It’s not often that you meet someone whose painting instructor was Reginald Marsh, the New York City social-realist artist of the Jazz Age who also happened to be one of this magazine’s first cartoonists. But Hilary Knight, an illustrator most celebrated for his work on the “Eloise” books, was genially holding forth about Marsh from his wheelchair the other day, on the patio of a restaurant in Sierra Madre, California.“I learned so much from him,” Knight said. “He was drunk all the time but a great teacher.”

It was Knight’s hundredth birthday, and a small party had been organized by a niece, Lily Knight. Hilary, a diminutive man with no children of his own, moved in with Lily in 2018, when, because of age-related limitations, he became unable to maintain his homes in Manhattan and East Hampton.

Though Knight remains mentally and verbally sharp, his hearing isn’t what it used to be. At the restaurant, Lily distributed pink notepads and Sharpies, so that guests could pose questions and offer tributes. Knight responded either verbally or in writing.
Does he still draw?
“Not as much as I should,” he said. “My parents were both great artists. My mother was a naturalist and a real inspiration to me. She needed to draw to keep going. I should be doing the same thing.”

Had he heard that the Plaza, the hotel where Eloise resides in the books—and where tourists regularly visit Knight’s portrait of her, insouciantly posing in the lobby with her pug, Weenie, and her turtle, Skipperdee—will be closed for at least four years?
Knight’s eyes widened with alarm: “No! Why on earth would they do that?”
Renovations to the façade, mostly.
“God, I hope they find a safe place to keep my painting.” (In 1988, when Donald Trump bought the hotel, Eloise fans worried that she might be evicted.)

The party guests included Lily’s twin, Kitty; their brother, Chris; and a strapping young towhead named Alvin, who amused his great-great-great-uncle Hilary with his Eloise-like mischievousness. There were also some swells and characters from Knight’s old life who had flown in from New York, among them the mustachioed pianist and historian Peter Mintun and the musician, artist, and downtown fixture Phoebe Legere, who, to Knight’s delight, had dressed up in a sequinned minidress, fish-net tights, and a plumed fedora.

Knight himself has always been, as Eloise might say, rawther fond of visual whimsy and extravagance. He wore amber-tinted glasses, a bird-print shirt, and a baseball cap to which a spray of peacock feathers had been affixed. The feathers were a nod to Knight’s love of India, a country he adores but has not—yet—had the opportunity to visit.

Legere led the crowd in “Happy Birthday” as a cake was carried out. There followed a reading of testimonials from absent friends: Bernadette Peters, Anderson Cooper, the British actress Sally Hawkins, and Liza Minnelli, whose godmother was the singer and actress Kay Thompson, the author of the Eloise books. Minnelli is believed to have been at least a partial inspiration for Eloise.

“In 1955, you and my beloved Kay Thompson introduced the world to a little girl named Eloise, and nothing has been quite the same since,” Minnelli wrote. “Seventy-one years later, Eloise is still six years old, the Plaza is still her playground, and your drawings remain as enchanting as ever. What a magnificent legacy. What a magnificent life.”

There is a new live-action “Eloise” movie in the works, directed and co-written by Amy Sherman-Palladino. Knight has mixed feelings about this. Hawkins, who became his friend after he admired her performance in Guillermo del Toro’s “The Shape of Water,” is in the film, which is a mark in its favor. “But I’ve seen images from the set, of Eloise as a real girl, which is kind of strange,” Knight said. “Eloise isn’t real! She’s a fantasy, an invention. That’s what I like about her.”

As the party entered its third hour, the New Yorkers, jet-lagged, made their apologies and headed out. The birthday boy, however, showed no sign of fatigue. He commandeered one of the pink notepads and wrote the following:
WHO is readyTo go to INDIAWith me—I will guaranteeElephant ridescurry dinners ♦

theguardian.com/environment/2026/nov/13/.headline: Storm Charles causes floods and flight cancellations across southern Europe
theguardian.com/environment/2026/nov/13/.author: Guardian staff reporter

paragraphs.text: Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninsula this week, particularly in Portugal and the far south of Spain. Heavy rain and strong south-westerly winds arrived first in the Portuguese island of Madeira, before the system headed towards the mainland on 11 November. A wind gust of 84.5mph (136 km/h) was recorded at Funchal airport, alongside rainfall totals reaching 355mm (13.97in) in 12 hours. In Lisbon, 183 flights were cancelled on Wednesday, about a third of its normal daily traffic, while Madrid Barajas airport had 155 cancellations.

After causing widespread flooding in Spain and Portugal, the system moved on a north-easterly track through southern France and then towards northern Italy. This resulted in significant flooding in parts of Cannes, some of which caused rock falls and led to the closure of roads along the French Riviera. The Italian weather service issued a red rainfall warning, its highest level, for the area extending from Tuscany to Venezia. Further heavy rain is expected to fall in Italy and the Balkans over the next few days, with the latest forecast models indicating an additional 100mm could accumulate widely, while totals close to 200mm are likely in more mountainous areas.
Successive rounds of heavy rain and strong winds have caused flooding, landslides and disruption across British Columbia, Canada through the last week or so.

Between Monday and Friday last week, severe rainfall and strong winds left more than 400,000 customers without power in British Columbia. These unsettled conditions continued into the weekend, with further heavy rain leaving 135,000 customers without power, alongside downed trees, flooded roads and landslides. Strong winds were also recorded on Sunday, with a gust of 72.1mph (116 km/h) on Herbert Island and a gust of 60mph (96 km/h) at Victoria international airport.

Heavy rain warnings were then issued on Wednesday for British Columbia’s Vancouver Island and southern coastal areas as multiple stations recorded rainfall totals in excess of 100mm. Additionally, the River Forecast Centre issued flood warnings on Wednesday across the south coast with heavy rain and high streamflow continuing to bring an increased risk of flash flooding and landslides.

A further area of low pressure is expected to bring torrential rain and strong winds across this same region over the weekend. More than 100mm is likely across central and southern parts of Vancouver Island on Saturday, with gusts in excess of 60mph likely too.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cklyw3neqg2wo.headline: Africa Miss Universe beauty queens in limbo as US visa restrictions bite
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cklyw3neqg2wo.author: Ondiro Oganga

paragraphs.text: Miss Universe Zimbabwe Roseanna Hall and several other contestants from Africa could miss this year's competition in Puerto Rico as they race to secure a US visa.
Hall is due to represent Zimbabwe at the 75th edition of the Miss Universe pageant, with the winner set to be crowned on 24 November. But she has yet to obtain a visa to travel to the US territory.
"We have been back and forth, trying to get my visa approved," Hall said in a video posted on her Instagram page.
Hall is not the only African contestant to be affected by the restrictions. Zambia has withdrawn its representative, Pamela Mubanga, from the competition because of US travel restrictions.

Contestants began arriving in Puerto Rico on 8 November for registration, fittings and other pre-pageant activities, putting pressure on Hall, and others including the representative from South Sudan, to secure their visas.
"Officially, today is the day I was supposed to be leaving for Puerto Rico for the 75th edition of Miss Universe," Hall said.
Zimbabwe is among 19 countries subject to partial US travel restrictions introduced under the Presidential Proclamation 10998, which took effect on 1 January 2026.

The measures suspend the issuance of visitor, student and exchange visas, as well as immigrant visas, to nationals of the affected countries. They also impose restrictions on other categories of non-immigrant visas.
In a statement, the Miss Universe organization in Zambia said Mubanga's situation was a consequence of the travel restrictions rather than individual circumstances.

"Unlike situations where a contestant's visa is denied due to personal circumstances, documentation or organisational challenges, Mubanga's situation is linked to the United States' presidential travel restriction affecting Zambia and other African countries," the statement read.
Mubanga, 25, a registered nurse, was crowned Miss Universe Zambia on 8 October and was due to represent the country at the international pageant.
The statement said five other African countries faced similar difficulties, although it did not name them.
Hall said she shared their concerns, adding that she had spent the past few weeks in South Africa trying to secure her visa.
"I am not alone in this predicament. Some of my African sisters are facing the same predicament, and I know exactly what they are going through," she said.
Miss Universe South Sudan also expressed uncertainty about her participation, commenting on Hall's video: "It is 50/50 whether we will make it, Miss Universe."
In another video posted three days earlier, Hall said she was still hoping to make it to Puerto Rico.
She captioned the video: "The fight to get Zimbabwe to Puerto Rico continues,"
The pageant's final is scheduled to take place at the José Miguel Agrelot Coliseum in San Juan.

npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-6039312/spacex-.headline: SpaceX's giant rocket may leave NASA in the dust
npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-6039312/spacex-.author: Geoff Brumfiel

paragraphs.text: Later today, SpaceX is planning the most ambitious test yet of its massive new rocket Starship. If all goes well, it will lift off from a pad in South Texas, circle the Earth and then land vertically at the same pad 22 and a half hours later.

The test would be a major milestone for a rocket that company founder Elon Musk says he hopes will one day carry astronauts to Mars. But experts say the rapid development of Starship could also end up stranding one of the company's biggest boosters over the years: NASA.

That's because as SpaceX ramps up its new rocket, it has said it will stop flying a much smaller one called Falcon 9. Falcon 9 launches the company's Dragon capsule, which is currently the only American spacecraft capable of ferrying NASA astronauts to and from the International Space Station.

"Because Dragon has become such a successful and reliable vehicle, it became the de facto way for astronauts to get to orbit," said Caleb Henry, director of research at Quilty Space, a firm that tracks the space industry.

According to a NASA announcement in September, the space agency has contracted with SpaceX for three additional flights to the International Space Station. That would only allow Dragon to fly through 2028, assuming the missions were flown consecutively in six month increments and no further flights are contracted with SpaceX.
The space station is currently set to retire in 2030.
"I love you guys"

The current problem facing the space agency marks a stark reversal from earlier times, when it was SpaceX that was depending heavily on NASA. In 2008, following multiple failures of the Falcon 9, the space launch company was on the ropes.
"We were running on fumes at that point, we had virtually no money," Elon Musk told CBS' 60 Minutes in a 2014 interview.
Then, just days before Christmas, NASA came through with a big contract.
"I couldn't even hold the phone, I just blurted out, 'I love you guys!'," Musk said.

For the next decade, a steady diet of NASA and eventually Pentagon contracts were responsible for a big share of the company's revenue. But all that changed in 2020, when SpaceX launched a subscription satellite internet service called Starlink. Starlink subscriptions quickly eclipsed the money made from launching rockets.

Today, according to SpaceX's latest financial report, the company made around $2.1 billion in revenue from space launches through September of this year. By contrast, Starlink pulled in around $12.8 billion, while its rapidly growing AI business made around $10.9 billion.
Winding down Falcon

Starship is central to SpaceX's newer, larger businesses. The space launch company is already using it to send its new, powerful V3 satellites for Starlink into orbit. Further down the road, Musk has said he wants the rocket to deliver data centers to space.

"Once Starship is flying reliably several times per week, it makes sense to shift super scarce SpaceX engineering and production resources to Starship to get launch rate to several times per day, which means winding down Falcon," Musk said on X earlier this year.

"We definitely want to move from the older technology to the newer technology," SpaceX president Gwynne Shotwell said at the All In summit in Los Angeles in September. "A Falcon 9 with a Dragon capsule on top is like a minivan. … The road trip to Mars is six months — so you don't want to be in the minivan."
The problem is that the minivan is perfect for taking astronauts on a short jaunt to the space station. In fact, it's currently the only American option for making the trip.

Henry said building space capsules is time-consuming and expensive. And as it turns out NASA is about the only one willing to pay, making it a very small market for a company like the one SpaceX has become.
"Today there is not a strong commercial market for human spaceflight," he said.
Launch gap

The retirement of the Falcon rocket will have huge impacts beyond human spaceflight. A recent analysis by Quilty Space finds that the commercial market may end up short by some 150 launches between now and 2030, and the Pentagon has reportedly been left scrambling to find rides for national security satellites. In a statement to NPR, the U.S. Space Force said it had secured Falcon 9 launches through 2028 and that it was "confident" other suppliers would be able to pick up the slack.
None of that is likely to change SpaceX's mind, according to Tim Farrar, the president of TMF associates, a telecom analysis firm that tracks SpaceX.
The company has grown far beyond its launch business, he said. "SpaceX has now got an enormous amount on its plate."
In particular, "it's not making a lot of money out of NASA," he said. "Although it seems likely that the individual missions are profitable, they're small potatoes."

It's still not clear when SpaceX will retire the Falcon 9 rocket. The company did not respond to NPR's request for comment, but in her public comments at the summit, Shotwell implied that a rival company, Boeing, could fly to the station instead.
"Boeing has been paid, I think, probably more than we have been paid to develop their human capsule. So we're just going to let them have some business," she said. "They should fly their capsule."

The Boeing capsule, known as the Starliner, has been beset by problems throughout its development. In 2024, failures with the vehicle's first attempt to take astronauts to space resulted in a planned eight-day mission aboard the ISS becoming a nine-month stay. The astronauts returned home on a SpaceX vehicle in March of the following year. The next Starliner test flight is set to take place over the winter, with a crewed flight sometime in 2028.

For Farrar, SpaceX's choices make sense for its business, but he wonders whether NASA deserves better. "They were responsible essentially for SpaceX not going bankrupt," he said. "One would hope that there's a bit of loyalty."

politico.com/news/2026/11/11/hill-republ.headline: ‘Draft Marco’ effort grows on Capitol Hill after midterms bloodbath
politico.com/news/2026/11/11/hill-republ.author: Meredith Lee Hill and Mia McCarthy

paragraphs.text: A growing number of Republicans on Capitol Hill want to draft Marco Rubio for a 2028 presidential bid as they grapple with their midterms wipeout — and look beyond Vice President JD Vance.

The generational losses are sparking new discussions among Hill Republicans about who should lead the party. Many argue the race to carry the mantle is now wide open — including a faction who view Rubio as a better fit, given that voters may continue to tie Vance to the president’s unpopularity, interviews with roughly two dozen GOP lawmakers reveal.
“I hope he runs. I think he's the best person to communicate, to unify,” Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-Ind.) said of Rubio in an interview.

“I think he's the most talented Republican by far,” Stutzman said when asked about why he supported the secretary of State over Vance. “We're going to have to continue to re-message, put some new faces up.” The vice president still has his supporters. And he got a boost Tuesday by fellow Ohio Republican Jim Jordan being elected as the incoming House minority leader.
But the election wipeout “certainly makes it harder for Vance,” said one GOP senator, who like others in this article, was granted anonymity to speak candidly.
“I think Rubio is our best hope to lead Republicans out of this wilderness, and I hope he makes his break from Trump and JD early next year,” said one House Republican in the wake of the election.

The openness toward Rubio — or any other candidate that’s not Vance — is a complication for the vice president, who was picked by Trump for the role that’s next in line to the presidency. Now, Vance has to grapple with being closely associated with an agenda that even GOP lawmakers argue voters harshly rebuked last week.

Several lawmakers said they’ve spoken to people close to Rubio who have suggested he isn’t interested in pursuing a 2028 bid, even after Tuesday’s results. Rubio himself this week has stood by Trump’s decision to go to war against Iran and told reporters Monday he was “just not going to talk about 2028 anymore.”

A person close to Rubio said the secretary of State is the only person who knows what he will do regarding a presidential bid. Right now, he’s “fully focused on doing his many jobs and isn’t thinking about 2028.”
But some Hill Republicans aren’t giving up hope.

“I’m a big supporter of Marco Rubio, and I’m very excited about the potential of his candidacy,” said Florida Rep. Mike Haridopolos, who has known the secretary of State for nearly three decades. “No question he’s ready to be president if he chooses to pursue the office.”
“Some of us are still hoping we can draft Marco,” said another GOP senator.
A State Department spokesperson declined to comment. Vance’s office didn’t respond to a request for comment.

In reaction to Stutzman’s comments, a Vance ally argued that Stutzman has been one of the biggest supporters within the GOP of amnesty for unauthorized immigrants for over a decade — and that he was likely never going to support Vance, who is extremely hawkish on border security.

Vance, for his part, has tried to distance himself from the unpopular Iran war, blaming it for the party’s losses in the immediate aftermath of the midterm election. His allies argue that the vice president would’ve always faced some internal opposition, like Trump did within the GOP ahead of the 2016 election.

However, as the Rubio talk swirls, even some of Trump’s top MAGA allies on Capitol Hill are unwilling to publicly declare Vance the presumptive GOP nominee for 2028. “Can I skip this one?” one House GOP hardliner said. “Not wading into 2028 yet.” Some Republican senators also declined to back Vance just yet, citing their own reelections.
GOP Rep. and Sen.-elect Barry Moore of Alabama said he thought Vance would certainly “have a shot” at the presidency in 2028. Moore was the first member of Congress to back Trump for the 2016 race.
But Moore for now is leaving his endorsement up in the air: “We got a great bench," he said. "Whoever steps up, we'll be happy to support.”

Rubio’s supporters say that he’s not as closely associated with the 2026 GOP wipeout as Vance, but he could face his own obstacles. Rubio, unlike Vance, has continued to show strong support for the war in Iran, a conflict he’s tied to as the country’s top diplomat. Some GOP lawmakers have also grown frustrated with the amount of information the Trump administration, including Rubio at times, has been willing to share about the ongoing conflict.
Rubio also has his failed 2016 presidential run to contend with, including an infamous debate performance where he awkwardly repeated the same rehearsed line multiple times.

One thing is clear, the 2028 presidential race is now wide open, many Hill Republicans argue as they process Tuesday’s results. And other potential candidates only appear encouraged after the midterms wipeout.

Several Hill Republicans believe outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, who has been one of the most outspoken Republicans urging a course correction after the midterms bloodbath, will get in the race as well. Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) this week also didn’t rule out a presidential bid. Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) also appears likely to run.

“I think everybody reserves the right to adjust. You know, learn from this,” GOP Rep. and incoming Oklahoma Sen. Kevin Hern said. Asked his favorite candidate of the three he expected to run: Vance, Rubio or DeSantis, he replied with a smile: “Everybody.”
Vance does have ardent supporters, including Sen. Jim Banks of Indiana who said before the midterms he would enthusiastically back him for president in 2028.

“If JD runs, he has my full support,” Banks said in an interview this week. “He continues to lead in all the polls on the Republican side to be the nominee. He's my friend. We come from the same part of the country, the same background, and he's what the country needs. I hope he runs. But I don't know if he's running or not.”
Rep. Brandon Gill (R-Texas) called Vance “a friend who I’ve had the honor to work alongside. He’s the vice president, of course he’s a front-runner.”

Rep. Riley Moore (R-W.Va.) said in an interview that it was the Republican “party” and not its “policies” that suffered massive losses last week. But he doesn’t blame Vance, and he supports him for the 2028 presidential race.

Vance, for his part, made his own allusion to the situation he’s found himself in. "I wanted to talk, of course, about the devastating loss last week. …There are a lot of people, I think, unfairly criticizing the leader of the team … a lot of staff infighting. … And of course, there's a conversation about whether the No. 2 has what it takes to ultimately lead the team.”
He finished: “I'm talking, of course, about the Ohio State Buckeyes."

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Anthropic’s IPO Is About Six Times Oversubscribed
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Bailey Lipschultz

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Anthropic PBC's initial public offering has drawn about six times the orders for the shares available, according to people familiar with the matter, as interest increases for potentially the biggest first-time share sale ever.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The Claude AI model firm and its co-founders are seeking to raise as much as $64.4 billion in the IPO and $26 billion in a private placement, its filings show. Taken together, the offering would be bigger than SpaceX's IPO, making it the biggest listing of all time.
Bankers have told prospective investors that existing backers will be prioritized by Anthropic, and some would-be buyers will receive smaller allocations than they expect, some of the people said.

Details of the IPO including the demand for shares could change, said the people, who asked not to be identified as the information isn't public. A representative for Anthropic didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

The surge of interest in Anthropic shares contrasts with investors pulling back support for Nvidia Corp. after Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang was ousted from his post after reports of several affairs, including one with a woman suspected of spying for China.

The chipmaker has agreed to buy about $10 billion worth of shares in Anthropic as part of a $26 billion private placement concurrent with its IPO, the AI model firm's filings show. Anthropic counts Nvidia as a strategic partner, and has committed tens of billions of dollars to deals securing access to its most advanced chips.

Anthropic is looking to bolster demand for the IPO with a campaign of events for prospective investors, including a live-streamed event with its Chief Executive Officer Dario Amodei and JPMorgan Chase & Co. CEO Jamie Dimon on Friday, a person familiar with the matter has said.

The company is targeting a fully diluted valuation of about $1.4 trillion, below where some investors expected the company to settle, Bloomberg News reported. Some companies set terms conservatively when they begin formally marketing their IPO, in the expectation that strong demand will push up the final figure and set them up for robust trading in their debuts.

Anthropic's filing Tuesday supported the case for AI spending as sales continued to increase. The company reported a revenue run rate of $81 billion as of Oct. 31, up $10 billion from the end of September, the filing showed. Anthropic had a $65 billion run rate figure at the end of July, Bloomberg News reported. Anthropic defines the metric as annualizing consumption-based fees for a trailing 28-day period and subscription-based fees for a single month.

Some investors are offering a portion of their Anthropic IPO allocation to other prospective backers, letting them collect additional fees and reduce their risk before trading begins, while others with pre-IPO stakes are marketing them to buyers via special purpose vehicles.

Goldman Sachs Group Inc. and Morgan Stanley are leading Anthropic's IPO, with participation from 20 other banks, the filing shows. The stock is expected to trade on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol ANT.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/googles-latest.headline: Google’s latest Search upgrade promises better answers to your most complicated questions
techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/googles-latest.author: Sarah Perez

paragraphs.text: Google Search is getting better at understanding complicated questions, including those with multiple parts, highly specific requests, or confusing typos. The updates are coming via the company’s newly released Gemini 4 Hydrogen model, which Google claims is its “biggest model improvement to Search yet.”

While Google’s frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon, are best at deep reasoning for hard problems, Hydrogen is designed for fast execution across a variety of agentic workflows, or tasks in which an AI carries out multiple steps on its own, the company explained in an announcement.

The idea behind the model’s release is that using the most powerful model isn’t always needed — sometimes a faster, cheaper, and reasonably smart one will do. Google says Hydrogen completes tasks 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash, its previous fast model, but it’s still pretty smart, even beating the more powerful Gemini 4 Argon on one broad intelligence benchmark, the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, at its default high thinking level.

In Search, Hydrogen brings several improvements, including a better understanding of user intent, the ability to offer more helpful links and visual responses, and better answers across the different languages supported by Google’s AI Mode.

In terms of intent, Google says Hydrogen can handle more nuanced and complicated questions more quickly. This means people can ask their questions in their natural train of thought, including those that have multiple parts or that include highly specific requests. Hydrogen is also better at navigating hard-to-understand typos, Google says. Because of its improvements and better ability to follow instructions and call the right tools, Hydrogen is able to more precisely address each part of a user’s question.

Its advanced reasoning also improves Search’s fan-out technique, which breaks down a single user’s prompt into multiple subqueries. This allows people to discover websites related to the query that they may have otherwise missed, the blog post explains.
The addition of Hydrogen to Search will also mean more images, structured responses, comparison tables, and custom tools will appear as visual responses to users’ queries in AI Mode.

Google also says Hydrogen can work on its own for everyday work in areas like writing code, running tests, or verifying code changes, or it can be paired with Carbon and Argon in workflows that combine several models.
The model offers four thinking levels: low, medium, high (default), and a new, extra-high tier (“xhigh”), all of which are designed to complete tasks faster with fewer output tokens.
On multi-step tasks like deep research, data analysis, and broad codebase navigation, Hydrogen ranks No. 5 on Agent Arena’s benchmarks, the company pointed out.

In addition to Search, Gemini 4 Hydrogen is coming to all tiers of Google’s AI Studio, the Gemini API, the Gemini App, and the paid AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google’s Antigravity development platform.
Google says the Hydrogen update is rolling out to all Search users globally.

Josh Homme, a guitarist and vocalist in the art-rock band Queens of the Stone Age, paid a visit to Regan MacNeil, the demonically possessed adolescent girl at the center of the 1973 film “The Exorcist,” the other day. Actually, it was an animatronic-doll version of Regan, complete with head-whirling, and it was on display in a Plexiglas box at the Museum of the Moving Image, in Astoria. Somehow, the doll’s bleached-out eyeballs seemed to follow a visitor around the room.

Homme, who is fifty-three years old, first saw “The Exorcist” when he was twelve. His parents weren’t home. “My brother was supposed to watch me, and, of course, he didn’t,” he said. “I started it at around six-thirty. The sun went down, and I’m in my parents’ waterbed, just gently jiggling. Sheets and blankets pulled up to my nose. And this movie just happened to me. I couldn’t get up.” He continued, “ ‘The Exorcist’ deals with things that are sort of esoterically possible: possession, the Devil. I had a pretty sincere Christian upbringing, so it seemed like nonfiction. To me, this was a documentary.”

In an adjacent gallery, an exhibition on Jim Henson’s Muppets was visible. Homme looked up from Regan and locked eyes with Kermit the Frog. “Oh, shit!” he said. “Seeing all this horror stuff and then looking over at Kermit, it feels like Kermit’s doing something dark.”

Homme founded Queens of the Stone Age in 1996, shortly before he returned to his home town of Palm Desert, a sunbaked oasis in the Coachella Valley. “I grew up right where the desert starts,” he said. “There are pine forests at the top of Mt. San Jacinto, in Palm Springs. It’s snowy, and then the snow melts and it comes down, and that’s right where the desert begins. I love transition, the braiding together of worlds. I think that’s where the interesting stuff is.”

His songwriting has always embraced heavy and devious themes: lust, death, menace. The day before Halloween, the band released its ninth album, “Perfecth.” It’s a record about making reluctant peace with love gone asunder—“Letting go of you is beautiful,” Homme sings—and it was inspired, in part, by an acoustic show that the band played in the Paris catacombs, a subterranean ossuary containing the bones of about six million people, in 2024. “There’s a lot of gravel on the floor, so you crunch your way through,” Homme said. “It makes you feel really insignificant, which makes me feel comfortable.” He went on, “I took a dark alleyway and got on my knees and said, ‘I promise to try as hard as I can.’ It was very special to be alive there.” At the time, Homme was dealing with some health issues, and the band would soon cancel a tour. “The line between where they were at and where I was at—it felt paper thin,” he said, of the piled-up bones.

These days, Homme likes to watch horror movies with his twenty-year-old daughter, Camille. “She calls it Satan-ing,” he said. “She’s, like, ‘Do you want to Satan tonight?’ We just scratch each others’ arms and eat popcorn. I can tell it’s soothing to her, and it’s my chance to get unadulterated time—kid-straight-off-the-tap is hard to come by.” He finds the experience of being frightened cathartic, even calming: “You get on a roller coaster, and by the time you get off all anxiety is gone. It’s been replaced with adrenaline, endorphins. Jump scares flush the body of anxiety.”

At the museum, Homme paused to examine a vomit device that, on the set of “The Exorcist,” was attached to the actress Linda Blair, who played Regan. It resembled a single-jointed horse bit, with plastic tubing at the center; this was glued to Blair’s face and then concealed under prosthetics and makeup. Crew members fed bile-colored porridge into a hand-cranked pump hidden under her bed. Homme marvelled at the mechanics of the thing. “I think, nine times out of ten, the fascination with horror is that it lets us deal with death in a way that’s a little campier. It initiates a conversation,” he said. “Modern society kind of tells you not to look at the sky. Don’t think about death, especially in the United States. Sweep it under the rug. But sending someone off into the ether, into the great parent that made us, should be revered and ritualized.” ♦

politico.com/news/2026/11/11/biden-2024-.headline: Biden says he wouldn't have run in 2024 if he knew about his cancer
politico.com/news/2026/11/11/biden-2024-.author: Gregory Svirnovskiy

paragraphs.text: Former President Joe Biden would not have run for reelection in 2024 if he had known about his cancer, he said in an interview released Wednesday in which he also sought to downplay the historic debate performance that helped end his political career.

"If I had known that I was feeling lousy because I had cancer, I would have not gone forward because I don't think an 80-year-old man with cancer should be running," he said in the interview with People magazine, which was conducted last week following Democrats’ big midterm wins and ahead of his upcoming memoir’s release.

The former president announced his diagnosis — Stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer — in May 2025, just four months after leaving the White House. It triggered an outpouring of public support — but it also raised questions about how doctors failed to catch the cancer earlier and whether it might have contributed to Biden’s apparent decline toward the end of his term.

“I think it’s very sad, actually. I’m surprised that it wasn’t, you know, the public wasn’t notified a long time ago because to get to [a Gleason score of] 9, that’s a long time,” President Donald Trump told reporters shortly after Biden’s announcement.
Prior to his diagnosis, Biden hadn’t been screened for prostate cancer since 2014. U.S. guidelines have long recommended that men shouldn't be screened for the cancer once they hit their 70s.
Biden also downplayed his poor June 2024 debate performance against Trump that contributed to his exit from the Democratic ticket a month later.

“To me, it was not very consequential,” he said. “First of all, I thought there would be another debate, which there wasn’t. But notwithstanding the fact that there wasn’t another debate, it didn’t disturb me because it wasn’t consequential.”

Biden’s son, Hunter, has said he believes the cancer was responsible for the performance. His weak showing on the debate stage led to mounting calls within his party for him to withdraw, an effort eventually backed by longtime friends and allies such as former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi.

The former president’s memoir, “Promise Me, America,” will go on sale next week. Biden wrote Sunday on X that the cancer meant he “won’t be able to do as many conversations about my book as I’d hoped.” But he still feels sharp, he told the magazine.
“I’m not saying I’ll live forever, but the point is that, you know, I have all my faculties, I have access to all the things I had before and, you know, I feel good,” he said.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: SpaceX and Tesla Talks on Record Merger Are Said to Progress
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Ryan Gould, Siddharth Philip and Dinesh Nair

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- SpaceX and Tesla Inc. are progressing in their merger negotiations, setting the stage for a combination that could redefine the limits of global dealmaking.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Elon Musk's two largest companies could announce what would be the biggest-ever deal as soon as in December, according to people familiar with the matter. That aggressive timeline reflects Musk's tendency to move quickly when it comes to corporate maneuvers.

The companies have also discussed a scenario in which an announcement slips into early 2027, said the people, who asked to not be identified because the discussions are private. Their boards and advisers are hammering out the terms of the tie-up and governance structure of the combined entity, among other matters, the people said.
Representatives for Tesla and SpaceX didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.
Tesla shares jumped to a session high, rising as much as 1.9%, while SpaceX stock gained 0.5% as of 3:20 p.m. Thursday in New York.

The merger would be a blockbuster for Wall Street's dealmakers, creating a conglomerate housing electric vehicles, energy storage batteries, rockets and satellites. The rationale for bringing all those assets under one roof lies in a shared ambition to leverage artificial intelligence across space, driverless cars and humanoid robots.
But both companies will have to grapple with obstacles before they can close a transaction, including how to ring-fence Tesla's operations in China, according to the people.

National security sensitivities around SpaceX's US government and defense contracts, and Tesla's large, profitable China manufacturing footprint, loom as "key dynamics that are at odds with each other" when it comes to getting regulatory and shareholder approvals for a deal, JPMorgan analyst Rajat Gupta told clients in a research note last month.

The merger would be a major test case for political sentiment following the US midterm elections. Democrats, which took control of Congress, have pledged to probe Musk's business and political dealings.
Musk in October said the boards of the companies had formed special committees of independent board directors to consider combining.
SpaceX has a market value of more than $1.9 trillion following its initial public offering, while Tesla is worth about $1.5 trillion. Tesla is slated to host its annual shareholder meeting on Dec. 3.

Bloomberg News had reported that SpaceX and Tesla were pushing to announce a deal by the first half of next year, with the aim of closing the merger before the end of President Donald Trump's term. One of the factors being discussed is the number of shares SpaceX will have to offer Tesla investors in the transaction.

SpaceX and Tesla already have business ties, including a joint effort to build a semiconductor plant in Texas called Terafab. The companies also increasingly have been laying the groundwork for joint operations.
SpaceX, formally known as Space Exploration Technologies Corp. and based in Starbase, Texas, went public in June in a landmark listing in New York that made Musk the world's first trillionaire.

The company has transformed in recent years from a leading rocket manufacturer and launch provider into a crucial supplier of AI infrastructure to companies including Anthropic PBC as well as a top provider of internet beamed down from space.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/nectar-launche.headline: Nectar launches an AI agent to automate creator discovery and outreach for brands
techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/nectar-launche.author: Lauren Forristal

paragraphs.text: Nectar, an AI-powered operating system for marketing, is launching a new AI agent designed to take a lot of the manual work out of influencer marketing, from finding the right creators to contacting them, managing partnerships, and tracking results.

Founded by sisters Misbah and Farah Uraizee, both former Meta employees, Nectar came out of stealth last year and uses AI agents to help brands manage social media, customer conversations, content moderation, creator partnerships, and competitor research.

Announced Thursday, its new “Creator Agent” can search for creators, check their content and brand partnerships, send personalized messages, coordinate collaborations, and monitor how campaigns perform. Instead of having marketing teams spend weeks scrolling through social media, building spreadsheets, and sending individual DMs, Nectar wants its agent to handle much of that work automatically.

Nectar joins other companies introducing agentic AI assistants designed to automate influencer outreach, including Aspire and GRIN. The launch also comes as more brands turn to creators to reach customers. U.S. spending on creator advertising is expected to reach $44 billion in 2026, according to the Interactive Advertising Bureau. As companies work with hundreds or even thousands of creators, keeping track of relationships and measuring results can get pretty difficult.

Nectar says its Creator Agent searches more than 300 million creator profiles to find potential partners, including smaller creators who may not yet have a large following but are gaining traction. The system analyzes videos to understand what creators post about, how their content fits a brand, and whether their previous partnerships are appropriate. It also checks brand safety by reviewing content in context rather than simply searching for specific keywords.
Nectar then creates ranked lists of recommendations and adds new matches as creators become more popular.

Once it finds a potential match, the agent can draft and send messages in a brand’s voice, create custom landing pages to collect creator information, and help manage contracts, product gifting, and shipping details. It also remembers previous conversations and interactions, so brands can keep track of relationships without relying on spreadsheets.

“Brands can share voice guidelines in any format, and Nectar picks up the rest from their history,” CEO Misbah Uraizee tells TechCrunch. “On top of that sits a set of proprietary guardrails that keep every draft on tone and in context. Nectar understands what is being said in a video, reads the tone of the conversation, and knows the difference between a quote post on X and a TikTok comment section. A brand should not sound identical in both, and with Nectar it doesn’t.”

Another feature looks for personal milestones in creators’ lives, such as an engagement, a new baby, or completing a marathon. The agent can then suggest a personalized message or gift, helping brands build relationships that feel less like one-off advertising deals.
Creator Agent is available today globally and covers Instagram creators and TikTokers.

The company plans to make the agent available through its Model Context Protocol (MCP), allowing teams to use it through AI assistants such as Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot, as well as their own custom-built agents.
This past May, Nectar raised a $30 million Series A round led by Menlo Ventures and its Anthology Fund, which is a joint initiative launched with Anthropic.

paragraphs.text: Nvidia founder Jensen Huang was having a separate affair with an employee that has not been previously reported, Reuters reported on Thursday.

Huang stepped down as CEO and board member for the company earlier today, in the wake of news of extramarital affairs with accused spy Alice Huang and Nvidia VP of Healthcare Kimberly Powell. CFO Colette Kress has stepped in as interim CEO, but no permanent successor has been named.

latimes.com/business/story/2026-11-12/no.headline: Notorious Graffiti Towers wiped clean in downtown Los Angeles
latimes.com/business/story/2026-11-12/no.author: Roger Vincent

paragraphs.text: The skyline of downtown Los Angeles got a lot less colorful in the past few months as crews wiped florid, eye-catching graffiti off the towers of a stalled $1.2-billion real estate development.

City officials joined the buyers of Oceanwide Plaza on Thursday to celebrate the removal of spray-painted graffiti splashed as high as 54 stories that threatened to become an unwelcome icon for the city during the 2028 Olympics as the bankruptcy sale of the hotel, residential and retail complex dragged on for almost two years.

Removing the graffiti was a top priority of the city, which imposed the job on expected buyers KPC Group and Lendlease as a condition of the sale set to close in January. Completion of the project itself is set to begin after that, said KPC executive John Petty.
“This is the end of the medieval period and the beginning of the renaissance,” he said Thursday.

The buyers will complete Oceanwide Plaza as designed, Petty said, with 504 residential units, a luxury hotel and a shopping center in three skyscrapers that stand across Figueroa Street from Crypto.com Arena and the L.A. Live event and entertainment center.
“The original design was amazing, and when it comes to life and actually opens it’s going to just completely transform this area of downtown Los Angeles,” he said.

The original developer, Beijing-based Oceanwide Holdings, spent about $1.2 billion on the project before running out of money in 2019 and halting construction at about 60% completion. It will take about another $850 million to finish it, Petty said.

Early in 2024, taggers began turning Oceanwide Plaza’s skyscrapers into canvases for graffiti. BASE jumpers parachuted from its heights, and a performance artist recorded himself teetering along a one-inch-wide slackline strung between two of the property’s 42-story towers.

While some found the graffiti-clad towers an engaging art installation, others including some downtown residents and stakeholders regarded the graffiti as embarrassing blight that sent the message that downtown was a disorderly place where mischief could go unpunished.

Removing the graffiti by hand with with a biodegradable solution was an arduous process that is not quite complete, Petty said. Most of the graffiti was applied by taggers who reached outdoor balconies in the two residential towers, he said, but some of the paint was sprayed on windows by daredevils who sidled from the balconies onto ledges little more than a foot wide.
“Our guys could not remove that safely,” Petty said, so cleaners will next lower themselves on window washing platforms known as swing stages to remove the last of the renegade paint.

“For too long, this property has been a symbol of what was left unfinished,” said Kali Chaudhuri, chairman of KPC Group. “Removing the graffiti is about more than improving the appearance of a building. It’s about restoring pride, rebuilding confidence and demonstrating our commitment to bringing new life to this property.”

After the $517-million bankruptcy sale closes, the developers’ next goal will be to make Oceanwide Plaza — which is expected to be renamed at some point — presentable for the Olympics, Petty said. That includes erecting a massive electronic sign on its facade intended to bring a flavor of Times Square to Figueroa Street.
The sale is contingent securing a construction loan to complete the project and Petty said the developers are negotiating financing terms with domestic institutional and private equity lenders.
“It’s a beautiful project,” Petty said. “It will be the gem in the crown of downtown Los Angeles once people see it come alive.”

“The graffiti removal at Oceanwide Plaza marks a milestone step toward this neglected development finally becoming a transformative asset for Downtown Los Angeles,” Councilwoman Ysabel Jurado said in statement. “Angelenos deserve to see the real benefits this property promises to deliver new housing, jobs, economic opportunity, investment, and energy in the heart of our city.”

politico.com/news/2026/11/11/welcome-to-.headline: Several Dem women leaned into their identity this cycle. Not in the way you think.
politico.com/news/2026/11/11/welcome-to-.author: Lauren Fedor and Erin Doherty

paragraphs.text: When Annie Andrews announced her longshot campaign for U.S. Senate last May, the Democrat from South Carolina pitched herself as a “busy mom.”

“Lindsey [Graham] is going to tell you I am radical, that I am crazy,” Andrews said in her launch video. “But here’s the thing: I am literally a busy mom and a pediatrician who plays peek-a-boo with my patients, watches Bluey with my kids … and spends most of my free time shuttling them to dance, Tae Kwon Do and football.”

Now, she is one of a record number of women who will serve in the next Congress. And as a 46-year-old mother of three school-aged children, she’s among several Democratic women who flipped seats and governor’s mansions this November with campaign messages centered on parenting and affordability.

It’s a notable campaign shift from previous election cycles: This year, female candidates focused less on the historic nature of their bids, or culture war issues that have long fomented divisions over gender and electability. Instead, they zeroed in on an economic message emphasizing bread-and-butter concerns — like how rising costs were squeezing families, including theirs.

“Moms understand kitchen table issues better than perhaps anyone,” said Jessica Mackler, president of EMILY’s List, the group that recruits and backs female Democratic candidates who support abortion rights. “They understand how to stretch a paycheck. They understand what it is like to walk through a grocery store and have to put something back on the shelf.”

Senate, House and gubernatorial campaigns spent a combined $72 million on ads featuring the words “mom” or “mother” in 2026, according to AdImpact — a 50% increase from the $48 million spent in 2024 and double the spending on these kind of ads from 2022.
In many races, Democrats leaned on their experiences as parents to dismiss the kind of culture war attacks that have been effective for Republicans in recent years.

“They want to run an entire campaign saying that I’m too woke … I plan to spend an entire campaign focused on the fact that working people are too broke,” Democratic Texas Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa said in one of her final TV ads. “My pronouns are mom, Texan and soon-to-be governor.”

Campaign messaging around gender and representation can be fraught: In 2016, Hillary Clinton’s “I’m With Her” campaign slogan fell short as she failed in her pledge to break the “highest, hardest glass ceiling.” In 2024, Kamala Harris’ campaign was decidedly less overt in its messaging about the barrier-breaking potential of her candidacy. But debates about gender seemed inescapable as Trump called her “weak” and then-Sen. JD Vance said the Democratic Party was run by “childless cat ladies.”
This cycle was different.

In a 2026 environment driven by concerns about affordability and the cost of living, Democratic operatives said it was an easy decision for women and mothers in particular to lean on their home lives to connect with voters.

At least 159 women will serve in the 120th Congress, according to the Center for American Women and Politics, with Democratic women outnumbering Republicans by roughly five-to-one. Many of the newly elected Democrats are younger moms.

Their victories, especially in battleground districts and states long seen as Republican strongholds, have emboldened Democratic groups dedicated to electing more women, who argue the candidates offer a blueprint for winning races going forward.
Veteran Democratic pollster Celinda Lake said her party’s female candidates “really got points for having the right priorities and being in touch with real people's lives."

"It used to be that women with young children just didn't run, and we were electing all these women who had grown children or no children, and then we were electing women with young children, but they were hiding them, if you will,” Lake said. “Now [candidates] were bringing them out as major credentialers, and that has been changing over time."
Winning Democratic candidates told POLITICO they did not hesitate to talk about their families and personal experiences on the trail.

“I didn’t need anyone giving me talking points on how expensive groceries are,” said Representative-elect Teresa Benitez-Thompson, who won a heavily Republican House district in northern Nevada. “I don’t need anyone telling me how expensive gas is because I am filling up my tank … running kids all around town.”
JoAnna Mendoza, a single mom who flipped a swing district in the Tucson, Arizona, suburbs – said she spent the night before the election in the emergency room with her 10-year-old son.

“That is what parents face. That is what moms go through. Their kids are sick, they have to take time off of work, or they have to leave work,” Mendoza said. “It is important for people to see themselves in their elected leaders.”

Uncomfortable questions surrounding gender and electability nevertheless persist in the run-up to the next presidential election. Some in the Democratic Party at least privately question whether they should nominate another woman at the top of the ticket in 2028.

“My message to people who would say that is: cut it out,” said Mackler. “This election clearly demonstrates that women are the drivers of Democrats' path to power, and we should embrace their leadership at all levels of the ballot.”
Lake, the Democratic pollster, said the surge in female Democratic victors showed how fed up voters are with the status quo, calling it a “Hail Mary for change.”

“It is so bad, it is so failed, we're going to elect these women who will hold people accountable,” she said, adding that voters, particularly women, “were really upset with how out of touch the older white men seemed with their families' lives” after a decade of Trump and Joe Biden running the country.

Democratic candidates do not have a monopoly on talking about family life. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, the Republican governor of Arkansas, sailed to reelection last week with a campaign that highlighted her three children and efforts to cut grocery taxes and bring down the cost of living for other families. Messages around motherhood also featured prominently at the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention in Dallas, Texas, earlier this year.
The messaging is part of a broader shift in the public conversation, said Abby McCloskey, a conservative policy analyst.

“For a long time, to be taken seriously in politics, your professional side went first and your personal side went far after, and that was especially the case for women,” she said. “I think there's been broader cultural shifts that, and probably in a desire for authenticity and connection, why that is no longer necessarily the case.”Democratic campaign veterans said the renewed focus on motherhood gave their candidates an edge as they try to counter swing voters’ deep-seated biases against female candidates.

One Democratic pollster, granted anonymity to speak candidly about voters’ biases, said voters still have “bad reactions” to women running for office who are perceived as “cold.” Talking about motherhood and family life, the pollster said, allowed candidates to come across as warm while pushing back against the idea that their candidates are too radical or left-wing.
“In some of these places where you have to win over a bunch of conservative folks, the candidate can come across as just a regular mom,” the pollster said. “Not a scary, left, woke lady.”

The beginning of Jocelyn Benson’s campaign launch video showed the Democrat hugging her son in their family’s kitchen. Now Michigan’s Democratic governor-elect, Benson told POLITICO she was “very intentional” about inviting kids to join her on stage during her celebration on Election Night.
“I think leaders in this moment, and I think parents, moms in particular, recognize this as an opportunity to show a different way of leading and of being a good person and a good citizen,” she said.

washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/13/m.headline: Most top Fed officials blame AI for fueling inflation. Not Trump’s Fed chief.
washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/13/m.author: Steve Thompson

paragraphs.text: When President Donald Trump chose him to lead the Federal Reserve, Kevin Warsh argued that the artificial intelligence boom would help tame inflation.

More than a dozen of his colleagues, including two other Trump appointees, now say it’s doing the opposite, playing a role in fueling inflation, which could soon mean even higher interest rates on credit cards, car loans and mortgages.

Warsh will get a chance to revisit that argument on Monday, when he opens a conference in San Francisco meant to inform the work of a task force he created to study AI’s effects on jobs and productivity. He heads into it looking increasingly out of step with many other Fed officials.

This week, Fed governor Michelle Bowman, a Trump appointee who like Warsh once predicted AI would help push inflation down, conceded that is not yet happening. She said the AI buildout accounts for roughly a quarter of the excess inflation the Fed is fighting, about as much as the pressure from tariffs or energy prices.

Fed governor Christopher Waller, who said a big interest rate hike should be on the table in December, on Tuesday pointed to research by Fed economists on AI and high energy prices. Their findings, the Trump appointee said, “do not encourage me to think that these factors will be fading anytime soon.”

Hotter-than-expected inflation numbers out this week underscored the concerns raised by Bowman and Waller. Electricity prices jumped in October, and smartphones also logged their largest monthly increase since the government began tracking them separately in 2019. The data center buildout has been driving up electricity prices over the past year, as well as demand for chips that are also critical for consumer electronics.
Warsh has acknowledged that the artificial intelligence boom is increasing the price of computer chips, but he has questioned whether it is driving inflation more broadly.

“Economic growth is higher, but that doesn’t tell me that economic growth is somehow causing inflation and making our job harder,” he said at his news conference last month after the Fed held rates steady a week before the midterm elections. Warsh said politics played no role in the decision.

The debate over AI’s role in inflation comes down to timing. Right now companies racing to build AI are competing for the same chips, electricity and electricians, which pushes prices up. But AI could eventually make businesses more efficient, allowing them to produce more for less and helping hold prices down.

If that payoff comes in the near term, as Warsh suggested before he took over the Federal Reserve, the central bank can afford to be patient. If the productivity gains are years away, as many at the Fed now fear, Fed officials may need to keep raising interest rates to cool things off.

So far, Warsh’s views haven’t kept the Fed from acting. The Federal Open Market Committee voted unanimously to raise rates in September for the first time in more than three years. Several officials have said they expect another increase at the Fed’s December meeting.
Warsh was openly enthusiastic about AI before he took the job, arguing last year in an op-ed that it could help bring about a “new golden age” for the economy if the Fed changed some of its policies.
“AI will be a significant disinflationary force, increasing productivity and bolstering American competitiveness,” he wrote.

At a Senate hearing in July, Warsh called a disagreement over whether AI investments were driving inflation one of the Fed committee’s “good family fights” and said his view “might be somewhat nuanced” from “some of my colleagues.”

“I don’t view a one-time change in prices as necessarily being inflationary,” Warsh told the senators, because he expects higher prices to prompt companies to produce more. He predicted AI would increase “measured prices” over the next year. “But whether that’s inflationary or not, that’s up to the Federal Reserve, and we’re going to have something to say about that,” he said.

Michael Strain, an economist at the right-leaning American Enterprise Institute, said he sees AI’s effect on the economy playing out in two steps. First, companies spend heavily on data centers and other AI investments, and “all of that pushes up the prices.” Then “businesses figure out how to use this technology to make money. That translates into productivity increases, and that is disinflationary,” he said. The challenge for the economy is that he expects that second step “no earlier than 2028 and maybe later.”

Jacob Robbins, an economist at the University of Illinois at Chicago and a nonresident scholar at the Washington Center for Equitable Growth, a left-leaning think tank, said Warsh’s view has sometimes seemed too relaxed about rising prices.

“He has been very persistent with his view of AI, and he’s essentially stuck to it,” Robbins said. He added that Warsh’s embrace of the idea of near-term productivity gains from AI looks rosy next to the data.
AI was barely a topic at the Fed’s policy meetings in early 2025. When it did come up, officials mostly talked about it as a force that could help hold prices down.
But as early as this past February, Fed Vice Chair Philip Jefferson warned that a surge in AI-related spending “could raise inflation temporarily.”

At Warsh’s first meeting as chair in June, most officials said strong AI investment was helping push the economy past what it could sustain, which “could contribute to more persistent inflationary pressures,” according to the minutes.

By July, some Fed officials were pointing to higher prices for everyday purchases, including “smartphones, computer equipment, software, and electricity,” the minutes said. Since then, several officials have gone further.
“While the impact of AI on productivity remains unclear, its effect on prices is not,” Anna Paulson, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, said in a September speech.

John Williams, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York, said days later that AI spending’s effect on inflation was becoming harder to ignore. And Fed governor Lisa Cook said in a speech that month that “in the short term, AI appears to be adding inflationary pressures to the economy, postponing inflation’s return to our 2 percent target.”

On Monday, Austan Goolsbee, president of the Chicago Fed, said at an event that the AI buildout is “starting to look more just like old-fashioned demand overheating,” with everyone “out trying to hire an electrician at the same time.” That kind of inflation, he said, isn’t something that “just goes away on its own.”

Bowman said Tuesday that she still expects AI to “raise productivity and put some downward pressure on inflation” over time, and many other Fed officials share that long-run hope. The question is when.

Warsh’s AI task force that will convene Monday is led by Marc Andreessen, a Trump ally and one of the AI industry’s best-known venture capitalists, along with a Microsoft executive and a Stanford economist on leave at the AI company Anthropic.
Warsh has said Monday’s conference in San Francisco is meant for “a lot of listening,” including on whether AI will make it “harder or easier” to keep inflation in check over the next several years.

“Is this a productivity miracle that’s going to happen, or will it happen slowly?” he said at last month’s news conference. “I know I, for one, am keenly interested in refining my own views on that question.”
Federica Cocco contributed to this report.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/jensen-huangs-.headline: Jensen Huang’s exit puts Nvidia’s support for open source in question
techcrunch.com/2026/11/12/jensen-huangs-.author: Rebecca Bellan

paragraphs.text: The open source community just lost one of its strongest advocates.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday after he admitted to an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, raising concerns about U.S. national security and the motives behind the executive’s support for softer chip export controls on China.

Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI, framing the ecosystem as good for safety, innovation, diffusion, and sovereignty. And as frontier AI labs increasingly move to reduce their reliance on Nvidia and build their own chips, supporting open source is also a good way for the company to diversify its customer base by selling chips to nation-states, enterprises, and any organization that wants to own its own models.
Still, Huang’s resignation raises questions about whether Nvidia will carry on his legacy by continuing to support the open model community.

Huang’s departure also comes as Nvidia has yet to finalize a deal to acquire open source platform Hugging Face for $13 billion. Hugging Face CEO Clem Delangue said in a post on X that the company would continue to fight for open source, whatever happens next.
Nvidia also agreed to pay $6 billion for a non-exclusive license for open AI coding startup Poolside’s technology.

Within Nvidia, Huang pushed for the development of the Nemotron family of open-weight AI models built for long-running agentic AI systems and reasoning workloads — potential competitors to closed frontier models. One company insider told TechCrunch that they don’t expect a change in leadership to have an impact on Nemotron development.
Huang also backed companies that would make American open models more competitive, investing in startups like Reflection AI and Thinking Machines Lab.

Huang’s influence extended beyond Nvidia’s investments and product roadmap. He also emerged as one of the most prominent voices pushing back against Washington’s efforts to restrict the open AI ecosystem.

Earlier this year, Huang wrote an open letter signed by 25 companies, including Microsoft, Meta, IBM, and Palantir, urging the U.S. government not to over-restrict open-weight AI models, many of which come from China.

The impetus for that letter was Washington’s debate over how the U.S. should respond to allegations that Chinese AI labs are stealing intellectual property from American counterparts like Anthropic and OpenAI, both of which have reportedly appealed directly to Washington on the matter, urging stronger protections.

That combination of Huang’s personal visibility and Nvidia’s market power made him the strongest counterweight to arguments from closed-model providers like Anthropic and OpenAI, which have advocated for greater restrictions on advanced AI models due to safety reasons.

Without Huang, the concern among open source community members is that whoever takes over will be more cautious. Nvidia has named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO. It’s not clear how Kress will approach the Hugging Face deal or support for the open model ecosystem, but founder-driven priorities tend to get a downgrade when leadership changes.

Huang’s exit could also strengthen the arguments of those in Washington who are arguing for tougher restrictions on Chinese AI companies, particularly as the scandal surrounding his relationship with Alice Huang, the Megaspeed executive and alleged spy, puts renewed scrutiny on his efforts to loosen chip export controls.
Restrictions on open-weight models from China could kneecap competition for American companies, the most powerful of which have kept their models closed.
Still, supporting open source isn’t simply a passion project Huang pursued out of idealism. It’s increasingly central to Nvidia’s business strategy.
As some of Nvidia’s biggest customers, including Google and OpenAI, develop their own chips, Nvidia has an incentive to cultivate a much broader ecosystem of AI developers and customers.
More players training, fine-tuning, and running models mean more GPUs sold, and less dependence on a handful of frontier labs.
Huang may be gone, but Nvidia still needs an open AI ecosystem. The question now is whether that commitment can survive without the man who made it a priority.
TechCrunch has reached out to Nvidia for comment.
This article has been updated with information from an Nvidia employee.

Rebecca Bellan is a senior reporter at TechCrunch where she covers the business, policy, and emerging trends shaping artificial intelligence. Her work has also appeared in Forbes, Bloomberg, The Atlantic, The Daily Beast, and other publications.

theguardian.com/global-development/2026/.headline: Boxer on death row in Iran vows ‘not to bow before oppression’ after winning rights prize
theguardian.com/global-development/2026/.author: Sarah Johnson

paragraphs.text: A boxer and political prisoner on death row in Iran said he will “never surrender” as he accepted a prestigious human rights prize on behalf of “the generation that is paying the price of freedom with their lives”.

Mohammad Javad Vafaei Sani, an Iranian boxing champion, coach and political prisoner, has been sentenced to death three times and is one of seven athletes at risk of execution in Iran. He was given the Magnitsky award for outstanding human rights activist at a ceremony in London on Thursday night.

In a written message from Vakilabad prison in north-eastern Iran, he said: “I accept this award in the name of all those who, for the ‘crime’ of aspiring to a free Iran, have been imprisoned, tortured, threatened, or sentenced to death; in the name of my comrades in the resistance units and the generation that is paying the price of freedom with their lives.”
He added: “The regime demands repentance, televised confessions and surrender from us. But our answer is clear: ‘We will never surrender; we will never submit to humiliation.’”
Vafaei Sani, 31, was arrested in 2020 for taking part in nationwide democracy protests in 2019 and accused of supporting an opposition group, the People’s Mojahedin Organization of Iran (MEK).

He was convicted of “corruption on Earth” and sentenced to death for a third time in September 2024 after “a grossly unfair trial”, according to Amnesty International. The supreme court upheld his death sentence on 4 October 2025. Since his arrest he has been tortured and held in solitary confinement for extended periods.

His continued imprisonment has drawn widespread international condemnation from prominent sportspeople, human rights organisations and legal experts who have called for his immediate release and the annulment of his death sentence.

The Magnitsky awards are named after the Russian lawyer, Sergei Magnitsky, who died in Russian police custody after exposing government corruption. They began in 2015 as a way to recognise journalists, politicians and activists in the field of human rights.

Sir William Browder, head of the Magnitsky Justice Foundation and the chair of the awards committee, said Vafaei Sani’s case was emblematic of the plight of many Iranians who face execution for standing against the regime. “Most important, Mohammad Javad is still alive,” he said. “That is why this award matters. Every time the world pays attention, it becomes harder to kill him quietly.”
According to the Hengaw Organisation for Human Rights, at least 710 people have been executed in Iran since the beginning of 2026, including 79 political and religious prisoners.

In an October report, the organisation documented at least 106 death sentences against January protest detainees, 35 of whom had already been executed. In Vakilabad prison, where Vafaei Sani is detained, five people have been executed linked to the protests and 15 others are facing death sentences.

Vafaei Sani’s award comes at a time when there are growing fears for imprisoned Iranian athletes, who are considered role models in the country. Zohreh Abdollahkhani, founder of Human Rights for Sport, said: “The situation is really dire … We have seven athletes at risk of execution now, including Vafaei Sani.”

Ali-Sina Mostafavi, a mountaineer, was executed on 14 October after the anti-government protests. His death followed the killing of Siavash Jamshidi Kheirabadi, a taekwondo athlete, earlier that month, and the mixed martial arts fighter Gholamreza Khani Shakarab, who was hanged in May.

Abdollahkhani said people had been celebrating Vafaei Sani’s award. “Even people who don’t support his political view are supporting him to be heard,” she said. “I find it very inspiring that different political groups are coming together to say no to execution.”

In his message, Vafaei Sani said he wanted “a free and democratic Iran … where the people vote freely, women and men are equal, there is no discrimination on the basis of ethnicity, religion or belief, and no one is imprisoned or executed for political opposition”.
He added: “I remain steadfast in my pledge, and I will not bow before oppression until the people of Iran are free.”

finance.yahoo.com/markets/options/articl.headline: Buyers of $22 Billion Bank Securities Are Trapped in Losing Bet
finance.yahoo.com/markets/options/articl.author: Tasos Vossos

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- A $22 billion group of US bank preferred shares has been slumping harder than even the riskiest junk bonds this year — and investors have no good way out of the trade.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Some fixed-for-life preferred shares sold by banks during the pandemic era have lost 8.5% in total return terms this year, making the group one of the worst-performing parts of the global credit market. The securities have plummeted nearly 40% since they were sold and every issuer so far has skipped repayment options that would have been investors' way out without a loss. A pending decision by Morgan Stanley may make it a clean sweep.

Unlike other types of preferred shares, fixed-for-life coupons never change, making them extremely sensitive to interest rates. Now, with rates significantly higher than in 2020 and 2021, when lenders sold the securities with sub-5% coupons, the banks have no incentive to replace them.
That's left investors, who were attracted by their relatively high yields at the time, effectively trapped in a losing bet.

"Would you buy 100-year bonds? No? Well, that's what you're buying," said Frank Sileo, senior fixed income strategist Americas at the UBS Chief Investment Office. "These are truly perpetual preferreds."

The losses for this group of preferreds are outsized even in a fixed income market that has come under intense pressure this year. Government bond yields have been rising on the back of inflation and public spending concerns, while the lowest-rated junk bonds are coming under strain.

The selloff has left the pandemic-era securities trading at deeply discounted levels. The group is indicated at a price of 61 cents on the dollar on average, based on data compiled by Bloomberg. Among the issuers are major banks like JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Wells Fargo & Co., which have already skipped call options.

Morgan Stanley's $1.3 billion issue, which has a call option in January, is indicated at 61.4 cents on the dollar, implying virtually no chance of early repayment. A representative for Morgan Stanley declined to comment.
Preferreds are a type of hybrid security similar to Europe's Additional Tier 1 bonds, and are popular with US banks because they help meet capital requirements without diluting common shareholders.

The fixed-for-life flavor — also known for their retail investor-friendly par amount of $25 — proliferated when interest rates were slashed during the pandemic. Banks seized the opportunity to lock in cheap capital, with lenders selling about $10 billion of the securities in 2020 and $16 billion in 2021.

"Some banks had the foresight that rates might not always be zero forever. Given demand for those instruments, why not issue some fixed-for-life," said Arnold Kakuda, senior financials credit analyst at Bloomberg Intelligence.

For buyers of fixed-for-life preferreds, coupons that were multiple times the Treasury yield seemed generous at a time when yields on all bonds had collapsed. And their bet may have worked out if rates had stayed lower for longer.

But now, the fixed coupons on these securities — many of which are below 5% — look far too low. The lowest-coupon issue in the group, a 3.75% series by US Bancorp, is now indicated at 55 cents on the dollar.

By contrast, fixed-for-life bank preferreds sold in 2026 have carried coupons of 6.69% on average, though this type of preferred shares has fallen out of favor. Banks are now issuing more fixed-to-reset preferreds, where the coupon switches to a market-based level after a certain period.

To be sure, "when we talk about perpetuity, anything can happen," said BI's Kakuda. "Never say never. Who would have thought negative rates would be possible but it happened," he said, referring to the potential for the securities to rebound in price and be repaid in the future.

Still, it's highly unlikely that rates will move in favor of the preferred-share investors anytime soon. If anything, Treasury yields rose back toward 5% this week after new evidence of sticky inflation boosted the odds of interest rate increases by the Federal Reserve.

At the same time, regulatory requirements prevent banks from adding any clauses to preferred shares that would give an incentive to call them, meaning the decision is purely based on whether it is economic for the lender to do so.
This points to an extended period of pain for holders of fixed-for-life preferred shares, and no way out apart from selling at deeply depressed levels.
"The seeds of dramatic losses were sown in 2020 and 2021," said UBS's Sileo. "I was talking about it at the time. What's going to happen when the music ends?"
