finance.yahoo.com/technology/articles/ch.author: Bloomberg News

paragraphs.text: Thu, November 12, 2026 at 1:38 AM CST 1 min read

(Bloomberg) -- The US should stop using allegations of Chinese spying on Nvidia Corp. Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang to justify technology restrictions, Beijing said, adding that it was in touch with American counterparts before a planned meeting of the nations' leaders.
Most Read from Bloomberg

"China's scientific progress relies on independent innovation and open cooperation," Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said at a regular press briefing in Beijing on Thursday when asked about the Nvidia episode and its potential impact on bilateral ties.
"The US should stop fabricating the so-called Chinese spy narrative as a pretext for imposing technology restrictions," she added.

The scandal surrounding Huang is complicating a meeting next week between Chinese leader Xi Jinping and President Donald Trump — a summit that comes with less than two months remaining on a trade ceasefire. Lawmakers in Washington have called for tightening restrictions on tech products since allegations that Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy arose.

Mao also said her country would "work with the US to act on the important common understandings reached between the two presidents, and build a constructive relationship of strategic stability on the basis of respect, fairness and reciprocity."

finance.yahoo.com/technology/articles/nv.headline: Nvidia Turmoil Lifts AMD, Broadcom on Bets for Business Gains
finance.yahoo.com/technology/articles/nv.author: Abhishek Vishnoi

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Nvidia Corp.'s leadership turmoil is boosting potential beneficiaries, with Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Broadcom Inc. and Alphabet Inc. gaining after hours on bets they may win business from the chip giant.
Most Read from Bloomberg

AMD and Broadcom each rose more than 3% as Nvidia sank 9% after hours on reports its board is preparing to oust Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang, who led its rise to become, at one point, the world's most valuable company. Alphabet rose 0.3% in extended trading.

The selloff followed reports about Huang's extramarital affairs and intensified after the Wall Street Journal said the board was preparing to remove him. Nvidia is working with an outside firm to identify potential replacements for Huang.

As Nvidia confronts leadership uncertainty, rival hardware makers are gaining as investors seek continued exposure to the AI trade while hedging Nvidia-related risks. The turmoil underscores the potential for further volatility as investors assess its impact on AI development and the extent to which customers diversify their spending worldwide.

"This is where competitors like AMD, like Google Tensor Processing Units and Amazon will probably have a chance to improve their market share when it comes to that accelerator market that Nvidia dominates," Mandeep Singh, global head of technology research at Bloomberg Intelligence, said. "There is no doubt that Nvidia won't be as aggressive as they have been in the past two to three years when it comes to setting goals and overachieving them."
Huang's potential replacement will likely be "quite conservative" in company leadership, given the recent developments.

AMD and Broadcom stand to likely gain the most if Nvidia's leadership issues disrupt its customer relationships. AMD is Nvidia's closest rival in AI accelerators, while Broadcom has a growing role in custom AI chips and networking.

While a Nvidia leadership shakeup may push customers to rethink their reliance on a single supplier, competitors like AMD and Broadcom are already pursuing business in AI accelerators, custom silicon and networking.

"AMD as a direct competitor, and Alphabet and Broadcom in the TPU space, are natural beneficiaries in the short term," said Anna Wu, an investment strategist and founder of Floodlines Research. "Huang's scandal has raised public doubts about Nvidia's commercial secrets and its product edge."

Alphabet's TPUs are custom-built for AI, while graphics processing units are multi-purpose chips originally made for gaming. TPUs can't replace GPUs across the board, and moving AI workloads away from Nvidia is slow and costly, she added.

Alphabet announced plans to roll out a broader array of AI chips, aiming to capitalize on its rapid rise as a major challenger to Nvidia in a market worth hundreds of billions of dollars. The company is introducing two new variations of its TPUs.
Other beneficiaries include the companies powering hyperscalers' in-house chips.

In Taipei, MediaTek Inc., which works with Google on custom silicon, rose as much as 3.3% in Taipei on Thursday. Design houses Alchip Technologies Ltd. and Global Unichip Corp. both jumped more than 8% in Taipei on hopes that rising budgets will flow into custom hardware.

Meanwhile, Nvidia's manufacturing partners appear insulated regardless who leads the company, since they also supply its rivals. Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. was little changed, while South Korean suppliers SK Hynix Inc. and Samsung Electronics Co. both rose more than 2%.
Roughly 27% of SK Hynix's revenue comes from Nvidia, versus 0.3% of Samsung Electronics, according to Bloomberg's supply-chain data.
Because Samsung shares a closer relationship with Nvidia rival AMD, some market watchers see potential for new leadership at Nvidia to warm up to Samsung.

"A potential leadership change at Nvidia could create a strategic opening for Samsung," said Jung In Yun, chief executive officer at Fibonacci Asset Management Global. "If Jensen Huang were to leave, new management could reassess supplier relationships and place greater emphasis on diversifying its supply chain, giving Samsung an opportunity to deepen its partnership with Nvidia and compete for a larger share of future HBM orders."
The scandal could also benefit Chinese companies working to replace Nvidia in their home market, as stricter export rules in the US intensify scrutiny of chip sales to China.
Any resulting tightening would provide a tailwind for local chipmakers such as Cambricon Technologies Corp., Hygon Information Technology Co. and Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp.

npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-6031982/this-we.headline: This week in science: PTSD prediction, phishing while tired, an exoplanet
npr.org/2026/11/12/nx-s1-6031982/this-we.author: Emily Kwong

paragraphs.text: SCOTT DETROW, HOST:
It's time now for our science news roundup from Short Wave, NPR's science podcast. I am joined by the show's hosts, Emily Kwong and Regina Barber. Hello to both of you.
REGINA BARBER, BYLINE: Hey.
EMILY KWONG, BYLINE: Hey.
DETROW: You were in stereo just now.
BARBER: Yeah.
DETROW: It was great.
BARBER: We planned that.
DETROW: So you've brought us three science stories that caught your attention. What are they?
KWONG: How AI can help emergency room workers identify patients who may develop PTSD.
BARBER: A new technique that helps us find really faint planets beyond our solar system.
DETROW: You know how I feel about space.
BARBER: That's right.
KWONG: We put it in there for you.
BARBER: That's why I picked it.
KWONG: (Inaudible) put this story in there for you (laughter).
KWONG: And why daylight saving time could be bad for cybersecurity.

DETROW: All right. Let's start with - this is interesting. There's been so many stories about AI identifying healthcare trends that might be hard for doctors to spot. Let's talk about this. Identifying...
KWONG: Yeah.
DETROW: ...PTSD in emergency departments.

KWONG: This is very interesting. So researchers took trauma patients answers' to a routine screening question - what brought you to the emergency department today? They fed the answers to that question into an AI model that was designed to predict the patient's risk of developing PTSD a month later.
DETROW: Huh. I mean, how good was the model making that prediction?

BARBER: So it got it right around 95% of the cases. A psychologist and lead researcher, Katharina Schultebraucks, says that these results are exciting because they're using a patient's story in their own words.

KATHARINA SCHULTEBRAUCKS: Some people talk, like, very elaborative of what happens. Some are in such high distress they may only say a few words and a few sentences. And we are looking not on PTSD symptoms right now, but we're looking in what happens in the future.
BARBER: They published their findings in the journal Nature Communications.
DETROW: I'm curious, is this something that clinicians have been missing?

KWONG: Yeah, so when trained clinicians are screening for PTSD risk, they do tend to find it. The problem is that giving a PTSD risk assessment is an extra step that a lot of emergency departments just simply do not have time for. You know, they're, like, tending to the emergency. There's also the stigma around mental health that might clam up some patients. So using this model could streamline the process, and medical professionals can act sooner to prevent PTSD from developing.
BARBER: And Scott, what's unique about this work is that the model gave its reasoning at each step of the analysis.
MUNMUN DE CHOUDHURY: What this work does, it says that the AI doesn't have to be a black box.
BARBER: So this is Munmun De Choudhury, a computer scientist not involved in the work. She said this work has real potential to guide clinicians to the right kind of interventions.
DETROW: Perpetual question with this stuff - are there worries about privacy of sending a patient's words to an AI model?

KWONG: Good question. Katharina says that the model did not share the data on a cloud service and was HIPAA-compliant. But she adds that it is important any patient consents to having their information recorded and used by an AI model.
DETROW: So new topic.
DETROW: Gina.
DETROW: Exoplanet.
BARBER: (Laughter) Yeah.
DETROW: New exoplanet. Let's - this is a - meaning a planet beyond our solar system.
DETROW: What is this technique that scientists used to find it?

BARBER: So this exoplanet was actually already known. A team of researchers studied existing images of the star it orbits to see if light from 51 Eridani b could be found, just to kind of verify this technique. And this is important because often it's hard to see exoplanets in images.
KWONG: And that's because the light that exoplanets reflect from the closest star is often much fainter than the light the star gives off.
DETROW: Right.
KWONG: So the star, like, kind of hides the planet.
DETROW: I mean, so how did they uncover it, then? Because again, stars, very bright.
DETROW: Planets, when they're far away, not very bright.

BARBER: So they subtracted light from the image until they could clearly see the planet and not the stars. The paper was published in Nature last week. And this new technique corrects that issue and corrects for millions of more issues that can make it harder to find an exoplanet, like the telescope being unstable or instrumental errors or temperature fluctuations.
DETROW: Is this kind of like in a - in, like, a cops TV show where they're looking at the security camera and they say, oh, enhance on that one image, and they zoom in?
BARBER: I mean, kind of (laughter). But Scott, what I'm actually surprised about is that they did all of this with just physics knowledge and algorithms and no AI.
DETROW: No AI.
DETROW: All right.
KWONG: (Laughter).
DETROW: So what can these images tell us about this planet?
KWONG: So yeah, because these images were taken in infrared by the powerful James Webb Space Telescope, they can tell us more about what these exoplanets are made out of.
RODRIGO FERRER-CHAVEZ: With this, it is the first time that we can actually get this specific information-rich image of this planet that might tell us a lot about how it formed.

KWONG: That's lead author Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, a Ph.D. candidate at Northwestern University. He also says that this tool can be used to find even more exoplanets hiding out in James Webb Space Telescope images.

BARBER: This technique can also be used to make future telescopes, that are already supposed to be more powerful, even better at finding exoplanets. But I do want to say that other astronomers I talked to said that this is just one cool technique of many that scientists are developing for future research in finding these faint, distant worlds.
DETROW: OK. All right, back here on Earth. Third story. It's about sleep.
KWONG: Mm-hmm.
BARBER: Mm-hmm.
KWONG: And daylight saving.
BARBER: Yeah. So, Scott, did you know that nearly one-third of U.S. adults don't get enough sleep?
DETROW: Honestly, I would assume the number is higher.
DETROW: One-third actually sounds promising (laughter).
KWONG: Oh, gosh.
BARBER: And we know that it's bad for our health, right? It's bad for decision-making.

KWONG: But just how bad is it for decision-making if you lose a modest amount of sleep? That's what Eitan Schechtman, an assistant professor at the University of California, Irvine wanted to know. And he found a fun way to test this with phishing attacks.
BARBER: (Laughter).

KWONG: His university regularly sends fake phishing emails to staff to train them on cybersecurity. These emails contain suspicious links you are not supposed to click. But would they click if they were a little sleepy?
DETROW: Interesting. Did this become a full experiment?

BARBER: Yeah, so Eitan worked with the university's security team to divide 11,000 participants into two groups. Some people got the fishing email the Monday before daylight saving, and some got it the Monday immediately after, you know, when we can assume some may have lost an hour of sleep. So people emailed after daylight saving were 13% more likely to fall for the phishing attack the following morning and click that bad link. The study was published in the Proceedings of National Academy of Sciences this week.

KWONG: I spoke to Muhammad Adeel Rishi, a sleep specialist at Indiana University School of Medicine who wasn't involved in this study. He found the finding compelling and said it adds to growing evidence about the consequences of daylight saving. Spring forward has been linked to an increase in heart attacks and fatal traffic accidents.
DETROW: And apparently cybersecurity problems. What's the solution here?

BARBER: So Eitan wants cybersecurity companies to be aware of this finding so they can beef up their security for any moments where there's widespread sleep loss. So think about holidays or major sporting events.

EITAN SCHECHTMAN: There might be more of these - more susceptibility to click these links or generally to make impulsive decisions, whether it's on the road, in the stock market or cybersecurity-related decision.
DETROW: Some places have just, like, gotten rid of time changes, right?
DETROW: Like most of Arizona and Hawaii.

KWONG: Yes. This is a whole other debate. But just to put science's finger on the scale, multiple studies have shown that standard time is healthier for our bodies. Standard time has more natural light in the morning, which better aligns to our bodies' circadian rhythms.
DETROW: All right. Good thing we're in standard time right now.
DETROW: That is Emily Kwong and Regina Barber with NPR's science podcast Short Wave, where you can listen for new discoveries and the science behind the headlines. Thanks to both of you.
KWONG: Thank you.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Blackstone Courts Dubai’s Rich in Race to Tap $1 Trillion Market
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Swetha Gopinath

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Blackstone Inc.'s top private wealth executives held their first-ever gathering in Dubai to court the city's deep-pocketed investors, as the alternative asset manager seeks to expand its business across the Gulf.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The US firm pitched its range of products, including private credit and infrastructure, to an audience of more than 100 high-net-worth individuals and representatives from family offices and platforms that distribute private investments to wealthy clients at the Waldorf Astoria in the Dubai International Financial Centre.

Speakers at the Wednesday event included Farhad Karim, chief operating officer of Blackstone Private Wealth; Carlos Whitaker, president of BCRED, its flagship private credit fund for individual investors; and Greg Blank, chief executive officer of BXINFRA, its infrastructure vehicle for retail investors.
The gathering also coincided with the opening of Blackstone's new Dubai outpost — its first dedicated private wealth office outside Zurich.

Blackstone's push into Dubai, where the financial hub alone is home to family offices controlling more than $1 trillion in assets, is the latest sign of the United Arab Emirates' continued appeal to financial firms, wealth managers and family offices despite the monthslong Iran war.

"The UAE has built an extraordinary position as a global finance and investment hub and is becoming an increasingly important center for wealth management," Blackstone Chief Operating Officer Jon Gray said in an emailed statement.

Private capital firms and alternative asset managers are increasingly turning to wealthy individuals and family offices as institutional fundraising has slowed. Blackstone has been at the forefront of that shift, with its private wealth business managing $330 billion, nearly a quarter of the firm's $1.4 trillion in assets.

The push hasn't been entirely smooth. Blackstone is navigating pressures hitting many private credit firms as some investors have rushed to redeem their capital on concerns on exposure to software companies and credit quality.
Get the Mideast Money newsletter, a weekly look at the intersection of wealth and power in the region.

The Gulf has become a prominent dealmaking destination for Blackstone. Despite the Iran war, the firm has struck several deals in the UAE, partnering with a Dubai firm on an aircraft-leasing venture and committing $250 million to a payments infrastructure platform in Abu Dhabi. It also joined other global firms in a $16 billion infrastructure partnership involving Kuwait's oil-export pipelines, the largest foreign direct investment in the country's history.
Blackstone is also expanding its Abu Dhabi office, already its largest in the region, to support further dealmaking.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/12/bro.headline: Eight dead and at least 18 injured after Brooklyn building collapse
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/12/bro.author: Tim Craig, Violet Jira, Dhruti Shah

paragraphs.text: NEW YORK — Eight people were killed and at least 18 injured after a three-story building in Brooklyn collapsed into an adjacent construction site Wednesday, New York City officials said.

Two of the dead were children, and two were construction workers, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani told reporters Thursday. The injured included four firefighters. Mamdani said most of the hospitalized were in stable condition, and one was considered critical.

New York Police on Thursday night identified the victims as: Nicole Daniela Salvada Rodriguez, 9; Kevin Santiago Reyes Gonzalez, 10; Juan Daniel Salvada Guzman, 31; Ndiaye Mamadou, 31; Barry Mamadou, 23; Gabriel Siguencia, 22; Edgar Sapon, 26; and Jose Luis Caguana Cosquillo, 26.
The fire department ended its search for survivors just after 3:30 p.m. on Thursday. The cause of the collapse is under investigation.
Department of Buildings officials are conducting safety checks at 100 locations across the city associated with five entities involved with the construction site, Mamdani said.

“A tragedy of this magnitude demands a comprehensive and thorough investigation that includes both the construction site and the building which collapsed,” he said, adding: “We will find out what happened, and we will share that information with New Yorkers.”

The remnants of people’s lives were visible Thursday in what remained of a next-door building, whose walls were partly sheared off. Pink sheets and a pile of clothes covered a bed, and clothing closets were visible nearby. Mamdani said immigrants from countries including Colombia, Mexico, Ecuador and Trinidad and Tobago were among the dead.
More than 250 emergency responders, including fire, medical and police workers, responded to the scene on Flatbush Avenue after the alarm was raised just after 4 p.m. Wednesday.
Rescuers used pickaxes and power saws to make their way through the rubble, according to photos from the scene and local media reports. Fire and police dogs were also deployed.
Some construction workers on-site at the time of the collapse dug other people out of the rubble after barely surviving themselves, Mamdani said at Thursday’s news conference.
“People are alive today because of their heroism yesterday,” he said.
Video footage showed survivors being pulled from the wreckage. One woman’s husband told ABC7 that she was six months pregnant and that he was very happy she had been found alive.
“This has been an incredibly challenging and fast-moving situation with precarious wreckage to navigate and dangerous voids beneath the surface,” Mamdani said at a news conference Wednesday.
Authorities shut down city water mains early Thursday to allow emergency responders to continue working, affecting around 100 buildings.

Records filed in the months leading up to the tragedy warned of the potential for adverse impacts to other buildings in the area due to excavation and vibrations from construction. The collapsed building was built in 1930. Like many in the area, the building was aging, said Rodneyse Bichotte Hermelyn, a New York State assembly member with an office across the street from the collapse.
She told The Washington Post on Thursday that city leaders were examining the excavation plans and whether the crew was digging deeper than authorized by their construction permits.
The three-story apartment building is owned by Isolag Realty Corp with Olufemi Falade listed as its registered agent, according to city property records.

The collapsed building has been cited for 11 violations of the city’s housing and maintenance code this year, according to the Department of Housing Preservation and Development. In April, the property received a citation for inadequate water supply to the building’s sprinkler system. The property was also instructed to repair a roof leak and exposed electrical wiring that same month.
In total, the property has 25 open violations that the city classifies as hazardous or immediately hazardous.

The same records show Falade owns multiple properties throughout Brooklyn which, like the property that collapsed, have unresolved violations of city building code going back several years. He was jailed for 12 days in 2006 over hazardous conditions and unpaid fines at his properties, the New York Post reported at the time.
Falade did not respond to multiple phone calls from The Washington Post.

Brooklyn District Attorney Eric Gonzalez said his office was “working closely” with the Department of Buildings and law enforcement “to determine whether any criminal conduct contributed to this tragedy.”

Construction was ongoing at a lot next to the north wall of the building that collapsed. The construction site had a plan approved for a three-story building, said Ahmed Tigani, the Department of Buildings commissioner. He said further plans for a nine-story building had been filed but not yet approved. Publicly filed zoning documents outline a plan for a mixed-use building, including a food store, apartments and businesses.

Robert Fischman owned the lot where construction was taking place, records show. He sent a required notice to a local advisory board in February notifying the community that construction would start in 30 days.
“All precautions will be taken to protect your property at 1321 Flatbush Avenue that is adjacent to our referenced property,” Fischman said in one of the letters.

The construction site was fined $10,000 for failing to abide by a stop-work order from the Department of Buildings in April. The fine was paid in October. Excavation work to construct the building’s cellar started on Sept. 10, according to records, and that work was ongoing on the day the building collapsed, James Williams, who works nearby, told The Post Thursday.
Williams, 60, said he heard loud bangs from the construction site the day of the collapse.
“They were hitting that structure tremendously,” he said. “Every five minutes after five minutes — bang. Like they were trying to break something down there to get through to something.”
Williams questioned whether enough was done to make sure the residents in the adjacent building were safe during the construction.
“What did y’all do to secure those people who lived over there?” he asked.
A stop-work order was issued for the construction site Wednesday, according to the Department of Buildings.
Victoria Bisset contributed to this report.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Long US Bonds Reopen With Gains as Risk Sentiment Sours Again
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Ruth Carson

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Long-end Treasuries drifted higher as trading resumed after a holiday as turmoil at Nvidia Corp. fueled doubts about the artificial intelligence trade and fueled demand for haven assets.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Yields on 30-year US government bonds slipped two basis points to 5.34% ahead of an auction of similar-maturity securities on Thursday. Those on 10-year notes dipped briefly before steadying at 4.99%. There was no cash trading on Wednesday due to the Veterans' Day holiday.

Risk sentiment took a hit after a report said Nvidia's board was considering the removal of Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang following allegations of multiple extramarital affairs. The chipmaker sits at the heart of the AI trade, meaning any sign of trouble risks undermining confidence far beyond the firm itself.

"All these headlines on Jensen Huang are further sowing doubt about the AI story and triggering a small safe haven bid in Treasuries," said Carol Kong, strategist at Commonwealth Bank of Australia. "There is no doubt every market participant is watching this closely given how critical Nvidia is to the AI investment boom, and by extension, the global economy."
Other government bonds were also in demand in Asia trading, with yields on Australian and New Zealand debt slipping at least one basis point.

Nasdaq futures dropped almost 1% and S&P contracts declined 0.5% after Nvidia tumbled about 10% in late trading. The company's board is meeting to discuss Huang's future after he admitted to an affair with a woman US officials reportedly believe is a Chinese spy, according to a person familiar with the matter.
What Bloomberg Strategists Say...
"Aggressive traders will likely view any modest Nasdaq bounce as a window to re-set macro hedges. It may also revitalize the bid for bonds, which have been struggling this week."
Mark Cranfield, strategist at Markets Live

But shorter-end Treasuries edged lower as traders held fast to bets for more Federal Reserve interest-rate hikes, leading to a flattening of the curve. Yields on two-year notes climbed three basis points to 4.77% and those on five-year debt rose one basis point to 4.83%.

The swaps market indicates that traders are pricing in a quarter-point rate increase at the Fed's December meeting after a key gauge of US consumer prices posted another firm advance in October. The print prompted Fed officials to open the door to more aggressive rate increases over the coming months, with Governor Christopher Waller saying a half-percentage-point hike in December may be needed.

"Higher short-end US yields this morning likely reflect a continuing hawkish repricing, post the hotter US CPI and some fairly blunt and hawkish Fedspeak since that release," said Andrew Ticehurst, a senior rates strategist at Nomura Holdings Inc. in Sydney. "It's very interesting to see the best part of 30 basis points priced for the next Fed meeting, the market is clearly considering the risk of a 50-basis-point hike in December."

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Janice Huang

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Alphabet Inc. began marketing its inaugural Hong Kong and Singapore dollar bond sale, testing investor interest at a time of increasing volatility for companies focused on artificial intelligence.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The Google parent set initial price guidance for its proposed 2-year, 5-year and 10-year Hong Kong dollar bonds at around 4.6%, 5% and 5.5%, respectively, according to a person familiar with the matter. The company is also marketing 2-year, 5-year, 10-year and 30-year Singapore dollar-denominated notes, with guidance around 2.75%, 3.25%, 3.65%, and 4%, the person said.
Proceeds from the offering will be used for general corporate purposes, which may include the repayment of outstanding debt. The bonds could be priced as early as Thursday, the person said.

The deal comes at a challenging moment for technology industry borrowers. Investors have become more cautious toward AI-linked assets after a broad market selloff last week fueled by concerns that a Democratic sweep in the US midterm elections could lead to greater scrutiny of data center development and AI infrastructure spending.

The sector has also been shaken by market turmoil sparked by Nvidia Corp., the leading maker of AI chips, which has been working with an outside firm to identify potential replacements for Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang.

Alphabet's fundraising effort is part of a broader push by global hyperscalers to tap new debt markets as they seek financing for AI-related projects. The company sold its first Australian dollar bonds in August and has also issued notes in Swiss francs, British pounds, Canadian dollars and Japanese yen this year.

Alphabet and other firms, including Microsoft Corp., Amazon.com Inc. and Meta Platforms Inc., have been borrowing at a record pace while simultaneously committing tens of billions of dollars to build out AI capabilities.

Earlier this month, Alphabet raised €6 billion ($6.7 billion) through a multi-tranche euro bond sale, its second offering in the currency this year. The company paid materially higher borrowing costs than in its inaugural euro deal in May as concerns over the pace of AI spending rose.

latimes.com/business/story/2026-11-12/nv.headline: Jensen Huang’s exit tests whether Nvidia can run without its co-founder
latimes.com/business/story/2026-11-12/nv.author: Ella Chakarian

paragraphs.text: Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia has shaken up not only his company but also the booming artificial intelligence industry, which was largely built around his success and leadership.

In a regulatory filing on Thursday, Nvidia said Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO while keeping her finance role until a permanent successor is named. Harvey C. Jones was appointed the board’s first-ever chair. Huang, who owns about 3.6% of Nvidia, will also leave the board.

Huang’s resignation follows reports of two extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a Singapore-based businesswoman whom U.S. intelligence officials reportedly suspect of working for Chinese intelligence. Nvidia’s board launched an independent investigation into national-security concerns raised by the reports. Since his resignation, Reuters reported that Huang had intimate relationships with a second Nvidia employee.
Representatives of Nvidia and Huang did not respond to a request for comment.
Nvidia’s stock dropped more than 11% in pre-market trading on Thursday and closed at $166.19, down more than 4%. Shares have fallen 13% since Friday.

“Jensen’s contributions to NVIDIA are profound,” the company said in its statement. “NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. The Board and the company thank Jensen for his immeasurable contributions to the company and the industry.”

Huang has been a key player in the growth of the AI industry and his ouster sparked worries about the effects it would have on Santa Clara-based Nvidia and other companies that depend on its computer chips.

The revelations have also highlighted national security concerns in Washington, where federal lawmakers have called for an investigation into accusations that China targeted the powerful tech mogul. The U.S. has been locked in an AI race with China, raising more scrutiny over Nvidia’s business with the country.
“It’s absolutely stunning news,” said Brian Colello, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar. “It was not something that was on the minds of investors a week ago or prior.”

Executive scandals are hardly rare, Colello said, but “not to somebody at his scale, not to somebody who helms a company the size of Nvidia” and “who is at the epicenter of such a transformative technology as AI.”

Huang was deeply embedded in the company’s operations. He had 60 direct reports, and both of his children work at Nvidia. Colello said Nvidia appeared to have done little succession planning, given how much of the company’s leadership and decision-making centered on Huang.
“The market hates uncertainty, and there’s far more uncertainty about Nvidia now than there was a week ago,” Colello said.
Global equity research firm Bernstein SocGen Group downgraded its rating on Nvidia’s stock and lowered its price target from $400 to $200, saying “there will no doubt be more allegations to come.”
Building a colossus
Huang co-founded Nvidia and led it to an unprecedented rise, making it the world’s most valuable company for some time and the first ever to reach a $5-trillion market capitalization last year.

While Nvidia’s powerful chips were first popular for gaming and cryptocurrency mining, they became the core component in building AI. Huang and his signature black leather jacket became the technology’s public face.
As other tech leaders have called for a slowdown of the AI race, Huang has called for faster AI innovation, saying it could help improve safety.

Huang is seen as a visionary, dealmaker and politically savvy, forging strong ties with President Trump, who suggested former Apple Chief Executive Tim Cook take over Huang’s role in a Truth Social post.

Some Silicon Valley tech leaders have shown support for Huang. When reports started to swirl that Nvidia’s board of directors was preparing to oust Huang, SpaceX Chief Executive Elon Musk said in an X post that it would be “an honor” to hire Huang.
In an interview with Bloomberg this year, Huang said he would prefer his transition out of the role to happen two decades from now.

“This is a company that was synonymous with Huang,” said Patrick R. Riccards, a crisis communications expert. “He was the company. He was the face, but he was also the heart and soul of this company.”

Riccards, who has consulted for Fortune 500 companies and presidential administrations, said the tech industry has grown increasingly volatile, with persistent layoffs and restructuring creating a “wild west.” Nvidia, which has not had any major recent layoffs, was the exception.
“It was the stable unicorn,” Riccards said.
That stability is facing its first test with the ousting of Huang, who was, up until now, the only CEO Nvidia employees have known.
“Those employees were ready to slay dragons with a butter knife for him,” Riccards said.
Absence of a succession plan
Such larger-than-life leaders can unintentionally become a liability, governance experts say.

Michael Useem, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School of Business, said there is no evidence the company invested in preparing a successor, and that the board shares responsibility if it didn’t press the issue.
“It looks like they’re making up for lost time,” Useem said.

Rene Haas, the chief executive of chip design company Arm Holdings, who worked at Nvidia from 2006 to 2013, told the New York Times that Huang was resistant to establishing a formal succession plan because “he felt it would create competition among executives and be divisive.” Nvidia has been working with an outside firm to identify potential replacements for Huang, according to Bloomberg.
“You can fault the board for not understanding what was going to be needed in the long term,” Useem said, “on the valid premise that nobody lives forever.”
The race in shareholder lawsuits against Nvidia has since commenced. A class-action shareholder lawsuit was filed Monday in federal court in San Francisco against Nvidia and Huang.

Still, Nvidia’s GPUs and software ecosystem underpin much of the AI industry, which makes the company hard to replace, Morningstar’s Colello said, even as the largest tech companies try to reduce their reliance on it.
“AI is still running on Nvidia gear today,” Colello said.
The larger risk, he said, is to customer relationships.
“Nvidia will have to work hard and work quickly to solidify any customer relationships that might be damaged.”

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a senior associate dean at the Yale School of Management, said he does not expect Nvidia’s business to shrink, though he said the turmoil could create opportunities for other semiconductor companies, including AMD, Texas Instruments and Analog Devices.
While some commentators predicted a market crash Thursday morning, Sonnenfeld said there have been bright spots in the market.
“This is giving opportunity for a lot of others,” he said.

Huang’s exit also hit the “neocloud” companies, the newer AI data center operators that rent out computing power, according to Steven Tian, research director at the Yale Chief Executive Leadership Institute.

Those companies were already under strain, Tian said. They must raise large amounts of debt to build data centers, and rising interest rates make that harder. Huang’s departure could add to those pressures, he said, contributing to Thursday’s selloff in neocloud shares.
The turmoil could benefit hyperscalers, including Amazon, Microsoft and Google, which have their own large-scale cloud infrastructure businesses, Tian added.
Investors will get their first look at the new leadership soon. Nvidia will report third-quarter fiscal 2027 results Tuesday as previously scheduled, followed by an earnings call.
Lawmakers have requested for Huang to appear for a closed-door congressional briefing the day after.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Index Provider MSCI Removes Strategy From Equity Benchmark
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: David Pan

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- MSCI Inc. has dropped Strategy Inc. from its global equity benchmarks, potentially triggering billions of dollars in stock sales and adding fresh pressure to the financing model behind Michael Saylor's vast Bitcoin holdings.
Most Read from Bloomberg

Strategy is among the firms that the major index provider is removing its MSCI USA Index after it adopted new eligibility rules, according to results of the November 2026 Index Review for the MSCI Equity Indexes released Wednesday. Last month, MSCI said it would exclude companies classified as non-operating businesses under a new framework that takes effect at the close of Nov. 30.

Strategy has said it expects the firm's class A common stock to be excluded from the MSCI Indexes as part of the review, according to the quarterly report in late October. Strategy didn't immediately reply to a request for comment.
Shares of Strategy fell almost 2% in after-hours trading. The stock is down almost 20% this year. Bitcoin has dropped around 15% during the same period.

The exclusion can add more stress to the Bitcoin accumulating model in which the firm sells a variety of securities, including common stock and preferred shares at a premium in order to fund its token purchases. Pioneered by Saylor, Strategy's co-founder and executive chairman, the firm has acquired over $60 billion in Bitcoin since the middle of 2020.

MSCI will also remove Tokyo-based Bitcoin treasury Metaplanet Inc. from its Japan Small Cap Index as part of the review. The company holds 44,000 Bitcoin. Metaplanet didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

As index-tracking funds rebalance, they usually sell billions of dollars in shares. Last year, JPMorgan Chase & Co. estimated that such an event could trigger as much as $2.8 billion of Strategy sales, and potentially another $8.8 billion if other indexes follow suit.

Saylor has downplayed any potential impacts by the decision. In an October interview with Bloomberg Television, he said the index provider was "imposing prejudicial values on digital assets." He called their decision a "value judgment" that sets a bad precedent.
