theguardian.com/environment/2026/nov/12/.headline: China rules out hosting Cop33 climate summit in 2028
theguardian.com/environment/2026/nov/12/.author: Fiona Harvey

paragraphs.text: China has ruled out hosting the Cop33 UN climate summit in 2028 after months of deliberations, leaving the field open for other Asian countries to hold it, the Guardian understands.

The decision will disappoint many countries and climate experts, who had hoped the world’s biggest emitter would take the lead on the global stage, as the US under Donald Trump has vacated all forms of international cooperation on the climate.

Al Gore, the former US vice-president, was among those left disheartened by the decision. “I would be very much in favour of that idea [of China hosting the summit],” he told the Guardian. “It’s too bad.”

China is in the midst of an economic transformation, from being heavily dependent on coal to becoming an “electro state”. John Kerry, the former US secretary of state, told the Guardian that China was leaving the rest of the world behind in forging and using the low-carbon technologies of the future.
Renewable energy generation capacity has now outstripped coal in China, and its greenhouse gas emissions appear to have declined slightly this year.

Sales of electric vehicles in the country have also taken off, making up nearly two-thirds of the market last month, and China’s clean energy industries drove more than 90% of the country’s investment growth last year.
The rules of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) mean an Asian country should host in 2028.

Gareth Redmond-King, the international lead at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit thinktank, said China’s position as an industrial powerhouse would have made it a formidable contender to hold the summit.
“It would undoubtedly be significant for the world’s biggest emitter and second-biggest economy to host a climate Cop,” he said.

“They’re leading the world on investment, manufacture and deployment of clean energy tech, and their emissions have started to tick down. As a leadership story, China hosting Cop33 would be a big deal.”

It is not clear why China has decided against hosting the conference, but several experts that spoke to the Guardian suggested that the US electoral cycle was likely to have been a factor. The next US presidential election will take place on 7 November 2028, and Cop33 is scheduled for 6 to 17 November that year.

After the strong showing by Democrats in the recent midterm elections, in which voter concern over the climate crisis was thought to be a factor, the Democrats will be hoping to elect a climate-friendly president in 2028. But even if they succeed, Trump will still be in office until the following January.
The US president rejects climate science and withdrew the US from the Paris agreement, and is also withdrawing from its parent treaty, the 1992 UNFCCC.

China seeks to be seen as a leader among developing countries, but has been wary of stepping into the gap left by the US. Under the Democratic presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama, the US and China enjoyed a close partnership on climate issues, setting joint targets on reducing methane and developing clean technology.

Cop33 will be an important meeting because it will include the “global stocktake” – a mechanism under the 2015 Paris climate agreement that examines countries’ progress on cutting emissions in line with the goal of limiting global temperature rises to 1.5C.
That limit is now certain to be surpassed, but experts say countries should now try to minimise the temperature “overshoot”, to avoid worse ravages from extreme weather.

India’s government considered offering to host Cop33 for several months earlier this year, but also decided against it. India’s coal use has been increasing, even as the country exceeds its own renewable energy targets.
The Guardian understands that other countries mulling a bid to host Cop33 include Uzbekistan, South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand.
No decision on a host is likely to be made at this year’s Cop31 meeting, which is ongoing in Turkey, with the Turkish and Australian governments jointly presiding over the summit.

cnbc.com/2026/11/12/scout-motors-reserva.headline: Scout Motors has 212,000 vehicle reservations as $2 billion South Carolina plant nears completion
cnbc.com/2026/11/12/scout-motors-reserva.author: Michael Wayland

paragraphs.text: BLYTHEWOOD, S.C. — Electric vehicle startup Scout Motors has notched roughly 212,000 reservations for its upcoming EVs as the company nears completion of its new $2 billion plant here, CEO Scott Keogh told CNBC.
The reservations are for the Volkswagen-backed company's Terra pickup truck and Traveler SUV, which are expected to start full production next year before deliveries begin to customers in 2028.

Reservations do not necessarily translate to sales, as the U.S. automotive industry has learned during the past decade, especially with highly anticipated all-electric trucks such as the Ford F-150 Lightning, Tesla Cybertruck and others that garnered strong interest that didn't lead to meaningful numbers of purchases.

Keogh said he expects Scout could roughly double those reservations by the time customer production begins, but he said the more important thing is to convert early interest into actual sales as production nears.

"It's been a consistent drumbeat," Keogh said during an interview at Scout's plant site outside Columbia. "I think we could easily be up over 400,000 with reservations without doing too much effort. The big thing for us is how much of the initial production can we 100% presell."

Keogh said achieving an order book of 12 to 18 months "would be great" and is something he thinks the company can do before production. Scout on Thursday said plant construction is "in its final phase."

Scout's vehicles will be offered as all-electric versions as well as electric hybrid variants, known as extended-range electric vehicles, or EREVs, that include an internal combustion engine as a backup generator for the electric motors and batteries.

Scout, a former American vehicle brand from 1961 to 1980, was expected to exclusively offer EVs in a bid for the German automaker to expand its presence in the U.S. However, slower-than-expected adoption of EVs and higher costs led the company to decide to offer EREVs as well.
Keogh said extended-range and SUV models are dominating reservations thus far, with roughly 87% choosing EREV models and 75% being SUVs.

The CEO also said the company is drawing interest from its target markets, which include owners of off-road vehicles such as the Ford Bronco and Jeep Wrangler as well as full-size pickup trucks and U.S. EV leader Tesla.

Given the interest signaled by reservations, Keogh said the company is expected to launch with the EREVs first, followed by the EVs. He also said the company plans to launch with mid-level models first, a deviation from many companies that begin with their highest-priced models.

Both the Traveler and Terra are expected to start at under $60,000. The EREV models are expected to feature more than 500 miles of range, according to the company, compared with 300 miles of range for the all-electric models.

"The No.1 thing for me is I want to go get the best volume as soon as possible," Keogh said. "In my mind, it's how quick can you get to 100,000 units? It's at 100,000 units where you can start to punch through."

His comments come months after Rivian Automotive received criticism online for launching its R2 SUV with its highest-priced models first, despite that being a common practice across the automotive industry.
Keogh said Scout's South Carolina plant is about 85% complete, but supporting infrastructure and a $300 million supplier park continue to be installed.

Reservations for Scout's vehicles initially opened in October 2024, when it revealed the Traveler and Terra, which feature sleek, yet rugged, exteriors that pay some homage to the brand's historic models.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/12/for.headline: 3 exonerated inmates urge Florida’s governor-elect to halt executions
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/12/for.author: Alex DeLuca

paragraphs.text: Joaquín José Martínez grew up believing in the death penalty.
Then he wound up on death row.

Arrested in 1996 for a double murder in Tampa, he was convicted and sentenced to death in 1997. He spent four years on the state’s death row before a jury acquitted him of all charges at a retrial in 2001. He was the first European exonerated from death row in the United States.
Twenty-five years later, with Florida poised to set another state record for executions, Martínez is asking the state’s next governor to rethink the death penalty as he himself once did.

At a news conference Thursday morning at the Leroy Collins Leon County Public Library in Tallahassee, Martínez and two other men exonerated from Florida’s death row, Herman Lindsey and Seth Penalver, urged Gov.-elect Byron Donalds (R) to pause executions when he takes office and review state laws they say leave room for wrongful convictions.
“Don’t be the governor that kills an innocent person,” said Lindsey, the executive director of Witness to Innocence and who, in 2009, became the 23rd person exonerated from Florida’s death row.

Donalds, who takes office Jan. 5, will succeed Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) and assume authority to sign death warrants. His campaign told the Florida Trib last month that he “firmly supports the death penalty.” Donalds told the Famuan, Florida A&M University’s student newspaper, that he would review cases individually.
Donalds’s campaign did not respond to a request for comment Thursday from The Washington Post.
Florida, with 234 inmates on death row, carried out its 19th execution of the year on Nov. 5, tying the modern state record set in 2025.

The execution of Thomas Mitchell Overton, scheduled for Nov. 19, would break that record. Overton was convicted in 1999 of killing Michael and Susan MacIvor in the Florida Keys. He has maintained his innocence for more than three decades, according to Floridians for Alternatives to the Death Penalty, which organized Thursday’s news conference with Witness to Innocence.
Florida’s surge in executions comes as some states are moving away from capital punishment.

In California, Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) began the process last week of commuting the death sentences of all 548 people on the state’s death row. A Gallup poll released Tuesday found that 49 percent of U.S. adults favor the death penalty for people convicted of murder, the first time support has fallen below half since 1971.
Gallup conducted the poll in early October, in the weeks after Christa Pike survived Tennessee’s attempt to execute her by lethal injection.

Florida has exonerated 30 people from death row, more than any other state, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Penalver spent 18 years in prison, including 13 on death row, before a jury acquitted him in 2012. On Thursday, he spoke about what he had lost in those years.
“I don’t talk to my oldest son. I lost my grandmother. My father, my mom,” he said through tears.
Martínez recalled a time when opposing the death penalty could seem almost “anti-American.”

He now spends part of his time in Europe. To explain how American executions are viewed from abroad, he asked listeners to imagine visiting Rome’s Colosseum and wondering how the Romans ever accepted putting people to death in front of a crowd.

“I mean, how barbaric! Well, you know what? People in Europe, in other countries, they’re thinking that same thing about the U.S.,” Martínez said. “And the U.S. is not barbaric, and Florida is not barbaric. It just needs to evolve. It just needs to grow.”

theguardian.com/uk-news/2026/nov/12/two-.headline: Two men found guilty of helping Iran try to ‘eliminate’ UK-based journalists
theguardian.com/uk-news/2026/nov/12/two-.author: Rajeev Syal

paragraphs.text: Two men of Iranian origin who were hired through social media as part of a plan to “eliminate” journalists in the UK have been found guilty of assisting Tehran’s intelligence services.
Mostafa Sepahvand, 41, and Farhad Javadi Manesh, 46, carried out surveillance and reconnaissance between August 2024 and March last year in an attempt to inflict violence on “subjects” in the UK.

These subjects included two journalists for the London-based Persian broadcaster Iran International, Mojtaba Pourmohsen and Kambiz Hosseini, and a founder member of UK Lawyers for Israel, Jonathan Turner.

The defendants visited addresses linked to their targets, took photos and videos and used platforms such as ChatGPT to research them online. They appear to be part of a growing new tactic used by hostile states in which “proxies” are hired to work for foreign security forces, with often little idea who they are targeting or why.

Last month the Norwegian teenager Johannes Natland, 19, was jailed for life after he agreed to carry out a hit in Huddersfield for the Foxtrot Network, a Swedish organised crime group backed by the Iranian regime.
The Iranian men came to the UK illegally between 2016 and 2022 – Sepahvand in the back of a lorry and Manesh in a small boat.

Sepahvand used the AI platform ChatGPT to find the home address of Pourmohsen, who worked for the London-based Persian language broadcaster Iran International. He hoped to be paid £150,000 to carry out a violent attack and help to “finish off” Pourmohsen.
Sepahvand chatted on WhatsApp to his handler, an Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps commander called Amin, as he spied on Pourmohsen in December 2024, Woolwich crown court heard.
Amin wrote: “These are new pictures of the guy/bloke.”
Sepahvand replied: “I’ll go tomorrow.”
Referring to a picture, Amin said: “And that dot is their office?”
Sepahvand said: “Love you brother, I’ll go there tomorrow.”
The pair also discussed surveillance of the Iranian satirist Kambiz Hosseini, who eventually had to leave home because of the threats made against him.

Bill Emlyn Jones KC, prosecuting, said Iran and its rulers did not and could not tolerate dissent. “One organisation critical to the regime, and therefore very much in its sights, is Iran International, a news organisation which has come under particular attack because of its explicit support for opposition groups and its editorial stance, which is anti-Islamic Republic of Iran.
“Eliminating hostile, critical or dissident actors overseas is a staple policy of the Islamic republic. Together, the defendants were engaged in what is very obviously a form of spying,” Jones said.

Hosseini, 51, had to leave home and stop work as a standup comedian as a result of the threats he received. He was sent a message with a picture of his car saying the next time he started the engine it would blow up. Hosseini’s family in Iran also received threats, and his family had to leave the country.
The court heard Sepahvand had been convicted of theft in Iran and was drawn into the plan to “eliminate” dissidents in the hope of reducing his criminal record.
He told his Iranian handlers he was prepared to escalate from surveillance to violence, the court heard.

He hoped to receive a final payment of £150,000 for “finishing the job”, a reference to killing one of the journalists, the court was told. “If the person [the target] is inside, they pay the £150,000, and I’ll finish him off,” said Sepahvand in a voice note.
Sepahvand claimed his family was being threatened and that he never intended to go through with the hit. He also denied plotting to kill Turner.
Manesh claimed he took a picture of the Iran International site because it was “a beautiful building” and did not know they were working with the Iranian intelligence services.

Earlier this year, Roman Lavrynovych, 22, and Stanislav Carpiuc, 27, were jailed at the Old Bailey for seven and two years respectively for arson attacks on property connected to Keir Starmer. An anonymous Russian-speaking figure named El Money had recruited Lavrynovych and Carpiuc on Telegram.

Last year, six Britons were jailed for their parts in a Russian-ordered arson attack on a London warehouse providing aid to Ukraine. The ringleader, Dylan Earl, was recruited by the Wagner group, a mercenary organisation that acts on behalf of the Russian state.

Sepahvand was convicted by the jury of assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct. Manesh was convicted of assisting a foreign intelligence service, but cleared of preparatory conduct.
Shapoor Noori, 57, of Ealing, was cleared by the jury of assisting a foreign intelligence service and preparatory conduct.
Sepahvand, Manesh and Noori had claimed asylum in the UK and received temporary leave to remain. None of them had regular full-time employment.
It is understood they met by chance and were then directed by Sepahvand and his contacts in Iran. There appeared to be no evidence of any wider plot.
Mrs Justice Cheema-Grubb remanded Sepahvand and Manesh before sentencing at the Old Bailey on 17 December.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/12/san.headline: San Francisco approves first gay bathhouse since AIDS epidemic
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/12/san.author: N. Kirkpatrick

paragraphs.text: San Francisco, the crusading city for gay rights and sexual liberation, closed its last legal bathhouses during the ravages of the AIDS epidemic.
Now, for the first time in nearly 40 years, the city has authorized a new gay bathhouse.

The San Francisco Planning Commission approved permits last week for Sanctum Baths. The plans call for the conversion of a two-story, 7,516-square-foot commercial building into a bathhouse and “adult sex venue” in The Hub neighborhood, next to the historic Leather & LGBTQ Cultural District. Backers of the project, first reported by the Bay Area Reporter, expect it to open by the end of next year.
Sanctum is first adult bath to be approved since the San Francisco Board of Supervisors rescinded its AIDS-era ban on them in 2020, according to the San Francisco Chronicle.

San Francisco had as many as 20 baths at their peak in 1982, according to Jacob Binder writing in the Berkeley Journal of Gender, Law & Justice. The spaces, which typically included saunas and steam rooms, served as gathering spaces and safe havens for sexual contact without harassment by law enforcement. In the 1970s, they became political symbols for the gay liberation movement.

“The baths were hallowed sites of queer community-building and epicenters of the city’s sexual subcultures,” Binder wrote. At first the bathhouses had few regulations or legal restrictions and hosted as many as 12,000 patrons a month. But the AIDS epidemic devastated the lives of gay men and became a new catalyst of prejudice against them. A “mix of caution, declining business, and government persecution” closed all the bathhouses by 1987.

Now, as new drugs for the treatment of HIV and AIDS have vastly reduced the transmission of the virus and the lethality of the disease, other cities such as Minneapolis and San Diego have rolled back AIDS-era policies.
“For decades sex positive spaces were systematically stigmatized and forced out of existence,” Jonathan Ohene, a local business owner and cultural district board member said in public comment.
”Approving this project is a vital step towards healing that painful chapter of our history," he said. “It’s exactly what our neighborhood needs.”

theguardian.com/sport/2026/nov/12/lewis-.headline: Lewis Hamilton says ‘Israel’s genocide in Gaza is appalling’ after Rafah visit
theguardian.com/sport/2026/nov/12/lewis-.author: Guardian sport

paragraphs.text: Formula One driver Lewis Hamilton said on Wednesday that Israel must allow aid ⁠trucks into Gaza, a day after he visited the Rafah border crossing in Egypt.

Hamilton, a seven-time ⁠world champion, arrived ⁠in El Arish on Tuesday, where he was briefed on how aid is prepared and coordinated before it ⁠is sent into Gaza, as he toured the Rafah crossing and the Egyptian Red Crescent’s aid warehouses.

He has frequently posted on social media about children killed in Israeli airstrikes in Gaza and called for a ceasefire. A ceasefire agreement reached last year has halted major combat operations in Gaza, but the amount of aid reaching the territory continues to fall far short of the agreed-upon minimum of 600 trucks a day.

“The past ⁠three years of Israel’s genocide in Gaza is appalling. It’s an injustice for people to be denied their freedom, their safety and their dignity. No human being should be treated as though their life matters less,” the Ferrari driver wrote on Instagram.
Israel strongly denies accusations of genocide and says its military campaign in Gaza targets Hamas militants.
Hamilton described seeing food trucks lined up and ready to go at the border that were regularly held up or faced major delays.

“I saw walls stretching for miles, built to keep them in. Standing there, outside what felt like an open-air prison, all I could think about was getting in to help,” he said in the post. “At the Rafah border, I saw food trucks lined up ready to go, but they’re regularly not allowed in or face major delays. The first driver in line that I spoke to had already been waiting over 12 hours. At the nearby logistics centre, I saw the hard work of the aid workers, but I also saw what gets rejected for crazy reasons. Sleeping bags, first aid kits, medical equipment, wheelchairs even footballs for kids.

“Israel needs to fulfil its obligations under the ceasefire and let the aid trucks in. I know so many people feel that same helplessness. That same need to do something rather than just watch. No excuse. I don’t want ⁠us to get used to their suffering. I don’t want us to look away.”
Hamilton, 41, is an advocate for humanitarian causes. In 2021 he founded Mission 44, a charity that supports young people and works to improve their access to education and employment.
“I think we need to make sure we’re pushing to free Congo, free Sudan, free Syria, free Palestine,” Hamilton said last month. “I think there’s a lot of peace that I’m hoping we get to at some stage.”
At the crossing on Tuesday, Hamilton greeted aid workers with “Assalamu alaikum” a widely used Arabic greeting meaning “peace be upon you”. He shook hands and briefly spoke to workers and officials.

Hamilton is fourth in the drivers’ championship. Mercedes’ Kimi Antonelli has won the title with three races to go. The Las Vegas Grand Prix is 21 November before the Qatar Grand Prix on 29 November and the season-ending Abu Dhabi Grand Prix on 6 December.

washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/12/h.headline: Home sales in worst slump since the aftermath of the Great Recession
washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/12/h.author: Rachel Lerman

paragraphs.text: The housing market slumped further in October as U.S. home sales fell again, hitting the lowest level in more than 16 years.

Mortgage rates have soared past 7 percent while home prices stay stubbornly high, keeping buyers on the sidelines and discouraging would-be sellers from listing their homes and moving. Sellers don’t want to give up their lower mortgage rates, so they don’t have much incentive to drop prices enough to attract buyers.

“People can’t afford the price that people are trying to sell their houses for, with mortgage rates what they are,” said Richard Green, director of University of Southern California’s Lusk Center for Real Estate.

Existing-home sales fell to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of 3.75 million last month, according to a report from the National Association of Realtors. That’s a 5.5 percent decrease from September and the lowest level since August 2010, when the economy was recovering from the Great Recession.
“Home buying is difficult when mortgage rates have climbed to their highest levels since 2000, aside from a single month in 2023,” NAR Chief Economist Lawrence Yun said in a statement.

At the same time, home prices are still increasing for existing homes, rising 0.4 percent from a year ago, according to NAR. Home prices are significantly elevated from their pre-pandemic levels, further discouraging buyers from jumping into the market.

The housing market fell into disarray during the Great Recession amid the collapse of a housing bubble and a subprime mortgage crisis. Several factors are different now, said Jessica Lautz, deputy chief economist at NAR. Distressed home sales are only a tiny part of the market. People are hanging onto their homes because of low mortgage rates and because rising values mean they’re building wealth.
Housing prices are rising on a year-over-year basis, but not as fast as inflation.
“That means people do have buying power, but it really comes down to ability to find a home they can afford,” Lautz said.

With rising rates and costs, buying a median-priced home now means shelling out far more — an estimated $2,468 per month, or an 85 percent increase over what typical homeowners pay, according to a new report from Realtor.com.

The typical current homeowner with a mortgage spends $1,332 in monthly principal and interest and holds a 4 percent rate. Realtor.com’s calculations assume new buyers pay a 14.3 percent down payment and hold a mortgage rate of 7.32 percent.

For years, Americans have been reluctant to sell their homes and buy new ones, even if they are looking to expand, downsize or relocate, because they have locked in relatively low mortgage rates. Rates have been on the rise this year, as the Federal Reserve has started increasing borrowing costs, and Treasury yields surge under geopolitical uncertainty.

That has kept inventory low and some would-be buyers on the sidelines. Though that dynamic has started to ease slightly, and inventory has picked up a bit, Realtor.com’s report shows that moving still often means taking on a significantly larger monthly payment.

theguardian.com/books/2026/nov/12/zimbab.headline: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story
theguardian.com/books/2026/nov/12/zimbab.author: Rachel Savage

paragraphs.text: The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.
Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.

Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara said the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated.

The Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement: “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.”
She said: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation.

“Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama said. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.”

Kundizeza, who had strongly denied using generative AI to write the story, said he was “relieved” that the allegations had been dismissed after the investigation. “It was not necessary in the first place, I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey,” he said.
Vara’s article prompted outrage online, with many claiming that Black writers, and Africans in particular, were being unfairly singled out by allegations of the use of AI.
Associated Press contributed to this report

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/12/thursd.headline: Thursday briefing: What we do (and don’t) know about Alice Huang and the Nvidia affair
theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/12/thursd.author: Hettie O'Brien

paragraphs.text: Good morning. Espionage is supposed to be a secretive business, and spies are supposed to be virtually invisible. That hasn’t been the case for Alice Huang, the mysterious Shanghai executive who formed a romantic relationship with Jensen Huang, the founder of Nvidia, one of America’s most powerful tech companies.

Many questions have arisen since it emerged that US intelligence believes that Huang (no relation of Jensen’s) is an asset recruited by the Chinese intelligence services to spy on behalf of Beijing. This morning’s newsletter explains what we know about the story, and what it tells us about the effectiveness of Chinese espionage. That’s after the headlines.
Five big stories

• UK | Ministers are considering changing the law to force the entertainment industry to better protect women and children in the wake of the revelations over David Walliams and the conviction of Russell Brand.
• Climate | The UK government has appointed the world’s first special representative for climate security, in the strongest sign yet of fears that climate breakdown will bring chaos to the country.

• US midterms | Democrat Scott Colom has become the first Black senator in Mississippi to be elected since Reconstruction, in a stunning upset after more than a week of vote counting in one of the country’s most reliably red states.

• Europe | Millions of people across Spain have joined the country’s first general strike in 14 years, setting up picket lines to protest against soaring housing prices before an election in which the far right could be catapulted into power.
• Technology | Police officers risk arresting innocent people, especially from ethnic minorities, if they treat inaccurate facial recognition data as evidence, an official report has found.
In depth: Everything we know (or don’t) about the Nvidia affair

Last month, the New York Times reported that Jensen Huang had formed a “close relationship” with Alice Huang, the former executive of a Singapore-based computing company, Megaspeed. Megaspeed is a customer of Nvidia; it buys the extremely valuable chips they produce, which are essential for powering AI, and rents computing space to Chinese companies. The US government had already been investigating whether Megaspeed could be flouting US restrictions and smuggling chips into China – allegations that both Nvidia and Megaspeed deny.

US intelligence officials, who had been conducting surveillance on Alice Huang, eventually concluded she was a Chinese intelligence asset who had been passing on information to Beijing. The intelligence behind this assessment is classified, so we don’t know exactly what they found – or which intelligence body was conducting the surveillance. Nvidia said Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual or unexpected”, but on Sunday, Huang admitted in a letter to his employees that he had been having an affair. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children,” he said, adding that he was “deeply sorry”.

Nvidia’s valuation is inextricably linked to Huang. By yesterday, $430bn (5.5%) had been wiped off its share price, and in the early hours of this morning, that figure ballooned to about $600bn following reports that Nvidia’s board was deciding whether to oust Huang (you can follow the latest on that here). The company has appointed outside counsel to review the pair’s relationship and says it has no reason to believe that secrets or national security were compromised.

The most interesting aspects of this story are the questions we can’t (yet) answer. Did Nvidia’s board know that US intelligence suspected Alice Huang was a spy? What evidence led US intelligence to conclude she was spying for China? What information could she have passed to Beijing? And …
Who is Alice Huang?

Reporters and sleuths on Chinese social media have been trying to get to the bottom of who the Megaspeed chief really is. On Tuesday, the Financial Times published an interesting report (£) about Alice Huang’s backstory. She was born in the rural area of Hunan, worked as a journalist at China’s state broadcaster, then at HSBC and the investment bank Citic Securities. In 2015, she joined an investment management company Hexi.

There, she met financier Kang Wei. The two became romantically involved, and together they reinvented themselves as AI entrepreneurs. In 2023, Huang and her business partners acquired Megaspeed, a Singaporean subsidiary of a Chinese gaming company, which she and Wei aimed to turn into a datacentre business. According to the FT’s report, the two pitched investors on their ability to secure access to Nvidia chips.

Nobody knows exactly when Jensen Huang met Alice Huang, when their relationship became romantic, or what information she might have passed to Beijing while it was going on. The earliest picture of them together is at an after-party following a tech trade show in Taipei, taken in 2024. As Aisha Down and Dan Milmo pointed out earlier this week, Jensen Huang is close to Donald Trump, so it’s possible that Alice Huang could have gained glimpses into US AI policy as it was being formed, into Trump’s thinking on AI, or into Nvidia’s company strategy. But without seeing the evidence, all this is speculation.
What does this reveal about Chinese espionage?

The US has been historically cautious about allowing AI chips to end up in Chinese hands. In 2022, Joe Biden’s administration introduced the Chips and Science Act, which restricted the sale of US chips in China, banning the export of most Nvidia chips. “The Chinese have a very strong pedigree for industrial espionage and copying other nations’ technologies,” Steve Tsang, the director of the SOAS China Institute, tells me. “They’ve been doing this for decades. And now it’s no longer engines they’re interested in, but AI.”

Both the US and China have an interest in gathering intelligence about each other’s AI firms. What’s more remarkable is the possibility that the Chinese spy agency, the MSS, could have recruited Alice Huang as a “honeytrap” to ensnare Jensen Huang – a method fraught with risk, which seems more reminiscent of 1970s spy fiction than contemporary counterintelligence (China, for its part, has rejected claims that Alice Huang was a spy).

“The facts clearly aren’t established, but it seems more likely that if Alice Huang was working for Beijing, the MSS would have recruited her after they became aware of her relationship with Huang, not before,” Nigel Inkster, the former director of operations and intelligence for the British Secret Intelligence Service, tells me.

China has built a large intelligence gathering operation: the MSS is now bigger than the CIA, and various national security laws mean that Chinese nationals can be required to provide assistance to the Chinese state. “You have a lot of people who can be co-opted into intelligence gathering, all of whom can be tasked with different requirements,” Inkster says. “Business delegations travelling abroad can be tasked with gathering information. So can visiting academics.”
“The big question, to my mind, is whether the Chinese intelligence agencies have actually been willing to deliver unwelcome information to the party leadership,” Inkster adds.
What approach has the US taken?

Jensen Huang is the most influential figure in the US AI industry outside major labs such as Anthropic, and has cultivated a close relationship with Donald Trump. He’s successfully lobbied the Trump administration to loosen regulations on AI and roll back restrictions on the sales of Nvidia’s chips to China (last year, Trump controversially approved the sale of Nvidia’s H200 chips directly to China in exchange for the federal government taking a 25% cut). Huang was present at the White House twice last month: once for a state dinner with Xi Jinping, and again for a meeting of tech and AI executives.

Huang’s close relationship with Trump could help explain why the president has so far played down concerns about Chinese espionage, appearing remarkably ambivalent about the recent allegations. The president was reportedly briefed last year about US intelligence conducting surveillance on Alice Huang, and in spring this year, his secretary of state, Marco Rubio, supervised the drafting of a classified memo warning that Jensen Huang was in a relationship with a Chinese spy. In May, Trump issued a last-minute invitation to Jensen Huang to board Air Force One in Alaska and join a delegation of executives bound to China. A US government official told reporters at the New York Times that when Rubio learned that Huang would be joining the trip in Alaska, he briefed Trump on the memo.

But on Monday, Trump, who is due to meet Xi Jinping later this month, said he had not known at the time of the trip about Huang’s relationship. He said the FBI had been investigating a matter relating to Huang, and defended the Nvidia CEO, describing him as an “honourable guy” who “built a great American company”.
What else we’ve been reading

• I loved Arifa Akbar’s story on theatregoers donning costumes to watch their favourite shows, though I’m not entirely convinced that wearing feline ears to watch Cats absolves her from “veering into fandom” … Michael

• Joanna Moorhead uncovers the growing disquiet surrounding a little known collection of Indigenous artefacts handed over to powerful Catholic missionaries and now held at the Vatican Museums in Rome. Libby

• Martin Lewis writes about his Small Ideas Initiative – quick fixes to make Britain work better, suggested by the public – with infectious enthusiasm. I just hope the government reads to the bit where he reminds us small fixes have to work alongside bigger structural change. Libby
• Providence, Rhode Island, has become the second US city to divest Israel (Somerville, Massachusetts was first) in a landslide vote. Claire Wang has the details. Michael
• Wire in, as they say in Scotland: our Comfort Eating podcast is back with a new host, the magnificent Siobhán McSweeney. Libby
Sport

Football | Harry Kane says he still feels a pressure to prove his worth, even as he prepares to become England’s most capped men’s player, as he outlined his determination to set records that will stand for years.
Cricket | White-ball tour begins in Perth on Friday, but there is only one story in Australian cricket and the tourists are not it.

Fifa | A complaint has been filed to the United States Internal Revenue Service calling for an investigation into claims an individual on the Fifa payroll was working privately as a housekeeper for Gianni Infantino.
The front pages
“TV industry must tackle abuse or face crackdown, ministers warn”, is the Guardian’s splash today. Metro writes “Another mystery star bids to block claims”.
The Times writes “Milburn: Cut sick benefits to force young into work”, and the i Paper has “Under-25s with ADHD won’t get £217-a-month benefits in new welfare reforms”.

The FT leads with “Democrats pledge to expose ‘absolute avalanche of corruption’ under Trump”, the Mail has “Even Cameron tells PM: Don’t rejoin the EU”, and the Telegraph writes “SAS issues warning over troop witch hunts”. The Mirror says “Not even a bed for an OAP with cancer”, and the Express has “‘Sanctuary in nature helped me to recover’”.
The Latest
Trump’s $10bn BBC battle: judge rules lawsuit can go ahead

Donald Trump’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC has been granted permission to proceed, after the corporation’s attempt to get it dismissed was thrown out by a Trump-appointed Florida judge. The case focuses on an edit in a 2024 Panorama documentary that spliced two comments together that were made by the president during a rally before the January 6 Capitol riots, for which the BBC has apologised. With the lawsuit now set to continue, what’s at stake for press freedom? Lucy Hough speaks to global editor, Devika Bhat.
Cartoon of the day | Nicola Jennings
The Upside
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad
Researchers from the Hoag Family Cancer Institute have made a potential breakthrough in the early diagnosis of ovarian cancer – a disease often detected after it has spread.

For decades, efforts to detect the cancer earlier have focused on finding smaller tumours. “We asked … what if we could identify the earliest molecular warning signs before invasive cancer even develops?” said study leader Rajan Gogna.

Ovarian cancer often begins with microscopic changes in the lining of the fallopian tubes. The study found that women experiencing these changes have elevated levels of a molecule called Tu-Stroma in their blood.
The study’s co-author Dr Esha Madan says the discovery “could transform how we approach prevention”.

Bored at work?
And finally, the Guardian’s puzzles are here to keep you entertained throughout the day. Until tomorrow.

theguardian.com/news/2026/nov/11/harvard.headline: Two skulls likely belonging to enslaved people returned to Brazil after Harvard used them in eugenics studies
theguardian.com/news/2026/nov/11/harvard.author: Tiago Rogero

paragraphs.text: Two skulls, including that of a man believed to have taken part in Brazil’s greatest slave revolt but whose remains were taken to the United States and used in racist eugenics studies at Harvard University, were repatriated on Wednesday.

The remains had been outside Brazil since the 19th century. One was taken about 190 years ago from Salvador, the capital of the state of Bahia; the other, about 160 years ago, from Rio de Janeiro – and were welcomed back in moving, subdued ceremonies in both cities.
The skulls are believed to have belonged to Africans or Afro-Brazilians in the country that received more enslaved Africans than any other during the transatlantic slave trade.

Each was brought back in a padded box inside a reinforced suitcase, carried on flights by Brazilian diplomats after a four-year campaign to recover the remains from Harvard’s Peabody Museum of Archaeology and Ethnology in the US.
Brazilian researchers from local universities will now try to learn more about who the two individuals were.

The skulls will not be displayed in museums or have their images released, and the Brazilian government has pledged that they will be buried with funeral rites as soon as the identification process is complete.

“It’s very important to restore the dignity of these people, which was taken from them in life and in death,” said Carolina Dias dos Reis, a government official who travelled to Boston to sign the agreement with Harvard.

The existence of the skulls was revealed in 2022, and Brazilian researchers sought their repatriation from Harvard, but said they faced a drawn-out process that only moved forward after the Brazilian government became involved in late 2024.
In recent months, concerns grew that Donald Trump’s sometimes hostile behaviour towards his Brazilian counterpart, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, could derail the repatriation. But everything worked out.

“We need to recover our past as a country, however difficult and violent it was, so that we can understand what we are living through in the present: the consequences and scars of structural racism,” added Reis.

Slavery was abolished in 1888, but nearly a century and a half later, Afro-Brazilians make up the majority of the population while occupying the bottom of every socioeconomic indicator, dominating the statistics on hunger, poverty, gender-based violence and victims of homicides committed by criminals or the police.

During the repatriation ceremony in Rio de Janeiro, Ivanir dos Santos, a history professor and a cleric of the Afro-Brazilian religion Candomblé, poured a glass of water on to the ground as researchers received the suitcase.

“It was a ritual act because you cannot deal with the remains of our ancestors without paying reverence to them. This is not a research object … for us, that person is still alive in memory and as our ancestor,” he said.

It is not precisely known who the skulls belonged to. The one taken to Salvador is believed to have belonged to a man who took part in the most significant urban slave revolt in Brazilian history, in 1835, when about 600 African Muslims attempted to seize control of what was then the country’s second most important city. They were ultimately defeated by police, who killed 70 rebels.
The man died at a hospital, and a US diplomat, Gideon T Snow, is believed to have sent the skull to Boston.
The Bahia Islamic Cultural Centre, one of the most active campaigners for its repatriation, has named the man Arakunrin, meaning brother in Yoruba.

Even less is known about the other person: initially, only that they were “an individual … exhumed from the ‘streets of Rio de Janeiro’” in the 1860s. Brazilian government officials, however, said on Wednesday that Harvard researchers had told them that some features – including that the skull was smaller than that of an adult man but larger than that of a child – suggested it may have belonged to a woman.

Bruno Veras, a historian who was part of the group that closely followed the repatriation, cross-referenced diaries, letters and maps of the city and believes the skull may have been taken from a cemetery for newly arrived Africans who either did not survive the long Atlantic crossing or died soon after disembarking.

The person believed to have taken it to the US was Walter Hunnewell, a student from a wealthy Boston family. He was part of an expedition led by the Harvard professor Louis Agassiz, who was in Brazil trying to document physical types to support his racist theories.
“To steal a skull and take it to another country was violent even in the context of racist research,” said Veras.

Researchers in forensic anthropology will now try to confirm the sex of the individuals and other information through measurements of the skulls – the one in Salvador is complete, while the one in Rio is missing its jaw – and microscopic analyses. If necessary, they will seek authorisation to carry out genetic or dating tests.

“This history of slavery cannot be undone,” said Irina Feisthauer Silveira, a diplomat who carried one of the skulls. “But acknowledging the mistakes of the past with transparency is a first step towards building a more equal, just and less violent future.”

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/11/red-br.headline: Ex-member of radical Marxist group scales balcony, escapes house arrest in Argentina
theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/11/red-br.author: Facundo Iglesia

paragraphs.text: A 74-year-old former member of Italy’s radical Marxist group the Red Brigades has escaped from house arrest in Argentina, the country’s security ministry confirmed on Wednesday, after he reportedly hid his ankle monitor inside a tube of pork and lowered himself from a fifth-floor balcony.

Authorities placed Leonardo Bertulazzi under house arrest in Buenos Aires in 2024, prior to his extradition to Italy to serve a 27-year prison sentence. He had received the sentence in 1987 for joining a subversive association and belonging to an armed group.

After years on the run, Bertulazzi was first arrested by Argentine authorities in 2002. He was freed a few months later and secured refugee status in 2004, but was arrested again in 2024 after it was revoked.
On Wednesday, Argentina’s security ministry offered a $13,000 reward for information leading to Bertulazzi’s recapture after he slipped out of detention.

The fugitive held a senior position in the Red Brigades, a radical Marxist organization responsible for attacks from 1969 to 1980, dubbed Italy’s “Years of Lead”. The group most notoriously kidnapped and assassinated former prime minister Aldo Moro in 1978.
Security footage showed Bertulazzi dropping from a building into a public road as cars drove past.
A detective tracking the former member of the Red Brigades reportedly told La Nación that Bertulazzi rappelled down from the fifth floor using a harness.

“First, he removed his electronic ankle monitor and placed it in a tube filled with pork, along with a blood pressure monitor to maintain the temperature. He then climbed on to a roof and, using a rope, lowered himself five meters until he jumped onto a vacant lot behind the building where he lived, and then scaled a metal gate to reach the street,” the detective said, according to the publication.
The footage, which indicated the time was 6.01am on 10 November, showed a possibly shaken Bertulazzi sitting down to rest for a few moments.
Police noticed his ankle monitor had stopped transmitting movement data and headed to the house, where they found the device discarded and Bertulazzi nowhere to be found.
Argentina approved his extradition to Italy in July 2025 after the country’s supreme court rejected a final appeal.

theguardian.com/uk-news/2026/nov/11/arge.headline: Argentinian lawyer mocks UK’s sovereignty claim in Falklands oil case
theguardian.com/uk-news/2026/nov/11/arge.author: Daniel Boffey

paragraphs.text: Britain should not be permitted to act as a 17th-century colonial power treating the waters around the Falkland Islands as a Dominium maris Britannici, Argentina has told an international tribunal.

Marcelo Kohen, representing Argentina at a hearing in Hamburg, mocked Britain for apparently believing in the historic doctrine that the British crown has sovereignty over expansive parts of the oceans.

Argentina has applied to the international tribunal for the law of the sea (Itlos) for a ruling that would force Britain to suspend the drilling for oil in the North Basin of the Falkland Islands ahead of further arbitration.
The Sea Lion oilfield is about 130 miles north of the Falkland Islands, a British overseas territory over which Argentina has a longstanding sovereignty claim.

Argentina’s president, Javier Milei, reportedly shared among his cabinet on Tuesday a photograph of the Argentinian legal team in Hamburg, describing it as “tremendous”, adding that “we are working on the Falklands issue like no one else in history”.

Addressing the tribunal on the second day of hearings, Kohen said that the dispute over the archipelago of 700 islands in the south Atlantic – known in Argentina as the Malvinas – did not mean that the area was a “legal black hole” and that the UK could do as it wished with its natural resources.

“The fact that the parties dispute sovereignty does not turn the areas surrounding the Malvinas into some kind of Dominium maris Britannici,” he said. “We are not in the 17th century … We are in an era where we should put an end to the last vestiges of colonialism.”

Ellie Reeves, the attorney general for England and Wales, told the tribunal’s panel of judges on Tuesday that Argentina was seeking to further its sovereignty ambitions by applying for suspension of the drilling.

She claimed that such a move would kill the Sea Lion project, with “disastrous consequences” for the Falkland Islanders and the companies involved. The UK claimed that the tribunal, which adjudicates over maritime matters, does not have jurisdiction to wade into matters of sovereignty.

Kohen, switching from French to English, said the UK had failed to mention in its submissions the “elephant in the room” or the “whale in the bathtub”. The UN regarded the Falkland Islands as a non-self-governing territory, he said, and had called in 1976 for both sides to refrain from taking decisions that would unilaterally change the situation before the sovereignty dispute was settled.

The exploitation of hydrocarbons would put the islands among the “highest ranks of wealth just below the principality of Monaco” while depriving Argentina of its rights to those resources, Kohen told the tribunal.

Argentina’s legal team claimed that suspension of the drilling, which is due to start in March next year and which could double the GDP of the islands, was urgent given the irreparable damage to Argentina’s rights.

In his closing remarks to the panel of 22 judges, Mario Oyarzábal, a legal adviser to Argentina’s ministry of foreign affairs, said they rejected the UK’s attempt to characterise the proceedings as an attempt to litigate the sovereignty dispute.

He said: “The question before this tribunal is a much narrower one: whether, while the underlying dispute remains unresolved, the UK may unilaterally authorise or carry out new drilling for the exploitation of hydrocarbons in the disputed maritime area.”

Sam Wordsworth KC, responding for the UK, said there was nothing in the convention on the law of the seas, over which Itlos has jurisdiction, which obliged a state not to “aggravate” a sovereignty dispute and that the UN resolution cited by Kohen as the “elephant in the room” was not legally binding.

The UK further claims there is no need for urgent suspension of drilling as oil extraction would not take place until 2028, before which an arbitration panel would have come to a conclusion on Argentina’s wider claim that its rights have been breached.

During his recent speech at the UN general assembly, Milei described the reclaiming of the Falklands as a “national cause”. Argentina invaded the islands in 1982 on the orders of the dictator Gen Leopoldo Galtieri. The 74-day conflict ended with the surrender of the Argentinian forces and cost the lives of 649 of its military personnel, 255 British military personnel and three Falkland Islanders.
Itlos is expected to make its ruling on Argentina’s case on 28 November.

wsj.com/economy/the-global-economy-looks.headline: The Global Economy Looks Vulnerable to an AI Bust
wsj.com/economy/the-global-economy-looks.author: Kanebridge

paragraphs.text: ’s shores. S. this year but for the whole global economy.

The Silicon Valley bounty is spreading as other economies join the party. Assembly hubs such as Vietnam and Mexico are seeing exports take off. Malaysia, Thailand and Australia are building data centers of their own.
Europe’s industrial giants are supplying the power and cooling systems that make the AI revolution possible. S. midterm elections shows this growing dependency on Silicon Valley has a downside.

A slowdown in AI investment would punish exports in economies that in many cases show few other signs of growth. A sustained stock slide would crush mom-and-pop investors all over the world who have piled into technology stocks in anticipation of bumper returns. Overstretched budgets mean governments have limited room to respond with more spending.

Economists calculating what might happen if the pace of investment slows or the AI boom turns to full-blown bust say the only real question is how severe the global consequences will be. “There is very little that can be done to prevent a global recession should the AI boom collapse,” said Frederic Neumann, chief Asia economist at HSBC in Hong Kong. S.

midterm elections sparked concerns that Congress will hit the brakes on data-center development. The latest upset in the industry has been the alleged spying scandal engulfing Nvidia, the linchpin of the AI ecosystem because of its deep pockets and advanced chips. Stocks have clawed back some losses in recent days, moves that suggest many investors think the selloff is overdone.

Even so, key stocks and indexes remain well below recent peaks. The tech-heavy Nasdaq index closed Wednesday 8% below its year-to-date high. Japan’s Nikkei index is down 16%, and South Korea’s Kospi, home to major memory-chip maker Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix, is down 43%.

For now, the stock-market gyrations haven’t spilled over into real economic activity, with global data pointing to the AI boom still going strong. Jensen Huang is under scrutiny after an affair with an alleged spy. Sean Gallup/Getty Images Asian economies are still seeing bumper export growth, with many of the gains driven by surging prices for chips and other hardware.

China’s exports were up 35% year-over-year in October, according to figures from data provider CEIC. South Korea’s were up 93%, with Japan, Taiwan, Singapore and others also posting double-digit gains. Economists at Capital Economics said the export bonanza means global trade is on track for its best spell of annual growth this year since the days of hyperglobalization in the early 1990s, excluding the big rebounds after Covid-19 and the 2008-09 financial crisis.
S. spending on data centers. China, South Korea and other major economies are beset by weak consumption, meaning a drop-off in trade would have an outsize hit on growth.

Political and regulatory hurdles could drag on data-center investment. So, too, could rising interest rates or disappointments on earnings if AI firms’ revenues fail to keep up with outlays. The AI splurge already eclipses past infrastructure booms such as the railroads, and even without external pressure it might struggle to maintain that breakneck rate of growth.

As data-center investment slows, “AI capex will turn from a major prop to a drag on world trade,” Marcel Thieliant, head of Asia-Pacific at Capital Economics, said in a report. Some economists have looked back to the dot-com bubble of the early 2000s as a yardstick to measure the possible costs to the global economy of an AI blowup. S.
S. consumer spending and crushing imports. S.

midterm elections. S. imports of IT-related equipment fell 55% in two years from their mid-2000 peak, according to Oxford Economics—a drop that hit Asian and other economies that were suppliers of the goods.

Global trade plummeted, and world growth in 2001 collapsed to just 2%, consistent with a global recession. The globalized financing of the AI boom would in a bust spread financial pain around the world, adding to the damage from a steep fall in trade. Gaurav Ganguly, head of international economics at Moody’s Analytics in London, said the world would struggle to absorb a sharp AI stock slide on top of an oil shock, tariffs and rising interest rates.
“The result could be a severe economic shock with global recessionary consequences,” he said.

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/11/ecuado.headline: Killing of journalist underscores deteriorating conditions in Ecuador
theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/11/ecuado.author: Tiago Rogero

paragraphs.text: Tomás Beltrán was manoeuvring his car into his garage on Sunday night when the Ecuadorian journalist was shot dead.

Beltrán ran a Facebook page with news about Calceta, a small city in the province of Manabí, whose Pacific coastline has made it a key flashpoint in the gang warfare over drug trafficking routes that has transformed one of Latin America’s safest countries into one of its most violent.

Police and the public prosecutor’s office have not said much about the case, and little was known about the killers except that they were armed and then fled the scene. It was also unclear whether the crime was linked to Beltrán’s work, though he had previously reported allegations of corruption involving local authorities.

Regardless, many press freedom groups already cite his murder as the latest example of how conditions for journalists have deteriorated dramatically in Ecuador. Six journalists were killed in the country last year alone.
Artur Romeu, Reporters Without Borders’ Latin America director, said in a statement that months ago Beltrán had told the organisation “about his fears and the threats he was receiving”.

“We took part in efforts to get him to safety,” he said, adding that Beltrán had been placed in a protection programme run by the public prosecutor’s office, although it was not known whether that protection was still in place when he was killed.

“Reporters Without Borders calls on the public prosecutor’s office to investigate as a priority whether there is a link to his journalistic work, identify any possible masterminds and protect his family and colleagues,” said Romeu.

The Ecuadorian civil society organisation Fundación Periodistas Sin Cadenas (FPSC) reported that at least 19 journalists have had to go into exile since gang violence exploded in 2023. Although Ecuador does not produce cocaine like neighbouring Colombia and Peru, it has become a major trafficking hub, particularly through the Pacific.
Journalists have received death threats with photographs of their homes and details of their routines and families.

“Practising journalism in Ecuador is now an extremely high-risk job,” said María Fernanda Almeida, a project coordinator at FPSC, adding that all of last year’s killings of journalists “remain completely unpunished”.
“And one of the many terrible effects of this violence is self-censorship: at least in the coastal provinces, colleagues no longer want to report on violence,” she added.

Almeida said another problem for journalists has been the stance of the government of the far-right president Daniel Noboa, who has responded to the surge in crime with a controversial “iron-fist” approach to the gangs, repeatedly declaring states of emergency and expanding the role of the armed forces in measures that have been widely criticised by human rights groups.

While covering military operations, reporters have had their phones confiscated, a search warrant was executed at a reporter’s home and a journalist was threatened by soldiers simply for filming them stopping university students.

There have also been several reports that Noboa, one of US president Donald Trump’s key allies in Latin America, has pressured media organisations to dismiss journalists critical of him, including the columnist Roberto Aguilar, who said he was fired from the newspaper Diario Expreso after the government reportedly threatened private advertisers with audits if they continued advertising with the outlet.
Noboa’s administration did not respond to requests for comment.
“I don’t think there is complete freedom of expression in Ecuador today,” said Almeida. “And that is very worrying because the more violence and silencing there is, the more journalism is needed.”

cnbc.com/2026/11/12/star-wars-cosm-dome-.headline: Disney's 'Star Wars' is coming to Cosm domes ahead of 50th anniversary as part of multiyear film deal
cnbc.com/2026/11/12/star-wars-cosm-dome-.author: Sarah Whitten

paragraphs.text: The Force is strong with Cosm.

On Thursday, the immersive entertainment technology company announced a new studio partnership with The Walt Disney Co. that will bring the original "Star Wars" to its domes early next year as part of a multiyear, multifilm collaboration.
The financial terms of the deal were not disclosed.
Cosm's massive concave screens will drop film fans into a galaxy far, far away starting in March, just ahead of the Academy Award-winning film's 50th anniversary in May.

"We are thrilled to add the Disney partnership," Alexis Scalice, head of Cosm Studios, told CNBC. "We do look for those opportunities of these like anniversary and commemorative moments. We look for those opportunities to celebrate with the fans, but also find this mutually beneficial partnership between both parties."

This will be Cosm's sixth theatrical collaboration with Hollywood, having already partnered with Warner Bros. to bring "The Matrix," "Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory," "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone" and "It" to its locations. The company is set to launch immersive screenings of Universal's "Shrek" in December.

Each Cosm dome has stadium-style seating, with booths and tables set on each level. The dome's width fills much of the viewers' periphery, giving the sensation that they are part of the onscreen environment.

In this case, "Star Wars" will be displayed in a large rectangle in the center of the dome while the background is transformed into the iconic planets of Tatooine and Yavin IV that are featured in the film as well as the infamous Death Star. Audiences will also see elements that will make it appear like they're traveling at lightspeed and getting trapped in an intergalactic trash compactor.
Cosm is working directly with studios Lucasfilm and Industrial Light and Magic as well as creative studio MakeMake to create the visuals and the sound mixing for the unique presentation of the film.

"We look for those moments where sound, music ... listening to Darth Vader's breath for the first time ... you feel those moments differently in an 87-foot diameter dome and 12k resolution with the sound system we have," Scalice said. "And it's one of the things that with experiential cinema and our technology that we were so excited and honestly privileged that we can take these defining moments for fans and work closely with our partners that doesn't really change the authenticity of it, it just enhances it in a different manner."

The premium experience will also be paired with a themed menu. Cosm has done this with other titles, such as "Harry Potter and the Sorcerer's Stone," serving guests throughout the screening with house-made shepherd's pie, pretzel wands with cheese dip and a box of Bertie Bott's Every Flavour Beans.

Cosm is trying to establish itself as a destination for fandom — both for sports and for film. It has a wide variety of live event offerings, which it telecasts using proprietary cameras mounted in arenas that broadcast back to the dome, as well as its expanding library of movies.
"What I love is that we really are kind of building these Cosm communities built on fandom," Scalice said. "It's the No. 1 foundation for our business."

And Star Wars is a powerful fandom. The franchise remains one of the top-ranking pieces of intellectual property across film, television and retail annually, and Disney is gearing up for a massive celebration of its semicentennial including merchandise launches, theatrical re-releases, its biannual Star Wars Celebration convention and collaborations with other brands.
Correction: This story has been updated to correct the spelling of Alexis Scalice's name.

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.headline: What’s behind Australia’s surge in teen extremism?
theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.author: Ariel Bogle

paragraphs.text: In March, Guardian Australia revealed that most people who have been charged with the new federal crime of possession of violent extremist material are under 18.
This week Australian federal police sounded the alarm about a surge in teen extremism: 32 of the 37 young people prosecuted in counter-terrorism cases since 2020 were charged in the past two years.

The growth in youth extremism is happening within a sprawling online ecosystem. My investigations have tracked the rise of online networks that urge violence and nihilism for their own sake, in which perpetrators coerce victims not much younger than themselves to commit brutal and degrading acts.

In a review of 55 youth terrorism cases, the AFP has found that the profile is mixed. They are often young men. Many have received some support or intervention for a mental health condition. Some are from stable homes, others not.
What they have most in common is that they are young people on the internet. Experts say the age of those caught up in these crimes is decreasing.
In the last month two teenagers in Darwin have been charged with collecting documents that could facilitate acts of terrorism.

The arrests came five months after another NT teenager was charged with making posts with “pro-Nazi, anti-immigration, anti-trans and white nationalist themes”. The charge sheet alleges he also possessed videos of white nationalist terrorist attacks, including the 2019 Christchurch mosque shooting and the 2022 Buffalo shooting that it partly inspired.
All matters are still before the courts.
Experts involved in harm prevention programs, including the Victoria University professor Debra Smith, have watched the age of this cohort decrease dramatically over the past decade.

Instead of considering the challenge exclusively through the lens of radicalisation, Smith says we need to recognise that some young people are being socialised and finding identity in online spaces that may appear exciting and transgressive but are ultimately harmful to themselves, and may encourage them to do harm to others.
She has seen cases where teenagers are being found with “hard drives full of what can only be described as gore”.

“It’s like getting involved in any other … unhealthy subcultural aspect of life … [such as] gangs or crime for payment,” she says. “There’s this offering of what young people can look at and get involved in that just simply wasn’t there years ago.”

The Guardian’s investigation into the growth of extremist material charges, as well as the surge of young people in Australia ensnared in sadistic online extortion and gore networks, reveals an amorphous online ecosystem in which young people may easily come into contact with extreme and violent content.

A teenager in New South Wales who pleaded guilty to possessing violent extremist material, among other charges, described how he first came across such content on TikTok when he was 14 and sought validation by talking to others online. He used ChatGPT to research the Boston marathon bomber Dzhokhar Tsarnaev as well as security arrangements at the Sydney Opera House. He was sentenced to a three-year community corrections order.
Others have told police how they became involved in so-called “gore” channels on Telegram, where more and more extreme footage – including of animal abuse – is traded.

Given the age of many involved, Levi West, a research fellow at the Australian National University, says they may be considered as much victims as perpetrators, which is a significant challenge for how authorities respond.

It’s important for parents, schools and others to think about what’s sitting underneath the uptick in numbers, he says, and not just the “algorithms”. He points to the legacies of Covid-19 and lockdowns as well as the presence of screens and digital technologies in the lives of young people.
“We are not going to arrest our way out of this problem,” West says.
With people as young as 13 before the courts, Australia must consider if authorities are taking the right approach and have the right resources for this challenge.

The Guardian’s investigation into the possession of extremist material charges in South Australia and around the country found that many of those who had been before the courts faced a range of health and social difficulties, including autism diagnoses and learning challenges – and raised questions about whether some young people understand a crime has been committed.
Smith has seen many young people caught up in these activities who come from troubled family backgrounds, while others have had every opportunity in life.

There is a role for everyone involved in caring for young people, she says, from parents and schools to sporting clubs, to recognise when someone might be engaging in harmful behaviours long before there is a risk of violence, then help them access non-punitive pathways for help.
“It’s really important to understand it through a developmental lens – that these are young people who are making decisions with young brains,” Smith says.
“My grave concern is that if we are just giving everyone terrorism offences at [age] 12, 13, 14, 15, we’re starting to label them the thing that they will become.”
• This article was amended post-publication for legal reasons.

latimes.com/opinion/story/2026-11-13/chu.headline: Column: Schumer's political era is over. Democrats need a public servant to lead them
latimes.com/opinion/story/2026-11-13/chu.author: LZ Granderson

paragraphs.text: Kennedy Brewer and Levon Brooks, two Black men wrongly convicted of murder in rural Mississippi in the early 1990s, spent a combined 30 years behind bars before DNA evidence freed them. Still, the district attorney who brought the murder charges — a white man by the name of Forrest Allgood — used taxpayers’ dollars to fight to keep the two in jail.

Even after the prosecution’s key witness was exposed as discredited and the actual murderer confessed, Allgood fought to keep the innocent in jail. In 2015, Allgood lost his reelection bid to a 32-year-old by the name of Scott Colom. That year, in capturing nearly 54% of the vote, Colom became the first Black person elected DA in that part of Mississippi. A little over a decade later, he has defeated incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith, the senator who once blocked his nomination to the federal bench in part because of his win over Allgood. In January, Colom will become the state’s first Black senator since the Reconstruction era.
In one sense, it all reads like a fairy tale, given Mississippi’s history.
In another, Colom’s historic victory is seen as an upset, given the Republican Party’s strong hold on the state.
However, when juxtaposed with the statewide results in similar Southern, traditionally red states such as Texas and Georgia, it is clear something more transformative is happening.
And that change is the reason Sen. Chuck Schumer’s leadership should be in question.
The New York Democrat has been a public servant since 1975, including 45 years in Congress.
He’s also been in politics for half a century.
The two sound like one and the same, but they’re not.

Public service unfolds in the lives of the people you were sent to represent. Politics happens inside: the caucus, the donors, the whip counts, the long memory of who owes whom. Schumer is a master of the inside game. That isn’t an insult. He recruited the candidates, and his allies’ super PAC raised a record $151 million at a time when Republican groups were outspending Democrats by more than $400 million. So of course Senate Democrats should make him majority leader in December, and by most counts they will.

But when Schumer swings and misses on the movement brewing in his own back yard, it’s clear he has significant blind spots. The 2025 election of Zohran Mamdani as New York City mayor — without Schumer’s full-throttle endorsement — said a lot about this moment in public service versus politics. As do the historic elections of Colom and Michigan’s Abdul El-Sayed and the close but failed Senate bid by Florida’s Angie Nixon — who says national Democrats wrote off her state almost until it was too late, with Schumer directing some funds to Nixon’s race only “the day before the election.”
These aren’t candidates who waited their turn.

And just as Napster signaled the end of the music industry’s grip on who became a star or as content creators diverted the revenue stream away from traditional media, the 2026 midterms mark the end of industrial kingmaking.

Sens. Chris Van Hollen (Maryland) and Elissa Slotkin (Michigan) could challenge Schumer. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) says he won’t support him. The International Assn. of Machinists and Aerospace Workers sent Schumer a letter directly asking him “not to seek another term” as Senate leader and to let the next generation lead.

That’s a message that should hit home. When Schumer took his seat in Albany in 1975, he was the Assembly’s youngest member since Theodore Roosevelt. In some ways, he was the Colom of his day, the young man who wasn’t supposed to be there yet. Now he risks becoming the latest elected official to bookend a career that way: the face of change at the start, the resistance to it at the end.

There is leadership of the moment, and there is leadership of attrition. There is no one-size-fits-all equation. Each politician has to find their own moral balance. And my questioning of Schumer isn’t solely about age; there are 75-year-olds who should be running things. It’s about whether a member of Congress for 50 years treats succession to leadership as part of the job or as a threat. We’ve seen it too often recently — think of President Biden and Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine). They all make promises to move aside until it’s time to move aside.
That’s when they typically dig in. Sometimes that leads to being pushed out.

When it comes to the inside game of politics, Schumer is a master. But in this new political landscape, where voters are setting the agendas and choosing the leaders without D.C.’s blessings, it seems more often that the historic victories the Democrats are enjoying are happening whether Schumer wants them to or not.
YouTube: @LZGrandersonShow

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Goldman Sees S&P 500 Rising 14% on Cheap Hyperscaler Valuations
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Julien Ponthus

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Goldman Sachs Group Inc. strategists are bullish on US stocks for 2027, predicting the S&P 500 will advance 14% over the coming year after a selloff in the biggest technology companies left their valuations historically cheap.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The team led by Peter Oppenheimer are overweight on the US and Japan for next year. They said in a note to clients that they see the S&P 500 hitting 8,700 points in the next 12 months, even as they expect earnings growth for the benchmark to slow sharply. The S&P is up 11% so far in 2026.

Goldman's call comes after the Nasdaq 100 dropped 9% from its early October high, dragged down by concerns over the artificial-intelligence buildout and the scandal at Nvidia Corp. that cost Chief Executive Officer Jensen Huang his job this week. The declines have left so-called hyperscalers trading "well below" their historical valuations, the strategists said.

"We see Technology — and the Hyperscalers in particular — as relatively defensive," they wrote. "True, the biggest companies have turned cash flow negative, but overall balance sheet measures such as net debt/equity remain healthy."

With global earnings growth expected to ease in 2027, the team recommended investing in US and Japanese stocks and in industries that typically thrive amid lower bond yields, easing inflation and falling oil prices. They forecast a rapid deceleration in earnings-per-share expansion, with EPS growth on the S&P 500 sliding to 11% next year from 36% in 2026, and to 7% from 18% for the Stoxx Europe 600.
That, in turn, means markets are likely to assign a premium to the companies that continue expanding rapidly, according to Goldman.

"We expect investors to seek companies that can sustain growth as it becomes more scarce," the Goldman strategists wrote. "Attractive opportunities are emerging in long-duration growth companies, which should become more valuable as growth rates slow."

The bank is underweight European stocks, with Oppenheimer's team arguing valuations haven't come off as much as in other regions, while government debt "issues" and "a heavy political calendar" mean risks are higher. The Stoxx Europe 600 hit a fresh record this week, boosted by an upbeat earnings season and investors rotating out of the AI trade.
--With assistance from Michael Msika.
