scottjg.com/posts/2026-11-11-reverse-eng.headline: Reverse Engineering My Coway Air Purifier to Ditch the Cloud
scottjg.com/posts/2026-11-11-reverse-eng.author: Ian Carroll @iangcarroll

paragraphs.text: November 11, 2026 16 min read
The year is 2017. A string of annual wildfires rocks the West Coast. The sky looks like this in the daytime:
My home, like many in the Bay Area, has no insulation and isn’t really air sealed. To avoid choking on soot, a lot of people started buying air purifiers like this one:

It’s an overpriced box fan with a HEPA filter and an air quality sensor. It has some controls for the fan speed, and it can also automatically ramp up if the air quality is bad. It’s ugly, but they’re so ubiquitous around here that I feel like no one even notices them anymore. Also, FWIW, the device works. It really does improve air quality.

This device became a staple item in our household when my wife eventually started cranking up the fan at night for white noise (a dual purpose!). Over time, I have become accustomed to it and now also require it to sleep.
The Good Night button#

Our home also has smart lighting, and it’s all integrated with Apple Home. At night, I always press the “Good Night” button, which shuts off all the lights. I really wanted to tie the fan into that. I’d press Good Night, the lights would shut off, and the fan would crank up to my wife’s preferred white noise volume.

The old Airmega didn’t have Wi-Fi, so there was no easy way to integrate it with Apple Home. When it eventually broke, I bought the now-discontinued Coway Airmega IconS (for non-discontinued Wi-Fi models, check out the Airmega 250S or Airmega MightyS). It’s still just a box fan with a HEPA filter, but it’s considerably more expensive, aims to look like a piece of fancy mid-century furniture, and most importantly, can be controlled over Wi-Fi (sort of).
The existing Home Assistant integration#

Coway’s iPhone app is an absolutely classic IoT affair. It takes forever to load, and it asks me to change my password nearly every time I launch it. Thankfully, a brave soul reverse-engineered the app and wrote an integration for Home Assistant. The integration more or less pretends to be the phone app. It polls the Coway cloud service for status updates and sends commands through it to control the fan. Home Assistant bridges that to Apple Home and… voilà!
Why ditch the cloud?#
The downside of this approach is that you’re still at the mercy (or lack thereof) of the Coway cloud service. It seems like at least once or twice a year, it breaks.
Here are some of the reasons I have seen it break:
• Coway didn’t like the integration hammering their servers and banned it. After a protracted argument with the community, they eventually settled on allowing it.
• Coway rewrote their phone app and rebranded it from IoCare to IoCare+, so the integration had to be rewritten as well.
• Coway made minor changes to the layout of the HTML that the integration scrapes, which broke it.
• Coway’s servers were periodically offline, which prevented any remote control of the device.
• Coway banned my account at one point for running an old version of the integration. I couldn’t control the fan remotely for weeks while I waited for their support team to reverse the ban.

On top of this, it seems unlikely that Coway will maintain this service forever. I suspect that eventually, like all IoT manufacturers, they’ll either charge for this service or discontinue it. My fan model is already discontinued (though there are other Wi-Fi enabled models, so… who knows).
A way in#

I admit, I have been lazy. For years, I put off trying to figure out a way to ditch the Coway cloud, because if the device was really locked down, it would be pretty tough. Presumably, when the fan starts up, it connects to coway.com (or whatever) and checks that the server’s SSL certificate is valid. Most likely, I wouldn’t be able to make a fake certificate that passes that check, so the fan wouldn’t connect to my server.

Also, setting up a man-in-the-middle (MitM) environment is just a pain in the neck. The fan would have to connect to an isolated Wi-Fi network that routes all its traffic through my own server on the way out to the internet. To do that, you have to configure a bunch of routing and firewall rules to redirect traffic. None of this is impossible (I’ve done it before), but it’s a hassle to set up, and it’s always finicky to get right. And once you have it set up, that’s just step one.
All that said, two major things have changed.

First, there was a recent security incident (October 2026) where someone discovered that eMudhra, one of the trusted internet certificate authorities, had used a very weak parameter for some of its private keys.

So, if the device is unpatched AND it has hardcoded root certificates AND it doesn’t pin the cloud service’s certificate, then… maybe that’s a way in. Admittedly, that’s a lot of ifs, but assuming the device doesn’t have any major security mistakes in its design, this could be the foothold needed to take control of it.
The second thing is simply AI. An LLM can set up everything you need for a MitM environment, so you can get straight to sleuthing out how the fan works. It can do this unattended, in minutes.
Once you can sit between the fan and the internet, you can see how it communicates, which should help us understand how to get the fan to talk to us instead of the cloud.
Our man in the middle#
Initially, I tried to set it up like this:

This actually didn’t work, because a Raspberry Pi uses a smallish PCB trace antenna that doesn’t get a ton of signal strength. With the Pi in the room with my router, the signal was too weak to reach the fan. I guess I could’ve moved the fan into the room with the router, but why do that when I can solve this with a convoluted technical solution?

The Raspberry Pi uses its Wi-Fi radio to run its own access point for the fan to connect to. It can’t easily do that while also connecting over Wi-Fi to the home network. So, I moved the Pi into the room with the fan and plugged its Ethernet port into my laptop, which bridges it to the home network over Wi-Fi:
Next, we need to configure the Pi.
I’m not really making a value judgment here on whether this is a fair thing to block, but Claude will not oblige the request, not even for… uhh… testing purposes.
Luckily, ChatGPT has no such compunctions.
After a few rounds of that, here are the nftables rules it ended up with:

scottjg@pi:~ $ sudo nft -a list ruleset table inet mitmproxy_ap { # handle 8 set client_interfaces { # handle 4 type ifname elements = { "wlan0" } } chain prerouting { # handle 1 type nat hook prerouting priority dstnat; policy accept; meta nfproto ipv4 iifname @client_interfaces tcp dport { 80, 443 } counter packets 2 bytes 120 redirect to :8080 # handle 6 } chain input { # handle 2 type filter hook input priority filter - 10; policy accept; iifname != "lo" iifname != @client_interfaces tcp dport 8080 counter packets 0 bytes 0 reject with tcp reset # handle 7 iifname @client_interfaces meta nfproto ipv6 counter packets 9 bytes 2397 drop # handle 8 iifname @client_interfaces ct state established,related accept # handle 9 iifname @client_interfaces udp dport { 53, 67 } accept # handle 11 iifname @client_interfaces tcp dport { 53, 8080 } accept # handle 13 iifname @client_interfaces ip protocol icmp accept # handle 14 iifname @client_interfaces counter packets 23 bytes 4697 reject with icmpx admin-prohibited # handle 15 } chain forward { # handle 3 type filter hook forward priority filter - 10; policy accept; iifname @client_interfaces meta nfproto ipv6 counter packets 0 bytes 0 drop # handle 16 oifname @client_interfaces meta nfproto ipv6 counter packets 0 bytes 0 drop # handle 17 iifname @client_interfaces udp dport 443 counter packets 1 bytes 57 reject # handle 18 iifname @client_interfaces oifname != "eth0" counter packets 0 bytes 0 reject with icmpx admin-prohibited # handle 19 } } table ip nm-shared-wlan0 { # handle 12 chain nat_postrouting { # handle 1 type nat hook postrouting priority srcnat; policy accept; ip saddr 10.42.0.0/24 ip daddr != 10.42.0.0/24 masquerade # handle 2 } chain filter_forward { # handle 3 type filter hook forward priority filter; policy accept; ip daddr 10.42.0.0/24 oifname "wlan0" ct state { established, related } accept # handle 5 ip saddr 10.42.0.0/24 iifname "wlan0" accept # handle 6 iifname "wlan0" oifname "wlan0" accept # handle 7 iifname "wlan0" reject # handle 8 oifname "wlan0" reject # handle 9 } }
Basically, the masquerade rule translates the traffic from the isolated Wi-Fi network out through our home internet, and the redirect rule forwards HTTP/HTTPS to a running instance of mitmproxy.
Also on the Pi, mitmproxy runs with its web interface, mitmweb, using a command line like this:
mitmweb \ --mode transparent --showhost \ --listen-host 0.0.0.0 --listen-port 8080 \ --web-host 127.0.0.1 --web-port 8081 \ --set web_open_browser=false \ --emudhra-old
Yes, off the shelf, mitmproxy has a built-in option (--emudhra-old) to automatically use the eMudhra root CA to intercept traffic.
Snooping on the fan#
Next, I used the iPhone app to set up the fan on our Pi-MITM-Test Wi-Fi network. Partway through, the app reported that setup failed. Let’s glance at the mitmproxy web interface:
So, we know there was some kind of connection issue, since the app said the fan failed to connect. But it clearly got onto our isolated Wi-Fi, because it made a request.

The request is very suspicious. It looks like the fan is downloading the root certificate for Amazon’s certificate authority over plain HTTP. This interface only shows connections that got far enough to make an actual HTTP request. If, for example, the fan doesn’t accept the eMudhra cert we’re using to impersonate the real servers, its HTTPS connections will fail before that point and never show up in the list.

Hypothesis: The device downloads this public certificate over HTTP so it has something to validate its later (currently unseen) HTTPS connections against. It doesn’t have any root certificates built in at all.

mitmproxy has a plugin mode where you can modify specific requests. We can use it to swap in mitmproxy’s own generated CA certificate in place of this public one. If our hypothesis is correct, the fan will trust that CA, and we can intercept the rest of its traffic.

"""Serve this lab's public RSA CA only to the authorized Coway test device.""" from pathlib import Path from mitmproxy import ctx, http def response(flow: http.HTTPFlow) -> None: if ( flow.client_conn.peername[0] == "10.42.0.93" # device IP and flow.request.scheme == "http" and flow.request.method == "GET" and flow.request.pretty_host == "rootca-fs.iocareus.com.s3.ap-northeast-2.amazonaws.com" and flow.request.path.split("?", 1)[0] == "/AmazonRootCA1.pem" and flow.response is not None and flow.response.status_code == 200 ): certificate = Path("/var/lib/mitmproxy-ap/mitmproxy-ca-cert.pem").read_bytes() flow.response = http.Response.make( 200, certificate, { "Content-Type": "application/x-pem-file", "Cache-Control": "no-store", }, ) flow.metadata["coway_test_ca_served"] = True ctx.log.info("Served lab RSA CA to the Coway's HTTP CA bootstrap request")
Sure enough, the device now fully connects, and we can see some new requests:
Hypothesis confirmed

We can intercept the traffic between the fan and the server, which means we could probably build our own server to replace the Coway IoCare cloud. It also turns out we don’t need the eMudhra hack at all. The fan downloads its root CA cert over plain HTTP. It was always MitM-able.

The one thing missing is that none of these requests have anything to do with changing the fan speed or anything else you can do in the app. That’s easy to figure out, though. If you run tcpdump on the Pi while clicking buttons in the app, you can see encrypted traffic on port 8883, the standard port for MQTT over TLS. MQTT is a message bus protocol commonly used in IoT devices.
Going back to the POST in the request list above, here’s what that API call returned:

{ "header": { "success": true, "result": "S1000", "message": "SUCCESS" }, "payload": { "macAddr": "<redacted>", "certToken": "<redacted>", "host": "a29vouc2qruduj-ats.iot.ap-northeast-2.amazonaws.com", "port": 8883, "serial": "<redacted>", "certSvrUrl": "https://cert.iotp.coway.com/iot/v1/cert/r0", "caUrl": "http://rootca-fs.iocareus.com.s3.ap-northeast-2.amazonaws.com/AmazonRootCA1.pem", "privateUrl": "https://icert-fs.iocareus.com/<redacted>/55d66923e9-private.pem.key", "certUrl": "https://icert-fs.iocareus.com/<redacted>/55d66923e9-certificate.pem.crt", "svcCode": "002AIR007", "countryCd": "US" } }
So, if we control the response to this call, we control which keys the fan uses to connect to the MQTT server, and also where that MQTT server is.

For now, we can write another mitmproxy plugin that injects our own key into this response, and then use that to proxy the MQTT traffic. The plugin code gets kinda long, so I didn’t include it here, but AI generates it fairly quickly. mitmproxy doesn’t decode MQTT, but it can still show us the raw stream:

The data looks like a mix of binary and ASCII gibberish, but it’s a standard MQTT protocol stream. When I adjust the fan speed in the app, you can see a new message come from the Coway server to the device. Usually, I’d load this into a traffic dissector and make a table of what gibberish comes in when I press each button in the app, but now…
and after a few minutes…

There’s enough here now to build our own web server that hands the fan its certificates and configuration during setup, plus our own MQTT server to send it commands. That completely cuts the Coway cloud out of the picture during normal operation, but we’re still using the Coway app to set the device up. We also still need a fairly annoying MitM environment to get the fan to connect to us instead of Coway.
Bluetooth setup process#

When you use the Coway app to set up the fan, it searches for the device via Bluetooth. I was hoping we could figure out a way to configure the device ourselves, without the app. Plus, if we’re lucky, we might find something else useful along the way.

I have reverse-engineered Bluetooth devices before. My old strategy was to get the Android version of the app, decompile it, and then just pore over the code. It’s not always as straightforward as it sounds. Developers often obfuscate their apps, which makes the decompiled code harder to read. Some bytecode also doesn’t decompile cleanly back to source code, which means you end up having to read the raw bytecode.

Still, in my opinion, this is usually easier than dealing with iPhone apps. Android apps are usually written in Java (or Kotlin), and it’s just easier to reverse-engineer Java apps than apps compiled from Swift or Objective-C.
This time, I tried a new strategy, which was to use the built-in Android Bluetooth debug logs.

Then, I connected the phone over USB and asked the AI to drive the phone via adb, look at the Bluetooth logs, and reconstruct the protocol. The AI took a while to churn through this task. Eventually, it identified that the message carrying the Wi-Fi configuration was encrypted. Since we would ultimately need to figure out what algorithm was used for the encryption, we would probably have to look at the decompiled app. Sure enough, the next thing it did was pull the Coway app off the phone, decompile it. Then, it started matching up the source code with the Bluetooth logs.
After all that, we can see the provisioning works like this:

• Read the fan’s identity over Bluetooth from characteristic FFA0 (a “characteristic” is a Bluetooth endpoint you can read or write). This gives you some basic information about the device, including its MAC address.
• Write an encryption key (20 random lowercase ASCII letters) to characteristic FFA2:"P001" + protobuf { command: 1, key: Base64(random_letters) }
• Construct the AES key by concatenating the key from step 2 with the 12 uppercase ASCII characters of the MAC address.

• Build the configuration payload, which looks like this:{ "cmd": 2, "ssid": "Example Wi-Fi", "pwd": "example-wifi-password", "bssid": "AABBCCDDEEFF", "type": 1, "macAddr": "112233445566", "caUrl": "http://192.0.2.1:8080/ca.pem", "certSvrUrl": "https://192.0.2.1:9443/iot/v1/cert/r0", "certToken": "example-enrollment-token", "serial": "EXAMPLE000000000001" } That gets wrapped in protobuf, padded with PKCS#7, and encrypted using the AES key from step 3. Then it gets prefixed with the string “P002” and sent to FFA2 as well.

Needless to say, figuring this out end to end from the decompiled Android app would have been very time consuming to do by hand. It’d be at least hours of work (likely days). AI really comes in clutch here. It took the AI about 20 minutes.

The good part, though, is that all the data you need to decrypt that payload is in the Bluetooth logs we captured from the phone, so we can check that our reimplementation is correct just from those. From there, the AI made quick work of reimplementing the whole setup flow in a little Python script.

I was watching the progress pretty carefully while this was going on. The AI never actually showed me the full payload, but I could see it in the intermediate output of the scripts it was writing. And that’s when I noticed something. Two of the URLs from our capture are set right in this payload (caUrl and certSvrUrl). The first tells the fan where to download the root CA cert over plain HTTP, and the second tells it where to POST over HTTPS to get its MQTT configuration.

Since we’re the ones sending this payload now, we can point those URLs anywhere we want. Most importantly, that means we don’t have to do any MitM anymore. We just have to run our own server and plug in its URLs when we set up the fan.
Home Assistant integration#

Based on the findings in this article, I was able to build a Home Assistant custom integration for the fan. My Home Assistant server doesn’t have Bluetooth, and it’s pretty far away from my fan, so I opted to do the provisioning with Web Bluetooth. That way you can bring your laptop next to the fan and provision it to talk to Home Assistant directly.
After that, the device talks directly over Wi-Fi to Home Assistant.
And, more importantly, it gets bridged from Home Assistant to my Apple Home.
All in a day’s work. Now, I can finally click Good Night.

washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/13/t.headline: Bessent blames Commerce for not restricting Nvidia customer’s chip exports

paragraphs.text: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the Commerce Department on Friday for failing to restrict Megaspeed, a Nvidia customer and the company at the heart of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s spy-sex scandal, from exporting chips.

Officials at the Treasury Department, the Pentagon and the State Department wanted to put restrictions on Megaspeed for months, “but Commerce has the pen,” and did not add the company to the export control list, Bessent said on CNBC’s “Squawk Box.”
“You will have to have to ask them about their internal processes,” Bessent said.

Generally, the Commerce Department is charged with managing exports of sensitive U.S. technologies. Commerce had been investigating whether Singapore-based Megaspeed was routing Nvidia’s cutting-edge chips to Chinese firms in breach of U.S. export restrictions.

Bessent’s comments mark the first time Bessent has publicly attacked the agency run by Howard Lutnick, after revelations that Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with Megaspeed employee and suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang.
Huang resigned Thursday amid reports of two affairs that included a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, a stunning downfall for one of the world’s most powerful executives.

In response to Huang’s advocacy, the Trump administration last year green-lit the sale of certain Nvidia chips to Chinese firms in exchange for a cut of sales. China hawks have contended that allowing Chinese companies to access the powerful chips hurts U.S. standing in the AI race.

Now, lawmakers on Capitol Hill are pushing Huang to testify about his relationship with Alice Huang, a technology executive for Megaspeed who is suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset. (Alice Huang and Jensen Huang have no relation.)

bloomberg.com/news/features/2018-10-04/t.headline: The Big Hack: How China Used a Tiny Chip to Infiltrate Amazon and Apple
bloomberg.com/news/features/2018-10-04/t.author: Jordan Robertson, Michael Riley

paragraphs.text: The attack by Chinese spies reached almost 30 U.S. companies by compromising America’s technology supply chain, according to extensive interviews with government and corporate sources.

In 2015, Amazon.com Inc. began quietly evaluating a startup called Elemental Technologies, a potential acquisition to help with a major expansion of its streaming video service, known today as Amazon Prime Video. Based in Portland, Ore., Elemental made software for compressing massive video files and formatting them for different devices. Its technology had helped stream the Olympic Games online, communicate with the International Space Station, and funnel drone footage to the Central Intelligence Agency. Elemental’s national security contracts weren’t the main reason for the proposed acquisition, but they fit nicely with Amazon’s government businesses, such as the highly secure cloud that Amazon Web Services (AWS) was building for the CIA.

To help with due diligence, AWS, which was overseeing the prospective acquisition, hired a third-party company to scrutinize Elemental’s security, according to one person familiar with the process. The first pass uncovered troubling issues, prompting AWS to take a closer look at Elemental’s main product: the expensive servers that customers installed in their networks to handle the video compression. These servers were assembled for Elemental by Super Micro Computer Inc., a San Jose-based company (commonly known as Supermicro) that’s also one of the world’s biggest suppliers of server motherboards, the fiberglass-mounted clusters of chips and capacitors that act as the neurons of data centers large and small. In late spring of 2015, Elemental’s staff boxed up several servers and sent them to Ontario, Canada, for the third-party security company to test, the person says.

Nested on the servers’ motherboards, the testers found a tiny microchip, not much bigger than a grain of rice, that wasn’t part of the boards’ original design. Amazon reported the discovery to U.S. authorities, sending a shudder through the intelligence community. Elemental’s servers could be found in Department of Defense data centers, the CIA’s drone operations, and the onboard networks of Navy warships. And Elemental was just one of hundreds of Supermicro customers.

During the ensuing top-secret probe, which remains open more than three years later, investigators determined that the chips allowed the attackers to create a stealth doorway into any network that included the altered machines. Multiple people familiar with the matter say investigators found that the chips had been inserted at factories run by manufacturing subcontractors in China.

This attack was something graver than the software-based incidents the world has grown accustomed to seeing. Hardware hacks are more difficult to pull off and potentially more devastating, promising the kind of long-term, stealth access that spy agencies are willing to invest millions of dollars and many years to get.

There are two ways for spies to alter the guts of computer equipment. One, known as interdiction, consists of manipulating devices as they’re in transit from manufacturer to customer. This approach is favored by U.S. spy agencies, according to documents leaked by former National Security Agency contractor Edward Snowden. The other method involves seeding changes from the very beginning.

One country in particular has an advantage executing this kind of attack: China, which by some estimates makes 75 percent of the world’s mobile phones and 90 percent of its PCs. Still, to actually accomplish a seeding attack would mean developing a deep understanding of a product’s design, manipulating components at the factory, and ensuring that the doctored devices made it through the global logistics chain to the desired location—a feat akin to throwing a stick in the Yangtze River upstream from Shanghai and ensuring that it washes ashore in Seattle. “Having a well-done, nation-state-level hardware implant surface would be like witnessing a unicorn jumping over a rainbow,” says Joe Grand, a hardware hacker and the founder of Grand Idea Studio Inc. “Hardware is just so far off the radar, it’s almost treated like black magic.”

But that’s just what U.S. investigators found: The chips had been inserted during the manufacturing process, two officials say, by operatives from a unit of the People’s Liberation Army. In Supermicro, China’s spies appear to have found a perfect conduit for what U.S. officials now describe as the most significant supply chain attack known to have been carried out against American companies.

One official says investigators found that it eventually affected almost 30 companies, including a major bank, government contractors, and the world’s most valuable company, Apple Inc. Apple was an important Supermicro customer and had planned to order more than 30,000 of its servers in two years for a new global network of data centers. Three senior insiders at Apple say that in the summer of 2015, it, too, found malicious chips on Supermicro motherboards. Apple severed ties with Supermicro the following year, for what it described as unrelated reasons.

In emailed statements, Amazon (which announced its acquisition of Elemental in September 2015), Apple, and Supermicro disputed summaries of Bloomberg Businessweek’s reporting. “It’s untrue that AWS knew about a supply chain compromise, an issue with malicious chips, or hardware modifications when acquiring Elemental,” Amazon wrote. “On this we can be very clear: Apple has never found malicious chips, ‘hardware manipulations’ or vulnerabilities purposely planted in any server,” Apple wrote. “We remain unaware of any such investigation,” wrote a spokesman for Supermicro, Perry Hayes. The Chinese government didn’t directly address questions about manipulation of Supermicro servers, issuing a statement that read, in part, “Supply chain safety in cyberspace is an issue of common concern, and China is also a victim.” The FBI and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, representing the CIA and NSA, declined to comment.
Read: Statements from Amazon, Apple, Supermicro and Beijing

The companies’ denials are countered by six current and former senior national security officials, who—in conversations that began during the Obama administration and continued under the Trump administration—detailed the discovery of the chips and the government’s investigation. One of those officials and two people inside AWS provided extensive information on how the attack played out at Elemental and Amazon; the official and one of the insiders also described Amazon’s cooperation with the government investigation. In addition to the three Apple insiders, four of the six U.S. officials confirmed that Apple was a victim. In all, 17 people confirmed the manipulation of Supermicro’s hardware and other elements of the attacks. The sources were granted anonymity because of the sensitive, and in some cases classified, nature of the information.
One government official says China’s goal was long-term access to high-value corporate secrets and sensitive government networks. No consumer data is known to have been stolen.

The ramifications of the attack continue to play out. The Trump administration has made computer and networking hardware, including motherboards, a focus of its latest round of trade sanctions against China, and White House officials have made it clear they think companies will begin shifting their supply chains to other countries as a result. Such a shift might assuage officials who have been warning for years about the security of the supply chain—even though they’ve never disclosed a major reason for their concerns.

Back in 2006, three engineers in Oregon had a clever idea. Demand for mobile video was about to explode, and they predicted that broadcasters would be desperate to transform programs designed to fit TV screens into the various formats needed for viewing on smartphones, laptops, and other devices. To meet the anticipated demand, the engineers started Elemental Technologies, assembling what one former adviser to the company calls a genius team to write code that would adapt the superfast graphics chips being produced for high-end video-gaming machines. The resulting software dramatically reduced the time it took to process large video files. Elemental then loaded the software onto custom-built servers emblazoned with its leprechaun-green logos.

Elemental servers sold for as much as $100,000 each, at profit margins of as high as 70 percent, according to a former adviser to the company. Two of Elemental’s biggest early clients were the Mormon church, which used the technology to beam sermons to congregations around the world, and the adult film industry, which did not.

Elemental also started working with American spy agencies. In 2009 the company announced a development partnership with In-Q-Tel Inc., the CIA’s investment arm, a deal that paved the way for Elemental servers to be used in national security missions across the U.S. government. Public documents, including the company’s own promotional materials, show that the servers have been used inside Department of Defense data centers to process drone and surveillance-camera footage, on Navy warships to transmit feeds of airborne missions, and inside government buildings to enable secure videoconferencing. NASA, both houses of Congress, and the Department of Homeland Security have also been customers. This portfolio made Elemental a target for foreign adversaries.

Supermicro had been an obvious choice to build Elemental’s servers. Headquartered north of San Jose’s airport, up a smoggy stretch of Interstate 880, the company was founded by Charles Liang, a Taiwanese engineer who attended graduate school in Texas and then moved west to start Supermicro with his wife in 1993. Silicon Valley was then embracing outsourcing, forging a pathway from Taiwanese, and later Chinese, factories to American consumers, and Liang added a comforting advantage: Supermicro’s motherboards would be engineered mostly in San Jose, close to the company’s biggest clients, even if the products were manufactured overseas.

Today, Supermicro sells more server motherboards than almost anyone else. It also dominates the $1 billion market for boards used in special-purpose computers, from MRI machines to weapons systems. Its motherboards can be found in made-to-order server setups at banks, hedge funds, cloud computing providers, and web-hosting services, among other places. Supermicro has assembly facilities in California, the Netherlands, and Taiwan, but its motherboards—its core product—are nearly all manufactured by contractors in China.

The company’s pitch to customers hinges on unmatched customization, made possible by hundreds of full-time engineers and a catalog encompassing more than 600 designs. The majority of its workforce in San Jose is Taiwanese or Chinese, and Mandarin is the preferred language, with hanzi filling the whiteboards, according to six former employees. Chinese pastries are delivered every week, and many routine calls are done twice, once for English-only workers and again in Mandarin. The latter are more productive, according to people who’ve been on both. These overseas ties, especially the widespread use of Mandarin, would have made it easier for China to gain an understanding of Supermicro’s operations and potentially to infiltrate the company. (A U.S. official says the government’s probe is still examining whether spies were planted inside Supermicro or other American companies to aid the attack.)

With more than 900 customers in 100 countries by 2015, Supermicro offered inroads to a bountiful collection of sensitive targets. “Think of Supermicro as the Microsoft of the hardware world,” says a former U.S. intelligence official who’s studied Supermicro and its business model. “Attacking Supermicro motherboards is like attacking Windows. It’s like attacking the whole world.”

Well before evidence of the attack surfaced inside the networks of U.S. companies, American intelligence sources were reporting that China’s spies had plans to introduce malicious microchips into the supply chain. The sources weren’t specific, according to a person familiar with the information they provided, and millions of motherboards are shipped into the U.S. annually. But in the first half of 2014, a different person briefed on high-level discussions says, intelligence officials went to the White House with something more concrete: China’s military was preparing to insert the chips into Supermicro motherboards bound for U.S. companies.

The specificity of the information was remarkable, but so were the challenges it posed. Issuing a broad warning to Supermicro’s customers could have crippled the company, a major American hardware maker, and it wasn’t clear from the intelligence whom the operation was targeting or what its ultimate aims were. Plus, without confirmation that anyone had been attacked, the FBI was limited in how it could respond. The White House requested periodic updates as information came in, the person familiar with the discussions says.

Apple made its discovery of suspicious chips inside Supermicro servers around May 2015, after detecting odd network activity and firmware problems, according to a person familiar with the timeline. Two of the senior Apple insiders say the company reported the incident to the FBI but kept details about what it had detected tightly held, even internally. Government investigators were still chasing clues on their own when Amazon made its discovery and gave them access to sabotaged hardware, according to one U.S. official. This created an invaluable opportunity for intelligence agencies and the FBI—by then running a full investigation led by its cyber- and counterintelligence teams—to see what the chips looked like and how they worked.

The chips on Elemental servers were designed to be as inconspicuous as possible, according to one person who saw a detailed report prepared for Amazon by its third-party security contractor, as well as a second person who saw digital photos and X-ray images of the chips incorporated into a later report prepared by Amazon’s security team. Gray or off-white in color, they looked more like signal conditioning couplers, another common motherboard component, than microchips, and so they were unlikely to be detectable without specialized equipment. Depending on the board model, the chips varied slightly in size, suggesting that the attackers had supplied different factories with different batches.

Officials familiar with the investigation say the primary role of implants such as these is to open doors that other attackers can go through. “Hardware attacks are about access,” as one former senior official puts it. In simplified terms, the implants on Supermicro hardware manipulated the core operating instructions that tell the server what to do as data move across a motherboard, two people familiar with the chips’ operation say. This happened at a crucial moment, as small bits of the operating system were being stored in the board’s temporary memory en route to the server’s central processor, the CPU. The implant was placed on the board in a way that allowed it to effectively edit this information queue, injecting its own code or altering the order of the instructions the CPU was meant to follow. Deviously small changes could create disastrous effects.

Since the implants were small, the amount of code they contained was small as well. But they were capable of doing two very important things: telling the device to communicate with one of several anonymous computers elsewhere on the internet that were loaded with more complex code; and preparing the device’s operating system to accept this new code. The illicit chips could do all this because they were connected to the baseboard management controller, a kind of superchip that administrators use to remotely log in to problematic servers, giving them access to the most sensitive code even on machines that have crashed or are turned off.

This system could let the attackers alter how the device functioned, line by line, however they wanted, leaving no one the wiser. To understand the power that would give them, take this hypothetical example: Somewhere in the Linux operating system, which runs in many servers, is code that authorizes a user by verifying a typed password against a stored encrypted one. An implanted chip can alter part of that code so the server won’t check for a password—and presto! A secure machine is open to any and all users. A chip can also steal encryption keys for secure communications, block security updates that would neutralize the attack, and open up new pathways to the internet. Should some anomaly be noticed, it would likely be cast as an unexplained oddity. “The hardware opens whatever door it wants,” says Joe FitzPatrick, founder of Hardware Security Resources LLC, a company that trains cybersecurity professionals in hardware hacking techniques.

U.S. officials had caught China experimenting with hardware tampering before, but they’d never seen anything of this scale and ambition. The security of the global technology supply chain had been compromised, even if consumers and most companies didn’t know it yet. What remained for investigators to learn was how the attackers had so thoroughly infiltrated Supermicro’s production process—and how many doors they’d opened into American targets.

Unlike software-based hacks, hardware manipulation creates a real-world trail. Components leave a wake of shipping manifests and invoices. Boards have serial numbers that trace to specific factories. To track the corrupted chips to their source, U.S. intelligence agencies began following Supermicro’s serpentine supply chain in reverse, a person briefed on evidence gathered during the probe says.

As recently as 2016, according to DigiTimes, a news site specializing in supply chain research, Supermicro had three primary manufacturers constructing its motherboards, two headquartered in Taiwan and one in Shanghai. When such suppliers are choked with big orders, they sometimes parcel out work to subcontractors. In order to get further down the trail, U.S. spy agencies drew on the prodigious tools at their disposal. They sifted through communications intercepts, tapped informants in Taiwan and China, even tracked key individuals through their phones, according to the person briefed on evidence gathered during the probe. Eventually, that person says, they traced the malicious chips to four subcontracting factories that had been building Supermicro motherboards for at least two years.

As the agents monitored interactions among Chinese officials, motherboard manufacturers, and middlemen, they glimpsed how the seeding process worked. In some cases, plant managers were approached by people who claimed to represent Supermicro or who held positions suggesting a connection to the government. The middlemen would request changes to the motherboards’ original designs, initially offering bribes in conjunction with their unusual requests. If that didn’t work, they threatened factory managers with inspections that could shut down their plants. Once arrangements were in place, the middlemen would organize delivery of the chips to the factories.

The investigators concluded that this intricate scheme was the work of a People’s Liberation Army unit specializing in hardware attacks, according to two people briefed on its activities. The existence of this group has never been revealed before, but one official says, “We’ve been tracking these guys for longer than we’d like to admit.” The unit is believed to focus on high-priority targets, including advanced commercial technology and the computers of rival militaries. In past attacks, it targeted the designs for high-performance computer chips and computing systems of large U.S. internet providers.

Provided details of Businessweek’s reporting, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs sent a statement that said “China is a resolute defender of cybersecurity.” The ministry added that in 2011, China proposed international guarantees on hardware security along with other members of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization, a regional security body. The statement concluded, “We hope parties make less gratuitous accusations and suspicions but conduct more constructive talk and collaboration so that we can work together in building a peaceful, safe, open, cooperative and orderly cyberspace.”

The Supermicro attack was on another order entirely from earlier episodes attributed to the PLA. It threatened to have reached a dizzying array of end users, with some vital ones in the mix. Apple, for its part, has used Supermicro hardware in its data centers sporadically for years, but the relationship intensified after 2013, when Apple acquired a startup called Topsy Labs, which created superfast technology for indexing and searching vast troves of internet content. By 2014, the startup was put to work building small data centers in or near major global cities. This project, known internally as Ledbelly, was designed to make the search function for Apple’s voice assistant, Siri, faster, according to the three senior Apple insiders.

Documents seen by Businessweek show that in 2014, Apple planned to order more than 6,000 Supermicro servers for installation in 17 locations, including Amsterdam, Chicago, Hong Kong, Los Angeles, New York, San Jose, Singapore, and Tokyo, plus 4,000 servers for its existing North Carolina and Oregon data centers. Those orders were supposed to double, to 20,000, by 2015. Ledbelly made Apple an important Supermicro customer at the exact same time the PLA was found to be manipulating the vendor’s hardware.

Project delays and early performance problems meant that around 7,000 Supermicro servers were humming in Apple’s network by the time the company’s security team found the added chips. Because Apple didn’t, according to a U.S. official, provide government investigators with access to its facilities or the tampered hardware, the extent of the attack there remained outside their view.

American investigators eventually figured out who else had been hit. Since the implanted chips were designed to ping anonymous computers on the internet for further instructions, operatives could hack those computers to identify others who’d been affected. Although the investigators couldn’t be sure they’d found every victim, a person familiar with the U.S. probe says they ultimately concluded that the number was almost 30 companies.

That left the question of whom to notify and how. U.S. officials had been warning for years that hardware made by two Chinese telecommunications giants, Huawei Corp. and ZTE Corp., was subject to Chinese government manipulation. (Both Huawei and ZTE have said no such tampering has occurred.) But a similar public alert regarding a U.S. company was out of the question. Instead, officials reached out to a small number of important Supermicro customers. One executive of a large web-hosting company says the message he took away from the exchange was clear: Supermicro’s hardware couldn’t be trusted. “That’s been the nudge to everyone—get that crap out,” the person says.

Amazon, for its part, began acquisition talks with an Elemental competitor, but according to one person familiar with Amazon’s deliberations, it reversed course in the summer of 2015 after learning that Elemental’s board was nearing a deal with another buyer. Amazon announced its acquisition of Elemental in September 2015, in a transaction whose value one person familiar with the deal places at $350 million. Multiple sources say that Amazon intended to move Elemental’s software to AWS’s cloud, whose chips, motherboards, and servers are typically designed in-house and built by factories that Amazon contracts from directly.

A notable exception was AWS’s data centers inside China, which were filled with Supermicro-built servers, according to two people with knowledge of AWS’s operations there. Mindful of the Elemental findings, Amazon’s security team conducted its own investigation into AWS’s Beijing facilities and found altered motherboards there as well, including more sophisticated designs than they’d previously encountered. In one case, the malicious chips were thin enough that they’d been embedded between the layers of fiberglass onto which the other components were attached, according to one person who saw pictures of the chips. That generation of chips was smaller than a sharpened pencil tip, the person says. (Amazon denies that AWS knew of servers found in China containing malicious chips.)

China has long been known to monitor banks, manufacturers, and ordinary citizens on its own soil, and the main customers of AWS’s China cloud were domestic companies or foreign entities with operations there. Still, the fact that the country appeared to be conducting those operations inside Amazon’s cloud presented the company with a Gordian knot. Its security team determined that it would be difficult to quietly remove the equipment and that, even if they could devise a way, doing so would alert the attackers that the chips had been found, according to a person familiar with the company’s probe. Instead, the team developed a method of monitoring the chips. In the ensuing months, they detected brief check-in communications between the attackers and the sabotaged servers but didn’t see any attempts to remove data. That likely meant either that the attackers were saving the chips for a later operation or that they’d infiltrated other parts of the network before the monitoring began. Neither possibility was reassuring.

When in 2016 the Chinese government was about to pass a new cybersecurity law—seen by many outside the country as a pretext to give authorities wider access to sensitive data—Amazon decided to act, the person familiar with the company’s probe says. In August it transferred operational control of its Beijing data center to its local partner, Beijing Sinnet, a move the companies said was needed to comply with the incoming law. The following November, Amazon sold the entire infrastructure to Beijing Sinnet for about $300 million. The person familiar with Amazon’s probe casts the sale as a choice to “hack off the diseased limb.”

As for Apple, one of the three senior insiders says that in the summer of 2015, a few weeks after it identified the malicious chips, the company started removing all Supermicro servers from its data centers, a process Apple referred to internally as “going to zero.” Every Supermicro server, all 7,000 or so, was replaced in a matter of weeks, the senior insider says. (Apple denies that any servers were removed.) In 2016, Apple informed Supermicro that it was severing their relationship entirely—a decision a spokesman for Apple ascribed in response to Businessweek’s questions to an unrelated and relatively minor security incident.

That August, Supermicro’s CEO, Liang, revealed that the company had lost two major customers. Although he didn’t name them, one was later identified in news reports as Apple. He blamed competition, but his explanation was vague. “When customers asked for lower price, our people did not respond quickly enough,” he said on a conference call with analysts. Hayes, the Supermicro spokesman, says the company has never been notified of the existence of malicious chips on its motherboards by either customers or U.S. law enforcement.

Concurrent with the illicit chips’ discovery in 2015 and the unfolding investigation, Supermicro has been plagued by an accounting problem, which the company characterizes as an issue related to the timing of certain revenue recognition. After missing two deadlines to file quarterly and annual reports required by regulators, Supermicro was delisted from the Nasdaq on Aug. 23 of this year. It marked an extraordinary stumble for a company whose annual revenue had risen sharply in the previous four years, from a reported $1.5 billion in 2014 to a projected $3.2 billion this year.

One Friday in late September 2015, President Barack Obama and Chinese President Xi Jinping appeared together at the White House for an hourlong press conference headlined by a landmark deal on cybersecurity. After months of negotiations, the U.S. had extracted from China a grand promise: It would no longer support the theft by hackers of U.S. intellectual property to benefit Chinese companies. Left out of those pronouncements, according to a person familiar with discussions among senior officials across the U.S. government, was the White House’s deep concern that China was willing to offer this concession because it was already developing far more advanced and surreptitious forms of hacking founded on its near monopoly of the technology supply chain.

In the weeks after the agreement was announced, the U.S. government quietly raised the alarm with several dozen tech executives and investors at a small, invite-only meeting in McLean, Va., organized by the Pentagon. According to someone who was present, Defense Department officials briefed the technologists on a recent attack and asked them to think about creating commercial products that could detect hardware implants. Attendees weren’t told the name of the hardware maker involved, but it was clear to at least some in the room that it was Supermicro, the person says.

The problem under discussion wasn’t just technological. It spoke to decisions made decades ago to send advanced production work to Southeast Asia. In the intervening years, low-cost Chinese manufacturing had come to underpin the business models of many of America’s largest technology companies. Early on, Apple, for instance, made many of its most sophisticated electronics domestically. Then in 1992, it closed a state-of-the-art plant for motherboard and computer assembly in Fremont, Calif., and sent much of that work overseas.

Over the decades, the security of the supply chain became an article of faith despite repeated warnings by Western officials. A belief formed that China was unlikely to jeopardize its position as workshop to the world by letting its spies meddle in its factories. That left the decision about where to build commercial systems resting largely on where capacity was greatest and cheapest. “You end up with a classic Satan’s bargain,” one former U.S. official says. “You can have less supply than you want and guarantee it’s secure, or you can have the supply you need, but there will be risk. Every organization has accepted the second proposition.”

In the three years since the briefing in McLean, no commercially viable way to detect attacks like the one on Supermicro’s motherboards has emerged—or has looked likely to emerge. Few companies have the resources of Apple and Amazon, and it took some luck even for them to spot the problem. “This stuff is at the cutting edge of the cutting edge, and there is no easy technological solution,” one of the people present in McLean says. “You have to invest in things that the world wants. You cannot invest in things that the world is not ready to accept yet.”

Bloomberg LP has been a Supermicro customer. According to a Bloomberg LP spokesperson, the company has found no evidence to suggest that it has been affected by the hardware issues raised in the article.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/uber-confirms-.headline: Uber confirms hackers stole thousands of drivers’ license information in data breach
techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/uber-confirms-.author: Zack Whittaker

paragraphs.text: Uber is notifying thousands of drivers that their personal and driver’s license information was stolen during an October data breach at one of the company’s tech providers.

In notices filed this week with several U.S. attorneys general, including California, the ride-hail giant said it was notified on October 9 by the provider that hackers broke in and stole internal credentials, which were used to access Uber’s data.
The company said it subsequently began notifying affected drivers that their personal information was stored with the provider.

TechCrunch has learned that the provider is Fireworks AI, which lets developers access and use open AI models. Fireworks reported a data breach last month in which hackers stole its customers’ information, including billing data and some private AI datasets.
Online productivity startup Notion confirmed its data was also stolen in the Fireworks hack.

“The notices to drivers are in relation to a security incident impacting one of our third-party vendors, Fireworks.ai, which had access to some Uber data,” an Uber spokesperson told TechCrunch, deferring our questions to Fireworks.
Uber did not say how many customers are affected by the breach, nor how many drivers it was notifying about the incident. A spokesperson for Fireworks did not respond to questions about the incident.

According to data breach notices seen by TechCrunch, the stolen data includes driver’s licenses of 2,567 individuals in Massachusetts, 3,430 people across South Carolina, and 1,873 residents of Rhode Island. A filing with Illinois showed that some state residents had their driver’s license information stolen, but that the number of affected people was pending. Uber also notified drivers who live in California, but did not say how many had their information stolen.
The number is expected to rise as more data breach notifications roll in.
Fireworks attributed its breach to a financially motivated cybercriminal group whose goals are to sell stolen tokens for accessing large language models, or LLMs.
No known cybercriminal group has taken credit for the data theft.
This is Uber’s second known data breach this year. The company reported a security incident at its Uber Freight truck shipping unit, for which an extortion gang took credit for stealing data.

Zack Whittaker is the security editor at TechCrunch. He also authors the weekly cybersecurity newsletter, this week in security.

nytimes.com/2026/11/13/science/spacex-la.headline: SpaceX Aims for Starship Launch on Friday. Here’s What to Know.
nytimes.com/2026/11/13/science/spacex-la.author: Kenneth Chang

paragraphs.text: SpaceX hopes to make history on Friday with the latest launch of the giant Starship rocket.
The company will try to catch both parts of the rocket as they return to Earth. This milestone “double-catch” maneuver is a key step toward SpaceX’s goal of developing a fully reusable rocket.

Until recent years, rockets have generally been expensive, single-use throwaways. If all of Starship, which is the largest rocket ever built, can be repeatedly flown, it would revolutionize the space industry, enabling launches of bigger, heavier satellites and other cargo at lower costs.

In addition, NASA is counting on a version of Starship to serve as a lunar lander for its Artemis program. The catches are not needed for NASA’s Artemis III mission next year, but any failures would make it even more unlikely that NASA could meet its goal of landing astronauts on the moon in 2028.
A success would keep SpaceX on schedule, at least for now.
When is the launch, and how can I watch it?

SpaceX is aiming to launch Starship at 5:45 p.m. Eastern time on Friday from its Starbase site outside Brownsville, Texas. As of Friday morning, the Federal Aviation Administration, which regulates rocket launches and spacecraft re-entries to ensure public safety, had not yet issued a license.
If weather, technical problems or paperwork cause delays, the countdown can be postponed by up to 75 minutes.
SpaceX plans to provide live coverage of the test flight on its website, starting about 30 minutes before liftoff.
What is Starship?

At 407 feet tall, Starship is the largest and most powerful rocket ever built. It consists of two pieces: a powerful booster stage with 33 engines known as the Super Heavy, and an upper-stage spacecraft, also called Starship and often shortened to Ship.

“It’s designed for not just full reusability but also rapid reusability, like an aircraft,” Elon Musk, the founder and chief executive of SpaceX, said in September during the All-In Summit, a business and technology conference.

A previous Starship test flight in September was the first to enter orbit around Earth. The mission successfully deployed 26 of SpaceX’s newest Starlink satellites, which have become operational pieces of the internet communications network.
What will happen during this flight?
This will be the 15th test flight of Starship. After launching from the southern tip of Texas, the rocket will head eastward over the Gulf of Mexico.

After completing its main task of accelerating the rocket through the densest part of the atmosphere, the Super Heavy booster will drop off and head back to the launchpad, where it is to be caught by two mechanical arms on the launch tower. SpaceX successfully pulled off this technological tour de force three times in 2024 and 2025.
The upper-stage Ship will continue upward to orbit, about 170 miles above Earth. It will then deploy another batch of 26 Starlink satellites.

After 22 hours and about 14 trips around the planet, Ship will drop out of orbit and head back to the launch site, where it will also be caught by the mechanical arms on the launch tower. By that time, the booster will have been lowered from the tower and moved away.
Is there any danger as Ship crosses the United States toward landing?
During Flight 14, SpaceX showed that it could restart an engine on the upper-stage Ship, allowing the craft to first enter a circular orbit and then to drop out of orbit.
If something on the spacecraft is not performing quite as expected, the return schedule can be moved up so that it will land in an empty swath of the Pacific Ocean.

That is what happened during Flight 14. Although SpaceX was not going to try to catch the Ship, it did plan to re-enter over the United States and then simulate a landing over the Gulf of Mexico. However, because one of the upper-stage engines had failed during ascent, SpaceX decided to be cautious and have the Ship return early, splashing down in the Pacific.
What comes after this test flight?

Flight 16 could be the first Starship launch from SpaceX’s revamped launchpad at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The launch site in Texas is not sufficient to serve SpaceX’s planned acceleration of Starship launches. Another Florida launchpad is under construction at the nearby Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, and SpaceX has announced plans to build a huge launch complex in Louisiana.

SpaceX could also hit a major milestone next year if it can launch two Starships in quick succession, dock them together in orbit and then move liquid methane and liquid oxygen propellants from one Starship to the other.

The refueling maneuver is essential for Starship to leave low-Earth orbit and head to more distant destinations like the moon and Mars. That is because by the time the upper-stage Ship reaches orbit, its tanks are almost empty.

SpaceX’s plan is to put up the equivalent of an orbital gas station. A series of tanker Starships will bring propellants to fill up the station. When it is full, the Starship that is headed to the moon or elsewhere beyond low-Earth orbit will launch, dock with the gas station, refuel and then continue on its journey.
Why is Starship important for NASA?

In the second half of 2027, NASA plans to undertake its Artemis III mission. That trip will not go to the moon but will remain in orbit around Earth to practice docking procedures. Like the Artemis II mission that flew to the moon and back this year, the Artemis III astronauts will sit inside an Orion spacecraft, launched atop of NASA’s Space Launch System rocket.
After they reach orbit, the astronauts will practice docking with prototype moon landers, first with the Blue Moon spacecraft built by Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin company and then with Starship.
NASA has not yet decided which lander it will use for Artemis IV, which will try to land two astronauts on the moon near its south pole.
Wasn’t Starship supposed to be heading to Mars already?
In March last year, Mr. Musk said on X that Starship would be heading to Mars by the end of 2026. The two planets line up to provide an optimal trajectory every 26 months.
On board would be Optimus humanoid robots built by Tesla, Mr. Musk’s car company.

But failures during Starship test flights last year meant that the craft would fall behind schedule. The Optimus robots have appeared in demos but do not appear to be ready for official space missions, either.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/elevenlabs-new.headline: ElevenLabs’ new app combines meeting note-taking and dictation for teams
techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/elevenlabs-new.author: Ivan Mehta

paragraphs.text: In the last few months, Fireflies, Wispr Flow, and Granola have all released competing capabilities in the dictation and meeting note-taking space. The newest entrant in that category is voice AI giant ElevenLabs, which this week released an experimental app called ElevenAI that combines meeting note-taking, dictation, and agent integration.

Launched during its 11/11 Summit in New York, ElevenAI is still in preview, and you have to sign up for early access instead of just downloading an app. ElevenLabs, valued at $22 billion, is very much positioning this as a product that lives within a team as compared to a productivity tool for an individual.

ElevenAI packs all the features typically found in other apps in the category. It can take meeting notes across your meetings and notify other participants that the conversation is being recorded. Users can query data across meetings and get live assistance during a chat, helping them recall a key detail from older conversations. ElevenLabs also allows companies to integrate ElevenAgent and take follow-up actions such as writing a draft email based on meeting notes.

Plus, there’s a dictation feature, which lets users convert speech to cleaned-up text in any app with support for over 90 languages. The company said that the app is capable of understanding industry-specific terms across dictation and meeting transcription.

ElevenAI allows the company to use its own model as a showcase and also utilize its agent platforms for better context funneling. The startup’s positioning might not be to directly compete in the productivity market, but rather to give enterprise teams an option to not buy licenses to a notetaker and use its solution instead. All meeting-related tools are rushing to become central knowledge hubs for companies while aiming to automate knowledge extraction and follow-up actions

In the last week, the company also launched its v3 series of Scribe speech-to-text models with live transcription capabilities and the ability for companies to fine-tune models using their own data, a tool to pick the right language model based on use case, and a routine creator that automates tasks based on the transcript.

nytimes.com/2026/11/13/science/babysitti.headline: These Male Dolphins Do Something Rare: Day Care
nytimes.com/2026/11/13/science/babysitti.author: Fanni Daniella Szakál

paragraphs.text: Franciscana dolphins are one of the most elusive dolphin species in the world.

They’re quite small — measuring only about five feet at full size — and they spend most of their time living in the often murky coastal waters of Argentina, Uruguay and Brazil. Most of what scientists know about them comes from studying their remains after they’ve been tangled up in fishing nets as bycatch.

So when Marcos César de Oliveira Santos, a marine biologist from the University of São Paulo, noticed them in the blue-green waters by his research station near Ubatuba, Brazil, he was astonished. He started flying drones over the dolphin’s pods, hoping for insights into how these animals live.
That’s when he saw something curious: The males were babysitting, an extremely rare behavior for male mammals.

When looking over the footage, Dr. Santos and his teammates often observed dolphins traveling in groups of three: a mother with her calf, and a smaller dolphin that the researchers presumed was male. (The adult males are noticeably smaller than females; and the researchers also caught attempts at mating or a look at genitals.) These males seemed to be following the mother-calf duo, tagging along on the hunt for food.

Sometimes, after the three dived together, only the calf and the male dolphin would surface. The mother remained below looking for a meal. The male would stay close to the calf until the mother came up for air, and then he often helped guide the baby back to its mother. Almost as if he were babysitting. “It’s amazing,” Dr. Santos said.
Dr. Santos and his team recorded males babysitting calves almost 300 times during their study over the course of a year and a half. They published their findings in the journal Marine Mammal Science.

Male mammals who actively participate in parental care are extremely rare, but there are a few examples. “In monogamous mammals, like gibbons, the males have quite a big role,” said Hal Whitehead, a marine mammal researcher at Dalhousie University in Canada who was not involved in the study. Gibbon dads groom, defend and play with their babies.
Dr. Whitehead has also observed male pilot whales looking after unrelated calves.

Babysitting is relatively common in dolphins and whales, because the calves can’t spend as much time underwater as their mothers. But this job is almost always done by females. So when Dr. Santos presented his initial observations at a conference two years ago, “it was jaw-dropping for everyone in that room,” he recalled.
How would babysitting benefit the males?

In other dolphin species, males might fight each other to get the opportunity to mate or they might compete by producing more sperm. Franciscanas, though, show no signs of aggression and have small testes, suggesting that they use neither of those strategies. The scientists proposed that these dolphins babysat as a different way to ensure their success.
“A potential reason is that they’re trying to impress the females,” Dr. Whitehead said. “‘I’m a nice guy, wouldn’t you like to mate with me?’ kind of thing.”

The biggest mystery is whether these males are related to the calves or not, which would change the interpretation of the behavior. Are they attentive fathers making sure their baby survives and their genes live on, or just optimistic mates-to-be? To answer this, Dr. Santos wants to get DNA samples from the dolphins.
He hopes that there is enough time. Franciscana dolphins are classified as vulnerable to extinction, and their numbers are decreasing, largely because they’re being scooped up in fishing nets.

As the only surviving species in their taxonomic family, these dolphins are perhaps hiding more unexpected behaviors. Researchers now have the first documentation of male babysitting in dolphins, which “we never thought we would describe,” Dr. Santos said. “We are losing the only species of a family that we know almost nothing about.”

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: Anthropic IPO to Cap Year of Record-Breaking Equity Megadeals
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Bailey Lipschultz

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Anthropic PBC is poised to add to a blockbuster year of transactions that are orders of magnitude larger than those seen in the past decade, with the biggest initial public offering of all time joining a half dozen other jumbo equity deals.
Most Read from Bloomberg

If Anthropic's first-time share sale prices at the top of its marketed range on Nov. 18, the artificial intelligence lab's IPO and private placement would together raise $90.4 billion, easily surpassing the $86.2 billion in Elon Musk's SpaceX listing in June.

Exercising the so-called over-allotment option after the trading begins, bringing it to more than $100 billion, would surpass Meta Platforms Inc.'s roughly $98 billion equity deal announced last month, also to fund its AI business.

More than $425 billion has been raised across US-listed companies when accounting for IPOs, completed at-the-market share sale programs and marketed share sales, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. That tops the 2021 total of roughly $408 billion raised, the data show.

Including Anthropic, the US's three biggest-ever IPOs landed in a matter of months of each other, a sign of how deals are being turbo-charged by AI companies' need for cash on a scale never seen before. Even adjusted for inflation, this year's biggest IPOs are far larger than previous record-holders like Saudi Aramco and Visa Inc.

While SK Hynix Inc.'s $26.5 billion US listing in July marked the largest for a company based outside of the country, its size after adjusting for inflation is actually more in line with deals from decades ago. By that measure, the South Korean company's US first-time share sale trails debuts from Alibaba Group Holding Ltd. in 2014 and SoftBank Corp. in 2018.
First Deals in Decades
The hunt for AI funding has not only broken records, it has also prompted a handful of tech giants to sell stock for the first time in decades.

Meta, led by Mark Zuckerberg, would likely hold the title for the biggest equity fundraise with its $98 billion of offerings including a marketed stock sale and preferred shares. The bulk of the total comes in the form of a planned $60 billion at-the-market share sale program, which allows companies to periodically sell shares in the open market.
Like IPOs, ATMs have metastasized in the AI era. Bitcoin treasury firm Strategy Inc. raised $21 billion in 2024 via an ATM and did another of the same size in 2025, data compiled by Bloomberg show.

This year, Alphabet Inc.'s roughly $85 billion funding plan includes a $40 billion ATM program. Oracle Corp. sold roughly $20 billion of shares through an ATM program, on top of raising tens of billions of dollars through the sale of additional equity and debt.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Fed’s Collins Says Inflation Fight Outweighs Housing Woes
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Maria Eloisa Capurro

paragraphs.text: Fri, November 13, 2026 at 6:10 AM PST 1 min read
(Bloomberg) -- Federal Reserve Bank of Boston President Susan Collins signaled Friday that tighter monetary policy may be needed to cool prices.
Most Read from Bloomberg

In a speech centered on the housing market, Collins said higher interest rates can limit housing affordability. Still, she added, ensuring price stability will benefit both the housing market and the overall economy in the long run.

"In the near term, the higher interest rates sometimes needed to cool the economy and keep inflation in check can make homes more expensive to buy and to build," Collins said in remarks prepared for the Boston Fed's annual economic conference. "But over the longer run, stable prices create predictable economic conditions that are good for housing."

After tightening monetary policy for the first time in three years in September, Fed officials held their benchmark rate steady last month. Several policymakers have signaled their support for a rate increase in December following hotter-than-expected inflation data for October. Investors currently anticipate hikes in December and January, with a third in either March or April, based on federal funds futures pricing.
