finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: Disney Embraces AI It Once Fought, From Animation to Finance and Film
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Dawn C. Chmielewski and Thomas Buckley

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- A century after Walt Disney Co. transfixed moviegoers with a hand-drawn mouse appearing on a silver screen with synchronized sound, the world's biggest entertainment company is now exploring a new frontier in animation: artificial intelligence. In December, the company will bring Ozzy Fox, a children's series rendered by AI, to its flagship Disney+ streaming platform.Ozzy Fox, about an orange character who regularly bursts into song, is the product of a year-long collaboration with French startup Animaj, whose AI tools convert artists' hand-drawn images and text instructions into three-dimensional animation. It's just one example of a wider mission, led by Chief Executive Officer Josh D'Amaro, to bring the 103-year-old home of Disney princesses, Pixar and Star Wars into the AI era.Just one week into D'Amaro's tenure as CEO, OpenAI shuttered its Sora text-to-video platform, scuttling a planned three-year partnership that would have seen Disney invest $1 billion into the startup and license more than 200 of its characters for use in AI-generated short videos. Since then, the company has charted its own course and is leaning on artificial intelligence to upgrade every one of its units from finance to film. At the same time, Disney has been looking to cut costs, moves that have resulted in regular rounds of layoffs as the company's traditional TV channels struggle to retain viewers and advertisers.
Most Read from Bloomberg

D'Amaro's embrace of AI marks a new approach for Disney. Under former CEO Bob Iger, Disney employed the carrot and the stick. It litigated against startups including Midjourney Inc. and MiniMax over alleged copyright infringement, after images featuring Mickey Mouse brandishing a machine gun or crude depictions of Disney princesses appeared on social media, while collaborating with one, OpenAI, which promised to act responsibly.

The false start of Disney's collapsed deal with OpenAI and the threat of AI replacing artists speaks to Hollywood's struggle to reconcile the promise of cheaper, faster filmmaking with fears that it could undermine the creative talent and intellectual property on which the industry depends. Those concerns fueled the crippling actors' and writers' strikes in 2023 and are simmering throughout an economic downturn in Los Angeles.

Few companies have more on the line than Disney. After more than $100 billion worth of acquisitions in the past two decades, from Marvel to Pixar, Star Wars owner Lucasfilm and The Simpsons owner 21st Century Fox, Disney has one of the industry's richest troves of characters, stories and franchises. Disney hasn't articulated an overall AI strategy, but teams across the company are experimenting with different applications, hinting at the potential for broad use of the technology. In September, the company named Karandeep Anand — a technology veteran who most recently lead an AI startup — as Disney's first chief technology officer, in a broad signal of the role AI is likely to play in the entertainment giant's future.Like other Hollywood studios, Disney began by introducing AI in parts of the business where it is least likely to encounter creative resistance.The company is building Disney Financial Insights — or D-Fi — an AI-enabled collaboration platform that can replace and automate manual budget reports, bringing visibility, approvals and insights into one place, people familiar with the plans said. It's also testing AI-powered suggestions with some US subscribers to the flagship Disney+ streaming service. People can speak or choose from suggested prompts to describe what they want to watch, and the algorithm will promote relevant titles.Documents filed with the US Patent and Trade Office hint at bigger ambitions.In Disney's parks division, a filing earlier this year describes a scenario where an AI-enabled character at the company's resorts asks guests about their favorite memories to compare them with the character's own programmed memories, in an exchange that mimics a meaningful conversation between humans.

Disney also patented a mechanism by which AI-enabled microphones can detect minor changes in the sounds of rides to signal to operators what maintenance is required to avoid a potential issue. Patents give an indication of the company's thinking but don't guarantee the ideas will come to life.

At a media event earlier this month at Disney's headquarters in Burbank, California, the company showcased how the AI technology of five startups that participated in its annual Accelerator program could improve operations. There were autonomous robots built in the style of characters from the Pixar movie Cars to guide resort guests to parking spaces, and tools for disrupting traditional filmmaking with a hybrid production process that places an actor's performance into an AI-generated environment."We're being very aggressive about exploring emerging technologies and seeing how they can support our creators and help us deliver even more engaging and even more personalized experiences all across the globe," D'Amaro said at the function.In October, Dana Walden, Disney's president and chief creative officer, and Alan Bergman, chairman of the entertainment studios, visited Amazon.com Inc.'s MGM studios in Los Angeles to see a demonstration of how the tech giant is using AI to accelerate live-action moviemaking and animation, according to people familiar with the matter. The two companies routinely meet, according to one of the people, who asked not to be named discussing information that's not public.

The same month, Disney also disclosed that it's acquiring some of the assets of Character.AI and hiring 60 employees. The chatbot startup filed for bankruptcy after a deluge of lawsuits related to negligence and wrongful deaths. The $20 million deal would give Disney expertise in conversational AI and help it build systems in-house, with more robust safety procedures, that could create new ways for consumers to interact with its characters. Disney could add conversations with characters as a feature on Disney+, though nothing is imminent, the people said.

Disney's new CTO, Anand, is the former CEO of Character.AI. At Disney, he'll oversee and centralize the company's AI efforts. Jamie Voris, who previously oversaw adoption of AI at Disney at the Office of Technology Enablement, and Eddie Drake, who replaced Voris in his previous role of CTO at Walt Disney Studios in 2024, are retiring, according to people familiar with the matter. Neither Voris nor Drake responded to Bloomberg's requests for comment.

Another way that Disney is expanding its use of AI while retaining control of its intellectual property is through its partnership with Adobe Inc. That relationship got an upgrade earlier this month in a new multi-year agreement that will give Disney early access to Adobe tools, including generative AI and video- and photo-editing software, to support creative endeavors across the company, from ESPN to Disney cruises.

Disney is more focused on controlling the use of their characters and preserving their exclusivity than getting paid by AI companies for training their models on the studio's content, according to one senior executive familiar with its strategy.

Like Disney's acquisition of Pixar Animation Studios in 2006, which revolutionized the company's use of groundbreaking computer graphics and ushered in a new era of animation, D'Amaro sees AI investment as a logical evolution of the Hollywood model."Technology itself is not the goal," D'Amaro said at the Accelerator event. "It's to put technology in the hands of our creators again to create these incredible and immersive stories."

cnbc.com/2026/11/13/openai-chatgpt-walle.headline: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Wallet, allowing its 'dots' AI agents to make purchases for users
cnbc.com/2026/11/13/openai-chatgpt-walle.author: Ashley Capoot

paragraphs.text: OpenAI on Friday announced ChatGPT Wallet, a new payment feature that enables its "dots" artificial intelligence agents to make purchases on behalf of users.

The company built ChatGPT Wallet in partnership with American Express, Mastercard and Visa, and it allows cardholders to maintain their existing credit card rewards and protections. Eligible users enter their card information once, prompt their dot to find items to buy and approve each purchase with a security check.

OpenAI said its dots agents will never actually access a user's card details. Instead, their payment networks will provide the dot with a "payment token," which contains a scoped card number, security code and expiration date that is specific to a given transaction.

"Our goal here is to really focus on merchants and our network partners and start building out a really great foundation that's safe and easy to use," Chaya Nayak, who leads product for monetization and payments at OpenAI, told CNBC in an interview.

ChatGPT Wallet comes as a growing number of consumers are exploring how to use personal AI agents to manage their calendars, book travel and complete other day-to-day tasks. OpenAI introduced the dots agents during its annual developer conference in late September, shortly after Meta's Muse offering topped the App Store charts.

Purchases made through ChatGPT Wallet could eventually kickstart a new revenue stream for OpenAI, but the company said it is not taking a cut of transactions to start. With the initial launch, OpenAI is working to build relationships with merchants and position itself as a serious platform for shoppers, especially as vendors are beginning to experiment with personal agents.

OpenAI has pushed deeper into AI-enabled commerce over the last year, but some of its early attempts failed to take off. The company introduced an "Instant Checkout" feature last fall, which it quickly pivoted away from. By March, it had rolled out a revamped shopping experience that aimed to make it easier for users to find and compare products.
Nayak said ChatGPT Wallet builds on OpenAI's previous efforts, particularly around product discovery.
"We think that this is the next step, where if someone found something they're really excited to buy, then we want to be able to get them through to that endpoint," she said.

ChatGPT Wallet is initially available to OpenAI's Pro subscribers in the U.S. who are over 18 years old. The limited rollout is intentional, and the "right approach to make sure things are working," said Luke Gebb, executive vice president and global head of innovation at Amex.

OpenAI's ChatGPT chatbot supports more than 1.2 billion weekly active users and nearly 100 million paying users as of the end of the third quarter. With such a broad user base, Gebb said OpenAI can decide to "turn up the volume" on ChatGPT Wallet when it wants to.
"It just makes sense to watch it, start it in a contained environment, and then keep rolling from there," Gebb told CNBC in an interview.

Merchants and vendors are still reckoning with the rise of personal AI agents, and some companies have opted to forgo them entirely. United Airlines said Wednesday that it will block agents from accessing its systems to book tickets, and Amazon prevents the agents from purchasing products on its platform.

OpenAI said Friday that agentic commerce is still in its "early days," and it published tools and guidance alongside its ChatGPT Wallet announcement to help businesses start to navigate the transition. The company explained how merchants can make sure their websites aren't inadvertently blocking OpenAI's agents, for instance.

"It's going to take time for the ecosystem to build the right infrastructure to be able to make this experience really amazing and seamless across all of their sites," Nayak said. "Really, who we are speaking to here is the networks and the merchants."

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-13/.headline: Rain, dangerous surf and snow to hit Southern California this weekend. Here’s where and when
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-13/.author: Karen Garcia

paragraphs.text: A storm series has arrived in Southern California, bringing with it rain, heavy surf and the potential for flooding in coastal communities.
The brunt of the rainfall from the first storm already arrived in Northern California and provided scattered showers to Southern California Thursday.
But the heaviest part of the storm begins Friday. Here’s what’s expected over the next several days.
Rain and potential flooding
Forecasters say widespread rainfall is anticipated to begin late afternoon and continue into Saturday morning.
Rainfall totals can top out between a quarter-inch to an inch by Saturday.
“The rain is generally going to be on the lighter side, but we can’t rule out some heavier rain at times,” said Mike Wofford, meteorologist with the National Weather Service’s Oxnard office.
Despite the lower amount of anticipated rainfall, meteorologists won’t rule out the possibility of minor flood advisories being issued over the weekend, Wofford said.

“There is potential for moderate coastal flooding impacts at times, especially Saturday” for Los Angeles County beaches, the National Weather Service warned. “Some of these impacts may be moderate to significant beach erosion and shallow flooding of normal dry beaches and walkways.”
Dangerous, high surf and rip tides
Gusty southwest to northwest winds are expected throughout the day Friday, with sustained wind speeds around 20 mph with possible gusts of 30 to 35 mph across the inland region of Los Angeles County.

A high surf advisory is in effect through Tuesday because of two large swells, the first arrived Friday and is expected to last into Saturday and the second is due Monday, said Bryan Lewis, meteorologist with the National Weather Service’s Oxnard office.

“We should see ... surf heights in some of those west-facing beaches in that 8- to 12-foot range, some areas may be a little bit lower,” Lewis said. “It just kind of really depends on that orientation of that coastline there.”
Forecasters caution swimmers to be on alert for dangerous rip currents and only swim near a lifeguard, stay off rock jetties and heed the advice of local officials.
Mountain snow and blocked roads

For those looking to hit the slopes, the storm is bringing heavy snow to the eastern Sierra, particularly around Mt. Whitney north up to Aspendell, where up to a foot of snow could fall over the weekend.

“Travel could be very difficult to impossible,” the weather service warned Friday. “The hazardous conditions will impact the Friday evening commute. Strong winds could cause extensive damage to trees and power lines. Roads, and especially bridges and overpasses, will likely become slick and hazardous.”
Cooler temperatures
It’ll feel warm during the day; however, temperatures are anticipated to drop about 10 degrees more in the evening and remain in the mid to high 60s throughout the rest of the week starting Friday.
The cooler temperatures are coming from a long-anticipated offshore pattern that is finally swinging onshore, forecasters with the National Weather Service’s Oxnard office said.

Additionally, expect gusty southwest to northwest winds throughout the day Friday, with sustained wind speeds around 20 mph with possible gusts of 30 to 35 mph across the inland region of Los Angeles County.

cnbc.com/2026/11/13/chicago-feds-goolsbe.headline: Chicago Fed's Goolsbee says central bank 'has definitely got work to do' on inflation
cnbc.com/2026/11/13/chicago-feds-goolsbe.author: Jeff Cox

paragraphs.text: Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee expressed concern about the latest inflation data, telling CNBC on Friday that the central bank likely will need to take action.
"I believe that the the central bank has definitely got work to do to continue to reestablish its credibility," the policymaker said during an interview on "Squawk Box."

His remarks came shortly after the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the producer price index, considered a proxy for wholesale prices, posted a 0.3% increase in October, which was slightly less than expected, but also indicated a 6.5% annual gain, the highest since November 2022.

With data in hand earlier in the week showing that the consumer price index rose a bit more than expected during the month, Goolsbee said the Fed is slipping further away from its 2% inflation target.
"We've been above 2% for almost six years, and while it sometimes we were making progress, lately we're not making any progress, and if anything, it's going the wrong way," he said.

"Inflation is rising. It's proved far more persistent than we predicted at the beginning from the supply shocks, and now we're adding this old-fashioned demand overheating coming from the AI data center buildout, that looks like it's starting to spread out of its lane," Goolsbee added.

Markets are fully pricing in a quarter percentage point increase when the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee meets next on Dec. 8-9. There also is a better than 10% probability of a half-point hike, according to the CME Group's FedWatch gauge of futures markets. Goolsbee is not currently an FOMC voter but will be in 2027.
Earlier in the week, Fed Governor Christopher Waller indicated he would entertain a 50 basis point move depending on this week's inflation data.
Goolsbee did not speculate directly on whether the Fed might need to be more aggressive.
"It's it's all going to be about this ... question: What is happening to inflation, and are we on path back to 2%?" he said. "My feeling is, right now we're not."

nytimes.com/2026/11/13/technology/anthro.headline: Why Anthropic’s Dario Amodei Has Angered OpenAI and Other A.I. Peers
nytimes.com/2026/11/13/technology/anthro.author: Kalley Huang, Mike Isaac, Cecilia Kang

paragraphs.text: Jensen Huang and Satya Nadella had a problem.

Anthropic and OpenAI, the leading artificial intelligence companies, were lobbying the White House to prevent some A.I. models from being developed and widely shared because, they argued, they were too dangerous. But Mr. Huang and Mr. Nadella’s companies, Nvidia and Microsoft, saw those A.I. models as a big business opportunity.

At the end of July, Mr. Huang — who resigned from his job on Thursday after Nvidia’s board launched an investigation into his conduct — and Mr. Nadella intervened. They emailed each other drafts of a letter saying those A.I. models should remain open, according to four people familiar with the discussions. When they asked other technology executives whether they’d like to sign on, two dozen companies quickly agreed before the letter became public. Over the next week, 200 more companies — including a chastened OpenAI — signed onto the letter.
Anthropic’s chief executive, Dario Amodei, refused.

Dr. Amodei has for years exasperated his peers with warnings about extreme risks of A.I., even as his company has built some of the most powerful A.I. systems in the world. Frustration has turned to hostility as Anthropic leaped into the lead in A.I. development, experienced stunning revenue growth and moved toward what is likely to be one of the largest initial public offerings ever later this month.

Along the way, Anthropic — which has cultivated an image as a company that tries to do the right thing — has also gained a reputation for playing hardball with customers and competitors. It has cut some off from its service and lobbied against other companies’s free alternatives to its A.I.

Over the last year, other technology companies and investors have organized to push back, according to more than 20 people in the technology industry, many of whom spoke on the condition of anonymity to preserve their relationships with Anthropic.

They have tried to show a united front to counter Dr. Amodei’s warnings about A.I. They have leaned on their ties to President Trump to keep regulators away. They have publicly complained about Anthropic’s business practices. They have even spoken with another Anthropic executive about Dr. Amodei scaring people with his rhetoric.

But the message on A.I. safety from Dr. Amodei, who appears unbothered by criticism from other executives, is breaking through. A.I. agents going rogue and attacking websites have become increasingly common. And in the midterm elections, the threat of job losses from A.I. and data center construction were significant issues for voters in both parties.
(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and Microsoft, claiming copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. The two companies have denied those claims.)
The Schism That Launched Anthropic

Anthropic started with a split. In 2020, a group of OpenAI employees led by Dr. Amodei left the company amid disagreements over how to safely develop A.I. Those employees founded Anthropic in San Francisco the next year.

Its founders’ ties to effective altruism — a philosophy where donors try to measure and maximize the benefits of their philanthropy — created a foundation for the company, particularly its approach to A.I. safety.
But Anthropic played second fiddle to OpenAI, which made everyday use of A.I. tools mainstream with the release of ChatGPT in 2022.

That changed in February 2025, when Anthropic surprised competitors with a preview of Claude Code, an A.I. coding tool. Software engineers started using the tool to generate computer code instead of writing it themselves. Anthropic’s revenue exploded.
Then, its critics say, Anthropic got tough with customers.

A start-up called Windsurf had talks to sell to OpenAI, and those negotiations became public in April 2025. Anthropic later cut off Windsurf’s direct access to its models, which the start-up used to power its own A.I. coding tool.
“I think it would be odd for us to be selling Claude to OpenAI,” said Jared Kaplan, one of Anthropic’s founders and its chief science officer, in an interview in June.

The move crippled Windsurf and potential customers went elsewhere, according to three people familiar with the discussions. Even as Windsurf’s talks with OpenAI broke down, Anthropic kept Windsurf cut off.

Windsurf struck a licensing deal with Google in July 2025. But the message was delivered to the rest of the start-up world: Their businesses were being built on Anthropic’s models, but they had to stay in the good graces of Anthropic to maintain that access.

“Somehow, in the United States, we’ve convinced ourselves that innovation should be in the hands of a few organizations,” said Manos Koukoumidis, chief executive of the A.I. start-up Oumi, in an interview.

Last February, about a year after Anthropic previewed it, Claude Code was on track to make $2.5 billion in annual revenue. In a financial filing, Anthropic disclosed overall revenue of $17 billion in its most recent fiscal quarter.
‘Only They Should Do It’
In early 2025, Dr. Amodei ruffled feathers at Nvidia by backing U.S. trade restrictions on chip sales to China. That June, Mr. Huang said he disagreed with Dr. Amodei on almost everything.
“He believes that A.I. is so scary that only they should do it,” Mr. Huang said of Dr. Amodei and Anthropic at a conference in Paris.
Anthropic responded: “Dario has never claimed that ‘only Anthropic’ can build safe and powerful AI.”
But industry leaders worried about public sentiment turning sharply against A.I. and asked Anthropic to tone down the doomsday talk.

Over the summer, Marc Andreessen and Ben Horowitz, of the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, met with Tom Brown, a co-founder of Anthropic. Anthropic was scaring the public with its predictions of extreme job loss, Mr. Andreessen and Mr. Horowitz said, and should cool it down, according to three people familiar with the discussion.

Mr. Andreessen then took out his phone, where he had pulled up one of Dr. Amodei’s television appearances. The text below Dr. Amodei’s face summarized his prediction of a white-collar blood bath and mass unemployment. Mr. Brown appeared taken aback by the confrontation.

Then, last June, Anthropic released Fable, a version of its most advanced model. The company said it would make the model less effective if it thought Fable was being used to research or develop A.I. But Anthropic wouldn’t tell a user it was degrading the performance, infuriating some researchers.

“It is a very real sign of concentration of power that businesses can make such obviously user-harmful behaviors and still lead in the market,” said Nathan Lambert, a co-founder of Trillium Labs, an open-source A.I. nonprofit, in a social media post.
Within a day, Anthropic walked back the policy. Now, if it thinks Fable is being used to research or develop A.I., it switches to a worse model, and then tells the user.
“We made the wrong trade-off,” Anthropic said at the time.

Anthropic also said it would store the data of those using its most advanced models for 30 days “to support our safety work.” In a sign of how paranoid Silicon Valley had become about Anthropic, the change stoked fears that the company could train its models on customer data, and then compete with those customers, according to four people familiar with the changes.

In September, Anthropic started allowing customers to store their data on their own cloud computing services. Danielle Cohen, a spokeswoman for the company, said it treats customer data as confidential and, by default, prohibits training on it.
‘It’s a Hoax’

At the end of July, Silicon Valley’s anger toward Anthropic peaked as Anthropic and OpenAI lobbied the White House to act against open-source A.I. models. Their campaigning came after OpenAI said its A.I. had gone rogue and hacked into other companies, including a start-up called Hugging Face.

So Mr. Huang and Mr. Nadella shared the letter supporting open-weights A.I., which make the rules that govern a model publicly available. It opened the floodgates against Anthropic, according to five people familiar with the discussions. So many companies asked to sign the letter that Microsoft set up an email address so it could accept signatures for the letter more easily. They included Amazon and Google, which are both investors in Anthropic.

OpenAI eventually signed the letter, but Dr. Amodei said he disagreed with parts of it and Anthropic didn’t sign it. He said in a blog post that all A.I. models, no matter how they are developed and shared, “should go through mandatory safety testing.” He said he believed bad actors would exploit open-weights A.I. models.

Silicon Valley’s executives continued discussing how to present a united front on safety concerns, mostly keeping Anthropic involved in those discussions. In calls and texts, executives from Nvidia, Microsoft, Google, Meta, Anthropic and OpenAI kicked around ideas, according to five people familiar with the discussions. Some had informal discussions about making a joint statement or commitment on slowing A.I. development. Others brainstormed regulatory proposals.

But in September, three days after an Anthropic employee quit over A.I. safety concerns and the issue burst into the mainstream, Dr. Amodei ran ahead of the other companies and made his own call for the industry to slow down.
About three weeks later, Dr. Amodei struck a different tone at the White House during a lunch with Mr. Trump and more than 30 other technology executives, venture capitalists and politicians.

Seated near the end of a long table, Dr. Amodei said the United States had to win in A.I., and that the technology should be built with maximum speed, according to two people familiar with the discussions.
It was, other guests thought, the opposite of what he had been telling the world.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/chatgpts-new-w.headline: ChatGPT’s new Wallet lets AI agents shop and check out for you
techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/chatgpts-new-w.author: Sarah Perez

paragraphs.text: ChatGPT can now shop for you. On Friday, OpenAI launched a new wallet feature that lets its agents, called dots, help you decide what to buy and then complete the purchase on your behalf. The option will initially be available to a limited number of U.S. ChatGPT Pro subscribers, ages 18 and up, with a U.S.-issued Visa, Mastercard, or American Express.

OpenAI says that users are fully in control of the purchases, as they’re able to review the items, the total, and the payment card that will be used to complete the transaction before the checkout occurs. In addition, users will approve the purchases directly with a security check like Face ID or a fingerprint, which creates a record of their transaction.

The addition comes as consumer-facing AI tools are working to find the right product-market fit, in terms of how they can help people be more efficient as they complete various tasks. While companies like DoorDash and Uber have so far reported low numbers of orders placed by AI agents, Meta’s Muse, which now has over 10 million users, has seen AI-assisted shopping become a top activity on its app.
Other personal AI agents, like Instinct, also support making purchases on users’ behalf.
It’s no surprise, then, that OpenAI would want to enter this space more with an agentic shopping feature of its own.

To get started, ChatGPT subscribers add their eligible payment cards to the new ChatGPT Wallet, then ask their dot to help with a purchase. (This setup is a one-time thing; users don’t have to re-enter their payment information every time they buy.) When it’s time to transact, ChatGPT’s Wallet charges the selected card using a payment token, which is a substitute for the user’s actual card details, so that information isn’t shared with either the dot or the merchant.

The merchant will automatically receive what it needs to fulfill the order from the dot, like the shipping address and contact information, OpenAI says. The company notes that customers who shop via their dots will still be able to earn their credit card rewards and be able to take advantage of protections that typically come with cards, like being able to dispute transactions.

The limited availability at launch will allow OpenAI to test and improve the feature and its capabilities before rolling it out more broadly. In the future, the company plans to offer users more control over the feature by allowing them to set spending limits or configure other parameters around purchase categories or time periods, so they can pre-approve purchases that their agent can then handle more autonomously.

It also aims to make the agentic shopping feature an option at a broader number of supported retailers. This could be a challenge in some areas, where retailers are blocking AI agents from using their site; on the shopping front, the largest retailer to ban AI agents is Amazon, as it aims to steer users to its own AI agent, Alexa, instead.
To help retailers adapt to agentic commerce, OpenAI also published a Commerce Partner Playbook that offers tools and guidance to sites that want to support customers using agents.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/13/sto.headline: The story behind the viral ad that helped Scott Colom win in Mississippi
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/13/sto.author: Joanna Slater

paragraphs.text: Ryan Sayles filmed the ad in a few hours and edited it while sitting on his cousin’s couch. The 27-year-old kept tinkering, trying to get the rhythm just right. The final product was good, he thought, and the candidate loved it.
He never imagined it would help change the course of Mississippi political history.
The 30-second digital ad for Democratic Scott Colom — “Pick Another Protein” — ricocheted across the state, the country and the internet. (At last count, it had 3.7 million views on TikTok.)

The spot riffed off a comment by incumbent Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R) about the rising cost of beef. “You have so many proteins to choose from,” she noted in February. The ad’s response: Pick another senator instead.

On Wednesday, the Senate race was called for Colom, a historic upset. When Colom stepped up to deliver his victory speech at Tougaloo College in Jackson, the sign in front of the lectern read, “Picked another senator.”
Sayles was in the audience, thrilled and overwhelmed. “Seeing everybody I know and grew up around take the moment in, that was a lot,” he said in an interview Thursday. “That was a whole thing.”

A freelance videographer and content creator, Sayles grew up in Jackson and studied mass communications at Alcorn State University. He never had worked on a political campaign. Last year, a Colom staffer asked Sayles to produce a one-off video for an event. The campaign liked his work so much they decided to keep him.

For “Pick Another Protein,” Sayles said he worked off a script written by Colom; Colom’s twin brother, Andrew; and Colom’s campaign manager, Gerard Henderson. In a post on X, Colom credited Patrick Gaspard, a former official in President Barack Obama’s administration, with the idea of taking Hyde-Smith’s gaffe and “doing something edgy with it.”

When it came to producing the ad, Sayles said he was a “one-man band.” There were no professional actors. The first scene of a man flipping burgers was filmed in the backyard of Colom’s parents’ home in Columbus, Mississippi.
Shooting on his trusty Sony Alpha 7R V camera, Sayles gave a crucial piece of direction to the man in the first scene, who gives a profane response to the suggestion he pick another protein
“Sheeeeeet,” the man drawls. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”
The first word is key, Sayles told him. “You got to drag that part out,” he said.
The ad took three hours to shoot and about four hours to edit. For music, Sayles chose a sample from “Rapper’s Delight,” a 1979 song by the Sugarhill Gang.
“The old funk beat is always a feel-good type thing,” he said. It “gave the cookout vibe.”

The campaign released the ad Oct. 13. A day earlier, Obama had released a video endorsing Colom. Sayles knew the ad had gone full-scale viral when the number of views eclipsed the Obama endorsement and just kept going.
“It’s still hard for me to conceptually understand that something I edited on my cousin’s couch could make it to L.A., could make it to New York, could make it all across the country,” Sayles said.
Colom called Sayles the breakout star of the election cycle. “He did GAME CHANGING work with SO little,” Colom wrote on X.
Sayles hasn’t made any decisions about his future. For now, he’s still savoring the monumental nature of Colom’s win.

Sayles grew up in a family that emphasized “how important it is to take advantage of the rights we have because we did not always have them,” he said. His grandmother marched with the Rev. Martin Luther King Jr., and Sayles used to go to the same church once attended by Medgar Evers, the civil rights activist killed in 1963.
“I know Mississippi is going to be a better place because of what we was able to pull off,” Sayles said. “That means more to me than anything.”

wsj.com/business/autos/stellantis-offers.headline: Stellantis Offers to Repay C$24 Million to Canada but Government Says Automaker Breaching Commitments

paragraphs.text: By Robb M. Stewart

Stellantis is offering to repay some of the money that Canada's government wants to see returned for past support, but it won't say if it's prepared to defend in court the proposed sale of an Ontario plant.

The company said it will voluntarily return the 24 million Canadian dollars (US$16.8 million) in federal government support it received for a planned retooling of its idled Brampton assembly plant in the Toronto area.

Stellantis early this week unveiled a deal to sell the assembly facility to Canadian armored-vehicle company Roshel, a move the labor union for the plant branded as a betrayal of workers and which Prime Minister Mark Carney said was unacceptable.

Following a meeting Thursday between the company, the union Unifor and government officials, Industry Minister Melanie Joly said Ottawa has issued a notice of default on a 2022 federal funding agreement. Joly said Stellantis was on the hook for hundreds of millions of dollars. The minister has given the company 30 days to take "corrective action."
"The battle for Stellantis workers in Brampton is one worth fighting," Joly said Friday in a post on X. "Bringing back the jobs is our number one priority."
The minister said the government planned to meet with the global chief executive of Stellantis, Antonio Filosa, in the coming weeks to "secure a more acceptable solution."

The Brampton plant has been halted since 2024, when Stellantis began retooling the factory to prepare for the production of its Jeep Compass, affecting some 2,000 jobs. The automaker changed course last year amid hefty U.S. tariffs on foreign vehicles and said Jeep Compass production would be shifted to a factory in Illinois.
Federal accounting records suggest officials forwarded more than C$220 million related to the retooling of the company's factories in Brampton and Windsor, Ontario.

"We recognize the disappointment and uncertainty surrounding the future of the facility," Stellantis Canada Chief Executive Trevor Longley said in a statement. "While our decision to sell the plant represents a change from the original plans for Brampton, the agreement we have advanced with a Canadian manufacturer provides a path to return the facility to productive industrial use, create new jobs with priority hiring consideration for Brampton workers and secure a long-term future for the site."

A spokeswoman for Stellantis declined to say if the company would consider reversing the planned sale of the plant or it is prepared to defend the move in court if Ottawa follows through on a threat to use every legal option available.

The Brampton assembly facility has 2.95 million square feet of floor space on 269 acres. It was built in 1986 and bought by Chrysler with its acquisition of American Motors in 1987. Stellantis in 2023 announced the plant would be used to produce the next-generation Jeep Compass, but retooling efforts were paused in early 2025.
On Monday, Stellantis said it was selling the Brampton plant and associated equipment to Roshel, with a deal slated to close by the end of the year.

Lana Payne, national president of Unifor, said it was critical efforts be made to save the auto industry in Canada and its industrial economy. "Our position hasn't changed in terms of where this needs to go. Unfortunately, we don't have a resolution here," she told reporters Thursday following the meeting.

latimes.com/opinion/story/2026-11-12/unh.headline: Contributor: Authorities need more tools to help unhoused Californians who don't want help
latimes.com/opinion/story/2026-11-12/unh.author: Matt Mahan

paragraphs.text: There’s a woman on the streets of San José who has spent a quarter of her life there. For the past decade she’s been cycling between the streets, the county jail, a shelter bed and the ER.
She keeps falling through the cracks. The specifics of her case are unique, but the pattern is ubiquitous and familiar in every city across California.

This woman in San José is nearly 60 years old. And without a change to state law, she could spend the rest of her life cycling through the same broken system. She could take her last breath on the pavement, in a jail cell or, if she’s lucky, receiving care in our public hospital.
Because in California, people are dying and we don’t have the political will to stop it.

I learned this constituent’s story when San José recently ran a pilot with our county focused on targeted intervention. She is one of the 60 most vulnerable residents living in our downtown — the “frequent flyers,” the people suffering on our streets and straining both emergency services and neighbors’ patience. The people who, frankly, we don’t know what to do with: They are too sick to remain in a shelter but not sick enough to be compelled into care.
We tried to get them help, including clinical evaluation. We offered all 60 people multiple housing options — a motel room, a tiny home, a permanent supportive housing unit.
Forty accepted. Twenty refused.
Of the 40 who came inside, 24 needed the county’s intensive behavioral health treatment, and 15 chose to immediately return to the streets.
We had less than a 50% success rate with the initial pilot.

By actually focusing on the hardest people to help, we confirmed a scary truth that should be obvious based on the state of our streets: We don’t have the tools to help more than half of the most vulnerable people living on our streets.
More than 1 in 5 Americans live with a mental illness.

Imagine going through a mental health crisis alone with no one to advocate for you. Imagine you are past the ability to recognize you need help. And no one is there to require the life-saving care you need.
In fact, in California, your right to remain ill and to overdose has a stronger legal foundation than your right to get well.
I’ve advocated to change this alongside state senators such as Susan Eggman and Catherine Blakespear, whose bills I’ve watched get watered down until access to care is essentially a suggestion.
We have to acknowledge that some of the people on our streets, often the ones who have languished the longest, are no longer able to make a rational decision regarding their own well-being.

Their addiction won’t let them say yes when offered services and care. Their psychosis stands between them and a treatment bed. And the end result is: We are allowing them to be controlled by chemicals in their brain telling them they are OK when anyone watching can see the truth.
So by taking the teeth out of initiatives such as the CARE Court, we’ve left people to face a much harsher bite: life and death on the streets.

It’s a philosophical question as much as a constitutional one: Where do we draw the line between personal liberty and moral responsibility? Especially when someone exercising their individual liberty is affecting our collective safety and quality of life. And even moreso, when our current policies allowed more than 30,000 people to die on our streets over the last decade, mostly from drug overdose, homicide and suicide.

We call 911 when someone is standing on a ledge. But when someone is slowly killing themselves on the sidewalk, we watch them deteriorate until they finally meet the legal threshold for intervention — or until it’s too late.

We have a collective responsibility to do better. And what we need to do next is clear to those of us closest to the system’s gaps: First, we need to significantly expand, by 50% or more, the number of treatment beds in California, including facilities capable of handling complex cases that involve both substance abuse and co-occurring mental illnesses. This also requires a significant investment in our healthcare workforce. Second, we need to create the legal tools to mandate care when those beds are available, including by allowing CARE Court proceedings to result in involuntary treatment.

I’m calling on our state leaders — our next governor and our leaders in the Legislature — to confront this moral failing head on. We can’t keep leading people to their graves while patting ourselves on the back for protecting the autonomy they are using to kill themselves.
Matt Mahan is the mayor of San José.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-ceo-jen.headline: The unfolding Jensen Huang scandal: a timeline
techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-ceo-jen.author: Amanda Silberling

paragraphs.text: Nvidia co-founder and now former CEO Jensen Huang has never been as prone to controversy as AI leaders like OpenAI’s Sam Altman or SpaceXAI’s Elon Musk. But the 63-year-old industry kingpin recently admitted that he cheated on his wife of 40 years in affairs that could have ramifications beyond Huang’s personal life and U.S. national security.

U.S. officials believe that one of Huang’s likely romantic interests, Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, is a Chinese spy who has been feeding information back to Beijing. (Alice Huang, a Chinese citizen, is of no relation to Jensen Huang.)

Megaspeed is a Singapore-based AI infrastructure company that reportedly purchased $4.8 billion worth of Nvidia chips over the last two years. The U.S. and Singapore have both previously investigated Megaspeed over suspicions that the firm was illegally sharing chips with China. The Justice Department has since taken over the federal investigation into the company, The New York Times has reported.

The story took a sudden turn on Wednesday. Citing five people who worked at Nvidia, the Times reported that Huang also had an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, the company’s vice president of healthcare, who reports directly to him. Nvidia, Huang and Powell have not confirmed the report. Reached by a Times reporter, Huang reportedly said, “I don’t think you should be talking to me directly,” before hanging up.

By early Thursday morning, Huang was no longer CEO of the company he co-founded 33 years ago. Then, Thursday afternoon, Reuters dropped another bombshell, publishing a report alleging that Huang had yet another extramarital affair with another unnamed Nvidia employee.

The U.S. and China are embroiled in a fierce technological arms race to build the most advanced AI infrastructure, which could shape each country’s economic future, military prowess, and capacity for innovation. Nvidia is valuable in this competition as one of the world’s largest makers of AI chips, which are essential for accelerating AI development. But as an American company, Nvidia faces government restrictions on the sale of its most powerful chips to Chinese entities.
As the controversy unfolds, we are organizing the most relevant events into a reverse-chronological timeline to keep you up to date.
November 13, 2026: Huang was not confident in his successor, Colette Kress; reports describe Huang as ‘broken’
More reports continue to roll out that illustrate the shock and severity of Huang’s resignation from Nvidia.
Bloomberg reported that Huang looked “broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted” by the time he surrendered his role on Wednesday night, uttering phrases like “whatever” and “I don’t care.”

Separately, the Wall Street Journal reported that Huang had been critical of his CFO and current interim CEO, Colette Kress. Huang is said to have described Kress as “a deer in the headlights” during a presentation this summer, and he had described Kress as someone who could not help him steer strategy or decision-making.

In a scathing letter sent to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Representative Richard Neal (D-MA) and Senator Ron Wyden (D-OR) said they will investigate how the Trump administration handled Nvidia’s chip sales to China, especially after Trump was briefed about Huang’s relationship with a purported Chinese spy.

“Although [Lutnick] and President Trump were reportedly briefed on this intelligence, the Administration did not appear to acknowledge this evident national security threat. On the contrary: despite reportedly learning of Mr. Huang’s compromising relationship last fall, President Trump granted Nvidia permission to sell its advanced H200 AI chips to China in December 2025 in exchange for a cut of the export sales,” the letter states.
That same evening, Senator Tim Scott (R-SC) requested that Huang and Lutnick both testify before the Senate Banking Committee.
“The American people deserve answers,” Scott wrote on X.
November 12, 2026: Huang was having a third affair with another Nvidia employee, according to Reuters

After Huang was already ousted from Nvidia, we continued to learn more incriminating claims about the former CEO. According to Reuters, Huang had a third affair with an additional, unnamed employee of Nvidia.
November 12, 2026: Jensen Huang resigns, CFO Colette Kress named as interim CEO; Huang agrees to testify before Congress

Nvidia said its board had accepted Huang’s resignation on Wednesday. The company’s current CFO, Colette Kress, will take over as interim CEO while still fulfilling her CFO duties. Nvidia is expected to conduct a larger search to determine a permanent successor to Huang.

Harvey C. Jones, a managing partner of Square Wave Ventures and former CEO of Synopsys, was appointed as the company’s first-ever chair of the board of directors. Jones has been on Nvidia’s board since 1993.
Later in the day, Huang confirmed that he would testify in Congress at some point before Thanksgiving, which falls on November 26.

“Jensen and I have been very at odds as some of you already know on export controls, but Nvidia is a very important company to the United States of America,” House Foreign Affairs Committee Chairman Brian Mast said to reporters. “I don’t want to see anything hurt in Nvidia, but he has some very serious questions to answer.”
The testimony is expected to take place behind closed doors, but Mast believes the briefing will be recorded and transcribed.
November 11, 2026: Nvidia’s stock drops as board reportedly preps to oust CEO Jensen Huang
November 11, 2026: Huang also had an affair with an Nvidia executive who reports to him, NYT says
The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang also had an affair with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell, who reports directly to the CEO.
According to the report, Huang and Powell were captured on film “being affectionate” at a hotel during a conference earlier this year.
November 11, 2026: Congress plans to subpoena Huang to answer questions about affair

Huang has not responded to a request from three Republican congressmen to appear for a closed-door briefing for questioning about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy. House China Committee Chairman John Moolenaar said Wednesday on Fox Business that if Huang doesn’t agree to the briefing, he’ll likely be subpoenaed.
November 9, 2026: Huang pulls out of various speaking engagements
The Nvidia CEO pulled out of upcoming speaking engagements at the ElevenLabs Summit and Anthropic CEO Forum.
November 9-10, 2026: Details emerge about the business relationships between Nvidia and the alleged spy

Alice Huang and her family reportedly built a network of companies in China and Singapore to acquire Nvidia chips, including founding a Chinese company called Shanghai Century Litong. Founded in 2023, it became an Nvidia-preferred cloud partner, giving it priority access to chips, The Information reported. The Information also reported that Shanghai Century Litong facilitated buying $7.5 billion worth of Nvidia’s chips, including banned chips.

Nvidia’s head lawyer, Tim Teter, intervened in a 2025 U.S. government probe surrounding the suspected smuggling of AI chips by Megaspeed International, Bloomberg reported. Teter contacted Commerce Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler asking questions about whether the Trump administration played a role in detaining Alice Huang.
In early 2025, Alice Huang and a business partner sought China-based investors for an Asian data center, promising they had no problem in securing GPUs, the Financial Times reported.
November 8, 2026: Trump shows support for Nvidia CEO, calls him a “fine person”
On Sunday night, President Trump weighed in on Huang’s controversy and showed support for the Nvidia CEO.
“I have not spoken to him about it. I just know he’s a fine person, but you never know what’s going on,” Trump said.
When asked if Huang should remain chief of Nvidia, Trump said, “I think so. Oh yeah, sure.”
November 8, 2026: Huang admits to affair in public message to Nvidia employees; Nvidia board of directors begins investigation
Jensen Huang wrote in a letter to Nvidia employees — which was also published as a press release — that he cheated on his wife.
“I owe my family and all of you an apology,” Huang told his company. “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”
Huang did not mention Alice Huang by name in the message, but linked his infidelity to “the national security concerns raised in news reports.”

“Nvidia’s Board of Directors has initiated an independent investigation. I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American,” Huang wrote.
Nvidia shares slid over 5% the following day.
November 5, 2026: Three Republican committee chairmen ask Huang for closed-door briefing

Three Republican congressmen — Chairman John Moolenaar of the House Select Committee on China, Chairman Brian Mast of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, and Chairman Rick Crawford of the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence — sent a request to Huang for a closed-door joint briefing with their three committees.

“Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the [People’s Republic of China]’s access to sensitive U.S. technology and information,” the chairmen wrote. “The issue of PRC infiltration and access to cutting-edge U.S. technology is core to the investigative work of our three committees this Congress. It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk.”
October 29, 2026: Jensen Huang publicly revealed to have developed ‘close relationship’ with suspected Chinese spy
U.S. officials had been investigating Alice Huang and Megaspeed for more than a year when the New York Times broke the story in late October that the two executives also had a close relationship.
An Nvidia spokesperson denied that this relationship was something out of the ordinary.

“Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected. Meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year,” Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said. He added that “if the U.S. government believes that any person is a threat to American industry, it would let us know.”
Spring 2026: A secret memo circulates in the Trump administration about Nvidia CEO’s alleged relationship with Chinese spy

U.S. officials circulated a secret memo among policymakers that warned that Megaspeed’s Alice Huang, who had a relationship with Jensen Huang, was a spy for China’s Ministry of State Security. This memo was not public knowledge until it was later reported by the New York Times.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio supervised the drafting of the memo.
Late 2025: President Trump briefed on U.S. surveillance of Alice Huang and her relationship to Nvidia CEO but does not take action

Around the same time, per the New York Times’ report, U.S. President Donald Trump was briefed about intelligence findings that possible Chinese spy Alice Huang had formed a close relationship with Jensen Huang. Trump did not act on this information.
The Nvidia CEO, an ally of Trump, has repeatedly advocated for the U.S. government to let Nvidia expand its business in China.
October 2025: U.S. and Singapore each investigate Megaspeed over possible Chinese export violations

Megaspeed was confirmed to be under investigation by both the U.S. and Singaporean governments in October 2025. As a customer of Nvidia, Megaspeed was suspected of helping Chinese companies get around American embargoes on chip exports.

Megaspeed, a neocloud that used Nvidia chips, had been renting computing power to Chinese internet giant Alibaba and other Chinese companies, the Times reported. A Commerce Department official who had visited Megaspeed’s data center in Malaysia in 2024 had found a hoard of Nvidia equipment that was still packed in boxes and the concern was that this equipment was being directly shipped somewhere else, like China, rather than installed and sold as a cloud service.
Jensen Huang had been spotted socializing with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang as early as 2024 in Taiwan, where the Nvidia CEO was born.

These investigations into Megaspeed highlighted concerns about the degree to which Nvidia is able to track its chip exports. At the time, an Nvidia spokesperson told press that the company did not have “any reason to believe products had been diverted.”

“NVIDIA visited multiple Megaspeed sites yet again earlier this week and confirmed what we previously observed — Megaspeed is running a small commercial cloud, like many other companies throughout the world, as allowed by U.S. export control rules,” the Nvidia spokesperson said at the time.
