finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: K-Beauty Boom Becomes Wall Street’s Latest Investment Play
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Micah Barkley

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Korean beauty products have long filled American medicine cabinets. Now, a new exchange-traded fund is set to test whether there's room for them in US investors' portfolios as well.
Most Read from Bloomberg

This week, Guinness Atkinson Asset Management launched the Guinness Atkinson K-Beauty ETF (ticker KBTY), aimed at capitalizing on the rapid growth and popularity of South Korea's $15 billion "K-beauty" industry.

The fund holds shares of companies that might be unfamiliar to Wall Street investors but are fixtures on social media and behind the beauty counter. Amorepacific Corp., PharmaResearch Co. and Kolmar Korea Co. — some of its top holdings — own or manufacture products for widely recognized brands including Laneige, COSRX and Summer Fridays.

"The products tend to be very effective and good, and they tend to be cheaper," allowing them to "fill a sweet spot" with consumers, Jim Atkinson, chief executive officer of Guinness Atkinson, said in an interview. K-beauty is "going global very rapidly."

The bet is that K-beauty's popularity will translate into an investment theme that will catch fire with investors, even as other consumer-themed ETFs have stumbled. Working in its favor, the K-beauty trend does have considerable momentum.

South Korea exported $11.4 billion in cosmetics in 2025, a 12% jump from a year prior, according to the South Korean Ministry of Food and Drug Safety. The country also overtook the US as the world's second-largest cosmetics exporter in 2025, trailing only France, with the US becoming its largest cosmetics export market.

Still, in the world of ETFs, a popular consumer trend doesn't necessarily translate into a sticky investment. Issuers behind many such thematic ETFs have had a spotty record of trying to turn cultural niches and fads into long-term wins, as they often struggle to attract enough cash to survive.

"Investors have been really interested in tech, AI, and disruptive technology themes," said Roxanna Islam, head of sector and industry research at VettaFi, an index provider and financial-services firm. "It's a difficult environment for thematic ETFs outside of that range."

The graveyard of thematic ETFs is littered with funds that tried to draw on a popular fad but failed to gain enough investor attention to survive. So far, more than 320 ETFs have closed this year, with around two dozen of them being thematic ETFs.

One Korean-theme casualty is the US-listed Jakota KPOP & Korean Entertainment ETF (KPOP), which, prior to its liquidation last year, had been designed to capitalize on the global K-pop music phenomenon made popular by groups such as BTS and BLACKPINK. That fund only had $1.4 million in assets when it closed.
Similarly, the MUSQ Global Music Industry Index ETF (MUSQ) was meant to serve as a way for investors to tap into the global music industry, but it liquidated in October after just three years.

The more specific the theme, the harder it can be to attract enough assets to offset a fund's operating costs, creating a "shrinking floor working against you," said Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Athanasios Psarofagis. In the case of niche ideas like K-beauty and K-pop, being a fan doesn't necessarily mean wanting to invest in the companies behind them.
"I like certain musicians. Would I invest in their label? Those usually don't make good investments, so that's where the gap lies," Psarofagis said.

When it comes to the KBTY fund, Atkinson at Guinness Atkinson says the investment case is built on much more than the industry's social-media buzz. The ETF is also reaching beyond traditional cosmetics, including Korean medical-aesthetics companies such as PharmaResearch, Classys, and Hugel whose skin fillers and aesthetic treatments could benefit from the explosive popularity of health treatments like GLP-1 weight-loss drugs.
Atkinson said he expects the fund to appeal first to retail investors, but believes its growth potential could eventually draw institutional interest as well.
"I do believe that excitement, knowledge, and interest is going to grow," he said.

(Bloomberg) -- Drivers of nearly 721,000 BMW AG vehicles should park outside due to a defect that could cause a fire, the US National Highway Traffic Safety Administration said Friday.
Most Read from Bloomberg

BMW last week recalled 14 models from model years 2012 to 2018 over an improperly sealed electrical connector on the water pump that may be exposed to water and short circuit, increasing the risk of a fire while parked and turned off.

The vehicles were previously recalled in 2024 due to a water pump issue and must be repaired again. BMW identified 10 incidents that could be related to the issue in vehicles that had been repaired under the previous callback, NHTSA said. No crashes or injuries have been reported.
"If you have one of these vehicles, you should park your vehicle outside and away from buildings and other vehicles until the vehicle is repaired," the agency said in consumer alert on Friday.
The company does not yet have a fix available, though one is under development. Notifications are expected to be mailed starting December 25, NHTSA said.
BMW didn't immediately respond to a request for comment.

BMW is seeking to cut costs and overhaul its management ranks to contend with increasing competition from Chinese automakers. The German carmaker last week trimmed its profit outlook and laid out plans to boost production of its next-generation models to shore up profitability in the coming years.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.headline: DraftKings’ Predictions Bet Has Bulls Reeling From Sticker Shock
finance.yahoo.com/markets/stocks/article.author: Peyton Forte

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- DraftKings Inc.'s plans to pour money into prediction markets is worrying Wall Street analysts who view the lack of regulatory clarity as a key risk, spurring a flood of downgrades for the stock.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The sports betting company is accelerating spending to acquire more customers for its prediction-market product, DraftKings Predictions. That growth is coming at the expense of its near-term profitability goals, with the company reducing its adjusted Ebitda forecast for this year by $575 million at the midpoint and initiating a 2027 outlook that disappointed.
The weak print forced at least five brokers, including JPMorgan, Wells Fargo and UBS, to drop their once bullish positions and step to the sidelines.

"What surprised us was the construction of the investment. It's the operating expenses related to startup costs around new states that were significantly higher, both this year and next, than our expectations," Wells Fargo analyst Trey Bowers, who cut DraftKings shares to equalweight from overweight Monday, said in an interview.

Shares of the Boston, Massachusetts-based firm tumbled 21% after it reported results postmarket Nov. 5, marking its worst single-day plunge in four years. The stock is down roughly 45% this year, on track for its worst annual performance since 2022.

After the recent wave of downgrades, the number of analysts with buy-equivalent ratings on the stock dropped to 26, the fewest since February 2024. Still, roughly two-thirds of the 40 DraftKings analysts tracked by Bloomberg rate the stock a buy. The average price target of $25.88 assumes a roughly 35% increase from where the shares closed Thursday.

The post-earnings rout came as DraftKings raised this year's prediction-market-related investments target to $675 million from about $250 million, both at the midpoint. For 2027, the expected size of the investment rises another $300 million from there.

Platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket are facing mounting legal challenges as states argue sports-related trades skirt local gaming rules and taxes. Analysts say the fight could end up in the hands of the US Supreme Court within the next two years, which could outlaw sports event contracts altogether.

"We've become more cautious on the digital gaming sector as the year progresses as the competitive intensity, in terms of sales and marketing spend as well as promotional spend, has continued to escalate against a backdrop of a very uncertain future for prediction-market-based sports-betting," Bowers said.

DraftKings' earnings estimates have started to come down as Wall Street resets its expectations. The average Ebitda estimate for the current fiscal year has slumped 64% over the past week, according to data compiled by Bloomberg. Expectations for 2027 profits are down almost 19% in that same period.

Some on Wall Street are sticking with their bullish calls despite the recent weakness. Bernstein analyst Ian Moore says the traction that DraftKings Predictions is gaining justifies the price tag, with the company noting that October consumer volumes were up nearly three times since July.
Here are other notable analyst calls and commentary this week:

• William Blair upgraded shares of Advanced Micro Devices Inc. to outperform from market perform, saying that the chipmaker's stock has a runway from here as its largest competitor, Nvidia, contends with the ouster of its CEO. Oppenheimer also upgraded shares of AMD to outperform from market perform this week.
• General Mills shares were cut to neutral from overweight at Piper Sandler, with analyst Michael Lavery saying that the risk of a dividend cut is too high.
• Capricor Therapeutics Inc. shares were raised to buy from hold at Jones ahead of its PDUFA date later in the month, which presents an "attractive catalyst" despite regulatory risk.

haddyalchaer.com/jepa.headline: After 600 experiments, here's what I discovered about JEPA world models
haddyalchaer.com/jepa.author: Haddy Alchaer

paragraphs.text: World models · JEPA · Planning

There's a big debate in AI right now about what a world model should be. Most of the attention goes to generative world models, which predict the future by generating it, usually in pixels. Many scientists, including Yann LeCun, argue that this is wasted effort. Most of the pixels don't matter for deciding what to do, and many of them can't be predicted at all. [1]

The proposed alternative is JEPA, the joint-embedding predictive architecture. It has three parts: an encoder, a predictor and a planner. The encoder turns each frame of observation into a learned embedding, a compact vector that describes the scene. The predictor takes that embedding plus an action and predicts the embedding of the next frame. The planner then tries hundreds of action sequences inside the predictor and picks the one whose predicted end state lands closest to the embedding of the goal. The whole loop runs in embedding space, so the model only has to learn the parts of the scene that are important for deciding actions.

This year a team including LeCun released LeWM [2], a JEPA world model whose main benchmark is Push-T [3], a simulation where a robot pushes a gray T-shaped block across a table until the T sits in the green target position shown in a goal image. I've spent the last few months running 600 experiments on it.

The first thing I wanted to know was how much LeWM is held back by its predictions, so I started by swapping out the predictor for the simulator's perfect physics, while keeping everything else the same. I then gave both versions long-horizon tasks, with the goal 75 steps away, along with the same subgoals: frames from an expert demonstration, one every 25 steps. Vanilla LeWM succeeded 78% of the time. The version with true physics succeeded 77%. Along the kinds of paths it was trained on, LeWM's predictions are already as good as perfect physics for planning.
That means the next gains for a JEPA world model come from how the trained architecture is used, and that's where most of my 600 experiments went.

Without retraining the model once, I found four new planning methods. The first two together took LeWM's success rate on long-horizon tasks from 22% to 85%, about the same as a planner that is handed the ideal subgoals from an expert demonstration. The other two methods extend LeWM to harder goals, and one of them, a single change to how the goal is scored, raised the success rate by 60 points, three times as much as swapping in perfect physics did.
1. Plan through subgoals 25 steps apart

Used exactly as published, LeWM succeeds on 22% of long-horizon tasks, where the goal is 75 steps away. [2] When the goal is 25 steps away, it reaches it 89.7% of the time, within a point of the exact-physics version at 90.5%.

So the model is accurate over 25 steps and struggles over 75. The usual explanation is that small prediction errors compound over a long plan, which would call for a better model. I tested that against the alternative on the same 250 long-horizon tasks.

Exact physics added 20 points. Splitting the task into 25-step segments, each the length LeWM already handles almost perfectly, added nearly 60. LeWM's useful planning horizon is about 25 steps, so it was clear that the way to go further is to chain segments of that length together.

This is hierarchical planning: a high level picks subgoals and a low level reaches them. It's widely considered one of the main open problems for world models, and on Push-T it's worth three times as much as swapping in perfect physics.

Extra search doesn't substitute for it. Running the planner four times and keeping the lowest-cost plan took four times the compute and added less than one point, because the four runs almost always succeeded or failed together.
The subgoals in this experiment came from an expert demonstration, which a deployed robot won't have. The second method removes that dependence.
2. A latent memory graph with a cost on every jump

LeWM was trained on expert demonstrations of the task, and its encoder can embed every frame of them, giving about 460,000 embedded states that I connected into a graph. Each state links to the states that follow it in its own demonstration, and to states in other demonstrations that are close in embedding space. To solve a long-horizon task, the planner searches this graph for a path from the current state to the goal and uses the states along that path as subgoals.

This only works if distance in embedding space means something physical, and it does. Take one subgoal the robot can reach within 25 steps and one it can't, and LeWM's embedding distance ranks the reachable one as closer 87% of the time. So the embedding space doubles as a map of what the robot can reach.

The first version had a flaw. A jump between nearby states in two different demonstrations cost the same as a real step, so the search strung jumps together into paths the block could never follow (318 of 1,015 plans tried to use six or more jumps). The fix was adding a cost on every jump between demonstrations in the graph. Using nothing but LeWM's own embeddings of past demonstrations, success on the same 250 long-horizon tasks (goal 75 steps away) went from 62% to 85%, which is the same score received by the planner using expert subgoals. Can't get much better than that, right?
The standard Push-T test is easier than it looks

The caveat is that the standard test takes a demonstration, starts the robot partway through it, and sets the goal a fixed number of steps further along the same demonstration. That's a reasonable design, but in Push-T every demonstration ends with the block in the same place. So every test goal sits on a path that demonstrations already travel, heading for the spot they all end at. For 84% of the standard test's goals, the memory graph already held a nearly identical state from another demonstration.

The usual sample is also small. On the official 50 episodes, LeWM succeeded 68% of the time with the goal 50 steps away. On 250 fresh episodes drawn the same way, it succeeded only 44%. Changing nothing but the planner's random seed flipped 38 of 250 episodes between success and failure.

That's where I decided to build a harder test, where each task takes its start from one demonstration and its goal from another, so the robot has to travel between states that no single demonstration connects. It only counts as a success if the block stays on target for the last 10 steps. Under these rules the memory-graph planner succeeds 75% of the time on standard tasks and 45% on the new ones. The third and fourth methods I found work on that gap.
3. Fill gaps in memory with transformed memories
A memory graph is only as good as its coverage. When I deleted every stored state near the goal, success fell from 93% to 32%.

Push-T has a useful symmetry here. The physics of pushing a block doesn't change if you shift, rotate or mirror the whole table. So when the graph has no states near a goal, it can take demonstration segments from elsewhere, transform them to fit the gap, and plan through those. With these transformed segments, success came back to 85%. They also stretch a small memory a long way (a graph built from 1% of the demonstrations plus transformed copies did about as well as one built from 10%).

On the harder test, transformed segments raise success from 45% to 56%, and they help most where demonstrations are thinnest. When the goal lies in the direction the demonstrations flow, the memory-graph planner already succeeds 69% of the time. When it lies the opposite way, plain memory gets 27% and transformed memory gets 46%.
4. The cost was “wrong”

I also built an interactive demo where I could place the block anywhere and pick any goal. A goal has to be an image, and an image of the scene has to show the pusher somewhere, so I placed the pusher just behind the goal. In one run, the robot pushed the block to within 14 pixels of the target, close enough to count as solved. Then it pushed the block away from the goal, and kept moving the pusher toward where the pusher was in the goal image.

The goals in the harder test are frames from expert demonstrations, so each one also shows where the expert’s pusher happened to be at that moment. A planner that compares its prediction with the whole goal image is trying to put the pusher there too.

To measure how much this matters, I took the model out of the question. I ran the exact-physics planner twice on the same 50 tasks from the harder test, and the only difference was whether its cost included the pusher’s position as well as the block’s.

Thirty tasks went from failure to success when the pusher was left out, and none went the other way. A split like that happens by chance about twice in a billion. The physics here is from the actual simulator, not predicted, so the 4x in success comes from how the goal was created.

The planner that scored the pusher did exactly what it was asked. On the 30 tasks that flipped, it got the pusher to within half a pixel of where the goal image put it, and lost the block on the way. Placing both the T and the pusher in the exact goal position is a much harder problem to solve.

But LeWM can’t simply be told to ignore the pusher. It scores a plan by the distance between two embeddings, and its embedding of a goal image holds the block and the pusher together, with no part labeled “pusher”. So, as a test, I measured how far a planner gets by searching over the pusher instead. It compares each prediction against 16 versions of the goal image, all with the block in the same place and the pusher moved to positions taken from stored demonstrations, and keeps the closest match. That doubled LeWM’s success on the harder test, from 11% to 23%, without retraining.

This applies to any robot because a goal should just be a set of end states, not a copy of an image. “Put the cup on the shelf” is solved wherever the robot’s arm ends up, but a goal image picks one arm position and makes the planner match it. A good goal accepts every end state that solves the task, and still includes what the task needs from the robot, like coming to rest at the end.

The good news is that large sets of demonstrations already contain many real frames of the same object in the same place, each with the robot somewhere different. Scoring a plan against the closest of those goals allows for a larger set of valid end states to plan for.
What comes next
None of these four discoveries change the model's weights. They apply to LeWM as published, and they should carry over to larger JEPA world models that plan the same way, at no extra training cost.

The biggest open problem remaining is generalizing to tasks that don't have perfect demonstrations. On the harder Push-T test, the best planner holds the block on target 56% of the time, and most of the remaining failures are goals that run against the direction of the data. Closing that gap needs a higher level that can propose its own subgoals beyond the demonstrations, and do it better than today's learned hierarchies like H-JEPA [4], which so far match or slightly beat flat LeWM on Push-T.

Going in, I assumed LeWM's predictions would be the bottleneck, but a JEPA small enough to train in a few hours already predicts about as well as the simulator itself, and there are several gains that can be achieved simply by changing the way it plans. What it can't do yet is choose its own subgoals where no demonstration has been. That's what I'm currently working on, and if you want to see more, I'll post about it first on X, @haddyalchaer.
References
• [1] Y. LeCun, A Path Towards Autonomous Machine Intelligence. OpenReview, 2022.
• [2] L. Maes, Q. Le Lidec, D. Scieur, Y. LeCun, and R. Balestriero, LeWorldModel: Stable End-to-End Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture from Pixels. arXiv:2603.19312, 2026.
• [4] W. Zhang, B. Terver, M. Rabbat, Y. LeCun, and R. Balestriero, H-JEPA: End-to-End Learning of Hierarchical World Models for Visual Planning. arXiv:2610.06805, 2026.

cbsnews.com/news/microsoft-battling-majo.headline: Microsoft says it is seeing "continued recovery progress" as it battles major worldwide outage

paragraphs.text: From Asia to the U.S., a Microsoft outage involving services like Outlook and Teams has dragged on into a second day on Friday, impacting users, companies and government operations around the world.

The outage was affecting a wide range of Microsoft 365 offerings that interact with its Exchange Online and email services. Services including Outlook, Teams and AI assistant Copilot were reported by users to be down.

On Friday morning, the Redmond, Washington-based company said it was making "encouraging recovery progress," noting improvements in email delivery. However, users may still experience "intermittent issues" as the company continues its recovery efforts, Microsoft said.
The company also reported "broader improvements" in North America and "sustained improvements across much of Europe," as well as "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia-Pacific region.

"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," Microsoft said Friday on X. "We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. "

The outage affected Microsoft's suite of business products, as well as those geared toward personal use for individuals, students and families. Users in more than 70 countries and territories experienced disruptions, according to Downdetector, a website that tracks technology outages.

"Microsoft in a Friday the 13th moment as global outage [causes] a very bad day in Redmond," Yorkville Ives and Co. tech analyst Dan Ives said in an X post Friday. "There will be major questions for MSFT in this global outage."

Microsoft said the outage was linked to a technical issue, not malicious or cyber activity. In an update posted Friday at 11:40 a.m. EST, the company said it had resolved the underlying issue and was working on restoring service to its customers.
Microsoft promised to issue a full incident report after it finished its review of the outage.
Widespread impact

Microsoft first flagged technical issues just before 1 p.m. Eastern time Thursday. The company updated users about its recovery progress through a series of posts on its Microsoft 365 Status X account.
More than 130,000 users reported issues with Microsoft on Thursday, Downdetector's website shows. However, those reports started to wane by Friday morning as Microsoft worked to restore its services.
The outage disrupted email for hours, hampering work activity for some employees.
"It's just challenging sending reports or things that needed to be approved," one woman told CBS News Los Angeles.
However, some took delight in the slowdown, with social users posting videos celebrating the freedom of not having access to email.
It's unclear how many people were impacted. Over 430 million people use Microsoft 365 apps, according to Microsoft's website.
Companies worldwide report issues

OpenAI and Anthropic each reported problems connecting to Microsoft 365 tools, underscoring the ripple effects of outages as more people use artificial intelligence platforms to interact with other companies' software.
U.S.-based industrial technology company Workhorse Group Inc. delayed a conference call on its quarterly earnings because of the outage.
In Australia, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Friday Microsoft had likened the widespread outage to the CrowdStrike outage in 2024.
Burke said he had spoken to Microsoft's top executive in Australia and the government's national cybersecurity coordinator about the global disruption.

"They (Microsoft) don't believe they are dealing with a cyberattack. They believe that they are dealing in some ways (with something) similar to what we saw with respect to CrowdStrike where there is an update that has gone awry," Burke told reporters in Sydney.

Texas-based cybersecurity company CrowdStrike blamed a bug in an update that allowed its systems to push bad data out to millions of customer computers, setting off a global tech outage in July 2024 that grounded flights, took TV broadcasts off the air and disrupted banks, hospitals and retailers.

Hong Kong businessperson Danny Lau, who runs an aluminum firm, said his company's Outlook accounts couldn't receive updates from its U.S. customers due to the outage. If the situation dragged on further, this could "impact the production timeline," he said.

Air India said its flight operations were unaffected by the Microsoft outage. However, it temporarily rerouted its email services to ensure customer queries continued to reach the airline without interruption, the company said in a statement.

IndiGo, another Indian airline company, said it also reported disruptions to its email support services, which affected its ability to receive customer queries. The airline in a statement on X said its other support channels remained operational and its flight operations were unaffected.
Singapore's Government Technology Agency said government email services were down and that it is working with Microsoft to resolve the issue.
The Philippines' Supreme Court said in a statement on social media that the ongoing Microsoft 365 service outage has affected some of its operations, including email responses.
In Japan, Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki said the outage impacted the government's IT infrastructure and that officials were "keeping a close eye on the developments."

techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/export-banned-.headline: Export-banned Nvidia chips are behind China’s most powerful AI models—uh oh, Jensen!
techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/export-banned-.author: Tim Fernholz

paragraphs.text: The leading open-weight models developed by Chinese companies were trained on Nvidia chips that the US government restricted from shipping to its largest geopolitical rival, a new research effort claims.

The apparently widespread access to Blackwell GPUs among Chinese frontier labs shows the magnitude of the problem facing the leading chip designer. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang left the company this week after admitting to his affair with Alice Huang, executive of Megaspeed, a company implicated in smuggling Nvidia chips into China. Alice Huang has also been alleged to be an agent of China’s intelligence service.

While Jensen Huang’s relationships with a customer and two employees have drawn the most public interest, Nvidia’s potential corporate liability for export control violations likely factored into its decision to part ways with Huang.

US export controls are intended to protect the country’s leadership in AI capabilities against China, but Huang has long sought to open up that market. Blackwell GPUs are banned from export to China or Chinese-owned firms, while the Trump administration allows Nvidia to export the H200, a less powerful chip, provided shipments take a circuitous shipping route that allows the US to claim a 25% tariff.

Will DePue, a former OpenAI researcher who leads the nonprofit research group Unemployment Labs, analyzed the weights—the unique structure—of large language models released openly by DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group. The weights still reflect the configurations of the chips used to train them, and DePue was able to find compelling evidence that the most closely watched models, including Moonshot’s Kimi’s K3 releases and DeepSeek’s V4 models, bear fingerprints from training on Blackwell chips.

White House technology adviser Michael Kratsios said earlier this year that Moonshot had used export-banned Nvidia chips, citing US intelligence sources. Epoch AI, a nonprofit research organization, estimates that about two million advanced chips entered China in 2024 and 2025 through schemes designed to hide their final destination.

That doesn’t mean that these models were trained entirely on Nvidia chips, or that export control laws were necessarily violated; the chips could have been in an offshore data center, which has proven a popular way for Chinese firms to access compute and driven an industrial revolution in Malaysia. Epoch’s data estimates that 275,000 Nvidia AI accelerators were imported to Malaysia in 2024 and 2025.

However, the ostensible goal of the export bans is to prevent exactly that: Chinese AI labs training on the most powerful chips. China hawks have long called for stronger controls on who uses chips, not just who owns them or where they are installed.

“If we care about the U.S. tech edge, it doesn’t make any sense to me that you would not allow Chinese companies to access chips in mainland China or Hong Kong and Macau, but then say, actually, if you just go over to Malaysia, you can do whatever you want,” Sam Bresnick, a researcher at the Georgetown Center for Security and Emerging Technology, told TechCrunch this summer.

Megaspeed, the company led by Alice Huang, has been at the center of that trade for several years through its subsidiary Speedmatrix, and has been the subject of investigations by both the US and Singaporean government. Friday, Bloomberg also reported that a company with links to Alice Huang was involved in smuggling banned Nvidia chips to a data center in Shanghai.

In May, the short-selling research firm Culper published a report arguing that Nvidia had a “China problem” because a significant share of its revenue was driven by Chinese demand, either through remote data centers or smuggling in violation of US law. It detailed Megaspeed’s relationship with Nvidia and alleged that Alice Huang’s companies are backed by Chinese firms that are barred from accessing US chips.

Ironically, short-seller Culper’s bet against Nvidia wasn’t driven by the expectation of a US government crackdown. Instead, it was focused on the Chinese government’s response to the bans, which was to recommit to its domestic chip industry.

If China succeeds, billions of dollars in Chinese demand for Nvidia chips could dry up. Some 600,000 H200 chips are reportedly stockpiled in Hong Kong, awaiting shipment into China. While Chinese companies might want the chips, observers have no consensus on why they’ve haven’t been cleared for import.

Graham Webster, a research scholar at Stanford who focuses on US-China technology policy, said he doesn’t buy the idea that holding the chips back would drive domestic production, since demand for chips is so large. Other theories for the hold-up include preparation for a potential trade deal that would involve importing a large volume of US goods, or concerns about potential surveillance technology in the chips.

For now, US companies have limited obligations to track what their customers do with controlled goods like AI chips. However, Jensen Huang’s personal and professional entanglements with Alice Huang create a much bigger problem for Nvidia if government investigators confirm that chip smuggling took place and that he was aware of it. Nvidia and Huang have both vouched for Megaspeed’s data centers, saying Nvidia officials had visited them to confirm they were legitimate.

The US government’s treatment of Nvidia and Megaspeed is also under scrutiny. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, who oversees the agencies that licensing chip exports, could reportedly lose his job after reports that his investigators failed to uncover suspicious chip buyers and were too cozy with Nvidia officials.
When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission. This doesn’t affect our editorial independence.

latimes.com/entertainment-arts/business/.headline: Savannah Guthrie extends her contract with NBC News
latimes.com/entertainment-arts/business/.author: Cerys Davies

paragraphs.text: With 15 years under her belt at NBC, Savannah Guthrie is sticking with the “Today” show.

The morning show anchor recently extended her contract with NBC News. The network confirmed her extension to The Times on Friday. Her current contract was reportedly expected to end later this year or in early 2027. It’s unclear how long her extension is.
The news combats the idea that Guthrie will be taking a step back from the public eye, after the tragic abduction of her mother, Nancy, earlier this year.

Guthrie first joined the “Today” show in 2011 as a co-host in the third hour and as NBC News’ chief legal analyst. By 2012, she was promoted to co-anchor of the show. Over the years, she has become a key fixture on the No. 1 morning broadcast news show. In addition to covering the daily news, she was among a panel of the network’s hosts anchoring midterm election night coverage and has interviewed movie stars, athletes and presidents alike.
The “Today” show is currently led by Guthrie, Craig Melvin, Al Roker, Carson Daly, and Jenna Bush Hager. Daly recently expanded his role at NBC News, as he was named co-anchor of “Saturday Today.”

On top of her “Today” show duties, Guthrie is also set to co-host the upcoming Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade alongside Roker and former “Today” co-host Hoda Kotb. In the coming months, she is poised to lead a new NBC game show, based on the popular New York Times “Wordle” game.

As much of the broadcast landscape continues to morph in the streaming era, Comcast is expected to spin off NBCUniversal in the coming months. The company will then operate as a separate publicly traded company. Comcast already offloaded its cable channels, like MS NOW, CNBC, and USA, into a separate company called Versant earlier this year.
L.A. Times Staff Writer Stephen Battaglio contributed to this report.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwg7l8n7dx5mo.headline: Pope Leo visits the Peruvian city that has embraced him as one of its own
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cwg7l8n7dx5mo.author: José Carlos Cueto

paragraphs.text: BBC News Mundo in Chiclayo, Peru
Pope Leo XIV has celebrated mass near the Peruvian city where he made his name as a compassionate bishop who worked closely with poor and migrant communities.
The ceremony was held on Friday at a park in Pimentel, about 10km (six miles) from Chiclayo in northern Peru as part of his tour of Latin America.
The Vatican estimates more than 1.5 million people gathered to welcome the pontiff.
"Thank you for your affection, support and prayers," the Pope told followers.
"Especially for my health during this time of trial which, with God's help, I am overcoming," he added, referencing the surgery he had for lung cancer which took place just weeks ago.
Some of the crowd arrived 12 hours in advance to wait in vigil before the mass began.
"We spent the night praying, alongside family, excited to welcome the Pope from Chiclayo," said Isa Orderique.
Many came from across Peru and even neighbouring countries to attend.
Merli Cruz Guerrero, from an area near the Ecuadorean border, travelled several hours by bus to attend. She also spent the entire night waiting.
Of all the events the Pope has attended so far during his visit to Peru, this felt particularly emotional.
The crowd fell into a hushed silence as the pontiff's motorcade approached.
They waited eagerly for his arrival despite spending long hours out in the open with the temperature pushing past 30C.
For many living here, the fact that the Pope worked extensively in this region before becoming the head of the Catholic Church has put them in the spotlight.
"The Pope has come home and Chiclayo is celebrating," said Lisbeth Díaz, a teacher who worked with Pope Leo when he served as the city's bishop between 2015 and 2023.
Peru is the longest stop on the first tour of Latin America by the pontiff, who was elected in May 2025.
The trip has also taken in Argentina and Uruguay, but his time in this country carries particular significance.
The Pope not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities.
Around Chiclayo, it is hard to meet anyone who doesn't claim to be a friend of the Pope or have a special anecdote about him.
Some recall how he would enjoy sampling Peruvian delicacies at El Trébol, a restaurant next to the city's cathedral. Others remember his love of tennis.
But for many it's the more serious moments of his time here, such as helping launch soup kitchens during the Covid-19 pandemic, or wading through deep waters on horseback when floods hit the area.
Several of these images are on display in a small museum dedicated to him at the entrance to the bishop's residence.
But for the city, and for a country that calls him the "Peruvian Pope", his return home means much more than a collection of photographs and anecdotes.

"It is the return of the man who brought Peruvians closer to the Church," said Samuel David Miranda Atoche, a local parish priest from Chiclayo who was ordained by the Pope back when he was still the bishop and known under his birth name of Robert Prevost.
And it is not just local people he connected with, according to Díaz, who came to Chiclayo from Venezuela.

"It was difficult for him to see so many migrants living on the streets," she added, recalling the time when large numbers of Venezuelans came through Chiclayo escaping the political and economic crisis in their home country.
"So, he got in touch with the migration authorities and coordinated with other organisations to speed up the paperwork needed for many of us to obtain legal residency and work permits."

Robert Prevost's time here as bishop also involved difficult decisions, such as having to deal with the controversy and scandal surrounding the dissolution of Sodalitium of Christian Life, a Peruvian Catholic organisation that had faced decades of sexual abuse allegations.

Santiago Roncagliolo, a Peruvian writer and journalist who has studied the Pope's life, believes his handling of that crisis earned him the favour of his predecessor, Pope Francis, and helped set him on the path to the papacy.
Father David also stressed the role the now-pontiff played in bringing people together.
"If there is one thing Bishop Prevost worked for here," he added, referring to the Pope by his previous title, "it was unity".
That unity has been on display in the run up to the mass, with the square in front of Chiclayo Cathedral filled with joyous celebrations for days.
Normally, 800,000 people live in the city and its surrounding area, but estimates say the Pope's visit has caused that to double.
Local businesses have been capitalising on the Pope's popularity to boost sales and hotels have sharply increased their nightly room rates.
But that didn't seem to put off the faithful who gathered for the mass.
Shouts of: "The Pope is from Chiclayo!" echoed across the field during the event.
Their affection was clearly reflected by the pontiff.
"As I look at your faces, a prayer of thanksgiving to the Lord arises in my heart," he said from the stage, "for the blessing you have been and continue to be in my life."

cnbc.com/2026/11/13/howard-lutnick-nvidi.headline: Lutnick faces questions over Nvidia spy scandal. His sons’ firm has deep ties to the chipmaker
cnbc.com/2026/11/13/howard-lutnick-nvidi.author: Luke Fountain

paragraphs.text: In late September, Cantor Fitzgerald hosted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and other top executives from the chipmaker for investor meetings in New York, according to a Cantor research report reviewed by CNBC.
The Wall Street firm liked what it heard.

"We continue to view NVDA as the best risk/reward in our coverage," Cantor analyst C.J. Muse and his colleagues wrote in a research report dated Oct. 3 that maintained a $350 price target and overweight rating on the stock.

Yet the firm formerly run by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and now led by his sons, Brandon and Kyle, reported a nearly 50% decline in the number of Nvidia shares it held between September 2025 and March 2026, according to a CNBC analysis of securities filings that excludes options. Nvidia had been one of the largest stock positions reported in Cantor's filings.

The decline coincided with White House and U.S. intelligence officials pressing Lutnick to crack down on Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company suspected of funneling Nvidia's advanced artificial intelligence chips to China. Lutnick repeatedly resisted those efforts, according to Axios.

By the time Cantor hosted Huang in New York, Lutnick had also received a classified intelligence warning, according to Axios, about Huang's ties to a suspected Chinese spy and had appeared alongside the CEO at a G20 technology summit in North Carolina.

Even as Cantor pared back its Nvidia stake, it continued doing business across the chipmaker's AI empire. A CNBC review of securities filings, corporate announcements and Wall Street research found the firm has helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for Nvidia's business partners while maintaining close ties to the chipmaker's leadership.

Those ties have drawn fresh scrutiny following Huang's resignation Thursday and Axios' reporting that Lutnick repeatedly resisted a crackdown on companies suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, despite President Donald Trump authorizing new export restrictions on those companies for a third time on Nov. 5.
An ethics expert said the relationship between Lutnick and his former firm's investments may raise questions, given what the secretary knew about Nvidia.

Richard Painter, the former chief White House ethics lawyer for President George W. Bush and now a corporate law professor at the University of Minnesota said that while "there's no proof of" Lutnick sharing nonpublic information with Cantor Fitzgerald, "the appearance doesn't look great."
"His conversations with his sons better be about publicly available information," Painter told CNBC.

There is no evidence that Lutnick's sons had advance knowledge of the intelligence concerns, that changes in Cantor's reported holdings were tied to any warnings or that the firm's business interests influenced their father's decisions.

"Cantor has to date from time to time had only immaterial stand-alone proprietary positions in Nvidia, unlike the positions reflected in 13F filings which were entered into in the ordinary course of business in connection with client swap transactions, that are common in institutional markets," a Cantor spokesperson told CNBC.

Cantor declined to answer CNBC's other questions. The Commerce Department, the White House, Howard Lutnick and his sons did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment or detailed questions about the findings.

As scrutiny of Huang intensified, Cantor Chairman Brandon Lutnick was publicly praising the chipmaker's leadership. "Nvidia is one of the great companies on the planet, and they have an amazing leadership team," Brandon Lutnick told Fox Business on Wednesday.
Trump is standing by Howard Lutnick. A White House official told Reuters on Thursday that the president maintains "complete confidence" in the commerce secretary.

But cracks in the administration's unity emerged Friday, when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that the Departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months."

Bessent pointed to Commerce as the department responsible for imposing the entity list, which identifies restricted businesses and other groups, adding, "You will have to ask them about their internal processes."
A shrinking Nvidia position

Nvidia was Cantor's second-largest reported stock position before Howard Lutnick left Wall Street to become commerce secretary in February 2025, behind only bitcoin investor MicroStrategy, now known as Strategy. At the end of 2024, the firm disclosed more than 3.5 million Nvidia shares worth $479 million, according to its quarterly securities filing.

That share count held steady through September 2025, but its value climbed 36% to $652 million, according to Cantor's quarterly securities filing, as the Trump administration moved over the summer to ease restrictions on Nvidia's H20 chip sales to China.

Over the following six months, however, the number of Nvidia shares Cantor reported holding fell by 49%, to 3 million in December and 1.78 million by the end of March 2026, with their value dropping from $652 million to $310 million, according to a CNBC analysis of securities filings.

Pressure on Howard Lutnick was also mounting on Capitol Hill. Sens. Jim Banks, R-Ind., and Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., in March urged the secretary to suspend or reconsider Nvidia's export licenses after three people linked to Nvidia customer Super Micro Computer were indicted on charges of conspiring to smuggle AI chips to China.

"The Trump administration, I think, leaks like a sieve when it comes to non-public government information getting to various hedge fund guys," Painter said, though he stressed there is no evidence Howard Lutnick had shared such information with his sons.

The filings do not establish why Cantor's reported share count fell or whether its overall financial exposure to Nvidia declined. Nvidia’s stock had more than doubled from its April 2025 lows by late October, before retreating in the following months. The stock fell about 6.5% between the end of September and the end of March.
Cantor's reported Nvidia holdings remained near that lower level through June 30, the latest quarter covered by public disclosures, at 1.81 million shares. Its next quarterly filing is due Monday.
Cantor has not publicly explained the decline.

Most of those shares were attributed to CF Secured, a Cantor brokerage subsidiary that uses stocks and derivatives to hedge customer transactions, according to its audited financial statements. Cantor also disclosed substantial Nvidia options positions during the time period CNBC examined, overwhelmingly skewed toward put options, which can protect against declines in the stock price.
Classified warnings and a $3 billion deal

As concerns about Huang escalated inside the Trump administration in May, according to Axios, Cantor was helping finance the expansion of one of Nvidia's newest business partners, securities filings show.

On May 7, Nvidia and Australia-based cloud computing provider IREN announced a five-year, $3.4 billion cloud computing contract and a strategic partnership giving the chipmaker the right to invest up to $2.1 billion in IREN.
"That's not a passive financial investment. Nvidia is a partner who wins as we deliver," IREN co-CEO Daniel Roberts told investors on the company's quarterly earnings call that day.

Five days later, as Trump headed to China aboard Air Force One, Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned him about Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, The New York Times reported on Tuesday. Huang, who had not initially been invited on the trip, joined the president's delegation during a refueling stop in Alaska.
Howard Lutnick had already been sent a highly classified intelligence memo detailing concerns about Huang's relationship, Axios reported.

On May 12, the day Trump departed for China, IREN announced the pricing of a convertible bond offering that ultimately raised $3 billion when it closed two days later. Cantor was one of seven bookrunners on the deal, alongside JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs.

On the day the offering closed, May 14, Lutnick's Commerce Department quietly cleared roughly 10 Chinese companies, including Alibaba and ByteDance, to buy Nvidia's advanced H200 chips, though some of those approvals predated the intelligence memo.
It is unclear when IREN hired Cantor for the offering or how much the firm earned from the deal. Cantor declined to answer CNBC's questions about its work with IREN.
Still, Cantor reported a substantial position in IREN's stock.

By the end of June, Cantor reported $115 million in IREN shares and $362 million in Nvidia shares. Together, the two companies accounted for more than 9% of the value of Cantor's reported $5.2 billion in securities holdings, excluding options, according to CNBC's analysis of the filing.
Cantor didn't answer CNBC's questions about its work with IREN.
Beyond the stock
IREN was not the only company in Nvidia's orbit that turned to Cantor for financing.

In October 2025, Cantor advised AI infrastructure developer Lancium on a $600 million financing deal to support its data center campus in Abilene, Texas, the first site of Stargate, the massive AI infrastructure project backed by OpenAI, SoftBank and Oracle.
Newmark, a commercial real estate firm controlled by Cantor, also helped finance the Abilene campus, arranging a $7.1 billion construction loan in May 2025.

Ten months later, Nvidia agreed to invest $2 billion for a roughly 20% stake in Lancium, with up to $1 billion more tied to future milestones, The Information reported in August. Lancium, which is also backed by Blackstone, confirmed an investment and a technology partnership on Aug. 24 without disclosing financial terms.
It's unclear whether Cantor continued advising Lancium after the financing deal or played a role in Nvidia's investment. Neither Cantor nor Lancium responded to questions about the investment.
Cantor's reported ties also extend to Nvidia's supply chain.

In May 2025, days after Howard Lutnick announced the transfer of his ownership stake in Cantor to his children via trusts, Semafor reported that bankers at the firm had informally advised executives at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., which makes Nvidia's most advanced chips, on navigating Washington. Cantor called Semafor's report "baseless and false."
TSMC received billions of dollars in federal subsidies created during the Biden administration and administered by the Commerce Department to fund its U.S. manufacturing expansion.
Democratic senators called for an ethics investigation in December into whether the Lutnick family stood to benefit from his push to expand AI data centers.

And on Wednesday, Sens. Warren and Chris Coons, D-Del., demanded that Howard Lutnick, Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller preserve records on Nvidia's chip exports to China and intelligence warnings about Huang.
The senators questioned whether "prudent defensive counter-intelligence action was taken or national security recommendations were overruled."

"The place where I think the Trump administration has most failed here is in being persuaded by Jensen Huang and others to license the export of some advanced chips," Coons said Friday on CNBC's "Squawk Box," accusing the administration of turning a blind eye to the black market for more advanced chips.

cnbc.com/2026/11/13/robinhood-supreme-co.headline: Supreme Court will hear Robinhood effort to toss IPO info omissions lawsuit
cnbc.com/2026/11/13/robinhood-supreme-co.author: Dan Mangan

paragraphs.text: The Supreme Court on Friday agreed to consider an effort by Robinhood to block a class-action lawsuit over the company's omission of interim financial data from the online broker's initial public offering in 2021.

Robinhood wants the Supreme Court to overturn a ruling by the 9th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals that revived a lawsuit by investors against the company and firms involved with the IPO, including Goldman Sachs and J.P. Morgan Securities.
A San Francisco federal court judge had previously dismissed the lawsuit.
The Trump administration had urged the Supreme Court to hear Robinhood's appeal.

In its order granting Robinhood's request, the Supreme Court said it would focus solely on the question of whether a company that issues stock can be found liable under the misleading-omissions prong of Section 11(a) of the Securities Act of 1933 based on a determination that the issuer failed to disclose interim financial information that is material within the meaning of Section 11(a), without an additional inquiry to determine whether the omission rendered any affirmative statement misleading.
Robinhood's IPO came on the heels of a surge in investor interest during the Covid-19 pandemic of so-called meme stocks, and trading in the crypto asset Dogecoin.

In July 2021, Robinhood conducted its IPO, "for which it prepared a registration statement" that "contained only limited information about Robinhood's performance during the second quarter of 2021," the 9th Circuit panel that heard the case noted.
"After the initial public offering, Robinhood reported financial results from that second quarter, and its stock price dropped," the panel wrote.
The investors who sued Robinhood and the other defendants alleged that the registration statement omitted material information that was legally required to be disclosed.

npr.org/2026/11/13/g-s1-153578/whats-tru.headline: What's Trump's strategy now with Iran? To keep things as they are
npr.org/2026/11/13/g-s1-153578/whats-tru.author: Aya Batrawy

paragraphs.text: DUBAI, United Arab Emirates — President Donald Trump is confronting new realities nine months into the war with Iran that leave him with dwindling options to ending the conflict.
On Thursday, he waved away the need for a deal with Iran, saying the U.S. has billions of Iran's dollars frozen in overseas accounts.
"We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We've got their money," he wrote in a Truth Social post.

Negotiations with Iran are stuck with mediator Qatar working to bridge the divide. Trump met Qatar's prime minister at the White House this week, and said afterward that Gulf Arab allies prefer "the status quo" of continued economic pressure on Iran. He wrote that while the U.S. remains "locked and loaded", an attack at this point "seems to be quite unlikely."
That's a pivot from his threats to carry out quick, intense strikes on Iran in the days before he had to contend with two election setbacks.
Trump's wartime ally, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, whom he'd thrown his support behind, is on the cusp of being ousted from power after elections there.

Meanwhile, at home, Trump's party lost its majority in Congress in midterm elections. Vice President JD Vance blamed Republican losses on the unpopular war with Iran and the nature of U.S. relations with Israel.
With less room to room maneuver and Iran still defiant, Trump's strategy appears to be to keep things as they are, for now. That means the possibility of escalation still looms.

Senior UAE diplomat, Anwar Gargash, told an audience in Abu Dhabi this week the region must "prepare for a prolonged period of uncertainty, in which neither a decisive resolution nor a stable regional order can be taken for granted."
Here's what keeping the status quo looks like.
Iran's chokehold on the Strait of Hormuz persists

Official Iranian social media accounts frequently post videos of attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz for violating Iran's new rules requiring permission to navigate the waterway, which was open and free to ships before the war.

The U.S., meanwhile, is assisting oil tankers through the Strait of Hormuz using a route that's close to Oman's coastline. While this has helped Arab states export their oil, it does not solve the bigger problem of how to bring back the pre-war production levels of other vital products like liquified natural gas, fertilizer and aluminum. Nor does a status quo allow countries like Kuwait, Qatar and Bahrain to import goods to their ports.

The International Monetary Fund says Gulf Arab states are in economic recession as a result of the war, despite higher oil prices. It says Kuwait, Qatar and Iraq's economies are contracting approximately 16% this year. Bahrain's is down 11%.
More limited strikes that could rapidly escalate
The U.S. is sending a third aircraft carrier with thousands of troops to the region, leaving open the possibility of another planned military escalation.
This week, Iran unveiled what it says is a new underground missile production site.
The U.S. and Iran are also still occasionally carrying out tit-for-tat for strikes.

On Friday, Iranian media said the U.S. struck one of its islands in the Strait of Hormuz. It's an area where Iran has radars and drone launch sites. Iran's Revolutionary Guard said it hit back, targeting an early warning U.S. radar in Bahrain.
Iran remains economically battered, starved of oil revenue
Secretary of State Marco Rubio told reporters this week there's no need for military action against Iran at this stage because economic sanctions are doing the job.
"The pain that they're feeling is, eventually you have to eat. Eventually you have to be able to pay your own fighters and your own security forces," Rubio said.

There's also a U.S. naval blockade at sea barring Iranian ships from transporting oil to countries like China. This blockade, according to the U.S. military, has cut Iran off from at least $25 billion in revenue so far.

One of the biggest economic blows, though, has come from the United Arab Emirates. The UAE announced over the summer it was severing all economic and trade ties with Iran. The UAE had been among Iran's biggest trade partners and local bank accounts were allegedly used by Iran's supreme leader and Revolutionary Guard to move money around.

Meanwhile, the U.S. military's Central Command announced a new operation, dubbed "Iron Gate", with other U.S. government agencies, aimed at preventing Iran from using land routes to transport advanced weapons across its borders and the Caspian Sea.
War in Yemen intensifies, draws in more countries
Another consequence of the conflict with Iran is the resumption of all-out war between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis in Yemen.

The Houthis, who are not a direct proxy of Iran but are supported by it, say Saudi airstrikes across Yemen have killed scores of people in past months, including nearly 60 this past weekend, many of them women and children in a village near the capital Sana'a.

Saudi Arabia, meanwhile, faces daily missile and drone attacks by Houthis, including some this week that hit its key East-West pipeline carrying crude oil to bypass the Strait of Hormuz. Another Houthi attack hit Saudi oil company Aramco's skyscraper headquarters in Riyadh's financial district.

Deadly Houthi attacks on Saudi airports have led to flights and high-profile events being cancelled. https://www.npr.org/2026/11/02/nx-s1-6007693/wars-in-iran-and-yemen-dent-saudi-modernization-mega-projects
As the Yemen war drags on, Pakistan, Turkey and Egypt are among the countries entering the fray with defensive support to Saudi Arabia. The U.S. is assisting with intelligence on the Houthis.
The United Nations says some 330,000 Yemenis have been displaced by the renewed fighting between the Houthis and the Saudi-backed Yemeni government, exacerbating an already dire humanitarian crisis.
Efforts by mediators continue, neither side budges
Iran says it's prepared for a short-term pause on attacks on ships in the Strait of Hormuz, but insists that seven demands be met before entering into direct talks over its nuclear program.
"The message has been only one thing. These seven items are on the table. Take it or leave it," Hamidreza Gholamzade, Tehran municipality spokesperson, told NPR.

These demands include lifting sanctions, ending the naval blockade, unfreezing Iran's dollars in overseas accounts and enforcing a ceasefire across all fronts, which includes halting Israeli attacks in Lebanon and Gaza.
Rubio has described the conditions as "absurd".

There's also discussion on diluting and moving Iran's enriched uranium abroad. However, the head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, told Iran's state broadcaster Wednesday: "We will not remove even a shred of enriched nuclear material from Iran."
It's another indication of the gridlock.
NPR's Hadeel al-Shalchi in Antalya, Turkey, and Ahmed Abu Hamada in Cairo contributed reporting.

cnbc.com/2026/11/13/retirement-401k-ira-.headline: Retirees sometimes tap savings for one-off expenses. Here’s what advisors say to consider first
cnbc.com/2026/11/13/retirement-401k-ira-.author: Sarah Agostino

paragraphs.text: Retirees facing a large expense that's not in their regular household budget may turn to their traditional 401(k) or individual retirement account balances to cover it.
While retirement savings may be the easiest place to turn for the money, financial advisors say there are a few things worth considering before making one-off withdrawals.

"Be aware of the fact that it's not as simple as just taking out the amount of money that [covers] what you want it for," said certified financial planner Victoria Trumbower, managing member of Trumbower Financial Advisors in Bethesda, Maryland. The firm ranked No. 19 on CNBC's Financial Advisor 100 list for 2026.

At the same time, research shows that many retirees aren't even spending their nest egg. About a third still have 100% or more of their initial assets when they reach their mid-80s, according to a May study by the Employee Benefit Research Institute, a nonpartisan research group.

"Retirement savings are meant to be spent," said CFP Alex Canellopoulos, director of wealth and a partner with Vista Capital Partners in Portland, Oregon. "A one-time withdrawal isn't necessarily a bad decision, as long as it fits within a sustainable retirement plan."
Unplanned withdrawals often go toward debt

In 2025, about 15% of 401(k) owners ages 60 to 72 with balances of at least $100,000 who had left their employer made an ad hoc withdrawal from their account, according to Vanguard's How America Retires 2026 report, which analyzed more than 125,000 ex-plan participants.

This age group falls between the onset of penalty-free withdrawals — age 59½ — and the threshold for starting required minimum distributions — currently age 73. RMDs are amounts that retirees must withdraw annually from traditional 401(k)s and IRAs.

Not all 401(k) plans allow occasional withdrawals from ex-employees — about 43% did in 2025, up from 16% in 2015, the Vanguard study says. If a plan doesn't offer such ad hoc distributions, a former employee who wants to tap that money would have to withdraw or roll over the entire balance. Typically, they roll it over to an IRA and take withdrawals from there.

The most common reasons for retirees taking irregular distributions, based on a 2025 Vanguard survey of 8,000 clients noted in the recent report, are paying off debt, with 31% of respondents citing it; covering unforeseen expenses such as medical care and home repairs, noted by 23%; and discretionary spending, with 22% citing it as a reason.
Don't overlook the tax hit
Regardless of why you take the money, advisors say a key consideration is the impact on your tax situation.

Distributions from a traditional 401(k) or IRA are generally taxed as ordinary income. If you don't have other means to cover the tax bill, you may have to withdraw extra from your retirement account to compensate — which creates a tricky situation.

"It's like a double whammy because you have to pay income tax, but you don't have any money to pay income tax, so you've got to withdraw more money to pay the tax, and then you've got to pay taxes" on the extra amount, Trumbower said.
It's going to cost you a lot more than you think.Victoria TrumbowerManaging member of Trumbower Financial Advisors

For illustration: If you need $50,000 after taxes and assume a combined federal and state income tax rate of 25%, the math says you would need to withdraw about $66,667. That's because the money withdrawn to cover the tax bill is itself taxable. A $66,667 withdrawal taxed at 25% would result in about $16,667 in taxes, leaving $50,000 after tax.
"It's going to cost you a lot more than you think," Trumbower said.
There may be an undesirable ripple effect
A taxable withdrawal from retirement savings can also trigger additional costs elsewhere.

For example, if you're receiving Social Security retirement benefits, the added income could cause a larger portion of that money to become taxable. Depending on how much other income you have, 0%, up to 50%, or up to 85% of your Social Security benefits may be subject to federal income tax. A large retirement-account withdrawal can increase that other income and make more of your benefits taxable.
For retirees on Medicare, a large taxable withdrawal also could increase their Part B and Part D premiums through the income-related monthly adjustment amount, or IRMAA.

For 2026, that surcharge applies when modified adjusted gross income exceeds $109,000 for an individual filer or $218,000 for a married couple filing jointly. Medicare generally bases the surcharge on tax information from two years earlier, meaning 2026 premiums are typically based on 2024 income.

"What catches many people off guard is that they often don't feel that impact until a couple of years after the withdrawal," said CFP Ciano Villaquiran, a partner with CURO Financial Planning in San Diego.
Consider delaying part of the withdrawal

For some retirees, it may be worth delaying the additional withdrawal needed to cover the tax bill until the next calendar year, Trumbower said. That second distribution would be taxable in the following year, potentially spreading the income — and its tax impact — across two tax years.
"Pushing the [additional] distribution from the IRA into the following calendar year may possibly avoid jumping up into a higher tax bracket," Trumbower said.

However, she said, retirees should still withhold enough tax from the initial distribution to avoid an underpayment penalty. The federal income tax system is generally pay-as-you-go, meaning taxpayers must pay enough tax through withholding or estimated payments during the year rather than waiting until they file their return.

Generally, taxpayers can avoid an underpayment penalty if their withholding and estimated payments equal at least 90% of the current year's tax liability or 100% of the prior year's tax liability. For certain higher-income taxpayers, the prior-year threshold is 110%. Any remaining tax due generally can be paid when the return is filed.
Other ways to cover the expense
If you have a brokerage account, that may be a better source to fund a one-off expense, Trumbower said.

Taxes on long-term capital gains — profits on investments such as stocks held for more than one year — are generally lower than ordinary income tax rates. Depending on your taxable income, some long-term capital gains may even be taxed at 0%.

For 2026, the 0% long-term capital gains rate applies to taxable income of up to $49,450 for single filers and $98,900 for married couples filing jointly. Above those thresholds, most long-term capital gains are taxed at 15%, with a 20% rate applying at higher income levels.
Weigh the pros and cons of borrowing the money
Depending on the expense, retirees may be able to borrow money instead of tapping their savings, Trumbower said.

For example, a home equity loan or line of credit could help pay for a major home improvement project, while a car purchase could be financed with an auto loan rather than a large withdrawal from retirement savings.

Of course, borrowing comes with its own costs and risks. The loan payments would need to fit within the retiree's budget, and the interest paid could outweigh the potential benefits of leaving retirement savings untouched.
The withdrawal could have long-term repercussions
Additionally, it's worth considering how the withdrawal could affect your savings over time.
"Pulling a large amount out for a one-time expense doesn't just reduce the account balance today; it can reduce what that money could have grown into down the road," Villaquiran said.

For illustration: $50,000 earning 5% annually would grow to about $81,400 after 10 years, according to the Securities and Exchange Commission's Investor.gov compound-interest calculator. If a retiree withdrew $10,000 at the start and left $40,000 invested under the same assumptions, it would grow to about $65,200 — a difference of roughly $16,300 after 10 years.

cnbc.com/2026/11/13/is-a-bottom-in-for-t.headline: Is a bottom in for the Nasdaq-100? Charts to watch
cnbc.com/2026/11/13/is-a-bottom-in-for-t.author: Frank Cappelleri

paragraphs.text: (See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.)
Is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in? We're going to look at several charts to help answer that question.

First, let's remember how we got here. In September, the NDX broke out from a bullish cup-and-handle pattern, producing a 33,200-upside target. That breakout quickly failed, however, and gave way to a bearish pattern that broke down aggressively two weeks ago.
The decline brought the index relatively close to its 26,350 downside target before the current rebound began.
Zooming out, it's telling to see where the bounce originated. Three important forms of support converged in the 25,000-26,000 area:
• The uptrend line extending from the early 2025 low through the early 2026 low.
• The 38.2% Fibonacci retracement of the entire 2025-2026 rally.
• The former 2025 highs, which represented resistance before becoming a key breakout zone earlier this year.
This confluence of support helped encourage buying after a roughly 15% decline.
For perspective, we also see what larger drawdowns of 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% would look like … a lot worse.

The following chart tracks NDX drawdowns from 52-week highs going back to just after the financial crisis. Only a handful of declines exceeded 20%, and three produced relatively quick reversals: late 2018, the Covid lows in 2020 and April 2025.
Historically, buying into declines of approximately 15%–25% has generally paid off, even when additional downside occurred first (yellow highlights).
The chart also highlights previous declines of 10%–16% in green, putting the current pullback into perspective.
The major exception was 2022, when the NDX eventually declined nearly 36% over approximately 10 months ... a much worse outcome, which many investors are concerned could happen again now.
That raises the key question: Are we experiencing another routine correction, or the early stages of a larger bear market?
One important clue will be how far this bounce progresses.
Any rally that fails to reclaim the previous highs could establish a significant lower high. Additional lower highs would provide stronger evidence of a developing, longer downtrend.
We saw this in March 2022, when that first sharp rebound effort failed to reach the previous high before a much more severe decline followed.
The bottom line: The current bounce is encouraging, particularly given where it originated and knowing how well buying prior 10-20% drawdowns has paid off.
From here, it's all about the follow through. We don't need to see new highs right away, but any rally from here that's met with another wave of strong selling could reignite downside momentum.

Frank Cappelleri is the founder and president of CappThesis, an independent research firm that helps active investors through time-tested chart and statistical analysis. Prior to starting CappThesis, he spent 25 years on Wall Street as an equity sales trader, technical analyst, research sales specialist and desk strategist.

cnbc.com/2026/11/13/kevin-hassett-white-.headline: Hassett denies report he's leaving White House: 'Not true'
cnbc.com/2026/11/13/kevin-hassett-white-.author: Kevin Breuninger

paragraphs.text: National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett on Friday poured cold water on a report that he's expected to leave the White House in the coming weeks.
That report is "not true," Hassett told CNBC's Eamon Javers in a text message.
Semafor reported earlier Friday afternoon that Hassett "has been inquiring about roles outside the administration," even before Republicans' drubbing in last week's midterm election.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, and his counselor David Zervos, are among the names being floated to replace Hassett, according to Semafor, which cited unnamed people familiar with his plans.
But a White House official told CNBC in a statement later Friday, "There is no factual basis for this reporting."

"Kevin Hassett is a key member of President Trump's economic team and will continue working to advance President Trump's economic policies," the official said on condition of anonymity to discuss the matter.
Zervos, reached by phone after Semafor's story published, declined to comment.
