bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5gm3gnwl42eo.headline: Aide to pro-Kremlin Ukrainian ex-PM badly hurt in Moscow car bomb
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c5gm3gnwl42eo.author: Dan Sales

paragraphs.text: A car bomb attack in Moscow has wounded a former adviser to Ukrainian ex-prime minister Mykola Azarov, Russia's Investigative Committee says.
Sergei Zavorotny, now a journalist and commentator, was behind the wheel of his black Toyota when the explosion happened and Azarov told Russian TV his condition in hospital was "rather critical".

The car bomb went off a day after a Russian colonel was killed in another explosion in St Petersburg, and both blasts are seen as part of a series of attacks on military and prominent figures linked to Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
Zavorotny, 72, worked as a press aide to Mykola Azarov in Kyiv until 2014.
But when pro-Kremlin Ukrainian president Viktor Yanukovych was toppled from power, Azarov fled Kyiv for Russia and tried unsuccessfully to set up a government in exile.

In a 2020 US Senate report on interference in the 2016 American presidential election, Zavorotny is described at the time as an SVR [Russian foreign intelligence] officer involved in influence operations.

Russia's Investigative Committee said on Telegram on Friday: "Serhiy Zavorotny, a former adviser to the former Ukrainian Prime Minister Mykola Azarov, was injured while driving a car. He was taken to one of the city hospitals, where he is receiving medical care."
It added: "A set of necessary investigative actions is being carried out. A number of examinations will be appointed, including medical and explosives."
According to several unconfirmed reports, Zavorotny suffered a number of serious injuries after an explosive device was detonated remotely.
Russia said the car bombs are the latest in a series of attacks targeting pro-Kremlin figures.
On Thursday a car bomb in the Pushkinsky District of St Petersburg killed a member of the Russian military, again after it was attached to the base of the car and detonated remotely.
The man targeted in the attack is yet to be named officially, but reputable sources suggest he was a high-ranking figure in the 6th Guards Air and Air Defence Forces Army.
Overnight into Friday, Ukraine and Russia exchanged attacks on each other's territories.
Ukrainian authorities said a hospital had been targeted by Russian bombardment.
They added that three people, including a 17-year-old boy, were also killed in attacks across southern Odesa and Zaporizhzhia.
Russia said a Ukrainian strike on an industrial facility in the central Samara region killed four people.
And in the southern Volgograd region another four died after an industrial zone was hit by drones. A further person died in the Bryansk border region, an area that is often fired upon.
Ukraine said these were retaliatory attacks in response to Russia's persistent targeting of its cities.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/ai-agent-start.headline: AI agent startup LangChain hits $3B valuation
techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/ai-agent-start.author: Julie Bort

paragraphs.text: Agent management startup LangChain has raised a $300 million Series C at a $3B valuation led by CapitalG, with participation from investors including Singapore’s GIC, DFJ Growth, IVP, and Sapphire Ventures, the company announced on Friday.
That’s more than double its $1.25 billion valuation when it raised $125 million about a year ago, led by IVP.

LangChain began in 2022 as a popular open-source project that handled the kinds of tasks that early-stage LLMs found difficult, like searching the web, calling APIs, and interacting with databases. As the frontier AI labs delivered harnesses that now competently do those tasks, LangChain turned its focus towards managing AI agents. It has apparently found its stride in this highly competitive area with a simple message: letting businesses own their own intelligence.

With its open-source roots, the startup says its agent creation and management software, LangSmith, is not trying to lock users into any particular model, cloud, or ecosystem, unlike the major clouds or frontier AI labs. It also promises that LangSmith will contain agent behavior and is easy to use.

True, there are plenty of other startups pitching similar advantages these days and also doing well (case in point is newcomer Mintive). However, LangChain has had a head start and now claims 7,000 LangSmith customers, including big-name startups like Harvey, Rippling, and Clay, and enterprises like NVIDIA, Toyota, and Salesforce.

cnbc.com/2026/11/13/a-trading-strategy-t.headline: A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process
cnbc.com/2026/11/13/a-trading-strategy-t.author: Michael Khouw

paragraphs.text: Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct. 6. The market despises uncertainty, and losing a visionary founder, particularly one without a well-telegraphed succession plan, makes it worse.

However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive. Trading in the $160s, Nvidia's valuation has taken a big haircut, yet its underlying business fundamentals remain largely intact. While Huang was the architect of Nvidia's AI dominance, the company's moat — superior GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, and networking expertise — does not walk out the door with him. The company's structural advantage in the global artificial intelligence rollout persists.

Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options. Huang's departure guarantees that Nvidia will be operating under a cloud of transition for the foreseeable future. Executing a permanent CEO search while navigating global regulatory scrutiny takes time. Consequently, Nvidia's implied volatility (IV)—the market's pricing of expected future price swings — has spiked to highs not seen since the tariff tantrum in the first half of 2025, and this elevated IV is highly likely to persist for several months as the leadership drama slowly unfolds.

This prolonged period of high implied volatility can be a goldmine for option sellers, specifically those executing options overlays such as covered call strategies. When you buy NVDA shares at these depressed levels and simultaneously sell out-of-the-money call options against your position, the premiums you collect are directly tied to IV. Because fear and transition-related uncertainty have dramatically inflated these option prices, the income generated from selling covered calls is now significantly higher than usual.

This lowers the risk profile of holding the stock considerably over time. Consistently collecting these inflated premiums systematically lowers your overall cost basis in the underlying shares. If the stock trades sideways or recovers slowly during the CEO search, you are generating an outsized cash yield on a stagnant asset. If the stock experiences further downside turbulence, the heavy premium income acts as a substantial downside buffer, meaningfully reducing the strategy's overall risk over time.
The trade:
• Buy 100 shares Nvidia
• Sell 1 Dec 18 $185 call

By deploying a persistent covered call strategy, investors can leverage the exact fear driving the stock down to generate robust, risk-reducing income while maintaining exposure to the undeniable future of AI.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/this-young-sta.headline: This young startup wants to power floating data centers with the ocean’s heat, and investors are already on board
techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/this-young-sta.author: Tim De Chant

paragraphs.text: Anyone who has weathered a hurricane can tell you that the oceans — which fuel the storms — contain a tremendous amount of energy. Thanks to global warming, they’re holding more than ever.
A new startup wants to harness that energy to power data centers.

Drogue, which has kept a low profile until now, is building a system that harvests heat from the ocean to power data centers on board floating vessels. According to co-founder and CEO Sam Sipe, the first prototype should be bobbing around the ocean, crunching bits, less than two years from now.

The goal, Sipe said, is to help data center developers deploy servers in AI-friendly timelines. “The data center industry is a real estate game, and so they’re playing on 8- to 10-year timelines, including interoperability with utilities and [independent system operators]” that manage regional power grids, he said. “AI demand has increased 10x in just the last three years. It’s completely incompatible.”

Drogue was founded just six months ago in Washington, D.C., and the startup told TechCrunch exclusively that it has already raised $20 million, including from XYZ Venture Capital, Toyota Ventures, Tamarack Global, Dream, FDVC, Garuda Ventures, Flexcap, Boost VC, and Slow Ventures, among other investors.

In those six months, Drogue has designed a multi-megawatt prototype that will be installed on a traditional oceangoing ship and sent out to sea in early 2028. Future versions will be built on floating structures that more closely resemble offshore oil platforms.
To Sipe, the decision to turn to the ocean was obvious.

After years flying E-2D Hawkeyes off U.S. Navy aircraft carriers, he had an appreciation for the ocean’s immense power. “Most people think, oh, ocean — hard waves, storms, corrosion, biofouling. And I just see this majestic place and resource that we just ignore,” he said.

As the planet warms, the oceans have been absorbing an additional 5.8 million terawatt-hours of energy every year. By comparison, all of human civilization uses about 180,000 terawatt-hours each year. If Drogue were to take some, surely the ocean wouldn’t miss it.

The startup’s technology works like a heat pump run in reverse. A heat pump uses electricity to move heat from one place to another; Drogue’s system instead uses a difference in temperature to generate electricity. This approach, known as ocean thermal energy conversion, or OTEC, was first developed in the 1950s.

Surface waters are warmer, heated by the sun, while down-deep temperatures are much colder, about 39°F on average (4°C). “There’s basically no amount of heat we can pull out of that that will collapse that temperature differential,” Sipe said.

To leverage the temperature differential, the startup’s system draws in warm surface water, uses it to cool the data centers, and then sends the now-warmer water to boil ammonia, a chemical that turns to gas at -28°F. That ammonia gas is then sent through a turbine to generate electricity. Once through the turbine, it courses through a condenser, which turns the gas back into a liquid. There, cold water drawn from 1,000 meters deep passes over the condenser’s fins to absorb the heat. The warmed water is then pumped back down to 1,000 meters, where it dissipates into the ocean. The ammonia gets sent back to the start of the sealed loop, and the cycle repeats.
The basic idea was tested in the 1980s but tossed aside. “A lot has changed since the ’80s, specifically manufacturing techniques around the pipe and the heat exchangers,” Sipe said.

To find out why, Sipe sought out people who had worked on those early efforts. “I just talked to everyone, basically interviewed them and figured out what went wrong, what went right, what would you do next. And everyone was like, dude, this stuff works. It’s just a matter of being able to raise enough capital to build something big enough, because there’s a sweet spot,” he said.

There also had to be customers who could use that power while still at sea. Sending power to shore would require lengthy, expensive cables, and manufacturing on board would require similarly expensive shipping of materials and finished goods. Data centers are ideal — the servers are compact relative to other equipment, and shipping data off the platform is incredibly cheap. Each vessel would live at sea for about a decade, Sipe said.

Drogue already has “approval in principle,” a preliminary sign-off, from the American Bureau of Shipping, which sets and checks safety standards for ships. Now it’s in the process of buying its first ship to start building a prototype ready for the open ocean.

In many ways, Drogue’s concept is similar to Elon Musk’s plan for orbital data centers: find a cheap source of power, and get the data centers as close to it as possible. Except unlike orbital data centers, Drogue’s don’t need to launch expensive rockets to get there. They can just sail a ship on the ocean, something humanity has been doing for millennia.

thebignewsletter.com/p/blocked-emboldene.headline: BLOCKED! Emboldened State Regulators Just Scuttled a Major Money Merger
thebignewsletter.com/p/blocked-emboldene.author: Lee Hepner

paragraphs.text: When Hiram Johnson was elected the 23rd Governor of the State of California in November 1910, the Southern Pacific Railroad was so powerful that most people thought of it as the fourth branch of government. In his 1911 inaugural address, Governor Johnson referred to Southern Pacific as “the political master of this State.”

Johnson was a Progressive Republican, one of many who had broken with President Taft over high tariffs and conflicts over conservation, corporate regulation, and the influence of monied interests. As he put it in his inaugural address:

In some form or other nearly every governmental problem that involves the health, the happiness, or the prosperity of the State has arisen, because some private interest has intervened or has sought for its own gain to exploit either the resources or the politics of the State. I take it, therefore, that the first duty that is mine to perform is to eliminate every private interest from the government, and to make the public service of the State responsive solely to the people.

Johnson saw it as his mission to replace every appointee who represented a “political machine or a corporation” and bring in a new uncorrupted workforce, so as to confront the “apostles of big business.” He realized the result would bring “a storm of indignation,” but also, the liberty of a free people.

Governor Johnson’s election was not a blowout; he won by just 5 points. But by October, just 10 months into his governorship, he had persuaded the legislature to deliver him a package of constitutional amendments, establishing the statewide ballot process, the ability to recall public officials, women’s suffrage and, critical to this column, the strengthening of the Railroad Commission. And the legislature delivered the constitutional amendments by a vote of 35-1 in the Senate and 71-0 in the Assembly. California’s era of popular democracy had arrived.

Strengthening the Railroad Commission was a direct rebuke of the power and influence of Southern Pacific Railroad and transitioned the entirety of the Commission’s appointment authority to the Governor. The other central reform to the Commission was found in Section 51, the Commission’s “change of control” authority, which gave it new powers to approve any sale, lease, mortgage, merger or consolidation of any utility property.

In many ways, we still live in the California that Governor Johnson reinvented in 1911. The “change of control” authority first established in the Railroad Commission is now integrated in several agencies, from financial regulators to insurance oversight. In other ways, we don’t. No one would argue that the lofty ambition to rid government of every appointee with loyalties to private interests has endured as anything but an ambition. And yet, in many places across the country, including in some parts of California, last week’s midterm elections resembled a populist wave, not unlike the rebuke of corporate power that carried Johnson to Sacramento.

Then, on Wednesday of this week, an under-the-radar state agency, under the leadership of former Consumer Financial Protection Bureau Director Rohit Chopra, invoked its change of control authority to thwart a merger that had until then escaped condemnation of political leaders across the country. And it involved a corporation that was well known to late 19th- and early 20th Century progressives, Western Union, which had faced allegations of monopolizing the telegraph industry dating back to at least 1889.

But it is very much a scandal of 2026, and wed to the political climate of 2026. One week after an election were economic populism rippled across the country, a state agency was using the authority first established in the wake of a populist revolt over a century ago to confront corporate power.

The parallels to the 1910 populist election wave and Governor Johnson’s creation of administrative merger controls are too enticing. Could this be the dawn of a new era in American politics? There are reasons to say yes, and perhaps more reasons to be skeptical. But one thing is clear: public officials at every level of government are waking up to new opportunities to serve the public. With the right attention, those opportunities might well become expectations — as envisioned by Governor Johnson — that government should be singularly committed to representing the public’s interest, free from the influence of private interests.
The Western Union-Intermex Merger

Last August 2025, Western Union announced an agreement to acquire International Money Express (Intermex) for approximately $500 million. What are these companies, and why did they want to merge? Western Union and Intermex are two publicly-traded companies that provide money transfer services, like the services provided by Venmo and CashApp. But whereas Venmo and CashApp primarily service domestic money transfers, Western Union and Intermex facilitate international money transfers.

Western Union is one of the world’s largest money transfer companies, whose customers – mostly individuals sending money to family, friends, and businesses – can transfer money domestically, internationally and across borders in more than 200 countries. Western Union makes money by charging a transfer fee and earns revenue from the foreign exchange spread when converting currencies.

Intermex specializes in transfers from the United States to Latin America and the Caribbean. Like Western Union, Intermex’s customers send money across borders, and Intermex makes money by charging transfer fees and from foreign exchange spreads.

Another distinguishing characteristic of both Western Union and Intermex is that they both operate through retail locations, which requires having sprawling and robust partnerships with grocery stores, convenience stores, neighborhood businesses, and other independent retail agents. These retail partnerships are valuable in a merger transaction because, for services that rely on physical locations, it’s a pathway to automatic geographic scale without having to compete for those relationships on your own. And Western Union wanted Intermex’s robust network of retail partnerships to expand its own reach throughout Latin America.

Cross-border money transfers are also big business and are a vital resource to immigrants, in particular, who can use the services to transfer money back to their families. As former FTC Commissioner Alvaro Bedoya pointed out when this deal was announced:

Millions of people send money to help their family in Latin America. I've been sending money more or less monthly since I graduated law school almost 20 years ago. It's really important to have a range of companies competing for that business. When you're sending $35 or $50 to just get someone to their next paycheck (which is a pretty common thing), the fee for that can really eat at what you're sending.So I'm pretty shocked to learn that Western Union is buying a company that *already* holds >30% market shares in U.S. to Ecuador and U.S. to Nicaragua remittances, and a 29% share in remittances to Guatemala. Intermex also claims to hold a 20% share in remittances to Mexico, and public reporting suggests that Western Union is #1 -- in other words, *above* Intermex -- in that corridor.

These types of transfers reach into the billions of dollars per year. In 2025, the New York Times reported that they had seen an uptick in international transfers attributable to heightened concerns around deportation caused by expanded and increasingly aggressive ICE enforcement. So the threat of retail locations closing down, or fees going up, was a source of particular concern for immigrant populations and other customers with family abroad. Here’s Mayor Zohran Mamdani earlier this year making the point, too:

It’s not every day that Mayors, even of major cities, are out front on merger issues, so Mayor Mamdani’s statement isn’t just compelling as it relates to this particular merger, but because it’s evidence that more and more cities are starting to think of themselves as agents in the organization of fair and competitive markets.

Now, cross-border money transfers are also used for less savory purposes. Since 2001, the U.S. Attorney of Pennsylvania had convicted dozens of Western Union agents for conspiring with international fraudsters to conduct mass marketing scams. And there’s a relevant connection to Secretary Chopra here, too. In late 2017, just a few months before Secretary Chopra was himself appointed to the Federal Trade Commission, Western Union was investigated by the FTC and agreed to disgorge $586 million after admitting to crimes like failing to stem money laundering schemes and aiding and abetting wire fraud. Fast forward a few years, while Chopra was serving as Director of the CFPB, that agency warned Western Union and other remittance services they should not charge potentially illegal junk fees. This was not Chopra’s first encounter with Western Union or Intermex.

Since 2025, the Trump Administration has slowed or eviscerated this oversight work. In August 2025, right as Western Union was announcing its intent to acquire Intermex, Trump’s CFPB was cutting its oversight of international money transfer services. When the Western Union acquisition of Intermex came before Trump’s FTC in late 2025, the merger didn’t get so much as a second look.
That could have been the end of the story. But it wasn’t.
Enter the States

Here’s where things get interesting, because federal agencies weren’t the only ones with authority to review the transaction. State level financial regulators, like those in New York and California, also had authority to review the acquisition under their respective change of ownership regulations. And following the election of Mamdani in New York City, the deal started encountering turbulence, as the mayor called on the State’s Department of Financial Services to review the merger.

New York financial regulators, in collaboration with NY Attorney General Letitia James, ultimately approved the merger on August 13, 2026, subject to various commitments made by Western Union. Those conditions included maintaining all of the combined company’s retail locations throughout the state, continuing to offer remittance services to key Latin American countries, and capping fee increases, all for a period of three years following the acquisition.

California financial regulators had also provided tentative approval to the deal in February 2026, with a built in clock to allow other regulators to review the deal. But the same day that New York DFS approved the Western Union-Intermex deal, newly-appointed California Secretary Chopra, who oversees the State’s equivalent financial regulator, suspended its approval of the merger. The stock prices cratered.

We love that you are reading, and we hope you will continue. With the recent election, the work of promoting a government that takes on monied interest will become far more potent. Every additional paid subscriber means we can invest in more education for leaders and citizens, and annoy Wall Street just that much more. So please, subscribe. And together we’ll pop the damn AI Bubble. Or at least, we’ll have fun trying.

California’s authority to review the Western Union-Intermex deal derives from its licensing regime, which requires anyone who engages in the business of money transmission to be licensed by the state. Critically, the law also requires the Department of Financial Protection and Innovation (DFPI) to approve or disapprove any acquisition of a licensee, which includes the power to impose conditions in furtherance of the “safety or soundness” of the licensee, or to enhance consumer protection. That change-of-control authority is a direct descendant of Governor Johnson’s 1911 expansion of the Railroad Commission.

Fast forward to Tuesday of this week, and California’s DFPI announced that it would allow Western Union to acquire Intermex, but, as in New York, subject to some conditions. Like New York, California prohibited Western Union and Intermex from shutting down agent locations. Then, California went further in a couple of ways. First, Western Union would be required to adopt anti-fraud and anti-money laundering measures. That’s basic consumer protection, anti-crime stuff, if not also a call-back to Chopra’s encounters with Western Union and other remittance services during his time at the FTC and CFPB.

California financial regulators also required Western Union and Intermex to continue operating , at least partially with respect to a consumer’s ability to choose between their preferred agents, as separate entities. This condition reflects the state’s authority to preserve competition, too, and to make sure that consumer choice is not sacrificed, even if Western Union and Intermex are integrating other back-end functions.

Imposing conditions on a licensee has the valence of regulation. And the authority to impose conditions is expansive. Operating within the bounds of its statutory authority, the conditions imposed by DFPI did not resemble a negotiation with private interests, like a mutually-agreed upon consent decree, but were principally about protecting consumers, preserving market competition, and enhancing the public interest by whatever means necessary.

However one thinks of it, for Western Union, the prospect of not doing crime was apparently a raw deal, and Western Union pulled out of its deal to acquire Intermex the next day. Western Union was not specific as to why, but deemed the conditions “unacceptable,” adding that they “would have required material changes to Western Union’s business model.”

Part of me is skeptical that Western Union was actually frustrated by the conditions, because I don’t see the conditions as anything more than rational mitigation of the public risk flowing from the combination. While Intermex shareholders were no doubt looking forward to the payout of a deal, Intermex seems to be similarly flummoxed by the termination and is demanding Western Union take all steps necessary to consummate the deal subject to DFPI’s terms.
So there may still be a thorny road ahead for Western Union and Intermex. In the meantime, here’s former FTC Chair Lina Khan celebrating the outcome:
People-First Deal-Blocking at the State Level

Khan’s final statement is one to sit with: “As newly elected state officials take the helm in coming months, they will have significant opportunity to use and activate all their tools to halt corporate abuse and make life better for working people.” While a lot of people are focused on the change of control in Congress, on a Federal level there is still split government. It is at the state and local levels where more nimble governance can actually occur.

You can hear in Khan’s comments, urging state legislators to “use and activate all their tools,” the echoes of Governor Johnson’s clarion call from 1911. And many state agencies are now possessed of the authority to oversee mergers and other changes in control that Johnson first established in the state’s Railroad Commission. These kinds of authorities exist across states and cities that are now controlled by populist Democrats. In 2026, a dozen state legislative chambers flipped from red to blue, and a host of administrative positions, from the Ohio Attorney General to the Texas Agricultural Commission to the Georgia Public Service Commission, are now run by populists, many of them operating outside the polarization of left-right politics. I could easily imagine state and city regulators all over the country reaching out to block or regulate mergers like the DoorDash-Instacart transaction.

I know California best, so that’s what I’ll speak to. In this state, the California Public Utilities Commission can block a person or corporation from directly or indirectly merging with, acquiring, or controlling a California public utility without prior authorization of the Commission. That authority extends to entities organized outside the State of California, and requires the Commission to consider things like ratepayer interests, service quality, and impacts on workers and local economies. There’s a specific provision stating that ratepayers must receive at least 50% of forecasted benefits of any transaction.

The State’s Department of Managed Healthcare and Department of Public Health are similarly authorized to review and block material changes involving health insurance plans and the sale of hospitals, skilled nursing facilities, and other licensed facilities. Similar merger controls exist under the Department of Cannabis and the Department of Alcohol and Beverage Control, and they also fall under Secretary Chopra’s purview. Veterinary practices, private cemeteries, pharmacies, and automotive repair businesses do, too.

The California Insurance Commissioner oversees changes in control of insurance providers. In California, the Insurance Commissioner is an elected statewide seat, and voters just elected another populist, Jane Kim, to the role.

State legislatures are also expanding this authority, interestingly not under the guise of expanding antitrust law, even though this type of oversight can serve the same pro-competition and consumer protection ends. California recently passed a law requiring licensure of small business lenders, an attempt to give DFPI more authority to oversee usurious merchant cash advance providers. If you want to be genuinely outraged at the perversity of merchant cash advances, take a look at this recent report by Protect Borrowers.

The bottom line is that economic fairness, consumer protection, and the general welfare of workers, consumers and small businesses in the face of increased corporate concentration is not just a litigation or enforcement project. It is woven by law into the oversight obligations of little-recognized bureaucrats. Some of them are captured by the industries they are commissioned to oversee. Others are more likely to heed the call to advance the public interest through whatever means necessary, untethered from the influence of private interests. They will face blowback for doing so, from business and from the press, but as Governor Johnson recognized, that’s the obvious price for the pursuit of government by and for the people.

As for Governor Johnson, that was a successful political calculation. The rift within the Republican Party between Taft and the insurgent progressives cost them the Presidency in 1912. But Johnson would become the first Governor in California history to serve two consecutive terms in office. He would go on to serve four terms in the United States Senate. At an inflection point in California’s history, he governed hard and fast, leaving a legacy that just this week scored another win for Californians and Americans more broadly.

persuasion.community/p/what-havel-teache.headline: What Havel Teaches Us About Freedom
persuasion.community/p/what-havel-teache.author: Carl Gershman

paragraphs.text: I’m very happy to announce that Mike McFaul and Larry Diamond have agreed to become regular columnists for American Purpose.

Mike is currently Ken Olivier and Angela Nomellini Professor of International Studies in the Department of Political Science at Stanford University, and a senior fellow at Stanford’s Freeman Spogli Institute (FSI) and Hoover Institution. He was also a former U.S. ambassador to Russia and NSC staff member.
Larry is Mosbacher Senior Fellow in Global Democracy, also at FSI, and Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution. He is one of the world’s leading experts on global democracy.
We welcome Mike and Larry to the American Purpose family, and look forward to their future regular contributions.
– Frank Fukuyama on behalf of American Purpose at Persuasion.

At a recent conference held in Prague by Forum 2000 conference, the organization co-founded by Vaclav Havel in 1996 to discuss the challenges facing mankind on the threshold of a new millennium, special attention was paid to Havel’s legacy, since the event coincided with the 90th anniversary of his birth. That legacy is especially important today when the future of democracy, which Havel believed was essential to the preservation of human well-being and world peace, is more threatened than at any time in the last 30 years.

When the Journal of Democracy published a collection of tributes to Havel after his death in 2011, it referred to him as “probably the most revered democratic leader and thinker of our time”—and so he was. He was not just a national leader and democratic intellectual of global stature, but also a renowned playwright, a political dissident, and a global democracy activist. He continued to be all of these things until his very last days, when he issued a statement of solidarity with political prisoners in Belarus and received his friend the Dalai Lama, who said after Havel’s death that the best way to remember him was to promote his legacy.

There are several components of Havel’s legacy that can help to guide us in addressing the challenges we now face. He was, first of all, an unrivalled democracy strategist. His actions—such as nominating for the Nobel Peace Prize brave democratic leaders —were always calculated to strengthen activists at the forefront of the struggle for democracy and to give them hope.

Charter 77, the civic initiative he co-founded and helped lead, not only revived the dissident movement in Czechoslovakia after the 1968 Soviet invasion, but also inspired dissidents in China three decades later to create Charter 08, which was signed by over 10,000 Chinese democrats. Havel’s Chinese friends said after his death: “Your Charter 77 and our Charter 08 are iron cousins.” Soon after Oswaldo Paya’s Varela Project had created the first democratic opening in Cuba since the revolution, Havel told him that “each democrat who opposes a totalitarian regime should behave today as if power were to be handed over tomorrow.” This spurred Paya to initiate a secret national dialogue among more than 10,000 citizens in totalitarian Cuba that led to the drafting of an “All-Cuban Plan” that Paya called “a bridge between our current situation and democracy.”

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6rrg51rkz09o.headline: Microsoft 'deeply sorry' for global outage after almost 24 hours of disruption
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c6rrg51rkz09o.author: Rachel Clun

paragraphs.text: Microsoft has said it is "deeply sorry" for the service outage to its products, including Outlook and Teams, which has caused disruption around the world.
Services were broadly recovering by Friday afternoon, nearly 24 hours after issues first began, as Microsoft said it was making "encouraging progress" and email queues were nearing normal levels.
The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide.
Microsoft said the problem was a technical issue introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and not related to cyber or artificial intelligence agents.
Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers.
Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday.

By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America.
In the UK, some parts of the NHS, including GPs and hospitals, were affected, as were some schools and police forces.
UK cyber minister Liz Lloyd said the incident had "limited" impact on critical frontline services such as 999 calls, and there had been no disruption to the transport network.
In Canada, however, the national rail network said passengers may not be able to receive email updates about their trips, and hospitals across the country also had issues with emails.
In the US, staff members from the House of Representatives told Politico it had set back an entire day of legislative work as everything was on Microsoft's Outlook.
Singapore's government acknowledged some of its systems had been impacted, and in India, the outage disrupted work for many on Friday.
In Turkey, advisers and officials attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya were left frustrated by being unable to access Outlook.
The issues also affected smaller businesses and individuals.
Peter Pentz, a winemaker in South Africa, said his entire business was basically brought to a "standstill".

His winery's communication with exports was also brought to a standstill, he said, and "critical production work" was been halted as the Cape West Coast winery "relies on these systems for parts of our day-to-day operations".
Georgia from Staffordshire in England said she was due to complete her first house purchase today after waiting eight months to get to this point - but the outage has delayed that.
"The solicitor mentioned there may be a delay due to not being able to contact other agencies.
"We're not the only one completing today, there are hundreds of houses and for them to ring everyone in time is unfeasible," Georgia said.
'Encouraging recovery signals'

Microsoft first acknowledged users in the Americas were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes at 17:54 GMT on Thursday, and shortly after warned the disruption was possibly affecting Microsoft 365 globally.
While it launched an investigation and engineers began working to restore services, by 04:36 on Friday Microsoft was reporting only a "partial recovery" in some parts of the world.
By 13:32, the tech giant said there were "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" across much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia Pacific region.
Microsoft said it restored services gradually due to the scale of the problem and to help ensure services remained stable once they were up and running again.
"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," a Microsoft spokesperson said.
"We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously."
A full post-incident report will be released once Microsoft has completed a review.
Experts said while workers may have been happy to not have email access for the day, the incident showed the dependence many organisations have on these cloud-based services.
"The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of big tech providers," said Rob Demain, chief executive of cybersecurity firm e2e-assure.
Matt Saunders, field chief technology officer at tech consultancy Adaptavist, said it would be challenging to mitigate against a similar problem.
"Classic IT disaster planning strategies suggest using a second service for resilience, but in practice, it's almost impossible for a business to function without tools such as Microsoft," he said.
"In the wake of this outage, organisations must have a plan in place for how to work without such tools, for when incidents like this occur."

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/13/tan.headline: Tanker strikes cruise ship in New Orleans, sending passengers into river
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/13/tan.author: Brady Dennis

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
National correspondent covering the Southeast

A tanker on Friday afternoon hit a passenger cruise ship that was docked along the Mississippi River in New Orleans, causing a massive emergency response that included firefighters rescuing people from the water.

Kimberly Curth, a Port of New Orleans spokeswoman, said the incident happened at approximately 12:30 p.m. local time when an Atlantic Asphalt tanker crashed into the docked American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage ship that had docked about two hours earlier.
An estimated 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, were aboard the American Heritage at the time, Curth said.

Port NOLA Harbor Police, the New Orleans Fire Department, the New Orleans Police Department, the U.S. Coast Guard and emergency medical personnel were on scene, conducting rescue and response operations.
Curth said passengers were being brought inside the port’s administration building “for triage and assistance.”

“Our immediate priority is the safety of all passengers, crew members and first responders,” she said in a statement. “This remains an active and evolving incident. The number of injuries and the cause of the collision have not yet been confirmed.”
Reporter covering politics with a focus on campaigns
Van Hollen ‘no longer pursuing’ possible 2028 bid as he seeks Senate leader job
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland) is abandoning his presidential ambitions for 2028 as he seeks instead to oust Sen. Chuck Schumer (D) from his leadership role.

“I’m no longer pursuing that,” Van Hollen said Friday of his potential 2028 presidential bid, after a speech to Democrats gathered in Denver to celebrate the party’s huge wins in the midterm elections and chart a cohesive path forward.

“I believe that the size and scale of these majorities provides an opportunity for the United States Senate to answer the call of the American people,” Van Hollen said. “We can’t go back to business as usual.”

He announced his challenge to Schumer, the Senate minority leader, late Thursday, sparking a public power struggle alongside the work to unite Democrats. Until this week, Van Hollen had been “kicking the tires” on a presidential bid.
Van Hollen, 67, said the election called for a generational shift and that Schumer, 75, represented a style of politics that voters wanted to change.

He again characterized himself as an underdog in his leadership competition with Schumer, who has led the chamber’s Democratic caucus since 2017. And he declined to publicly reveal how many fellow senators have agreed to support him. But Van Hollen said he spoke directly with Schumer about it.
“We understand that this will be a competition. I think it’s important to give Senate Democrats a choice. That’s what we just gave voters all over the country a choice. They chose change,” he said.
Reporter covering arts and culture
Stacey Abrams told Ava DuVernay to hold ‘14th’ until after midterms

Ava DuVernay’s first documentary in 10 years — titled “14th,” after the constitutional amendment that it traces — will arrive on Netflix on Dec. 4. That wasn’t always DuVernay’s plan: At one point, she wanted it to be released ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.

“It was Stacey Abrams who said to me, ‘You shouldn’t do that,’” DuVernay said Thursday at the Global Women’s Summit hosted by The Washington Post. She added that Abrams, the former two-time candidate for Georgia governor and voting rights activist, thought the film “will be more needed and more instructive after” the elections.

Abrams is interviewed in “14th,” which follows the history of the amendment that grants birthright citizenship, protects due process and guarantees equal protection under the law. DuVernay felt compelled to make the documentary after the Trump administration tried to end birthright citizenship via executive order, setting off a wave of litigation before the Supreme Court affirmed in June that nearly everyone born on U.S. soil is a citizen.

“What she really was saying to me is that the opposition is not going away,” DuVernay told The Post’s Geoff Edgers, explaining why Abrams thought it made sense for “14th” to arrive after Nov. 3. “These ideas are not going away, the money behind it is not going away, and it will come back with a vengeance.”
Anchor of the Early Brief newsletter
Trump gives Scott Colom ‘a lot of credit’ for campaigning at a MAGA rally
President Donald Trump doesn’t often give Democrats much credit.
But in an interview Thursday, he praised Democrat Scott Colom, who defeated Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R) in Mississippi in the midterms, for meeting with voters outside a Trump rally last month.

“I heard it the other day, where I had a rally there, and we had lines that went 10 miles long, and he campaigned on that line, telling everybody on the line what a good job he did,” Trump said during an interview on Stephen A. Smith’s “Straight Shooter” podcast. “I give him a lot of credit for that.”

Colom made reaching out to Trump supporters central to his campaign in Mississippi, reflecting how the state has consistently voted for Republicans and backed Trump by 22 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election. Colom’s visit to the Trump rally gained widespread attention online.

“What are you expecting? I’ve never been to a Trump rally,” Colom asked people in line. “What matters to you as a veteran right now?” he asked one man, who told him about gun rights. Other voters told him they were worried about high gas prices and the Iran war.
“I walked the Trump rally line to listen, not make assumptions. I talked with voters, asked questions and heard what matters to them,” Colom wrote about his interactions.
Meteorologist covering significant weather events and climate trends
Why the polar vortex has forecasters on alert for Arctic cold in the U.S.
For weeks, the weather community has been buzzing about an unusual phenomenon unfolding one atmospheric layer above us in the stratosphere.
It’s called a sudden stratospheric warming and involves temperatures rising rapidly and winds weakening significantly some 20 miles above the North Pole.

These warming events are most common during winter, but they can sometimes can happen in late fall or early spring — and right now, the earliest one on record is occurring, among records dating to 1958.

This warming is destabilizing the polar vortex and has caused it to stretch beyond its typical length. The vortex normally keeps frigid air locked up near the pole, but this disturbance could unleash it southward into areas where more people live.

That would only happen if stratospheric patterns filter down to the troposphere, which is the atmospheric layer where weather takes shape. Meteorologists liken this atmospheric-filtering process to “dripping paint.”

Late last November, a stratospheric warming event quickly dripped from the stratosphere to the troposphere, influencing a cold and snowy stretch across the United States that lasted for a month or two.

This year, the influence of this polar vortex disruption is looking less concrete, though some meteorologists are increasingly flagging the potential for it to play some role in U.S. weather patterns from late November into December.
However, its effects could be muted by a record El Niño, which has fueled an exceptionally mild start to November across much of the country.

If the polar vortex unleashes even a brief surge of icy air into the U.S., it would probably increase the chances for a blockbuster winter storm or two before the end of the year — especially when combined with El Niño’s heightened levels of atmospheric moisture.
The next ‘Bachelor’ star is Commanders quarterback Sam Hartman
Sam Hartman, a 27-year-old quarterback on the Washington Commanders’ practice squad, will be the next star of ABC’s “The Bachelor.”
Hartman, who will be asked to date 20 to 30 women at once before choosing a fiancée, said Friday on “Good Morning America” that he’s “very nervous.”
“I have a tough time holding conversation with one girl,” he said. “30 is going to be pretty tough.”

Hartman set various school records while playing college football at Wake Forest. In 2022, he was diagnosed with Paget-Schroetter syndrome and received the ACC’s Brian Piccolo Award for courage. He transferred to Notre Dame for his final season in 2023.
Hartman signed with the Commanders as an undrafted free agent in 2024. He has not yet appeared in a regular season game, spending most of his time on the team’s practice squad.
Asked what he looks for in a partner, Hartman said he likes “competitiveness.” He continued, “They have a drive for something that motivates me to wake up every day and chase them.”

His casting came after ABC pulled Taylor Frankie Paul’s season of “The Bachelorette” three days before its debut in the wake of domestic abuse reports. Season 30 of “The Bachelor” will premiere March 21 on ABC.
Reporter covering food news and trends
3 recipes that show sweet potatoes are more than just a Thanksgiving side
Sweet potatoes aren’t just for holiday dinners.

Beyond a marshmallow crown, they seemingly can do it all, including main courses, salads and even desserts. And their flavor offers loads of options, too — the vitamin-packed tubers’ earthy sweetness works just as well with the heat of chili powder as it does with baking spices.
Celebrate the sweet potato every day with these recipes. And if those don’t hit the sweet (potato) spot, you’ll find more here and in The Washington Post’s vast recipe database.

Loaded Sweet Potatoes With Chili Black Beans (pictured above): Potatoes sub for tacos when topped with all kinds of Tex-Mex fillings, such as cilantro and pickled jalapeños. (You can get creative with whatever condiments and bits of vegetables you have in your fridge, and do a taco-bar-style serving setup.) This hearty dish is a meal in itself.

Sweet Potato Salad With Orange-Maple Dressing: This side dish can be a vibrant accompaniment to a holiday meal, but you don’t need to wait for a special occasion to break it out. The ingredients both lean into the potatoes’ sweetness (that’s a job for raisins and maple) and serve as a foil for it (think zesty orange and verdant parsley).

Sweet Potato Spice Cake: Molasses and baking spices are classic companions in this Bundt cake, which is so beloved by readers that it made our hall-of-fame lineup. You can swap in a can of pumpkin puree if you have one left over from holiday pies.

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/13/russia.headline: Russia is ‘setting traps’ in Ukraine talks, EU foreign policy chief warns
theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/13/russia.author: Jennifer Rankin

paragraphs.text: The EU’s foreign policy chief has warned against “walking into the traps that Russia is setting” as she said Moscow was trying to start a debate about European security in order to divert attention from its aggression.

“We have one aggressor and one victim, and the aggressor does not have security concerns,” Kaja Kallas said on arrival at an EU leaders’ summit in Dublin. “Nobody has ever attacked them. They have attacked others. I mean, keep the focus, people.”

In talks on the Ukraine war, Russia has revived its hardline demands for a total overhaul of European security – demands that were rejected in 2021 because they were seen as an infringement of the sovereignty of central and eastern European countries. The latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US was held this week in Abu Dhabi.

Donald Trump’s envoy and son-in-law, Jared Kushner, said on Thursday night that Russia and Ukraine had agreed to expand the next round of peace negotiations to include the Europeans. However, Russia quickly contradicted that assurance.

European leaders have long said they will support Ukraine in any peace talks, but want to see a ceasefire before negotiations. They also stress the continent has an extensive web of security agreements that Russia has violated.

Friedrich Merz, the German chancellor, said: “Russia wants to talk about questions of a European security architecture. We do not need to discuss that; it already exists.” He added that it was a “given” that his country would be part of any European delegation.
The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said it was “self-explanatory that Europe is included in the peace talks to safeguard our interests, but also to support Ukraine”.

The Kremlin said on Friday: “Once we understand [Europe’s] real intentions and their willingness to contribute to the peace process, then we can make a decision on holding talks in an expanded format.” Russia’s lead negotiator in Abu Dhabi, Vladimir Medinsky, said it was “unclear what there is to discuss” with Europe.
The US call to involve Europe in talks has turned the spotlight on who would represent it.

Speaking after a summit of EU leaders in Dublin on Friday, the European Council president António Costa said leaders had agreed on a negotiating team: the EU institutions and E5 countries, namely Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland.
“Europe must speak with one clear and united voice in all discussions that shape the future of Ukraine and the security of our continent,” he said. “This is ultimately a team effort.”

The format had already emerged in recent months, but the need to formalise the grouping gained momentum after Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, this week urged his European allies to decide who will represent Europe in negotiations.

Kushner also mocked the absence of a single person to speak for the entire continent. “If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiations,” he said earlier this week.

But there was an increasingly settled view that Europe would not be represented by a single person, but by different interlocutors from the wider continent. Paris and Berlin had argued for a continued role for their own envoys in the E3 format of Britain, France and Germany, alongside EU representatives. Smaller member states put the emphasis more firmly on the EU representatives: Costa and Kallas, the EU’s high representative for foreign affairs and security policy.
Earlier in the day, Sweden’s prime minister, Ulf Kristersson, said the discussion on who should represent Europe was “slightly overstated” as it had differing interests.

Some of the issues in peace talks were “pure EU interests”, he said, citing financing Kyiv and Ukraine’s future membership in the bloc. He also supported other formats, such as the “pretty uncomplicated” E3 and the “very legitimate” E5, which includes Italy and Poland, as well as a role for EU representatives. He said: “I am quite flexible on that. I think what we actually say is more important than the exact configuration of the people in the room.”

Several at the summit, including Kallas, also pointed to the importance of including the UK, a founder member of the coalition of the willing, a broad group of countries committed to future peacekeeping in Ukraine.
Ireland’s taoiseach, Micheál Martin, said the UK and Norway each had a significant role and “that all has to be taken into consideration because it’s a European, continent-wide issue”.

The British prime minister, Andy Burnham, said it was for the EU to decide who would represent the bloc. He said there was a strong view among European leaders that it was for Europe – in the wider sense – “to decide its own arrangements” on security.

latimes.com/politics/story/2026-11-13/su.headline: Supreme Court agrees to rule on Trump's asylum ban at the southern border
latimes.com/politics/story/2026-11-13/su.author: David G. Savage

paragraphs.text: WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court announced Friday it will rule on President Trump’s ban on asylum claims at the southern border, testing a key part of his hard-line policy on immigration.
At issue is a clash between the promise of asylum for those fleeing persecution and the reality of a border overwhelmed by hundreds of thousands who arrived seeking to apply.
Trump’s lawyers said his ban on asylum claims in January 2025 was his “single most effective policy” in ending the chaos along the border.

“Over preceding four years, at least eight million illegal aliens were encountered along the southern border,” Solicitor Gen. D. John Sauer told the court, “and countless millions more evaded detection and illegally entered the United States.”

The sheer numbers of people coming to the border had “overwhelmed the system,” making it impossible for U.S. officials to screen and interview asylum seekers, he said. Lacking facilities to detain applicants, most were released into the country.
But the American Civil Liberties Union and other immigration rights advocates said the right of individuals to seek asylum was recognized in U.S. law and could not be abolished.
The law authorizes asylum for people who can demonstrate they are fleeing persecution based on race, religion, nationality or belonging to a particular social or political group.

Federal judges in Washington agreed that asylum must be preserved. They said immigration officials were free to reject claims for asylum but they could not eliminate the right for the entire category of potential applicants.
However, their ruling was put on hold while the administration appealed to the Supreme Court.

“The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger,” said Lee Gelernt, lead counsel and deputy director of the ACLU’s Immigrants’ Rights Project. “The courts are right to reject this unprecedented power grab that would put countless lives in danger. We look forward to making our case before the Supreme Court.”

Keren Zwick, executive director of the National Immigrant Justice Center, said the plaintiffs in the case “fled persecution and torture, including political imprisonment and threats from the Taliban. Yet, the Trump administration refused to honor its obligation to consider them for asylum.”
Instead, some of them “were removed to third countries and then pushed back to the very place they fled. This vicious attack on due process and human rights has put thousands of lives in danger.”
Federal immigration law gives the president broad authority to close the border to most migrants.

It says he “may by proclamation, and for such period as he shall deem necessary, suspend the entry of all aliens or any class of aliens as immigrants or nonimmigrants, or impose on the entry of aliens any restrictions he may deem to be appropriate.”
The court said it would hear the case of Mullin vs. Refugee and Immigrant Center early next year and rule by June.

finance.yahoo.com/markets/commodities/ar.headline: Microsoft Outage Disrupts Oil Trader Data and Dealmaking
finance.yahoo.com/markets/commodities/ar.author: Nathan Risser and Mia Gindis

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Around noon on Thursday, Oklahoma-based commodities trader Dennis Kissler's inbox went eerily quiet, even as new comments on the Iran war by US President Donald Trump sent oil into a volatile stretch.
Most Read from Bloomberg
It took another hour for his team to realize emails weren't going through and start calling clients instead.
"We were in a one hour black hole. It definitely threw us off," said Kissler, who uses Microsoft Corp.'s Outlook to communicate with clients, many of whom are executives at shale producers.

A major outage of Microsoft's flagship software starting Thursday hit government offices, businesses and traders around the world, leaving many, like Kissler, who serves as senior vice president for trading at BOK Financial Securities Inc., to try other forms of communication. In some cases, traders reverted to old-school methods, including employees taking orders and relaying fills by phone and fax machine.

For oil traders, the outage added another layer of complexity to a market already upended by months of conflict in the Middle East. Any delay to putting on or unwinding a trade can prove costly in today's headline-driven market, where prices can turn on a dime as traders parse every development tied to US-Iran peace talks.

Microsoft on Friday said it was making progress in efforts to restore access and service availability. Still, the company warned that users of more than 20 products and services may continue to encounter errors.
One of the key pain points for traders during the outage has been commodity price data.

In Iowa, refined products broker Ken Malloy realized just before noon local time on Thursday that he couldn't access his email. He tried for hours but ultimately couldn't send out a report detailing fuel prices for clients of Kembro Fuel Brokers that he publishes four times a day. He continued to try late into the night but the issue wasn't fixed and he ended up sending Thursday's report early Friday morning.

Commodity traders and the oil and gas industry more broadly — from drillers to refiners — rely on prices published by several reporting agencies. One of the main agencies, S&P Global's division Platts, alerted clients Thursday that price updates may be delayed due to the outage and asked market participants who share information with them to communicate via phone or instant messenger as the company was unable to receive data via email.

Natural gas and biofuels prices were delayed and 22 biofuels prices would not publish until the outage is resolved, according to Platts. As of Friday afternoon in New York, Platts' alert system says the "incident has now been resolved."
Meanwhile, an oil trader in Houston faced several internal issues as email stopped working and key reports showing profits and risk exposures broke down.
Some traders were relatively insulated from the outage, either using alternative email services not tied to Microsoft or relying on instant messaging services like ICE Chat to conduct business.

The Microsoft malfunction has been felt across commodities markets. For metals, trading itself wasn't disrupted because traders could execute electronically through CME Direct, Trading Technologies or OTC platforms.
John Porter, managing director of special metals at CCMA LLC, said the outage was an "inconvenience for sure." But there was another takeaway: "A phone call still works," he said.
--With assistance from Yvonne Yue Li and Grace Asenov.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Fed on Track to Raise Interest Rates Next Month And Maybe Again in January
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Enda Curran

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- The US monetary policy debate has already moved on to January.
Most Read from Bloomberg

In a blitz of speeches and interviews this week, Federal Reserve officials locked in market expectations for an interest-rate hike in December and opened the prospect of the first back-to-back increases since 2023.
The case for higher rates was given new urgency Tuesday when the October consumer-price report showed inflation accelerated and broadened across everyday goods and services.

"Inflation is far too high," said New York Fed President John Williams, while Chicago Fed's Austan Goolsbee described the data as "borderline disturbing." Dallas Fed President Lorie Logan said officials may need to hike "more rapidly" than she expected, while Fed Governor Christopher Waller went as far as warning that a 50-basis-points move may be needed next month.

"December is clearly locked and loaded for a 25-basis-point hike," said Olu Sonola, head of US economics at Fitch Ratings. "The real questions are how quickly the next hike follows and how many more will ultimately be needed."

About half of the 19 officials who sit on the Federal Open Market Committee, and about half who will vote at the December and January meetings, have spoken over the course of the week. On the last two questions, the signals were mixed.

They ranged from Waller's reference to an outsized move to the Cleveland Fed's Beth Hammack reiterating her preference for more frequent, smaller rises, and Philadelphia Fed President Anna Paulson favoring a gradual pace for increases.

There was more bad news on Friday when data showed wholesale prices, which feed into the Fed's preferred measure of inflation, climbed in October from a year earlier at their fastest pace since 2022. Transportation and warehousing costs jumped, adding to evidence of persistent price pressures throughout the economy.

"It now sounds like there's a worry to get ahead of the re-acceleration and increase the frequency and potentially increase what the FOMC views as terminal," meaning how high the rates should ultimately go, said Michael Reid, head of US economics at the Royal Bank of Canada.

Economists at Bank of America and at Santander US Capital Markets increased the number of hikes they expect following the week of data and the flurry of speeches. Bank of America now sees increases at the next three Fed meetings, while Santander is projecting two raises, in December and March.

The case for caution rests on parts of the economy that are vulnerable to higher borrowing costs, such as the housing market. Economic data this week highlighted how depressed that sector is, with sales of previously owned homes falling last month to a 16-year low.

Boston Fed President Susan Collins on Friday acknowledged that higher interest rates can hurt housing affordability, but added that price stability, in the long run, is more important for housing and the overall economy.

"It does seem to me that the appropriate direction for monetary policy is clear," she said, referring to the need to raise rates. But, in an interview with Bloomberg Television, she stopped short of revealing what she thought would be the right pace.
"I don't want to get ahead in terms of how high we should go or how fast," she said.

Stock market volatility linked to concerns about a slowdown in the artificial intelligence boom is another concern. Fed Governor Michelle Bowman cautioned of risks that include a sharp downturn in share prices if returns on investments in AI fall short of expectations.

"Lower equity prices could undermine the resilience in consumer spending," she said. "And higher interest rates could further strain interest-rate-sensitive sectors of the economy, like housing and small business investment."
Another variable is the potential for a decline in energy prices over coming months that would take pressure off fuel costs and offer relief to households and businesses.
Richmond Fed President Tom Barkin, who spoke on Monday, said rates need to go higher but at a careful pace.

"Most Fed officials seem aligned on the need for hikes and the preference to not rush things," Eric Wallerstein, chief macro strategist for Clocktower Group and previously an adviser to former Fed Governor Stephen Miran.
Fed officials raised rates by a quarter-point in September to a target range of 3.75% to 4%, and then held steady when the FOMC last met in October.

Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh, who hasn't spoken publicly since his October press conference, is due to talk about his task force on AI and productivity at an event on Monday. Few expect him to deviate from his stated preference not to give any guidance on the near-term outlook for policy.
Yet investors aren't waiting and have already priced quarter-point increases in for December, January and March. Before this week, investors had anticipated increases in December and March.

In an example of how jolted markets were by this week's Fed communication, Treasury yields spiked after the remarks from Waller and Logan, who spoke before and after the hotter-than-expected inflation data on Tuesday. The yield on the two-year note rose 19 basis points to 4.75% that day, its largest gain since President Donald Trump's tariff announcements roiled global markets in April 2025.

"The guidance from the Fed is a bit confusing and has sparked large swings in Treasury yields, and again — with Chair Warsh refraining from commenting — others are filling the void," said Nationwide Chief Economist Kathy Bostjancic.

Ultimately, accelerating economic growth may offer cover for the Fed to hike. Data last week showed jobs growth surged in October and the unemployment rate edged lower. Officials will receive one more jobs report and another read of October inflation before they gather again in December.
Few observers expect that set of data will reveal a meaningful slowdown.

"Gradualism is a policy mistake in an economy with strong growth and high inflation," said Robert Sockin, chief US economist at PGIM. "History suggests a high risk that this approach ultimately leads a central bank to need to tighten faster and more overall than it would have had to do otherwise."
