latimes.com/entertainment-arts/music/sto.headline: U2 'Carnaval de Luz' review: A rock band at the end of history
latimes.com/entertainment-arts/music/sto.author: Mikael Wood

paragraphs.text: Eight songs into U2’s new album, and there it is: the silvery thrum of the Edge’s electric guitar, echoing into infinity as Adam Clayton and Larry Mullen Jr. lock into a driving groove and Bono starts crooning about how “love’s the hardest easy thing.”

More than any other passage on “Carnaval de Luz,” which dropped Friday, the beginning of “The Greatest Show on Earth” is instantly identifiable as the work of these four veteran musicians — and clearly an assertion, 50 years after they formed the group, that they’ve still got it.
Except, hold on: What’s that Bono sings when he gets to the song’s sweeping chorus?
If this is love, don’t act surprised when you get hurt
Even if our dreams lay in the dirt
We were once the greatest show on Earth
Stuck in a moment you can get out of — that’s the spirit of U2’s 16th studio LP, a grippingly honest if typically idealistic meditation on the value of a rock ’n’ roll band at the end of history.

The quartet’s first album of new songs in nearly a decade, “Carnaval de Luz” might easily have not happened: After touring the world to celebrate the 30th anniversary of “The Joshua Tree,” Mullen was in such bad shape physically (thanks to a long-standing neck injury) that he sat out U2’s residency at the Las Vegas Sphere in 2023 and 2024. And even if the drummer was able to play — a necessary precondition, his bandmates have said, for the group to make a record — it’s not as though anyone was clamoring for one after the increasingly tedious “Songs of Innocence”/“Songs of Experience”/“Songs of Surrender” project.

But then Mullen met a young neurosurgeon willing to perform a risky surgery; back together as a foursome, U2 found enough inspiration in various global outrages — Gaza, Ukraine, the state-sponsored killing of Renée Good — to bust out a couple of surprise EPs early this year.
Having worked through an animating fury, “Carnaval de Luz” aims for what the Edge has called “defiant joy,” which I’m sorry to say yields some deeply embarrassing lyrics.

“I see a summer down the road of songs and a silver sea,” Bono sings in “Can’t Stop Us Now,” “Where the rainbow refuses the gold, and that’s revolutionary.” In “Superficiality,” he proclaims, “You and me are breaking news because the news can’t break us.” (Bro.)

Yet what comes through is U2’s earnest belief that these songs matter — that the band has something to offer a world in crisis, even if that something is just a righteously crunchy guitar riff, as in “La Reina” and the title track, or a soaring vocal melody like those in “Superficiality” and “The Greatest Show on Earth.” Indeed, Bono sounds better here than he has in years — supple and sensual but with just the right touch of desperation — which bodes well for the band’s 2027 stadium tour.

The achievement of “Carnaval de Luz” is an emotional state somewhere between nostalgic and thirsty; the music seems to know more about life (and death) than it actually says, at least until the album’s closer, “Torn.” Recorded shortly before Dolly Parton’s death in August, it’s a stirring yet unflowery duet between her and Bono about a mother who has no idea how to get her warring sons to reconcile.
The song’s beauty is in its intertwined voices; its wisdom is in its acceptance that no fix is assured.

cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-stock-jensen-.headline: Nvidia stock suffers longest weekly losing streak since 2012 as market value sinks by $1.7 trillion
cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-stock-jensen-.author: Ari Levy

paragraphs.text: Nvidia investors turned bearish before this week's Jensen Huang saga. But the selling on Wall Street accelerated in the past few days, sending the stock to its sixth straight weekly drop, the longest losing streak since 2012.

The chip giant, which spent most of the year as the world's most valuable company, has lost 30% of its value during losing streak. That's a drop of roughly $1.7 trillion in market cap, and it fell below Apple in the process.

Huang, who co-founded Nvidia and led it for 33 years, resigned on Thursday after two separate extramarital affairs — one with an alleged Chinese spy and the other with an employee — were made public. The board named finance chief Colette Kress as interim CEO while it conducts a search for a full-time successor.

Nvidia shares fell 13% this week, the most since April 2025. News of the first reported affair hit the front pages over the weekend, when Huang sent a letter to employees apologizing for being "unfaithful to my wife." The board convened late Wednesday after The New York Times reported on the other affair, this one with the company's vice president of health care.
By early Thursday morning, Huang was out, capping a stunning fall for the Nvidia co-founder, who had emerged as one of President Donald Trump's top allies in the corporate world.

"With the unfortunate departure of CEO Jensen Huang we expect a challenging transition for NVIDIA over the next few months," Gil Luria, an analyst at D.A. Davidson, wrote in a report on Thursday. Luria lowered his price target to $200 from $300, but maintained his buy rating. "We believe the market has appropriately adjusted for this transition," he wrote.

Last week, prior to Huang's departure, Nvidia shares dropped about 9%. Much of the decline came after the midterm elections, which resulted in sweeping victories for Democrats and the passage of dozens of ballot measures that could slow the artificial intelligence buildout.

In the weeks before the election, Nvidia's stock was sliding alongside the rest of the AI trade on concerns that rising interest rates would punish debt-heavy companies. While Nvidia is wildly profitable, big customers like neoclouds are reliant on the debt markets.

Heading into next week, the pressure is on Kress. Nvidia is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday. Analysts are projecting 91% year-over-year revenue growth to $108.9 billion, according to LSEG. That's up 18-fold from the same quarter in 2022, just before OpenAI launched ChatGPT and kicked off the generative AI era.
Analysts at Oppenheimer wrote in a report on Thursday that, even though they see the company reporting solid earnings, "we expect fundamentals to take a backseat near term."
"The departure of Mr. Huang could, in our view, translate to a lingering share overhang," they wrote.

washingtonpost.com/world/2026/11/13/ukra.headline: Ukraine critic injured in Moscow car bombing, Russia says
washingtonpost.com/world/2026/11/13/ukra.author: Natalia Abbakumova

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following

A car bombing in Moscow on Friday seriously injured a former adviser to Ukrainian Prime Minister Mykola Azarov who fled to Russia after his boss’s resignation in 2014 and became a pro-Kremlin commentator.

The explosion came a day after a Russian military officer was killed in a similar attack in St. Petersburg, and it follows a string of assassinations of Russian military figures and high-profile supporters of the war in Ukraine.
According to Russian officials, the car exploded while Sergei Zavorotny, 72, was driving, and he was taken to a hospital in critical condition.

Zavorotny, a former journalist with Komsomolskaya Pravda, served as Azarov’s adviser from 2010 to 2014 and moved to Russia after the ouster of Azarov and President Viktor Yanukovych, who both also fled to Russia. Yanukovich’s decision in late 2013 to abandon an association agreement with the European Union in favor of closer ties with Moscow sparked the Maidan protests.

Since then Zavorotny has been a prominent pro-Russian commentator, who regularly claimed that the Maidan revolution was orchestrated by Western governments. A 2020 U.S. Senate Intelligence Committee report identified him as an officer of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service.

Azarov told Russian state TV he was “shocked” by the attack and accused Ukrainian intelligence services of targeting Zavorotny over his criticism of Ukraine, without providing evidence. Ukrainian officials did not immediately respond to questions about the attack.
National correspondent covering the Southeast
Tanker strikes cruise ship in New Orleans, sending passengers into river

A tanker on Friday afternoon hit a passenger cruise ship that was docked along the Mississippi River in New Orleans, causing a massive emergency response that included firefighters rescuing people from the water.

Kimberly Curth, a Port of New Orleans spokeswoman, said the incident happened at approximately 12:30 p.m. local time when an Atlantic Asphalt tanker crashed into the docked American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage ship that had docked about two hours earlier.
An estimated 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, were aboard the American Heritage at the time, Curth said.

Port NOLA Harbor Police, the New Orleans Fire Department, the New Orleans Police Department, the U.S. Coast Guard and emergency medical personnel were on scene, conducting rescue and response operations.
Curth said passengers were being brought inside the port’s administration building “for triage and assistance.”

“Our immediate priority is the safety of all passengers, crew members and first responders,” she said in a statement. “This remains an active and evolving incident. The number of injuries and the cause of the collision have not yet been confirmed.”
Reporter covering politics with a focus on campaigns
Van Hollen ‘no longer pursuing’ possible 2028 bid as he seeks Senate leader job
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland) is abandoning his presidential ambitions for 2028 as he seeks instead to oust Sen. Chuck Schumer (D) from his leadership role.

“I’m no longer pursuing that,” Van Hollen said Friday of his potential 2028 presidential bid, after a speech to Democrats gathered in Denver to celebrate the party’s huge wins in the midterm elections and chart a cohesive path forward.

“I believe that the size and scale of these majorities provides an opportunity for the United States Senate to answer the call of the American people,” Van Hollen said. “We can’t go back to business as usual.”

He announced his challenge to Schumer, the Senate minority leader, late Thursday, sparking a public power struggle alongside the work to unite Democrats. Until this week, Van Hollen had been “kicking the tires” on a presidential bid.
Van Hollen, 67, said the election called for a generational shift and that Schumer, 75, represented a style of politics that voters wanted to change.

He again characterized himself as an underdog in his leadership competition with Schumer, who has led the chamber’s Democratic caucus since 2017. And he declined to publicly reveal how many fellow senators have agreed to support him. But Van Hollen said he spoke directly with Schumer about it.
“We understand that this will be a competition. I think it’s important to give Senate Democrats a choice. That’s what we just gave voters all over the country a choice. They chose change,” he said.
Reporter covering arts and culture
Stacey Abrams told Ava DuVernay to hold ‘14th’ until after midterms

Ava DuVernay’s first documentary in 10 years — titled “14th,” after the constitutional amendment that it traces — will arrive on Netflix on Dec. 4. That wasn’t always DuVernay’s plan: At one point, she wanted it to be released ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.

“It was Stacey Abrams who said to me, ‘You shouldn’t do that,’” DuVernay said Thursday at the Global Women’s Summit hosted by The Washington Post. She added that Abrams, the former two-time candidate for Georgia governor and voting rights activist, thought the film “will be more needed and more instructive after” the elections.

Abrams is interviewed in “14th,” which follows the history of the amendment that grants birthright citizenship, protects due process and guarantees equal protection under the law. DuVernay felt compelled to make the documentary after the Trump administration tried to end birthright citizenship via executive order, setting off a wave of litigation before the Supreme Court affirmed in June that nearly everyone born on U.S. soil is a citizen.

“What she really was saying to me is that the opposition is not going away,” DuVernay told The Post’s Geoff Edgers, explaining why Abrams thought it made sense for “14th” to arrive after Nov. 3. “These ideas are not going away, the money behind it is not going away, and it will come back with a vengeance.”
Anchor of the Early Brief newsletter
Trump gives Scott Colom ‘a lot of credit’ for campaigning at a MAGA rally
President Donald Trump doesn’t often give Democrats much credit.
But in an interview Thursday, he praised Democrat Scott Colom, who defeated Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith (R) in Mississippi in the midterms, for meeting with voters outside a Trump rally last month.

“I heard it the other day, where I had a rally there, and we had lines that went 10 miles long, and he campaigned on that line, telling everybody on the line what a good job he did,” Trump said during an interview on Stephen A. Smith’s “Straight Shooter” podcast. “I give him a lot of credit for that.”

Colom made reaching out to Trump supporters central to his campaign in Mississippi, reflecting how the state has consistently voted for Republicans and backed Trump by 22 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election. Colom’s visit to the Trump rally gained widespread attention online.

“What are you expecting? I’ve never been to a Trump rally,” Colom asked people in line. “What matters to you as a veteran right now?” he asked one man, who told him about gun rights. Other voters told him they were worried about high gas prices and the Iran war.
“I walked the Trump rally line to listen, not make assumptions. I talked with voters, asked questions and heard what matters to them,” Colom wrote about his interactions.
Meteorologist covering significant weather events and climate trends
Why the polar vortex has forecasters on alert for Arctic cold in the U.S.
For weeks, the weather community has been buzzing about an unusual phenomenon unfolding one atmospheric layer above us in the stratosphere.
It’s called a sudden stratospheric warming and involves temperatures rising rapidly and winds weakening significantly some 20 miles above the North Pole.

These warming events are most common during winter, but they can sometimes can happen in late fall or early spring — and right now, the earliest one on record is occurring, among records dating to 1958.

This warming is destabilizing the polar vortex and has caused it to stretch beyond its typical length. The vortex normally keeps frigid air locked up near the pole, but this disturbance could unleash it southward into areas where more people live.

That would only happen if stratospheric patterns filter down to the troposphere, which is the atmospheric layer where weather takes shape. Meteorologists liken this atmospheric-filtering process to “dripping paint.”

Late last November, a stratospheric warming event quickly dripped from the stratosphere to the troposphere, influencing a cold and snowy stretch across the United States that lasted for a month or two.

This year, the influence of this polar vortex disruption is looking less concrete, though some meteorologists are increasingly flagging the potential for it to play some role in U.S. weather patterns from late November into December.
However, its effects could be muted by a record El Niño, which has fueled an exceptionally mild start to November across much of the country.

If the polar vortex unleashes even a brief surge of icy air into the U.S., it would probably increase the chances for a blockbuster winter storm or two before the end of the year — especially when combined with El Niño’s heightened levels of atmospheric moisture.
The next ‘Bachelor’ star is Commanders quarterback Sam Hartman
Sam Hartman, a 27-year-old quarterback on the Washington Commanders’ practice squad, will be the next star of ABC’s “The Bachelor.”
Hartman, who will be asked to date 20 to 30 women at once before choosing a fiancée, said Friday on “Good Morning America” that he’s “very nervous.”
“I have a tough time holding conversation with one girl,” he said. “30 is going to be pretty tough.”

Hartman set various school records while playing college football at Wake Forest. In 2022, he was diagnosed with Paget-Schroetter syndrome and received the ACC’s Brian Piccolo Award for courage. He transferred to Notre Dame for his final season in 2023.
Hartman signed with the Commanders as an undrafted free agent in 2024. He has not yet appeared in a regular season game, spending most of his time on the team’s practice squad.
Asked what he looks for in a partner, Hartman said he likes “competitiveness.” He continued, “They have a drive for something that motivates me to wake up every day and chase them.”

His casting came after ABC pulled Taylor Frankie Paul’s season of “The Bachelorette” three days before its debut in the wake of domestic abuse reports. Season 30 of “The Bachelor” will premiere March 21 on ABC.

cnbc.com/2026/11/13/ai-risks-financial-s.headline: AI risks are the biggest threat to the financial system, Fed survey finds
cnbc.com/2026/11/13/ai-risks-financial-s.author: Jeff Cox

paragraphs.text: Threats from artificial intelligence topped the list for greatest risks to the financial system, far exceeding any other dangers, according to respondents who participated in a Federal Reserve survey released Friday.

The central bank's twice-yearly look at a variety of dangers saw a surge in respondents saying that the biggest danger comes from AI along several fronts including debt, stock market valuations and security risks.

"Respondents noted three distinct areas of concern: (1) elevated equity valuations and the possibility that lower-than-expected earnings could result in lower valuations and a market correction; (2) cybersecurity risk, stemming from either a malicious attack by sophisticated state actors or damage caused by frontier AI models themselves; and (3) risks associated with complex forms of AI-related financing," the report stated.

The report comes with Wall Street on edge over high-flying AI hyperscalers, while communities are on alert for the rapid spread of data centers used to power the technology. Some 56% of voters in this month's midterm elections said data centers were of crucial or major importance in their choices, according to exit polling.

Respondents to the Fed survey released Friday include a variety of market participants, economists, analysts and institutional sources. The report covers the period up to Oct. 28, just a few days shy of the election.

Of the group, 87% cited AI as a "salient risk" to the system. That was up from 50% in the survey during the spring of this year and well ahead of the next most-cited danger, a risk asset correction, which was mentioned by 52% of those surveyed.

Other leading risks were higher long-term rates (48%), cyberattacks (43%) and fiscal debt sustainability (43%), the latter coming with the U.S. debt over $40 trillion and the budget deficit near $2 trillion.
The report otherwise found the system fairly stable, though it mentioned that hedge fund leverage is at its highest since 2013 and concentrated on a relatively small group.

washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/13/s.headline: Supreme Court to review Trump policy blocking asylum seekers at border
washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/13/s.author: Julian Mark

paragraphs.text: The Supreme Court said Friday it will review President Donald Trump’s policy restricting entry to asylum seekers at the border between the United States and Mexico, a policy central to his immigration agenda.
The case is one of several high-profile immigration matters the Supreme Court has agreed to review in the coming months.

On the first day of his second term, Trump issued a proclamation barring entry to people seeking asylum for public safety, health and economic reasons until the administration found that “the invasion at the southern border has ceased.”

Advocates for immigrants challenged the policy, arguing that the president lacked the authority to impose the restriction. Federal law gives migrants the right to seek asylum if they fear persecution based on their political opinions, race or other reasons.

“The president does not have the right to unilaterally override the protections Congress has afforded those fleeing danger,” Lee Gelernt, deputy director of the American Civil Liberties Union’s Immigrants’ Rights Project, said in a statement Friday.

Crossings at the southern border have plummeted in recent years. Border encounters have fallen from more than 2.4 million in 2023 to just under 140,000 last fiscal year, which ran from Oct. 1, 2025, to Sept. 30, according to U.S. Customs and Border Protection figures.

“The single most important factor in the President’s success at the border has been this executive order, which he signed on day one,” James Percival, general counsel at the Department of Homeland Security, wrote in a social media post about the court taking up the case. “After successfully preserving this authority in lower courts for two years, we look forward to presenting our arguments to the Supreme Court.”
The high court’s decision to hear the asylum issue adds it to the mounting list of immigration-related cases awaiting the justices.

Next month, the justices will hear arguments about the Trump administration policy of deporting immigrants to countries that are not their own. It will also hear arguments regarding the Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s mandatory detention policy — in which undocumented immigrants who have lived in the country for years are detained until their deportation cases are resolved, which could take weeks or months.
The court’s 6-3 conservative majority has been largely sympathetic to the Trump administration’s immigration policies.

This year, the court allowed the administration to cancel temporary humanitarian protections for hundreds of thousands of immigrants living legally in the United States. The justices also said immigration officials are allowed to physically turn back asylum seekers from crossing the U.S.-Mexico border.

But the court also has handed Trump high-profile defeats, including rebuffing his attempt to ban birthright citizenship. The court in June narrowly upheld the Constitution’s guarantee of birthright citizenship.
Maria Sacchetti contributed to this report.

cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/13/honeypot-sca.headline: They train people to avoid 'honeypot' scams—here are the common red flags they spot: 'It feels so good to be wanted'
cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/13/honeypot-sca.author: Tom Huddleston Jr.

paragraphs.text: Shawnee Delaney often kicks off a training session by telling a room full of corporate workers: "OK, raise your hand if you've ever gotten a flattering message on LinkedIn just complimenting your background and your profile and your experience."
"Every hand goes up," she says. Then, she tells attendees how responding to a simple adulatory message could unwittingly open the door to a potential romance scam.

Delaney is a corporate security expert, well-versed in teaching people how to avoid “honeypot” schemes, in which a bad actor uses romantic or sexual interest to build trust and gain information, access or leverage over a target. The term is currently making headlines in the wake of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation from the company, following reporting on his admitted affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Honeypots, also known as "honey traps," are a very human form of social engineering attack, a category that also includes various forms of phishing and use of deepfake technology. And you don't have to be a billionaire tech CEO to possess information that scammers may value.

As competition in the global artificial intelligence race heats up, OpenAI is reportedly training employees to recognize espionage tactics including bribery, romantic manipulation and blackmail, according to The Wall Street Journal. On Nov. 3, cryptocurrency exchange Binance revealed that a recent cyberattack — which saw roughly $6 billion of digital assets stolen — was partially made possible by a fake job interview scheme that infected an employee’s work computer with malware.

"People can get solicited, bribed, romanced, etc.," says Kevin Tian, co-founder and CEO of Doppel, an AI-powered platform meant to help identify and deflect social engineering attacks. He adds: "If you've got access to sensitive IP [intellectual property] — it's not just AI companies — you can be a target."

Increasingly, scammers can use AI to scour websites ranging from Reddit to Pinterest for an individual's personal information and customize a ploy designed specifically for them, Tian says. Once they have relevant data points, attackers tend to use "the oldest tricks in the book: elicitation, flattery, ego," says Delaney, a former intelligence officer with the Defense Intelligence Agency and the founder and CEO of Washington, D.C.-based corporate security consulting firm Vaillance Group.

In many cases, Delaney notes, targets have an inkling that something is suspicious — but they'd rather allow themselves to believe the interest is legitimate. So how do you keep yourself from falling victim? Trust your self-awareness, common sense and ability to identify situations that feel too good to be true, she says.
"The bottom line is, we're all human," says Delaney, adding: "It feels so good to be wanted, or to be respected, or to be appreciated, or loved."
How to spot red flags and do some vetting

Delaney, who has worked with Fortune 500 companies such as Uber and Merck, advises corporate clients on cybersecurity risks and develops training programs to improve employees' awareness of security threats. Her sessions aim to build awareness of manipulative connections, such as romance scams, from how they begin to the natural progression they often take. "Introduction, then repeated contact, favors, sensitive requests — the secrecy, the pressure," she says.

Bad actors may tap into any information you post online to find an interest that can be mirrored and exploited, or an acquaintance who can be infiltrated and make an introduction. If someone you know and trust makes an introduction, you might be less likely to "go do due diligence" on the new person, even if they're a stranger, Delaney says.

One of Vaillance's services includes building a "targeting package" around an executive or C-Suite member, says Delaney. "We can show how they are vulnerable and how we would target that organization just by leveraging the people around them in that circle: spouses, friends, kids, parents, administrative assistants, neighbors," she says. "That's when people's eyes open."

From there, she discusses red flags to spot. Conversations that begin with flattery and seemingly innocuous small talk can gradually shift toward digging for information, introductions to colleagues or access to documents, says Delaney. It's human nature to want to be helpful and fulfill friendly requests, she adds. Add a potential romantic connection to the mix, especially amid an ongoing "loneliness epidemic," and the urge to comply can be even harder to resist, she says.

If you feel yourself getting cornered in a situation where a recent acquaintance or romantic partner keeps asking for information you're not comfortable revealing, Delaney says it helps to have first practiced polite refusal. "One of my favorites is: They could just respond with: 'Why do you ask?'" she says. "Put the other person on the defensive. You could give a nondescript answer. You can say you don't know. You can say you can't respond."

If you're ever suspicious of a new connection — even if you don't want to be — do yourself a favor and conduct some basic vetting, she recommends. You might examine their social media profiles and other publicly available information, for example, to see if their story checks out.

If you can't find enough information to allay your suspicions, don't be shy about alerting your employer's security or human resources team, she says. For smaller companies, or scams outside the workplace, you can file a complaint for cyber threats or romance scams with the Federal Bureau of Investigation's Internet Crime Complaint Center.
And pay attention if your new paramour starts asking you specific questions about your finances or work credentials, says Delaney.
"If you have no game at home, and you get off an airplane somewhere and suddenly everyone's all over you, we call that a red flag," she says.

cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-jensen-huang-.headline: Nvidia is done with Jensen Huang. The fallout in Washington is just beginning
cnbc.com/2026/11/13/nvidia-jensen-huang-.author: Garrett Downs, Justin Papp, Karen James Sloan, Irit Skulnik

paragraphs.text: Jensen Huang is out at Nvidia. Washington is just getting started with him and the company he co-founded.

Huang, the leather-jacket-clad CEO of the world's most important chipmaker, resigned from Nvidia on Thursday after revelations that he had an affair with a suspected Chinese spy. But the spy saga is gripping Washington, and lawmakers are preparing for investigations into how the now-ex-CEO's affair may have damaged U.S. artificial intelligence dominance, the national security implications and the executive's close relationship with President Donald Trump and his Cabinet.

Republicans will have their chance first during their last six weeks controlling both chambers of Congress. GOP leaders immediately summoned Huang to Capitol Hill and said they would subpoena him if he doesn't agree to show up. In January, Democrats, who are already eager to make their mark with oversight when they take over the U.S. House and Senate, will be in the driver's seat.

"In this environment where there's some really high stakes when it comes to our national security, I would expect there would be some follow-up, yeah," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., told reporters at the Capitol on Thursday.

Huang and the woman with whom he reportedly had a relationship, Alice Huang, an executive at the Singaporean technology company Megaspeed and an alleged Chinese spy have drawn congressional attention. And Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has drawn fire after reports this week that he stalled President Donald Trump's crackdowns on firms routing Nvidia chips to China.

Some Congress members have also called for an investigation into the role of the Bureau of Industry and Security, a subagency of the Commerce Department that manages and enforces export controls, in the Huang scandal.

The New York Times reported on Monday that Nvidia's general counsel, Tim Teter, claimed in emails to Commerce investigators probing Alice Huang's company that he'd been in touch with Jeffrey Kessler, who leads BIS. The Commerce investigation into Megaspeed, which allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China, was then transferred to the Justice Department.

By Thursday night, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott, R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick to testify before his committee in December. Later that same night, Lutnick had "proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement.
Scott threatened to subpoena Huang if he does not appear. A banking panel spokesperson did not immediately respond Friday morning when asked if they'd heard from Huang.
"Recent reports raise serious concerns about our national security and the protection of sensitive U.S. technology," Scott wrote to Huang. "The American people deserve answers."

And with Democrats poised to take control of both chambers come January, the tech mogul's close ties to the White House will add fuel to an already burning fire as the new majority spools up myriad investigations into the Trump administration.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., in a post to X on Thursday, said "Congress must demand answers from Mr. Huang and others at Nvidia about how they may have put U.S. national security at risk." Schumer is in a contested race to become Senate majority leader in the next Congress.
The senators who will lead those investigations, and hold subpoena power in the new Congress, are gearing up for Nvidia to take center stage.

Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., the likely incoming chair of the Senate banking panel, said in a statement Thursday that "Mr. Huang, NVIDIA executives, and NVIDIA's board of directors still owe Congress answers about the company's compliance with U.S. export controls

Warren and Sen. Chris Coons, D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter Wednesday to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
Even before Democrats take control in January, Huang is expected to appear before Congress.

House Foreign Affairs Committee Chair Brian Mast, R-Fla., is actively negotiating for Huang to testify before House committees and told reporters Thursday the Nvidia CEO has agreed to appear in the coming weeks.

Details of that testimony are still being worked out, Mast said. It would likely include his committee, as well as the House intelligence panel and the House Permanent Select Committee on China, and it would be under oath and transcribed. It's not clear at this point whether it would be public.
"We want to see him basically in a week … Sooner rather than later," Mast told reporters Thursday, adding that he believed it would happen before Thanksgiving.
If Huang doesn't willingly appear, Mast said he will subpoena him.

Mast, along with House Select China Committee Chair Rep. John Moolenaar, R-Mich., and House Intelligence Committee Chair Rick Crawford, R-Ark., send a second request Thursday to Huang and Teter requesting they appear and giving them an 8 p.m. ET Friday deadline to respond. Mast sent a second request to Kessler.

Rep. Josh Gottheimer, D-N.J., a member of the House Intelligence Committee, said Friday during an appearance on CNBC's "The Exchange" that he wants answers from Huang on the national security and export implications of the affair.

"From an intelligence committee perspective, you can imagine from an AI perspective, how important this is for our national security, for our critical infrastructure and understand when it comes to chip policy, what exactly got to China and ... did Megaspeed divert chips?" Gottheimer said.

The calls for immediate investigation into Huang and Nvidia on the day of his resignation represent a stunning fall from grace in the halls of power for the former CEO. Huang was one of the most effective voices for the AI industry in Washington — able to toggle between leveraging his relationship with Trump and defending his industry from fears about AI's risks to lawmakers.

"He is always the TED Talk guy," one senior Democratic staff member who was granted anonymity to describe private meetings they had attended with Huang, told CNBC. "He's really good and articulate, and really good at explaining why AI is important and why it's so important for the United States to be leading here."

The staffer said Huang was a "happy warrior" for AI, and stayed longer than scheduled or anticipated for questions from lawmakers. But in the meetings with lawmakers the aide attended, they said Huang did not aggressively push against export controls or get too "deep in the weeds" to really "lobby one way or the other" with the lawmakers.
Huang has repeatedly resisted export controls publicly, a move that has rubbed some lawmakers the wrong way.
Some lawmakers even lamented the loss of Huang, despite the inevitable buzzsaw he now faces on Capitol Hill.
"It's just sad all around," Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., said of Huang's resignation.

politico.com/newsletters/new-york-playbo.headline: Trump and Zohran sitting in a tree…
politico.com/newsletters/new-york-playbo.author: Molly Reinmann and Joe Anuta

paragraphs.text: FRIENDS WITH (SNAP) BENEFITS: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani unveiled the latest perk of his chummy relationship with President Donald Trump, announcing a deal today that will give stores across the country more time to comply with changes to federal food assistance rules.
New rules from the Department of Agriculture, which took effect last week, required retailers to stock a greater diversity of products in order to continue receiving SNAP benefits.

Just before they kicked in, Mamdani signed onto a bipartisan letter to USDA Secretary Brooke Rollins urging the Trump administration to delay implementing the new requirements. He warned the rules would threaten the viability of the city’s more than 10,000 bodegas and corner stores, as well as the New Yorkers who rely on them, if the stores could not meet the mandates in time and lost the ability to accept SNAP payments.

Now, after negotiations with Rollins and foe-turned-bro Trump, Mamdani secured a 90-day extension for small retailers to comply with the rules — not just in New York City, but nationwide. The extension starts Friday.
Mamdani said he personally escalated the extension request to President Trump after City Hall reached out to the federal government.

“What I told the president was that this is a rule that, if allowed to be implemented on the timeline as it was scheduled, would be one that would throw the lives of so many working New Yorkers into a real place of anxiety and chaos,” he said. “And the president took that concern seriously.”
Mamdani declined to share how often he chats with Trump — “I’ll keep the cadence of that between the two of us,” he said — but he emphasized their conversations are ongoing.
As the two executives approach the one-year anniversary of their unexpected bromance, today’s announcement serves as a reminder that Mamdani’s Trump strategy has largely paid off.

After a seemingly love-struck Trump emerged from the duo’s first Oval Office meeting on Nov. 21, the threat of an immigration enforcement surge on par with Minneapolis largely evaporated, eliminating a potentially explosive situation that at the time loomed over the mayor’s early days in office.

In February, Mamdani successfully petitioned Trump to release a Columbia University student who had been taken into the custody by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and, as POLITICO reported this week, Mamdani has continued to make those requests privately to the president. The two have also discussed the federal government’s involvement in a massive development project that would span the Sunnyside Yard rail depot in Queens.
The price for these spoils has so far been one Mamdani’s base is willing to accept.

The mayor rarely, if ever, criticizes Trump directly. He demurs when asked by reporters about their private phone calls. And during a joint appearance outside Gracie Mansion in late September, when asked about Trump’s short-lived White House media ban, Mamdani only said that he himself supported having a variety of news outlets covering City Hall. — Molly Reinmann and Joe Anuta
From the Capitol
NVIDIA AND BEYOND: Gov. Kathy Hochul isn’t worried that the scandal engulfing former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang will impact the broader semiconductor sector.

“It’s a resilient industry,” she said today. “We’ve already planted the flag in places from Malta and all the way to Syracuse. New York’s economy will continue to be sound and continue to grow. This will not have an effect on meeting our obligations to continue the investments and create more jobs.”

New York has placed a massive, long-term bet on the industry, which has toeholds in the Syracuse area and the Saratoga County town of Malta, where Hochul appeared today to tout the groundbreaking of a new chip manufacturing facility.
Huang resigned amid allegations of multiple affairs, including a relationship with a woman who may be a potential Chinese spy.
The tech boom has helped lift Wall Street and swell New York’s coffers. A slowdown may spell trouble for the economy. — Nick Reisman
LEADERSHIP MOVES: State Sen. Liz Krueger told Playbook today she isn’t angling to chair the body’s housing committee.
“I’m not going to be the housing chair and I’m not lobbying to be the housing chair,” the Manhattan lawmaker said. “Several other people have voiced active interest and I think that’s great.”

“I actually think that whoever is willing to be the housing chair should recognize they need to probably make a six-year commitment to this assignment,” she added. “And I’m not actually planning necessarily to make an additional six-year commitment to the Senate.”

One member who has voiced interest in the role is state Sen. Julia Salazar, a democratic socialist who represents north Brooklyn. The committee is currently chaired by outgoing state Sen. Brian Kavanagh.
“I’m a huge Julia Salazar fan,” Krueger said. “I think she’s an underestimated young talent in the Senate.”
Decisions on chairmanships will be up to Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins, as the Senate navigates leadership turnover and the largest Democratic majority in 150 years.

Krueger has chaired the Senate finance committee since Democrats took control of the chamber in 2019. She suffered a stroke earlier this year but has recovered and was recently elected to serve another full term.

“The finance committee has about three times the workload of any committee,” Krueger noted. “I have told Andrea if she would like me to stay on in finance, I would be happy to do so, but I would need some kind of vice-chair or co-chair arrangement.”

She added: “If nobody wants to give me any chairmanships because we have too many mouths to feed, that’s okay also. This will be my 25th year [in the senate]. I feel like people either know who I am and respect what I try to do or not, and it’s irrelevant what the title is on my door.” — Janaki Chadha
FROM CITY HALL
HE’S NO SCHU-IN: Mamdani pointedly declined to back Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer’s bid to continue leading the caucus when asked about it at a press conference this morning.

“The American people made their voices very clear. They sent a message that they want Democratic leadership across the board that will deliver material improvements for the working class. And as the mayor of New York City, that's exactly what I want to see for New Yorkers across our five boroughs,” Mamdani said. “So I care less about who it is, and I care more about what they do.”
Schumer is facing a leadership challenge from Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, who has the support of Mamdani allies like Sen. Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan.
Mamdani’s hand-off approach to the Senate leadership race stands in stark contrast to the House, where the mayor has backed Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries’ bid to become speaker. — Joe Anuta

JOGGER PROBE: The New York City Law Department is launching an independent review of the school system’s hiring and background check procedures following revelations that the suspect in the recent high-profile murder of a Brooklyn jogger had worked at an elementary school.

At the request of schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels, the Law Department will conduct a review that will include an examination of employee screenings and verifications, how information is shared between government agencies and what safeguards are in place after an individual is hired.

“The Law Department stands ready to conduct a review, follow the facts, and make recommendations based on what we find in order to make sure New York City Public Schools, and all collaborating agencies, continue to take all necessary measures to ensure the safety and well-being of students and staff,” Corporation Counsel Steven Banks said in a statement.
Details of the review and the full scope are currently being developed, according to the Department of Education.
Read more in POLITICO Pro from Madina Touré

ULRICH TRIAL LATEST: As former New York City Correction Department Commissioner Louis Molina took the stand today in the trial of former Buildings Department Commissioner Eric Ulrich, a series of wiretapped calls and emails gave a behind-the-scenes peek at how patronage works within municipal government.

Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg has accused Ulrich of using his position as a senior adviser to former Mayor Eric Adams to obtain perks like cash payments and season tickets to the Mets. The former Queens City Council member has pleaded not guilty and is in the midst of a bench trial in Manhattan criminal court.
As part of the case, prosecutors summoned Molina to the stand today to discuss how exactly the daughter of Ulrich’s close friend came to be hired as a policy analyst at the Department of Correction.
“In my mind, it was her job if she wanted it,” Molina told Assistant District Attorney Guy Tardanico at one point during the proceedings.

Shortly after Adams took office in 2022, Ulrich came to Molina with a candidate for open positions at the department. He impressed upon the correction commissioner that the candidate’s father, Michael Mazzio, who is on trial alongside Ulrich, was a friend of the mayor and that hiring his daughter was a top priority.
Molina said that context spurred him to give her an interview and offer her a job — something that might not have happened had she applied via traditional routes.

Defense attorneys for Ulrich and Mazzio, however, cross examined Molina and sought to show that recommendations for jobs from senior City Hall staffers were nothing out of the ordinary. And those attorneys noted that Ulrich never demanded Mazzio’s daughter be hired, nor complained when she was given an entry-level position instead of a loftier job title that came with a six-figure salary. — Joe Anuta
FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL
HAKEEM’S HECKLERS: House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries took a victory lap today at the Majority Democrats’ confab in Denver. The welcome he received wasn’t entirely warm.

Right after moderator Jessica Tarlov’s first question, protesters interrupted with demands that Jeffries support the Green New Deal, Medicare for All and an arms embargo against Israel. Tarlov then asked for his response to the criticism that his “leadership is too timid for the moment.”
“As House Democrats, we're honored by the trust that the American people have placed in us to get the job done, and so we’ve got to work hard to deliver,” he replied.
That didn’t quiet the hecklers.
As Jeffries spoke about reversing Medicaid cuts and working to extend the Affordable Care Act tax credit, one tarred him as a “fucking liar.”
“I'm from Brooklyn,” Jeffries said in response. “This is light work.”
During the talk, he said he’s “absolutely a yes” on banning mid-cycle redistricting and partisan gerrymandering.

“I said this when this all started in Texas last July, that Republicans and MAGA extremists started this redistricting war,” he said. “We're going to end it. And last Tuesday, that's what we did, decisively all across the country. So we're not going to unilaterally disarm, but at the same period of time, as we've done in two prior Congresses, we need to ban mid-decade gerrymandering and partisan gerrymandering.”
New York Democrats are still mulling a mid-decade redistricting effort. — Madison Fernandez
IN OTHER NEWS
— DOWN WITH THE DSA: Veteran campaign strategist Hank Sheinkopf is repurposing his super PAC to block the DSA’s expansion in New York. (The New York Post)
— NY-21 SHORTFALL: Rep-elect Anthony Constantino received more than 30,000 fewer votes in his district than GOP gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman. (Times Union)
— RIDE OR DIE: Ingrid Lewis-Martin, a longtime advisor to former Mayor Eric Adams, has made frequent cameos in the corruption trial against Eric Ulrich. (Gothamist)

washingtonpost.com/transportation/2026/1.headline: FAA grounds flights at all U.S. airports, citing communications issue
washingtonpost.com/transportation/2026/1.author: Liam Scott, Maegan Vazquez, Todd C. Frankel

paragraphs.text: The Federal Aviation Administration issued an unexpected nationwide ground stop Friday afternoon, citing a communication issue.
“FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide updates,” the agency said in a statement. The FAA said its information was preliminary and subject to change.
Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy said on X that the FAA’s nationwide ground stop followed “a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.”
This is the second national ground stop since Sept. 11, 2001. The FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop in January 2023 over a systems outage.

About 3,115 flights were still inbound to U.S. airports at about 4:40 p.m. Eastern, according to flight-tracking platform AirNav Radar. These were the last planes to get off the ground before the ground stop.
At Los Angeles International Airport, a United Airlines gate agent announced to passengers that there had been a nationwide ground stop but said she did not know why.
Air traffic control audio pilots and air traffic controllers across the United States learned about the ground stop Friday afternoon.

“Why is there a ground stop?” a pilot asked Friday afternoon at Dallas-Fort Worth International Airport, according to air traffic control recordings on ATC.com. “We are not aware of a reason. We just know it’s indefinite and U.S.-wide,” an air traffic controller replied.
At Seattle-Tacoma International Airport, an air traffic controller told a Southwest Airlines pilot, “Just a heads up, we went into a national ground stop, all aircraft, with update unknown.”
“Okay,, thank you,” the pilot replied.

In a statement, a spokesperson for the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority said passengers should expect flight delays related to the ground stop, but Reagan National Airport and Washington Dulles International Airport remained open.

A United spokesperson said the airline was responding to the ground stop. United flights that are already airborne will continue, the spokesperson said, but new domestic flights will not depart while the ground stop remains in place.
“United will work with our customers to get them to their destinations once this issue is resolved,” the spokesperson said.
This is a developing news story and will be updated.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/u-s-government.headline: US government grounds all flights across the United States ‘due to extraordinary circumstances’
techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/u-s-government.author: Zack Whittaker

paragraphs.text: The Federal Aviation Administration said Friday afternoon that it has grounded all flights across the United States due to “extraordinary circumstances” and issues related to safety.

The FAA’s website said the cause is an “equipment outage.” The site itself was down for a brief period at the time of publication, with a note that the website was “experiencing technical difficulties.”

Per an alert sent by the Air Traffic Control System Command Center, or ATCSCC, the FAA said the ground stop means that aircraft cannot take off from departure gates. The message said that the disruption was “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” but did not specify further. The alert was not visible on the ATCSCC website at press time.
The alert stated that all departing flights must remain on the ground “until further notice.” Inbound international flights will be “managed on a case-by-case basis,” it said.
A spokesperson for the FAA told TechCrunch that it issued the ground stop “following communication issues impacting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers.”
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a post on X: “FAA technicians are investigating the issue.”

It’s not clear what caused the ongoing FAA equipment outage. The outage comes in the same week that the administration rolled out an AI-powered tool for air traffic controllers to save aircraft flight time and fuel costs — though it’s unclear if the ongoing outage is related.
Updated with comment from the FAA.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-13/.headline: FAA issues nationwide ground stop due to 'extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety'
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-13/.author: Terry Castleman, Hannah Fry

paragraphs.text: The Federal Aviation Administration has issued a temporary ground stoppage on all flights in the United States.
“Due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” the FAA advisory read, “all departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice.”

The stoppage was announced Friday afternoon and impacted flights nationwide, including at Los Angeles International Airport, following a communication issue that affected air traffic control centers. It marks the second full ground stop since 9/11 and it’s unclear how long it will last. The last full ground stop was in 2023 when a pilot notification system went down.
“FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them,” Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said in a post on X.
Inbound international flights would be handled “on a case by case basis,” according to the FAA advisory.
In Air Traffic Control audio posted by the ATC, a controller could be heard announcing the ground stop to pilots on the runway at San Diego International Airport.
“That’s a joke, right?” a pilot responded in disbelief.
The air traffic controller then confirmed that it was not a joke, and said the ground stop was due to an issue with equipment.
Multiple voices on the channel then speculated that the outage was related to the Microsoft Outlook outage from Nov. 12, but the controller said he could not confirm the cause.

In Chicago Air Route Traffic Control Center audio, an air traffic controller said they “lost all frequencies and automation for handoffs and strips,” likely in reference to handing off which towers handle which flights and the electronic records used to track individual planes.

At Denver International Airport, a pilot and controller confirmed that the stop was expected to last for more than six hours. In audio from the ATC, the controller said the ground stop was in effect until 9 p.m. local time, or 8 p.m. in California.

California’s Office of Emergency Services is reaching out to federal and state officials to determine the extent of the impacts on the state’s airports and passengers, Gov. Gavin Newsom’s press office wrote on X.
This is a developing story and will be updated.

nytimes.com/2026/11/13/upshot/gerrymande.headline: Did the Redistricting Wars Backfire on Republicans? In a Word, No.
nytimes.com/2026/11/13/upshot/gerrymande.author: Nate Cohn, Eve Washington

paragraphs.text: When Republicans started redrawing congressional maps in the summer of 2025, they hoped to gain enough seats to give the party a chance to hold the House in this year’s midterm elections.

That gambit did not come close to working. The Democrats won so overwhelmingly that they easily overcame the G.O.P.’s newly drawn lines. In many cases, Democrats wound up winning the seats that the Republicans targeted. Sometimes, Democrats even gained seats in the very states where Republicans redrew the maps to their advantage.
But do Democratic gains mean the Republican effort backfired? Did Republicans lose more seats in 2026 than they would have had they left the maps alone?

Our preliminary estimate is no, the Republican effort didn’t backfire. In fact, Republicans still gained anywhere from four to seven seats as a result of the new maps, even if they didn’t pay off as Republicans hoped.
There is one state where the Republican effort seems to have backfired, if only barely: North Carolina. Elsewhere, Republicans came out ahead or the new maps didn’t make a difference either way.

And even beyond the new maps enacted for 2026, Republicans still benefited enormously from partisan gerrymandering — not only in the states where they redrew maps in recent years, but elsewhere in the country as well. They may have even gained more seats in this election thanks to gerrymandering than they have in prior elections.

If every congressional map had been drawn fairly, with party-blind nonpartisan methods, Democrats might have come close to winning a veto-proof two-thirds majority in the House, with the party winning nearly 20 additional districts in Texas, Florida and Georgia alone.

It’s important to caution that these findings are still preliminary. Votes are still being counted in many states; in others, the detailed results by precinct aren’t yet available. Many districts are so close that even slight differences between our estimates and the actual outcome could be enough to flip the projected winner on the old map.
Nonetheless, it’s not too early to suggest that mid-cycle redistricting helped the G.O.P.

Texas is a good example. Republicans targeted five of the state’s 13 Democratic-held seats when they redrew the map last August, but Democrats came out of the midterms gaining a seat. While that might suggest that the Republican gerrymander backfired, Democrats would have won all of those same districts — including the one they gained — on the old map, even if the Republicans hadn’t redrawn the lines. Indeed, none of those districts were even close.
In reality, Republicans came out ahead with the new map in Texas. Democrats did gain a seat to win a total of 14 on the current map, but they would have won 15 if Republicans hadn’t redrawn it.

That’s because there’s a district — the 32nd, around Dallas — that Democrats would have won on the old map, but that Republicans successfully flipped this time. They redrew it to include much more Republican-leaning rural areas.

If anything, the Republican gerrymander in Texas played an enormous role in the results. Democrats won the U.S. House vote in Texas by about six percentage points, 53 percent to 47 percent, but Republicans still won a lopsided 24-to-14 congressional majority. On a hypothetical party-blind map, like one drawn by computer simulations, Democrats almost certainly would have won a majority of Texas’ House seats — with the simulations yielding an average of nine more Democratic seats in Texas.
Besides Texas, Republicans also did better on the new maps in Florida — and are projected to do better in Louisiana — than they might have on the old ones.

Did the Republican gerrymander backfire anywhere? North Carolina is the one state where Republicans may have been better off leaving the 2024 map alone — although so many districts are so close, on either the old or the new map, that a definitive answer will depend on the final vote count and the results by precinct.
But more often, the new maps didn’t make much of a difference. Democrats managed to hold the seats that Republicans sought to win in states like Ohio, and Alabama.

Even the Democratic gerrymander in California may not ultimately move a seat. Democrats redrew that map to try to cancel out the Republican effort in Texas. But as it turns out, Democrats appear to have been able to flip all the seats that they sought to flip even on the old map.

And oddly enough, Democrats may have been hurt in a state where a Republican gerrymander was dismantled ahead of the election: Utah. On the G.O.P.-drawn map — which was intended to be unanimously Republican — Democrats might have won two districts (though we’d need the exact precinct results to be sure). Instead, Democratic votes were concentrated in a single Salt Lake City district, guaranteeing them one seat, but only one.

Utah isn’t the only state where a seemingly favorable map for Democrats might have hurt the party in this year’s election. Based on computer simulations, Democrats probably fared worse in Arizona and New York than they would have on a party-blind map. In both cases (as with Utah), the current map solidifies Democratic-leaning seats but, in doing so, nudges a larger number of Republican-leaning districts out of play. In this year’s wave, Democrats would have been better off with more Republican-leaning seats in play.

Of course, all of this could work out differently in 2028. In a more competitive year, Republicans might be favored to win back the seats they failed to pick up this cycle. Similarly, Democrats wouldn’t be favored to win those light-red districts in New York, Utah and Arizona.

But even if the new maps fail to yield the decisive gains that Republicans had hoped, gerrymandering would still give the Republicans a meaningful structural advantage. And this cycle, that structural advantage made a major difference.

In a hypothetical world without gerrymandering, Democrats would have won many more seats in the big red states with successful Republican gerrymanders — Texas, Florida, Georgia and Tennessee — along with a longer list of districts where Republicans shored up seats that could plausibly be competitive, like those around Oklahoma City, Columbia, S.C., and Little Rock, Ark.

That would add up to 20-plus more seats, and Democrats would have been awfully close to winning the 290 seats necessary for a veto-proof majority. The last time any party held that many seats was in the 1970s, when Democrats won large gains in the House in the post-Watergate era.

marketwatch.com/story/faa-declares-rare-.headline: FAA declares rare, widespread ground outage

paragraphs.text: Nearly 8,000 flights are delayed so far
Jets on the tarmac at LaGuardia Airport.
The Federal Aviation Administration declared a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday, citing a "communication issue" impacting traffic control centers.
According to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, FAA technicians are investigating the issue.
Nearly 8,000 flights within, into, or out of the U.S. are delayed on Friday, according to FlightAware. Total cancellations for the day hit 930 flights.
Most affected airports included New York's JFK airport as well as Boston's Logan and San Francisco's airports.
"This has been in the making for the last 20 years, in terms of air traffic-control modernization," said Ernie Arvai, president of AirInsight Group.
"We have talked about it forever, and not done much about it," he said. "I feel bad for all the people today who are going to be stuck."

The last time there was a nationwide ground stop was in January 2023, after a failure of a pilot-alert system. Before that, the last such nationwide stop was after the Sept. 11, 2001 terrorist attacks.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/13/for.headline: Former death row inmate Richard Glossip pleads guilty to lesser charge
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/13/for.author: Maegan Vazquez

paragraphs.text: A former Oklahoma death row prisoner who had been incarcerated for nearly 30 years and whose execution was halted several times pleaded guilty to a lesser charge this week, his attorney said.

Richard Glossip had been sentenced to death in the 1997 killing of Barry Van Treese, the owner of an Oklahoma City motel where Glossip worked. Van Treese was beaten with a baseball bat. Glossip has long claimed his innocence in what prosecutors have alleged was a murder-for-hire plot.
Glossip’s co-worker at the motel, Justin Sneed, confessed to killing Van Treese but testified that Glossip paid him to do it. Sneed was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole.

Glossip on Thursday pleaded guilty to accessory after the fact in exchange for the prosecution dropping its first-degree murder charge against him. Glossip’s attorney, Don Knight, said he will be sentenced in December.

“In May, the court determined that Rich could be released on bond, and since that time he has been living a peaceful and law-abiding life,” Knight said in a statement. “In 1997, had Rich been given the longest possible sentence for the crime he pleaded guilty to today, he would never have been on death row and would have been released ten years ago. We look forward to an opportunity to show why returning him to custody would not serve the interests of justice, and to ending this nightmare for Rich and all concerned.”
The plea agreement is the latest twist in a decades-long saga that at one point led Oklahoma to put its lethal injection protocols on indefinite hold for a review.
Since being sentenced to death in 1998, Glossip has been scheduled to die nine times and served three last meals only to have his execution halted by the state, sometimes at the 11th hour.
Glossip’s scheduled execution was repeatedly postponed in 2015 amid legal back-and-forth over the kinds of drugs the state used in its execution protocols.

That January, after Glossip was served a last meal, the U.S. Supreme Court halted his execution and the executions of two other prisoners while considering Oklahoma’s use of midazolam, a sedative, during executions. In June 2015, the court upheld the state’s use of the drug.

But hours before Glossip’s scheduled execution on Sept. 16, 2015, the state appeals court granted a two-week extension to review new evidence. Then, on Sept. 30, 2015, as prison officials were again preparing to execute Glossip, the state’s governor issued a stay because the execution drugs being used did not match Oklahoma’s execution procedures.
Oklahoma then put state executions on hold from 2015 through 2020 to review its lethal injection protocols.

In May 2023, the Supreme Court issued a stay of execution for Glossip at the request of the state and Glossip’s legal team, who alleged that the prosecution had known that Sneed made false statements in court. Glossip had been scheduled to be put to death less than two weeks later.

The U.S. Supreme Court ultimately ordered a new trial for Glossip in 2025. He was released from prison on bond in May 2026. Oklahoma’s attorney general, Gentner Drummond, had previously said he planned to try Glossip again for murder but would not pursue the death penalty.

Drummond said in a statement that while allowing Glossip to plead guilty to the lesser charge “was a difficult decision for me and, more importantly, the Van Treese family, we both recognize that this path ensures a conviction related to Mr. Van Treese’s murder and gives us the best chance to secure additional prison time for Glossip.”
Drummond said he hopes the court will consider sentencing Glossip to the maximum 45-year sentence in prison.
Katie Mettler contributed to this report.

finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.headline: Anthropic IPO Buyers Have More Influence on Price Than SpaceX
finance.yahoo.com/technology/ai/articles.author: Anthony Hughes

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- Anthropic PBC will try next week to take SpaceX's title of the biggest public listing of all time, but unlike Elon Musk's conglomerate, major investors will have more sway on its initial share price at a time when the artificial-intelligence trade is in flux.
Most Read from Bloomberg

The Claude developer is gauging interest in its shares at a range of $70 to $78 for its initial public offering, a departure from SpaceX, which used a take-it-or-leave-it approach by setting a fixed price of $135 a share in the marketing phase.

And while Anthropic wants the bragging rights of having the biggest IPO ever, some market watchers are warning that it shouldn't be too aggressive on pricing so institutional investors will feel like they got a fair price and shares will have room to rise on day one.

"Anthropic is doing a more conventional roadshow and when you set the IPO price based on institutional demand that makes it less likely to trade below the IPO," said Harrison Rolfes, a senior research analyst for late-stage company research at Pitchbook.

But there are no guarantees. A challenging market backdrop — including the ouster of Jensen Huang at Nvidia Corp. — has made final stages of Anthropic's march to public markets more complicated than SpaceX's $86.2 billion listing in June.

SpaceX, whose shares now trade 3% above its IPO price, benefited from coming to market in a quarter in which the Nasdaq 100 Index jumped nearly 28%. The same index is down about 7% in the last three months after a US interest-rate hike, widespread worries about an oversupply of AI debt and a midterm election result where the data centers that power models like ChatGPT and Claude drew the ire of voters. Those factors have hushed earlier whispers about Anthropic having a $2 trillion valuation.

"It seems like they really are listening to the market," said Andy Tang, a partner at venture capital firm Draper Associates and a former technology investment banker. "They are bringing the IPO at a more conservative level."

Anthropic is now targeting a fully diluted valuation of about $1.4 trillion. It plans to raise as much as $64.4 billion in the IPO and $26 billion in a private placement, a total that would surpass SpaceX's IPO.
Jeff Zell, a partner and senior research analyst at IPO Boutique, also said "the timing likely contributed to Anthropic's lighter valuation and lighter cash raise."

The private placement is another difference between the two listings. While SpaceX's IPO went ahead without explicit anchor investors, Anthropic has lined up $26 billion from seven tech companies led by Alphabet Inc. and Nvidia.

The massive placement sends a positive signal to investors about outside support in choppy markets, said David Erickson, an adjunct professor at Columbia University and the former global head of equity capital markets at Barclays Plc. The transaction also doesn't come with banking fees, which Anthropic will pay on the actual IPO.

Investors in the placement won't be able to sell their shares until they're registered at a later date. And since they're a part of Anthropic's compute supply chain, they have an interest in maintaining their position for the long term, Erickson added.

The respective companies have another key difference: a long acquaintance with public markets. Musk has worked with bankers for well over a decade to raise capital for Tesla Inc., while Anthropic has relative newbie status as a five-year-old company.

"Obviously Elon Musk has had significant experience dealing with Wall Street, so he dictated the terms, whereas Anthropic has not had that experience before and I assume are doing what the banks recommend," Erickson said.

finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.headline: Kevin Hassett Says He Will Remain as Trump Economic Adviser
finance.yahoo.com/economy/policy/article.author: Saleha Mohsin and Courtney Subramanian

paragraphs.text: Saleha Mohsin and Courtney Subramanian
Fri, November 13, 2026 at 2:31 PM CST 2 min read
(Bloomberg) -- National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett denied a report that he plans to depart his post in the coming weeks.
Most Read from Bloomberg
"Not true," Hassett said in a text message Friday when asked about the report on his impending departure.

Semafor reported earlier that Hassett is expected leave his role as President Donald Trump's top economic adviser. The news outlet said his potential replacements include Scott Bessent, who would retain his role as Treasury secretary, and Bessent's counselor David Zervos.

Hassett said he joked about the report with the president on Friday afternoon. A White House official also said the report has no factual basis, adding that Hassett is a key member of Trump's economic team and will continue working to advance his policies.

Republican losses in the midterm elections have intensified speculation about a shake-up of the president's team. Days after the midterms, Trump's chief of staff Susie Wiles left and was replaced by Stephen Miller. That move is expected to lead to further changes on the president's staff.
Trump himself has said he expects some turnover among his advisers.

As NEC director, Hassett is responsible for coordinating economic policy across the federal government. A frequent presence on television, Hassett is staunch defender of the president's policies, including his sweeping use of tariff powers, as Trump moved in his second term to reshape US manufacturing and ties with trading partners.
