washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/13/m.headline: Musk joins calls for Jensen Huang to be reinstated as CEO of Nvidia
washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/13/m.author: Faiz Siddiqui

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
Reporter covering public health with a focus on infectious diseases
U.S. reports at least 10 measles deaths in 2026
Two more measles deaths were reported Friday, in Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, bringing the U.S. toll this year to at least 10 as outbreaks continue to erupt in several states.

Wisconsin health officials reported the death of a child, the second measles-associated death in the state this year. Officials did not release the child’s age or other details, including vaccination status, citing the family’s privacy.
The state has reported 649 measles cases across 20 counties since August, the Wisconsin Department of Health Services said. It is the state’s largest measles outbreak in more than 35 years.

Pennsylvania health officials also announced Friday that an unvaccinated resident of Montour County who tested positive for measles had died. It was the seventh measles-associated death in Pennsylvania this year. Officials did not disclose the person’s age or other identifying details.
Pennsylvania has reported 1,542 measles cases across 46 counties this year, making it the state hit hardest by the resurgence of a disease that the United States declared eliminated in 2000.
New York has reported one death.

The U.S. is on the brink of losing its status as having eliminated the continuous spread of measles as the country faces its worst outbreak in decades, driven largely by communities with low vaccination rates.

Measles is highly contagious and can cause severe complications, including pneumonia and swelling of the brain. Young children, pregnant women and people with weakened immune systems face a higher risk of serious illness.
Reporter covering technology with a focus on Tesla, SpaceX and Elon Musk's empire

Elon Musk called for the return of Jensen Huang to Nvidia on Friday, saying he’d signed a petition for Huang’s reinstatement a day after the chip executive resigned following his admission of an affair with a woman who is alleged to be a Chinese spy.
“A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I’m signing it too,” Musk told his more than 240 million followers on X.

It was not immediately clear which petition Musk had signed. Wired reported Thursday that a call for Huang’s return had internally circulated at Nvidia, with more than 1,600 comments — the majority of which supported him coming back.

Huang’s resignation came after he admitted to an affair with a woman alleged by some in the intelligence community to be a Chinese spy. Amid the fallout, Huang has garnered vocal support from President Donald Trump and Musk, who has spoken about the irreplaceability of founders and issued other messages backing Huang.
In response to one post suggesting that Musk hire Huang, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO replied: “That would be an honor.”
More than 1.5 million people welcome Pope Leo XIV in northern Peru
CHICLAYO, Peru — As the plane touched down in northern Peru, in the adopted home city of the first U.S.-born pope, a local TV station proudly announced: “Pope Leo XIV returns to his land.”

More than 1 million people lined the streets of Chiclayo, Peru, with 500,000 more gathered for a sprawling Friday Mass, according to Vatican estimates, nearly doubling the city’s population for the pope’s emotional homecoming.
“The pope is Chiclayan!” the crowd chanted. “Chiclayo is with you!”

Some in the crowd had been waiting nearly 24 hours for the papal Mass, standing or sitting on the sandy, rock-strewn flat in the scorching sun. Firefighters drove through the vast area spraying the faithful with water.

Yuri Romero, 58, had arrived at 3 p.m. the previous day with her 88-year-old mother. Romero did not sleep, and her arthritic knees ached. But tears filled her eyes as she spoke of her first, and perhaps only, chance to see a pope — a former local bishop who “made you feel like you knew him for a while,” she said.
As the pope passed by and waved at the crowd, a woman holding a Chiclayo flag began to sob. Another held up a bandanna with an image of his home cathedral.
Lenner Mercado, a 39-year-old from Trujillo, and his family drove five hours and walked for three more for the “opportunity to see the Peruvian pope.”
“He was born in the U.S.,” he said, “but his heart is in Peru.”
Reporter covering national politics and breaking news
Brian Monahan out as attending physician to Congress amid Pentagon probe

Rear Adm. Brian Monahan is no longer the attending physician for Congress and the Supreme Court, more than a year after the Pentagon launched an investigation into alleged misconduct at the office he headed.
“I am no longer serving with the Office of Attending Physicians,” Monahan said in a voicemail message he said had been recorded Wednesday.

Monahan had served since 2009 as the top doctor at the Office of Attending Physician, which provides in-house health care and emergency aid to Congress and the Supreme Court. Within the OAP, Navy medical personnel provide health care under the attending physician’s direction.
Monahan’s departure comes the same week as the Defense Department inspector general’s office published a report that said there had been insufficient oversight of Navy personnel assigned to the OAP.

“Without clinical quality management oversight, Navy personnel may face unclear guidance, inconsistent standards, and pressure to engage in practices that deviate from established medical requirements,” the report stated.

The report also found there had not been the number of regular inspections and inventories of the OAP pharmacy required by law. The most recent inspection, in February, found shortages of sleep aid medication held at the pharmacy versus how many tablets were listed on an inventory, according to the report. There were also discrepancies in the quantities of other controlled substances.

The Navy Times reported Thursday that sailors assigned to the OAP complained of a toxic work environment, including being pressured to work 70 to 80 hours per week and performing unwanted tasks, such as cutting a congressman’s toenails.

Monahan and representatives for the Navy did not immediately respond to requests for comment Friday about whether he had been fired or had resigned. The Defense Department referred questions to the Navy.
Meteorologist focused on explaining the atmospheric conditions behind significant weather events
Rare November tornadoes hit Delaware and New Jersey
Severe thunderstorms brought damaging hail and exceptionally rare tornadoes to portions of the Mid-Atlantic on Thursday.

A highly visible and uniquely unobscured tornado tracked southwest of Wilmington, Delaware, near Newark, Delaware. More northeast, another tornado occurred just east of Interstate 95 in Mercer County, New Jersey.

It’s exceptionally rare for tornadoes to happen this time of year in the Mid-Atlantic. It also marked the 115-year anniversary of a damaging F2 tornado that carved through Wilmington on Nov. 12, 1911.

The National Weather Service’s Storm Prediction Center had issued a tornado watch in advance of the storms. A low-pressure system was pulling just enough moisture northward for strong thunderstorms to form, and there was ample wind shear along a warm front. Wind shear describes changing winds with height. Tall storms feel those changing winds and rotate.
Temperatures were rather cool — only around 64 degrees — but it was exceptionally cold aloft. That’s why surface air was still able to rise and produce storms.

Thursday’s storms were supercells, or individual, discrete thunderstorms that were spinning. The Newark, Delaware, tornado occurred around 1 p.m. Radar suggests it was an EF1 on the on the 0-to-5 scale for tornado damage, give or take, with maximum winds around 100 to 110 mph. The weather service will be surveying the damage to make the final call.
Large hail up to the size of golf balls was reported in Burlington and Ocean counties in New Jersey. And in Parkside, Pennsylvania, poor drainage carried hail into piles several feet deep.
Ukraine critic injured in Moscow car bombing, Russia says

A car bombing in Moscow on Friday seriously injured a former adviser to Ukrainian Prime Minister Mykola Azarov who fled to Russia after his boss’s resignation in 2014 and became a pro-Kremlin commentator.

The explosion came a day after a Russian military officer was killed in a similar attack in St. Petersburg, and it follows a string of assassinations of Russian military figures and high-profile supporters of the war in Ukraine.
According to Russian officials, the car exploded while Sergei Zavorotny, 72, was driving, and he was taken to a hospital in critical condition.

Zavorotny, a former journalist with Komsomolskaya Pravda, served as Azarov’s adviser from 2010 to 2014 and moved to Russia after the ouster of Azarov and President Viktor Yanukovych, who both also fled to Russia. Yanukovich’s decision in late 2013 to abandon an association agreement with the European Union in favor of closer ties with Moscow sparked the Maidan protests.

Since then Zavorotny has been a prominent pro-Russian commentator, who regularly claimed that the Maidan revolution was orchestrated by Western governments. A 2020 U.S. Senate Intelligence Committee report identified him as an officer of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service.

Azarov told Russian state TV he was “shocked” by the attack and accused Ukrainian intelligence services of targeting Zavorotny over his criticism of Ukraine, without providing evidence. Ukrainian officials did not immediately respond to questions about the attack.
National correspondent covering the Southeast
Tanker strikes cruise ship in New Orleans, sending passengers into river

A tanker on Friday afternoon hit a passenger cruise ship that was docked along the Mississippi River in New Orleans, causing a massive emergency response that included firefighters rescuing people from the water.

Kimberly Curth, a Port of New Orleans spokeswoman, said the incident happened at approximately 12:30 p.m. local time when an Atlantic Asphalt tanker crashed into the docked American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage ship that had docked about two hours earlier.
An estimated 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, were aboard the American Heritage at the time, Curth said.

Port NOLA Harbor Police, the New Orleans Fire Department, the New Orleans Police Department, the U.S. Coast Guard and emergency medical personnel were on scene, conducting rescue and response operations.
Curth said passengers were being brought inside the port’s administration building “for triage and assistance.”

“Our immediate priority is the safety of all passengers, crew members and first responders,” she said in a statement. “This remains an active and evolving incident. The number of injuries and the cause of the collision have not yet been confirmed.”

npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-6040409/trump-m.headline: GOP state officials push to revive Trump's mail voting restrictions for 2028 election
npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-6040409/trump-m.author: Hansi Lo Wang

paragraphs.text: Voting for this year's midterm elections just concluded, but Republican officials in a number of states are already looking to shape how votes are cast in 2028.
Twelve GOP state attorneys general are pushing to revive the president's bid for mail-in voting restrictions in time for the 2028 election.

On Thursday, they started the process of appealing a September order by U.S. District Judge Carl Nichols, one of the two judges who blocked the U.S. Postal Service from carrying out a plan released in response to an executive order by President Trump.

The Republican state attorneys general represent Alabama, Florida, Indiana, Kansas, Louisiana, Missouri, Montana, Nebraska, Oklahoma, South Carolina, South Dakota and Texas. It's not clear, however, how long some of these states will continue this case, given that Democrats won up and down the ballot in the midterms. In Texas and Kansas, Democratic candidates are set to take control of their states' attorney general's offices in January.

In September, the Supreme Court refused to pause a similar ruling by U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani, who is based in Boston. That order stopped USPS from working on its revised rule for federal ballot mail, but it only applied to this year's midterm elections.
Nichols' preliminary injunction blocks USPS from implementing the plan for all federal elections, including the 2028 race.

It's not clear if the Trump administration plans to appeal Nichols' ruling by Friday's deadline for filing a court notice. Asked about the Justice Department's plans, DOJ spokesperson Matthew Tragesser replied in an email that the department doesn't comment on ongoing litigation.
The blocked rule — which the Postal Service released in late August — would require states to turn over lists of voters' names and addresses in order to have them delivered by USPS.
Nichols, a Washington, D.C.-based judge who was nominated by Trump, found that the mailing agency likely has no power to impose that requirement on states.

"As the Government concedes, the Postal Service could issue (and enforce) the Rule only if Congress gave it the authority to do so, but here no statute grants the Postal Service the power to issue key parts of the Rule," Nichols wrote.

The administration's earlier push to put these new restrictions in place for the midterms alarmed many election officials, who were concerned about last-minute changes causing major disruptions to the tens of millions who regularly vote by mail. Some voters with disabilities and those in places without polling sites, they feared, could have lost the ability to exercise their right to cast a ballot.

A whistleblower report claimed the online system officials would need to use to follow USPS' revised ballot requirements had not been properly tested and could have resulted in many eligible voters not getting their mail-in ballots in time or at all.
While the Supreme Court ultimately stopped implementation of the USPS rule for the midterms, Justices Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas dissented from that ruling.

Fellow conservative Justice Brett Kavanaugh said in a concurring opinion that he believed state and local election officials did not have enough time to "reasonably implement the rule" this time. But Kavanaugh noted that "there is at least a fair prospect that the final rule falls within the Postal Service's statutory authority."
Edited by Benjamin Swasey

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/13/hungar.headline: Hungary seizes $19.5m in cash found buried in forests amid graft inquiry
theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/13/hungar.author: Guardian staff reporter

paragraphs.text: Hungary’s anti-corruption agency said on Friday it had seized cash worth $19.5m (£14.8m) buried in forests and hidden elsewhere while investigating an ex-minister of nationalist former leader Viktor Orbán’s cabinet.

Miklós Seszták, Hungary’s minister of national development between 2014 and 2018, is accused of taking bribes in a scheme involving the state transport company, purchasing secondhand buses at inflated prices.

The prime minister, Péter Magyar, won a landslide election victory in April, ending Orbán’s 16 years in power after promising to investigate alleged corruption and abuse of office during his rival’s rule.
Seszták, two other Orbán-era ministers and the former premier’s brother have been taken into custody in different cases as graft inquiries have gathered pace in recent weeks.

The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH), an anti-graft body with sweeping powers established as part of Magyar’s accountability drive, said it searched several locations on Thursday and Friday as part of the criminal proceedings against Seszták.

“During the search, investigators found large amounts of cash: buried in forests, hidden in agricultural and warehouse buildings as well as residential properties, and stored in high-value safes in secluded locations,” the statement said.
“The total amount of cash found during the two-day search was 5,071,632,000 forints, €2,658,350 and US $1,257,100,” it added, bringing the combined value to $19.5m.
NVVH said its staff deposited the cash into the Hungarian State Treasury’s account.
“Upon receipt, 12 Treasury employees spent 8 hours counting the money using 5 counting machines,” the finance minister, András Kármán, said on Facebook.
Magyar hailed the seizure as a potential turning point.
“This officially marks the end of the Fidesz-KDNP mafia!” he said in reference to Orbán’s former governing coalition.
The former leader did not react to the latest development. Orbán had previously denounced the probes targeting his inner circle as “political persecution” aimed at imprisoning him.

cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/13/binance-hack.headline: Hackers stole $6.3 billion from Binance—2 habits that take 'a few seconds' can help you avoid similar traps
cnbc.com/make-it/2026/11/13/binance-hack.author: Joel Breakstone, Nadav Ziv

paragraphs.text: The biggest heist in cryptocurrency history began with small mistakes many internet users make. A hacking group tied to North Korea recently stole $6.3 billion from the crypto exchange Binance. The operation was sophisticated, involving fake job interviews and malicious code.

But it was also mundane. Although artificial intelligence played a role in the hack, this was not a cyberattack of the future, propelled by swarms of AI agents. Rather, it relied on humans who made some basic errors, like clicking a link because it appeared first on a search results page or trusting strangers at a fake company without taking a few seconds to look them up.
We work at the Digital Inquiry Group, a nonprofit that researches how people evaluate online information and creates free, evidence-based curriculum that helps people decide what to trust.

In over a decade of research, we've found that people frequently engage in online behavior that makes them more likely to get duped. Two simple strategies can help you better navigate today's information landscape, from traditional phishing to misleading social posts to AI fakes. Here's how.
When searching online, the first result is not always the best or the safest

The Binance heist began when one of the company's engineers downloaded compromised software. That engineer, according to the Reuters investigation of the hack, clicked on a sponsored search result that appeared higher on the results page and directed them to the malicious code.

Our research at the Digital Inquiry Group suggests internet users frequently behave as if first is best. They click on the first thing they see. They incorrectly associate a higher placement with vetted content, ceding judgment to tech company algorithms. Students have gone so far as to tell us "Google is almost never wrong" or "AI is always right."

Professional fact-checkers commonly practice click restraint. They understand that whether you're searching on the internet or querying a chatbot, first isn't always best. If you're researching an organization, the first link will often be to its own site, which is hardly likely to disclose anything that's wrong with it.

So the next time you search for something online, be wary of links to sponsored content, the organization you're investigating, or to open platforms where anyone can post and information isn't verified, such as Quora or Reddit. Read the brief snippets beneath each link, and make a more informed choice about what to open.

Always ask yourself: Who is behind this information? What makes them credible? Look for people and organizations that have direct expertise on the topic at hand, or have processes to ensure the accuracy of information, such as news outlets that employ editors and fact-checkers.
'The internet is a precarious place'—always get external verification

Binance says it caught that first malicious download, replaced the device and changed passwords. But later, another engineer downloaded compromised code as part of what they thought was a job interview, which included a virtual meeting with the supposed CEO of a fake company.

It's tempting to think that the engineer should have seen something was off. But the internet is a precarious place because bad actors know how to make content feel legitimate. Binance says its employee was snared by a hacker posing as an HR rep who "shared a social media account with him, including personal photos and videos posted on the platform, in order to build trust."

When they encounter a piece of unfamiliar content, professional fact-checkers don't just read it closely — they read laterally. They open new browser tabs to see what other, credible sources have to say. Fact-checkers know that bad actors make themselves look good on their home turf, but that it's a lot harder to fake a good reputation across the internet.

The next time you encounter something unfamiliar online, look for authoritative sources that can shed light on the person or organization. You might find a news article that confirms the claim you're looking into, or a report that identifies a supposedly neutral source as biased.

In some cases, you may find nothing at all, which is a signal in itself: if you look up a company that reached out to you and find no external confirmation of its existence, that should be an immediate red flag.

Had that first Binance engineer engaged in click restraint and verified the source of the software, they might have avoided the malicious download. Had that second employee taken time to seek external verification about the supposed HR rep, rather than trusting a polished social media profile, they might have realized that something didn't add up.

The internet and AI have made it harder to know whether what we see is authentic. They've also made it easier than ever before to investigate who or what we encounter online. It's always worth pausing to check. A few seconds up front can save us all a lot of time, grief and money later on.
Nadav Ziv is a researcher at the Digital Inquiry Group. Joel Breakstone is co-founder and executive director of the Digital Inquiry Group.

washingtonpost.com/world/2026/11/13/more.headline: More than 1.5 million people welcome Pope Leo XIV in northern Peru
washingtonpost.com/world/2026/11/13/more.author: Samantha Schmidt, Anthony Faiola

paragraphs.text: The 7LIVEDeveloping stories we're following
Reporter covering technology with a focus on Tesla, SpaceX and Elon Musk's empire
Musk joins calls for Jensen Huang to be reinstated as CEO of Nvidia

Elon Musk called for the return of Jensen Huang to Nvidia on Friday, saying he’d signed a petition for Huang’s reinstatement a day after the chip executive resigned following his admission of an affair with a woman who is alleged to be a Chinese spy.
“A petition is underway to reinstate Jensen and I’m signing it too,” Musk told his more than 240 million followers on X.

It was not immediately clear which petition Musk had signed. Wired reported Thursday that a call for Huang’s return had internally circulated at Nvidia, with more than 1,600 comments — the majority of which supported him coming back.

Huang’s resignation came after he admitted to an affair with a woman alleged by some in the intelligence community to be a Chinese spy. Amid the fallout, Huang has garnered vocal support from President Donald Trump and Musk, who has spoken about the irreplaceability of founders and issued other messages backing Huang.
In response to one post suggesting that Musk hire Huang, the Tesla and SpaceX CEO replied: “That would be an honor.”
CHICLAYO, Peru — As the plane touched down in northern Peru, in the adopted home city of the first U.S.-born pope, a local TV station proudly announced: “Pope Leo XIV returns to his land.”

More than 1 million people lined the streets of Chiclayo, Peru, with 500,000 more gathered for a sprawling Friday Mass, according to Vatican estimates, nearly doubling the city’s population for the pope’s emotional homecoming.
“The pope is Chiclayan!” the crowd chanted. “Chiclayo is with you!”

Some in the crowd had been waiting nearly 24 hours for the papal Mass, standing or sitting on the sandy, rock-strewn flat in the scorching sun. Firefighters drove through the vast area spraying the faithful with water.

Yuri Romero, 58, had arrived at 3 p.m. the previous day with her 88-year-old mother. Romero did not sleep, and her arthritic knees ached. But tears filled her eyes as she spoke of her first, and perhaps only, chance to see a pope — a former local bishop who “made you feel like you knew him for a while,” she said.
As the pope passed by and waved at the crowd, a woman holding a Chiclayo flag began to sob. Another held up a bandanna with an image of his home cathedral.
Lenner Mercado, a 39-year-old from Trujillo, and his family drove five hours and walked for three more for the “opportunity to see the Peruvian pope.”
“He was born in the U.S.,” he said, “but his heart is in Peru.”
Reporter covering national politics and breaking news
Brian Monahan out as attending physician to Congress amid Pentagon probe

Rear Adm. Brian Monahan is no longer the attending physician for Congress and the Supreme Court, more than a year after the Pentagon launched an investigation into alleged misconduct at the office he headed.
“I am no longer serving with the Office of Attending Physicians,” Monahan said in a voicemail message he said had been recorded Wednesday.

Monahan had served since 2009 as the top doctor at the Office of Attending Physician, which provides in-house health care and emergency aid to Congress and the Supreme Court. Within the OAP, Navy medical personnel provide health care under the attending physician’s direction.
Monahan’s departure comes the same week as the Defense Department inspector general’s office published a report that said there had been insufficient oversight of Navy personnel assigned to the OAP.

“Without clinical quality management oversight, Navy personnel may face unclear guidance, inconsistent standards, and pressure to engage in practices that deviate from established medical requirements,” the report stated.

The report also found there had not been the number of regular inspections and inventories of the OAP pharmacy required by law. The most recent inspection, in February, found shortages of sleep aid medication held at the pharmacy versus how many tablets were listed on an inventory, according to the report. There were also discrepancies in the quantities of other controlled substances.

The Navy Times reported Thursday that sailors assigned to the OAP complained of a toxic work environment, including being pressured to work 70 to 80 hours per week and performing unwanted tasks, such as cutting a congressman’s toenails.

Monahan and representatives for the Navy did not immediately respond to requests for comment Friday about whether he had been fired or had resigned. The Defense Department referred questions to the Navy.
Meteorologist focused on explaining the atmospheric conditions behind significant weather events
Rare November tornadoes hit Delaware and New Jersey
Severe thunderstorms brought damaging hail and exceptionally rare tornadoes to portions of the Mid-Atlantic on Thursday.

A highly visible and uniquely unobscured tornado tracked southwest of Wilmington, Delaware, near Newark, Delaware. More northeast, another tornado occurred just east of Interstate 95 in Mercer County, New Jersey.

It’s exceptionally rare for tornadoes to happen this time of year in the Mid-Atlantic. It also marked the 115-year anniversary of a damaging F2 tornado that carved through Wilmington on Nov. 12, 1911.

The National Weather Service’s Storm Prediction Center had issued a tornado watch in advance of the storms. A low-pressure system was pulling just enough moisture northward for strong thunderstorms to form, and there was ample wind shear along a warm front. Wind shear describes changing winds with height. Tall storms feel those changing winds and rotate.
Temperatures were rather cool — only around 64 degrees — but it was exceptionally cold aloft. That’s why surface air was still able to rise and produce storms.

Thursday’s storms were supercells, or individual, discrete thunderstorms that were spinning. The Newark, Delaware, tornado occurred around 1 p.m. Radar suggests it was an EF1 on the on the 0-to-5 scale for tornado damage, give or take, with maximum winds around 100 to 110 mph. The weather service will be surveying the damage to make the final call.
Large hail up to the size of golf balls was reported in Burlington and Ocean counties in New Jersey. And in Parkside, Pennsylvania, poor drainage carried hail into piles several feet deep.
Ukraine critic injured in Moscow car bombing, Russia says

A car bombing in Moscow on Friday seriously injured a former adviser to Ukrainian Prime Minister Mykola Azarov who fled to Russia after his boss’s resignation in 2014 and became a pro-Kremlin commentator.

The explosion came a day after a Russian military officer was killed in a similar attack in St. Petersburg, and it follows a string of assassinations of Russian military figures and high-profile supporters of the war in Ukraine.
According to Russian officials, the car exploded while Sergei Zavorotny, 72, was driving, and he was taken to a hospital in critical condition.

Zavorotny, a former journalist with Komsomolskaya Pravda, served as Azarov’s adviser from 2010 to 2014 and moved to Russia after the ouster of Azarov and President Viktor Yanukovych, who both also fled to Russia. Yanukovich’s decision in late 2013 to abandon an association agreement with the European Union in favor of closer ties with Moscow sparked the Maidan protests.

Since then Zavorotny has been a prominent pro-Russian commentator, who regularly claimed that the Maidan revolution was orchestrated by Western governments. A 2020 U.S. Senate Intelligence Committee report identified him as an officer of Russia’s Foreign Intelligence Service.

Azarov told Russian state TV he was “shocked” by the attack and accused Ukrainian intelligence services of targeting Zavorotny over his criticism of Ukraine, without providing evidence. Ukrainian officials did not immediately respond to questions about the attack.
National correspondent covering the Southeast
Tanker strikes cruise ship in New Orleans, sending passengers into river

A tanker on Friday afternoon hit a passenger cruise ship that was docked along the Mississippi River in New Orleans, causing a massive emergency response that included firefighters rescuing people from the water.

Kimberly Curth, a Port of New Orleans spokeswoman, said the incident happened at approximately 12:30 p.m. local time when an Atlantic Asphalt tanker crashed into the docked American Cruise Lines’ American Heritage ship that had docked about two hours earlier.
An estimated 129 passengers, in addition to crew members, were aboard the American Heritage at the time, Curth said.

Port NOLA Harbor Police, the New Orleans Fire Department, the New Orleans Police Department, the U.S. Coast Guard and emergency medical personnel were on scene, conducting rescue and response operations.
Curth said passengers were being brought inside the port’s administration building “for triage and assistance.”

“Our immediate priority is the safety of all passengers, crew members and first responders,” she said in a statement. “This remains an active and evolving incident. The number of injuries and the cause of the collision have not yet been confirmed.”
Reporter covering politics with a focus on campaigns
Van Hollen ‘no longer pursuing’ possible 2028 bid as he seeks Senate leader job
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Maryland) is abandoning his presidential ambitions for 2028 as he seeks instead to oust Sen. Chuck Schumer (D) from his leadership role.

“I’m no longer pursuing that,” Van Hollen said Friday of his potential 2028 presidential bid, after a speech to Democrats gathered in Denver to celebrate the party’s huge wins in the midterm elections and chart a cohesive path forward.

“I believe that the size and scale of these majorities provides an opportunity for the United States Senate to answer the call of the American people,” Van Hollen said. “We can’t go back to business as usual.”

He announced his challenge to Schumer, the Senate minority leader, late Thursday, sparking a public power struggle alongside the work to unite Democrats. Until this week, Van Hollen had been “kicking the tires” on a presidential bid.
Van Hollen, 67, said the election called for a generational shift and that Schumer, 75, represented a style of politics that voters wanted to change.

He again characterized himself as an underdog in his leadership competition with Schumer, who has led the chamber’s Democratic caucus since 2017. And he declined to publicly reveal how many fellow senators have agreed to support him. But Van Hollen said he spoke directly with Schumer about it.
“We understand that this will be a competition. I think it’s important to give Senate Democrats a choice. That’s what we just gave voters all over the country a choice. They chose change,” he said.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/jensen-huangs-.headline: Jensen Huang’s departure blasts big hole in AI startup funding, VCs and founders say
techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/jensen-huangs-.author: Marina Temkin, Dominic-Madori Davis

paragraphs.text: It was the resignation heard across the world. Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s embattled CEO who co-founded and led the company for 33 years, had officially stepped down. “It’s like a bomb went off,” one neocloud founder told TechCrunch when he first heard the news.

Over the last several years, Nvidia has been a prolific investor, pouring tens of billions into startups annually, and participating in 105 rounds this year alone often as the largest investor, according to PitchBook. “If that direction changes, it’ll be a big blow to so many young companies,” said Maria Davidson, founder of Relational Capital.

Huang’s absence leaves the startup ecosystem without one of its biggest champions and with far less capital for now, investors say, which could have a massive impact on dealmaking, valuations, funding, and even competition.
“Nvidia is carrying almost every AI-native startup from application to neocloud,” Dawn Capital’s Shamilla Bankiya told TechCrunch.

Most of the significant decisions to invest in startups often came from Jensen himself, according to Umesh Padval, managing partner at Seligman Ventures. Padval has known Huang since serving on the board of Mellanox Technologies, a networking chipmaker Nvidia acquired for approximately $7 billion in 2020. While there is hope that Huang’s eventual successor will resume his dealmaking spree, investors aren’t hopeful that it will happen in the short term.

Nvidia’s interim CEO, Colette Kress is expected to institute some changes, especially when it comes to Nvidia’s investments into AI startups at the crux of the billion-dollar data centre build-out. Huang’s rampant dealmaking in this sphere has been a source of concern for Wall Street.
“She’s much more conservative,” one investor said of Kress. “I don’t think she’s going to commit the same amount of money to keep the early-stage ecosystem going.”

Nvidia’s biggest bets were backing neoclouds, inference providers, and open weight models, which are expensive for smaller companies to build. “Jensen’s initiatives are a big reason an ecosystem has emerged despite that,” Zain Javid, co-founder of the hardware company Ghost, said.

For instance, Nvidia backed CoreWeave back when it was still private, and participated in two of Crusoe’ rounds, including its $1.4 billion Series E. It bought Hugging Face this year for $13 billion (expected to close in 2027) and holds investments in Mistral AI, Lambda, and Black Forest Labs. Nvidia was often the largest investor in the deals. Last year, it wrote an $800 million check into a $2 billion Series B round for Reflection AI, before the open-source startup began to earn meaningful revenue, according to the Wall Street Journal.

“Jensen believed in open source and frankly speaking, Europe,” Bankiya said of how Huang invested so much in AI across the world. The cease of that support in other regions outside of America, like Europe “would be a massive funding and honestly ecosystem gap that no one can fill.”

It’s also true that Nvidia was such a dominant player in the ecosystem that at times, it felt like a monopoly. By backing so many companies with such generous checks, Nvidia effectively locked those startups into using its chips which helped reinforce its dominant market position.

If the company does grow more conservative with its startup investments, that could leave more room for rivals and smaller competitors. (Coincidentally, Google announced two new chips this week amid Huang’s Nvidia fallout).
Some investors with whom TechCrunch spoke hope that large cloud companies and other chipmakers will step in to back startups and fill some of the void that will likely be left by Huang.

Dharmesh Thakker, a general partner at Battery Ventures, for example, expects big tech rivals to vie for Nvidia’s investment crown, “depending upon who brings the best combination of a great product, an ecosystem and community to compete with CUDA, and the financial power to bankroll the ecosystem,” he said. CUDA is Nvidia’s software platform that enables developers to run AI models on its GPUs.

While companies like Google, Amazon, Microsoft, and AMD may back mature startups to drive adoption of their chips and clouds, Thakker doubts they will pour hundreds of millions into pre-revenue infrastructure startups the way Nvidia did.

Under Huang, infrastructure companies that needed $100 million to $500 million in GPUs would often raise half of that amount at valuations of $1 billion or more from Nvidia just to get started, one VC said. The chipmaker’s participation gave other investors the comfort in backing these companies at the lofty valuations.
Now, Nvidia is expected to be more selective in the new companies it backs, while writing smaller-sized checks into its existing portfolio, contributing to a drop in valuations.

“When Nvidia was on the cap table, everyone felt safe,” Padval said. Without that backing, investors say traditional VCs are likely to think twice before writing checks into these startups and may even pause certain dealmaking.
Even so, few believe that Nvidia’s investment slowdown will by itself halt the broader AI boom.

Though everyone agrees that Huang is a massive loss for Nvidia, one of his ex-employees, Amulya Vishwanath, who now runs her own VC fund, said that “founders and leaders must be held accountable,” and that the ecosystem is bigger than one person. “That talent will, and must, continue to thrive.”

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/13/eisenk.headline: Eisenkot accuses Netanyahu of ‘racist’ campaign against Israel’s Arab minority
theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/13/eisenk.author: Guardian staff reporter

paragraphs.text: Israeli prime ministerial hopeful Gadi Eisenkot accused caretaker premier Benjamin Netanyahu on Friday of fuelling a “racist” campaign against the country’s Arab minority, after he sought to delegitimise the community’s lawmakers by linking them to Hamas.
Eisenkot’s statement was a rare instance of a prominent Jewish political leader taking a strong stand in defence of Arab Israelis, who make up more than 20% of the population.

Two Arab-majority parties, Raam and the Joint List, secured a combined 19 seats in last month’s election, winning nearly a sixth of the 120-seat parliament and potentially emerging as kingmakers in efforts by Eisenkot to form a government.
“Arab citizens of Israel are an integral part of the Israeli story,” Eisenkot wrote on X on Friday.
“They have been subjected to a racist and aggressive campaign of delegitimisation, fuelled by the outgoing prime minister and those around him for political purposes,” he added.
“The attempt to marginalise them and vilify them collectively is a profound violation of the principles of civic responsibility.”
Netanyahu and his allies have repeatedly criticised leaders of Arab parties for refusing to describe Hamas as a “terror group” following its unprecedented 7 October 2023 attack on Israel.
All leaders of Arab parties have condemned the attack, in which Arab Israelis – descendants of Palestinians who remained in what became Israel in 1948 – were also among those killed.
Netanyahu has also repeatedly alleged electoral fraud by Arab-majority parties, but electoral authorities have rejected the claims.
In a speech, Netanyahu lamented that the two Arab lists refused to recognise Israel as a Jewish state, although Raam leader Mansour Abbas has done so in the past.
He further claimed that they sought to establish either an “Islamic state” or a “nationalist Palestinian state”.
During the same ceremony, national security minister Itamar Ben Gvir heckled Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen during his oath of allegiance, accusing him of having “pledged allegiance to Hamas”.

“It is entirely legitimate to disagree with representatives of the Arab parties, even to strongly disapprove of some of them. But it is neither legitimate nor acceptable to malign an entire community, and I will not allow it,” Eisenkot said.

President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with forming a new government on Sunday after consultations in which a majority of political parties, including the two Arab lists, recommended him for the role.
But one of Eisenkot’s rightwing allies, Avigdor Lieberman, has said he will back out of the coalition if Arab Israelis are part of it.
If Eisenkot fails to form a government within 28 days, he may request a 14-day extension. Should he still fall short, the mandate would pass to another lawmaker, most likely Netanyahu.

techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/amazons-new-ki.headline: Amazon’s new Kindle Colorsoft is a premium e-reader with a premium price
techcrunch.com/2026/11/13/amazons-new-ki.author: Aisha Malik

paragraphs.text: Amazon recently unveiled its refreshed Kindle lineup introducing a new basic Kindle, Paperwhite, and Colorsoft. The new Kindle Colorsoft starts at $290, while the Signature Edition, which I’ve spent the past few weeks testing, costs $320.
The base model comes with 16GB of storage, while the Signature Edition doubles that to 32GB and is available in graphite or a maroon-like Fig finish with an aluminum back.

Amazon first brought color to its Kindle lineup in 2024 with the launch of the original Colorsoft. The latest model is lighter and thinner than its predecessor and features an edge-to-edge display. If you already own the first-generation Colorsoft, there’s little reason to upgrade.
The core reading experience remains largely the same. Both models have a 7-inch color E-Ink display, 300ppi resolution for black-and-white content and 150ppi for color.
However, if you’ve been eyeing a color e-reader, the new Colorsoft is worth considering if you can get past the hefty price tag.

Unlike standard Kindles, which display everything in black and white, the Colorsoft brings your digital bookshelf to life with their original colors. This makes it a particularly appealing option for readers who enjoy comics, graphic novels, or cookbooks, where color makes a big difference. It’s also great for readers who like highlighting passages in different colors.

It’s worth noting that colors on the Colorsoft are still relatively muted and not as vibrant as what you’d see on an iPad. Still, they add a welcome splash of color and make a noticeable difference compared to the black-and-white displays of standard Kindles.

The Colorsoft lets you adjust the screen’s color temperature, so you can switch to a warmer, more yellow-toned display that’s easier on the eyes when reading at night. There’s also an auto-adjusting brightness option that comes in handy.

When it comes to battery life, Amazon says that the Colorsoft can last up to eight weeks on a single charge, compared to up to 12 weeks for the Paperwhite. During my testing, I didn’t have to stress about charging the Colorsoft because like other Kindles, its battery lasts a relatively long time compared to other everyday electronics.

One small but welcome improvement on the new Colorsoft is the repositioned power button. On the previous generation, it was on the bottom of the device next to the charging port, making it easy to accidentally press it when handling the Kindle. On the new model, Amazon has moved it to the top-right edge, where it’s less likely to get in the way. I quite like this change, and found the new location more intuitive when powering the device on and off.

I enjoyed the premium feel of the aluminum back on the Signature Edition. Although Amazon provided a case with my review unit, I rarely used it, and the finish held up well. While the slimmer design isn’t a major change, I found the new Colorsoft quite comfortable to hold compared to older Kindle devices.
For those who enjoy reading in the bath or by the pool, the Colorsoft is waterproof, so you don’t have to worry about accidental splashes or spills damaging the e-reader.

One thing I appreciated about the Colorsoft was how infrequently the screen needed to refresh, which was something I noticed more often with the larger Kindle Scribe Colorsoft. I also didn’t experience any noticeable ghosting, where text from previous pages lingers on the screen, which is common on some e-readers.

The Signature Edition supports a magnetic cover with built-in page-turn buttons that connects to the pogo pins on the back of the device, but I can’t speak to this experience because I didn’t have access to the case.

The biggest drawback of the Colorsoft is its price. It’s a steep investment for a device that’s just used for reading. That said, if you really want a color display, the Colorsoft is definitely worth considering. For everyone else, it’s a nice upgrade, but far from a must-have. Many readers would be better off with the basic Kindle or Paperwhite, which start at $169.99 and $199.99, respectively.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck1exevgql4qo.headline: Nvidia: How the Jensen Huang scandal exposed a headache for business-friendly Singapore
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ck1exevgql4qo.author: Tessa Wong, Osmond Chia

paragraphs.text: A major scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy based in Singapore has cast a spotlight on the city-state's success as a global chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade.

On Thursday, Huang stepped down from the US chip giant after admitting he had an affair. He was reportedly involved with a woman named Alice Huang, who ran Singaporean data centre company Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's chips.
For decades, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy offering easy access to both the US and Chinese markets.
With the AI boom, it has become a major hub for the trade of high-end semiconductor chips in recent years.
Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the US chip giant earns.
But notably, less than 1% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, as the island acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.

Since 2022, when the US restricted advanced American semiconductors from being exported to China or acquired by Chinese companies, US officials have been concerned that other countries such as Singapore could be used by Chinese companies to gain access to the chips.
Megaspeed is a case in point.

It became the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia and is suspected of giving backdoor access to these chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.
The city-state has had some success in policing this.

It has charged four companies and five individuals - including Chinese nationals - for various offences including fraud, following US concerns that Chinese AI company DeepSeek had been buying Nvidia chips from third parties in Singapore, among other places.
They also tried to probe Megaspeed, but were faced with a number of difficulties.

In a statement released on Thursday, the government said that since February 2025, they had been looking into whether Megaspeed and other firms had made false declarations about data servers which were purchased and exported through Singapore.
The companies stated the equipment would end up in neighbouring Malaysia, but Singapore authorities suspect the equipment's final destinations were elsewhere.

Singapore said it sought assistance from US authorities several times to get more information from one of the investigated companies - Supermicro, a US-based company which the BBC understands was supplying computer servers to Megaspeed.
But "despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance", it said in its statement. The BBC has sought comment from the US State Department.
Singapore authorities said they had also investigated Alice Huang - not for espionage, but for any possible role in Megaspeed's suspected fraud.
In the end, they found "insufficient evidence" of crime and let her leave Singapore in February this year, after holding her passport for several months.
Since launching their probe nearly two years ago, Singapore has yet to bring any charges against Megaspeed or any of the companies and individuals linked to the case.
Singapore and US investigations into Megaspeed are still ongoing.

In 2024, US officials had paid a visit to a Malaysian data centre owned by Megaspeed and saw Nvidia technology still in their boxes, raising concerns that Megaspeed was shipping high-end chips out elsewhere, according to a report by the New York Times.
Last year, Megaspeed appeared to have imported 50,000 more chips than Nvidia could account for, according to a Bloomberg report. Nvidia later adjusted its own figures after visiting more warehouses.
Megaspeed has maintained it has always acted lawfully and that previous inspections by authorities found no evidence of illegal activity.
On Thursday, the company said it "welcomes appropriate government scrutiny" and that it is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government".
China has also long refuted accusations that its companies and institutions are illegally obtaining high-end US chips.
How Megaspeed and Alice Huang came to Singapore highlights other vulnerabilities stemming from the city-state's openness.

In recent years, the city-state has become a prime destination for Chinese companies, with tech firms such as TikTok and Manus making it their global headquarters. Besides Singapore's ease of doing business, it has a population that is mostly ethnically Chinese and largely views China positively.

For a Chinese firm, Singapore offers a base near the mainland and a "neutral address" that global customers and investors accept, said Winston Ma, adjunct professor at New York University's School of Law.
But critics say this has given rise to "Singapore-washing", where Chinese companies use the city-state's clean image to obscure their origins, reduce suspicions and even cover up dubious activities.
Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS told the BBC they had assessed Alice Huang's setup of Megaspeed to be such a case.
BBC checks of corporate records in China, Hong Kong and Singapore found that in 2019, Huang sold a gaming company and its subsidiaries to Chinese gaming firm 7Road.
In March 2023, a 7Road subsidiary in Singapore named Huang as its executive director. The next day it changed its name - to Megaspeed.
Huang was in charge for eight months before she transferred the company to a Singaporean man.

During this period, Megaspeed went through "a critical period of corporate restructuring and regional expansion", and her corporate relationships raised questions about whether "Megaspeed's Singaporean identity is genuine or effectively Chinese-controlled", according to C4ADS.

Even after she transferred Megaspeed, C4ADS assessed that she was still "practically in control" of the company, based on her links to Megaspeed via another company as well as LinkedIn posts where she continued to identify herself as Megaspeed's "chairwoman" at conferences.
Megaspeed has not answered BBC queries regarding the company's and Alice Huang's links to China and the Chinese government.
All this reinforces the dilemma faced by Singapore.

"For the longest time, Singapore has managed to enjoy the best of both worlds with excellent relations with US and China," Nanyang Technological University politics and international studies lecturer Dylan Loh said.

Singapore has long positioned itself as a neutral party between the two superpowers. Its prime minister Lawrence Wong has insisted that his country is neither pro-China nor pro-America, but "pro-Singapore".
But Loh says this balancing act "has now fast become very difficult to manage and sometimes quite fraught too" with the US-China dispute over chips.
With the Megaspeed case, the tightrope Singapore has walked is set to get even narrower, according to analysts.

Beijing may ask why Singapore is investigating issues pertaining to US restrictions and whether they are siding with the US' interests, says Chong Ja Ian, a Singaporean political scientist and non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.
Washington, in turn, might read Singapore's latest statement as "pushing blame" on the US, which could lead to backlash from the White House, he said.
"Singapore has made a policy position not to take sides. But by not choosing a side, they run the risk of being seen as complicit" in either side's agenda, he said.

But Benjamin Ho, an assistant professor and China expert at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies, noted that this was "not the first or last time Singapore will be caught between the US and China".
"This is the price that an open economy has to grapple with - you get caught in the middle when things turn sour."
Additional reporting by Jack Lau of the BBC's Global China Unit.

engadget.com/2316687/some-physical-copie.headline: Some International Physical Copies Of GTA VI Can Allegedly Be Redeemed Without Opening The Box
engadget.com/2316687/some-physical-copie.author: Ian Carlos Campbell

paragraphs.text: Less than a week before Grand Theft Auto VI is released into the wild, online reports have started to bubble up about a potentially serious issue with the retail version of the game. According to posts on ResetEra and X, the download code for the game may be visible from the outside without opening the box if you have a strong enough flashlight.

The code is visible because, rather than including a paper insert with the code or covering it with a scratch-off coating, it's reportedly printed on the inside cover of the GTA VI box. Only a few photos are currently circulating of codes illuminated through the side of the game box, so it's hard to say if this is truly a widespread issue. The ResetEra post says it may be limited to international copies of the game, because the US game box includes a backing that camouflages the code from the outside.

Fans have discovered the entire GTA 6 redeem code on the physical copy can be seen without opening the box by shining a powerful flashlight through the side at an angle. pic.twitter.com/YtN5QhC81R — GTA 6 Countdown ⏳ (@GTAVI_Countdown) November 13, 2026
Engadget has asked Take-Two to comment on the reports and whether it's aware of any issues with GTA VI game boxes. We'll update this article if we hear back.

If the issue is widespread, it could pose a serious problem for anyone trying to buy a physical version of the game. All you need is a code, your console and an internet connection to download GTA VI, and if you're able to get those codes without buying or even opening the retail box, it could be possible to purchase a copy of the game that's already been redeemed.

All of this hinges on Take-Two and Rockstar Games' strained definition of what a "physical" version of a game is. Traditional physical releases include a disc or cartridge that, even if it doesn't include all of the game or its final version, acts as a kind of key that you need to play. And importantly, those keys can be given to someone else if they want to play. Rockstar's physical GTA VI release is just another way to purchase the digital version of the game, and because of the nature of digital game licenses, not really something you can own. If this issue does affect a large number of copies, it could also be a game you can't play, too.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckregdgnl0xpo.headline: Elon Musk’s SpaceX to attempt double catch of Starship rocket
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckregdgnl0xpo.author: Rebecca Morelle, Alison Francis

paragraphs.text: SpaceX will attempt to catch both parts of its huge Starship rocket after it launches on its next test flight on Friday.
Elon Musk's company will use the mechanical arms - nicknamed chopsticks - on its launch tower to grab the rocket parts mid-air as they return to Earth.
If successful, this will be the first full recovery of a rocket that's been to space, paving the way for making Starship reusable so it can fly repeatedly.
Nasa will be closely watching the flight: the SpaceX rocket is set to play a vital part in its Artemis programme, which will see astronauts land on the Moon.
The 124m-tall rocket is scheduled to blast off from the Starbase launchpad in Texas at 1645 local time (2245 GMT) with a 75-minute-long launch window.
After six and a half minutes, the first planned catch will be attempted when the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - returns to the launch tower.

The top part of the rocket, called the Ship, will continue its journey to space and deploy 26 satellites. These will form part of the Starlink constellation that provides high speed internet from space.
The Ship is then due to complete 14 orbits around the Earth before returning for the second catch attempt about 22 and a half hours after taking off.
Until now, SpaceX has managed to catch the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights.
But the upper stage of the rocket, which only reached orbit for the first time in September, has never been grabbed by the chopsticks. Instead it's splashed down in the ocean.
SpaceX said it would only decide to try to catch the Ship after carefully assessing the vehicle while it's in space.
If any problems are detected there are various points during the flight when the rocket stage can be brought down in the ocean.
Building a fully reusable rocket is a long-held ambition for SpaceX.
In 2015, it became the first company to vertically land part of a rocket with its Falcon 9 booster.
Falcon 9 rockets now fly more than a hundred times a year, and the ability to reuse the bottom part of the rocket has dramatically cut the costs of launch.
But landing an entire Starship rocket could take this to the next level, says Prof Malcolm Macdonald, President of Royal Aeronautical Society.
"A successful double catch would be visually spectacular, but full reusability has the potential to fundamentally change the economics of accessing space," he said.
"One successful flight will not prove that model, but it could mark an important transition: from demonstrating that Starship can fly, to demonstrating how Starship could operate."
After SpaceX went public earlier this year, its shareholders will be carefully monitoring this flight, as will the US Space Agency.
The progress of Starship has direct implications for Nasa's attempt to land humans on the Moon in 2028 - a highly ambitious timeline.
SpaceX has been given a Nasa contract to configure the Ship into a lander that will eventually take astronauts down to the lunar surface.

But it's not the only company working with the US Space Agency. Blue Origin, owned by rival tech billionaire Jeff Bezos, also has a contract to use its New Glenn rocket and lander for the Moon touch down.
Both companies will also play a key role in Artemis III, which is currently planned for summer 2027- another challenging schedule.
This mission will see four astronauts in Nasa's Orion spacecraft attempt to dock with both SpaceX and Blue Origin's landers.
Starship will need to make a lot of progress in the coming months to meet these commitments - the pace of the rocket's development has been far slower than SpaceX had intended.
But Blue Origin also has much work to do. The company suffered a major setback earlier this year when its rocket exploded, totally destroying its launchpad in Florida.
Blue Origin had said they would be back in action by the end of this year, but a return to flight has now been delayed to early in 2027.

Nasa is under pressure to meet its timelines. Its administrator Jared Isaacman has said America is in a race with China to get to the Moon. China plans to land its Taikonauts on the lunar surface by 2030.

cnbc.com/2026/11/13/spacex-launches-star.headline: SpaceX launches Starship in key test flight of massive rocket
cnbc.com/2026/11/13/spacex-launches-star.author: Lora Kolodny

paragraphs.text: SpaceX launched its 15th Starship test flight on Friday, the company's first attempt to catch both the Super Heavy booster and upper stage spacecraft of the rocket at its launch site in Starbase, Texas.

The flight lifted off at 4:47 p.m. local time, or 5:47 p.m. ET. Earlier on Friday, SpaceX obtained authorization from the Federal Aviation Administration. Hours later, the FAA issued a nationwide ground stop after reporting communication problems affecting "multiple" air traffic control centers. The SpaceX license wasn't effected by the flight stoppage, a spokesperson for the FAA told CNBC.
SpaceX, which began test flights of its massive Starship rocket in 2023, had to abort plans to catch and reuse the booster, instead diverting it to splash into the ocean.

Starship's success is critical to Elon Musk's company and its ambitions to eventually lift cargo and people to the surface of the Moon and Mars. In the near-term, SpaceX needs to send more satellites into orbit to expands its Starlink satellite internet service, which is currently the company's profit center.

With Friday's test flight, SpaceX plans to release a batch of its new Starlink v3 satellites into orbit. The company's constellation already includes over 11,000 active satellites in low Earth orbit. One Starship rocket has the capacity to carry up to 60 Starlink v3 satellites into orbit, the company has said, representing about 20 times the capacity of earlier Falcon 9 rockets.

In the previous Starship test flight, the company released 26 Starlink v3 satellites, and was planning to release another 26 in the Friday test flight with the goal of "Starlink becoming 51% of the internet," SpaceX said in a post on X.

When it comes to launches, "SpaceX is likely a full decade ahead of peers on this front," William Blair analysts wrote in a note out on Friday. "Even if tonight's catch is unsuccessful, a delay by a few months is not that consequential."

Meanwhile, SpaceX is facing fresh criticism over restrictions imposed on its Starshield satellite internet service in Ukraine. Starshield is built on Starlink technology and is the military-tier of SpaceX's satellite internet service.

Earlier this week, Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said his country's military forces had experienced limits on Starshield without warning again, harming their ability to defend against Russia's ongoing aerial attacks. Similar limits on Starshield in Ukraine were temporarily imposed last month.
Some U.S. senators have condemned the restrictions, and urged Congress to investigate SpaceX.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-13/.headline: O.C. Sheriff probes whether employees alerted ICE before man’s arrest
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-13/.author: Ruben Vives, Suhauna Hussain

paragraphs.text: An internal investigation is underway at the Orange County Sheriff’s Department after surveillance footage captured two department employees briefly speaking with federal immigration agents shortly before a man was detained while leaving the jail.

The department said in a written statement that it had received a complaint early this month about the Halloween incident alleging that the two employees may have alerted U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents, enabling them to detain the man.
The department said it had launched an internal investigation to determine if the employees had violated state law or department policy.

A state law called the California Values Act prohibits local police and sheriff’s departments from using public resources to help enforce federal immigration laws, such as detaining people solely for immigration purposes or sharing certain personal information with ICE. The law allows limited exceptions, including cooperation involving people convicted of certain crimes.
The department identified the two employees only by title. They said one was a deputy and the other was a sheriff’s special officer.
An internal review found that surveillance video from the Oct. 31 incident showed ICE agents parked on a public street outside the Orange County Jail in an unmarked black SUV.

The deputy and special officer are seen exiting the sheriff’s building before approaching the black SUV, and engaging in what appeared to be a five second conversation with the agents inside the vehicle, video released Friday by the department shows. Footage shows a man who appears startled jogging to a corner of the courtyard and standing and waiting as federal agents approach and then arrest him.

“Shortly after the deputy and sheriff’s special officer left, a second vehicle arrived,” the department’s statement read. “ICE agents exited both vehicles and entered the public courtyard outside the visitor’s entrance. The ICE agents contacted and arrested a man who appeared to be hiding in the public courtyard.”

News outlet NBCLA reported that the man taken into custody by ICE had been visiting his son at the Men’s Central Jail. A family member identified the man as Jesús Esparza to Telemundo 52 earlier this month.

His daughter, Adriana Esparza, told Telemundo 52 that her father had called her from the jail saying ICE was outside and hung up just after telling her they were capturing him. The Times could not immediately get in touch with Esparza’s family.

His daughter set up a GoFundMe campaign earlier this month to raise money for an immigration attorney. She wrote in the online fundraiser that after her mother’s passing, her father had became the sole head of household supporting her younger brother.
“We are brokenhearted about the situation we are in,” she wrote in Spanish.
The department said upon receiving the complaint it immediately opened a personnel investigation into the conduct of the employees and placed both of them on administrative leave.

“Securing the border and enforcing immigration law are important federal responsibilities,” said Orange County Sheriff Don Barnes. “The Orange County Sheriff’s Department does not enforce federal immigration law. That has not and will not change.”
Barnes said the department will cooperate with ICE to the extent the law allows to prevent serious criminal offenders from returning to communities they have preyed on.

“We will enforce state and local laws equally, without bias, and without concern for anyone’s citizenship,” Barnes said. “I want the community to continue to feel safe in calling for assistance, reporting crime and visiting the jail regardless of their immigration status.”

nbcnews.com/news/us-news/faa-orders-nati.headline: Ground stop ordered for all airports nationwide for ‘reasons of safety’
nbcnews.com/news/us-news/faa-orders-nati.author: Corky Siemaszko, Tom Costello, Joy Y. Wang

paragraphs.text: Much of the air traffic across the U.S. was suddenly shut down Friday after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered a nationwide ground stop for all departing flights “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”

The unexpected and highly unusual alert, which was issued at 3:54 p.m. ET, contained no other information beyond stating that “all departing traffic should remain ground stopped until further notice.”
Follow along for live coverage.
“Inbound international flights will be managed on a case by case basis,” the FAA said.
When the FAA issued the alert, 4,042 flights headed for U.S. destinations were airborne, according to Flightradar24, a Swedish service that displays real-time aircraft flight tracking information.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was “no indication as of yet” that there was anything “nefarious” that caused the ground stop. He said it was the result of a telecommunications outage “as of now.”

Mullin said President Donald Trump has been briefed and they are “are not ruling out anything at this point” in terms of what caused the communications issue. He said those currently on flights have no reason for concern. “We are assured that everybody is safe,” he said.

While the investigation into the failure is in a very early stage, there is no indication that the incident has been caused by malicious activity, officials from multiple agencies that are involved in the situation tell NBC News.
They say they haven’t seen the type of activity that would normally be associated with a cyberattack. The officials, however, cautioned that the assessment could change as investigators learn more.
Three senior officials say there’s nothing that indicates a connection between Friday’s incident with the FAA’s systems and the Microsoft outage.

By 6 p.m., Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Virginia, was at capacity, and Chicago O’Hare International Airport was nearing capacity, meaning there was no place for the planes to park, a source with knowledge told NBC News.
With planes stranded on runway, the likelihood increased that some of these planes would have to be diverted to other airports, the source said.

Meanwhile, Air Space Intelligence, the AI tech startup that is a vendor for the FAA on its new SMART system for air traffic control, insisted its software was not responsible for nationwide ground stop.
“The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said in a statement posted to X.
Aviation safety expert Jeff Guzzetti called the outage “extraordinary” and said he doesn’t know what would cause it.

Guzzetti emphasized that pilots are trained to operate through communications outages and that there are redundancies in place for such instances. Pilots “could get information relayed through other means” to ensure planes are spaced properly for landing.

He added that the situation is moving from a safety issue to instead becoming a massive logistics problem. Airports are becoming crowded with planes trying to land as the aircraft currently on the ground aren’t able to depart. Planes on the ground may have to move and park on taxiways, Guzzetti said.
There are different layers of communications — high-altitude, midlevel and then the towers on the ground. The high-altitude control centers are affected by the outage.

At Newark Liberty International Airport, personnel in the control tower said the situation is “a whole mess right now,” according to LiveATC. “We’re running out of space” and “there’s significant gate issues” were comments also heard on the live audio feed.
“I’m as much in the dark as everyone else. I’m not getting any information from anybody,” one controller at Newark said, according to the feed.

Shortly before the FAA issued its alert, both major airports in Chicago — O’Hare and Midway International Airport — were listed on a ground stop alert due to an “equipment outage,” NBC Chicago reported.
Deveren Werne was on an American Airlines jet that was about to take off from Indianapolis to Chicago when suddenly the pilots announced that all flights were grounded.

“At first, the pilot announced that there was some kind of radio issue,” Werne, 55, of Greenville, South Carolina, told NBC News in a telephone interview. “Then a little while later, the pilot said something like, ‘There is something going on that’s more serious than that.’”

Werne, a consultant who helps manufacturers and other industries adapt AI technology, said he is a frequent flyer and this was a first for him. He said there was “a mixture of emotions” from his fellow passengers on hearing the announcement.

“Then I started hearing from other friends who were on planes, including one in Chicago who was stuck on a runway,” Werne said. “Right now, our plane is heading back to the terminal, so at least we’re going to be able to deplane.”

United Airlines issued a statement acknowledging the ground stop. “United flights that are already airborne will continue,” the statement said. “New domestic flights will not depart while the FAA ground stop remains in place.”
Nationwide ground stops are extremely rare.

After the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, the FAA ordered an unprecedented nationwide ground stop. All civilian air traffic across U.S. airspace was halted and airborne planes were ordered to land at the nearest available airports.
In January 2023, the FAA grounded all flights, blaming a failure in the Notice to Air Missions system, which alerts pilots to a host of potential dangers.
Corky Siemaszko is a senior reporter for NBC News Digital.
Tom Costello is an NBC News correspondent based in Washington, D.C.
Joy Y. Wang is a senior editorial director for NBC News.

washingtonpost.com/sports/2026/11/13/tea.headline: Teams scramble as FAA ground stop threatens to upend sports calendar
washingtonpost.com/sports/2026/11/13/tea.author: Stephanie Apstein, Noah White

paragraphs.text: Five buses carrying almost 200 members of the Washington Huskies football team’s traveling party had just pulled up to King County Airport on Friday night when they got the alert: The FAA had instituted a nationwide ground stop.
The team was headed to East Lansing, Michigan, to play Michigan State at 4:15 p.m. Saturday — until it wasn’t.
The team lingered at the airport for half an hour before deciding to return to campus, where the players milled around Husky Stadium in their team sweatsuits.
“There’s not much we can do until there’s some clarity as to when flights might resume,” assistant athletic director Jeff Bechthold said in an interview. “It’s a 30-hour drive.”

College football teams throughout the country are scrambling to rebook travel or find alternative routes as the nationwide FAA ground stop left them unable to fly to the sites of this weekend’s games, while teams in other leagues wait to see how long the ground stop will last.

The Knoxville News-Sentinel reported that Tennessee, which is scheduled to play Texas A&M in College Station, Texas, at 3 p.m. Saturday, was stuck at the airport, waiting for news on a 4 p.m. Friday flight that never took off. CBS Sports reported that Auburn, which is scheduled to play Mississippi State at noon Saturday in Starkville, Mississippi, was in the same position.

College football teams probably will be most affected by the ground stop, as many schools travel on Fridays for Saturday games. Team planes, which are often school-owned among Power Four programs, follow a strict itinerary, departing from regional airports sometime during the afternoon or evening the day before games, to avoid athletes missing their classes as much as possible. Only in rare instances do schools travel on the day-of for games.

NBA, NHL and college basketball teams could also face scheduling adjustments. Ten NBA teams are on the road Saturday, and a handful are playing Friday night in a different city, as well. After Friday night games, they’d usually fly to their next city on a red-eye rather than waiting until the following morning. NHL teams follow similar scheduling practices.
NFL teams typically fly on Saturdays for Sunday games.

Hope that the FAA full ground stop is quickly and easily fixed and everything's OK soon.Just a detail: The 49ers are scheduled to fly to Dallas tomorrow. They often fly out on Fridays if it's multiple time zones, but not this time.— Tim Kawakami (@timkawakami) November 13, 2026
If the ground stop were to continue into Saturday, NFL teams might consider driving, depending on the proximity of their Sunday opponent.

cbssports.com/college-football/news/faa-.headline: FAA flight stoppage leaves college football teams scrambling to find alternate travel plans
cbssports.com/college-football/news/faa-.author: Austin Nivison

paragraphs.text: On Friday afternoon, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a nationwide ground stoppage for all departing flights due to "extraordinary circumstances and reasons for safety." That announcement came as numerous college football programs were preparing to leave for road games across the country.

There is no timetable for when the issue will be resolved, and that has left teams scrambling for alternate plans. Fortunately, some teams have already arrived at their destination, but quite a few high-profile matchups could be affected by the disruption.

The @FAAnews issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.— Secretary Sean Duffy (@SecDuffy) November 13, 2026

There are a handful of top-25 teams that still haven't taken off, and they are looking for alternate forms of transit. That raises another set of questions, including timing and player safety. What if these teams can't get the proper rest after spending most of Friday night on a bus, and will games have to be pushed back due to late arrivals?
Those are questions without answers at the moment, as neither the NCAA nor the individual conferences have addressed how the ground stoppage might affect Saturday's schedule.
For now, here is the latest on how notable Week 11 matchups have been affected by the FAA's ground stoppage.
SEC

In addition to sorting out which teams will be able to arrive on time for kickoff, the SEC is still assessing if any officiating crews for Saturday's games have been affected by the groundstop, sources tell CBS Sports.
The conference issued a statement on the FAA's ground stoppage on Friday night, saying it's still evaluating the situation with all member institutions.

The Tigers have arrived in Athens for their showdown against the top-ranked Bulldogs, sources tell CBS Sports.

Ole Miss hadn't arrived at the airport prior to the ground stoppage. Per 247Sports, Rebels players have been instructed to go home and return to the airport at 7 p.m. local time, and pushing kickoff to Sunday is on the table.
