cnbc.com/2026/11/13/trump-nvidia-huang-c.headline: Trump doesn’t plan to raise Nvidia, spy issue during China trip: U.S. officials
cnbc.com/2026/11/13/trump-nvidia-huang-c.author: Dan Mangan

paragraphs.text: President Donald Trump does not plan to raise the issue of a suspected Chinese spy having an affair with former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during his upcoming trip to China, senior U.S. officials told reporters on Friday evening.
Officials also said that Elon Musk, the CEO of Tesla and SpaceX, will accompany Trump on the trip to Shenzhen, China, for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit.
The White House earlier Friday said that Trump plans to have a three-way summit while there with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

Jensen Huang's relationship with the suspected spy, Alice Huang, who is not related to him, has raised concerns that a Singapore-based company where she was an executive diverted restricted Nvidia chips to China.
"The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip," an official said on the press call, speaking on the condition that they not be identified.

"In all of our discussions and negotiations with the Chinese, we do not negotiate American export controls ... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there."

Asked if Trump would raise the allegations against Alice Huang to Chinese leader Xi Jinping, the official said, "The focus of a meeting with President Xi, at least on the economic side, is going to be about implementation of the trade agreement."

"When it comes to some of these national security matters and examinations and investigations that are going on in the U.S., [that is] probably not something that we're going to read the Chinese in on at this moment," the official said.
Another official said, "I don't expect the president to raise it — the Alice Huang issue."

Huang resigned this week as Nvidia's CEO after damning reports that he had an affair with Alice Huang, who was an executive of Megaspeed, a cloud-computing company that is being eyed for possible facilitation of sending billions of dollars worth of Nvidia chips in violation of U.S. restrictions on those chips.

The scandal has rocked Nvidia and raised questions about whether the Commerce Department, which is led by Trump's friend Howard Lutnick, has been aggressive enough at blocking advanced chips from ending up in China.
During Friday's call, a reporter asked why Musk was going on the trip with Trump.
"I don't want to speak for the president on exactly why Elon's going," an official said.

"Obviously, he has tremendous business interests in the U.S.-China relationship. He's a big part of our national security," the official said. "There are numerous reasons, given the engagement that the president is going to have, where I think Elon would be of tremendous benefit, just even as an advisor to the president."

cbsnews.com/news/democrats-post-election.headline: Democrats see mandate from voters to lower costs, but still figuring out how to deal with Trump factor
cbsnews.com/news/democrats-post-election.author: Anne Bryson, Zak Hudak

paragraphs.text: November 13, 2026 / 7:43 PM EST / CBS News

Democrats received the message loud and clear from the midterm elections that Americans want results, not "shallow litmus tests," as Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro put it at a conference in Denver this week. But it was evident that Democrats, who gathered at a summit on the way forward as they take control of the House and Senate next year, are still working out just how to achieve those results while President Trump is still in the White House.

Shapiro helped Democrats flip four House seats in his state, and he spoke after an election that delivered decisive majorities to Democrats in the Senate and the House. He said voters had rejected "chaos" and "corruption" and are demanding results-focused governance. Shapiro urged congressional Democrats to focus on lowering costs, building affordable housing, protecting consumers and expanding economic opportunity — and not on ideological fights.

The Pennsylvania governor, who has been mentioned as a possible 2028 presidential candidate, focused on national issues, arguing the "beginning of the mandate" from voters called for aggressive action on competition, AI, innovation and economic fairness. He advised Democrats to use their majorities to deliver a stronger "American bargain" for working families.

While some newly elected Democrats, like Sen.-elect James Talarico of Texas, have some optimism about the new Congress' ability to work with the Trump administration, others, including New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill, encouraged new members of Congress to be pragmatic in approaching dealmaking with Mr. Trump.
In his remarks Thursday, Talarico, who won his seat in a heavily Republican state, said that Democrats "must" work with President Trump because "the American people cannot wait two years for change."
"We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history," Talarico said.
But Sherrill suggested that may be harder than it sounds.

"The art of the deal to Trump is, he figures out what you want. He leverages the you-know-what out of you and keeps taking, taking, taking and never delivers. He does not follow through on his commitments," Sherrill said of her experience in working with him as New Jersey's governor.
She told Democrats to take advantage of the power they amassed this election cycle and use it to their advantage.
"My advice to Senator Talarico is, if Trump wants to work with us, we will lay out the agenda and he can sign it," Sherrill said.
Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger, who won the governorship in 2025, the same year as Sherrill, agreed that trying to make deals with Mr. Trump may be futile.

"It is foolish to think if you ever make a deal, if you ever give anything, you give an inch to the president, there is no reason to believe—he has no track record of ever following through—that if you make a deal with President Trump, he will ever actually abide by it," Spanberger said.

Spanberger, who represented Virginia in the House before she was elected governor, offered this advice to next year's Democratic Congress: "Congress should pass bill after bill after bill that is broadly, very clearly popular, and is responsive to what folks across the country campaigned on, and send it to the president's desk. No pre-negotiations, no discussions. Eventually he'll want to do a signing ceremony. And eventually, he might sign a couple of them. And if not, then in 2028, folks say, look at these bills that passed through the House, passed through the Senate. The president didn't take action."

Despite the celebratory mood in Denver, Democratic officials repeatedly sent the message that they understand that last week's victories do not represent a long-term realignment, and there's no guarantee that the voters who supported them will continue to do so.
"This isn't a blank check," Sen. Ruben Gallego of Arizona said. "If anything, it is a short-term loan that we need to keep paying — or we will lose it."
Democrats work to keep momentum in 2028

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-13/.headline: DUI suspect in deadly North Hollywood crash driver charged with murder
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-13/.author: James Queally

paragraphs.text: A 61-year-old Valley Village man has been charged with three counts of murder for a suspected drunk driving wreck that claimed the lives of three street food vendors near the North Hollywood Metro station on Tuesday night, officials said.

Ihor Demianenko faces life in prison if convicted as charged after his Nissan Sienna hopped the curb on Lankershim Blvd. near Chandler Avenue and plowed into a series of blue and white tarps that housed vendors who had been feeding Metro line commuters for years, according to a criminal complaint made public Friday. His blood-alcohol content was more than three times the legal limit, according to a news release issued by the Los Angeles County district attorney’s office.

Two other pedestrians were struck by the vehicle, and one remains in serious condition, according to LAPD Capt. Mike Bland, the department’s chief spokesman. Demianenko remains hospitalized and was unable to appear in a Van Nuys courtroom on Friday, Bland said.
The women who died in the crash were Francesca Krystine Esker, 39, Teodora De Jesus Villalobos, 57, and Maria Angelica Peck, 73, according to the district attorney’s office.

“Once again, an impaired driver has left a trail of carnage on our Los Angeles streets. The victims of this horrific crash included street vendors who were simply trying to earn a living when tragedy struck. My deepest sympathies are with the families of the three women who lost their lives, and I hope the two other victims who were seriously injured make a full recovery,” Los Angeles County Dist. Atty. Nathan J. Hochman said in a statement.

Demianenko is expected to be arraigned on Monday. It was not immediately clear if he had an attorney. He has not been previously convicted or accused of any prior driving offenses in California, according to state Department of Motor Vehicles records. He was involved in a car accident in 2024, records show.

Police said Demianenko was driving southbound on Lankershim at an “unsafe speed” around 6 p.m. Tuesday when his vehicle struck a row of street vendors that is normally stationed outside the transit hub that marks the end of the Metro B Line train and the G Line bus extension to Chatsworth. On the night of the crash, the car could be seen on the sidewalk come to rest under a blue tarp, while coolers, soda cans and racks of snacks the women usually sold were scattered across the sidewalk.
Area residents said the women who operated the row of food stalls there were beloved community members who had sold hot dogs, tamales, coffee and snacks to rush hour commuters for years.
LaDuke Warwick, 47, told The Times that an act of kindness from one of the women changed his life.
Warwick said he was homeless about five months ago and sleeping on a nearby vent near when one of the women approached him and told him to come with her.
“I haven’t watched you eat in three days,” he recalled her saying. She gave Warwick one of her hot dogs.
“Everybody in this area loved them,” Warwick said. “They were such sweet souls.”

On the night of the wreck, fellow vendors who operated in the area continued to sell their wares to the crowd of onlookers who arrived at the crash scene, hours after watching their colleagues get mowed down.
“I’m just glad it wasn’t my family, but it still hurts,” said 12-year-old Kassandra Guzman, as her father served someone a smash burger across the street.
Times Staff Writer Fedor Zarkhim contributed to this report.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-13/.headline: Thousands of flights affected by FAA ground stop. Here are your rights as a passenger
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-13/.author: Clara Harter

paragraphs.text: Thousands of flights across America were delayed, canceled or stuck on the tarmac Friday after the FAA announced a ground stop due to a communications issue with its air traffic control centers.
The sudden announcement left weary travelers scrambling and unsure about when they could make it to their destinations — and what sort of compensation they may be entitled to.
More than 10,000 flights within the United States were delayed and more than 5,000 were canceled as of 4:30 p.m. Friday, according to flight tracking website FlightAware.

Flights that already were in the air when the ground stop began were allowed to continue to their destinations, while all other domestic flights were held on the ground. International flights were being handled on a case-by-case basis, according to the Federal Aviation Administration.
The cause of the technical issue was unknown and there was no estimated time for resuming domestic flights Friday.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no reason to believe that the telecommunications outage was caused by a foreign or nefarious actor.
Here is what you should know if you are among the travelers affected.
If your flight is stuck on the tarmac

Under U.S. Department of Transportation regulations, all airlines at U.S. airports are required to allow passengers to deplane within three hours of a tarmac delay on domestic flights and within four hours on international flights. A tarmac delay applies to planes awaiting takeoff or planes that have just landed where passengers are unable to get off.

Airlines are generally required to provide water and snacks to passengers within two hours of a tarmac delay. Working toilets and comfortable air cabin temperatures must also be maintained and medical care must be provided if needed.
If your flight is delayed

Passengers are not automatically entitled to financial compensation if their flight is delayed. Passengers do generally have rights to a refund if there is a significant change to their travel plans and they choose not to continue traveling. The DOT defines this as departing or arriving at least three hours later than scheduled for domestic flights and at least six hours later than scheduled for international flights.
Several airlines have announced flexible travel policies to make it easier for passengers to change flights or receive refunds during the ground stop.

United Airlines released a statement Friday saying it would waive change fees and fare differences for passengers who opt to reschedule their trip for a new flight departing on or before Nov. 20. Passengers affected by the air traffic control outage who cancel or don’t take their trip are entitled to a full refund, the airline said.

Delta Airlines also announced a travel waiver allowing customers affected by the ground stop to change their flight at no extra cost. Alaska Airlines has a flexible travel policy in place allowing refunds for canceled flights and waived fees for certain flight changes.
If your flight is canceled

Passengers are entitled to a full refund if their flights are canceled and they choose not to accept alternative flights, per DOT regulations. Federal law does not require airlines to provide meal or hotel vouchers to passengers when a cancellation is caused by factors outside of an airline’s control.

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.headline: Stuart Bonds made ‘racist’ and ‘divisive’ comments. But One Nation is showing no sign of dumping the NSW candidate
theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.author: Penry Buckley

paragraphs.text: In a Facebook video from a Sydney anti-immigration rally on Sunday, as a man dressed like a medieval knight watches on, One Nation leader upper house candidate Stuart Bonds launches into a speech against “mass” migration.
“Make no mistake, we are being demographically replaced inside our own nation,” he says.
“If we don’t support Australian mothers having Australian children, we [are] going to pay for other cultures’ children to be brought up in our lands.”

In an apparent allusion to the “great replacement theory”, a far-right conspiracy theory that white westerners are being actively “replaced” by non-white immigrants, he continued: “That’s the socialist plan, is to destroy and bring down and tear down the fabric of your civilisation.”

The comments sparked a wave of criticism, but the party has shown no signs of taking Bonds off the ticket for the 2027 New South Wales state election. One Nation did, however, dump one candidate this week: the Victorian branch disendorsed a lower-house candidate over an old social media post describing Hitler as the GOAT, an acronym for the greatest of all time.

The rally was not a one-off. On a podcast released on Monday with the rally’s organiser, the Australian Lobby Group, Bonds appeared to double down on the remarks. He did not challenge host Scott Challen’s assertion that Labor governments were building “ethnic voting blocks with Middle Eastern and subcontinent people … to stack the numbers to entrench power for themselves”, instead responding: “Mate, and that’s why we’re going to get rid of all of the multicultural grants, right?”

On Wednesday, in an interview with ABC Upper Hunter, Bonds responded to questions about his comments by citing Australian Bureau of Statistics data that shows the proportion of Australians born overseas has trended upward since the end of the second world war, from 10% in 1945 to 32% in 2025. He did not mention that the proportion of Australians born overseas was at its highest – 32.4% – in 1891, the first year of available data.
Bonds said with the Australian birthrate beneath the 2.1 required to replace the population, “I would just like to know what people assume is going to happen.”
“Where are these people going to come from?” he said.

NSW Labor pounced on the rally comments immediately, with the state’s premier, Chris Minns, calling them “frankly outrageous and racist”. The government passed motions in both houses censuring Bonds, not yet a member.
The Coalition followed four days later. On Wednesday afternoon, the opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, said Bonds’ language was “clearly divisive”.
But she did not rule out a confidence and supply arrangement with One Nation after the March state election.
“We will not form a coalition with One Nation, [but] we’ll work with anyone post-election if we’re in a minority government,” she told reporters.

The Australian Financial Review has reported many of her MPs privately expect the party to go into a Coalition with One Nation. And with the Coalition consistently polling behind One Nation, that makes Bonds not a fringe candidate, but a potentially influential figure.
One Nation could ‘clean the deck’ in regions
The ABC’s former election analyst, Antony Green, said the remarks played straight into Labor’s hands.
“This will certainly be something the Labor party uses in all those multi-ethnic seats in Sydney,” he said – seats like those on the rural fringes of Sydney, which One Nation said it plans to target.

Indeed the deputy premier, Prue Car, who has Indian heritage and whose electorate of Londonderry is one of the seats in question, gave an impassioned critique of Bonds’ comments in question time on Tuesday.
“Who’s he [Bonds] talking about when he talks about this?” she said. “I tell you who he’s talking about – he’s talking about families like mine, and families that I represent.”

Kos Samaras, a former Labor strategist who is now a director of polling group Redbridge, said that while the comments likely won’t play well in Sydney seats – including alienating moderate Liberal voters worried about the party going into Coalition with One Nation – “you might be able to get away with it in certain parts of NSW”.
And Bonds, a former coalminer, has made his base in the Hunter.
Samaras said One Nation could “clean the deck” in the regions, including Labor-held seats in the Hunter, and “pretty much anything else the coalition hasn’t got bolted down to the ground”.

The NSW One Nation leader, Mike Newman, who in September said he “made a mistake” when he told a Sydney rally he wanted to stop abortions, did not respond directly when asked if he agreed with Bonds’ comments or if he would rein in his first-placed upper house candidate.
“What I will say is that what Stuart Bonds is a patriotic Aussie. He’s a coalminer. He has very, very strong views,” he said on Tuesday.

Newman, who previously rejected claims that One Nation was racist, said on Tuesday: “What we want to do is … protect Australian values, and that is the fundamental thing that Stuart Bonds is pushing for. It’s about assimilation.”
The NSW treasurer, Daniel Mookhey, whose parents immigrated to Australia from India in the 1970s, told the ABC that Bonds’ comments were not grounded in reality.
“I think he’s saying that there is a deliberate conspiracy to use migrants to replace the way he puts it, native-born Australians for political reasons,” Mookhey said.
The quota for election to the upper house is 4.5%, making Bonds all but guaranteed to be elected, with One Nation polling in the high 20s and low 30s in recent months.

Green expects the party to pick up four or five seats in the upper house; so far it has only named three candidates: Newman, Bonds and Jeff Bacon, a firearms manufacturer who is second on the upper house ticket.
But unlike Victoria, NSW has optional preferential voting, which means when that state goes to the polls in March, lower house preferences flows aren’t guaranteed.
But Bonds has downplayed whether he may have jeopardised a future preference deal with the Coalition.
“If the Coalition have a problem with facts, the same as the Labor party, then maybe it will,” he told the ABC.
“But I’m not here to impress the Coalition.”

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq99e0z4vg1eo.headline: CJP: India’s protesters face government crackdown after summer victory
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cq99e0z4vg1eo.author: Azadeh Moshiri

paragraphs.text: After a summer win, India's Gen Z protesters face a winter of uncertainty
South Asia Correspondent, Delhi
Cheers erupted at Delhi's Jantar Mantar protest site in July as news broke that Gen-Z protests had forced federal education minister Dharmendra Pradhan to resign.
One protester turned to me, beaming: "This is the youth's victory."

Just over three months later, the mood has shifted dramatically. Student protesters are now struggling even to assemble. Demonstrations by the Gen Z-led Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) last month over voting rights were met with sweeping restrictions and thousands of peaceful protesters were detained.
The summer had seen a new wave of dissent in India, driven by deep frustration among the youth and fuelled by irreverent online satire.

The movement spread across the country, and Prime Minister Narendra Modi, a leader with a strongman image, unaccustomed to open criticism or mockery, struggled to contain it. But the government's increasingly forceful security response suggests it has learned from its rare concession to protesters, invoking public order to curb dissent.

The ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) national spokesperson Syed Zafar Islam rejected accusations of heavy-handedness and told the BBC: "The right to protest and freedom of expression is mandated by the constitution, but it has to be done within the law. It cannot override the rights of others, at the cost of public security".
This is by no means the first time the Modi government has faced large-scale protests.
But the breadth of them pose a challenge for the BJP, according to Yamini Aiyar, former president of the Centre for Policy Research and visiting professor at Brown University.
"They are not defined by caste, gender or economic class," Aiyar said. "Even some of the core BJP base, the upwardly mobile, lower-income classes, were attracted by the movement."
The scale of the youth protests is also magnified by its online presence. Protesters have broken a longstanding political taboo, openly mocking the prime minister online.
"It's more than just laughs," said Sakhi, a student protester who identifies as they/them and affiliated with one of Delhi University's left-wing student organisations.
"The fear of repercussions in other generations isn't felt as much in ours," they said. "Comedy is a new language to challenge authority."
Previous protest movements posed serious challenges to Modi but were easier to dismiss as representing narrow sections of society or to label "anti-national", according to Aiyar.

In 2020, farmers protesting against controversial agricultural reforms were blocked from entering Delhi, leading to months of demonstrations and, at times, clashes on the capital's borders. After a year of protests, the government abandoned the reforms.
Protests against a contentious citizenship law in 2019 and 2020 are a stark reminder of the powers of the judiciary should anyone be deemed a national security threat.

Student activist Umar Khalid was arrested under anti-terror laws after violent clashes in Delhi that killed 53 people, mostly Muslims. He was accused of being a "key conspirator". He has now spent more than six years in jail without his trial having begun.
His partner Banojyotsna Lahiri told the BBC they have no regrets, but that the situation instilled "a kind of fear that has prevailed".
"We are just looking at a very dark mesh of empty space, because we don't know when the endpoint is," Lahiri said. Khalid's latest appeal was lodged this month.
Aiyar believes opponents are using a familiar "playbook" today to "de-legitimise" protests, but that it isn't resonating as convincingly.
Nevertheless, the youth protests have struggled to recapture this summer's momentum.

CJP leaders, including spokesperson Saurav Das, have faced repeated detentions and legal action. Das and fellow leader Ashutosh Ranka spent a week in Delhi's Tihar jail after being accused of trespassing at Jantar Mantar.
The site of their summer victory has since been struck off the list of authorised protest venues, a decision being challenged in court.
Protesters from other groups, including the left-wing All India Students' Association (Aisa), have also faced police action over allegations of defying orders.
"We were expecting some kind of crackdown," said Das. He added that "the government has learnt a lot" since the summer.
Legal experts warn the proceedings themselves can have a chilling effect.
"A lot of cases can lead to acquittals, but it can take years. The process is the punishment, and that can deter protesters," said Ali Khan, an assistant professor at Lloyd Law College.
The restrictions on demonstrations have become excessive, according to constitutional lawyer Vrinda Grover, who is advising the CJP.
"Those who are organising the protests have repeatedly emphasised that this is non-violent," she argued. "Rights have been whittled down in the name of law and order."
The BJP has rejected suggestions it is suppressing peaceful dissent.
Islam told the BBC that demonstrations "cannot override the rights of other citizens just because a handful of people want to protest and be responsible for violence".
Even dissenting online carries risk. Sakhi's viral social media posts have attracted targeted abuse and transphobic attacks. The BBC has seen posts threatening them with violence and rape.
Sometimes, it can deter Sakhi from protesting or even make them change the way they dress.
"Making people laugh can turn into being called anti-national," Sakhi said. "They want me to feel damaged," they added.
They claim some of their content was removed after getting millions of views.
Under India's information technology laws, the government can order platforms to block content on national security grounds. Notices on X and Instagram have shown accounts being withheld in India.
CJP leaders have likened the crackdown to the 1975 Emergency, when then prime minister Indira Gandhi suspended civil liberties and jailed political opponents.
Yet dissent has not been stamped out.

Opposition parties have, in part, filled the void. Tens of thousands gathered in Delhi on 1 November for a rally organised by INDIA bloc, an alliance of opposition parties led by Congress, and permitted by the authorities.
CJP leaders, meanwhile, insist the movement is bigger than their organisation.
When Das walked out Delhi's Tihar prison on 21 October, photographs showed him smiling.
"I would just say wait and watch," Das told us. "Time is on our side. We are a very young generation."

npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-6040403/faa-nat.headline: FAA issues nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports
npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-6040403/faa-nat.author: Joel Rose

paragraphs.text: The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a rare nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a "communication issue" which is currently under investigation, according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.
Friday afternoon, the FAA said in a post on X that there has been a "temporary telecommunications outage."
"Out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted. Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis," the post reads.
The outage hasn't been linked to a threat or attack, said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

"There is no indication, and we had no reason to believe as of right now that this was a threat to the United States," Mullin told reporters at the White House. "There's no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for your loved ones."

As of 7 p.m. EST, more than 10,000 flights had been delayed Friday and 4,000 had been canceled in the U.S., according to FlightAware, a flight tracking site. The turmoil comes on the heels of nearly 7,000 flight delays on Thursday.
The FAA said the issue was affecting Air Route Traffic Control Centers — the regional air traffic control centers across the country that handle high-altitude traffic.

This is only the second national ground stop since September 11, 2001. The U.S. last issued a ground stop of this scale in 2023, when all U.S. airports were shut down due to an outage in the NOTAM (Notice to Air Missions) system, which alerts pilots and airports of real-time hazards.
That outage prompted fears of a cyberattack, but the FAA later determined the issue was caused when contract workers inadvertently deleted critical files.

The telecommunication issue doesn't extend to the entire U.S., Mullin said. Without naming the regions in question, he stated, "there's two areas inside the United States that are still able to communicate just fine."
Mullin also said that other countries' aviation systems don't seem to be affected by the FAA outage.

The FAA has recently begun rolling out an AI-enhanced software tool known as the SMART system as part of its ambitious overhaul of the nation's air traffic control system. But Air Space Intelligence, the company that makes the tool, quickly dismissed speculation that its product could be connected to the flight disruptions.
"The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC," the company said on social media.
Passengers stranded
The nationwide ground stop has caused chaos in airports and headaches for travelers — many of whom are already too familiar with flight delays and cancelations during the holiday season.

At Dallas Fort Worth International Airport, Regina Harling said she waited hours — long past when her flight was supposed to depart — before she learned of the nationwide grounding by checking the news on her phone.
"There's still a sign right in front of me that says we're boarding in 16 minutes," she said.
Harling needed to travel last minute to San Diego for a family emergency. Stuck at the airport, she's thinking about how soon she can make it to her family, but she's not optimistic.
"I was just thinking to myself that it always feels like it's getting harder to travel than it used to be," she said.

At Chicago O'Hare International Airport, Giliann Karon was on board a plane when the nationwide ground stop was ordered. Karon said she had already experienced a flight delay the day before due to bad weather in New York City, where she is heading.
"It's just kind of like, 'Oh, of course this is happening,'" she said.
This is a developing story.
Deepa Shivaram contributed to this report.

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.headline: Microsoft ‘deeply sorry’ for global disruption that could have billion-dollar impact on Australia
theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.author: Henry Belot

paragraphs.text: The Microsoft outage could be a disaster for the Australian economy that forces some small businesses to close, with costs expected to run into the billions of dollars, experts have warned.

The US software company has said it is “deeply sorry” for a widespread outage that caused disruption to millions of users, organisations and businesses across the globe – and that it has “addressed the underlying issue”.
The company said the outage was a “technical issue” not related to cyber-attacks or AI agents, and that it continued to gradually restore services.
Experts have said the outage exposes “Australia’s reliance on foreign technology” and that people unable to be paid, send an invoice, or access government services “are entitled to be worried”.

The outage of Microsoft’s services, which began on Friday morning, lasted roughly 18 hours before services started to recover. Microsoft said it was bringing back services gradually to ensure a stable restoration.
Ashwin Pal, a partner at the risk advisory firm RSM Australia, said his clients had activated business continuity and disaster recovery plans, but many businesses didn’t have a fallback.
“A protracted event like this can easily be the straw that breaks the camel’s back for smaller entities,” Pal said.
Pal said Microsoft had obviously struggled to recover, which raised bigger questions.
“I’m a technologist and I’m actually flabbergasted as to how something like this could have happened … they pushed out a change which should have been tested,” Pal said.

The Australian Computer Society has renewed calls for the federal government to urgently review which critical IT systems rely on a single provider, and where backup options could keep the economy running.
The society’s chief executive, Prins Ralston, said the outage had “exposed Australia’s reliance on foreign technology”, particularly on small businesses.
“Australians who couldn’t get paid, couldn’t send an invoice, or couldn’t reach a government service this morning are entitled to be worried,” Ralston said.
Australian hospitals and health clinics were affected by the outage, although the Australian Medical Association (AMA) on Friday said had been no impacts for patient care.

“We’ve had some facilities return to using paper for scripts because authentication to get into lots of prescribing software requires multifactor verification, which requires you to be able to access your Microsoft-supported email,” said the AMA’s president, Dr Michael Bonning.
Courts in South Australia and Victoria reported that the outage had affeced its email system. Many schools across the country were also affected.
Service NSW, the one-stop shop agency for residents, drivers, and business owners to access government services, encouraged customers to delay their visits to its service centres.
Federal government departments have also been maffectedy the outage, including national security agencies.

The head the domestic spy agency Asio, Mike Burgess, on Friday said the organisation’s systems “operate on multiple levels”, adding that they had been affected “on one level, yes, but not completely”.
The outage has affected businesses and organisations across the world that use Microsoft products.
In the UK, healthcare systems were disrupted and several British police forces urged people not to try to report crimes online and to phone them in instead.

US government offices across the country have been affected by the outage, including congressional offices that heavily rely on Outlook email. The US House’s chief administrative officer that handles IT for the chamber sent out a “campus-wide alert” to staffers on Thursday about the outage, Politico reported.

In Japan, the shipping company Sagawa Express said it was unable to accept online reservations for some of its services at airports and train stations while Taisho, a leading pharmaceutical company, said it was having to handle orders by phone.
When stock market trading opened on Wall Street, shares in Microsoft dipped slightly, down 1.1% at $516.86.
Microsoft has suggested the outage may have been caused by problems with the settings applied to servers responsible for keeping Microsoft 365 up and running.
Microsoft’s executive vice-president of Copilot, Charles Lamanna, said: “We regret that today’s outages caused disruptions for our customers, and we are working to address the issue.”
Call me Dumb Nostradamus.

Two days ago, I was on my friend Pablo Torre’s podcast to discuss some of my recent reporting on artificial intelligence. A lot of accomplished cybersecurity people I’ve spoken with are convinced that the combination of rapidly advancing AI systems, the diffusion of those systems via open-source models, and the rickety state of the world’s software would lead to something like rolling waves of chaos. Paraphrasing those experts, I told Pablo, “There’s going to be stuff that doesn’t work that disrupts your daily lives—and that’s the best you can hope for.”

That I learned all domestic flights in the United States were being grounded minutes after my own flight this evening landed—safely, and with the country’s chillest passengers and Delta crew—just goes to show that predicting chaos and being prepared for it are two very different skills.

To be clear, I have no idea what caused this. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed a communications issue for interfering with air-traffic control. It could be a classic software-upgrade facepalm; the extremely rare ground stop coincided with the FAA’s recent rollout of SMART (Strategic Management of Airspace Routes and Trajectories), an $875 million AI-enhanced air-traffic-management system. The system’s maker, Air Space Intelligence, denies that its technology was at fault. Of course, the stop also coincided with yesterday’s Microsoft’s Outlook outage. That’s a lot of cyber smoke in two days.
Even if today has a boring explanation, the experts I’ve been talking with are pretty sure that plenty of days like this are coming, for two main reasons.
[Ian Bogost: Airport chaos began long before the ground stop]

First, anyone can be a bad guy now. Switching off a country’s power grid has technically been possible for a long time. What stopped anyone was the logic that kept the Cold War cold. The only people capable of that kind of chaos were governments, and governments know that turning off another country’s lights is exactly the sort of thing that gets answered with missiles. Deterrence works on parties who have something to lose and an address where you can send a reply. The trouble with AI (um, one of the troubles) is that it may hand state-grade capability to people who have neither.

You can’t deter a vandal. You don’t know who he is, and he doesn’t care, and he may currently be eating cereal in a gaming chair. The kids who used to grab a bat and swing at mailboxes can now grab some compute and turn off a town’s refrigerators—not for money or a cause, but because why not? Historically, that’s been the motive behind a great deal of human mischief.

Second, our best defense against this kind of chaos is amputation. None of the security people I’ve talked with has predicted an apocalypse. But they’re pretty convinced that the next 18 months are going to be a hassle, with regular disruptions to services that we rely on. That’s because, when cyber defenders find a hole they can’t patch fast enough, the rational move is to amputate: Switch the system off and wait. Big institutions already do this, more quietly and more often than you’d think. Whatever caused today’s ground stop, halting every departure in the country “for reasons of safety” until someone works out what’s going on isn’t a sign that the system is failing. More and more, it is the system. I’ve just watched it from 22C.

You can do some things to protect yourself, but they fall into the realm of flossing: Install the update when your phone nags you, use passkeys instead of text-message codes, keep a little cash and water around. There’s some safety in numbers. Gmail and your giant bank are obvious targets, but they also employ armies of very serious, very well-paid people whose whole job is looking for trouble. And if they go down, hey, we’ll all have problems big enough that the world reading your love letters and poring over your credit-card statement will be the least of them.

The disorientation will be harder to adjust to. Most of us have been privileged to live in a world of peace, prosperity, and above all, stability. We’ve gone to bed without having to wonder whether the traffic lights will work tomorrow. Now, if my sources are correct, we should plan to wake up in Software Beirut, where nothing is broken all the time, but anything might break at any time, and the main skill you need is not being surprised.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/13/wee.headline: For weeks, Brooklyn residents felt the shaking. Then came a deadly collapse.
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/13/wee.author: Tim Craig

paragraphs.text: NEW YORK — The residents who used to live 1321 to 1327 Flatbush Ave. in Brooklyn had grown used to constant banging and slamming that shook their buildings, from dawn to evening, as developers dug up an adjoining lot.
Ciahola Lawrence described the vibrations as a “thump and movement” that you heard “in your soul.”
But on Wednesday afternoon, as the grinding from the excavation equipment continued, Lawrence dozed off for a nap on her day off.
Then one especially loud cracking sound shook her awake.
“When I opened my eyes, there was light everywhere,” a tearful Lawrence said Friday during a news conference. “So, I got up and I couldn’t believe I was seeing outside.”
With the side of her apartment torn away, Lawrence looked through the opening at a pile of rubble. She could see some of her neighbors, apparently deceased, below.
“What is happening,” Lawrence shrieked. “We didn’t bother these people. They killed us.”

Lawrence’s emotions reflected the grief and anger of a community mourning eight neighbors killed when their apartment building collapsed. Officials suspect that the excavation project, which was being undertaken to construct an apartment building, triggered the collapse.

The tragedy, which has displaced Lawrence and dozens of other residents who lived in adjoining apartments, is renewing calls for stricter enforcement of building codes in New York City. It is also uniting a cross-section of New Yorkers grieving the dead, most of whom were recent immigrants to the U.S.

“Our community has been living through a nightmare,” said New York City Councilwoman Farah Louis (D), who represents the area. “Grief without accountability is not enough. Buildings simply do not collapse without systemic failures.”

Those killed include a 31-year-old man from Colombia as well as his 9-year-old daughter and another 10-year-old relative, also of Colombian descent. A relative from Spain told Gothamist, a local New York news outlet, the family had been mostly staying in their home in recent weeks because they feared U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents.
Two others killed were immigrants from Guinea, relatives said Wednesday.

Mamadou Saliou Diallo, president of the Guinean Community of America-New York, said the community is now asking President Donald Trump and federal officials to grant the parents of the men visas so they can travel from Guinea to the United States to attend their funerals.

“We call on our elected representative and appropriate authorities to ensure that this tragic incident receives the necessary attention and that its circumstances are thoroughly investigated,” Diallo said.
Two of those killed were also construction workers from Ecuador who had been working in the pit.
Winston Sanchez, a representative for the men, said the wife of one of the men is due to give birth on Sunday.

“It’s a sad day because it not only collapsed a building, it collapsed the lives of many relatives, brothers, fathers,” Sanchez said. “We are here today not only in solidarity but also demanding … that the city do more to protect our workers and protect our people regardless of their immigration status.”
Despite the grief, there was some relief over those who were rescued from the collapsed building.

On Wednesday evening, Mamadou Mouctar Balde made an impassioned plea in front of television news cameras for information on his pregnant wife, who had been pulled from the rubble by New York City firefighters.
On Friday, Balde, speaking in French, told reporters his wife remained in serious condition at a hospital, but she and her unborn child were expected to survive.
“To the firefighters, thank you,” Balde said.
The three-story apartment building that collapsed is owned by Isolag Realty Corp., with Olufemi Falade listed as its registered agent, according to city property records.
The same records show Falade owns multiple properties throughout Brooklyn that, like the property that collapsed, have unresolved city building-code violations dating back several years.

Robert Fischman owned the lot where construction was taking place, records show. The construction site had been fined $10,000 for failing to abide by a stop-work order from the Department of Buildings in April. The fine was paid in October, and the excavation work to construct the building’s cellar started on Sept. 10.
Neither property owner has returned phone calls from The Washington Post seeking comment.
New York Attorney General Letitia James (D) said Friday that both her office and Brooklyn County District Attorney Eric Gonzalez are scrutinizing the circumstances that led to the collapse.
“I have faith that investigators will follow the facts and anyone held responsible will be held to account,” James said.

New York City Council Speaker Julie Menin (D) also vowed Friday that the city will increase its spending on building inspectors. She noted that the Department of Buildings has a 9 percent staff vacancy rate.

A spokesman for the Department of Buildings said the agency is hiring an outside engineering firm to assist in its investigation of the building collapse. The agency is also investigating more than 160 other building sites that had been using the same contractors that were working next to the collapsed building.
“This is an unspeakable horrendous tragedy, and we must meet this moment,” Menin said.
But the increased focus on building safety has come too late for Zariah Coleman.
Coleman was not home when the building collapsed but has had to vacate her own apartment. She has since been unable to find her cat.

“Before all of the happened, we used to feel shakes in our building,” Coleman said, through tears. “We used to feel the shakes when they were working. … Now, I just really want them to come and get our cat.”
Violet Jira and Razzan Nakhlawi contributed to this report.

marketwatch.com/story/14-dividend-stocks.headline: 14 dividend stocks selected for long-term growth

paragraphs.text: These stocks feature attractive dividend payouts and are trading low to the companies' intrinsic value, according to John Buckingham of Value87 Investment Partners
These are three of 14 dividend stocks selected by John Buckingham of Value87 Investment Partners, who is also the editor of the "Patient Prospector" newsletter.

There are a variety of ways to select dividend stocks. John Buckingham, a veteran value-oriented stock picker, believes the best approach is to focus on a stock's total return potential, which means emphasizing long-term growth first, and income second.

Buckingham was the editor of "The Prudent Speculator" newsletter for more than 25 years until he and his colleagues Jason Clark and Christopher Quigley founded Value87 Investment Partners in May. The team now manages about $1.1 billion for individual clients following the same strategy they used to select portfolios described and shared through "The Prudent Speculator."

Their new newsletter, with Buckingham again editing, is titled "A Patient Prospector." While the team's value-oriented investment strategy has evolved over the years, the Hulbert Financial Digest has tracked its performance continuously, carrying through to the present. The renamed strategy ranks very high for total return performance against other investment newsletters tracked by Mark Hulbert, especially the 30-year and 1-year returns, which you can see here.

'In a world with people worried about viability and prospects for "growthy" stocks, you might want to put these in your portfolio as a hedge against the Nvidias of the world not living up to their potential.'John Buckingham, co-founder of Value87 Investment Partners and editor of "A Patient Prospector"

This has been a good year for stocks of dividend-paying companies. Before discussing Buckingham's dividend-stock selections, let's take a look at how four exchange-traded funds that take different passive approaches to holding portfolios of dividend stocks have performed against the S&P 500 SPX. These are total returns for 2026 through Thursday, with dividends reinvested:
Many exchange-traded funds holding dividend-paying stocks have outperformed the S&P 500 during 2026.

-- The Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF SCHD tracks the Dow Jones U.S. Dividend 100 Index, which is a group of stocks with high dividend yields, subject to a variety of quality screens done annually. The stocks in the index are weighted by a combination of market capitalization and quality scores. This ETF quotes a 30-day Securities and Exchange Commission yield of 3.06% and has been the best performer of 2026 among the four ETFs on the chart.

-- The iShares Core High Dividend ETF HDV has been the second-best performer among the four this year. It quotes a 30-day yield of 3.10% and holds 73 stocks to track the Morningstar Dividend Yield Focus Index, which also is designed to select high-yielding dividend stocks for quality. The index is reconstituted quarterly, with stocks weighted by the value of each component company's dividend payment.

-- The ProShares S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats ETF NOBL quotes a 30-day yield of 2.28% and holds 68 stocks as it tracks the S&P 500 Dividend Aristocrats Index XX:SP50DIV of companies that have raised their regular dividend payouts for at least 25 consecutive years. You can read more about the Dividend Aristocrats in this article from Nov. 6.

-- The Invesco S&P 500 High Dividend Low Volatility ETF SPHD quotes a 30-day yield of 4.26%. It tracks the S&P 500 Low Volatility High Dividend Index. This index is reconstituted twice a year, at which time S&P Dow Jones Indices narrows the list of 75 stocks in the S&P 500 with the highest dividend yields to the 50 that have shown the lowest price volatility over the previous year. These 50 stocks are then weighted by trailing 12-month dividend yields.
Buckingham's 'myth busting'

Investors are always concerned about inflation and the Federal Reserve's interest-rate policies. But Buckingham felt it was important to point out that the core consumer-price index (all items minus food and energy) of 2.6% for September wasn't particularly high. That is the most recent official core CPI number, because the government shutdown last year kept the Bureau of Labor Statistics from publishing the figure for October.
Buckingham said that according to Bloomberg's data, the average CPI going back to 1955 was 3.7%.

Then, using data going back to Jan. 31, 1958, from the Fama-French data library and Bloomberg, he showed that for the most part, stocks in various categories performed better during periods of higher inflation than during periods of lower inflation.
Stocks have tended to perform even better during periods of high inflation.

For the above and following charts, the value- and growth-stock camps are based on traditional price-to-book value measures used in the Fama-French data, Buckingham said, while emphasizing that his team's approach is more focused on earnings than book value.

Here's a similar chart showing how stocks have performed during periods during which the federal-funds rate has been higher or lower than the current target range of 3.75% to 4%. The tendency has been for stocks to perform better during periods of higher rates, which runs counter to the continual warnings to investors about rising rates.
Stocks have also tended to perform better during periods of higher short-term interest rates.
Buckingham's point was that most investors are better off sticking with their long-term strategies rather than reacting to headlines about inflation, Fed policy, elections or other events.
Buckingham's dividend-stock picks
Buckingham selected 14 dividend stocks with an average yield of 4.24%, which he called "fairly decent," especially when the main focus of his selection criteria is long-term growth potential.

The approach taken by Buckingham and his colleagues to stock selection makes use of various traditional measures of company valuations to sales, earnings, cash flow and other items. "We look out one to two years" to estimate companies' profit growth, "even though we are three-to-five-year investors," he said.
"We are applying what we think is a fair [price-to-earnings] multiple of where a stock should trade over that time span," he said.
So the 14 dividend stocks are "all trading at significant discount to our determination of long-term value," he said. Here they are, sorted alphabetically:
