theatlantic.com/ideas/2026/11/faa-ground.headline: Of Course Americans Blamed the Ground Stop on AI

paragraphs.text: For many hours, the Federal Aviation Administration did not explain why it issued a national ground stop in the United States this afternoon. The agency described the cause only as a “telecommunications outage” and cited “extraordinary circumstances,” but failed to say more. So speculation abounded: Was the problem connected with the onboarding of a new AI route-selection system this week? Is it somehow related to the Microsoft Outlook outage this week? Or is the cause some antiquated telecommunications system that just finally gave up trying?

In the absence of solid information from trusted authorities, people interpret crises through the prism of their pre-existing concerns. When the aviation system shut down, many Americans’ minds went to DOGE cuts, cyberattacks by hostile foreign actors, recent reports of renegade AI. A safety planner’s job is to envision the full range of possible threats and assess how likely each one is to occur. Even before recent advances in artificial intelligence, the list of factors that could jeopardize commercial aviation was already long: terrorism, extreme weather, staffing strains, the decay of outdated communications networks, and more. AI could theoretically help the aviation system manage risks and disruptions, but it also adds many more variables that could go wrong.

It’s no wonder many Americans were quick to envision rogue disruption caused by the new technology: When AI CEOs tell us that the risk of AI is so great that it is essentially uninsurable, people take notice.

The more prosaic reality is that America’s critical infrastructure systems are built without sufficient resiliency. As a result a single disruption can have national consequences. CNN reported tonight that the aviation problem may have originated with network routers at Chicago’s Midway Airport. In a fragile system, glitches spread unpredictably and potentially rapidly. So far, more than 10,000 flights have been disrupted.

Fortunately, our aviation-safety systems had sufficient backups to let planes land safely, and pilots have been communicating through emergency frequency lines. The best analogy is a spare tire: It’s good enough to get you to the nearest gas station but not much further.

The ground stop—which has now been lifted—has exposed either a new security vulnerability or a problem with old systems; either way, the economic impact could well be major. The high stakes are all the more reason that, in moments of crisis, authorities should quickly tell the public what is known, what is not known, and what they are doing to close the information gap. Finally, after four hours, the Trump administration held a press conference, at which Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that “things seem to be working, as we can say, in the right direction.” How long it will take for the mess at airports to clear is anyone’s guess.

cbsnews.com/news/howard-lutnick-scott-be.headline: Lutnick agrees to testify as Bessent blames him for not banning Nvidia chip exports to China-linked firm
cbsnews.com/news/howard-lutnick-scott-be.author: Jennifer Jacobs, Kathryn Watson

paragraphs.text: Washington — Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 10, according to a U.S. official, amid intensifying scrutiny of the Commerce Department's oversight of the export of powerful AI chips following the resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

A growing number of Republicans are calling on Lutnick to answer questions about the Commerce Department's apparent delay in adding Singapore-based company Megaspeed International to the U.S. government's Entity List, which would have restricted the company's ability to get access to advanced AI chips.

Megaspeed was previously led by Alice Huang, the suspected Chinese spy who had an affair with Jensen Huang. The U.S. government suspects Megaspeed of directing advanced Nvidia chips to China, circumventing a U.S. export ban.

GOP Sen. Jim Banks of Indiana, a member of the Senate Banking Committee, told Fox News on Thursday that "we know that the Department of Commerce, Secretary Lutnick, it appears, used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur even though President Trump has directed his administration and the Department of Commerce not to allow that to happen."

On Friday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent repeatedly emphasized that the Treasury Department and other parts of the executive branch had pushed for restrictions on Megaspeed, laying the blame for the delay at the feet of the Commerce Department.

"Treasury, War, [the U.S. Trade Representative] and State, they were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the Entity List for months, but Commerce has the pen," Bessent told CNBC. "And you will have to ask them about their internal processes."
Bessent declined to comment on reported tensions between himself and Lutnick. The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to CBS News' request for comment.

theguardian.com/australia-news/2026/nov/.headline: US-bound flights out of Australia delayed after telecommunications outage grounded American planes

paragraphs.text: Some US bound flights from Sydney Airport were grounded or delayed on Saturday after to American authorities halted departures and delayed landings at all US airports.
Flights from Melbourne Airport were also affected, with travel for passengers expected to depart for Los Angeles shortly after 10am being delayed by more than two hours.
Sydney Airport confirmed the US ban on flight arrivals was lifted shortly before 1pm, although it was not known how this would impact delays.
Earlier, the airport confirmed some US bound flights had been grounded.
“We are aware of the nationwide ground stop issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration and are monitoring the situation closely,” the spokesperson said.
“Passengers travelling to or via the United States should check with their airline for the latest information regarding their flight.”

The US Federal ⁠Aviation Administration announced the nationwide pause in response to “a temporary telecommunications outage”. It has since lifted the grounding order, as it continued to investigate the cause of the outage.
Passengers on two US bound flights from Melbourne Airport, which were due to depart at 12.00pm and 12.45pm, were also told to expect delays due to the situation in the US.
These include a Qantas flight to Dallas, and an United Airlines flight to San Francisco.
Flights to the US were also delayed at Brisbane Airport, where passengers on one US bound flight began boarding at around 1pm.

joshka.net/cell-borders.headline: Terminal borders that don't cost a cell

paragraphs.text: This post (and the code behind it) was written with a lot of help from AI. I'm not going to apologize for that. If that bothers you, feel free to close the tab.

I maintain Ratatui, so I see a lot of the TUIs people build. Many of them end up looking fairly same-ish: plain boxes on a boring background, missing a bunch of the things that good design in other mediums brings us.

Borders are part of the problem. They have to take up space, so they become part of the panels people want to build. One option is to drop them and just use color, but borders are really nice for delineating and surrounding things. There are lots of ways to sort of get borders in a terminal, but none that are 100% good. I've drawn enough ┌──┐ by hand to have opinions about this.
The usual way is the Unicode Box Drawing block, which has 128 characters for lines, corners and joins. Somehow that's still not enough:

So I've been working on a terminal protocol that draws thin lines on the edges of cells instead. I've got it working as a patch to Ghostty (and an earlier version in Rio before that), and I've built demo apps for it with Ratatui. I'd like feedback from terminal and TUI authors.

Every line in that screenshot is a cell border. None of them use up a row or column. The tab labels sit on the top edge of each pane, the text fields are underlined right under the text, and the buttons are one row tall and rounded.
Here's the same app in a terminal without cell borders, falling back to box-drawing characters:

Each pane loses a row and a column on every side, so the log pane shows two fewer lines and the notes wrap differently. The tab labels move inside the frame. The text fields use the underline attribute instead, and the checkbox and buttons turn into brackets.
What I'd use it for
• Borders, obviously. Panes and panels that don't eat a row and column on every side.
• Menus and popups that sit on top of other content and still look like they're on top.
• Panel style apps, where the layout is a set of regions that each want an edge.
• Widgets like text fields, buttons and checkboxes, which want a line right up against their text.
• Making things look neater in general. A border on the outer edge of a panel's background looks a lot cleaner, and text can run right up to it.
Up close
The settings form, with cell borders and then with the box-drawing fallback:
The tabs are the same story. With cell borders they sit on the pane's top edge. With box characters they need their own row inside the frame:
Charts

Lines between cells also work for charts. btop-style braille graphs fill every cell with dots, so there's nowhere to put a gridline or an average line without giving up a row. With cell borders they sit on the cell edges between the dots. Here's a monitor in that style, built with Ratatui:
And the fallback, which has to drop the gridlines:
In motion
Here's the tiling panes demo moving panes around, opening menus and the about dialog:
Partway through, it turns on a checkerboard of the cells, which shows how everything lines up with the grid. Toggle it here:
Show the cell grid
What box characters can't do
The root of it is that box-drawing characters are text. Each line is a glyph that takes up a whole cell, and pretty much everything annoying about them falls out of that.

Space is the obvious one. On my 16" laptop with a font I can actually read, the terminal is something like 200x50 (your prefs will move that around a bit). Columns are mostly fine at that size. Rows aren't. A layout with a couple of levels of nested panels can easily spend 6 or 8 of those 50 rows on nothing but lines. That's a lot of screen to give up for decoration.

You also can't put a line between two cells that both have something in them. So there's no way to underline a text field right under its text, or to outline a button, without adding padding around it. Rounded corners sort of work, except the corner glyph has one background color, and when the panel's background is different from what's around it you get a little square of the wrong color in each corner. And the line itself is whatever the font decides it is, weight and position included.

Then there's copy and paste. Select some text inside a box and you get the box too. Everyone who's pasted from a TUI into Slack knows the little │ cleanup dance. Sometimes you do want the box (pasting a table into a chat, say), but mostly it's junk. Cell borders aren't text, so they never get copied, which cuts both ways.
How it works

A cell border is a cell attribute, like a background color. Each cell can carry up to twelve line segments: the two halves of each of its four edges, and four arms from its center. Each segment has its own color, width, placement and style, and the terminal draws them over the cell grid. Borders are stored in the cells, so they scroll, erase, insert and reflow with the text. What happens on erase or scroll already has an answer, the same one as for colors.

The edges are split into halves so borders line up with quadrant block characters (▖▗▘▝ and friends). That makes it easy to draw a shape that's a half cell in from the grid and still put a neat border around it. Yes, that still uses a character for the fill, and there might be a better way to do that part. One problem at a time.
The same idea could stretch to sextants and octants, or to quarter and eighth widths, if designs need them.
Styles and joints

Lines can be solid, double, dashed or dotted. Each corner and center of a cell can be square or rounded, with a configurable radius and anti-aliased arcs. A rounded corner can name an outside color, so the area outside the arc is painted correctly when the panel's background differs from what's behind it.

When two neighboring cells both put a line on their shared edge, they merge into one line. The stroke with the higher priority wins, then the wider one, then the one to the right or below. That way a focused pane can raise its priority and keep its whole outline, whatever order its neighbors were drawn in. My first try was "right/bottom always wins", which lasted until the focused pane lost half its outline to its neighbor.
The wire format
Everything is one DCS string with a namespace:
ESC P 1 + b cell-border ; OP ; FIELDS... ESC \
The common path is a pen, held in the cursor like the current background color. Set it, print some text, and the printed cells get the borders:
ESC P 1 + b cell-border;pen;48;32;7aa2f7;0;0 ESC \ bottom edge, blue: an underline hello ESC [ 0 m SGR 0 clears the pen

There are also rectangle commands that set or clear borders on existing cells without touching the pen, and a capability query. An app sends the query followed by DA1. If the DA1 reply arrives without a cell-border reply first, the terminal doesn't support it, so the app falls back to box characters and reserves the space they need. Terminals that don't understand the DCS ignore it, the same as any unknown DCS.

The minimum a terminal needs is the pen, the rectangle commands and solid strokes. I've tried to keep that first cut small, because there's always one more "... and this" to add, and that's a slippery slope.

Line styles, rounded joints, priority and outside colors are extension fields listed in the capability reply, and unknown fields are ignored, so they can be added later. I'd rather the early decisions be two way doors where possible.

The spec calls itself version 1 (it's the 1 in DCS 1 + b). That's v1 in the old sense, before we all got bogged down in semver. It doesn't mean done or stable, it means it's the first one I was willing to write down. Read it as v0.1, or a draft, or whatever you prefer.
Prior art
Parts of this have been done before:

• DEC ruled lines in DECterm (extension 43 in the DA1 reply) draw lines around rectangles. They scroll with the text, but they're a separate layer: clearing the screen leaves them behind, and they're always one pixel wide in the normal text color.

• SGR 51 to 65: framed, encircled, overline and the ideogram side lines. Some terminals draw borders with them, but they're on/off attributes with no color, width or joins, and there's no attribute for the bottom edge.

• The Win32 console has per-cell grid flags for the top, left and right edges. PDCurses and X/Open curses (WA_TOP, WA_LEFT and friends) have similar attributes. These are the closest to this protocol, but they have no bottom edge (Win32), color, width or halves.
• IBM 3270 terminals can outline whole input fields.
What none of these give you is a line with its own color and width on each edge. The rationale document covers the prior art in more detail and explains each choice in the protocol.

My own first prototype was in Rio (raphamorim/rio#1947), with an earlier version of the spec that used APC instead of DCS. Feedback pointed out that APC isn't safe to reuse: Kermit 95 has run APC payloads as Kermit commands since the 90s. DCS is where structured terminal commands already live, and terminals ignore DCS strings they don't recognize, so I switched to that.
The awkward (edge) cases
When I first showed this around, most of the questions were about these. The spec goes into all of them properly, but here's roughly where I landed.

Multiplexers were the first thing people asked about. tmux and friends redraw panes from their own idea of the cell grid, so passing these sequences through would just put borders in the wrong place. A multiplexer that doesn't know about the protocol should drop them and answer DA1 itself, and then apps running inside it fall back to box characters like they would anywhere else. One that does know about it can store borders like any other attribute and redraw them.
Conflicting lines on a shared edge are settled when the terminal renders, using the priority rule above, so it doesn't matter what order the app wrote the cells in.

Erase, insert and delete all work the way they do for background colors. Erased cells pick up the current pen, and lines that get inserted or deleted take their borders along. Scrollback, the alternate screen and reflow mostly come for free, because the border lives in the cell.

On cost: the Ghostty change is about 1,650 lines, and a fair chunk of that is tests. Each cell gets a 16-bit border ID, which fits in padding that was already there, so cells don't get any bigger and a screen with no borders costs nothing extra. The IDs point into a table of distinct border sets (about 100 bytes each) that's shared by the whole terminal. A typical TUI only uses a handful of distinct sets, but the table is never freed, so in the worst case (all 65,535 IDs in use) it's somewhere around 10-15 MB.

Rendering only does extra work for cells that have borders. Each one looks at its four neighbors to resolve shared edges, so changing a row also rebuilds the rows either side of it. Straight lines are a few solid quads per cell. Rounded corners cost more, because the anti-aliased arc is drawn as rows of small quads, roughly one per edge pixel. I haven't benchmarked any of this properly yet, and it's the part I'd most like another set of eyes on.
Try it

The spec and rationale are on my Ghostty fork. The Ghostty branch implements all of version 1. I've only built and run it on macOS so far, so the GTK and OpenGL builds are untested. To build and run it (you'll need Zig 0.17 and Xcode):
git clone -b joshka/cell-borders https://github.com/joshka/ghostty.git cd ghostty zig build -Doptimize=ReleaseFast -Dxcframework-target=native open zig-out/Ghostty.app
Inside that Ghostty, the gallery script on the same branch draws the style gallery above. It detects support first, so it's also a quick check for another terminal's implementation:
python3 scripts/cell-borders.py # the default view python3 scripts/cell-borders.py --styles # line styles, joints and outside fill

Once it's running you can flip between views with keys: p placement, c colors, h blocks, j junctions, e halves, s styles and l live. w cycles the stroke width, b turns borders off so you can compare, and q quits. Each view also has a matching flag (--placement, --styles and so on) if you want to start on it.
The tiling panes demo is on the Ratatui branch. It falls back to box-drawing characters when the terminal doesn't support cell borders, which is how I made the comparison shots above:
git clone -b joshka/cell-borders https://github.com/joshka/ratatui.git cd ratatui cargo run -p tiling-panes

Drag panes around with the mouse to retile them. n and v split, x closes, and right click opens a pane menu. Press b to switch between cell borders and box drawing, or g to shade alternate cells and see where the edges are.
The btop-style monitor from the chart screenshots is in the same branch. Given how much of it an AI wrote, I did briefly consider calling it bslop:
To run it:
cargo run -p cell-border-top

It's a real system monitor (it reads your actual CPU, memory, network and processes), so it's a better test of how this looks on a busy screen than the panes demo. 1 to 4 show and hide the boxes, b and g work the same as in the panes demo, and h or ? lists the rest of the keys. It needs a newer Rust (1.95) than the rest of Ratatui because of the sysinfo dependency.
What I'd like to hear

I'm not attached to this being the exact solution, but I think it's a problem worth solving, and I'd like it to be more than one terminal's feature (and more than one weekend's worth of yak shaving). If you work on a terminal, would you implement this, and which parts look expensive? If you work on a TUI library or app, which of your widgets would use it, and what would they need that isn't here? Comments are welcome on the Ghostty discussion.

nytimes.com/2026/11/13/us/politics/nvidi.headline: Nvidia Scandal Prompts Questions of What It Means to Be a Spy
nytimes.com/2026/11/13/us/politics/nvidi.author: Julian E. Barnes, Maggie Haberman, Jonathan Swan

paragraphs.text: Alice Huang, the Chinese executive at the center of the Nvidia spying scandal, was believed to be using her affair with Nvidia’s founder to help China get around U.S. efforts to restrict access to advanced A.I. chips, people who have read U.S. intelligence reporting said.

But there remains much that intelligence agencies are still assessing about Ms. Huang including when she began working with China’s top spy agency, whether her cooperation was willing or coerced, how much direction Beijing gave her, and how much she relayed to officials there, the people said.

Her relationship with Jensen Huang, who stepped down as Nvidia’s chief executive on Thursday, gave her potential access to crucial information about the company’s technology, Mr. Huang’s strategic thinking and his knowledge of Washington’s debates about A.I. policy.

She also had a business interest in ensuring a flow of chips to her own company, one of a number in Southeast Asia that provided Chinese tech firms with the computing power needed to train advanced artificial intelligence models.

The aftershocks of the scandal continue to play out as President Trump prepares for a trip next week to Asia, where he is scheduled to meet with President Xi Jinping of China, who has made a top priority of catching the United States in the race for A.I. dominance.

The unknowns surrounding Ms. Huang have generated intense scrutiny of how Chinese intelligence operates, prompted questions of what it means to be a spy and given backers of Mr. Huang an opening to raise questions about the extent and nature of her role.

Mr. Trump, who has viewed Mr. Huang as an important ally in his push to maintain American superiority in A.I. as well as a key driver of the U.S. economy, has defended the former Nvidia leader. On Thursday he seemed to suggest that he was less sure than are U.S. intelligence agencies that Mr. Huang had been the target of a Chinese intelligence operation.

“The big thing is, was the woman a spy, and I don’t know if that’s been determined yet,” Mr. Trump said in an interview with Stephen A. Smith, the podcaster and sports commentator, when asked if Mr. Huang should have resigned. “But if the woman was a spy, yes. If the woman was not a spy perhaps it would be different.”

Still, the concerns in the U.S. intelligence community that Ms. Huang was spying on behalf of Beijing were taken so seriously that Mr. Trump was twice briefed on it, late last year and again this spring.

One of those briefings was by Marco Rubio, the secretary of state and national security adviser. Mr. Rubio had overseen the drafting of a memo, dated March 30, sent to a handful of Cabinet secretaries, that detailed Ms. Huang’s close relationship with the Nvidia founder and her contacts with China’s main civilian intelligence service, the Ministry of State Security.
Mr. Trump said this week that Mr. Huang had told him he did not know Ms. Huang was tied to Chinese intelligence. Ms. Huang has not responded to outreach from The New York Times.

Ms. Huang was a top executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that purchased Nvidia chips and built data centers in Southeast Asia whose customers included Alibaba, the Chinese commerce giant.

The Commerce Department launched an investigation into whether Megaspeed was helping illegally divert Nvidia chips to China, an inquiry launched well before the current scandal emerged and subsequently taken over last year by the Justice Department. Authorities in Singapore also questioned Ms. Huang last year. Her current whereabouts is unknown.

Attorney General Todd Blanche said at a news conference on Thursday that the Justice Department has a role in investigating whether advanced chips had been sold to China in violation of U.S. export controls.

“If there are chips that shouldn’t be sold it could potentially be a violation of our export laws,” Mr. Blanche said. “That could be civil, regulatory, it could also be criminal, depending on the case. And that investigation is ongoing.”
Mr. Blanche sidestepped a question about whether the Justice Department has made an assessment about the nature of Ms. Huang’s role.
Multiple people who have reviewed the underlying U.S. intelligence said that it showed that Ms. Huang was working with the Chinese intelligence agency.
People briefed on the intelligence say it appears that she was not a trained intelligence officer but rather an “asset,” someone providing information secretly to the Ministry of State Security.

Chinese espionage is complicated. There are a range of ways that Chinese business executives can conduct espionage for the Beijing government, from simply reporting what they know to taking active direction.
U.S. intelligence agencies have confidence in their information about her interactions with Chinese intelligence services, despite all that they do not know about Ms. Huang.

Current and former officials said that Chinese business executives often believe that they cannot advance their careers without being aligned with the state. Approached by the Chinese government to collect information or prod an American company for access to high-end chips, many Chinese executives might feel they have no choice but to comply.

The U.S. intelligence community has been gathering surveillance on Ms. Huang for well over a year. She was already in a close relationship with Mr. Huang when the surveillance began, people familiar with the situation said.

Determining when Ms. Huang started providing information to the Ministry of State Security is important as American intelligence tries to better understand what details she might have gathered during her affair with Mr. Huang.

Mr. Huang stepped down from Nvidia after admitting to an affair and after the company’s board began investigating his relationship with Ms. Huang. The board pushed for Mr. Huang’s resignation not just because of the spying allegations. On Wednesday, The New York Times reported Mr. Huang had conducted another affair with an executive who reported directly to him.

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-13/.headline: FBI disrupts crypto theft scheme by North Korean hacking group; billions stolen so far
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-13/.author: Ruben Vives

paragraphs.text: The FBI said it has disrupted a highly tailored, hard-to-detect cryptocurrency theft scheme by a North Korean hacking group that has managed to steal billions across the world in recent years.

The hackers have aggressively targeted people in the cryptocurrency and Web3 industries, as well as workers in the development and maintenance of open-source software, the FBI said in a written statement. Web3, in general, describes internet applications that interact with a blockchain — a digital ledger that stores data.

On Thursday, the FBI and Department of Justice announced the disruption of a cloud-based infrastructure used by the North Korean hackers, resulting in the seizure of more than 900 webcam videos of victims working in the crypto and Web3 industries worldwide. Before the operation was disrupted, the scheme resulted in the theft of more than $400 million over an 18-month period. FBI officials say the funds are used to bankroll its “rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft” and the videos are employed to impersonate and target more victims.
“North Korea’s government bankrolls its rogue regime and illicit weapons program through cryptocurrency theft,” said Principal Deputy Assistant Atty. Gen. for National Security M. Scott Proctor.

“The FBI attributes this activity to the North Korean hacking group commonly referred to in the private sector as Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, Stardust Chollima, APT38, and BlueNoroff,” the FBI said in a written statement.

“Cryptocurrency unfortunately has become fertile ground for North Korea to defraud victims and fund its malign activities,” Bill Essayli, the top federal prosecutor for Los Angeles, said in a written statement. “Today’s seizure shows that America will continue the fight against rogue states who financially gain from cybercrime.”
The federal agency said the hackers used several tactics to compromise victims, including a sophisticated social engineering scheme dubbed “FaceStealer.”

The scheme involves hijacking LinkedIn, Telegram, Slack and Discord accounts of people known to the victim, then impersonating those people to make contact and lure the victims into video calls using Zoom, Microsoft Teams and Google Meets.

As the victim waits for the call to start, the hackers secretly record them to impersonate them later. Once the call starts, the impersonator attempts to persuade the victim to download malware, often under the guise of resolving a technical issue.

“Their objective is compromise of the software supply chain. By infiltrating accounts of trusted developers and maintainers, the threat actors can potentially distribute malicious code through widely used software, impacting millions of downstream users,” the FBI said in its written statement.

FBI Cyber Branch Operations Director Brett Leatherman said in a statement that the “North Korean regime relies on proceeds from large-scale cryptocurrency theft to fund its illicit weapons program, stealing billions of dollars in recent years.”

Separately from the FaceStealer scheme, members of the North Korean military, referred by the FBI as “TraderTraitor,” stole more than $6 billion in cryptocurrency from the world’s largest crypto exchange Binance on Oct. 29, according to federal authorities. Binance said it has replaced the stolen assets to its customers, but not recovered the stolen loot.

Federal authorities said they have worked closely with private companies to recover the stolen funds, freezing more than $2.7 million and obtaining court approval to seize or restrict access to $1.2 billion of that amount.

FBI officials said efforts to trace, freeze, seize and forfeit the stolen virtual assets are ongoing. Additionally, the agency put out a flash alert on its website to inform the public of the FaceStealer campaign.

nytimes.com/2026/11/13/nyregion/flatbush.headline: Developer Avoided Stricter Oversight Before Fatal Building Collapse
nytimes.com/2026/11/13/nyregion/flatbush.author: Stefanos Chen, Mihir Zaveri, Amy Julia Harris, Bianca Pallaro, Dionne Searcey, William K. Rashbaum

paragraphs.text: New York City officials on Friday were examining whether a developer’s desire to construct a taller building in Brooklyn than had initially been approved factored in the fatal collapse of a neighboring structure earlier this week.

Records show that the city signed off on plans for a three-story, eight-unit construction project at 2625 Bedford Avenue in the Flatbush neighborhood in March 2026. But other filings reveal that, from as far back as November 2025, the developer had intended to build something much larger: It ultimately sought approval for a nine-story building with 64 apartments, a 9,000-square-foot community space and a grocery store.

The city had not approved the more ambitious plans by Wednesday, when the more than 96-year-old building next door collapsed into the construction site, killing eight people, injuring 18 more and leaving dozens displaced.

“We have approved plans for a three-story building,” Ahmed Tigani, the commissioner of the Buildings Department, said at a news conference on Friday. But, he added, “The nine-story plan is something they seek, not what they have approval for.”

The difference between the two projects could be a key to understanding what went wrong, building experts said. The developer, a limited-liability company tied to the real estate investor Robert Fischman, was excavating the Bedford Avenue site when the building fell.
Neither Mr. Fischman nor other representatives of the development company could be reached for comment on Friday, despite visits to their homes and phone calls.

It is not uncommon for developers to win approval for a more modest project and then seek to expand its size and scope, in part because obtaining permission to build taller structures can take several months.

But the Bedford Avenue site’s status as a three-story project created an important distinction: It meant that city rules requiring stricter safety oversight were not triggered, according to the building experts, who reviewed the site’s plans at the request of The New York Times.

The rules mandate projects over seven stories to have a site safety coordinator to ensure tasks like demolition and construction are carried out safely. Records the developer filed with the Buildings Department listed no such coordinator for the Bedford Avenue site.

Pablo Vives, the founder of a construction consulting firm called DVA Advisors, said the coordinators were supposed to provide “an extra set of eyes” on excavation and other sensitive work. The development team typically pays for the coordinator.

Jay Valgora, the founder of an architecture firm called Studio V, said past clients had specifically requested that their projects be smaller to avoid the added cost and scrutiny of hiring a site safety coordinator.
“The question is, did that play a factor in what happened” at the Flatbush building? he said.
Records show the developer of the Bedford Avenue site already had a spotty record of complying with city rules before the collapse.

In March, the Buildings Department put the project under a stop-work order after inspectors found that a building on the site was being demolished without proper overhead protection, like netting and sheds.

A follow-up inspection in April found that the building had been completely demolished in violation of the stop-work order, although no digging or excavation had begun. The Buildings Department fined the developer $10,000 before lifting the stop-work order in May.

Asked why the city gave the developer the go-ahead to begin excavation despite the developer’s stated plans to build a nine-story structure that had not received city approval, Andrew Rudansky, a spokesman for the Buildings Department, said the officials appropriately granted approval to the work that was authorized, not the larger job the developer had wished to see approved.
If and when the developer wanted to expand the scope of the project, it could have applied for an amendment to the permit, he said.

Excavating a construction site in New York City, where century-old buildings abut much larger projects, can be a delicate and painstaking process, because digging can destabilize neighboring structures.

Adding to the challenge is the nature of the soil in New York City. It can vary drastically, from being rocky in some places to sandy in others, sometimes even just 20 feet apart, engineering experts said. Groundwater or water from leaking pipes can also complicate things. Before excavation begins, workers must collect soil samples from across the site, boring into the ground and extracting cylinders of earth to be tested in a lab, said Anil Agrawal, the chairman of the civil engineering department at the City College of New York.
Another important step involves inspecting adjacent buildings to make sure they are sound, and shoring them up if they are not, the engineering experts said.

Older buildings like the one next to the Bedford Avenue site tend to have more shallow foundations than newer buildings and may have brittle exterior walls. Bricks used decades ago might not be as strong as modern bricks, and mortar can be more likely to give way when rattled horizontally by vibrations, which can happen during nearby construction.
At 1321 Flatbush Avenue, the building that collapsed, there were signs that the developer “didn’t do due diligence,” Mr. Agrawal said.

An inspection report from March — commissioned by the development team before construction began — identified signs of distress at the neighboring three-story apartment building, which was built sometime before 1930. The inspection report noted visible cracks in at least three of the building’s facades. The northern face of the building — the wall closest to the construction site — was in “poor condition,” the inspectors noted, meaning they had visually identified “a wide range of major deficiencies.”
It was not clear whether the developer or its contractors attempted to stabilize the structure while carrying out the excavation.

LMW Engineering Group, an engineering firm involved with the plans, did not respond to requests for comment on Friday. Jieming Wang, the engineer who drafted the excavation plans, answered the phone but hung up after a reporter inquired about the project.
The Brooklyn District Attorney’s Office has opened a criminal inquiry into the collapse as investigators work to determine what caused the Flatbush Avenue building to topple over.

One lead they were pursuing was a complaint filed with the city hours after the collapse, in which an anonymous tipster suggested that a “subcontractor may have excavated too much of the area along the neighboring foundation.” The tipster did not name the subcontractor in the complaint.
Whatever the cause, it was most likely a result of missed warnings, said Mr. Valgora, the architect.
“You have to do something — unfortunately, tragically — very wrong to have a catastrophic failure,” he said. “The real tragedy is that buildings tell you before they fall down.”

latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-13/.headline: Voters pass Proposition 42, barring new taxes on personal assets
latimes.com/california/story/2026-11-13/.author: Dakota Smith, Queenie Wong

paragraphs.text: California voters have approved Proposition 42, a statewide measure that bans new taxes on an array of personal assets.

While votes are still being counted across the state, the Associated Press on Friday declared that the ballot measure had passed. The measure had just over 51% votes in favor and nearly 49% opposed, with about 96% of votes counted.
Prop. 42 has led by a narrow margin since the vote count began on Nov. 3.

The proposition bars any new tax on personal property, such as 401(k) accounts, business interests, digital assets, intellectual property, and personal belongings. Real estate isn’t included. It also prohibits retroactive taxes, except in cases of a state-declared emergency.

Proposition 42 was put on the ballot as a “poison pill” to nullify Proposition 40, a one-time tax on billionaires’ assets that also appeared on the Nov. 3 ballot. Voters rejected Proposition 40, but passed Proposition 42, closing off a potential source of money for the state.
If Proposition 40 had passed, Proposition 42 would have nullified the wealth tax if it received more votes.
The state generally taxes income, but not the unrealized gains of assets.

Its passage means that “voters are concerned that the retirement savings that they have might have been a target for taxation in the future,” said Susan Shelley, vice president of communications at the Howard Jarvis Assoc., which opposed the tax.
Proposition 42 was put on the ballot by Building a Better California, a group funded by Google co-founder Sergey Brin, venture capitalists and other tech executives. The group opposed Proposition 40.
The California Small Business Assn., the California Senior Alliance, and the California Professional Firefighters organization also backed Proposition 42.
“Taxes and cost of living are already too high in California — we need protection against taxes on our personal property and retirement savings,” supporters wrote in favor of the measure.
Proposition 40 backers said they may return with a proposed wealth tax for the 2028 ballot. Any attempt to target personal assets would require asking voters to nullify Proposition 42.

latimes.com/entertainment-arts/story/202.headline: Christian Cousins, former child actor in 'Kindergarten Cop,' dead at 43
latimes.com/entertainment-arts/story/202.author: Emily St. Martin

paragraphs.text: Christian Cousins, the former child actor who starred as Dominic Palmieri in the 1990 movie “Kindergarten Cop,” has died. He was 43.
The actor’s half-brother, Jonas Roeser, announced the death on social media last month, writing that Cousins “had been very sick with liver disease.”

Cousins and his twin brother, Joseph, starred alongside Arnold Schwarzenegger in “Kindergarten Cop,” with the boys trading off in their portrayal of Dominic, the son of a dangerous drug dealer who had gone into hiding with his mother, Joyce. Schwarzenegger’s character, a Los Angeles police detective, goes undercover as a kindergarten teacher, falls for fellow teacher Joyce and becomes a father figure to Dominic.

“It’s hard to share that my brother, Christian Cousins, has passed away,” Roeser wrote on Instagram. “Christian and his twin brother, Joseph ‘Joey’ Cousins, are my brothers through my biological father. They grew up in California while I was in Washington and I didn’t get to know them until I was in college.
Roeser wrote that he grew up watching the twins on the CBS soap opera “Knots Landing” but that the acting roles were “only a small part of how I’ll remember Christian.”

“He was a character, full of passion and energy, with big stories and even bigger dreams,” Roeser wrote, adding that it “brings me comfort to believe he is now in heaven with his mother, free from the pain he was carrying.”
“Rest easy, Christian,” he wrote. “I hope your soul is at rest and that you’ve found peace. You are my brother and you will be missed.”

According to Cousins’ Facebook page, he was living in East Irvine and has struggled with health issues in recent years. Alongside a 2017 photograph of him cheekily lighting two cigarillos, he commented years later: “The good old days when I could be thin and smoke two bay Sherman’s in one hand. Now I’m regretting it all.”

Born March 17, 1983, in Orange County, Cousins was raised in Laguna Niguel. He and his twin brother shared roles across television and film in the ’80s and ’90s, including their portrayal of Bobby Ewing in “Knots Landing” from 1987 to 1993. Cousins also starred in the movies “Twin Sitters” and “Critters 3,” and the TV shows “Eerie, Indiana,” “Empty Nest” and “Intruders.”
During a “Kindergarten Cop” reunion Zoom call with the cast in 2020 hosted by Yahoo, Cousins described his experience acting in some of the most intense scenes of the film.

“I remember having to act more scared than I’d ever been on camera thus far in my career . . . it was actually a little difficult because despite how evil it seems my dad is, which is Richard Tyson — he’s like the nicest guy in the world in person,” he said. “It was really hard to act scared of somebody who after every scene [said] ‘That was awesome; you did great!’”

Cousins was 7 when he filmed “Kindergarten Cop,” and after the film hit theaters, Cousins said he was recognized and swarmed for autographs at shopping malls, airports and at Disneyland. He recalled a bus full of kids at the amusement park lining up and asking for personalized notes. He was so young that he struggled to spell “beautiful.”
During the reunion, Cousins also revealed that he had retired from acting and was working in the furniture business.

latimes.com/business/story/2026-11-12/ca.headline: Cancer institute backed by Larry Ellison plans major layoffs in Los Angeles
latimes.com/business/story/2026-11-12/ca.author: Ella Chakarian

paragraphs.text: The Ellison Medical Institute — a cancer research center funded by tech mogul Larry Ellison — will cut a chunk of its staff in a couple of months.

The Los Angeles-based research center, led by its founding chief executive and oncologist, David Agus, plans to permanently lay off 88 employees in January, according to a Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification filed Nov. 4.

The institute describes itself as a medical research and development center focused on artificial intelligence, molecular analytics and interdisciplinary disease research and treatment, with preventative medicine and cancer clinics, research laboratories and community education programs.
The 84,000-square-foot institute is at 12414 Exposition Blvd., near the Expo/Bundy Metro station. Its LinkedIn company profile lists it as having 51 to 200 employees.
The Ellison Medical Institute did not respond to requests for comment on the reasons for the layoffs.
Ellison has long focused on cancer research and has made substantial donations to the cause.
In his Oracle AI World 2026 keynote speech, Ellison said AI will make most cancers “gone in five years, and certainly in 10.”
In 2016, Ellison donated $200 million to USC to build the interdisciplinary medical center focused on cancer.
The Lawrence J. Ellison Institute for Transformative Medicine of USC was meant to combine research with the holistic prevention and treatment of cancer. It later moved from USC. .

The institute has also been active in drug development. In June, it signed an exclusive license with UniQuest, the commercialization company of the University of Queensland in Australia, to advance a new prostate cancer treatment. The drug could reach first-in-human trials as early as 2027, according to a news release.

In 2025, the institute announced a research partnership with Salt AI, a Los Angeles-based company offering AI-powered tools for drug design. The institute also runs educational programs, including a three-week summer program for high school seniors.
Ellison and Agus also founded the Ellison Institute of Technology in Oxford, England.
Ellison Medical Institute’s layoffs come as other medical institutes, hospitals and healthcare providers in Los Angeles have also implemented layoffs and cutbacks.

Kaiser Permanente has plans to cut 147 business and administrative jobs across California, with layoffs starting Nov. 20. According to a state employment report filed Sept. 21, the reductions affect 16 locations, including 21 employees in Los Angeles County. San Diego will see the biggest impact, with 72 jobs cut.

Last year, Children’s Hospital Los Angeles laid off 5.8% of its staff as a result of outside pressures, including reduced Medi-Cal reimbursement rates. Keck Medicine of USC also laid off 89 employees in October 2025 to address a university-wide operating deficit.

In March, L.A. Care Health Plan laid off 225 employees, or nearly 3% of its workforce. L.A. Care is the nation’s largest publicly operated health plan, serving more than 2.6 million low-income Los Angeles County residents. The layoffs came amid federal and state budget cuts.

latimes.com/politics/story/2026-11-13/wh.headline: What caused the national ground stop? Here is what we know
latimes.com/politics/story/2026-11-13/wh.author: Clara Harter, Richard Winton

paragraphs.text: WASHINGTON — For more than four hours, a ground stop of virtually all aircraft in the United States brought unprecedented chaos and delays that are expected to last days.
Here is what we know about what went wrong.
What caused the stop?

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy said switches and routers on the Federal Aviation Administration’s analog air traffic control system became overloaded with data, causing inconsistencies in communication with airlines. As a result, the decision was made to shut the system down shortly after 12:30 p.m.
“We have old, old switches, old routers, we use 1980s little copper lines,” he said. “It’s an old system that went down and went down everywhere.”
The ground stop ended around 5:15 p.m. Duffy said the FAA was able to deploy fixes to reduce the overloading and bring its towers and air traffic control facilities known as TRACONs back online.

Duffy said the problem was with the TDM — time-division multiplexing — a dated, still mostly copper-wire technology used to transmit air traffic control voice and radar data. He said there was no evidence to suggest a cyberattack or the involvement of foreign adversaries.
What problems did this cause?
The technological breakdown led to intermittent communication and radar, but not a complete blackout, Duffy said.

“We were able to keep some of those communications going, but when you have issues and you can’t immediately communicate and immediately see where aircraft are at — that’s a risk that we’re unwilling to tolerate,” he said.
What do we know about the technology?
Duffy lambasted the aging infrastructure that the FAA relies on and said that President Trump is pushing for the funding needed to update the equipment.

“None of your networks run on 1980 technology,” he said to the gaggle of reporters at a Friday evening news conference. “You have all got fiber, state-of-the-art, high-speed networks that cover all of your stations, but not the FAA.”

He said the FAA was in the process of upgrading its air traffic control system thanks to $12.5 billion in funding secured through Trump’s Big Beautiful Bill, but called on Congress to approve an additional $50 billion to complete the modernization of the system.
“I believe that should be a priority,” he said. “America, Congress, let’s make this system more safe.”

Duffy said that none of the newly upgraded technology was involved in the system overload Friday. He acknowledged that the air traffic control system had previously failed on a local level in Newark, N.J.
What is the impact?
There were more than 3,500 airplanes flying across America when the decision to close the airspace was made, Duffy said.

Tens of thousands of travelers were left stranded and FEMA was mobilized to ensure lifesaving medication was not being missed by passengers, said Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin. Some college football teams were left scrambling to find alternative transportation to this weekend’s playoffs.
Duffy said that air traffic control would try to move as many planes as possible Friday night, but noted that this will depend on the availability of flight crews and pilots.

perplexity.ai/hub/blog/perplexity-decide.headline: Perplexity Decider v1.3: Training, eval, and use cases

paragraphs.text: How we train, evaluate, and use it.
We are releasing Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3, the successors to our earlier decision models: v1, v1.1, v1.2, and Flash v1.2.
Decider Flash v1.3 is a smaller model distilled from Decider v1.3. Both models are available on Hugging Face under Apache license, through OpenRouter, and the Perplexity Decisions API.

Perplexity Decider is inspired by Jev, TypeSafe AI’s System One Model. It supports binary and multi-class classification with ordered or unordered labels, returning probabilities that applications can use to classify, route, rank, and evaluate inputs.

Both v1.3 models improve performance and robustness across a broad range of text and vision tasks through bidirectional attention, better-curated training data, and a refined training recipe. We also introduce locate, a new feature to highlight the selected content for named entity recognition, personal information identification, and extractive question-answering tasks.
In this post, we explain how we train and evaluate Decider and share how we use it internally at Perplexity.
What is a decision model?

A decision model is a general-purpose classifier. You give it an input and a set of questions each with its possible answers. For each question, it returns a probability distribution over the answers. It supports 3 question types:
• Yes / No: binary decisions.
• Multiple choice: custom multi-class labels.
• Score: ordered levels.
Decision models support a wide range of classification and scoring tasks:
• Judging outputs: assessing faithfulness, quality, and safety.
• Routing: directing requests to smaller or larger models based on difficulty.
• Moderation and security: detecting harmful content, phishing, and prompt injection in tool outputs.
• Filtering and tagging: organizing large collections of content.
• Retrieval and reranking: scoring search results by relevance.

Many of these tasks were previously handled by generative models like LLMs, even though they do not require free-form text generation. Decision models sit between LLMs and task-specific classifiers. They return probabilities for multiple questions about the same input in a single forward pass, avoiding token-by-token answer generation and sharing computation across questions. Unlike task-specific classifiers, they can handle new tasks through natural language prompts, a flexibility learned from training across diverse tasks in a shared question-answering format.
Training
Turning a generative LLM into a decision model

We build Decider by adapting strong generative LLM backbones. To explain the adaptation, we first describe how a request is represented. As illustrated below, a request consists out of a shared context (the state) and a number of questions. The state will be reused by all questions.

For example, given a document and its summary, a single request can ask whether the summary faithfully represents the document and whether it is intended for an expert or a general audience. After the state, each question block contains a question and its possible answers, each assigned a predefined label token such as A, B, or C. A special <|marker|> token indicates where to read out the model’s prediction. At this position, a learned linear output layer (a decision head), maps the hidden state to scores for the question’s answer options, which are then converted to probabilities.

We initialize the output layer from the base model, which normally scores next-token from the entire vocabulary, and only keep the rows corresponding to the predefined option tokens such as A, B, or C. This pruned layer is then trained to turn the hidden state of <|marker|> into answer scores. This approach covers all classification questions because they can all be formulated as a multiple choice.

For training, we take hundreds of public datasets spanning diverse tasks (sentiment, natural language inference, intent detection, entity matching, moderation, fact checking, ratings, etc.) and convert each example into the unified format described above: a state, one or more questions, their options and a target. The target can be the single correct option if we have gold labels, or a probability distribution over options.

In v1.3, we introduce locate, which extracts text from the state instead of selecting from predefined options. A locate question describes what to find, using either a short label such as “location” or an instruction such as “Extract the city name where the job is located.” The model returns the exact matching text from the state, along with its start and end character locations. If it identifies no matches, it returns an empty list.

Because of shared state, a single request can combine locate, classification, and scoring questions about the same input. For example, it can ask whether a job requires senior-level experience and extract the required skills.
Bidirectional attention: letting the model read both ways

Our models start from strong pretrained generative backbones, whose causal attention lets each token attend only to itself and preceding tokens. Our ablation studies showed that making the backbone’s full-attention layers bidirectional improves performance, so we adopt this design to let each token incorporate context from the entire input.

Bidirectional attention introduces another design choice: how should the state and questions interact? We considered three attention patterns, with different implications for performance, answer stability, and cache reuse:

• Everything sees everything (v1.2): The state and all questions are processed together with full bidirectional attention. Computation over the state is shared, but an answer to one question can change depending on what else is asked.

• Isolated questions (v1.3): The state attends to all the questions, while each question attends only to the state and its own tokens. Questions can still influence one another indirectly through the shared state but results are more stable.

• Fully cacheable: The state only attends to itself, while each question attends to the state and its own tokens. The state is question-independent and reusable across requests to take advantage of prompt caching. We don't use it by default, because letting the state see the questions matters a lot for several tasks, but a small fine-tuning can switch a model to it.
We ultimately chose isolated questions for their strong performance and stability.
Training recipe

Training proceeds in three stages for both model sizes. We first train the larger model, based on Qwen3.8-27B, using cross-entropy on large datasets, then distill it into the smaller Qwen3.5-4B model.

The first stage is generalist training, where we fully fine-tune the model on large-scale corpora. In this stage, we only accept data that helps the model across the board and is not specific to any benchmark; we thus exclude any benchmark training splits.

After this generalist model is trained, we run a second, more fine-grained stage using LoRA. The data used in this stage is targeted toward specific domains and tasks. We add data in the second stage rather than the first one if we observe narrow gains or if we observe some regressions on other tasks. We use LoRA to avoid drifting too much from the generalist model and risking losing performance to fit those specific domains. The goal is to improve performance while retaining the backbone’s general knowledge. We also use a weight when merging the LoRA back into the base model, to control the drift more precisely and favor held-out metrics above any in-domain gains.

Finally, we add a vision-specific step. Similar to the second stage, the vision step is treated as another fine-grained specialization step, using a LoRA adapter that is merged back to the base model with a weight. Some vision capabilities can come at the price of text performance. Since we observe much more usage of the models on text, we prioritize text metrics over vision metrics.
For both text stages, we use the average weights from three runs, each using a different random seed. We found this improves the performance and robustness of the aggregated model.

Once the final large model is obtained, we apply the same three-stage training procedure to the smaller model. Here, the large model acts as the teacher: its predicted output distribution replaces the gold labels, and the smaller model is trained to minimize the KL divergence between its predictions and those of the teacher. This distillation objective outperforms cross-entropy on the same training data. While cross-entropy performs better on benchmarks with dedicated training data, it generalizes less well to held-out data. We hypothesize that distillation better transfers the teacher’s output distribution, including its confidence over non-gold alternatives, whereas cross-entropy encourages overfitting to the benchmark-specific training distribution. We therefore adopt the KL-based distillation objective.

To mitigate train-test contamination, we remove any training samples that could overlap with any evaluation we use. This is important because some public training datasets contain large parts of some evaluation datasets. We also conduct extensive bias audits and removal to make sure our gains are reliable and not just driven by learned biases.
Adding the ability to extract information

The locate feature extracts information such as named entities from text, without changing how it answers ordinary requests. To do so, we introduce an additional training stage: we add a new special token, <|locate|>, a span head, and LoRA adapter to Decider.

We initialize <|locate|> ’s embedding from <|marker|> learned in the previous training stages. We train only this new embedding, the span head, and the LoRA adapters, while keeping the original backbone weights and decision head frozen. Each requested field gets its own <|locate|> token.

The span head uses <|locate|> ’s representation together with the state-token representations to score where matching spans start and end, and which start-end pairs belong together. It also uses the <|locate|> token’s representation to predict field-specific thresholds for these scores. Selected spans are returned as character positions in the original text.

We train the span head with an adapted InfoNCE loss that pushes every gold span above the threshold, and the threshold above every other span. The loss has two terms: The first one pushes the scores of correct spans above the threshold and the wrong spans. The second term pushes the threshold above the scores of wrong spans. Fields with no answer get only the second term, which teaches the model to return an empty list.

We train on a mix of span extraction tasks, including named entity recognition, PII detection and extractive question answering. We vary the field descriptions from short labels to detailed instructions, so the model learns to follow the request rather than memorize a fixed label set.

Locate teaches the model a structurally different task, and we want to add it without losing what the model already does well. Merging the locate adapters into the backbone causes some regression on decision requests. To limit this, we are running investigations such as more replay data from earlier stages and auxiliary objectives that keep the model’s outputs on decision requests close to those of the original model. However, we find that merging is currently still not lossless, so we keep the adapters unmerged and activate them only for locate requests.
Evaluation
We evaluate Decider v1.3 and Decider Flash v1.3 on external benchmarks from the Hugging Face Decision Index, Vals AI’s ClaimBench, and Artificial Analysis Decision Index.

Across these evaluations, our models demonstrate strong performance. Even though these leaderboards include privately held tasks, they can still be gamed through repeated submission and iterative tuning based on leaderboard feedback. To complement these leaderboards, we evaluate the models on an internal suite combining private production tasks with held-out evaluations drawn from public non-benchmark datasets. These evaluations provide an additional check on generalization beyond public benchmarks, helping us distinguish broader improvements from gains specific to familiar evaluation suites.

Internally, we built a suite of more than 200 tasks spanning various domains and tasks such as classification, scoring, reranking, and entity extraction. To honestly assess Decider’s real-world performance, all evaluations are performed zero-shot, without task-specific fine-tuning, giving us a clear signal of where to improve the model.
Query classification

At Perplexity, we use a multi-head classification system to process each user query. Each query is first passed through an embedding model that acts as a feature extractor. The resulting embedding is then fed into multiple separate classification heads, including both binary and multi-label classifiers. For example, one head determines whether a user query should trigger web search.

Across 63 classification tasks with independently relabeled references by a frontier LLM, Decider v1.3 achieves 91.6% mean accuracy, exceeding our production classifiers by 6.54 percentage points. Decider Flash v1.3 also outperforms the production baseline, while Decider v1.3 outperforms Jev 1.14.
Domain-specific classification

We assembled a domain-specific evaluation suite from public datasets to assess decision models’ classification performance across seven domains: claim verification (6 tasks), healthcare (7), cybersecurity (8), programming (16), government (7), law (9) and finance (9).

For example, “judge the time complexity of a Python program”, or “use an annual financial report to determine whether a company’s unrestricted cash covers debt principal due within the next twelve months”. Decider v1.3 leads across all seven domains, outperforming Jev 1.14 by up to 12.9 percentage points in finance and 9.3 points in law. Decider Flash v1.3 trails Jev 1.14 in finance, programming, and law, and performs similarly in other domains.
Retrieval and Reranking

Search is at the core of Perplexity. We maintain a broad suite of retrieval tasks to evaluate our models’ reranking performance. For each task, we first use a pool of embedding models to retrieve the top 50 candidate documents from each corpus. We then rerank these candidates using Decider and compare its performance against a strong reranker baseline, Qwen3-Reranker-8B.

We evaluate Decider in a zero-shot, pointwise setting, using the model to directly score each query–document pair independently and rank documents by relevance. Across 72 retrieval tasks, Decider v1.3 achieves a mean nDCG@10 of 83.99, outperforming Qwen3-Reranker-8B by 1.81 points and Jev 1.14 by 2.24 points.
On the BEIR benchmark, both models outperform Qwen3-Reranker-8B by 8.78 and 7.05 nDCG@10 respectively. Against Jev 1.14, Decider v1.3 is 1.33 points higher, while the Flash version scores 0.4 lower.
Multilingual classification

To evaluate decision models beyond English, we assembled a multilingual classification benchmark comprising 19 language-specific tasks from 8 public datasets, with 46,484 examples across eight languages: German, Spanish, French, Italian, Russian, Japanese, Korean, and Chinese. The benchmark covers intent detection, topic classification, sentiment analysis, natural language inference, paraphrase detection, offensive language detection, and grammatical acceptability.

We report mean accuracy across tasks within each language, weighting each task equally. Decider v1.3 outperforms Jev 1.14 in all eight languages and Decider Flash v1.3 does so in six, with mean task accuracies of 88.16% for Decider v1.3 and 86.50% for Decider Flash v1.3, compared with 85.41% for Jev 1.14.
NER, PII and Extractive QA

We evaluate the locate feature on 17 out-of-domain tasks that test its extraction across various domains, input formats (text, tables, structured documents) and instructions (short labels, questions and detailed descriptions). The domains range from Wikipedia to scientific papers, cyber-threat reports, technical support, privacy policies, resumes, and legal contracts. The requests range from short label names such as “person” or “email address”, through questions about a table or a support ticket, to detailed field descriptions for structured extraction, such as the parties of an NDA or the total on an invoice.

We evaluate NER and PII using exact-span F1, which requires predicted spans to match the reference boundaries exactly. Extractive QA uses character-level F1, giving partial credit for overlapping answer text, while structured extraction uses field accuracy, the proportion of fields extracted correctly. For CV parsing, we average the NER and PII exact-span F1 scores.

We compare our models against general-purpose extraction models of different sizes: GLiNER large v2.5 (0.5B), Liquid d1 (2B) and Cloudflare’s Clairic (undisclosed). Decider v1.3 reaches an average score of 69.0 (using each task’s primary metric) and Decider Flash v1.3 reaches 63.6, compared with 43.3 for Liquid d1, 41.5 for Clairic and 33.6 for GLiNER large v2.5. Both Decider models lead in every category.
Image classification

Decider has natively supported vision tasks since v1. To evaluate its performance beyond text, we assembled a five-task benchmark suite with a particular focus on document classification, including invoices, letters, and resumes. The suite also covers satellite image classification, texture classification, pet breed classification, and animal counting.

Decider v1.3 achieves a mean accuracy of 76.99% across the five visual tasks, outperforming Jev 1.14 by 1.47 percentage points. Decider Flash v1.3 achieves 72.77%, demonstrating visual classification capabilities in a smaller model.
Real-world decision requests

We sampled one million deduplicated, PII-masked requests submitted to the Perplexity Decision API during its first 18 days of availability. Because each request can contain multiple questions about the same state, the sample comprises 2,318,887 individual questions. All requests were included with explicit user permission for research.

Production requests do not come with ground-truth labels, so we use frontier LLM judges to generate reference answers and measure each model’s agreement with them. We also group the requests into 10 task categories, including information extraction, domain classification, sentiment analysis, intent and routing, relevance ranking, content moderation, quality and compliance review, entity matching, business analysis, and an “Other” category. This breakdown shows how performance varies across real-world use cases.

The task mix is uneven: information extraction accounts for 425,402 questions, domain classification for 409,564, and sentiment analysis for 344,158. Together, these three categories make up 50.8% of the sampled questions.

Decider v1.3 achieves the highest agreement with the judges at 93.98%, compared with 93.68% for Decider v1.2 and 93.35% for Jev 1.14. Decider v1.3 and Jev 1.14 are closely matched on domain classification and sentiment analysis, with gaps of 0.34 and 0.07 percentage points, respectively. Jev leads by 0.69 points on relevance ranking, while Decider v1.3 leads by 0.93 points on information extraction (the most common task in the sample) and by 1.21 points on intent and routing.
The chart below compares the reported cost of running the same one million production requests. Each request can contain multiple questions, so the unit here is requests, not individual questions.
Robustness

We evaluated label sensitivity on 372 multiple-choice questions, making 4,788 requests per model. We reordered options, reassigned labels to answer texts, and renamed labels while preserving each question’s meaning, then checked whether the model’s semantic answer changed. Lower flip rates indicate greater stability.

Decider v1.3 changed its answer on just 0.27% of questions under each transformation, compared with 2.69–4.84% for Jev 1.14. We also repeated identical inputs to measure serving variability: Decider v1.3 showed no changes, while Jev 1.14 changed on 1.88% of questions.
How we use Decider
Decider is built for workflows that need fast and structured decisions. In this section we explore how to leverage them to produce meaningful impact on the way we work. Here are some that stood out.
Self-improving security rules
Internally, we are already using Decider to improve our security policies.

The activity of our agents is recorded and a series of rule-based checks are performed to identify any problematic behavior. A rule-based approach means that we can monitor our agents in real-time with negligible latency added. Offline, we use Decider to look at samples from these recorded agent logs. In the case that no problematic behavior was flagged, Decider checks if there is something that our set of rules missed; and in the case that an alarm was raised, Decider checks whether this was a false alarm. Any records where our rule set fails in either case are sent to an agent for triage and a fix to the rules is proposed, to be approved by a member of our security team.

In one day, Decider read 1 billion tokens across 7,000 agent sessions and identified flaws that led to 14 rule fixes, 6 of which were approved and shipped within two days. Replayed on a week of logs, the fixes cut our busiest rule's volume by 52%, and the widened rules caught about 40% more legitimate actions to investigate.
Monitoring RL rollouts

When we post-train models with reinforcement learning, aggregate metrics such as a terminal reward do not explain why a rollout (an individual attempt at a task) succeeded or failed. It can lose reward unfairly because a tool service or the sandbox failed, or receive undeserved reward if the evaluator overlooks an unsupported claim, such as a made-up value that no tool returned.

We use Decider to monitor rollouts for these cases. Code first identifies parts of a rollout that warrant closer inspection: a failed tool call and the surrounding reasoning, code that ran without errors, or the final answer. Decider then answers multiple-choice questions about each part, such as what failed in a step (a tool service, an external site, the sandbox, the harness, or the agent’s own code) and whether the agent interpreted the result correctly. We bundle all questions about a given part into a single request and store the probabilities rather than a verdict, so we can adjust thresholds later without querying Decider again. The monitor only observes and diagnoses: it never changes a reward or stops a run.
Page quality filtering

When crawling web pages to index and serve to users, many pages are too low quality to be of any use. This includes anti-bot walls, CAPTCHAs, and error pages, as well as correctly loaded web pages that just don’t contain any helpful information, such as spam, SEO filler or navigation-only pages. These low-quality pages need to be identified and filtered out of our index.

Using Decider, we can judge the quality of pages as we crawl them. In the same forward pass, we perform a suite of other classification tasks such as identifying the domain and intended audience of the content and whether it contains harmful, illegal, or personally identifiable information. Compared to using an LLM judge, Decider is considerably faster and cheaper.
Beyond these internal uses, Decider also fits workflows such as the following.
Visual QA

Because Decider reads images, it also works as a visual checker, reviewing style changes to web pages or apps and identifying faults. It can review page screenshots for clipped text, overlapping elements, broken layouts before a change ships, or flag charts whose design could mislead a reader or break a brand guide.
Browser navigation

Agents can use Decider for the small decisions inside larger tasks. A browser agent can send a screenshot at each step and receive detailed information about the state of the page and the expected outcome of each possible action.
Planning research tasks

Users’ questions can greatly vary in their complexity, as does the depth of search that needs to be performed to find an answer. Decider can estimate this before search begins, allowing for fewer resources to be spent on simple questions.
Getting started

Decider returns probabilities. The appropriate decision threshold depends on the application. Label frequencies and the relative costs of false positives and false negatives vary across use cases. We therefore encourage users to tune thresholds on a small, representative labeled development set rather than assume that a fixed cutoff will work equally well across tasks.

We recommend using Decider v1.3 for nuanced judgments, detailed rubrics, and workflows where errors are costly. Choose Decider Flash v1.3 for high-volume routing, labeling, and filtering where latency and cost are the main constraints. Evaluate both models on representative examples from your workload, then choose the model that meets your quality, latency, and budget requirements.
Both models are available as downloadable weights on Hugging Face under Apache license, through OpenRouter, and the Perplexity Decisions API.
