theatlantic.com/technology/2026/11/fligh.headline: How to Land 4,000 Planes During a Ground Stop

paragraphs.text: For four and a half hours, the sky above the United States emptied out.

Normally, throughout the day and the night, thousands of planes are taking off, crisscrossing the country, and landing. When the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all U.S. flights around 4:00 p.m. today, because of “extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety,” some 4,000 airplanes were in the sky, headed for U.S. airports, according to Flightradar24, an aviation-tracking website. Even if no more flights took off, all of those planes needed to land.

For the people below, getting them down safely became an immediate preoccupation. This type of nationwide grounding had happened only twice before in recent history—once after the September 11 attacks, and once in January 2023 for about an hour and a half. Every aircraft still aloft needed to make it to its destination, despite apparently spotty communications.

Our formidable system of flight, a machine that’s constantly in motion and choreographed to the minute, has backups built in. Pilots have emergency systems they can rely on if they lose radio communications, as well as onboard systems to detect where other aircraft are around them, R. John Hansman, the director of the MIT International Center for Air Transportation, told me. Communications problems don’t generally mean an immediate safety risk, and planes can still fly toward their destinations, he said. “The problem is getting them safely down.”

“The risk is related to how many other airplanes you could bump into,” he said. “So if you stop putting new airplanes into the system, then it becomes safer and safer and safer, until there’s no airplanes in the air. But of course, nobody’s flying, right?”

At the moment that the ground stop was declared, planes would have been landing. They landed in the minutes afterward, and in the hours after that. Within three hours, the number of flights still in the air had dropped to 550, Ian Petchenik, a spokesperson for Flightradar24, told me. Wheels hit the ground; the people on the plane and the people tracking their flights exhaled; pilots offered reassurances from the cockpit. On a plane that landed in Austin, carrying a number of writers headed a book festival (including some of my Atlantic colleagues), the pilot explained the delay on the tarmac by telling passengers there had been a “little issue with the FAA, folks, so no one is taking off and so there are no gates free.”

In the first hours, the Trump administration offered little immediate reassurance, or clarification of what had gone wrong or how long it might take to fix. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said, “It’s just a telecommunication outage as of right now.” More than four hours after the outage began, Mullin told reporters at the White House that “we have seen zero evidence that this was a cyberattack” but also did not rule it out or explain a cause for the outage. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who was on an airplane from Dallas amid the ground stop, said at the press conference that the country’s air traffic controllers faced “instability” in communications and radar—that switches and routers “actually got overwhelmed with data.” He blamed old analog equipment and software, and demanded $50 billion from Congress to fix the system. “It’s going to continue to fail,” he said.

Some of the problems, Duffy said, affected communications with the Air Route Traffic Control Centers, a network of 22 regional hubs. Airplanes communicate with these centers as they fly across the country. The disruption also affected what are known as Terminal Radar Approach Controls, facilities where air traffic controllers help guide planes approaching and departing airports. During this outage, air traffic controllers could apparently communicate on some radio frequencies but not others, and they had to actively search for ways to talk with the airplanes in the sky, Nick Daniels, the president of the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, told CNN. “This is not just a bad day,” he said. The air traffic controllers were “handling something that’s never been seen before.”

As the hours dragged on and planes kept landing but not taking off, the airports got crowded. Thousands of flights across the country got canceled. Passengers waited for hours, trying to figure out new plans, and scrambled for rental cars. They went home, or back to their hotels. Good Samaritans on social media offered rides. At Ronald Reagan National Airport, just outside Washington, D.C., hundreds of grounded travelers waited around a baggage carousel that moved so rarely that people felt comfortable sitting directly on it. Dana Johannesson, an ultrasound specialist in black scrubs and gold hoops, had gotten on her plane then gotten off, before waiting for her bags for hours; while she had sat on the plane, the American Airlines app still attributed the delay to the weather, but the pilot got on the loudspeaker to say that a friend had told him to give up on flying into Tampa and book himself a rental, she said.

Then the ground stop lifted at 8:15 p.m. Thousands of planes that had been flying four hours earlier had landed. But fewer than 400 were still in the air. The passengers on those planes got on and off their plane as planned. The system started up again, and the planes could take off.
Hana Kiros contributed reporting.

latimes.com/entertainment-arts/business/.headline: Look dine-in theater chain to reopen former iPic theater in Pasadena
latimes.com/entertainment-arts/business/.author: Samantha Masunaga

paragraphs.text: The former iPic movie theater in Pasadena is expected to reopen in early December under the management of the Look dine-in theater chain.
The theater will be branded under the Look name.

The reopening comes after the iPic dine-in theater chain filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection earlier this year. At the time, the Boca Raton, Fla.-based company cited the “lasting” changes in moviegoer behavior after the pandemic, as well as the rise of streaming, as reasons for its bankruptcy filing.
The chain had 13 locations across the U.S., including in Pasadena and Westwood.
Look executives began negotiating with the former iPic owners on the day the Pasadena theater closed, said Brian Schultz, chief executive at Look Dine-In Cinemas. Discussions went on for months.
“This is a special location, a special theater,” he said in an interview. “It’s just really important to this community, which is a very creative, close community.”

Dallas-based Look plans to restore and renovate the six-screen theater before the reopening, including installation of new sound systems and laser projection technology. The Pasadena location, which already has a bar lounge, will also have a more upscale menu than other Look locations, as well as more intimate service.

Schultz said the company has begun speaking with members of the community to get ideas on how to differentiate the Pasadena cinema from the rest of the Look chain. Look has hired the location’s longtime general manager, as well as at least 25 hourly employees who once worked there.
“We plan to be there for a long period of time and really make this the shining jewel of the market,” Schultz said.

Look has faced its share of difficulties in the theater business. In February, the chain abruptly closed three of its Southern California locations, a decision Schultz attributed to an inability to come to an agreement with the landlord who controlled the master lease for the trio of theaters.
“As part of the COVID recovery, the industry is in a different spot,” he said. “We would have loved to keep those locations, but it wasn’t economical to do so.”
The landlord for the former iPic theater in Pasadena, he said, understood the different financial realities of the post-pandemic theatrical recovery.
Schultz declined to comment on the financial terms of the lease agreement with One Colorado shopping center owner Perform Properties.

“One Colorado has long been a premier destination in the heart of Old Pasadena,” Mark Ross, senior vice president and head of retail leasing at Perform Properties, said in a statement. “The cinema has been part of that experience. We’re excited to welcome Look and add another vibrant experience for the Pasadena community to enjoy.”

So far this year, the theatrical business has seen a remarkable turnaround, powered by major blockbusters including Sony Pictures’ “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” and Universal Pictures’ “The Odyssey,” as well as unexpected boosts from films like Focus Features’ “Obsession” and A24’s “Backrooms.”
As of Nov. 8, the domestic box office stood at about $8.63 billion, up 20.6% compared to the same time last year, though it still lags pre-pandemic 2019, according to Rentrak data.

latimes.com/politics/story/2026-11-13/tr.headline: Trump, Putin and Xi will meet in historic summit. Here's what to expect
latimes.com/politics/story/2026-11-13/tr.author: Michael Wilner

paragraphs.text: SEOUL — President Trump will get his wish for a historic meeting among the three most powerful men in the world — Xi Jinping of China, Vladimir Putin of Russia and himself — at a summit Thursday in southern China.
But Moscow, Beijing and Washington already know their leaders are arriving at the Shenzhen conference with disparate aims.

Trump hopes to focus the meeting on nuclear nonproliferation, urging the Russian and Chinese presidents to work with him to scale back the world’s largest nuclear stockpiles. Putin pressed for the meeting to discuss his ongoing war in Ukraine. And Xi wants to discuss neither, only embracing the idea of the summit to show the world China can help broker peace on the international stage, Chinese officials told The Times.
“That’ll be interesting,” Trump said earlier this week, teasing the trilateral summit before the White House formally confirmed the meeting Friday.
“We’re talking a lot of things, including denuclearization,” he added, “but we’ll be talking a lot of things.”

U.S. officials have acknowledged they do not expect the meeting to result in a breakthrough on arms control. China is openly racing to build up its nuclear capacity — a nonnegotiable policy in Beijing, which sees its arsenal dwarfed by an American stockpile nearly 10 times the size.

“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement. I would characterize this as the entry point,” one senior Trump administration official said. “This is the beginning of hopefully a conversation that can be productive going forward.”
The Chinese, too, threw cold water on the chances of a breakthrough, with one Chinese official telling The Times the central government saw no benefit to a pause.
“It is a matter of survival,” the official said.

The United States and Russia still command the world’s two dominant nuclear arsenals, with over 5,000 warheads each. China has an estimated 620 — but in catching up, it is developing new warheads with more sophisticated delivery systems.
Moscow, too, is modernizing its weapons, after the Trump administration allowed the last major U.S.-Russian nuclear arms treaty to expire earlier this year.
Though expectations are low for a nuclear breakthrough, Trump doesn’t want to discuss Putin’s priorities, either, the U.S. official added.
“He does not intend to talk about Ukraine in that meeting,” the official said. “China is not really part of that track, so it doesn’t really seem appropriate.”
Ukraine has grown increasingly concerned by Trump’s pressure campaign to force it into concessions to Moscow as he pushes to end the war.

The Trump administration has brought Russian and Ukrainian officials together at a working level to explore the viability of peace talks. But a long-standing U.S. policy on the war — not to negotiate about Ukraine without Ukraine — could be further compromised at a trilateral with Putin and Xi.

The only American business leader confirmed to join Trump in Asia is Elon Musk, the Tesla and SpaceX chief who was seen as instrumental in the decision last month to restrict Ukraine’s access on the battlefield to Starlink, the satellite internet service owned by Musk.

Beijing has struck a careful balance on Ukraine, publicly issuing its respect for sovereign borders — a position popular among Chinese voices who support Kyiv — while giving Moscow diplomatic cover, an economic lifeline and technological support throughout the war.

Their competing agendas could make the summit little more than a spectacle, yet still produce images that hark back to the famous Yalta conference — held in Crimea, the Ukrainian peninsula currently occupied by Russia, in 1945 — where Josef Stalin, Franklin Delano Roosevelt and Winston Churchill carved up a postwar order.
The summit on Chinese soil offers Xi a powerful image to broadcast worldwide, demonstrating an emergent superpower can bring together the leaders of two historic rivals in the name of peace.
Putin gets to present himself as a global player, despite the devastation wrought on Russia’s economy and military standing after four bruising years of war.

And it allows Trump to reassert his global relevance after this month’s midterms delivered the worst electoral rebuke to a president in half a century, rivaling the backlash against President Nixon during Watergate.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261112.headline: Yale scientists reveal what really slows aging and what doesn't

paragraphs.text: A growing body of research suggests that aging may be more flexible than once believed. Now, scientists at Yale have taken an important step toward identifying which treatments can actually influence biological aging and which ones show little measurable benefit.

Their findings suggest that certain prescription medications and lifestyle changes can reduce biological age as measured by DNA-based blood tests. Popular over-the-counter supplements examined in the research, however, showed little evidence of producing the same effects.

The findings, published in Nature Medicine, could help scientists evaluate anti-aging treatments more effectively, although researchers emphasize that changes in biological age markers do not necessarily mean people will live longer or avoid age-related diseases.
From Fighting Cancer to Understanding Aging

When Raghav Sehgal began graduate school at Yale several years ago, he planned to use advanced computer science techniques to investigate cancer. His background in engineering and experience launching a computational biology startup had given him a strong foundation for that work.

However, a question from his Ph.D. adviser at the Yale School of Medicine changed his research direction. Rather than focusing on individual diseases such as cancer or cardiovascular disease, why not investigate the aging process that contributes to their development?

"That put me on a different path," said Sehgal, now an associate research scientist in psychiatry who specializes in computational biology and bioinformatics. "As researchers, we have a long way to go in understanding the aging process and whether the steps we take to manage it really work."

Sehgal now studies the biological mechanisms behind human aging, how scientists can measure those changes, and why getting older increases the likelihood of conditions such as cancer, diabetes, and dementia. His work also explores whether interventions might reverse certain aspects of biological aging, even if eliminating aging itself remains beyond reach.
New DNA Tests Reveal Which Anti-Aging Treatments Work

Sehgal is the lead author of the new study, which was conducted in the laboratory of Albert Higgins-Chen, an assistant professor of psychiatry at the Yale School of Medicine. The research team set out to determine which existing approaches to slowing aging produce changes that can be reliably measured.

Their analysis found encouraging results for certain medications and lifestyle interventions. In contrast, the over-the-counter supplements included in the study generally failed to produce meaningful reductions in biological age.
The project involved the entire Higgins-Chen laboratory, including Daniel Borrus, Jenel F. Armstrong, John Gonzalez, Jessica Kasamoto, and Yaroslav Markov.

"For the first time we've shown that certain therapies have measurable impacts," said Sehgal. "This wasn't previously possible, because we didn't have enough data to say these biomarkers are consistently responsive to these interventions."

Biomarkers provide measurable information about what is happening inside the body. In aging research, they can help estimate a person's biological or functional age, which may differ from their chronological age.
How Scientists Measure Biological Age
To investigate whether treatments could influence aging, the Yale team relied primarily on blood-based measurements called epigenetic clocks.

These tools analyze chemical patterns attached to DNA, particularly methyl groups (basic chemical structures that act like tags). Previous research has shown that these chemical markers change as people grow older. Some interventions may reverse certain age-associated patterns, and computer algorithms use those changes to estimate a person's biological age.

The researchers brought together findings from 51 clinical studies investigating different anti-aging strategies. These ranged from dietary supplements and medications to lifestyle changes and medical procedures.

Across those studies, the team examined more than 110 DNA methylation biomarkers (including 16 major epigenetic clocks). By comparing measurements taken before and after interventions, they could evaluate which approaches were associated with reductions in biological age.

"What we did was pretty unique," Sehgal said. "We already know that certain things might prolong health span and lifespan. There is data from retrospective analysis as well as from animal models. We took all that knowledge along with the real-world clinical studies to identify which interventions in humans were slowing down aging across the board in these known biomarkers."
Which Anti-Aging Treatments Showed the Best Results?
The researchers divided the interventions into four main groups: prescription drugs, lifestyle modifications, over-the-counter supplements, and medical procedures.

One of the clearest findings involved diet and exercise. Combining regular physical activity with a healthy eating plan consistently reduced epigenetic age. The dietary approaches examined included Mediterranean, low-fat, and low-carb diets.

The strongest reductions in biological age markers were associated with certain pharmaceutical treatments. These included metformin and semaglutide, prescription medications used to manage metabolic conditions and body weight, as well as anti-TNF therapies that target a protein involved in the body's inflammatory response.
(TNF, or tumor necrosis factor, is an immune-system protein that helps fight inflammation-related injury.)
The findings were less encouraging for over-the-counter supplements and some medical procedures. In the studies examined, these approaches did not produce measurable reductions in epigenetic age.

The researchers also discovered that newer biological age clocks performed better than older versions. Another important finding was that people living with diseases generally experienced larger changes in their aging biomarkers than healthy participants.
Could DNA Blood Tests Transform Anti-Aging Research?

According to Sehgal, the next priority is to test these findings in larger, more diverse populations. This would help researchers determine how consistently different treatments influence biological aging across people with different health conditions and backgrounds.
The improved blood tests could also dramatically shorten the time needed to evaluate potential anti-aging therapies.

"If these new biomarkers are eventually validated to predict long-term health, scientists will be able to evaluate anti-aging therapies much faster," he added. "Instead of waiting decades for evidence from clinical trials, we'll be able to see which interventions are effective and in which people in a few years or even months."

That possibility could represent a major advance for aging research. Instead of relying entirely on clinical studies that follow participants for decades, scientists might eventually use validated biological age measurements to identify promising treatments much earlier.
However, senior author Higgins-Chen stressed that scientists must be careful about interpreting what changes in aging biomarkers actually mean.

"We have developed a rigorous, systematic approach to evaluating and comparing how biomarkers change across a wide variety of interventions, and that is a critical step in the right direction," he said. "However, the true meaning of that change must be fully understood."
Important Questions About Slowing Aging Remain
Although the results are promising, several major questions remain unanswered.

For example, researchers still need to establish whether changes in biological age are directly caused by a treatment or influenced by other factors that were not accounted for. They also need to understand how quickly those changes occur, whether they persist after treatment ends, and which biological processes produce them.
Most importantly, scientists have not yet established whether lowering epigenetic age leads to meaningful improvements in long-term health.
"And most importantly - what does the change mean for our long-term risk of age-related disease and functional decline?" Higgins-Chen said.
Further investigations into these questions are underway, with additional studies led by Borrus, Armstrong, and Grace Zou.
The Higgins-Chen laboratory is also affiliated with Yale's Department of Pathology, the Computational Biology and Bioinformatics Program, and the Y-Age Yale Center for Research on Aging.
What Appears to Work Against Biological Aging?
Based on the improved DNA-based blood tests, the Yale researchers identified two particularly promising approaches for reducing biological age markers:

• Prescription medications: Drugs used for metabolic regulation and weight management, including metformin and semaglutide, were among the treatments associated with the strongest reductions in biological age.

• Healthy eating combined with exercise: Regular physical activity paired with nutritious diets, including Mediterranean, low-fat, and low-carb eating plans, consistently produced favorable changes in aging biomarkers.
The analysis also identified benefits from certain anti-TNF medications, while the tested over-the-counter supplements and some medical procedures showed little measurable effect.

These results provide a clearer picture of which interventions may influence biological aging. However, more research is needed to confirm the findings and determine whether reductions in biological age markers ultimately translate into fewer age-related diseases, better health, or longer lives.

washingtonpost.com/health/2026/11/13/us-.headline: U.S. loses measles-elimination status, erasing a landmark public health achievement
washingtonpost.com/health/2026/11/13/us-.author: Lena H. Sun

paragraphs.text: International health experts have determined the United States has lost its status as a country that eliminated the continuous spread of measles, according to a person familiar with the matter who spoke on the condition of anonymity because the official announcement is pending.
Losing measles-elimination status erases a major public health achievement the country attained 26 years ago and comes as the United States faces its worst outbreak of the disease in decades.

A committee of the Pan American Health Organization, part of the World Health Organization, had been meeting this week to determine if the United States had uninterrupted transmission of measles for more than 12 months. The committee is expected to officially announce its conclusions Tuesday.
The global review follows a resurgence that began with a major outbreak in West Texas in January 2025 and was followed by sustained outbreaks in Utah, Arizona and other states.

The decision had been widely expected by infectious-disease and public health experts for months because publicly available data have showed at least two separate chains of transmission extending beyond 12 months. Outbreaks in recent years have been driven largely by communities with low vaccination rates.

The country has tallied more than 5,400 cases so far this year, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, more than double the total reported in 2025. Two more measles deaths were reported Friday, in Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, bringing the U.S. toll this year to at least 10. In 2025, three people died of measles.

“The ferocious return of measles to the U.S. is a clear indicator that our children are at grave risk,” said Noel Brewer, a professor of public health at the University of North Carolina and chair of an independent U.S. committee that verifies the annual report on measles elimination to PAHO. The committee presented its findings to PAHO on Tuesday.

“It is time for CDC to begin daily measles briefings, the Department of Health and Human Services to release a comprehensive measles plan, Congress to allocate more funds to measles control efforts, and the President to speak out forcefully in favor of measles vaccination.”

Measles is the most contagious disease on Earth, but widespread vaccination stopped sustained transmission in the United States for decades. But in recent years, especially the past two years, large outbreaks have spread across multiple states.

npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-6040264/is-ther.headline: Is there an opening for Nvidia's competitors, now that Jensen Huang is out?
npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-6040264/is-ther.author: Kai McNamee

paragraphs.text: SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

Nvidia has long been the kingpin of the semiconductor industry, a company whose huge technological bets paid off, making its chips the most in-demand chips in the world and crowning the company, for a time, the most valuable in the world. But with Nvidia's leader, Jensen Huang, out, does that leave an opening for Nvidia's competitors to catch up? We're going to put that question to Dylan Patel. He is founder and CEO of SemiAnalysis, an AI and semiconductor research firm. Welcome to ALL THINGS CONSIDERED.
DYLAN PATEL: Thank you for having me.
DETROW: So you and others have estimated Nvidia is probably a year, two years ahead of its competitors. With Huang out, can other companies catch up?

PATEL: I think that's the biggest risk at least. Over the last, you know, handful of years, Nvidia's lead has actually lessened, and so therefore, they've lost market share, albeit, the market has grown so fast, Nvidia's revenue and profits have skyrocketed so fast. But now, with, you know, many barbarians at the gate, when sort of Jensen is needed most, he sort of is disappearing or (inaudible) the game.
DETROW: Needed most by the company, the industry?

PATEL: I think most - the most to the company. The industry has for a long time tried to roll their own solution, you know, at least as far as the biggest customers. Google, Microsoft, Meta, Amazon all have been working on their own AI chips for, you know, a number of years. And yet, they all still relied on Nvidia. But their reliance is reducing to some extent, and that's their goal and has been their goal. And now, you know, the only way Nvidia can keep their market share and stay on top of the world is if they out execute everyone - right? - they keep innovating and bringing new technology to the market. But without Jensen, you know, the founder and the visionary of the company, it's going to be a lot harder for them to keep on top.

DETROW: One of the things you've written about that I think is really important to understand is the way that - like, sometimes I feel like a CEO's role in a company is overblown. But how much came to (ph) his personal decisions, his personal decision-making? Let's talk about this first on the supply side. How was his personal relationships with supply chain managers in Korea and Taiwan so key to Nvidia getting what it needed?

PATEL: There's no other company in the supply chain, including in the semiconductor supply chain, where the CEO is, every quarter, meeting with all his suppliers. And, you know, chips are such a complex supply chain. He has hundreds of suppliers. He's talking to every single one of them, going to Korea, going to Taiwan, going to China, meeting, having drinks with them, going to local fried chicken spots, or, you know, night food markets, everything to woo them. And given this is such a complex industry where, you know, products are improving by 2x a year - right? - it's at an incredible pace - you need your suppliers to have full focus and put their best engineers on your product. And this just keeps Nvidia ahead of everyone.

DETROW: I mean, a big part of the reason the company dominated this field the way it did was the really risky big bets that Jensen Huang took. Do you see another CEO taking those bets, or do you see another company trying to establish itself taking the types of bets that he took?

PATEL: You know, there's many visionaries within the company. The challenge is, are there visionaries who are willing to bet the entire company, right? Jensen with CUDA, the software that makes Nvidia what it is, he developed it in 2010, you know, and the company developed it in 2010. And everyone who was a technologist at the time, everyone who was on Wall Street at the time thought it was a waste of money, thought it was a waste of effort. And then it turned out to be the bedrock of all AI software. You know, is someone going to do something that is such a waste of money that, for a decade looks like a terrible bet? It really takes a visionary, and I don't know if too many people will make those kinds of bets. You know, if someone were to ask me, hey, Nvidia without Jensen, a decade from now, are they the one that's bringing the most important new technology to market? I'd probably wager no.
DETROW: Do you have any sense what some of Nvidia's next big bets could be?

PATEL: Yeah, so Nvidia sort of had this history where they started making chips, and then they started making servers, and then they started making systems. Nvidia now is really focused on the end applications. They're making - they're helping companies make medical devices. They're helping companies make satellites. They're helping companies make entire systems that include AI as a part of it. If they don't do this, then most small and medium-sized healthcare companies, and even many of the not - large-but-not-so-largest-ones can't afford to build their own systems out of AI.

And so I think that's where Jensen was heading - right? - was, hey, in automotive, in healthcare, in manufacturing, how do we make it so medium-sized companies, small companies can all start deploying AI throughout their businesses to make them more efficient, increase production, make their products better, make people healthier? Without that, only the biggest companies can do this. And then the profit motive sort of makes it so, you know, all of the profit is captured by a few, not diffused to the whole ecosystem.
DETROW: That is Dylan Patel, founder and CEO of SemiAnalysis. Thanks so much for talking to us about this.
PATEL: Thank you.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261112.headline: 5,000-year-old skulls reveal a disturbing secret of ancient Egypt's first kings

paragraphs.text: New forensic evidence suggests that some of ancient Egypt's earliest rulers had members of their royal households killed when they died, possibly so those individuals could continue serving them in the afterlife. The discovery sheds new light on a disturbing burial practice that archaeologists suspected more than a century ago but could not prove.

The evidence comes from ancient skulls recovered near royal tombs at Abydos, Egypt, where members of the First Dynasty were buried roughly 5,000 years ago. When archaeologist Flinders Petrie excavated the graves in the 1920s, he noticed that unusually large numbers of people had been buried around the kings. He suspected that these individuals had been sacrificed following their rulers' deaths, but he could not identify physical evidence of fatal injuries.

Now, a modern forensic examination has uncovered signs of potentially deadly head trauma in 18 of 46 skulls, representing approximately 39% of the individuals studied. The findings provide compelling new support for the theory that human sacrifice played a role in the burial traditions of ancient Egypt's first kings.

"I was drawn to these retainers partly because, even though they were buried around royalty, they are mostly relegated to footnotes in the grander narrative," said Dr. Roselyn Campbell of Purdue University, who led the research published in Frontiers in Environmental Archaeology. Campbell is also the author of the forthcoming book State-sanctioned Violence and Human Sacrifice in Early Dynastic Egypt (Routledge Press).
"Who were these people and how did they view the ruler and their own role in his or her life and death?"
A 5,000-Year-Old Mystery Surrounding Egypt's First Kings

Around 3000 BCE, the earliest kings of a unified Egypt constructed elaborate burial complexes at Abydos. These sites included royal tombs, additional burial chambers, and enclosed areas believed to have been used for funeral ceremonies.

Surrounding the main structures were numerous smaller graves arranged in rows. Some royal burial sites were accompanied by hundreds of these subsidiary burials, raising questions about why so many people had been buried in close association with a single ruler.

"Each subsidiary burial was a simple chamber in a row of dozens of others," said Campbell. "Some people had a simple coffin. Most people had a few grave goods, like ceramic vessels, and many graves also included small objects like copper tools, projectile points, or small ivory figurines. Petrie found a few grave markers that had names and sometimes official titles on them. The titles seem to mostly refer to lower- or mid-level officials as well as artisans."
The extraordinary concentration of graves led Petrie to propose that the people buried alongside the kings were victims of a practice known as retainer sacrifice.

"Retainer sacrifice is a type of human sacrifice where those close to a ruler are killed when the ruler dies," explained Campbell. "In many cultures, retainer sacrifice is practiced because of beliefs that the sacrificed individuals will continue to serve the ruler in some kind of afterlife, but retainer sacrifice can also be a visceral display of the ruler's power. Some retainers might have volunteered to die to achieve eternal life or honor, others may have been chosen or even forced."

Despite the suspicious circumstances, Petrie could not find convincing evidence that the individuals had died violently. Without identifiable fatal injuries, the possibility of human sacrifice remained an unresolved archaeological mystery.
Campbell decided to revisit the original excavation evidence, hoping that modern forensic techniques could reveal clues that had escaped investigators a century earlier.
Modern Forensics Reveals Evidence of Violent Deaths

Although Petrie documented his excavations carefully, he eventually reburied most of the human remains. He did, however, preserve a selection of skulls, some of which were transferred to the United Kingdom.
Campbell located 46 of these skulls in the Duckworth Collection at Cambridge University and examined them using contemporary forensic knowledge.

The results revealed injuries that had previously gone unrecognized. Eighteen skulls showed substantial cranial trauma, primarily in the form of linear fractures. Petrie had apparently interpreted these cracks as damage caused by natural processes rather than injuries sustained by living people.

Modern forensic methods made it possible to identify the fractures as perimortem injuries, meaning they occurred around the time of death. Their characteristics suggest that some of the individuals may have suffered deliberate, potentially fatal blows to the head.

"The injuries on the preserved crania are generally linear fractures, which would likely cause rapid unconsciousness, internal bleeding, and death," said Campbell, who also reported evidence of sharp-force trauma on some of the 18 skulls, including a chopping injury to one individual's eye.
These findings suggest that at least 39% of the examined individuals may have been deliberately killed, providing important new evidence in support of the long-standing human sacrifice hypothesis.
How Were Ancient Egypt's Royal Attendants Killed?
Although the skull injuries offer strong evidence of violence, the precise circumstances of the deaths remain uncertain.

Ancient Egyptian artwork frequently portrays kings striking enemies with maces, but Campbell noted that the royal attendants buried at Abydos were not enemy combatants. The injuries also do not match the damage typically associated with these weapons.

A mace would generally produce depressed skull fractures, while the injuries identified in this study were predominantly linear. Such fractures are more commonly associated with impacts from broad, flat objects or severe falls.

Accidental falls cannot be entirely excluded. However, a fall powerful enough to fracture the skull would likely have caused injuries elsewhere in the skeleton. Such damage should have appeared in Petrie's excavation records or photographs, yet no corresponding evidence was documented.

The researchers also cannot determine how the remaining individuals died. Some may have died naturally, while others could have been killed using methods that left no recognizable marks on their bones, such as asphyxiation.

Additional injuries might also have been found if the rest of their skeletons were available for examination. Unfortunately, most of those remains were reburied more than a century ago, leaving researchers with only part of the physical evidence.
Ancient Skulls Reveal New Clues to Egypt's Dark Past

The findings demonstrate how archaeological collections can preserve important clues long after their original excavation. Even when evidence is incomplete, advances in scientific techniques can provide new answers to questions that earlier researchers were unable to resolve.

For Campbell, the possibility of locating and examining the remaining skeletal material offers an especially intriguing opportunity to learn more about the people buried around Egypt's earliest kings.

"If I had unlimited resources, I would love to figure out where the bodies of these individuals might be and analyze them!" said Campbell. "Still, this study shows how much new information about the past can be revealed when we revisit previous data armed with updated methods and knowledge, even for datasets that are incomplete and imperfect like this one."

latimes.com/politics/story/2026-11-13/de.headline: Democrats demand answers on FAA outage, question aging air traffic control
latimes.com/politics/story/2026-11-13/de.author: Clara Harter, Ana Ceballos, Kevin Rector

paragraphs.text: WASHINGTON — Democrats are demanding answers about Friday’s temporary ground stop on all flights in the United States and the alarming communications issue that affected air traffic control centers.
The hours-long ground stop crippled air travel and raised myriad questions about the nation’s aging air traffic control systems.

The problem stemmed from a data overload on the 1980s-era copper-wire technology used to transmit air traffic control voice and radar data, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said at a Friday evening news conference. This caused inconsistent communications between airplanes and controllers, prompting the Federal Aviation Administration to stop flights from taking off until the system was safely brought back online.
For several hours, both the public and members of Congress were left in the dark about the cause of the crisis.

In an interview shortly after the ground stop was announced, Rep. Ted Lieu (D-Torrance) said the FAA telecommunications outage was completely unacceptable and that the agency needs to create systems that do not have a single point of failure.
“I urge the FAA and the Trump administration to make sure this never happens again,” he said.
The California congressman said there need to be congressional hearings on the cause of the technical issue and what improvements should be enacted to avoid similar future outages.
“What just happened is enormously damaging to trust in our air system,” he said, “and our air system is a vital component of our national economy.”
Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), the ranking Democrat on the Aviation, Space and Innovation Subcommittee, said she will be demanding answers from the FAA about the ground stop.
“The safety of our skies is built on redundancies,” she said in a statement. “Whatever led to the nationwide ground stop will warrant a thorough and complete investigation.”

Duffy said President Trump has been pushing hard to modernize the FAA’s infrastructure and secured $12.5 billion through his 2025 “Big Beautiful Bill” — a sprawling collection of tax breaks, spending cuts and other Republican priorities — to upgrade the nation’s air traffic control and airspace systems. Duffy noted that none of the recently updated technology failed on Friday and called on Congress to approve an additional $50 billion in funding to finish a complete system overhaul.
“I’m going to say it a million times: Congress has to give the resources to the president so he can finish this build,” Duffy said.
Duffy praised Trump for his interest in updating the aging infrastructure, saying “what’s just unique about the president is he loves aviation, he loves the airspace.”

The president did not issue any statements on the ground stop Friday or appear at either of the White House’s two emergency news conferences. When asked by a reporter about the president’s silence, Duffy said that Trump was “fully engaged” and had been in communication with his relevant Cabinet members throughout the duration of the ground stop.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there is no evidence that the telecommunications outage was the result of a cyber attack or any nefarious foreign actors. However, he did say that the country’s outdated air traffic control system itself was a national security risk.
“Our air traffic control system is outdated, and it hasn’t been a priority from Congress,” Mullin said. “This is what happens when Congress kicks the can down the road.”
Mullin noted that the communications failure was caused as the FAA was performing upgrades.
“That new equipment, new technology — it was overwhelming the older system,” he said. “The patchwork doesn’t work. We need one complete system.”
In the initial absence of answers, speculation was raised over whether the ground stop was tied to the use of an AI tool that assists air traffic controllers.

The FAA expanded the use of the tool to all of its 22 control centers on Tuesday, according to the agency. The tool — called Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories, or SMART — combines about 200 data streams, including flight paths, schedules and weather, on one cloud-based system, according to a fact sheet posted on the FAA’s website.

Congressional Democrats raised concerns after the platform’s initial roll-out in the Washington area, calling for a 90-day pause until they better understand how it is being used. In a letter to Duffy, lawmakers said there was an “egregious lack of transparency” about the tool.
“The air traffic control systems and processes currently in place are complex, and we don’t know what impact AI-enabled tools might have on these systems and resulting safety,” they wrote in October.

But in a post on social media Friday afternoon, the AI company that created SMART, Air Space Intelligence, said that the “current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.”
After some questioned whether this week’s Microsoft outage could have affected the air traffic control system, Mullin said there was no connection.

npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-6040044/dem-sen.headline: With his challenge to Schumer, Van Hollen forces a debate over Democrats' mandate
npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-6040044/dem-sen.author: Elena Moore

paragraphs.text: SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

Democrats say they have a mandate to deliver change next year, but as the party gets ready to retake a majority in Congress, there are divides over how far that change should go and who should lead it. It's a debate playing out in the Senate where minority leader Chuck Schumer now faces a challenge from fellow Democrat Chris Van Hollen for the top job next year. Here to break down what we know is NPR's Elena Moore in the studio with me. Hi, Elena.
ELENA MOORE, BYLINE: Hey, Sacha.
PFEIFFER: So last night, Van Hollen announced he's running. For people who don't know him, what should we know about him?

MOORE: Yeah, he's had a pretty long career in Washington, representing Maryland in the Senate since 2017 and serving more than a decade in the House before that, where he held some leadership roles. Ideologically, he's seen as more progressive than Schumer is, and he's tried to position himself in recent years as someone who pushes back hard against the Trump administration. Notably, last year, he lobbied for the release of Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the Maryland man who was wrongly deported to a prison in El Salvador, and Van Hollen actually traveled there to meet with him.
PFEIFFER: And what is Van Hollen's argument for why he should have the Senate's top job?

MOORE: Well, he argues that the midterms showed how much voters want Democrats to reject the status quo. You know, speaking to reporters earlier today at a Democratic conference in Colorado, he argued he's the best person to usher in that change.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

CHRIS VAN HOLLEN: This is about answering the call of the American people because what I'm very afraid of is that their calls to end political corruption, their calls to end a rigged economic system, will require that we organize the Senate in a different way.

MOORE: And, Sacha, those talking points may sound kind of familiar because we kind of just heard them on the campaign trail. Van Hollen is really embracing much of the same messaging used by successful Democratic Senate candidates this cycle, like Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan, who made, you know, their campaigns all about this idea of rejecting the establishment, which, in many ways, Schumer has long embodied.
PFEIFFER: And that message has been successful for some candidates, but...
MOORE: Right.
PFEIFFER: ...In many ways, Van Hollen kind of embodies older school politics. So what makes him think he is an embodiment of change right now?

MOORE: Yeah, and also he's only eight years younger than Schumer, which I think is also kind of important to mention. But it is an important question. On the issues, it's worth noting that he and Schumer are pretty aligned on the party's big-picture priorities. They've both emphasized the need to lower costs, you know, end the war and reverse some of the Trump administration's funding cuts.

I think the bigger difference between the two politicians is how they talk about reforming the Democratic Party. You know, Van Hollen has talked about the Senate being taken over by special interest groups, which hits on a pretty big rift within the caucus right now about campaign donations from super PACs as well as pro-Israel lobbying groups like AIPAC, which is a group that has supported Schumer in the past.

PFEIFFER: And I know that Van Hollen has said he hopes to rally support from the party's left flank. But can you tell if the opposition to Schumer is being driven mainly by progressives, or is there broader appetite for an alternative inside the party?

MOORE: Yeah. It's important to say Schumer is by no means universally loved inside the party, right? You know, towards the start of Trump's second term, he was actually criticized both within the halls of Congress and from voters who argued he wasn't doing enough to fight back against Trump.

Yes, some of that frustration is coming from progressives, like, you know, Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders, for example. But, Sacha, it's not just the party's left flank. You know, earlier this week, Sanders actually held a press conference alongside Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, who's way more of a moderate, I would say. And the two both announced that they wouldn't be backing Schumer for the job.

And, you know, when looking at the broader caucus, dissatisfaction with Schumer may not translate to a victory for Van Hollen, per se, but, you know, he knows he's the underdog here. Schumer says he's confident he has the support needed. But there's also time for both of these politicians to try to make gains. Ultimately, this is going to come down to a secret ballot vote in early December.
PFEIFFER: That is NPR political reporter Elena Moore. Thank you.
MOORE: Thank you.

sciencedaily.com/releases/2026/11/261112.headline: Forcing yourself to smile can actually make you miserable

paragraphs.text: A smile might brighten your mood, but new research suggests that forcing yourself to smile over and over can have the opposite effect. When smiling becomes an obligation, especially one tied to financial pressure, it may actually leave people feeling less happy and more irritated.

For years, psychologist Nicholas Coles, Ph.D., studied evidence suggesting that even an artificial smile could make someone feel a little happier. Yet those findings never quite matched his own experiences.

"I used to work in customer service. I actually got written up for my inability to keep smiling at work at an unnamed theme park in Florida," laughed Coles, a professor of psychology at the University of Florida. "So I'm looking at all this evidence I had accrued so far that smiling boosts happiness and realizing it flies in the face of my own experiences in the world."

That contradiction inspired Coles and his colleagues to investigate what happens when people must keep smiling, rather than simply trying it once. Their findings suggest an important distinction: A brief, intentional smile can provide a small emotional lift, but repeatedly putting on a smile under pressure can undermine happiness.
Testing How Forced Smiling Affects Happiness

To explore this difference, Coles worked with researchers Annabel Dang and Joao Francisco Goes Braga Takayanagi to design an experiment that more closely resembled the demands of customer service jobs. Their findings were published on October 1 in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology.

"We tried to combine the classic way of studying it in a lab with some extra ingredients that we might see in the real world. We told participants that we would pay them less if they weren't successfully smiling," Coles said. "We also controlled the number of times they have to do it, because in customer service, every interaction is another faked smile."

The online experiment initially enrolled 1,201 people, with data from 1,174 included in the final analysis. Participants were shown images designed to produce different emotional reactions. Some depicted appealing subjects, such as kittens and flowers, while others showed disturbing situations, including theft and mistreatment of animals.

During the experiment, participants either deliberately formed a smile or allowed their facial expressions to develop naturally. Depending on their assigned group, they completed the exercise once or repeated it 10 times.

To introduce an element of pressure, researchers warned half the participants that failing to follow the smiling instructions could cost them $2 from their $6 payment. However, nobody actually lost any money, and every participant received the full amount.
When Fake Smiles Start to Backfire

After completing each task, participants reported how happy they felt. The results showed that the emotional effects of smiling depended on how often people had to do it and whether they felt pressured.

When participants viewed unpleasant images, producing a single smile gave their mood a modest boost. This benefit appeared even among those who had been warned about a possible financial penalty. However, the positive effect weakened when smiling was repeated, and it disappeared when repeated smiles were combined with the threat of losing money.

The pattern was even more revealing when people looked at pleasant pictures. Smiling just once offered little additional happiness compared with allowing their faces to respond naturally. But when participants had to smile repeatedly or felt pressure to do so, their happiness ratings actually fell below those of people who responded naturally.
Further analysis revealed another unexpected consequence. In the pleasant picture conditions, forced smiling was also associated with increased irritation and anger.

"If you only force a smile once without any financial penalties, you can see the improvement in happiness. So what psychologists were seeing in their lab is right," he said. "But when you make it a little bit more like the real world, where you have to keep repeating it, and if you don't do it well, you get financial penalties, you see it completely reverse."
The Hidden Emotional Cost of Smiling at Work
These findings may help explain why expectations to appear cheerful throughout the workday can become frustrating rather than uplifting.

The issue has already sparked controversy in the workplace. In recent years, Target faced widespread criticism over a policy requiring employees to smile when customers came within a specified distance. Although the policy was intended to encourage friendly interactions, Coles argues that such requirements can interfere with people's ability to express their emotions naturally.

The problem may extend beyond employees. Customers can also feel obligated to respond positively to friendliness that is being imposed rather than offered spontaneously. According to Coles, these expectations limit the emotional freedom of both sides of the interaction.
Could Trying Less to Be Happy Make Us Happier?

After spending years investigating how people can improve their emotional well-being, Coles has begun considering a broader question. Rather than constantly searching for ways to increase happiness, might people be better off placing greater value on simply being content?
His research suggests that efforts to manufacture positive emotions do not always produce the intended results. Sometimes, trying too hard to appear happy can make the experience less pleasant.

"As a society, we have placed such an immense amount of emphasis on trying to make ourselves feel happier than we currently are," he said, "much less emphasis on just being content with what we have."

Qwen3.8-27B is a 27B parameter dense model Qwen, featuring vision and reasoning capabilities, a 256K context window, and runs locally on 17GB RAM/VRAM setups. Qwen3.8 excels at agentic coding, vision and chat tasks, and can now run via Unsloth GGUFs, NVFP4 and Unsloth Desktop.

Nov 11 Update: Qwen3.8-27B GGUFs now use Unsloth Dynamic V3.1 which improves average accuracy by 5-10% accuracy at comparable sizes including Terminal Bench, DeepSWE and more benchmarks. We're working on an even better version of Dynamic quants which will be applied to Qwen4 and future models.
Run Qwen3.8 GuideDownload Unsloth
Thank you Qwen for day zero access. Unsloth quants also include:
• Developer Role Support for agentic tools like Codex
• Tool calling: Improved parsing nested objects to make tools succeed more
Dynamic V3.1 Update (November 11th 2026)

We're excited to release new Qwen3.8-27B GGUFs using our updated Unsloth Dynamic V3.1 (preview) algorithm which improves Unsloth quants by 5-10% accuracy at the same size on most benchmarks and is the best in class for most tasks including coding, agentic workloads and general chat.
Most quants from 2bit until 6bit are updated. We found 3bit UD3 quants to do on par with UD3.1, so we do not update them. We are actively working on making all quants better!

We ran agentic benchmarks including Terminal Bench 2.1, DeepSWE v1.1, and general benchmarks like LiveCodeBench v6, GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro, AIME25 and many others. We used 256K context lengths for all agentic benchmarks, and 128K for the rest. We followed the same methodology for Qwen3.8-27B as DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next which also utilized our V3.1 preview algorithm.
Dynamic V3.1 Full Breakdown
Click below to see full details of benchmarking and more:
Exllama-v3 considerations
To compare GSQ-RCO and Exllama-v3, we had to exclude the token embedding layer from the x axis, as Exllama-v3 uses BF16 for it.

If you consider the full download size and total RAM usage for Exllama-v3, then adding the BF16 embedding table and including all embedding sizes changes the plots. Our main plots's x axis removes the embedding layer sizes from all quant providers. However on pure RAM usage and disk space usage vs accuracy, the below plot is the true reflection of actual usage.

We have not investigated why Exllama-v3 keeps token embeddings in BF16, but as the lm_head is still quantized heavily, the embedding layer might have "absorbed" most of the quantization damage from it. We would be glad to benchmark new Exllama-v3 non BF16 token embedding quants like using 8-bit for example, and see if benchmarks change.
GSQ-RCO results are misleading

For LiveCodeBench, GSQ-RCO showed Unsloth UD3 quants doing consistently worse than ISTA's. However we found the opposite - UD3 quants (our OLD quants) do better than ISTA on LCB on all sizes except the smallest. UD3.1 further improves on LCB as well.
We approximate that GSQ-RCO used a context budget of 96K, as that best fits the data for the runs we have. At 96K, GSQ-RCO does somewhat do better than UD3, but at 128K, UD3 does much better.
On another benchmark, for ISTA GSQ-RCO's AIME25 benchmarks, their quants reach 100%, 100%, 100% and 96.7% accuracy recovery. And they said our quants do worse.

Through out investigations, we estimate ISTA only did 1 trial - we did 14 trials, and we show on average the recovery rate is 93% to 96% - not 100% accuracy recovery. And in fact our UD3 old quants do BETTER on average than their quants on 14 runs vs 1 run of theirs, so we draw the opposite conclusion if you run the trials more.

We also checked and graded our answers using Math Verify Dynamic 3.1 GGUFs and also LightEval and we find exactly the same conclusions. We also tried greedy decoding (temperature of 0), and this could not get the 100% accuracy recovery ISTA found across multiple greedy runs, as GPUs themselves are non deterministic. That is why you benchmarks should be run multiple times. Greedy decoding is also not representative of real world use cases.
We also checked 96K (which is most likely ISTA's budget) and 128K, and our quants still do on average better.
KLD of Unsloth v3.1 vs v3

We did KLD for multiple domains for Unsloth UD3.1 quants and UD3 quants - we reduce KLD throughout most quants and most domains - we did not replace the 3-bit ones, as we found UD3 to do mostly great, and the accuracy recovery on benchmarks was not significant enough with UD3.1 to warrant an update, so we did not update them.
Benchmark details and setups

We follow the same procedure for all benchmarks as for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as well as discussed in Dynamic 3.1 GGUFs. We used temperature 1.0, top_p 0.95, top_k 20, min_p 0, no presence or repetition penalty, preserve_thinking and xhigh reasoning for Qwen3.8-27B.

paragraphs.text: Looking to bounce back in a big way from a lopsided loss to Georgetown last Saturday, Maryland instead squandered a lead at home Friday and lost to a highly ranked Virginia squad, 87-83.
The Terps fell to 1-2 in Coach Buzz Williams’s second season with the program, while the sixth-ranked Cavaliers improved to 5-0 with the win at Xfinity Center.

Maryland led by 11 after a stirring first half and by as many as 10 with over seven minutes gone by in the second before the Cavaliers began to reel the Terps back in. Virginia used a 9-0 run to quickly get within one point, tied the game with just under seven minutes to play and, moments later, took its first lead since an early 5-4 edge.

The teams went back and forth from there until the Cavaliers took advantage of a number of defensive breakdowns by Maryland to forge a 76-72 lead. Virginia then held off a still-feisty Terps team and got a dagger three from Belgian big man Thijs De Ridder, the ACC’s preseason pick for player of the year, with one minute 33 seconds to go. After De Ridder got a steal with around 30 seconds to play, fans began streaming for the exits.
De Ridder finished with 20 points and Virginia guard Sam Lewis, who was a menace all night, had 28 points as the duo combined to make 20 of 29 shots from the field.

Standout forward Pharrel Payne paced the Terrapins with 20 points but was mostly held in check in the second half. Teammates Kaden House and Mike McNair had 17 and 15 points, respectively, but overall Maryland shot just 37.9 percent in the second half, compared to 76.9 percent for Virginia.

Maryland went to halftime on a raucous note after McNair beat the buzzer with three-pointer that gave the Terps a 47-36 lead. By that time, the home crowd was in full throat, particularly after Mills threw down a dunk moments earlier.

Payne’s 12 points, followed closely by McNair and House at 10 apiece, led the Terps in that half. Maryland carried over the poor shooting from deep that marked its lopsided loss to Georgetown, but whereas the Hoyas scorched the nets from distance in an 86-74 win at Capital One Arena, Virginia had its own early troubles.

The Cavs made just one of five shots from three-point range, amid a hard-nosed defensive effort by the Terps that saw them also rack up major advantages in steals (5-1) and points off turnovers (13-2).

By stifling what had been a smooth-running Cavs attack, Maryland gave itself numerous chance in the first half to generate roars at the Xfinity Center, but for much of the time the Terps couldn’t quite finish an otherwise rousing sequence. Maryland missed several tough shots at the rim and misfired from distance until a final-minute stretch that featured an offensive rebound and layup by House, followed by Mills’s dunk and McNair’s three.

The dunk represented Mills’s first and only basket of the first half after he started 0-7 from the field, following a 4-for-15 performance against Georgetown. Unfortunately for the redshirt sophomore, a key cog in the Terps’ attack, he reverted to recent form over the final 20 minutes and finished with six points on 2-of-13 shooting.

Against Georgetown, Maryland looked like the overhauled team its is, following an offseason makeover by Coach Buzz Williams. The Terps showed more cohesion against Virginia, itself a squad that boasts notable continuity from last season, but left Williams still searching for a signature win in College Park after his first season ended with a 12-21 record.

According to Maryland, it entered the game with a 108-77 record all-time against Virginia in a basketball rivalry that dates back to 1913 (Virginia’s athletic department put the record at 107-77). Before Friday, though, the Cavaliers had won nine of the teams’ past 10 meetings.
The game ended a busy stretch for Virginia in which it played five games in an 11-day stretch. Friday’s contest marked the Terps’ third game in 12 days.

nytimes.com/2026/11/14/world/europe/stud.headline: A ‘Generational Clash’ Is Fueling Europe’s Protests
nytimes.com/2026/11/14/world/europe/stud.author: Jason Horowitz

paragraphs.text: Sébastien Ducros, a French data analyst who supports the widespread student protests in his country, has identified an obvious culprit for the lack of government funds for dilapidated schools.

“A huge portion of the money is going toward retirees, while many other things are being neglected,” said Mr. Ducros, 36. “I honestly think — even if it feels strange to say — that people like my parents are in a position where they should and could” surrender some of their pension payments, he added, saying that they were about to retire.

But Laurent Grinwald, 72, who retired recently after decades as a postal worker, isn’t eager for his pension to be reduced, particularly to pay for other state-funded services. Especially, he said, as rents and the cost of living have shot up.
“We’ve been working all this time,” Mr. Grinwald said, “and now, suddenly, the stance is, ‘Well, no, we’re going to start taking a bit more?’”

This disagreement embodies a broader question for Europe, one that is at the heart of mass antigovernment demonstrations planned for Saturday in France, as well as recent protests driven by frustrated young people in countries including Belgium, Germany, Greece, Italy and Portugal. As Europeans live longer, should the needs of the young be eclipsed by their parents’ and grandparents’ pensions, routinely the largest items in Europe’s national budgets?
“It’s a generational clash,” said Jorge Galindo, the director of EsadeEcPol, an independent think tank in Spain, which has some of the most generous pensions in Europe.
In much of Europe, spending on a growing population of older people has come at the expense of services and subsidies for young workers whose tax contributions help to fund pensions.

Spiraling defense costs, prompted by American pressure and Russian aggression, have also made it harder for governments to balance their books. And high interest rates have driven up the costs of servicing state debt.

All of that, coupled with rising rents and house prices, has compounded a sense of generational injustice among young people. Only 38 percent of people aged 15 to 30 think that policymakers consider the long-term consequences of their decisions, according to a recent European Union survey. Only a third believe that today’s young people have the same shot at success as young people 30 years ago did, the survey also found.
The enormous financial burden of pensions — they gobble up around 40 percent of the spending on social protections in the European Union — has not been lost on European governments.

Over the past decade, many countries have tried to tinker with pension formulas, trying to cut costs while postponing major political blowback. To many older Europeans, pensions are considered the sacrosanct base of the European welfare system.

Often, they have avoided cutting what each retiree is paid while gradually raising the age at which citizens qualify for those payments — to 67 from 65, for example, or older. Denmark plans to raise it to 70 by 2040.

Even that approach has had a political cost. When President Emmanuel Macron of France tried in 2023 to raise France’s retirement age to 64 from 62, it prompted such furious protests that the government eventually froze the measure. But that gave the country a different problem.
With one of the highest debt levels in Europe, France says it cannot afford to spend more on education — which has prompted the youth anger spurring the wave of unrest.

Other countries have tried other ways of softening the generational competition. Britain plans to save billions by slowing the speed at which its pension payments increase over time, while Spain has enlarged its pool of taxpaying workers.

Spain chose in 2011 to raise its pension age to 67 in most cases. Then the current left-wing government enlarged the pension bill by ensuring that pension payments would grow in line with inflation, protecting recipients from rising prices but putting an enormous strain on the budget.
To offset those costs, it has bucked the European trend and opened its doors to immigrant labor — more than 1.7 million foreigners have entered the Spanish work force since 2018.
Those workers have increased tax revenue, which in turn helps to fund pension contributions, but eventually, experts note, they will age, too.

Spain will spend 17.3 percent of its gross domestic product in 2050 on pensions, according to the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development — roughly four percentage points higher than now. That means the government would then be spending the equivalent in today’s terms of an additional $67 billion every year on pensions. It currently spends roughly $79 billion on education.
Despite the competition for resources, many of the young people protesting throughout Europe are loath to blame their elders.
“Honestly,” said Alice Cossa, 22, an Italian student who protested recently in Venice, “we’ve never talked about it.”

Left-wing demonstrators often say that pensions and other benefits can be funded by taxing the rich and corporations. Their right-wing counterparts suggest cutting immigration, blaming immigrants for soaking up welfare benefits.
Some feel, though, that at least some pensions, namely those received by wealthy older people, should be reassessed.

“We young people have less and less and less,” said Alejandro Rojano, 28, a bank employee who lives in a basement apartment in Madrid with a roommate. He said even his own nonagenarian grandparents received “way” more than his monthly salary, which was less than 2,000 euros, or less than $2,200. No political party would dare cut the benefits of such a dependable and powerful voting bloc as retirees, he lamented, adding of the pension payouts, “It makes no sense, you know?”

Mr. Galindo, the think tank director, said that given the entrenched political interests in protecting retirees, young people might need to form an essentially single-issue voting bloc. Because European governments are typically formed from coalitions of smaller parties, such a party could become pivotal and have its concerns taken seriously with only a handful of seats.
But young people are a shrinking demographic in Europe, and the number of older people, who are more likely to exercise political power through union and party memberships, is booming.
And young and middle-aged Europeans are reluctant to cut a benefit that they hope to enjoy in the future.

As Daniel Ramo, 46, left a recent teachers’ strike in Madrid protesting dismal salaries and packed classrooms, he said that he personally looked forward to receiving his generous Spanish pension after making €2,100 a month after taxes. In the meantime, the benefits of his parents’ pensions would trickle down to help him through tough times.
“I’m on strike knowing I’ll have to borrow money from my father,” said Mr. Ramo, who said his father’s pension made him the top earner in the family.
From the perspective of retirees, the hard-earned benefit helps keep families, and European society, going.

“We personally make more than our children do,” said Encarna Matilla, 72, as she took a walk in sunny Retiro Park in Madrid. She said her 88-year-old husband, who worked from 14 to 70, received a pension payment of €2,700, 60 percent higher than Spain’s median salary, and helped support her great-grandchildren.
“We are the safety net,” she said.
Ségolène Le Stradic contributed reporting from Paris, Josephine de La Bruyère from Rome and Carlos Barragán from Madrid.

npr.org/2026/11/14/g-s1-151719/midterms-.headline: Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins wins race for Alaska governor, replaces a Republican
npr.org/2026/11/14/g-s1-151719/midterms-.author: Eric Stone

paragraphs.text: Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state representative from the small island community of Sitka, won the race for Alaska governor, according to a race call by the Associated Press. At 37, he'll be the youngest governor in state history.
Kreiss-Tomkins will replace outgoing Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a term-limited Republican who has been governor since 2018. The state's last Democratic governor was Tony Knowles, who left office in 2002.
Kreiss-Tomkins, known by his initials JKT, made his "high-energy, bipartisan, problem-solving approach" a centerpiece of his campaign.

He's said he plans to build an administration of Democrats, Republicans and independents and described himself at a debate as a "man of the middle." He was endorsed by three former governors — a Democrat, a Republican and an independent — along with Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski.
Alaskans have had enough of zero-sum partisan politics, he said in an interview just before voting at a precinct in Anchorage on Election Day.
"I strongly believe people just want things to work, and want people to work together," Kreiss-Tomkins said.

The AP race call came after over a week of counting votes, including those coming in by mail and from remote parts of the state. In the ranked-choice system the state uses, he faced three Republican candidates, including one backed by President Trump. Winning requires getting a majority of the votes.
Voters were also facing a question on the ballot about whether to scrap that unique, ranked-choice system. That proposal failed, according to another AP race call, keeping the system in place.
With Kreiss-Tomkins' win and others in the midterms, Democrats will hold 30 governors' offices across the country, up from 24 now.
Kreiss-Tomkins will take office in a state where voters have loudly complained that things aren't working as they should.

Rising costs and relatively flat state funding have forced schools to close and class sizes to rise. Already-high costs for food, fuel and housing have risen sharply, and a looming shortage of easily accessible natural gas near the state's population centers is threatening to push prices higher. And Alaskans have been migrating out of the state for more than a decade.
The Republicans in the race were Trump-backed business owner Bernadette Wilson, former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson and former Alaska Attorney General Treg Taylor.
Kreiss-Tomkins is set to take office at noon Dec. 7.
Eric Stone covers state government for Alaska Public Media.

theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/14/univer.headline: University hounded out of Hungary by Orbán reaches out to new government
theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/14/univer.author: Jennifer Rankin

paragraphs.text: A university that Viktor Orbán tried to chase out of Hungary is open to expanding its presence in Budapest, in a mark of confidence in the country’s democratic future.

Carsten Q Schneider, the interim president and rector of Central European University (CEU), said it was interested in increasing its programmes in Budapest, as long as this did not damage the student experience.

So far the CEU has not held formal talks with Hungary’s new government, which has promised to restore academic freedom, “but our hand is reaching out, their hand is reaching out – it is just that they have many things to do”, the academic told the Guardian.

The CEU relocated its main activities to Vienna from Budapest in 2019, after pressure from the previous government led by Orbán. But the outlook changed when Péter Magyar won a landslide victory in April pledging to root out corruption and reform the state.

The CEU, founded by Hungarian-American financier and philanthropist George Soros in 1991 to entrench democratic change in the region, was forced to cease awarding degrees in Budapest in response to a law widely seen as targeting the institution.

The EU’s highest court struck down Hungary’s “Lex CEU” in 2020, finding that it violated the EU charter of fundamental rights, but the verdict came too late for the university. The CEU retains 312 staff in Budapest, mostly administrative, but the majority, 476, and all its teaching, are in Vienna.

Schneider said upgrading the status of the CEU, which is privately funded, in Budapest would be “a symbol for academic freedom [and] of resilience” but depended on goodwill and funding independent of the Hungarian government. He said a decision on its future in Hungary would be taken by the CEU’s 13-member board, whose members include Soros and his son, Alexander Soros.
“We don’t want special treatment,” Schneider said. ‘“We are a great asset, so let’s work out something.”

But the CEU, which he said was “thriving tremendously” in Vienna, does not plan a wholesale return to Budapest. Any change would have to ensure the quality of the student experience, for instance, assuring that students would be able to combine courses, say in economics and history, without having to travel the 200km-plus distance between the two cities.
Focused on social sciences, law and humanities, the CEU has more than 1,400 students from 103 countries, mostly doing master’s and PhD programmes.

According to Schneider, for the first time in the CEU’s 25-year history, students from the US now make up the largest cohort of master’s students (10%). The CEU has seen an increase in US applicants since Donald Trump returned to the White House and launched a sweeping campaign against elite universities, including slashing federal funding and seeking to exert control over internal policies.

The CEU rector has had informal talks with US academics on how to maintain academic freedom under pressure from rightwing populists. He described his message as: “Don’t be naive for a second. These people have a plan, so it’s not by accident that they attack universities. They want to have cultural hegemony.” He added, however, that Trump and allied movements, such as Germany’s Alternative für Deutschland, have identified “real problems”, such as in the US how universities have entrenched “a reproduction of elites”

When coming under political pressure, he said universities needed “to look for allies”, among other academic institutions, students, alumni and parents. Institutions also had to stand up for disciplines under attack, such as gender studies, Schneider added.
He recalled the outpouring of support for CEU – when tens of thousands of people protested in Budapest in defence of the university – as “one of the most humbling experiences I have had”.
Schneider, a German political scientist who specialises in the study of democracies and regime transition, said Magyar had successfully used Orbán’s political machine against him.

“Nobody has a better idea than [Magyar] how to defeat the most potent and the most skilled illiberal populist [Orbán]. So he knows something.” He added: “The people and skills that you need to bring a non-democratic regime down are not the same and sometimes the opposite of what it takes to establish a democracy. So the question now is whether he [Magyar] has the skills to basically reinvent liberal democracy for the 21st century.”

Schneider said Hungary could be the world’s first “post-illiberal democracy” – a model for democratic restoration, just as Orbán inspired rightwing populists around the world. But he also raised doubts about this thesis, saying there were questions about how Magyar and his Tisza party might develop in the context of Hungary’s “very difficult economic situation”.

The test would be, he suggested, when Magyar faces losing support and, eventually, defeat at the ballot box. “So what happens when he loses support and then cracks in his movement appear? Will he be the visionary leader who manages … to establish a three, four, five-party system, where people compete? That is to be seen.”
