nytimes.com/2026/11/13/us/faa-ground-sto.headline: What to Know About Friday’s Nationwide Ground Stop
nytimes.com/2026/11/13/us/faa-ground-sto.author: Karoun Demirjian

paragraphs.text: The Federal Aviation Administration issued a rare nationwide ground stop Friday afternoon, after outdated air traffic communications equipment became overloaded with data and began to fail, officials said.

The outage stranded thousands of passengers and caused widespread delays from which airlines and airports are still struggling to recover. It also highlighted persistent vulnerabilities in the aging U.S. air traffic infrastructure and a funding fight, as administration officials demanded lawmakers approve tens of billions of dollars more to accelerate systemwide upgrades.
Here’s what to know.
What caused the problem?

Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, told reporters at the White House Friday night that the radar and other air traffic communications started to falter at 3:36 p.m. when old routers became overloaded with data. While the failures were not universal, they were pervasive enough to prompt officials to issue the unusual nationwide moratorium on takeoffs, Mr. Duffy said.
Appearing alongside him at the White House, Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, stressed that there was no evidence that nefarious activity had triggered the technology failures.

“We’ve seen zero evidence that this was a cyberattack,” Mr. Mullin said, suggesting that new equipment and new technology the Mr. Duffy’s department had added to the old infrastructure was what had overwhelmed it.
Mr. Duffy insisted that the failure was caused by the antiquated, legacy communications equipment, not recent upgrades to the system.
“What we have is an incredibly old air traffic control system,” Mr. Duffy said, predicting that until significant upgrades are made, “it’s going to continue to fail.”
How long will it take to get things back to normal?

Mr. Duffy warned that it would take “some time” for air travel nationwide to recover from the ground stop, predicting flight schedules would be fully back to normal by the time the Thanksgiving travel season begins.
“I believe that it’s going to take us some time to get back to capacity,” he said, adding: “We’re going to have some makeup to do.”
Mr. Duffy said that the F.A.A. would prioritize larger commercial flights ahead of private and charter flights, to get previously grounded flights off the ground.
What does the administration say needs to be done?

Mr. Duffy has long been pushing for a sweeping overhaul of the U.S. air traffic infrastructure, routinely complaining that controllers have been hampered by the country’s failure to upgrade outdated equipment.
“We have old, old switches, old routers — we use 1980s little copper lines,” he said to reporters Friday. Only last week, the F.A.A. announced that it had begun to phase out the use of floppy disks.

Last year, Congress approved $12.5 billion to fund upgrades to the country’s aging air traffic facilities and networks, some of which has been directed toward communications system upgrades. Mr. Duffy noted Friday that air traffic facilities that had been upgraded to digital systems did not experience the same overloading issues that prompted the F.A.A. to issue the ground stop order.

But he stressed that having an air traffic control system dependent on a “patchwork” of upgrades and fixes was untenable, calling on Congress to spend tens of billions more to allow for more upgrades.
Why did Duffy blame Congress?

For months, Mr. Duffy has been calling on the Republican-controlled Congress to give his department another $30 billion to accelerate efforts to upgrade air traffic control systems. On Friday night, he upped the ante, telling reporters he wanted $50 billion — and that he wanted it before the end of the year.
“This is an emergency, I want Congress to give us emergency funding,” he said, adding: “How many more times does this have to happen for Congress to give the money to fix it?”

But it is unclear whether Republicans will prioritize such a sum before the end of the year, after which control of Congress shifts to the Democrats, who are expected to scrutinize how the F.A.A. has utilized air traffic funding they have received so far. Republican lawmakers have filed bills in the House and Senate to authorize $30 billion in air traffic upgrades, but neither piece of legislation has cosponsors.
Later on Friday, Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the House’s top-ranking Democrat, appeared to reject Mr. Duffy’s accusing tone and shifted the blame back to the Trump administration.

“Today’s unprecedented breakdown is the latest in a series of unacceptable air travel incidents under the Trump administration’s failed leadership,” he said in a statement, adding that “American travelers deserve timely answers from the Trump administration about how and why this happened and assurances that steps are being taken to ensure that our air travel system remains safe and functional.”

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckz74jzpy18do.headline: Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckz74jzpy18do.author: BBC News

paragraphs.text: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.

The historic meeting between the leaders of the US, Russia and China will take place as Trump attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," she said.
It is understood Iran may also be discussed during the meeting of the world's biggest nuclear powers, but not Ukraine. Moscow and Beijing are yet to comment.
No agreement was expected to follow the talks, an unnamed, senior American official said, according to news agencies AP and Reuters.

Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day summit between the 21 member states. He will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president returned to office in 2025.

"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People's Republic of China, and the president of the Russian Federation," Wales said.

She said Trump's trip, which will also include attending an Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo Pacific".

A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February, leaving the world's biggest nuclear arsenals without major guardrails and effectively marking an end to the arms control co-operation which helped to resolve the Cold War.
The UN has urged both sides to agree a new framework without delay. Trump however said he could replace the deal with a better agreement which included China, which has been building up its arsenal.
Former senior US officials and analysts told the BBC at the time that seeking Beijing and Moscow's co-operation could turn up major hurdles and take years.
Xi separately hosted both Putin and Trump in Beijing just days apart earlier this year, while the US president welcomed his Chinese counterpart to Washington in September.
Beijing has become a crucial trading partner for Moscow since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which has isolated Russia and left it subject to Western sanctions.

But a controversial US deal to import Russian diesel and the suspension of sanctions targeting the biggest buyers of Moscow's oil and gas - including China - heightened European concern about the Trump administration's softening towards the Kremlin last month.

Trump and Xi have meanwhile sought to project warmer ties at summits in Beijing and Washington this year - though little significant progress appeared to have been made on key issues such as trade, their race for AI dominance, and Taiwan. The war in Iran has also been a sticking point, with Beijing the largest buyer of Tehran's oil and its biggest trade partner.

Chinese state media reported on Friday that Xi would take part in "bilateral" talks on the sidelines of the Apec summit, citing a foreign ministry spokesman, but has not reported on the trilateral meeting.
Earlier this month, Russian state news agency Tass reported that Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov had said there were "signals confirming readiness" for such talks at the summit.

npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-6040418/dhs-hea.headline: DHS head Markwayne Mullin says there is not a threat to the U.S. amid FAA ground stop
npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-6040418/dhs-hea.author: Deepa Shivaram

paragraphs.text: SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

Travelers across the country are now stranded in airports and sitting on runways after the FAA issued a total ground stop this afternoon. There are very few details about why Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy made that call. All we know at this time is that it's being attributed to communication difficulties. Here is Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin speaking at the White House just a few minutes ago.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

MARKWAYNE MULLIN: We're getting a ton of calls saying, is this a terrorist attack? Is this a terrorist attack? Everybody's safe. There is no reason to be concerned about your loved ones, if they're flying or anything like that. I just want to make sure everybody's at ease about that.
PFEIFFER: NPR White House correspondent Deepa Shivaram was there listening to Mullin when he talked to reporters, and she's with us now. Deepa, what can you tell us about what's going on?

DEEPA SHIVARAM, BYLINE: Yeah. So this all happened in the span of the last 30 minutes, I would say. DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin came out to brief reporters just outside the White House, and he started off by saying that there is not a threat to the U.S., and they believe that this whole situation boils down to a telecommunications issue.
MULLIN: There was no prior indication. There was no indication as of yet that this was a nefarious attack against us. It is just a telecommunication outage as of right now.

SHIVARAM: He was asked about his wording there, as of yet, when he said that there, you know, wasn't any indication that this was a nefarious attack. He said that they're not ruling out anything. They're still looking into the details, and they're not at a point where they can rule anything out, hence his wording, as of yet. He said that all flights are accounted for, and he was very emphatic multiple times that this was not a 9/11 situation.

MULLIN: Out of abundance of caution, we have grounded all the flights, and all the flights are accounted for. As incoming flights, either internationally or the flights that are currently still in the air - we'll be dealing with those case by case.

SHIVARAM: The secretary also said that he does not think this is affecting other countries. He did have some information that was a little unclear, though. He added that there are two places in the U.S. that were not affected by this outage, this communications outage, but he couldn't quite share more details about that. So that part of this is a little bit unclear and, I think, underscores that there's still a lot of information that's coming in.

PFEIFFER: Interesting. I guess we'll find out later whether he means continental U.S. or otherwise. We'll try to answer that question for our listeners later. Did he give any details about what steps are underway to try to resolve this?

SHIVARAM: Yeah. So he said the first thing officials are working on is trying to restore communications to the full extent, make sure that all flights are on the ground. But no specific timeline was given here, Sacha. He was asked if this whole process was going to be, you know, a matter hours. Are people going to be stuck on tarmacs? Is it going to take days, months? He didn't really have an exact answer to that. All he said is that it's going to take some time. And he said this isn't going to be turned around within the hour. It's just going to take some time, and that part is still a little bit unclear as well.

PFEIFFER: Deepa, as I've been reading about this over the past 30 minutes, I saw some reporting that said there was some new system, possibly an AI-driven system, that was rolled out earlier this week by the FAA. Do you know anything?

SHIVARAM: Yeah. So at at this stage, the secretary said that this outage today is not connected to this AI system, and I'll just explain that really quickly. The FAA rolled out an AI air traffic tool nationwide earlier this week, and that tool is built to help assist with air traffic management. It was already piloted in D.C., actually, in September, and then this week, it was applied nationwide. The secretary said, though, that at this stage, they don't think those two things are connected. He also was asked about the Microsoft outage that happened yesterday and if there was any possible connection to that and what's going on today. And he said he didn't see any reason to connect those two situations.
PFEIFFER: Has President Trump weighed in on this at all?

SHIVARAM: We have not heard from the president yet. I have been refreshing his social media feed to try and see if we will hear from him imminently. He has been briefed on this, and the secretary said that, you know, everybody's involved with this right now. It takes the FAA, obviously. The transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, has been speaking with the president, the State Department. He called the situation unprecedented when you have something like this going on. I will say, in terms of Trump's travel plans, he is expected to stay in Washington this weekend, so no imminent travel for him, but he is planning on Monday to depart for Asia, where he'll be going to the Philippines and China for two summits.
PFEIFFER: You know, Deepa, I am supposed to fly tonight. I'm now bracing...
SHIVARAM: Oh.
PFEIFFER: ...Myself for probably not being...
SHIVARAM: My goodness.
PFEIFFER: ...Able to fly tonight. So I have so many questions. And I have a few I want to ask you that you actually may not know. Please feel free to say, I don't know.
SHIVARAM: Yeah.

PFEIFFER: We know they're grounded, and you touched on this, but do we know if planes that are actually in the air are going to be brought down, they have to get out of the air? Or that's a case-by-case situation?

SHIVARAM: Yeah. So that's, like, kind of a split ticket right now. The secretary did say that they're working on getting all flights grounded. So I think that's something that's in the process of happening. The split ticket that I referred to, I think, when it comes to international flights that are incoming - that is being treated as a case-by-case basis.
PFEIFFER: And in terms of where the planes who might have to come down quickly have to go, that's...
PFEIFFER: ...Just the challenge that air traffic controllers deal with. How do we get them down? Where do we put them?

SHIVARAM: Yes. So when they talk about this communications outage, I believe that the secretary said they're still able to communicate with certain planes that are in the air and things like that. And so the process of getting everybody on the ground sounds like it's obviously very complicated. The specifics on which communications elements here are, you know, up in the air, for lack of a better word and unclear - that part is sort of just broadly being spoken as a widespread telecommunications issue.

PFEIFFER: So I imagine a lot of people stuck in airports, a lot stuck in tarmacs. If people are trying to decide whether to go to the airport, maybe call your airline, but I'm sure they're overwhelmed by calls right now.

SHIVARAM: Yes. It sounds like the information is a little unclear, especially when it comes to grounding flights versus departing flights. I don't think there's been guidance that's been issued on that quite yet.
PFEIFFER: Thank you for that. That's NPR White House correspondent Deepa Shivaram.
SHIVARAM: Thank you.

nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/alaska-senate-.headline: Alaska Senate Race Between Dan Sullivan and Mary Peltola Still Counting Votes
nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/alaska-senate-.author: Tim Balk

paragraphs.text: Mary Peltola, a Democrat, widened her lead over Senator Dan S. Sullivan, a Republican, in the latest vote tally in Alaska’s Senate race, but the election remained uncalled on Friday as the count continued.
If neither candidate wins an outright majority, the race will be decided next week by ranked-choice tabulation.

Ms. Peltola had 49.8 percent of the vote and led Mr. Sullivan by nearly four percentage points in incomplete results as of Friday night. She is on track to eventually prevail, according to a New York Times analysis.
The race between Mr. Sullivan, a two-term incumbent, and Ms. Peltola, a former congresswoman, is the only Senate battle still uncalled in a midterm cycle that featured sweeping Democratic victories.
A spokesman for Mr. Sullivan, Nate Adams, said on Friday night after the latest release of results: “We’re still waiting for every ballot to be counted. And we’ll see what happens from there.”

The delay in Alaska is in part because of the time the state allows for mail ballots to be received and counted and in part because of the state’s unique ranked-choice system. Mr. Sullivan and Ms. Peltola faced two other candidates after emerging from a nonpartisan primary in August.

In Alaska’s ranked-choice voting system, voters can rank the candidates on the ballot in order of preference. If no candidate gets over 50 percent of the first-choice votes, the candidate with the fewest votes is eliminated and their supporters’ second-choice votes are counted. The tabulation continues until two candidates are left; the candidate with more votes wins.

In Alaska, Ms. Peltola and Mr. Sullivan contended with Gerald L. Heikes, a Republican, and Dan J. Sullivan, an unaffiliated candidate with a similar name to the Republican senator. Mr. Heikes and Dan J. Sullivan have combined to win about 4 percent of the vote so far.

Democrats had recruited Mr. Heikes and Dan J. Sullivan onto the ballot in an effort to dilute Senator Sullivan’s vote share. The Times analysis found that among voters who picked Dan J. Sullivan as their first choice, more selected Ms. Peltola as their second choice than picked Senator Sullivan.

Ms. Peltola, a centrist whose campaign slogan was “fish, family and freedom,” would be the first Alaska Native elected to the Senate. She would also be the first Democrat elected to the Senate from Alaska in nearly two decades.

Democrats, riding widespread voter frustration with high prices in President Trump’s second term, have won 55 Senate seats in the midterms, securing the largest majority held by either party since President Barack Obama’s first term.

The president’s war in Iran and his tariff fight with Canada adversely affected Alaska, where voters faced particularly high gasoline prices. Senator Sullivan decided to campaign with Mr. Trump, despite the president’s poor approval ratings, in a bid to activate conservative Republican voters.
Mr. Trump won Alaska by about 14 percentage points in 2024, but the state has been gradually shifting left in presidential elections over the last quarter-century.
If Ms. Peltola were to win the Senate race, it would give Democrats 56 seats in the chamber, more than they have captured in any election since Mr. Obama won the presidency in 2008.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqx2wyvyr3zzo.headline: What we know about the longest US nationwide flight ground stoppage since 9/11
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cqx2wyvyr3zzo.author: Grace Eliza Goodwin

paragraphs.text: The US Federal Aviation Administration has lifted the longest nationwide ground stop of flights since the 11 September 2001 terrorist attacks.
The FAA said Friday's stoppage, which lasted more than four hours, was "due to extraordinary circumstances" from a communication issue affecting all air traffic control centres.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of an attack and that everybody was safe.
Here's what we know.
How many flights were affected?
The ground stop led to more than 8,500 delayed and nearly 8,000 cancelled flights on Friday, according to FlightAware.
The FAA's initial announcement at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) said all flights departing within the US would be grounded until further notice.
More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air at the time. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.
Hours later, some flights were allowed to take off from San Francisco International airport.
The Federal Aviation Administration opened skies again at until 20:15 EST.
What about international flights?
All US-bound air traffic from Eurocontrol member states was suspended "on request of the FAA due to technical issues", according to Eurocontrol's website.
There are 42 Eurocontrol member states, including dozens of EU nations, the UK, Ukraine, and Turkey, as well as Israel and Morocco.
Australia's largest international airport, Sydney, grounded all US-bound flights until further notice.
Air Canada cancelled flights between the US and Canada.
When will normal service resume?
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a news conference on Friday night that the outage would cause a ripple effect for a few days.
"It's going to take us some time to unwind what's happened this afternoon," Duffy said.
Tens of thousands of people were stranded in airports around the country, many of them "without any knowledge of where they're going to sleep tonight", Duffy said.
Delta Air Lines and United Airlines said they were resuming operations.
American Airlines said it was "focused on operating as many remaining flights as possible this evening". JetBlue said it would resume flights on Saturday morning.
What caused the ground stop?
Duffy said a legacy air traffic control communications system became overloaded.
"So this is analogue telecom. Our switches, our routers actually got overloaded with data and they went down," Duffy said.
He said this had affected communications and radar. The system needs a complete overhaul, he said, estimating a $50 billion price tag.
"It's going to continue to fail," he said.
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told the news conference said they had seen "zero evidence" it was a cyber-attack.
He also ruled out any link to the global Microsoft outage that began on Thursday.
Mullin said the introduction of some new technology into an old air traffic control system had overwhelmed it.
Both cabinet secretaries insisted the public was never in danger during the stoppage.
When was the last ground stop?
It was only the second such nationwide stoppage since the immediate aftermath of the al-Qaeda plane hijackings of 11 September 2001.
"This looks like the worst since 9/11, but clearly not on that scale," Dr Guy Gratton, an associate professor of aviation at Cranfield University, told BBC Verify.
Dr Gratton pointed to a US grounding in 2023 due to a failure in the Notice to Air Missions (Notam) system.
"That lasted 1 hour and 52 minutes, delayed about 9,500 flights and cancelled about 1,300," he said.
The 2023 outage meant air traffic safety notices could no longer be published, and flights were grounded until that system was restored.
But Friday's incident lasted longer than the 2023 event.

npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-6040388/what-we.headline: What we know about the FAA nationwide ground stop
npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-6040388/what-we.author: Joel Rose

paragraphs.text: SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

The U.S. air travel system is slowly getting back off the ground. The Federal Aviation Administration has lifted the rare nationwide ground stop it issued earlier today, citing telecommunications failure. That grounded thousands of planes at airports across the country, stranding millions of passengers. NPR's transportation correspondent Joel Rose is here. We've been talking all afternoon and evening trying to sort this out. Joel, now we have a little bit of a resolution, but not really. What's the latest?

JOEL ROSE, BYLINE: Yeah. We just heard from the transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, that, as you said, the airspace has reopened. The ground stop is lifted. But it's going to take some time to get this hourslong - to get through the backlog of canceled and delayed flights. And it's going to take even longer to figure out, apparently, what happened here.

During the news conference, Duffy said that investigators are still trying to understand exactly what the problem was. Duffy blamed the - Duffy cited intermittent communications, intermittent radar and blamed this on outdated air traffic control equipment that was overloaded with data. We have old switches, old routers, he said. It's an old system that went down. It got overloaded. Here's more of what Duffy said.
(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)
UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: We're getting very little information. Our pilot's been great and has been giving us updates every 15 minutes, which has been really helpful and reassuring.
DETROW: I think we had the wrong tape there, Joel. But...
ROSE: That's the wrong cut. Well, you got...
DETROW: Yeah, yeah, keep going.
ROSE: I'll tell you more about Secretary Duffy.
DETROW: Sure.

ROSE: So he spent a lot of this press conference blaming old gear that failed. But when reporters pushed and asked for clarity on exactly what went wrong today, he wasn't able to give them a whole lot of specifics. He pivoted again and again to pushing for more money to rebuild the nation's air traffic control system, which has been a big priority for this administration but was - we just don't - we still have only Duffy's word that this was the old gear that failed. We don't have a lot of detail on what it was.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was at this press conference too. He said, there's no indication that this was a cyber attack, but he could not rule that out entirely - also started the press conference by saying that this outage is not related to the Microsoft outage that knocked out Outlook and some other services yesterday.

DETROW: Yeah, I feel like I had a lot of questions watching that briefing, as did many other people. And meanwhile, there's people all over the country trying to get home. Our reporter at Washington National Airport, Ava Berger, says she is hearing announcements that the hold's has been lifted, but the announcements are saying - urging people to please be patient. About half the board there is red with canceled flights. But she said people are now starting to optimistically slowly go back to their gates to see if their plane's ever going to leave. I mean, Joel, what is the situation like on the ground at other airports around the country?

ROSE: This is a mess, and it's going to be a mess for days. I mean, we've canceled - airlines have canceled thousands of flights. Thousands more are delayed. Planes are out of position. Crews are out of position. This is, you know, imagine if you had a giant blizzard at every airport in the country all at once.
DETROW: Ooh.
ROSE: You know, it's like the whole system is scrambled, and it's going to take days, optimistically...
DETROW: Yeah.
ROSE: ...Before we are back to normal in the U.S. aviation system.
DETROW: We've got about 10 seconds left. Remind us how rare something like this is.

ROSE: Very unusual. This is the second nationwide groundstop since September 11. The most recent was in 2023, and that one only lasted less than 2 hours. So this now appears to be the longest nationwide groundstop since September 11 of 2001.
DETROW: NPR's Joel Rose, thanks so much.
ROSE: You bet.

cnbc.com/2026/11/14/nvidia-jensen-huang-.headline: Companies love a ‘rockstar’ CEO. Until they depend on one
cnbc.com/2026/11/14/nvidia-jensen-huang-.author: Spriha Srivastava

paragraphs.text: When Jensen Huang quit, it struck me how quickly the conversation shifted from his departure to whether Nvidia could manage without him.

It wasn't about whether the company had the technology, customers or talent to keep growing, but whether anyone else could do what Huang had been doing for the business. That made me wonder: did investors believe in Nvidia, or just Huang?

The company is hardly short of capable people. Interim CEO and Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has been with Nvidia since 2013. Nvidia has experienced engineers, established customer relationships and a leading position in the artificial intelligence chip market.
But, listening to guests on CNBC this week, I noticed how much of their concern was about the influence Huang had built outside Nvidia.

On Friday, just a day after Huang quit, Dylan Patel of SemiAnalysis told CNBC's "Squawk Box Asia" how Huang would persuade executives at smaller companies that make critical components to commit capacity to Nvidia. This helped it secure "the majority of supply chain capacity," he said.

Without Huang, competitors could try to persuade those suppliers to allocate more capacity to them, Patel argued. And so the big question is, how much of Nvidia's advantage comes from its technology and how much comes from the relationships Huang built?
A rockstar CEO

There are obvious benefits to elevating CEOs to be rockstars. They can attract investors, open doors and give a company a new identity. A charismatic leader attracts attention, reassures investors and makes a company's strategy easier to sell.

Huang was particularly good at this. He helped shape the conversation about where AI was heading and made Nvidia central to it. Donning his trademark leather jacket, Huang took to stages around the world, courting world leaders to lay out his vision and explain why Nvidia would be at its center.
Before Huang resigned, Eric Ross told "Squawk Box Asia" that Huang "is the company."
That may sound like an endorsement, but it also helps explain why his departure has raised so many questions.

Bernstein's Stacy Rasgon made an interesting distinction on the same program, also before Huang's departure. Nvidia had capable executives who could keep the business running, he said. What was harder to replace was Huang's vision.
"They need a visionary like that," he said.
But for a company whose valuation reflects not just what it sells but expectations of what AI could become, replacing that vision may prove harder than replacing the CEO.
Duncan Clark pointed to another part of Huang's job. He had become a bridge between Silicon Valley, Asia and Washington, and one of the most prominent voices for the wider AI industry.
"I don't think you can replace him with one individual," Clark said on "Access Middle East" on Friday. Replacing him with multiple people is "going to take time, and it won't be the same," he added.

That distinction may be important. Nvidia's board has begun a search for a permanent CEO and said it will consider both internal and external candidates. But whoever takes the job may not personally assume every role Huang had come to play around the company. Some of his responsibilities and relationships could end up being spread across Nvidia's broader leadership team.

For now, the board is emphasizing continuity. New chair Harvey Jones said Kress is backed by an experienced leadership team and that Nvidia expected its operations, customer commitments and product roadmap to continue without interruption. Kress, meanwhile, pointed to Nvidia's people and leadership team as strengths as the company moves forward.
Governance risk
Other boards will be watching, particularly those that have allowed their CEOs to become the face of everything their companies do.
When a charismatic leader is the only person outsiders hear from, it becomes harder to convince them that anyone else can take over. There is also the question of accountability.

Clark described Nvidia's situation as a governance failure. And my colleague, "Squawk Box Europe" anchor Steve Sedgwick, raised a similar point on Friday about how corporate America has approached ESG.

Much of the political debate has focused on its environmental component, Steve said. President Donald Trump has repeatedly attacked environmental and climate policies using phrases such as "green scam." But Steve questioned whether the governance element has been overlooked, particularly at some of America's biggest technology companies.
"When you have a 'Rockstar' CEO you need way more governance, NOT less," he said, citing his recent conversations with CEOs and senior executives.

His point was that powerful leaders can come to believe the normal rules don't apply to them. Without strong governance to challenge them and prepare for their departure, the consequences for a company can be far greater.

Linda Ford, chief executive of The Chartered Governance Institute in the U.K., said Nvidia showed what could happen "when a company's leadership is built around one person." She noted that Nvidia had never previously had a board chair, adding: "A high-profile leader can be an asset, but the board needs to work hard to protect its independence and provide the scrutiny shareholders are entitled to expect."
And that gets to the bigger issue. How easily can a board challenge a CEO who has delivered extraordinary success, particularly when investors have come to see that person as indispensable?
Companies spend years putting leaders in front of investors and customers and making them central to the business. But how much effort goes into making sure the company can function without them?
Nvidia now has to show that the business Huang built can stand on its own. Other boards might want to ask themselves whether they could say the same.

npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-6040397/stuck-o.headline: Stuck on the tarmac without information: Travelers share their ground stop experiences
npr.org/2026/11/13/nx-s1-6040397/stuck-o.author: Erika Ryan

paragraphs.text: Stuck on the tarmac without information: Travelers share their ground stop experiences Passengers stuck on airplanes on tarmacs across the country during the FAA ground stop on Friday share their stories.
Transportation
Passengers stuck on airplanes on tarmacs across the country during the FAA ground stop on Friday share their stories.
SCOTT DETROW, HOST:
When today's FAA ground stop was announced, thousands of planes at airports across the country were on the tarmac with passengers on board. We spoke with one of them, Regina Heirlig (ph).

REGINA HEIRLIG: I am at the Dallas Fort Worth airport right now, and I'm trying to go to San Diego. I flew out of BWI in Baltimore this morning and connecting in Dallas Fort Worth, trying to go to San Diego. I'm trying to help a family member who had an emergency, and so I need to get there, and I hope it's today, but I'm not feeling really optimistic about it at this point.
SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:
We also heard from Gillian Karen (ph).

GILLIAN KAREN: I'm at O'Hare, and I'm going to LaGuardia. We boarded normal time, everything normal, sat on the tarmac for quite some time. And then flight attendant comes over the speaker saying there's a nationwide grounding.
DETROW: Allison Frankel (ph) said she was in a bit of an information vacuum.

ALLISON FRANKEL: You know, it's hard sitting here without information, so we're all looking for information and guidance from the government and for as much information as we can from news reporters. But at the end of the day, you know, we all want to stay safe, so grateful, at least, to be on the ground and safe.
PFEIFFER: And as we were talking to Gillian Karen, she got some news.
KAREN: Oh, wait, sorry. There's - hold on, they're...
UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: (Inaudible). Turn off seatbelts.
KAREN: Oh, OK. We are at the gate.
