cnbc.com/2026/11/14/ecuador-biodiversity.headline: Ecuador wants to monetize its biodiversity — while still drilling for oil
cnbc.com/2026/11/14/ecuador-biodiversity.author: Lucy Handley

paragraphs.text: Ecuador, known for its "megadiverse" Galapagos Islands, Amazon rainforest, Andes and Pacific coast, wants to protect its natural landscapes for years to come — but it faces a tricky balancing act.

As well as preserving its nature, the South American country also plans to capitalize on its critical minerals and continue to extract oil from parts of the Amazon — both of which have led to protests from Indigenous and environmental groups.

One way Ecuador is planning to channel funds into its nature is via new financial tools, such as "debt-for-nature" swaps and its first sovereign green bond. It is also aiming to raise its environmental profile on the global stage by hosting the U.N.'s biodiversity summit, known as COP18, in 2028.

Ecuador, which uses the U.S. dollar, is no stranger to green finance. In March, IDB Invest, the private-sector arm of the Inter-American Development Bank, and Ecuadorian lender Banco Bolivariano issued a $120 million biodiversity bond to back conservation projects. The government also completed two swaps in 2023 and 2024 — deals in which a country's debt is refinanced on better terms in exchange for commitments to spend the savings on conservation. Together, they freed up about $1.1 billion for conservation in the Amazon and Galapagos Islands.

We are being careful on that balance between biodiversity and natural resources use, renewables or not renewables, and it's a delicate matterJuan Carlos BlumMinister of Environment and Energy, Ecuador

Juan Carlos Blum, Ecuador's minister of environment and energy, said the country hopes to issue sovereign green bonds for the first time in 2027, to raise finance to protect its coastal and mountainous regions and the people whose livelihoods depend on them. The government is looking to the European Union for advice on such instruments, he said. The bloc set green bond standards in 2024.

For Blum, one of the challenges is public awareness. "A lot of us are not aware of how we depend on nature, how we depend on the biodiversity, how vulnerable we all are towards climate," he told CNBC by video call.
Oil and mining
Another challenge for Ecuador, as it looks to protect its biodiversity, is its reliance on oil.

The country is a significant oil producer in Central and South America and in October, the government announced plans to open up new tenders for oil exploration in parts of the Amazon, according to local media reports. The news was reportedly met with criticism from Indigenous leaders, who strongly oppose the plans.

"We are being careful on that balance between biodiversity and natural resources use, renewables or not renewables, and it's a delicate matter," Blum said. "That's my day-to-day reality, dealing with balancing this."

About 80% of Ecuador's energy was generated from oil and oil products in 2024, according to the International Energy Agency, while about two-thirds of its electricity was produced using hydroelectric power.
Cracking down on illegal mining is a focus for Blum, who told CNBC he was aware of the environmental impact of legal mining, but that illegal mining was a far bigger problem.
Biodiversity credits

At Ecuador's first Bio Summit held Nov. 4 to Nov. 6 in Quito — an event aimed at helping the country's natural assets "enter the global financial system" — a new way of monetizing nature was introduced.

Marcelo Salame, the event's president, told CNBC he is working on a project to bring so-called biodiversity credits to the country for the first time, to "preserve and monetize" a 260-hectare, or 640-acre, area of the Prosperina forest owned by ESPOL University in the port city of Guayaquil.
That can be potentially dangerous because then you have people that are optimizing for this one metric at the expense of all the other thingsJerry TothThird Millennium Alliance
Salame said biodiversity is "multidimensional," with credits reflecting a whole ecosystem rather than carbon emissions alone.

Biodiversity credits work in a similar way to the carbon credits that large companies buy to meet sustainability goals, but track a range of measures such as the number of species in a given area or tree canopy cover, with the money raised funneled back into nature protection.

But whereas carbon credits can be used to offset emissions, biodiversity credits cannot. "It's all about funding verified nature outcomes and not, to date at least, compensating for damage," Martin Vaquié, co-founder of Berlin-based Bloomlabs, a company that tracks the biodiversity market, told CNBC.

Jerry Toth, a conservationist and co-founder of Ecuador-based Third Millennium Alliance, a nonprofit that aims to protect the "last remnants" of Ecuador's Pacific Forest, told CNBC that carbon markets can reduce the ecological value of a forest to a single metric: how many tons of carbon it stores.

"That can be potentially dangerous because then you have people that are optimizing for this one metric at the expense of all the other things," he said. Toth hopes biodiversity credits can capture the nuances of an ecosystem.
Regenerative cacao

Toth also runs chocolate maker To'ak — which made headlines for producing the "world's most expensive chocolate bar" — using ancient Nacional cacao grown in Ecuador's Manabí province and processed in Quito.

Third Millennium Alliance works with farmers to restore degraded land by planting cacao in the shade of taller trees, and To'ak pays them around $1.20 per pound of cacao, about double the current market price, Toth said.
Ensuring that chocolate production does not deplete nature is "the key question," Toth said. "Our goal at the outset was, how do we use chocolate to reverse deforestation?"

Ecuador recognizes its "immense" ecological and biological resources, Toth said. "It's still trying to figure out how to … capture that value in a way that makes sense both for people in Ecuador and for the ecosystem."

engadget.com/2316792/faa-flights-resume-.headline: FAA Allows Flights To Resume After Hours-Long Ground Stop Across The US
engadget.com/2316792/faa-flights-resume-.author: Mariella Moon

paragraphs.text: Transport secretary Sean Duffy blamed the USA's 'incredibly old air traffic control system.'

The Federal Aviation Administration has lifted a nationwide ground stop in the US that brought all flights to a halt for hours, starting in the afternoon of November 13. Hundreds of flights were canceled, thousands that were already flying had been diverted and millions of passengers were stranded as the ground stop went on. After the FAA lifted the suspension at 8:15PM Eastern time, transportation secretary Sean Duffy held a press conference, blaming old equipment — and the Congress' unwillingness to fund their upgrades — for what happened.

Duffy explained that the USA's "incredibly old air traffic control system" malfunctioned. The US still uses TDM telecom, which is a legacy analog telecommunications technology, to transmit information between facilities. Duffy said that its routers got "overloaded with data," and by 3:36PM on the 13th, they started transmitting inconsistent information. The secretary said the equipment that had already been replaced weren't affected, only the old ones. He also clarified that the US didn't lose all communications and radar, but the FAA still decided to ground flights out of an abundance of caution.

"It's going to continue to fail," Duffy told reporters about the country's air traffic control system, according to the New York Times. "How many times does this have to happen for Congress to give the money to fix it?" The FAA has only issued ground stops thrice this century, and this was the second longest after the 9/11 attacks. While the Congress has already given the FAA $12.5 billion to modernize the country's air traffic facilities, Duffy has been trying to secure $30 billion more.

Markwayne Mullin, the secretary of Homeland Security, appeared with Duffy at the conference and said that there was no indication that the communication issues were caused by a cyberattack. Still, he said his agency was "still looking," and Homeland Security is "not going to rule it out." In addition, Mullin clarified that the incident wasn't related to the lengthy outage that took out Microsoft's services for over 24 hours.

cbsnews.com/news/alaska-governor-jkt-jon.headline: Alaska elects Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, the first Democrat governor since 1998

paragraphs.text: November 14, 2026 / 2:11 AM EST / CBS/AP
Alaska voters have elected a Democrat for governor for the first time since 1998, part of a national midterm elections wave that gave the party sweeping wins in state governments across the country.

Former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republicans, including one endorsed by President Trump. His victory means Democrats will control the governor's office in 30 states, including several they flipped after years of Republican control in places such as Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Texas.

Kreiss-Tomkins, often referred to as JKT, completed a political comeback three years after leaving the state House. He traveled throughout Alaska to build his coalition and focused on affordability, advocated for full funding of public schools and called for all oil and gas producers to pay corporate income tax. He also sought a moratorium on new data centers until state lawmakers pass regulations for their development.

He said Alaska had become "broken" under eight years of outgoing Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy and needed a change. He cited among other issues a state ferry system that he said has been left in shambles, with routes to many communities cut drastically. The ferry is a key mode of transportation for southeast Alaska communities not connected by roads, some of which also have limited air service.
Kreiss-Tomkins, 37, emphasized a willingness to work across party lines and said he wanted a Cabinet with Republicans, Democrats and independents.

"If they're competent, if they're service-minded, if they're entrepreneurial, if they're problem-solvers, you're on the team. Game on," he said during a candidate forum last month. "Let's go, and let's get Alaska back on track."

Republican U.S. Sen. Lisa Murkowski, who has at times been at odds with her party, including Mr. Trump, endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins a week before the election. She said Kreiss-Tomkins "understands that governing requires listening to people with different perspectives and finding common ground to solve the problems all of us face."
Three former governors including Democrat Tony Knowles, independent Bill Walker and Republican Frank Murkowski, the senator's father, also endorsed him.

In a statement declaring victory earlier Friday, Kreiss-Tomkins said voters wanted change and "a government that works across party lines to move Alaska forward. Our administration will not waste a single day getting to work to solve problems for Alaska." He said his campaign had more than 10,000 donors.
Why the Alaska and Mississippi Senate races remain too close to call

theguardian.com/travel/2026/nov/14/eurot.headline: UK-EU breakthrough will allow airport-style checks at Eurotunnel to avoid border ‘chaos’
theguardian.com/travel/2026/nov/14/eurot.author: Lisa O’Carroll

paragraphs.text: Airport-style passport and fingerprinting controls are to be introduced at Eurotunnel in an attempt to prevent “short-term and long-term chaos” in Folkestone and Calais.

In a breakthrough for travellers, the European Commission has agreed to a new system in which an “eagle eye” camera system, already used in Rome and Paris airports to supervise fingerprinting and facial imaging, will be used at the border between the UK and France.
Yann Leriche, the chief executive of Getlink, the Eurotunnel owner, said it had tried to replicate the “airport experience” but wanted to go much further.

Instead of getting out of the car and getting biometrics taken at a terminal building, holidaymakers and business travellers will now be greeted with special drive-through terminals in Folkestone and Calais.

Both sides are now equipped with 120 kiosks under the case of an eagle-eye camera that will be monitored by police, similar to e-gates at airports where police are not physically present at each gate.

In the coming weeks, Leriche will meet UK and French authorities presenting a 40-page proposal to allow Eurotunnel to become a “laboratory” for an “intelligent border” using emerging tech and lessons learned from the US and Singapore.

The entry and exit system (EES) requires all third-country citizens including British passport holders to submit fingerprints and facial images as they enter and exit the Schengen area, but has been delayed for years.
EES was supposed to be active across the EU by 9 September, but nine of the 27 EU member states, including France, have yet to be deploy it fully because of continued technical issues.
It has always been a logistical nightmare for Eurotunnel and a potential cause of miles-long tailbacks at the approach to the terminal.

Originally, Getlink had planned to use a tablet to hand to the passengers in their cars to allow them to self-fingerprint and capture a facial image. It also looked at a system involving passengers parking up and going into the terminal to get fingerprinting.
But both models would have required the physical presence of police officers for first-time fingerprinting.

Leriche said: “We told the authorities: it is going to be a mess. Many people are going to the wrong place and you can’t have police jumping from one place to the next to solve the issues. It would also means customers would have a bad experience, particularly at peak time.
“This is not something people in airports experience, but nobody approached this before, thinking we could have an airport experience at the border here. But we said: why not?”

He said that after “many, many discussions” with the European Commission and the French authorities, finally they were “authorised” to trial “eagle-eye cameras” at each kiosk. “The French authorities are also on board because for them it is more efficient, too, so we are all aligned on the trial,” he said.
The trial will last two years, but Eurotunnel hopes the experiment will become permanent.

Each car will be able to pull up to an individual kiosk, with two stands per vehicle to read passports and take fingerprints and facial images. “It will prevent the chaos in the long term and the short term and if the experiment works, as hopefully it will, then it will become permanent,” said Leriche.
He said the company had been inspired by visits to the US/Mexico border controls, where drivers and passengers remain in their cars.

The requirement of having a police officer present each time a first-time passenger, or “primo” as they are known, submits their fingerprints was designed as a safeguard against subterfuge. Criminals, for example, could use a fellow passenger for example with a “clean skin” fingerprint.

Leriche said he had no idea when the system will be introduced by France. “It has been delayed and delayed and delayed, but our kiosks are there, they are can function but the connection with the French system is still not working. It is a question was are asking all the time.”
This week it emerged that the EU had filed a lawsuit against IBM and two other companies involved in the implementation of EES.

cbssports.com/college-football/news/okla.headline: Oklahoma AD Roger Denny blasts SEC after game vs. Ole Miss pushed to Sunday under threat of forfeit
cbssports.com/college-football/news/okla.author: Brandon Marcello

paragraphs.text: Nov 14, 2026 at 2:05 am ET • 3 min read

Oklahoma's efforts to block the SEC from rescheduling its home matchup against Ole Miss to Sunday ended in defeat after a nationwide flight groundstop and a Friday night dispute with conference officials.

SEC commissioner Greg Sankey moved the Sooners' home game against No. 19 Ole Miss in Norman, Oklahoma, from Saturday afternoon to Sunday at 1 p.m. ET (noon CT) a decision Oklahoma athletics director Roger Denny said came "over our strong objection." When OU attempted to keep the game Saturday, Sankey told the school that failing to play at the directed time would result in a forfeit.

"Put simply, this decision isn't fair to our athletes, our institution or to Sooner Nation," Denny said in a statement released early Saturday. "But we've been given no other choice. We are obligated to play the game when directed, but we remain steadfast in our belief that the wrong outcome was reached this evening."

Ole Miss administrators couldn't secure a charter flight from Tupelo, Mississippi, to Oklahoma City after the groundstop, and the earliest they could book another flight was Saturday at 4:20 p.m., a team spokesperson told CBS Sports.

The trouble began Friday afternoon, when air travel across the country stopped. The Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports shortly before 3 p.m. CT after communication problems hit multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers, the facilities that manage high-altitude traffic between airports. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy blamed switches and routers that became overloaded and shut down after they began producing inconsistent data. Thousands of flights were delayed or canceled before the FAA lifted the order at 7:15 p.m. CT, more than four hours after it began. It was only the third full groundstop in the country's history.

Most college football teams do not travel to game sites until the day before games, leaving many scrambling after the groundstop was ordered. All games in the FBS managed to stay on Friday and Saturday, with Ole Miss' trip to Oklahoma the only exception. Kick times across the country were slightly altered, including No. 2 Utah's game at No. 23 Arizona, which is now set to begin at 10:30 p.m. ET on Saturday after the Utes were unable to leave Salt Lake City Friday.

Ole Miss and Auburn were among four SEC teams grounded for several hours. Auburn's game at Mississippi State was moved to 3:15 p.m. CT Saturday as the Tigers left an airport and booked buses for a four-hour road trip to Starkville. No. 6 Texas was delayed until after 10 p.m. CT until boarding a flight to play No. 21 LSU on Saturday.
Every other traveling SEC team found a way, including Tennessee, which managed to reschedule a flight after the groundstop for its longest road trip of the season at Texas A&M.

Ole Miss players were sent home Friday afternoon and told to return to the football facility that evening for updates. Ole Miss flies out of Tupelo, Mississippi, a 55-minute drive from Oxford, and flies about 90 minutes to Oklahoma City.
"We are continuing to work through our options and coordinate with the appropriate groups regarding both travel and the game," an Ole Miss spokesperson told CBS Sports earlier Friday.
Ole Miss wanted to play Sunday and Oklahoma wanted to keep the game Saturday, CBS Sports reported Friday night. The league sided with the Rebels.

"We were told that Ole Miss explored every avenue to travel to Norman and play on Saturday as planned," Denny said. "But, unlike every other team traveling for competition tomorrow, they were unable to find a solution."
The game had been scheduled for 3:15 p.m. CT Saturday on SEC Network. Television plans for Sunday have not been announced.

"Rescheduling the game has a significant impact, particularly on our fans," Denny said. "Those who have made travel arrangements, accommodations and personal plans around a Saturday game now face unnecessary disruption and hardship. Their time, commitment and investment deserve greater consideration than they were afforded in the conference's decision tonight."
Oklahoma (5-4, 4-4 SEC) is coming off a 23-7 win at Florida in Jason Witten's first game as interim offensive coordinator. The Sooners need one more win to reach bowl eligibility.
Ole Miss (6-3) fell to No. 19 in the College Football Playoff rankings after a 42-7 home loss to now-No. 1 Georgia.
"We will continue to fight in the best interests of OU Athletics and always on behalf of our student-athletes and fans," Denny said.

bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/cke891.headline: Will John McGinn take Kenny Dalglish and Denis Law's joint record for most Scotland goals?
bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/cke891.author: Andrew Petrie

paragraphs.text: As Scotland legend Kenny Dalglish watched one of his records equalled in Scotland's 2-1 win over North Macedonia, another of his feats loomed into view.
The night was supposed to be about Andy Robertson joining Dalglish as Scotland's most-capped man, the Tottenham left-back making his 102nd appearance for his country.
But instead, for the first time, the 75-year-old might be nervous that his crown as one of Scotland men's all-time top goalscorers is wobbling.
That is because, in Scotland's rather humdrum Nations League victory, John McGinn - in his 94th Scotland appearance - took two big strides towards the record.
The Aston Villa midfielder now has 24 goals for his country - six shy of Dalglish's long-standing record of 30, shared with Denis Law.
"It's something that's been in the back of my head," McGinn admitted in the post-match debrief. "If I start climbing that table, it means we've been successful as a team."
Now 32 years old, time is running out for him. But as he pulls level with Hughie Gallacher, one of the Wembley Wizards of folklore, his ambition is clear.
McGinn 'definitely capable' of reaching record
There was a time when talk of this record being toppled seemed laughable. Scotland has produced strikers in recent decades, but none close to Dalglish or Law.
The fact a midfielder might take the title makes McGinn's feat all the more astonishing.

His prowess in front of goal is no secret to the Tartan Army. There was the spell at the end of 2019 where he scored six in three games, his overhead kick against Austria, his late winner against Croatia in 2024.
But of late, his lack of goals and even his performances have had some fans questioning where he fits into the Scotland team.
"It has been a bit of a dry patch for me over the last year on the goal front," McGinn admitted, and he's not wrong.
He failed to find the back of the net for Scotland in 2025, the first time he'd done that since 2020.
But, just as his form at Villa has sky-rocketed, he came up big for his new international head coach Sebastien Pocognoli.
"Isn't it great to have a John McGinn in your team?" former Scotland winger Pat Nevin said on Sportsound. "He's somebody you'd want to have in your team to be taking a penalty for you.
"I'd be surprised if John McGinn doesn't get the goal record now. It might take him another year or two, but he is definitely capable of getting that record."
'The best person I've met in football'
Becoming Scotland's main penalty taker will help, a fact McGinn alluded to coyly post-match.
In his career, he had only taken one spot-kick before this season - scoring for Scotland in the 3-3 draw against Norway back in 2023.
In this campaign he has scored three and missed one, smacking the bar against Fulham on Halloween.

In classic McGinn fashion, he bounced back to slot home against Manchester United the following week, before being caught on ref-cam admitting to the official that he was nervous to take it after his hitting the woodwork.
That jovial, lovable personality has not just won him fans off the pitch. It is clear that his team-mates at both Villa and the national team adore him.
"He's not going to stop until he [gets the record]," said striker Che Adams, who helped set up McGinn's first against North Macedonia.
"Everyone's pleased for him, he's the best person I've met in football. For him to get the recognition he deserves is amazing."
McGinn's iconic status in Scottish football is secure and will not be tarnished if he fails to climb the mountain.

Whether it is being speared by Steven Thompson in training, calling Scotland performances 'jobby', or admitting he would "probably be at Yeovil" were it not for his backside, the midfielder has already won the heart of a nation.

bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/articles/cq7.headline: England v Japan: Warner Dearns on his unlikely route to leading Brave Blossoms
bbc.co.uk/sport/rugby-union/articles/cq7.author: Mike Henson

paragraphs.text: Warner Dearns didn't want to go to Japan. Now, he doesn't want to leave.

A decade ago, Dearns' father Grant got a job as a strength and conditioning coach with top-flight Japanese side NEC Green Rockets, taking the family from New Zealand's North Island to a satellite city outside Tokyo.
For Dearns, like most 14-year-olds, swapping class-mates, countries, continents and cultures didn't appeal.
"I said I didn't want to go," says the second row, who will co-captain Japan against England at Allianz Stadium on Saturday.
"My sister and I wanted to stay with our grandma and grandad [in New Zealand]."
But, reluctantly, they made the trip, with Dearns' mother Tanya, a former New Zealand netballer, giving up her own coaching job to help the family settle in Japan.
"The first year or two took a bit to adapt to, it is a very different culture from New Zealand, and the language barrier didn't help much either," remembers Dearns.
"At high school there was no-one else who spoke English. I was the kid who stood out, the only one with blond curly hair, so it was lots of fun."
There were other reasons that Dearns stood out.
Even as a teenager, he stood 6ft 8in tall and weighed more than 19 stone (120.6kg).
In New Zealand, Deans had been more interested in basketball than rugby. But at Kashiwa Senior High School – one of Japan's strongest rugby-playing schools – they moulded him into a monster prospect.

To supplement his size and galloping, long-legged sprint, Dearns' school coaches introduced gymnastics into his training schedule, having him hurdle team-mates and perform flips, to improve his agility around the pitch.
Away from school, he would hit the gym at his dad's employers, working out alongside the likes of former England full-back Alex Goode.
Given that super-charged rugby education, Dearns progressed fast.
England v Japan
Saturday 14 November, 16:40 GMT
Allianz Stadium, Twickenham
Live on BBC Radio 5 Live, the BBC Sport website and app
Having qualified on residency grounds, he made his Japan debut In November 2021 at just 19.
By France 2023, he was a regular, featuring in all four of the team's matches at the Rugby World Cup.
This past season, he has been a revelation.

He has spent the year back in New Zealand at the Hurricanes on a season's sabbatical, where his bottomless energy, soft hands and line-out prowess helped the Wellington side to their first Super Rugby title in a decade.
Playing alongside All Blacks Jordie Barrett, Ruben Love, Cam Roigard and Peter Lakai, broadened Dearns' horizons once more.
"It was awesome, I got to sit back and see how the boys prepare," Dearns added.
"The All Blacks guys especially lead the way and are part of the leadership group, I got to enjoy playing footy and watch how they do things."
The possibility of Dearns having a more permanent view was raised.

Various figures in New Zealand rugby's scene wondered whether Dearns would be amenable to returning to his homeland, waiting out a three-year Test stand-down requirement and then transferring his allegiance to the All Blacks.
Dearns, now 24, declined.
"It was nothing official, it was all sort of hearsay," he says of the possibility of switching sides.
"I had a couple of people coming up to me asking me if I would ever think about it. It was never an option for me."
Dearns is indebted to Japan for the country's role in his development. But Japan is also now home.
Dearns, who now speaks the language fluently and whose son was born in the country, was moved to tears during his adopted nation's anthem at the last World Cup.
His passion shows in the way he plays too.

On his last visit to Twickenham, back in 2022, Dearns set up a try with a break and offload to scrum-half Naoto Saito. In the teams' most recent meeting, in Tokyo in 2024, he assisted another two, one via a brilliant one-handed grab-and-go in midfield.
On both occasions however, Japan ended up on the wrong end of heavy scorelines.
If they are to shock Twickenham, Dearns will need to marshall an extraordinary forward effort, as well as produce showreel moments.
"It is always a set-piece battle and England do a very good job of scrum and line-out, they are obviously very physical," he says.
Dearns has come a long way. But victory on Saturday would be his biggest step yet.

noahpinion.blog/p/im-feeling-more-optimi.headline: I’m feeling more optimistic about American politics
noahpinion.blog/p/im-feeling-more-optimi.author: Noah Smith

paragraphs.text: “Partisanship is a helluva drug,” as they say. When your preferred party is in power, the sun seems to shine a little brighter, the birds sing a little more sweetly, and there’s a spring in your step as you walk past the homeless encampments and sterile single-family-home-only neighborhoods of your American city. Foreigners from countries where politics is less contentious, like Japan, will never know this joy.

Anyway, this natural partisan sentiment makes it very hard for me to write about developments in American politics. I would like to give you some analysis that’s more informative than “Yay, Democrats won an election!”. I do consider myself a Democrat, after all (even though I’m registered as an Independent). There has never been a point in my entire life when I’d have told you that the Republican presidential candidate was a better pick than the Democrat (though 2012 was fairly close). I regularly bemoan the state of the Democratic Party, but somehow the Republicans always find some way to be Even Worse.

This has been the unfortunate reality for most people in America for years now. Disgust and dissatisfaction with both parties have grown, as both have become more extremist. But there was little they could do except keep voting for the lesser of two evils, while tuning out political news and expressing anger at the whole system. It got so bad that in my New Year’s essay, I even entertained the notion that liberal democracy itself had suffered a generational failure:

To be honest, I still entertain that notion. Reading that essay again, there’s not much I would change. But on the margin, recent events have made me feel more optimistic about where American politics is going.

A lot of this is downstream of the midterm elections. Trump has turned the Republican Party into something truly awful, and it’s refreshing to see America punish the GOP for going along with that transformation:

But my optimism isn’t just about the fact that Democrats won — it’s also about how they won, and what they seem likely to do with their victory. Here I’ve been pleasantly surprised so far. And there are also some scattered signs that our leaders are starting to take our substantive policy challenges more seriously, instead of just relying on partisanship and culture wars. Basically, I see three broad positive trends:
• The Democrats are not becoming extremist at the rate I had feared.
• There is some real bipartisan movement on good policymaking at the federal level.
• The nation is waking up to the problem of corruption, and holding the perpetrators to account.
Liberals, not leftists, are leading the anti-Trump charge

Over the past few years, I’ve watched the emergence of a leftist faction within the Democratic Party, which I’ve likened to MAGA on the right. This faction had its roots in the Bernie insurgency of 2016-2020, but it has grown beyond that. The Palestine movement both invigorated the leftists and radicalized them, shifting the locus of power in left-of-center activism away from Black activists, identitarian movements, and anti-capitalism, and toward explicitly anti-American “decolonial” ideas.
As recently as this summer, I believed that a Democratic victory in the midterms would be led by this hard-left vanguard:
Here’s what I wrote:

Democrats have spent their political capital moving to the left…[They are selecting] candidates who are so far to the left that they end up frightening and/or offending many voters, and then basically daring people to keep voting for the Republicans…When DSA-type candidates were just winning in deep blue cities, it was possible to think that they would remain a small, limited faction within the party. But Francesca Hong is going to be the Democratic nominee in a statewide race. So is Abdul El-Sayed, who, while not a member of the DSA, is closely aligned with them (especially on Israel, which he focuses on a lot)…This, increasingly, is who the Democrats are now.

Well, happily, I was wrong about this. Francesca Hong was actually defeated in the Democratic primary race just a few days later in a stunning upset, showing that even partisan Democrats aren’t sold on the DSA faction.

Even more importantly, the hard left didn’t end up leading the anti-Trump charge in the midterms, as I had expected. Despite the blue wave, most of the high-profile DSA-faction candidates performed significantly worse than their normie Democrat counterparts. Jeff Maurer has great data on this:
And the same voters who powered the big Democratic victories also endorsed a lot of centrist policies at the ballot box. Here’s the Washington Post:

Voters in North Carolina elected a Democratic senator…giving former governor Roy Cooper an overwhelming win. At the same time, they approved three [Republican] measures…The first would add a constitutional requirement for a levy limit on property taxes…The second would cap the state income tax at 3.5 percent…The third would require photo ID for voting…In Wisconsin, Democrat David Crowley won the gubernatorial election…Those same voters approved an initiative…to ban affirmative action in state institutions…Iowa voters elected Democrats as governor and senator while amending their constitution to make it substantially harder to raise state income taxes…Ohio….went blue for Senate and governor. At the same time, two-thirds of voters backed an amendment to require photo ID for voting…Moderates and independents drove Democratic gains in all these places.
Voters in several blue and purple states also approved measures to restrict women’s sports teams by biological sex.

There’s also a general indefinable “vibe shift” in the air. Anecdotally, people I talk to are less ashamed to voice full-throated support for the kind of liberalism that Barack Obama typified in the early 2010s. Meanwhile, liberal influencers online are beginning to push back more strongly on leftist shouters.

And in Congress, the sheer scale of the Democrats’ victory means that the DSA faction will be effectively disempowered. Because marginal victories tend to be won by moderates in purple states, the leadership in both the House and the Senate is likely to be held by moderates like Hakeem Jeffries and Chuck Schumer. This is driving the DSA factionalist types apoplectic with rage:

Note that the knives are already coming out for Jon Ossoff, whose potential as a 2028 presidential contender surged after his massive midterm victory. But who can leftists run against Ossoff? Enthusiasm around AOC has dimmed, and there’s no obvious replacement.

If they fail to find a candidate for 2028, and if Democrats take back the White House with a normie liberal, the leftist faction faces the real possibility that the window of America’s decade of unrest will limp to a close without them. That would, of course, be good for the nation.
Smart policy is starting to win (and “the groups” are starting to lose)

Even moderate politicians, of course, often support unworkable or inadvisable policies. On the Democratic side, the worst problems are anti-development policies at the state and local level. “Progressive” policies have made it prohibitively difficult and/or expensive to build housing, roads, trains, power stations, and transmission lines across much of the country, freezing our built environment in the 1970s. I’ve been loudly complaining about this for years now:

This was a big part of my pessimism about politics. What’s the use of kicking out the Republicans, if the Democrats are just going to decide that “open space” and historic gas stations are more important than giving the middle class a place to live and power for their homes?
Now there are signs that at long last, America’s leaders recognize this problem and are taking action to fix it.

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw4gn0ky2pgdo.headline: Eurovision Song Contest is finally coming to Asia - meet the stars gearing up in Thailand
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/cw4gn0ky2pgdo.author: Jonathan Head

paragraphs.text: Eurovision, the pan-European competition famed for zany gimmicks, slick, sometimes over-the-top staging, the drama of its complex voting system and, occasionally, for outstanding music, celebrates its 70th birthday this year.
And to mark it, the European Broadcasting Union is trying out audiences in Asia.
It's an idea that's been talked about for two decades but never materialised, despite many false starts.
Until now - Eurovision Asia will hold its first grand final in Bangkok, starting at 20:30 ICT (13:30 GMT).

Transferring one of the most successful television formulas that has worked in Europe for 70 years to Asia has not been straightforward, says Sarun 'Note' Kungbunpot, a Eurovision enthusiast and Thai singer who has won several competitions in this region.
"It's still very new in Asia. I'm not sure many people have heard about it yet," he says, adding that he thinks it will take a bit of time for audiences to adjust.
"When we look at contests in Thailand, the Philippines and Korea, we actually compete based on the singer.
"It's all about popularity – fans are looking for their idols. But Eurovision is all about the song, not the singer. I think this needs to be communicated clearly."

Then there is the long history of Eurovision in Europe. It began in 1956 as a project to encourage greater cultural exchanges in a Europe which was trying to forge a common future after two world wars.

This was the very start of the age of mass television ownership, and Eurovision became such a fixture it is now an indelible piece of Europe's shared cultural heritage. It has no such resonance in Asia, and arrives in this region in the digital age, when traditional TV formats are struggling to cut through.

Only 11 countries are taking part in this first Eurovision Asia contest – host Thailand, along with Malaysia, the Philippines, Vietnam, Cambodia, Laos, South Korea, Mongolia, Bangladesh, Nepal and Bhutan.
Asian giants India, China, Japan and Indonesia are noticeably absent, although there are negotiations ongoing to try to get them into next year's contest, assuming there is one.
There have also been problems with the organisation of this event.

A sudden million-dollar (£760,000) budget cut just three weeks before the final meant many of the technicians familiar with staging Eurovision were not brought to Thailand, and there have been a number of staff resignations too.
Eurovision fans - and there are many passionate followers around the world - have noticed, criticising audio and lighting in rehearsal videos.

The contest's unusual voting system will be unfamiliar to Asian audiences. Like in Europe, Eurovision Asia will determine the winner through a 50/50 mix of public voting and national juries from each of the 11 contesting countries, as well as a 12th "rest of the world" category.
Anyone can vote - you get eight votes once you register - but you cannot vote for your own country's contestant and you must give your votes to at least three others.

The public and jury votes are then converted into points. The most popular song among the Bhutanese or Mongolians, for example, will get 12 points from those countries, while the song ranked last will get zero - the famous "nul points".

In Europe, there have long been reports of co-ordinated voting to back neighbours, for example the four Nordic countries voting for each other. This seems less likely in Eurovision Asia, but political differences, for example between Thailand and Cambodia after their border war last year, could influence how their audiences vote.

Filipinos, with their passion for singing, are expected to be enthusiastic participants and the 11 million who live overseas might make a difference. But as most live and work in countries which are not participating, their votes will only go into the "rest of the world" pool.

For Bhutan, with a population of less than a million, this is a rare chance to shine on a global stage, which puts some pressure on 24-year-old Thukten Nyendra, the singer representing the Himalayan kingdom in Bangkok with his song Lhayi Semo (The Angel). Before coming here he had never left his country or been on a plane before.

"I'm not a star. I'm just Nyendra over there," he told the BBC. "Nobody knows me. But Eurovision has given me a huge platform. Actually winning would mean the world to us... If I really make it through all of this, it would mean the entire freaking world to us."
The other characteristic of Eurovision is the song format – no more than three minutes, no more than six people on stage, and no backing band, only taped music.

This encourages performers to prepare elaborate, sometimes outrageous choreography and stunts to impress the audience – think Poland's My Słowianie in 2014 with models in traditional costume churning butter on stage, or the Finnish heavy metal band Lordi donning flamboyant monster outfits in its 2006 entry.

There has also been a long association of Eurovision with LGBTQ+ artists. Eurovision Asia includes Malaysia and Bangladesh – where same-sex activity is illegal – and there are no visible LGBTQ+ elements this year.

Performers have been using the last days of rehearsals before the final to try to make their stage acts as striking as possible. Thinla from Laos has abandoned the short, sequinned dress she wore in the first video of her infectious reggaeton song Bae and is adopting Lao hill-tribe costume for her and her backing dancers.
Perhaps the most ambitious choreography is in Vietnamese singer Tóc Tiên's song Em Tiên ("Fairy Maiden").
It has been exhausting just watching her rehearse the elaborate moves and costume changes for more than an hour at a time.
The entry from Bangladesh's Beatmosphere, Tumi Ele ("You Came"), is unusual as an a cappella and beatboxing performance by six men with little backing music.
The youngest contestant is 19 year-old Carmelle Collado from the Philippines, whose bubbling confidence and strong stage presence in her song Sobra-Sobra ("Too Much") belie her youth.
"I'm actually quite scared because I'm the youngest, but also really happy," she told us.
"The song is about feminine energy. It's about being brave, strong, fierce, and it's about how strong Filipino women are."

Eurovision is famous for putting unknown acts onto a global stage, and introducing musicians who went on to become megastars – think Abba, little known when they won in 1974 with Waterloo, and Celine Dion winning in Ireland in 1988.
Because of the lack of public awareness of Eurovision Asia many of the finalists chosen for this first contest are already well known in their home markets.

Aina Abdul is perhaps the most famous singer in Malaysia, known as much for dramatic costumes as her impressive vocal range. Her song Bluest Sky – which she told us was inspired by her late cat Hiro – is a strong contender to win the contest.

Abdul's spectacular dress, by Malaysian designer Melinda Looi, who has travelled to Bangkok with her, had taken 600 hours to make, she told me. She said its glistening texture, made from materials brought from Italy and China, is meant to represent moving water.

If all goes well on the night, the organisers are hoping this could be the start of an expansion of the hugely successful Eurovision brand into a region which, after all, has half the world's population.

bbc.co.uk/sport/articles/cm4gn9lvlgy2o.headline: Estonia latest country to ban Russian athletes as backlash intensifies
bbc.co.uk/sport/articles/cm4gn9lvlgy2o.author: Dan Roan

paragraphs.text: Estonia has become the latest country to say it will not allow Russian or Belarusian athletes to compete on its territory as a result of the ongoing war in Ukraine.
It comes after Norway, Finland and Canada made similar announcements.
The moves come amid a mounting backlash over the reinstatement of athletes from Russia and Belarus.

In September, the International Ski Federation (FIS) relaxed its rules, saying competitors from the two countries would be granted access to its events "provided that they sign a declaration of neutrality".
They had previously faced more stringent background checks on any voluntary link or paid duty with the military.
Participation remains limited to individual events, with athletes banned from displaying national symbols such as flags, anthems or uniforms.

However, it has now emerged that Estonia's government has written to the FIS, claiming that allowing entry to competitors from Russia and Belarus would undermine the country's support of Ukraine, and present an opportunity for propaganda. It said a ban issued in 2022 will be maintained.

In a statement issued to BBC Sport, the FIS said it "is committed to offering full support to athletes, national ski associations and local organisers - with most of which we have a long-standing relationship - in the process of navigating what we know to be a very complex situation.

"With that said, the Individual Neutral Athlete policy is clear in stating that notwithstanding eligibility, the host country visa and entry policies remain in place and are determined solely by the host country. FIS bears no responsibility for denial of visas or entry to any person granted eligibility under the FIS Individual Neutral Athlete Policy."
On Thursday, Scandinavian neighbours Norway and Finland both said they would also block visas for Russian athletes because of the war in Ukraine.

Norway is preparing to host the cross-country skiing World Cup next month, while Finland is due to stage the figure skating world championships in March. The International Skating Union (ISU) has said it "believes that athletes should not be punished for the actions of their governments in a world where, sadly, many conflicts are ongoing", and that it was "seeking clarifications" from officials in Finland.

This comes in the wake of last month's decision by the Court of Arbitration for Sport (Cas) to overturn a ban of Russia by the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF), a move condemned by the British, German, Finnish and Czech federations.

Russia have been suspended from competing in IIHF events since the country invaded Ukraine in February 2022, but the Russian Ice Hockey Federation (RIHF) then successfully appealed that decision at Cas. The court said that IIHF arguments citing safety and security were "not supported by sufficient evidence", but the Hockey Federation of Ukraine said the ruling caused "special outrage".

The Canadian government has since informed its hockey authorities that it will not issue visas for Russians to play in next month's World Junior Championship, including those who currently play for teams in Canada, as long as the war continues. A number of countries had said they would refuse to play against Russia, if they were allowed to take part.
Despite the controversy, the return of Russia and Belarus to international sport has been gathering pace this year.

In March, several athletes from the two countries were allowed to compete under their national flags at the Winter Paralympics after partial suspensions by the International Paralympic Committee were lifted.
In July, the International Olympic Committee (IOC) provisionally reinstated Russia to its competitions, stating a ban introduced in 2023 after the invasion of Ukraine was "no longer applicable".

However, sports federations can still enforce their own eligibility criteria. While World Gymnastics, World Aquatics and World Boxing have all removed restrictions on Russian athletes competing, a total ban has been maintained by World Athletics.

Last month, it was announced that Moscow will host the 2030 World Weightlifting Championships - the first time an Olympic federation has chosen to stage a global event in Russia since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

engadget.com/2316804/workday-outage-lock.headline: Outage At HR Platform Workday Locks Millions Of Employees Out Of Their Account
engadget.com/2316804/workday-outage-lock.author: Mariella Moon

paragraphs.text: The company placed its system in maintenance mode after discovering an issue.

A widespread Workday outage on the evening of November 13 left employees unable to clock in and out, access their pay info, request for time off or file for benefits. According to San Francisco Chronicle, the human resources platform said it placed some of its systems into maintenance mode to fix an issue it discovered during testing. Specifically, the problem left some information inconsistent, and the company said it could cause errors when users try to access their accounts or complete tasks within its system. There was a spike in reports at Downdetector at around 5:19PM Eastern time, though it has tapered off since then.

It's not quite clear if the outage affected all of Workday's customers. But the company said 11,500 organizations around the world use it for various HR tasks. Its clients include Target, Walmart, Charles Schwab, Nasdaq, Netflix and even the US Department of Energy and NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. The company has apologized for the disruption and said that it's looking for the best way to fix the problem.

livescience.com/health/genetics/links-wi.headline: 'Links with the British royal family would eventually prove crucial': How DNA solved the 70-year mystery of what happened to the executed members of the last Russian imperial family
livescience.com/health/genetics/links-wi.author: Turi King

paragraphs.text: In 1917, the Russian Revolution was in full swing. Tsar Nicholas II had abdicated, and he and his family were exiled to a remote Siberian town. There were plans to get the family to the U.K., but King George V (Nicholas' first cousin) and the British government withdrew their offer of asylum over concerns of the ramifications.

After the Russian Provisional Government was overthrown by the more extreme Bolsheviks in October 1917, Nicholas, his wife, their children and several members of the family's staff were moved to Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg, where, in July 1918, they were executed. Their bodies were hidden and remained lost to time ‪for nearly a century —‬ until modern technology, with some help from the British royal family, unraveled the fascinating story of their disappearance.

In this excerpt from "The Secrets of Our DNA: How Genetics Has Changed the World" (Pegasus Books, 2026), author Turi King, director of the Center for Evolution at the University of Bath, looks back at the incredible story of how DNA was used to solve a major mystery of modern history: What happened to the last members of the House of Romanov?

I was sitting in a lecture theatre at Cambridge University in 1994 when one of my lecturers, Erika Hagelberg, spoke about a new study she had just been involved in. It was the first major case to combine both mitochondrial DNA and DNA fingerprinting to identify human remains: those of the Russian imperial family.
But first I need to take you back to Russia in 1917 and the abdication of the tsar following the Russian Revolution.

The Russian royal family, the Romanovs, had been the reigning imperial dynasty since 1617, and three centuries later, Tsar Nicholas II was on the throne. Nicholas was the cousin of George V, king of the United Kingdom, their mothers being sisters, and had married George's cousin Princess Alix (Alexandra) of Hesse, who was apparently Queen Victoria's favourite grandchild. Nicholas and Alix had five children, four daughters (Olga, Tatiana, Maria and Anastasia) and a son, Alexei.

The tsar and his wife were not well liked by the Russian population and political unrest culminated in the revolution of 1917, when Nicholas was forced to abdicate. The family were kept under house arrest and in 1918 they were moved to Ipatiev House in Yekaterinburg with the royal physician, Dr Botkin, and three of their staff. On the night of 16 July, the family, their doctor and staff were herded into the cellar together and executed. Their bodies were then taken to a secret location and placed in a hastily dug communal grave, doused in sulphuric acid in an attempt to disfigure them and hinder identification, and then covered over, the location of the grave being lost for more than 70 years.

Ironically, the new Russian government had wanted to get the Romanovs out of Russia due to the risk of their becoming a rallying point, but a plan to grant asylum to the Romanovs in the U.K. because of their links with the British royal family fell through, owing to a reluctance on the part of George V to grant it. Yet those links with the British royal family would eventually prove crucial in their identification.

Fast-forward to 1991, when several skeletons were found in a shallow grave some 20 miles from Yekaterinburg. Many of the bones were badly damaged but it was possible to determine, based on examination of the skeletal remains, that there were nine individuals — two short of the 11 killed that night. The faces of the skulls were badly damaged in all of the skeletons, all of them showing evidence of violence either in the form of bullet holes or bayonet wounds or both. Before the genetic study, Russian forensic scientists had used numerous techniques alongside historical data to tentatively identify the remains as some of the members of the Russian royal family, their doctor and servants.

These included examining the bones, to determine approximate age and sex, and some of the teeth, the expensive dental work, incorporating gold, platinum and porcelain, indicating that certain remains must belong to members of an aristocratic family. The team worked out that the two missing individuals would have been two of the children, one of the daughters (while it was hard to determine which one it would be, given how close in age they were, it was thought that it was either Maria or Anastasia) and the son, Prince Alexei.

The Russian chief forensic medical examiner then contacted a team in the U.K., which included Erika, to see if genetic evidence could be used to confirm the identification. The U.K. team used the amelogenin genetic sex test, now part of standard forensic DNA testing, which confirmed the sex of the skeletons (four male and five female bodies), while an early form of DNA profiling showed that there was a family group here — two parents and three children — and four unrelated individuals. So far, so good.

Next, they needed to prove that this was the Russian royal family, and they did this using mitochondrial DNA analysis. As you'll remember, mitochondrial DNA is passed down by a mother to all her children, male and female, but only daughters can pass it on — so if female-line family members of Tsar Nicholas and Tsarina Alexandra could be found and would agree to give a DNA test, their mitochondrial DNA should match that of their royal ancestors. It just so happened that the late Prince Philip, husband of the late Queen Elizabeth, was related to the tsarina through the female line: she was his great-aunt, his maternal grandmother being the sister of the tsarina. He kindly gave a DNA sample.

The testing that they did was standard for the time in that they looked at two regions known as hypervariable regions 1 and 2 (HVR1 and HVR2). You'll remember that mitochondrial DNA has 37 rather crucial genes on it where any "typo" that occurs as the DNA is being copied could have serious consequences if the mutation is deleterious. By contrast, in those parts of the mitochondrial genome that don't code for anything, such as these two hypervariable regions, mutations can occur more freely without necessarily causing issues, meaning that these regions contain much more genetic variation. These are the sections of mitochondrial DNA that scientists began analysing for identification purposes. While it's not as precise as DNA profiling because many thousands of people will all have the same mitochondrial DNA type, it can be very helpful in a case such as this.

When the team sequenced these two regions, Prince Philip's mitochondrial DNA was found to match that of the putative remains of the tsarina and her daughters. Next they found two living female-line relatives of the tsar, descended from his maternal grandmother: a great-great-niece, Princess Xenia Cheremeteff Sfiris, and a first cousin twice removed, James Carnegie, 3rd Duke of Fife. The mitochondrial DNA from these two matched each other perfectly, and they, in turn, matched that of the tsar, except at one base where there was both a match and a mismatch.

This is because the tsar had what's known as a heteroplasmy at this position: some of the mitochondrial DNA sequences showed a T and others showed a C, his maternal relatives showing a T. Heteroplasmy is known to take place primarily through mutations occurring when the DNA is copied to make new cells in a person's lifetime, but it can be inherited from a maternal ancestor with heteroplasmy. Extremely rarely, it can come from paternal mitochondrial DNA making it into the cell. So the fact that heteroplasmy existed in the DNA sample didn't negate the match, and the probability that these were the Romanovs was still between 70 to 1 through to 840,000 to 1 in favour. But, it did sow some seeds of doubt. Incidentally, we now know that heteroplasmy is fairly common, with potentially over half of the human population having at least one heteroplasmy, albeit at a low percentage in terms of their mitochondrial DNA carrying it.
Exclusive to Live Science Pro

So, to be doubly sure, in 1996 the remains of the tsar's brother, Georgij, who had died in 1899, were exhumed and he was found to have exactly the same mitochondrial heteroplasmy. Given the very low chance of two people having this particular heteroplasmy if they weren't related, this pointed to the mitochondrial DNA data the researchers obtained being 130,000,000 times more likely if these were the Romanovs than if they were an unrelated family.

The case was solved in terms of identifying the tsar, tsarina and three of their daughters, but the mystery still remained as to what had happened to the two other children. In the scientific paper reporting the results, the authors conjectured that possibly the two children had been buried separately, or that they could have survived the massacre. Incidentally, there was a woman living in the U.S. who claimed to be Anastasia, saying she had managed to escape being executed, and so the fact that two of the children were missing from the Romanov family group only fuelled the idea that maybe she truly was the missing princess.

Then, in 2007, a group of amateur archaeologists, digging a mere 70 metres away from the previously discovered mass grave, came across more human remains. Skeletal evidence showed that they were the remains of two bodies, a young woman aged 15-19 and a probable male aged 12-15. DNA analysis was brought to bear and again showed that the two individuals were siblings and related to the Romanovs already identified. As an extra DNA test, Y-chromosome testing was carried out, the Y chromosome being passed from father to son, to confirm that the Y chromosome of the newly found male skeleton was indeed male and that it matched the Y chromosome of the tsar. This also then matched male-line relatives — a second cousin once removed of the tsar (third cousin of Alexei) through Tsar Nicholas I. The missing Romanov children had been found.
Adapted from The Secrets of Our DNA: How Genetics Has Changed the World by Turi King. Published by Pegasus Books. Copyright © 2026. All rights reserved.

bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/c60mdz.headline: Thomas Tuchel: England boss to remind players of anti-racism protocols before Spain game
bbc.co.uk/sport/football/articles/c60mdz.author: Matthew Henry

paragraphs.text: The match will be England's first in the Spanish capital since a notorious fixture at Real Madrid's Bernabeu stadium in 2004 which was overshadowed by racist chanting aimed at England players.

The Spanish federation was fined last month and ordered to play their next friendly match with a partial stadium closure after fans sang "Islamophobic and xenophobic" chants about Muslims during a game against Egypt.
"We had a same discussion before the Serbia game [in Belgrade in September 2025]," Tuchel said. "There is a protocol in place.
"Maybe we take our five minutes to inform the players about the protocol if there is a precedent [in Madrid]."

European governing body Uefa, the organiser of the Nations League, has a three-step protocol to handle incidents of discrimination inside stadiums, designed to give referees the power to halt matches, and even abandon games if racist behaviour continues.
In the first instance, referees halt the match and request an announcement on the public address system.
Then, if discrimination continues, officials can stop the game for five to 10 minutes and take the players from the field.
If issues continue after the second stoppage, then the game can be abandoned.
"It's important that the players know about the protocol," Tuchel said.
"And then, yeah, we will give our answers if stuff like this happens. Best answers are on the pitch."
Sunday's fixture takes place at Atletico Madrid's home, the Metropolitano.

Victory would ensure England win their Nations League group and earn a more favourable quarter-final draw but world champions Spain are unbeaten in 43 matches, including a 3-2 win at Wembley in September.
"It's important that we play with the same mindset that we played at home, and attack them and try to make it a physical game, and try to impose our strength," Tuchel added.
"It [Spain] is a team that has forgotten how to lose, so it requires a top performance first of all, and if we can deliver this performance, it will give us a big boost.
"I think we're there, and I think we're ready to win on Sunday,"

cnbc.com/2026/11/14/faa-ground-stop-flig.headline: U.S. flights resume after FAA ground stop, but travel chaos continues
cnbc.com/2026/11/14/faa-ground-stop-flig.author: April Roach

paragraphs.text: U.S. flights resumed Saturday after the Federal Aviation Administration halted flight departures across the country for more than four hours on Friday, leading to thousands of flight delays and cancellations.
The disruption is set to continue this weekend, even after the nationwide ground stop was lifted at 8:15 p.m. ET on Friday.
"The safety of the flying public is always the FAA's highest priority. The FAA lifted the ground stop and some flight departures are resuming," the agency said in a post on X on Saturday.
"Before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable," it added.
There were more than 6,200 delays and more than 3,400 cancellations as of early Saturday, according to FlightAware.
The disruption also upended travel for NBA, NHL and college teams struggled to reach their destinations in time for games this weekend.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said college football teams traveling on charter flights could receive priority.
"I would encourage those football teams to reach out to the FAA to schedule their flight times and make sure they have games going off tomorrow," he said during a Friday press briefing.
The Southeastern Conference announced on X that some games had been moved to Sunday due to the flight disruption.
"We are in close communication with our member institutions to assess potential disruptions and coordinate appropriate responses," the SEC said in a statement shared on X.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said the "outdated" air traffic control system posed a "national security risk." He told reporters that there was no evidence of a cyberattack of an "SI attack," referring to artificial intelligence.
Duffy added that telecommunications routers were overloaded with data. "They went down," he said.

theguardian.com/science/2026/nov/14/chil.headline: Hundreds of children in England prescribed weight-loss jabs, figures show
theguardian.com/science/2026/nov/14/chil.author: Nicola Davis

paragraphs.text: Hundreds of children in England are receiving prescriptions for GLP-1 medications, including some younger than 12, the Guardian can reveal.

GLP-1 medications were initially developed to help people with type 2 diabetes control their blood sugar levels, but have since become a popular slimming aid, with products such as Wegovy and Mounjaro becoming household names.
While social media is awash with adults who have lost weight with GLP-1s, data shows a number of children are also being prescribed them.
A Guardian investigation has revealed that in the financial year 2025-26 there were 419 prescriptions issued to children under the age of 18, 10 of which were for children under the age of 12.
And in the four months from April to July this year, 341 prescriptions for GLP-1s were issued to children, 15 of whom were under the age of 12.
The figures, obtained from the NHS Business Services Authority through freedom of information requests, relate to prescriptions in England and dispensed in a community setting anywhere in the UK.
However, they do not cover those prescribed and dispensed via private prescriptions, in prisons, and in hospitals, meaning the figures are likely to be a considerable underestimate.

One private clinic for children has previously revealed it has more than 200 patients receiving the jabs. It is also unclear whether the GLP-1 figures reflect medications that are being given primarily for weight loss.

Martin Whyte, a professor of metabolic medicine at the University of Surrey, said the number of prescriptions was still small relative to the scale of childhood obesity, but those taking the drugs needed long-term change to their lifestyles.
He said: “The important thing is that children who start them do so within specialist services, with support for diet, growth and wellbeing, and a plan for the long term.

“That includes regular monitoring of growth and puberty, nutritional intake, mental health and eating behaviours, and side effects. This matters partly because we know weight tends to return when the drugs are stopped, and partly because we still have limited data on use over many years in growing young people.”

The rising use of GLP-1s comes as levels of childhood obesity are increasing. Figures from the National Child Measurement Programme show that 10.7% of reception-year children (ages 4 and 5) are obese, while that rises to 22.8% for children in year 6 (ages 10 and 11).
According to the World Health Organization (WHO), 400 million children and adolescents aged between five and 19 were overweight in 2024, including 170 million living with obesity.
As part of efforts for early intervention, the NHS began piloting Complications from Excess Weight (CEW) clinics from 2021, aimed at children aged two to 16 with severe obesity.
In May, NHS England revealed almost 6,500 children have since been referred to such clinics, including more than 400 younger than four.

Hundreds of young people have received weight-loss medications through such services – although only some CEW clinics can access funding to offer GLP-1s, and these are typically dispensed through hospital pharmacies.

Dr Dunia Ismail, a consultant paediatrician who runs a CEW clinic, said experts were now looking at widening the use of GLP-1s in such settings. “We have been sticking to 12 [years], although now we are looking at expanding that to eight-plus once licence-approved,” she said.
Last month, new global guidelines from the WHO stated obesity medications, including GLP-1s, should not be given to children under the age of 10.

However, recent data from a trial involving 165 children aged 6 to under 12 – run by the pharmaceutical company Novo Nordisk, which produces Wegovy and Victoza – has suggested GLP-1s can help young children with obesity.

Julian Hamilton-Shield, a professor in diabetes and metabolic endocrinology and a clinician at the Bristol Complications CEW clinic, said typically children who receive semaglutide at CEW clinics had been unable to lose weight through standard dietary and nutritional advice and psychological support.

“Probably, in the vast majority of cases, they have a secondary comorbidity such as type 2 diabetes, obstructive sleep apnoea, liver disease, intracranial hypertension – you name it, they’ve got it,” he said. “So it’s been used as an adjunct after standard therapies haven’t really helped. However, it is used quite frequently and it is a very effective drug.”
Hamilton-Shield stressed GLP-1 medications were given to children who have very high excess weight. “You’d call it morbid obesity if you were classifying it as adults,” he said.
The use of GLP-1s in children has reignited a debate about the drivers of childhood obesity, but experts say it is important to avoid blaming patients or their families.

“We’re a health service that delivers health to the people who require it. We’re not one that makes moral judgments about people,” said Hamilton-Shield. “Nobody’s saying that every child who’s a bit heavy should have a GLP-1.”

Hamilton-Shield added: “These children and young people are from very complex backgrounds, have enormous lack of self-esteem. They’re not attending school. They’ve got all these complications. They’ve got all the stigma. And when you actually give them a drug that helps them to lose maybe 25, 30kg, [it is] the first time they feel they have any agency in their lives at all, and that will have a transformative effect in its own right.”

Ismail also stressed the importance of GLP-1s for children. “We know now that obesity is not a choice, it’s a condition,” she said. “We’re giving them GLP-1s because there is nothing else you can do at this stage. Otherwise, they will die young, they will have heart disease, they will have diabetes … It’s just terrible what could happen to them if we don’t.”

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/14/tex.headline: Texas’s Democratic gov.-elect vows to trade GOP culture wars for moderation
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/14/tex.author: Molly Hennessy-Fiske

paragraphs.text: AUSTIN — GOP Gov. Greg Abbott and conservative state lawmakers tried to label incoming Democratic governor Gina Hinojosa a closet progressive, warning that she’ll turn the deeply red state socialist.

But after Hinojosa’s historic upset win amid a blue wave that swept every state office, Texas’s first Latina governor-elect vowed during an interview with The Washington Post at the state Capitol on Friday to avoid culture wars in favor of something Texas hasn’t seen in a generation: moderation. On a number of key issues facing her state — affordability, border security, data centers and school vouchers — Hinojosa is staking out what she calls populist positions that seem calibrated to appeal to voters at both ends of the political spectrum. That includes her pledge to work with President Donald Trump on immigration.

“I agree with President Trump that our border needs to be secure and people should not be coming here to cross into the country,” Hinojosa said. “It’s a dangerous journey and I don’t think it will be fruitful for them.”

In a Truth Social post Thursday about migrant caravans forming in Mexico, Trump referred to her as “the very liberal new governor of Texas.” Hinojosa, seated near a photo of the state’s last Democratic Gov. Ann Richards, said Friday afternoon that the Trump administration had not contacted her and she had not spoken to the president, “but I welcome that conversation.”

“Trump and I won the same border communities: I won them this time, he won them last time” in 2024, said Hinojosa, who will preside over the country’s second-largest Latino population. Latino voters in places like her native Rio Grande Valley were instrumental in Democratic wins, including one county that swung away from Republicans by more than any other in the nation.

Asked if she would end Operation Lone Star, the more than $11 billion-dollar state border security operation Abbott used emergency powers to launch in 2021, Hinojosa said she would review its legality.
“It’s essential that we have strong partnership with Washington … to make sure our local border communities are safe,” she said.

But she drew a distinction between border security and federal immigration enforcement in Texas’s interior. “The election was a referendum on how people are treated within our state, not outside of it, certainly not outside the country,” she said.

After a migrant was fatally shot by an Immigration and Customs Enforcement agent last July in Houston and another ICE agent was indicted on federal assault charges there last month, Hinojosa stressed that federal agents securing the border was “very different from interior enforcement, which as we have all seen has been chaotic and dangerous and people died, people have been hurt. People are scared and angry and people’s rights are violated and that has to stop.”

Last week, Democratic Houston Mayor John Whitmire said he was directing police officers to limit their cooperation with ICE during traffic stops, challenging a policy imposed on the state’s largest city by Abbott, who had threatened to withhold state grant funding.

“That was wrong,” Hinojosa said, “requiring our city police to hold people for ICE who were, for instance, reporting domestic violence assault. That is not good for public safety. That makes us less secure when people don’t feel that they can report crimes freely or face being handed over to ICE.”

Hinojosa will not challenge Texas’s mostly Democratic municipal leaders if they block police from cooperating with ICE. But Hinojosa said she will not overturn a state law requiring sheriffs and counties that operate jails to comply with ICE.
“I will always follow the law. The law is what it is. It’s up to the legislature if that’s going to get changed,” she said.

The Texas governor has virtually unlimited emergency powers, which some GOP state lawmakers have said they fear Hinojosa will use to overturn conservative laws passed in recent years, including laws requiring people to use bathrooms that match their sex at birth, bans on abortion and gender transition medical care for minors.
Hinojosa said those fears are unfounded.
“I don’t see us trying to tackle culture wars. That was not the mandate we were given,” she said. “The mandate we were given was to deliver for Texans.”

On day one, she plans to declare a “high-cost emergency,” freeze electricity rates and suspend the 20-cent-per-gallon state gas and diesel tax. She also plans to immediately issue an emergency proclamation to the legislature to approve a measure that would send every Texas household $1,500.

“That is the emergency that families are experiencing in their homes right now: They just can’t afford basics. They can’t pay their electric bills. They can’t afford to put food on the table. They can’t afford to see the doctor,” she said.

Abbott had embraced Islamophobia, vowing to “ban sharia law,” blocking Muslim housing developments and designating the Council on American-Islamic Relations, the country’s largest Muslim civil rights and advocacy organization, a terrorist group. Hinojosa said she would remove that designation.

“We have to use public safety measures for public safety,” she said, dismissing what she called “nonsense happening with power that should be used for public safety, money that should use for public safety, that is not being used for safety.”

She promised once she’s inaugurated Jan. 19 to declare a moratorium on data centers, but only those that have yet to receive state permits because “if they’ve already received state permits, I don’t have the power just to shut them down.”
But Hinojosa acknowledged that “there are communities who are under the impression that their water will be shut off if there’s only enough water for either them or the data centers.”

“I would intervene with all my power to stop that from happening,” she said, citing recent water shortages in Corpus Christi. “It can just never be the case that industry is prioritized over people for water that they drink and need to live.”

Hinojosa, who like Abbott is Catholic, has said she personally opposes capital punishment. Texas has executed more than 600 death row inmates since the reinstatement of capital punishment in 1976, with an execution scheduled later this month.

But unlike outgoing Democratic California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who this month began the process of commuting the sentences of all 548 inmates on the state’s death row, Hinojosa said she would consider those on Texas’s death row “on a case-by-case basis and review and make a decision in accordance with the law.”

Hinojosa voted against the state’s abortion ban but during her campaign she also released an ad in which she spoke about her decision to carry her first pregnancy to term even after genetic testing revealed a fetal anomaly. Since the abortion ban went into effect, Texas lawmakers increased funding to $200 million for more than 100 antiabortion pregnancy centers under a state program Hinojosa said she would review and potentially veto.

“My understanding is a lot of that funding was not going to actually provide health care services for women. It should be,” she said. “I’m going to take a fine-tooth comb to that entire budget … If it is not serving Texans, not serving their health care needs, not serving families, then, yeah, I would veto that funding.”

While Hinojosa voted against a state school voucher program and vowed on the campaign trail to fight it, she said that instead of executive action, she plans to work with the legislature to reshape the program, potentially using it to expand access to prekindergarten.
“It’s going to all be one big negotiation,” she said.

Hinojosa spoke out during her campaign against mid-decade redistricting her GOP colleagues forced through the legislature last summer despite a Democratic quorum break. But she said she doesn’t have to power to reverse it.
”That’s something that the legislature would have to pass a law to do,” she said.

Republicans retained their majority in the state Senate, and some have suggested they may use Senate rules to strip the incoming Democratic lieutenant governor of her power to lead the senate, effectively blocking Democrats’ legislation and the governor’s priorities.
But Hinojosa said Lt. Gov. Vikki Goodwin has been “working with her team to ensure that the voice of the voters is heard, and the voters voted for change.”

Hinojosa was elected to the state legislature almost a decade ago, and said she has worked with Republicans on education and other issues, including a former GOP colleague she included on her transition team.
