She noted she’ll have help from two Democratic state senators — Nathan Johnson, who was elected attorney general, and Sarah Eckhardt, the comptroller-elect.

Walking the halls of the Capitol on Friday, Hinojosa shook hands with voters and children in tour groups, all of whom congratulated her. She visited the empty floors of the state House and Senate, pointing out the clear line of sight between them.

“I am hearing very positive feedback from senators who are looking forward to working with me,” Hinojosa said. “I know how the legislative process works. I know these people. I know what’s important to them. And I know how to get things done here.”

washingtonpost.com/investigations/2026/1.headline: A spy plane tied to covert attacks leads back to Florida’s largest senior community
washingtonpost.com/investigations/2026/1.author: Imogen Piper, Samuel Oakford, Zach Dorfman

paragraphs.text: A high-tech surveillance plane that repeatedly flew in the vicinity of CIA-linked attacks on boats near the Galápagos Islands this year had an unlikely first owner: a company based in The Villages, the retirement mega-community in Florida.

The company, Sunshine Aviation Capital, has no online presence or public profile. But corporate filings with the Federal Aviation Administration bear the signatures of members of the Morse family, the billionaire owners of The Villages and prominent longtime Republican Party donors.

The Galápagos attacks were part of a CIA “covert action” program that resulted in the disappearance of eight fishermen, The Washington Post previously reported. No government has claimed responsibility for the strikes.

This Post investigation used flight data and radio communications to trace the specially equipped business jet that flew near those strikes back to its origins. FAA filings and corporate documents revealed the Morse family’s role in the company that previously owned the plane — and a web of contractors that suggests the plane itself has ties to the CIA.

How, and why, the Morse family became involved with a plane that was later used in a CIA campaign in Latin America is unclear, as is whether family members had a financial stake in Sunshine Aviation. The plane appears to have never flown to the airport near The Villages where the Morse family maintains a private hangar, according to available flight data.

When Sunshine Aviation acquired the plane in November 2022, the Cessna Citation Longitude was already outfitted with unusual modifications such as infrared lighting and specialized cockpit interiors that allow pilots to don night-vision goggles, FAA records show. Additional surveillance modifications were made during the eight months the firm owned the jet, according to the records.

Sunshine Aviation delegated authority to manage the jet and approve those modifications to a mechanic who has worked for Triangle Aviation Solutions, a North Carolina-based firm previously known as Aero Contractors. That company had a well-documented role in the CIA’s “extraordinary rendition” program after 9/11, ferrying terrorism detainees around the globe.

In July 2023, several years before the action near the Galápagos, Sunshine Aviation transferred ownership of the plane — along with two other similar aircraft — to a trust at the Bank of Utah. Mark Morse, then CEO of The Villages, digitally signed the paperwork as manager of Sunshine Aviation.
FAA records show the aircraft was subsequently managed or inspected by two other individuals with employment histories at Triangle Aviation.

The CIA declined to respond to a list of questions about The Post’s findings. The Morse family and their representatives at The Villages did not respond to requests for comment. Triangle also did not respond, nor did the Bank of Utah.

Starting in November 2025, and continuing in the months surrounding the attacks, aviation data shows a series of flights across the southern United States and to and from El Salvador, each involving a Cessna Citation Longitude. Although the flights are recorded as having different registration numbers, The Post uncovered multiple overlapping “squawk codes” — transponder codes assigned by air traffic controllers — transmitted by the aircraft across some of the legs, showing that the seemingly unrelated flights were flown by a single plane.
The tactics mirror methods employed in the past to hide classified aviation activity, according to a former FAA official who worked with the CIA to disguise clandestine operations.
“One would have to believe that this is the agency hiding flights,” said the former FAA official, speaking on the condition of anonymity. “I can’t think of any other explanation.”
The FAA did not return a request for comment.

In January, the surveillance jet was tracked flying in the direction of an Ecuadorian fishing boat that went missing a short time later, The Post previously reported. Flying under the call sign FENIX701, the plane appeared again in March when two other fishing boats were attacked.

Survivors of the attacks said small quadcopter drones either dropped munitions on the vessels or detonated by crashing into them. They described being detained aboard a vessel by English-speaking armed men before being transferred to the Salvadoran Navy. They were ultimately returned to Ecuador, without criminal charges or an explanation.

The secretive attacks were distinct from the Trump administration’s highly publicized military campaign against alleged drug traffickers at sea. It is not clear whether other actors were involved in the Galápagos strikes, such as private contractors or authorities from other countries.
A secretive spy air wing
The CIA has long operated a covert fleet of aircraft for logistics, transport and intelligence-gathering and reconnaissance purposes.

Starting in 1949, the CIA secretly funded — and later outright purchased — an airline that ballooned into the storied Air America, a so-called agency “proprietary” that was central to CIA’s secret war in Laos and Southeast Asia and once boasted 8,000 employees.

CIA aviation front companies, which functioned as legitimate commercial businesses in addition to undertaking secret operations, brought in “at least” $658 million in outside income to the agency through 1975, according to a document fully declassified by the Trump administration in 2025.
After the Vietnam War, the CIA downsized, obscuring its aviation activities behind a tangle of modest, formally independent firms operating out of small airfields, particularly in the Sun Belt.

Aero Contractors was founded in 1979 by Jim Rhyne, the renowned chief special missions pilot for Air America, to carry out operations on the agency’s behalf, according to prior reports and books on the company’s activities. Those included CIA-sponsored counternarcotics missions in Colombia.

Most notably, in the 2000s, Aero Contractors was associated with the rendition of over four dozen terrorism detainees to so-called CIA “black sites” abroad or foreign custody. A web of dummy firms and contractors were linked to the transit of suspected terrorists across the globe.
A 2005 New York Times investigation into Aero Contractors called it “a major domestic hub of the Central Intelligence Agency’s secret air service.”
Rhyne died in an airplane crash in North Carolina in 2001.

A partially declassified 2007 CIA inspector general report into the botched rendition of Khaled al-Masri, a German citizen abducted by the CIA in Macedonia in 2004, refers to an Aero Contractors-operated plane that transported Masri to a CIA black site in Afghanistan as “an Agency aircraft.” In 2007, a German court issued arrest warrants for three pilots tied to Aero Contractors, alongside 10 other suspected CIA personnel working under aliases, with kidnapping Masri, but later decided not to seek extradition of the suspects.

In recent decades, the FAA has collaborated with the CIA and other federal agencies to prevent certain aircraft from being easily tracked, according to the former FAA official who worked with the CIA to obscure flights.

This enhanced FAA-CIA relationship became more critical after the widespread advent of plane-tracking technology that allows users to trace the movement of aircraft in real time, according to the former official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

“It’s near impossible to obfuscate these days,” said a former CIA official who interacted frequently with agency-affiliated aircraft conducting renditions in the 2000s and spoke on the condition of anonymity.
The Villages connection
Far from the remote waters of the Eastern Pacific and the U.S. militarized counter-drug campaign is The Villages retirement community in central Florida, nicknamed “Disneyland for seniors.”

The 57-square mile development of homes, golf courses and shopping centers is home to roughly 150,000 residents and has played an outsize role in Florida politics. Long known as a conservative bastion, the retirement community has provided a major reservoir of votes for Republican candidates statewide and in federal elections. The vision of developer H. Gary Morse and presided over by three generations of the Morse family, The Villages has grown into the largest senior-living estate in the country.

President Donald Trump visited The Villages during his first term in 2019, during his reelection campaign in 2020, and again in May 2026. In 2020, former CIA director and then-Secretary of State Mike Pompeo visited The Villages for what was reported as a private meeting with the Morse family.
Pompeo declined to comment for this report.
Members of the Morse family have given nearly $1 million to Republican candidates and party-affiliated entities since 2016, according to Federal Election Commission filings.
Why the Morse family had a role in a company that acquired planes outfitted with spy gear is unclear, and the family did not respond to outreach from The Post to discuss.

Sunshine Aviation was incorporated in Delaware in 2017. But the company’s address in purchase agreements filed with the FAA is a property located along Lake Sumter Landing, one of the town squares constructed within The Villages. The property is owned by The Villages Operating Company, which until 2018 listed it as its address in state filings.

In 2019, Sunshine Aviation acquired the first of four Cessna Citation Longitudes from Textron, the manufacturer, according to FAA filings. The combined value of the aircraft, including the three later outfitted with elaborate surveillance technology, likely ran over $100 million, according to market estimates.
It is not clear whether Sunshine Aviation arranged for the three planes it acquired in 2022 to be equipped with gear that is unusual for a civilian aircraft.

In March 2023, Kelsea Morse Manly, then a senior executive at The Villages and daughter of Mark Morse, signed a document on behalf of Sunshine Aviation giving Joe Galloway, a certified mechanic at the Georgia-based aviation leasing firm RGB Enterprises, authority to act on the company’s behalf for any maintenance, inspections, and modifications to the three planes. More recent FAA documents obtained by The Post identify Galloway as director of maintenance for Triangle Aviation.

Under Galloway’s supervision, the three aircraft were equipped with additional capabilities, including several specialized antennas and an anti-jamming GPS system, according to FAA documents. Galloway’s name appears on applications for special certificates permitting experimental test flights of aerial survey equipment. Galloway declined to comment.

The documents signed by Morse Manly also gave authority over the planes to Cheryl Bercegeay, who was described as general manager of RGB. Bercegeay’s name appears in FAA registration documents for all four planes, including the first purchased by Sunshine in 2019. Bercegeay did not respond to requests for comment.

In mid-2023, Galloway received approval from the FAA to conduct experimental test flights with the plane that later was tracked to El Salvador, according to filings. Flight data shows the aircraft then flying loops at an Air Force training range in Idaho where a nearby National Guard unit specializes in simulating electronic warfare threats for pilot training exercises.

After Mark Morse signed off on the sale of the planes to the trust at the Bank of Utah in July of that year, Galloway continued to manage the aircraft, according to FAA filings. The use of trusts is a common arrangement in private aviation that can shield the identity of a plane’s owner.
After the sale, FAA documents reviewed by The Post show the aircrafts’ connections to Triangle Aviation deepening.

In September 2023, the bank, operating on behalf of the trust that owned the planes, extended authority to manage the three aircraft to an “Andy Spears.” Spears is identified in Federal Communications Commission filings as general manager of Jamestown Companies, based out of Raleigh Regional Airport in North Carolina. Spears signs his name as “David Andrew Spears” in FAA filings.

A LinkedIn page for a David Spears lists Aero Contractors as his employer, an association that is corroborated through The Post’s review of public records and other online evidence. A 2018 Facebook post from an aviation training company celebrates Spears having been awarded the title of master technician. It identifies him as an Aero Contractors employee and shows an image of a celebratory cake ascribed with his name.

Another individual associated with Triangle Aviation, Richard Litka, conducted inspections on two of the aircraft over the span of more than a year, according to FAA filings. Litka’s LinkedIn page describes him as director of maintenance for Aero Contractors and more recently Triangle Aviation, stretching back more than a decade.
Spears and Litka did not respond to requests for comment.
The planes eventually caught the eye of aviation enthusiasts, who tracked them regularly at Raleigh Regional Airport in North Carolina, as well as at more unusual locations.

One was photographed in late 2023 flying in Fiji, where the U.S. embassy said in a statement the jet had been contracted to transport regional leaders. More recently, it and another of the planes were tracked flying in Eastern Europe, including in countries bordering Russia and Ukraine. An open-source aircraft research group JANN noted that the planes’ ownership and capabilities were unusual, and later used flight data — including one overlapping squawk code — to suggest that one of these three jets was FENIX701.

In November 2025, FENIX701 began conducting maritime surveillance flights near the Galápagos Islands. Two days earlier, Spears had signed documents adding a fully adjustable military-grade seat to the aircraft interior.
Meanwhile this summer, Brian Hudson, the general counsel of The Villages, dissolved Sunshine Aviation Capital, according to corporate filings. Hudson declined to comment.
Last month, the plane that had flown in the Galápagos began appearing over Colombia, where the U.S. is engaged in extensive counternarcotics activities.
Clara Ence Morse and Aaron Schaffer contributed to this report.

theguardian.com/science/2026/nov/13/spac.headline: SpaceX Starship megarocket blasts off before expected return for reuse
theguardian.com/science/2026/nov/13/spac.author: Uwa Ede-Osifo

paragraphs.text: SpaceX’s Starship megarocket blasted off from Texas on Friday afternoon as the aerospace company sought to make history with a double catch of its reusable rocket, but ultimately fell short.

Starship, the world’s largest rocket, standing at 407ft, is expected to orbit Earth about 14 times over the course of 22 hours, before the company catches the rocket at its launchpad at Starbase in south Texas.
The rocket, which is on its 15th flight, is composed of two elements: the lower booster, with 33 Raptor engines that fired off during takeoff, and the Starship at the top.
As smoke plumes wafted from the launch site, SpaceX employees erupted into cheers.
SpaceX had planned for both components to return to its tower, but the booster, named Super Heavy, was aborted, and splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico. The cause of that diversion remains unknown.

“That certainly isn’t the news that we had hoped to hear for today,” said Kate Tice, SpaceX’s director of quality management, but she noted the booster’s return was in line with “rigorous safety checks”.
Early in the webcast, SpaceX simulated the return. The entire rocket was expected to be grabbed in the launch tower’s “chopstick” mechanical arms.
Friday’s test did not rise to the double-catch mantle, which Elon Musk had described early in November as a “critical breakthrough needed to make life multiplanetary”.
Still, the flight is still poised to mark another milestone for the company. If all goes to plan, it would be the first time SpaceX has caught the rocket’s 171ft upper stage.
Previous tests focused on the retrieval of the booster.
The Starship, meanwhile, has continued to sail through space at over 26,000 km/h at an altitude of 270km.
The launch went on as scheduled despite a nationwide ground stop that disrupted hundreds of flights.
Flights to the west coast from Hawaii were temporarily paused, then resumed on Friday due to space debris from the launch, according to the island’s transportation agency.

As in the past, Starship carried satellites for Starlink, SpaceX’s internet service wing, three of which were fitted with cameras to analyze the rocket’s heat shield. The data plays a role in determining if the spacecraft is ready to return.
SpaceX chief executive Musk has sought to advance Starship’s “rapid reusability” as a vehicle, which he hopes will take humans to the moon and, controversially, to Mars.
Nasa has contracted SpaceX, along with Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin, to provide the lunar landers that will return astronauts to the moon in 2028.
Musk has cast his reusable rocket as a buffer against the enormous costs associated with future space travel.
SpaceX has launched a flurry of test flights in recent years, some of which have resulted in explosions that signaled major design flaws.
In September, the most recent flight test, SpaceX notched a victory, sending the spacecraft into Earth’s orbit for the first time, although its engine failed during the ascent.

washingtonpost.com/health/2026/11/14/doc.headline: Surging measles cases are forcing doctors to treat conditions they’ve never seen
washingtonpost.com/health/2026/11/14/doc.author: Lena H. Sun

paragraphs.text: John Goldman had seen only two cases of measles in more than 30 years as a physician. Now, in the midst of the nation’s largest measles outbreak, the infectious-disease specialist in Pennsylvania has helped care for about 50 infected patients in a single year.
And he is seeing the disease manifest in ways he never encountered before: adults with severe pneumonia, pregnant women and babies born infected.

All the patients recovered. But the resurgence of measles is forcing clinicians such as Goldman, 62, to relearn how to recognize and manage a disease that has been largely absent from medical practice since the U.S. eliminated measles in 2000. After years of falling vaccination rates and amid the worst measles outbreak the U.S. has seen in 35 years, doctors are confronting an illness many have never seen in practice.
“There is a tremendous amount of what I would describe as learning on the fly,” said Goldman, an epidemiologist at UPMC Harrisburg.

The magnitude of Pennsylvania’s outbreak — 1,542 cases and seven deaths, including one reported Friday — has made once-rare complications more visible, offering a glimpse of what doctors elsewhere could encounter as measles spreads among susceptible populations.

Some of the greatest unknowns involve the youngest patients — babies infected before birth or in the first months of life. Doctors have far less evidence or knowledge about what infection at such a young age could mean years later.

This week, an independent group of global health experts determined the United States has lost its status as a country that eliminated the continuous spread of measles, a landmark public health achievement attained more than a quarter-century ago. A committee of the Pan American Health Organization, part of the World Health Organization, met this week to determine whether the disease has spread uninterrupted for more than 12 months since a major outbreak in West Texas in January last year, — a conclusion many epidemiologists and infectious-disease experts had said was expected based on publicly available data.

For clinicians in Pennsylvania and elsewhere who have been battling outbreaks, that is a technical marker, and a lagging one. Doctors on the front lines are already seeing the real-life consequences of sustained transmission.
Measles in adults had been rare

For decades, measles was taught in textbooks as a disease that primarily affected children. Historically, most people were infected as children, “so as they got to adulthood, they were immune,” said Robert Hopkins, medical director of the National Foundation for Infectious Diseases who also takes care of adults and children at the University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences hospital in Little Rock.
But now doctors are seeing measles in adults, something they were not expecting.

Measles in adults is often more serious than it is in children, doctors say. One man developed such severe measles pneumonia that doctors placed him on a ventilator to help him breathe, Goldman said. Another, a woman hospitalized with sepsis, a life-threatening reaction to an infection unrelated to measles, turned out to have measles before she even had the characteristic rash.

Nationally, 41 percent of measles cases this year have been among adults 20 and older, up from 29 percent last year, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. There have been more than 5,400 measles cases so far this year, more than double the total reported in 2025.

Years of underimmunization mean there is a population of adults who were neither vaccinated nor infected as children and therefore remain susceptible. Declining vaccination rates have weakened the community immunity that once protected them by preventing a measles case from spreading.
In Pennsylvania’s outbreak, the shift has been even more pronounced: Two-thirds of the state’s cases have been in adults, some as old as 60.

The outbreak has been heavily concentrated in the state’s Plain community, which includes Amish and conservative Mennonite groups that follow traditional ways of life. Many Amish families do not routinely seek preventive care, are self-insured, and might interact with the health system mainly when someone becomes sick or injured, according to pediatricians who have cared for patients in the community.

As a result, there are people in the community who made the decision not to be vaccinated decades ago and remain susceptible today, said Goldman, who is also the epidemiologist for the system’s hospitals in central Pennsylvania, where the outbreak is centered. The average age of measles patients he has seen in the Pennsylvania outbreak is “probably in the 20s or 30s,” he said.

Goldman has been training younger physicians to recognize measles in people of all ages, starting with the basics. Get vaccinated. Know that you can’t spread the virus to family members unless you are sick. If you are vaccinated and pregnant, there is no risk to the baby.
“And then what we’re really doing is trying to teach them what measles looks like and when to be suspicious of it,” Goldman said.

For example, any rashes that start on the face. A person with a high fever, conjunctivitis or pink eye, and cough are classic measles symptoms. But early on, adults might not have the rash “and it can look like any other viral illness,” Goldman said.

Knowing that measles was spreading in communities with low vaccination rates put clinicians on heightened alert. Sometimes that led to “overcalling who could have measles,” he said. “We had people suspicious of any rash.”
Pregnancy: Another layer of complexity

As more susceptible people reach adulthood, doctors are also confronting a consequence that had become exceedingly rare: women contracting measles during pregnancy, putting them and their babies at risk.

Women who contract measles while pregnant face increased risk of serious illness, including pneumonia, as well as miscarriage, stillbirth and premature delivery, said Kevin Ault, an obstetrician-gynecologist at Penn State Health in Hershey, about 30 miles northwest of Lancaster County, the outbreak’s epicenter.

Scientists at the CDC sought to send an urgent nationwide alert to clinicians about the risks and management of measles during pregnancy as cases increased, but the alert was not approved, The Washington Post previously reported.

Last month, Pennsylvania health officials took the unusual step of issuing a statewide health alert specifically addressing rising cases of measles in pregnancy and measles passed on in utero. The notice urged doctors to immediately report suspected infections and said women should be vaccinated against measles before becoming pregnant. The measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine cannot be given during pregnancy.
Complications for children born with measles

If a woman contracts measles late in pregnancy, or gives birth prematurely, the baby might be born with congenital measles, Ault said. But much of what physicians know about the condition dates to the middle of the last century, he said. Those data suggest that about 30 percent of babies born to women infected during pregnancy develop congenital measles, he said.

What doctors are seeing in Pennsylvania appears consistent with that estimate, Ault said. In talking to obstetricians in other parts of the state, “I think they are seeing congenital measles about the rate you’d expect, about one-third of the time,” he said.
Still, the estimates of congenital cases predate modern diagnostic tools such as PCR testing and advanced imaging. Physicians might now “find a whole new crop of problems,” Ault said.

Children known to have been infected around the time of birth should be followed closely throughout childhood for developmental delays or learning disabilities, clinicians said. One particularly serious concern is subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE, a rare, progressive and almost always fatal brain disorder that typically emerges years after a measles infection.

Since the outbreak began in late April, at least 101 pregnant women in Pennsylvania have been diagnosed with measles as of Friday, an increase of 24 cases in three weeks, according to the state health department. Pennsylvania’s sixth measles-associated death was a 21-year-old woman who died after postpartum complications. The funeral director who handled her arrangements told The Post that her baby was healthy.

It’s unclear how many of the women have miscarried or delivered babies with congenital measles. The department said that state law prohibits it from releasing details of the outcomes of those pregnancies. There is no national database that tracks such cases. True numbers might also be higher because the outbreak has been centered in the Amish community, where many families have not sought conventional medical care.

Pennsylvania does not track congenital measles as a separate category because there is no national case definition or standardized reporting system, state health officials said. The state and CDC are working to develop definitions and tracking tools for measles in pregnancy and congenital measles cases.

Doctors estimate almost two dozen babies have either been born with the infection or became infected after delivery. Goldman, at UPMC in Harrisburg, said the hospital system has treated at least a dozen babies with congenital infections, meaning they tested positive at birth, or neonatal infections, meaning they tested negative at birth but became infected after delivery.

Ericka Hayes, senior medical director of infection prevention at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia (CHOP), said the Geisinger health system has had six congenital cases. In an email, Geisinger spokesman Joseph H. Stender III declined to comment.
CHOP has treated two infant cases of measles in its network, spokesman Ben Leach said.

Canada’s outbreak last year offers some clues about the potential consequences. In Ontario, 51 women contracted measles during pregnancy and 10 babies were diagnosed with congenital measles, according to a recently published study. Seven of the women experienced premature labor or delivery. One infant, who was born prematurely, died; researchers said measles contributed to the premature birth and death, although the baby had other serious medical conditions.

Alexandra Medoro, a neonatologist and pediatric infectious-disease physician at CHOP, said pediatricians worry there might be other babies whose infections are never recognized because their symptoms are subtle.

Measles in very young babies does not always look like the textbook illness. Maternal antibodies — or immune globulin given after known exposure — can lessen the illness, leaving a baby with a mild or atypical rash instead of the classic measles presentation.
“My biggest concern is not necessarily the loss to follow-up of the kids that we know about,” Medoro said. “It’s the lack of identification of kids that we can’t know about.”

Even when babies recover from the initial infection, doctors have little evidence to tell parents what comes next. Congenital measles has historically been so uncommon that much of the medical literature consists of case reports or small numbers of patients.
The risk is greatest among children infected at very young ages, and the disease can emerge sooner the younger a child was when infected.

Medoro, who is the mother of a 10-month-old, said the uncertainty leaves her unable to answer the questions she said parents ask in almost every difficult consultation: “Is my baby going to make it? And then what’s going to happen to my baby long-term?”
“Those are questions that I wish I had the answers to, too,” she said.

theguardian.com/science/2026/nov/13/kurt.headline: ‘Ahead of his time’: AI helps unlock discoveries hidden in notebooks of man who transformed maths
theguardian.com/science/2026/nov/13/kurt.author: Alex Bellos

paragraphs.text: The Austrian logician Kurt Gödel was one of the most original thinkers of the 20th century. His two incompleteness theorems, published in 1931, transformed mathematics and paved the way for the digital age.
After his seminal results of the 1930s, Gödel published only a few papers. His unpublished work, however, runs to tens of thousands of pages, and is of great interest to historians of science.

Since 2017, the Finnish logician Jan von Plato has led a project at Helsinki University to understand the contents of 16 notebooks that Gödel wrote in the early 1940s. This material – the “workbooks” – is 1,009 pages of densely written text about maths and logic. Much of it is written in a German shorthand, Gabelsberger, that was obsolete even when Gödel was using it.

Progress in the mathematical understanding of the text was painfully slow – about a page a week – until September, when von Plato enlisted the help of the AI model Claude. Within a couple of days, Claude had provided a comprehensive digest of the entire material, revealing Gödel had proved hundreds of theorems that no one knew about.
The most famous logician of modern times had, in fact, discovered significantly more than anyone had thought.

“I was flabbergasted,” said von Plato. “The workbooks not only contain dozens of anticipations of results not known until the 70s and 80s, but they also contain 14 themes in logic that have not been pursued. Gödel was far ahead of his time.”

Gödel changed the course of logic because he revealed the limits of mathematical knowledge. His incompleteness theorems show that in all mathematical systems there are true statements that can neither be proved or disproved. Yet while this result was a blow to previous generations of logicians, who had hoped that all truths were verifiable, Gödel’s work pushed the field in new directions, inspiring Alan Turing to write his 1936 paper that began the theory of modern computation.

In 1940, Gödel fled Austria under the Nazis. He settled in Princeton, New Jersey, and became a close friend of Albert Einstein at the Institute of Advanced Study. Increasingly paranoid in his later years, he refused to eat food that was not cooked by his wife, and died of starvation in 1978.

Von Plato said he had started his Gödel project in 2017 because he was facing mandatory retirement from Helsinki University. “What should I do to make myself indispensable? Oh yes, I’ll start reading Gödel’s enigmatic shorthand pages!” He received a €2.5m (£2.1m) grant from the European Research Council, taught himself Gabelsberger shorthand – “I am one of only six people who can read it in the world” – and assembled a small team.

In August, at a conference in France about AI and theorem proving, von Plato met computer scientists who suggested that he co-opt the help of Claude in trying to make sense of the workbooks. On his return to Helsinki he began the process, showing Claude his transcriptions of the workbooks, as well as six books he had previously written on Gödel and other secondary scientific literature.

“In a couple of days, I got to see a 650-page explanation of the workbooks. It had to be controlled page for page, but it’s basically a work that is impossible to do for human beings,” he said. “Humans read one page at a time and we tend to forget things. It takes us a year to read about 50 pages. We just are not able to keep in mind all the different parts.
“The AI can connect all the pieces in a thousand pages. It can see all of Gödel’s writings as one piece.”

Gödel’s incompleteness theorems revealed the existence of statements whose truths were independent of the system they were written in: that is, they could not be proved or disproved within the system. In 1966, the American mathematician Paul Cohen won the Fields medal, the highest honour in maths, for showing the independence of two well-known mathematical statements: the continuum hypothesis and the axiom of choice.
Gödel reacted to Cohen’s Fields medal by saying that he had already proved the result in the 1940s. Yet when pushed for a proof by his peers, Gödel was unable to reconstruct one from his notes.

The first task von Plato set Claude was to discover if Gödel’s workbooks had a proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, which would reveal that Gödel had been telling the truth in 1966. The answer came back: yes, almost. “He was just one step away,” said von Plato. “There’s one definition that Gödel got wrong, but he had the right definition two years earlier, and so the thought is that he would have arrived at the right definition anyway if he had just continued for a few months. For me, the architecture of his proof is just wonderful. It makes all of these results of set theory follow a uniform pattern.

“What strikes me especially is that he starts from ideas. He’s not like someone who plays with formulas and hopes to arrive somewhere. He has very, very clear ideas, and then he’s methodical. Step after step he goes ahead and he manages to fulfil the aims that he has in this formal work.”

Von Plato said that when Claude presented him with the reconstructed proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, he ran it through the proof assistant Coq, a program that verifies the validity of mathematical proofs, and it passed. Von Plato believes that had Gödel published his work on the axiom of choice, he would have won the 1940 Fields medal. “Maybe he felt that when Cohen got the medal, that that was something he sort of missed.”

In further discussions with Claude, von Plato asked the AI model to extract all theorems in the workbooks for which Gödel either had a proof, had sketched a proof or had an idea for a proof. Claude found 663. When these results were put into Coq: “About 400 were verified as stated, about 200 were repaired, meaning that perhaps the statement of the theorem had to be made more precise, or some assumption had to be added. About 50 were false, and this is no wonder. Gödel himself, when rereading his notes, would occasionally add a marginal remark: falsch! [incorrect] or schlecht! [bad].”

Von Plato added: “I am sure that the continued study of Gödel’s manuscripts will reveal further treasures. The workbooks contain, Claude says, more than a dozen themes in logic and foundations of mathematics that have not been found in the 80-plus years since they were written down. So this is one thing to explore. But there are many others. His physics and cosmology notebooks are an unknown territory I plan to start exploring once I am finished with my present logic projects.”

Joel David Hamkins, a professor of logic at the University of Notre Dame, Indiana, has not seen Claude’s reconstruction of Gödel’s proof of the independence of the axiom of choice, but said that if it stood up “it is remarkable and historically interesting. Although how much is Claude and how much is Gödel is a job for the historians.”

Hamkins said: “The fact that there are things in there that resemble [Cohen’s proof] does not mean he had it. It shows he was on the path. You don’t get credit for work you don’t tell anyone about. But Gödel had so many ground-breaking ideas that it is maybe not surprising that his notebooks are full of exciting things.”
Flatology, the study of flatulence, sounds more like a joke than a serious scientific discipline. But studying farts actually helps biologists understand an animal's diet and digestion.
We know that a host of creatures ‪— from whales, to snakes, to sloths ‪— pass gas. But do we know which animal is the top tooter? Experts told Live Science the answer is blowing in the wind.

"Getting quantitative measurements for farts per animal is pretty difficult," Nick Caruso, a data scientist and co-author of '"Does It Fart?: The Definitive Field Guide to Animal Flatulence'' (Quercus Publishing, 2017), told Live Science in an email.

What we can do is hypothesize using the data we do have. Expelled gas is made partially of methane, so comparing methane emissions produced by different species may provide a clue. However, this method does have limitations, experts pointed out.
Fart league

Researchers measure the methane animals produce by placing them inside respiration chambers, then inserting a capsule into the stomach that releases a tracer gas while strapping them with a harness that samples their breath. Alternatively, they capture their breath at stations where they feed or are milked.

Research points to livestock, especially cows, as major methane emitters. A recent report puts their total methane emissions at 117 teragrams per year. (One teragram is equal to 1 billion kilograms, or 2.2 billion pounds.) A buildup of cow-generated methane gas even caused a dairy shed in Germany to explode. However, contrary to what many people believe, the "overwhelming majority" of methane emissions from livestock is released through burping, not flatulence, Ermias Kebreab, a professor of animal science at the University of California, Davis, told Live Science in an email.

The reason comes down to where in the gut the gas is made. Herbivores can't break down plant material on their own; they rely on microbes in their guts to ferment it, and that fermentation releases gases such as methane and carbon dioxide, Dr. Marcus Clauss, head of research and co-director of the Clinic for Zoo Animals, Exotic Pets and Wildlife at the University of Zurich, told Live Science in an email. Some of this gas is absorbed into the bloodstream and exhaled. The rest tends to leave by the nearest exit ‪—‬ animals that ferment their food toward the front of the digestive tract mostly burp it out, while those that ferment it toward the back mostly pass it as wind, Clauss explained.

Cows and other ruminants ‪(such as buffalo, sheep, goats and camels)‬ ferment their food in a chamber called the rumen, located near the front of the digestive system, so most of the methane they produce is through belching, Matthew Hayek, an associate professor of environmental studies at New York University, told Live Science in an email.

So if it's not cows, which animal is the top farter based on their methane emissions? The best candidates are hindgut fermenters ‪—‬ herbivores that digest plant matter in the large intestine (the hindgut). Meat eaters, by contrast, typically produce far less methane than herbivores do, Clauss said.

One possible contender are termites, which break down wood and grass in their hindguts. Their global population is estimated to be around 27 quadrillion (that's 15 zeros) individuals, and they collectively emit 10 teragrams of methane per year.

But, per individual, the title might go to horses. According to a 2019 report from the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, horses have the highest methane emissions among hindgut fermenters — around 40 pounds (18 kg) of methane per horse each year.

However, Clauss is skeptical. "The ranking of horse as highest is only because it has been measured," he told Live Science in an email. "But there are so many hindgut fermenters not measured, like rhino ... Who knows?"
If we consider methane emissions per unit of bodyweight, the nutria (Myocastor coypus) ‪—‬ an herbivorous, semiaquatic rodent ‪—‬ would have higher methane emissions than the horse, Clauss said.

Clauss also questioned the accuracy of using methane emissions data as an indicator of flatulence. "There is some methane in flatulence, but most likely the majority of methane produced by an animal is exhaled, i.e. it goes via blood to the lungs," he said.

So until scientists figure out how to measure animal farts, any ranking remains speculative. For now, scientists have developed ways to track intestinal gas in people, including swallowable electronic capsules that measure gases inside the gut and clip-on underwear sensors that detect hydrogen in farts.
Does animal flatulence contribute to climate change?
Related mysteries

Methane is a particularly potent greenhouse gas when released into the atmosphere, and the quantities that large herds of cows and other ruminants emit through burping are enough to contribute to climate change. Indeed, scientists are experimenting with ways to reduce methane emissions from cattle — for example, by adding seaweed to their diet.
But animal flatulence is not a major contributor to global methane increases, Hayek said.

Even methane emissions from termite flatulence, while large, do not have an impact, Stefan Arndt, a professor of physiological and ecosystem ecology at the University of Melbourne in Australia, told Live Science in an email. "A large proportion of that methane is then consumed by methanotrophic bacteria in the soil," he said. These bacteria use methane as an energy source, thereby reducing the net methane emissions from termites substantially.

"Their emissions are part of the natural cycle of methane that has always been there for millennia," Arndt added. "The increasing methane concentrations in the atmosphere that are leading to climate change are caused by humans."

washingtonpost.com/world/2026/11/14/midd.headline: Middle East monarchies brace for Trump corruption scrutiny after blue wave
washingtonpost.com/world/2026/11/14/midd.author: Susannah George

paragraphs.text: Persian Gulf governments are preparing with dread for the inevitable: A damaging barrage of inquiries into alleged corruption involving President Donald Trump, his administration and family, by Democrats who swept the House and Senate in last week’s midterm elections, and who have pledged to follow the money wherever it may lead.

Democrats on Capitol Hill have warned the governments of Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar of the coming investigations, according to officials in Washington and diplomats in the Gulf states, who like others interviewed for this article spoke on the condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive diplomacy.

After decisive Democratic victories in last week’s midterm elections, the party vowed to launch sweeping probes into the Trump administration and those around it. Inquiries involving Persian Gulf monarchies are expected to focus on real estate deals, financial investments and other transactions, including the Qatari gift of a $400 million luxury jet.

Democratic lawmakers have warned the Persian Gulf states that a failure to comply with the impending inquiries could jeopardize their relationships with Washington. But the Saudi, Emirati and Qatari governments are not expected to be forthcoming with the kind of information lawmakers are seeking, such as private communications, according to two diplomats in the region and other people briefed on the matter, in what could set affected governments up for a clash with the incoming Democratic majority.
The embassies of Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar declined to comment on the planned inquiries.

The potential strain between the United States and some of its most important Middle Eastern allies would come at a critical moment for the region. The Iran war is in its ninth month without a resolution in sight and after withstanding months of devastating Iranian attacks on U.S. bases in the region, the Pentagon is rethinking its footprint.
Persian Gulf governments have defended their dealings with the Trump administration as aboveboard and have rejected allegations that they were attempting to curry favor with the Trump administration.
Regardless, the anticipated scrutiny has rattled officials in the region, according to diplomats based there and others familiar with the thinking of Persian Gulf monarchies.

The Emirati stake in a Trump family-backed cryptocurrency venture is expected to receive some of the most intensive scrutiny. Just months before the UAE was granted access to advanced U.S. microchips, an entity connected to a senior member of the Emirati royal family, Sheikh Tahnoon bin Zayed al-Nahyan, bought a $500 million stake in World Liberty Financial, the crypto firm founded by Trump’s three sons and Zach Witkoff, the son of senior Trump envoy Steve Witkoff.
“This is corruption, plain and simple,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass) said in a statement at the time.

Saudi Arabia has also allocated money to Trump family ventures. The kingdom’s sovereign wealth fund invested $2 billion with the private equity firm Affinity Partners — of which Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law is the founder and CEO — in 2021. Since Trump won a second term as president, the president’s family has dramatically expanded their real estate dealings with the kingdom, including plans for a Trump tower in Jeddah announced in 2024, a $1 billion Trump plaza in Jeddah announced this year and two luxury residential communities in Riyadh, the Saudi capital, announced in 2024.

An agreement the Trump administration signed in July that granted Riyadh the ability to build nuclear power plants with U.S. technology is also expected to come under close scrutiny. Saudi Arabia has long pushed for a civil nuclear program and the deal gave the kingdom a pathway to enriching nuclear fuel. However, after fierce opposition from Congress, including from Republicans, Trump seemed to backtrack, conditioning the deal on Saudi normalization with Israel.

The Qatari luxury jet is also expected to be a subject of investigation. After the Trump administration initially inquired about purchasing the Boeing 747-8, Qatar agreed to provide the plane as a gift. At the time, Democratic lawmakers called the transaction bribery and introduced legislation to block $1.9 billion in arms sales to Doha.

Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Connecticut), who visited the Persian Gulf in October, said he raised his concerns about corruption with Saudi Crown Prince Muhammed Bin Salman and Qatari Emir Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani. “There needed to be some hard messages delivered in Saudi Arabia and in Qatar. Our foreign policy has been corrupted,” he said at a Washington DC event shortly after returning.
Murphy said he warned the states against expanding those financial ties, cautioning that such moves would only further “jeopardize the relationship.”
The subpoena authority that Democrats will soon have in Congress does not extend to foreign governments, but Congress could use other levers of power.

Two congressional aides to Democrats briefed on the planned corruption inquiries, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to share sensitive details, said lawmakers could respond to corruption concerns in areas where Congress has oversight and influence, such as arms sales and security assistance. Lawmakers will be “less likely to want to be full partners with a country that we believe is involved in corrupting our system,” said one of the aides.

Congressional investigators are looking for information to help them “unpack the strategy” behind the investments and gifts, according to Donald Sherman, the president and CEO of Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a government watchdog group. He said lawmakers will be looking for communications between Persian Gulf officials, members of the Trump administration and Trump family members that link the investments and gifts to policy changes.
“The American public understands that money has influence, but how it influences, seeing how is very different,” he said. “It’s one thing to intuit, it’s another thing to know.”
Diplomats and others familiar with the thinking of Persian Gulf governments say they would be unlikely to hand over such information.

One of the diplomats based in the region said the kind of information U.S. lawmakers are after would be politically “embarrassing” for Persian Gulf states to reveal, and doing so would also open them up to punitive congressional action.

Allison Minor, who served during the first Trump administration as the director for Arabian Peninsula affairs on the National Security Council, said she expects the inquiries to further frustrate what was already expected to be a more acrimonious relationship.
“I think that Gulf countries have an uphill battle with Democrats,” said Minor.

“It’s not just corruption, it’s also Sudan and the Saudi war in Yemen,” she said, referring to the UAE’s alleged support for paramilitary fighters who have killed thousands in Sudan’s civil war and concern surrounding Saudi Arabia’s conduct of operations against the Houthi militia in Yemen, including allegations of high civilian casualties.
These are issues on which, Minor said, “Democrats have a lot of muscle memory and pent-up frustration.”

npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-6040299/hegseth.headline: Hegseth's failed impeachment was a warning to Democrats. Where will they go from here?
npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-6040299/hegseth.author: Domenico Montanaro

paragraphs.text: Democrats are not in the majority yet, but the first post-election test of their ability to get things done was a failure.

The House was unable to advance an impeachment effort of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Eleven Democrats were no-shows for the vote. Based on the math in this vote: If those 11 had been there and if no more Republicans showed up, the attempt would have gone forward.

Now, for those who want to see Hegseth impeached, it's fair to ask why only one Republican was in favor of it, Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who led the effort, especially after an election that saw GOP wipeouts in no small measure because of the Iran war? The GOP still controls the floor, so a Democratic speaker would have been able to leave the vote open longer for the 11 to be able to cast their votes.

But it's also fair to ask if this would have happened under Nancy Pelosi's watch? (Ironically, she was one of the 11 who didn't vote for advancing Hegseth's impeachment because she had flown back to San Francisco for a veterans' event.) Or if this kind of effort is what people want in the first place.

First, on the Pelosi point: The former House speaker and retiring congresswoman was known for the discipline she kept in her caucus. She knew where the votes were, who was voting how and why – and, most importantly, did not move forward with efforts that didn't have the votes.

Hakeem Jeffries, the heir apparent Democratic leader, is going to have the largest majority in Congress since the early 1990s. His leadership and agenda priorities are going to be scrutinized and compared to Pelosi – and this wasn't a great start to this new era.
Second, on whether impeachments are what people want to see: it depends on which people. Certainly, the Democratic base — and some beyond that — wants accountability for the Trump administration.
Voters more broadly also said corruption was a top issue in the campaign. But walking the line between reasonable accountability and oversight versus impeachments is a potential tight rope.

Democrats will have to balance the mandate they were given to bring down prices (sound familiar?) and end the war with the accountability of the Trump administration that many in the Democratic base feverishly wants and expects.
What do voters want?

A Reuters/Ipsos poll taken after the election, found that 8-in-10 people think Democrats' focus in the first 100 days should be on the cost of living, three-quarters said lowering health care costs, 7 in 10 said lowering gas prices, while 6 in 10 said ending the Iran war and eliminating President Trump's tariffs.

What about investigations and impeachment? Only 40% said investigating the Trump administration should be a priority in those early days. But 71% of Democrats do want this to be a first 100 days focus. Only 36% of independents said the same.
Almost two-thirds said they are concerned that Democrats will spend too much time on investigations, which included, by the way, half of Democrats.

When it comes specifically to pursuing impeachment of Trump, only 33% said they think it would be good for the country. On the other hand, 63% of Democrats do. Only 30% of independents said it would be good for the country.
More than half also said they think Democrats should at least make efforts to work with the Trump administration. That, however, only included 40% of Democrats.
So this is going to be tricky to navigate for Democratic leadership, but a major part of a speaker's job is messaging, particularly when that speaker's party does not control the White House.
So what will Democrats focus on when they're in charge?

People are going to be watching the new Democratic majority for what it focuses on, and even with the Hegseth effort, it was clear that many conservatives were thrilled with not only how it went but that Democrats were fueling Massie's effort.

It arguably backfired and strengthened Hegseth's position within the administration. The White House and Republicans rallied around him. Even if some Republicans on Capitol Hill might have misgivings with Hegseth for one reason or another, and they and Vice President Vance think the war in Iran was the main reason for the midterm losses, opposing Democrats is far more unifying.
Politics is often (some would say too often) a team sport, and no group is more conditioned to put the T-shirt on and run the playbook than the red team.
It certainly gave Republicans more of a chance to go on offense than talking about health care, the cost of living or the war and gas prices.

Democratic leadership is certainly aware of the line it has to walk, but Jeffries is going to have to make some decisions. Asked on PBS NewsHour this week if Democrats would be impeaching more Trump officials, he said, "We will cross that bridge when we get to it."
But a House speaker is the one who builds the legislative bridges. He or she controls the agenda.
Jeffries, of course, also noted, as he has elsewhere, that affordability is a priority.

"We're committed to driving down the high cost of living in every area," he said. "That's housing, that's health care, that's groceries, that's gas, that's caregiving – to making this country affordable again for everyone."
Democrats will be tested
Democrats have been given a huge opportunity with majorities in both the House and Senate — but the balance of priorities, timing, messaging and discipline are all going to be major tests.

The stakes couldn't be higher. Arguably, what Democrats focus on will lay the foundation for views of the party's competence heading into the 2028 presidential election, and they don't want to squander the advantages they have.
The Ipsos poll showed that Democrats have big leads on which party has a better plan, policy or approach for health care (42%-23%), the cost of living (40%-25%) and the economy (37%-30%).

But they have to be careful. A lot of people are not convinced that Democrats are focused on the issues that are important to them. Only 47% in the Ipsos poll said that, including only 40% of independents.
Only 44% said they're confident that Democrats are putting the best interests of the American people above their own personal interests.
So while Democrats have the wind at their backs, the jury is still out on whether people are confident in their leadership.

nytimes.com/2026/11/14/world/americas/tr.headline: Trump’s Oil Grab in Venezuela Is Testing the Country’s National Identity
nytimes.com/2026/11/14/world/americas/tr.author: Simon Romero, Isayen Herrera

paragraphs.text: Like generations before him, Leonardo Silva grew up steeped in beliefs about the extraordinarily abundant resource that made Venezuela special. All the oil under their feet was theirs, they felt. Virtually free gasoline was a birthright. To be born atop this bounty was like winning the lottery.

Mr. Silva, 38, said his generation viewed oil as a cornerstone of the country’s national identity, when a booming economy allowed Venezuela to occupy a privileged tier in the global order. His children, he said, have a far less rosy view.

“To them oil isn’t important, it’s secondary,” said Mr. Silva, who works at a foundation in Caracas helping people with disabilities. “They don’t have that culture of us being a rich country. They just know that if you don’t work, you don’t eat.”

Oil has shaped Venezuela to an extent that is rare outside the Middle East for more than a century, becoming a defining feature of the social fabric like baseball, beauty pageants or the veneration of the liberation hero Simón Bolívar.

But now the U.S. government is taking control of a huge portion of Venezuela’s oil. And, pressed by economic need, long-held nationalist convictions about oil, starting with the need for sovereign control, are giving way to a more complex web of perspectives.

The ways in which Venezuelans are re-evaluating oil, and by extension their reliance on it, are the result of immense upheaval over the last decade. Oil production plummeted because of mismanagement, political purges, corruption and sanctions.
The cratering of an economy overwhelmingly dependent on oil led to a financial crash marked by widespread deprivation and the exodus of millions of Venezuelans up and down the Americas.

The Trump administration then toppled Venezuela’s leader at the start of the year, took control of oil exports and went even further, forming a partnership with a scandal-plagued Venezuelan oil magnate that would enable the U.S. government to control a huge portion of Venezuela’s reserves.

Delcy Rodríguez, the interim president, has expressed full-throated support for the plan, a sweeping shift for a leader steeped in Chavismo, the political movement that made uncontested dominance over oil one of its tenets.

Ms. Rodríguez has little wriggle room with the Trump administration essentially dictating how she can operate. At the same time, some Venezuelans are so desperate for the economy to improve that they say ceding control over the oil industry is a small price to pay.
“Closing these deals is super urgent,” said María Ines Figueroa, 56, referring to the Trump administration’s takeover of Venezuelan oil reserves as well as other U.S. ventures under consideration.

Ms. Figueroa, a retired public-school teacher in Caracas, said inflation had eroded her pension before the U.S. deposed Venezuela’s last president to less than $1 a month. She now teaches at a private school where she earns $120 a month.
Her hope, she said, was that a revival of the oil industry would create a trickle down that reached into households like her own. “I’m no expert, but I think this could work,” Ms. Figueroa said.

Other Venezuelans are openly welcoming U.S. dominance over Venezuela’s oil, reflecting how opposing voices, including on the right, are becoming more bold after three decades of leftist rule marked by economic devastation and repression of dissent.

“I don’t care about the oil,” Maria Elisa Smith, a right-wing polemicist known for her racist vitriol, said recently on social media. “Oil never gave me anything good, just a miserable, socialist country.”
Still, sharp indignation bubbled up after President Trump announced the deal in August that gave the United States access to 65 billion barrels of Venezuelan oil, then repeatedly boasted about it.
Many across the ideological spectrum were angry, from opposition leaders to prominent figures of Chavismo, the movement that has controlled Venezuelan politics for three decades.

Luis Britto García, a playwright who has written widely about oil’s importance in Venezuela, said Trump’s deal laid bare the “unlimited pillage” Venezuela was experiencing as the Trump administration exerted tight financial control over oil revenues.

Long before Venezuela’s economy crashed, oil had ceased to be merely a geological resource or an export statistic, evolving into a prism through which Venezuelans contemplated their own society or compared it to others.
Some credited oil for creating modern Venezuela: Its reserves rank among the world’s largest, and since the first gushers were found, oil gave Venezuela an income neighboring countries envied.

Others saw oil as cursing Venezuela with corruption, dependency and dysfunction, citing how authoritarian and democratic leaders alike wielded the revenues to advance their own ambitions at the nation’s expense.

For decades until Venezuela’s economy collapsed, motorists viewed practically free gasoline as an entitlement, spawning a car culture of 1970s-style gas hogs and fuel-devouring SUV’s that can make the oversized vehicles filling Texas’s roads seem quaint.

Even today, oil permeates everything from rap lyrics to the memes Venezuelans share on their phones. Writers have wrestled with Venezuela’s entanglement with oil so much that there’s an entire literary tradition devoted to it.
Oil even shapes the Spanish that Venezuelans speak: “Este hombre trabaja más que un balancín,” is just one popular expression, a nod to an industry once considered a steppingstone to a better life.
It can be translated as “This man works more than a pump jack,” referring to the iconic machinery functioning nonstop to pull crude oil from subterranean wells.

Cósimo Mandrillo, the director of Monte Ávila, a state-owned publishing house, said that despite shifting political winds as the United States takes greater control of the country’s resources, Venezuelans maintain a connection to oil so intimate that it “borders on the subconscious.”
“Oil penetrates every fiber of national life,” Mr. Mandrillo said. “It is so deeply absorbed in the collective psyche that we navigate its presence almost by instinct.”

Hugo Chávez, who ruled Venezuela from 1999 until his death in 2013, seized on this visceral connection like few rulers before him. Constantly clashing with the United States, he made state control over oil the centerpiece of his socialist-inspired Bolivarian revolution.

At home, he used oil revenues to ease poverty and consolidate power. Projecting power abroad, Mr. Chávez propped up Cuba, built international coalitions to defy U.S. influence and launched Telesur, a pan-Latin American television network.

Nicolás Maduro, Mr. Chávez’s successor, doubled down on the approach. Even as the economy unraveled, he framed oil not as a commodity on a balance sheet but as the fuel for consolidating his authoritarian rule.

In a bid to circumvent U.S. sanctions, Mr. Maduro launched his own cryptocurrency called the Petro, claiming each token was backed by a barrel of oil. But the crypto scheme collapsed in connection to a corruption scandal at the national oil company.
Even before Mr. Maduro was overthrown by U.S. forces in January, the ways in which Venezuelans viewed oil had begun to change, largely because of economic desperation after production plunged.

It was not until 2020, under the cover of acute fuel shortages and the Covid-19 pandemic, that Mr. Maduro effectively ended the era of universal, nearly free gasoline, introducing a dollarized rate at most gas stations.

Until then, Chavismo had recast the Caracazo, the massive riots in 1989 sparked by a jump in fuel prices, as one of its spiritual catalysts. As a result, highly subsidized gasoline became an untouchable third rail of Venezuelan politics.

Standard gasoline in Venezuela for most motorists costs about $1.89 a gallon (still far less than the prevailing prices in the United States and many other nations), alongside a tightly restricted, subsidized and cheaper tier linked to a social rationing program.
In an energy-rich country where electricity shortages are a part of life in many cities, such rationing routinely produces the surreal sight of long lines of motorists waiting to fill up.
The dysfunction plaguing much of the economy comes as Mr. Trump is unsparingly direct about using his chokehold on Venezuela’s government to extract one deal after another.

As Venezuela emerges as essentially a vassal state of a pre-eminent superpower, Margarita López Maya, a historian, said it was not surprising some Venezuelans were prepared to accept U.S. control over the country’s oil, if only because they saw no other option.
“Chavismo,” she said, “has reduced us to a state of global humiliation, kneeling before the United States.”

washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/14/n.headline: Nvidia scandal hits Trump’s political vulnerabilities after Democratic sweep
washingtonpost.com/politics/2026/11/14/n.author: Isaac Arnsdorf, Cat Zakrzewski

paragraphs.text: Sex. Money. Power. Espionage. As Washington scandals go, this one has everything.

But what really makes ex-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy an explosive political problem for the White House is that it brings together the very issues that propelled Democrats to their largest congressional majority since 1990. Voters revolted against President Donald Trump’s handling of the economy, with widespread concerns about artificial intelligence, data centers, competition from China, and special access and favors for billionaires.

Those concerns vaulted the Nvidia scandal atop Democrats’ list for investigating the Trump administration, according to Rep. Stephen F. Lynch (D-Massachusetts), a member of the House Financial Services and Oversight committees. The latter panel will focus on national security dangers, including why Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick declined to blacklist companies suspected of smuggling advanced chips to China made by Nvidia, whose processors power much of the AI industry, and why Trump continued to talk to Huang and bring him on Air Force One.
“We really want to get to the bottom of this,” Lynch said, noting Nvidia committed $25 million for Trump’s White House ballroom. “Was there some type of quid pro quo there?”

The scandal is engulfing Washington as Trump prepares to travel to China next week and meet with its president, Xi Jinping. A senior U.S. official said Trump is unlikely to raise the Huang subject with his Chinese counterpart.
“The situation with Nvidia should not really have any bearing on the trip,” said the official, who spoke on the condition of anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the matter publicly.

Huang will not join this trip. On the last visit to China in May, Trump picked up Huang on Air Force One in Alaska, despite a warning from Secretary of State and national security adviser Marco Rubio that the U.S. had obtained intelligence that showed Huang was having an affair with a woman believed to be a Chinese spy.

Concerns over the national security and economic fallout are not limited to Democrats. Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott (R-South Carolina) asked Huang and Lutnick to testify, and House Republicans are demanding Huang come in for a transcribed interview, threatening him with a subpoena. The top Republican and Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee also asked Lutnick for a classified briefing.

“If you’re in bed with a Chinese spy and you’re an individual with top-secret clearances developing these things related to everything from military tech to AI across the board to data crunching and everything else, this is a very big concern,” said Brian Mast (R-Florida), the House Foreign Affairs Committee chairman who signed the letter to Huang along with House Select Committee on China Chairman John Moolenaar (R-Michigan) and House Intelligence Committee Chairman Rick Crawford (R-Arkansas). “It’s painful to see this happen to Nvidia because they are one of the most important American tech companies, probably the most American tech company right now.”
The Foreign Affairs Committee’s ranking Democrat, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York, who is seeking the gavel when Democrats take the majority in January, said he hopes the probe can be bipartisan.

“We’ve seen the tip of the iceberg,” he told reporters inside the U.S. Capitol on Thursday. “We need to know whether or not the Chinese government got any additional information, what information it was, how much, and then who knew what when.”
Trump has said little publicly on the scandal this week except to sympathize with Huang.
“I always thought of him as a fine man,” Trump said in an interview on Thursday with Stephen A. Smith, noting that he spoke with Huang the day before. “He’s going through hell.”

Others in the administration have pointed the finger at Lutnick, whose department is responsible for restricting exports of sensitive technology. “Commerce has the pen,” Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on CNBC on Friday. Last week, Bessent confronted Lutnick over why he hadn’t taken action despite directions from Trump on three occasions, according to a former administration official who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe a private conversation.
Lutnick agreed to appear voluntarily before Scott’s Banking Committee, a Commerce Department spokeswoman said.
Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana) said he would like to question Lutnick on why he allowed the sale of advance chips to the company of the suspected spy that Huang was having an affair with.
“Congress is not going to let this go,” he said.

In a sign of how the political winds have shifted since Nov. 3, Nvidia is counting on an experienced Democrat to help manage the crisis. In June, the company brought on Bruce Andrews, a former Commerce Department official in the Obama administration.

In the midterms, 56 percent of voters said AI and data centers were a crucial or major factor in their vote for Congress, and two-thirds of them voted for Democrats, according to the broadcast networks’ exit polls. Ninety percent said corruption was a crucial or major factor, and they favored Democrats to Republicans, 58 percent to 40 percent.

“Tech accountability was a winning message at the ballot box because of the AI industry’s cozy and corrupt relationship with Trump. Now we are learning Big Tech’s wrongdoing went far beyond corruption,” said Sacha Haworth, founder of the Tech Oversight Project, a watchdog group advising Democrats. “We want to see a Democratic Congress investigate Nvidia for anticompetitive practices that pass off costs to consumers, what the company knew about chip smuggling operations with China, and what Nvidia received in exchange for donations to the Trump campaign and ballroom.”
Some of those themes have crossover appeal to China hawks and tech critics within Trump’s coalition.

“This is going to end in tears unless we get some very smart people to start saying, ‘Hey, what is in the country’s interest?’” former White House strategist Stephen K. Bannon said on his influential online talk show on Friday. “Not the oligarchs. Not the stock market. … This goes to the beating heart of the modern world economy and who’s actually in charge.”
Mariana Alfaro, Jarrell Dillard, Noah Robertson and Nancy Cook contributed reporting.

npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-6040507/democra.headline: As Democrats win big, thirst traps of male candidates take social media by storm
npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-6040507/democra.author: Danielle Kurtzleben

paragraphs.text: If you're on social media, there's a good chance you've seen the videos: people getting hot and bothered about the young men Democrats just elected.

"I'm looking at you, Rob Sand. I'm looking at you, Jon Ossoff. I'm looking at you, El-Sayed," said fitness coach Jesse Barton, reacting to the midterm results. "I am looking, I am not the only one, and I'm very happy about what I see."
There are debates over candidates' relative levels of hotness. There are a lot of AI-generated images. And there are many, many montages of the politicians set to sexy pop music.
One of the most viral pieces of content was a parody Tiger Beat magazine cover featuring Democratic men … which Manoushka Guerrier, an LA-based chef and content-creator, took one step further.

"I created the entire Tiger Beat style personality quiz, complete with the different boy band personas," she said. The quiz gives people matches including "the Babyface" (Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico) and "the Heartthrob" (Colorado Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel).
Guerrier pays a lot of attention to politics, and she emphasizes that these guys' looks are just a bonus.
"They're young and they're ballsy and they're smart, and they're not just smart; they're brilliant," she says.

The tidal wave of attention on these young men creates a striking contrast to the first Trump midterm, in 2018. That election — after the Women's March, Me Too and the long list of assault and misconduct allegations against President Trump — yielded a record-setting wave of Democratic women. It all suggests that the thirsty social media posts aren't just a cheeky trend; they also say a lot about how Democrats have responded to the Trump era.
A response to Trump
Two main forces are behind the wave of attention on these men according to Christina Wolbrecht, a political science professor at Notre Dame University.
"I think it's a function of our kind of society-wide debate about masculinity," she said. "And I also think it's about age."

The age side is straightforward — just ahead of the midterms, a majority of likely voters said they favored candidates with new ideas over those with experience in the job, according to a NPR/PBS News/Marist Poll.
The masculinity side, meanwhile, is in response to MAGA and its elevation of a very specific type of manhood, Wolbrecht said.
"For 10-plus years, Donald Trump has presented one very distinct version of masculinity," she said. "It's very much power over [others]. It's very much power through wealth and status."

Manliness took center stage on the Democratic side this election. Candidates leaned into it, with people like Rutinel and Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El Sayed posting weightlifting videos. El Sayed at one point did a video spoofing Love Island.

Voters noticed, posting admiring videos well before the election. Meanwhile, the media noticed and amplified this narrative, with profiles and think pieces throughout the midterm cycle, and reporting on Democrats' "rugged" and "authentic" candidates.
'That's a girly thing to be, is a Democrat'

Amplifying young, "manly" men may have boosted the party in this election. That's because Democrats had a problem after Kamala Harris lost the presidency in 2024, according to Democratic strategist Monica Venske.

"The feeling within the straight male demographic, if you will, [was] that it just wasn't cool to be a Democrat," she said. "It wasn't sexy to be a Democrat. It's not manly to be a Democrat. That's a girly thing to be, is a Democrat."
That's why she started the Instagram account Boyfriends We Deserve, where she highlights attractive Democrats — mostly men, but a few women as well.
Venske explains she is careful in how she posts about women's looks — unlike when she talks about men, like Montana's incoming Democratic congressman.
"Like when I call Sam Forstag hot, it will most likely never, ever hurt him," she said. "But I can call someone like Keisha Lance Bottoms hot and that could hurt her every time."
She said she instead will call the women "baddies" or focus on their hair, as opposed to highlighting their bodies or overall looks.
To Venske, the Boyfriends We Deserve posts are part of making it clear that the Democratic party is a big tent that includes young men.

"I'm like, 'Look at all these manly guys who are Democrats,'" she said. "Sam Forstag is an example I usually give. He was like a smokejumper in Montana. And in his announcement video for Congress, he's fixing up a truck. If a guy who is jumping out of planes to put out fires and fixing up trucks can be a Democrat, you can be a Democrat, I promise."
…But Democratic women won, too

All of that said, plenty of Democratic women ran and won this year, including several historic firsts: Georgia's Keisha Lance Bottoms, for example, will be the first Black woman governor. New Mexico's Deb Haaland will be the first Native American woman governor. Minnesota's Peggy Flanagan will be the nation's first Native American woman senator.
That highlights a big difference between this midterm and 2018's wave of women.

Since that election, Democrats have seen Joe Biden defeat Trump, and then watched a second woman lose the presidency to Trump. And while Democrats most certainly do still elect women — far more than Republicans — the masculinity of their male candidates received outsized attention this year.
It's possible, then, that the attention on Democratic men isn't simply lighthearted, but is part of Democrats' continual conversation about electability.

"I hear it from all sorts of people with all sorts of engagement that 2016 and 2024 proved that it took old-guy, aviator sunglasses Joe Biden to defeat Trump," Wolbrecht said, "and we need more of that and not more Kamala Harrises or Hillary Clintons."

"I think that's a mistake," she added quickly. "I think it's a misunderstanding of what happened in '16 and in '24. But the meaning we put on elections has consequences and it really shapes what parties do strategically going forward."
Democrats have struggled to win over men in recent elections. For example, Harris won 43 percent of men overall in 2024. This year, the party won 50 percent of the men's vote.
Guerrier disagrees that the attention on candidates' looks is about electability, but she thinks that for a lot of voters, this election was about changing the Democratic Party's story.
"It was just like these guys came out of nowhere, and it was just so refreshing that, wow, we can get out of this darkness and into something that is hopeful," she said.
