nytimes.com/2026/11/14/nyregion/gold-bar.headline: This Man Stole $9 Million in Gold Bars on the Upper West Side, Police Say
nytimes.com/2026/11/14/nyregion/gold-bar.author: Neil Vigdor

paragraphs.text: The meeting point had been arranged: near 81st Street and Broadway on the Upper West Side.

It was there, in broad daylight, that two men approached each other on a Wednesday in April 2025. One of the men, a 67-year-old New Yorker, transported a bag of $9 million in gold bars, each one the size of a chocolate bar, that the police said someone online had instructed him to buy and hand over.
The man did exactly as he was told, believing that he could secure his financial assets, which an alert on his computer had led to believe were compromised, the authorities said.
The other man took sack of gold and fled on foot, according to the police. The first man had been the victim of an online fraud.

Now, more than a year and a half after the deceit, the New York Police Department is asking for the public’s help in identifying the man who ran off with the gold bars in connection with a grand larceny investigation.
Investigators this week released security camera footage and images of the man suspected of taking the bars.
Isaac Kahan, the owner of Bullion Trading LLC, a gold and silver dealer in Manhattan’s Diamond District, wondered about the sheer logistics that were involved in the heist.

Each of the gold bars weighs one kilogram, about 2.2 pounds, according to the police. While the dollar value of gold has fluctuated since 2025, the current cost of a one-kilo bar is about $130,000, according to Mr. Kahan, meaning that $9 million would buy about 69 gold bars and weigh more than 150 pounds.
“I don’t even know how he would be able to carry that,” Mr. Kahan said in an interview on Friday. “You can’t even lift that.”

From his decades as a precious metals wholesaler, Mr. Kahan said, he had become all too familiar with such fraud schemes, which he noted typically target people in their 70s and 80s, and seek to get them to liquidate their assets to buy gold.

About once every two weeks, Mr. Kahan’s business will receive somewhat cryptic requests from potential clients to buy gold bars, he said, adding that it used to happen on a daily basis. Unlike investors, victims of frauds show little interest in the weight and purity of gold, he said.
“When a person starts throwing the dollar amount first to me, that’s a telltale sign right away,” Mr. Kahan said.

A few years ago, while his company was closed for the Jewish High Holy Days of Rosh Hashana and Yom Kippur, it received several online orders from people who had been targets of such schemes, he said. The business was able to cancel some of the transactions, according to Mr. Kahan, who said one victim’s daughter had contacted him after noticing a suspicious wire transfer for $150,000.
“It was heartbreaking,” Mr. Kahan said, adding that gold is essentially “impossible” to trace.

An older woman in Florida was the target of a similar scheme this May, according to the F.B.I., which said the victim received an email claiming to be from Amazon and telling her to call a phone number because her bank account had been breached.

A person claiming to be associated with the bank told the woman that her identity had been stolen and that her Social Security number had been compromised, which would require her to speak with another individual, who claimed to be an agent with the Federal Trade Commission.

That individual instructed the woman to write a check for $101,220 to buy 21 gold bars that she delivered to a masked man in a Volvo at a Sunoco gas station near the victim’s home in McIntosh, Fla., the authorities said.

When the woman received directions to buy another $500,000 in gold bars, a friend became suspicious, according to federal authorities, who began an investigation and this month announced the indictments of 10 people in connection with the fraud scheme.
It was not clear if there was any connection between the cases in Florida and New York.
The F.B.I. field office in New York did not respond to a request for comment on Friday about the gold bars that were stolen from the man on the Upper West Side.
Mr. Kahan said that he flags suspicious gold purchases for the F.B.I. and arranges for agents to speak to people who he fears could be the targets of frauds.
“We do try to slow the process down,” he said.

npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-6032604/organ-t.headline: An organ transplant controversy tests 'the dead donor rule'
npr.org/2026/11/14/nx-s1-6032604/organ-t.author: Rob Stein

paragraphs.text: The U.S. organ transplant system has approved the first national policy for a controversial procedure used to remove organs from hospital patients. The guidelines are designed to protect potential donors. But critics say they do little to improve safety and fail to address deeply troubling ethical concerns.

The procedure is called normothermic regional perfusion, known as NRP. It can be used after a family has decided to withdraw care because there's no hope of meaningful recovery for the person. To perform NRP, doctors attach an external pump to a donor minutes after their circulation has ended and they've been declared dead. The pump restores blood flow to their hearts, lungs, kidneys, liver and other organs to keep them from deteriorating.

"The hope with NRP is that it increases the supply of organs and it increases the quality of the organs," says Dr. Raymond Lynch, the director of transplantation at the Health Resources & Services Administration, the federal agency that oversees the organ transplant system.

NRP could help solve the chronic organ shortage, Lynch says. More than 109,000 Americans are waiting for an organ transplant, according to HRSA. About 12 die every day because of a chronic organ shortage.

Critics, however, say NRP is unethical because it violates the Dead Donor Rule, which is the most important rule protecting potential donors. The rule says transplant surgeons can only take organs from patients after they are dead because of brain death or circulatory death. But because NRP restarts circulation, critics say the procedure reverses the very condition upon which the person has just been declared dead.

"In order to be dead by circulatory criteria it means we're not going to attempt to reestablish circulation. But that's exactly what they do in NRP," says Dr. Lainie Friedman Ross, a University of Rochester bioethicist. "So, yes, I have a real problem with NRP. I think it violates the dead donor rule. It's taking organs from people who are no longer dead."

The other aspect of NRP that troubles critics is what surgeons do to try to make sure the donor is also brain dead, after circulation has been restarted by a mechanical pump. They clamp off blood vessels that supply the head. But alarm bells started going off for organ retrieval teams when blood appeared to get restored – or "reperfused" – to the brain during some NRP cases.

"We have seen signs of life in NRP when the brain has been reperfused," says Dr. Claire Morgan, a transplant surgeon who serves on the transplant network's Patient Affairs Committee and was the first to report such cases to HRSA. "It's extremely disturbing."

Those cases prompted HRSA to instruct the Organ Procurement & Transplantation Network (OPTN), which runs the organ system, to investigate and develop a response. On Nov. 6, the OPTN board of directors approved the first phase of the first uniform national guidelines for how to perform NRP.
The new guidelines, which will go into effect Dec. 6, call for surgeons to do more than just clamp the blood vessels to the brain. They should also cut holes in them, according to the new policy.

"Clamping the blood vessels should stop blood flowing to the brain," says Lynch. "Cutting or venting above the level of the clamping is a second safeguard to make sure that if the clamping is insufficient that it immediately drains out of the head and is not supplying warm oxygenated blood to the brain."
The new policy also includes other protections, including recommending against giving donors drugs that would paralyze them and mask any movements.
But critics say the new safeguards are insufficient. Most surgeons already both clamp and vent blood vessels to the brain, for example, they say.

"I honestly don't believe they have created a policy that creates much or any more protection than these donors already had," says Morgan, who also disagrees with the decision to implement the first phase of the new guidelines on an emergency basis before the public had a chance to weigh in.

Critics also say the new policy doesn't begin to address the bigger concerns that NRP donors are not technically dead when surgeons remove their organs. They worry the adoption of the policy could speed the use of NRP before the troubling questions have been fully aired.
"I really think the policy is the cart before the horse," says Dr. Matthew DeCamp, a University of Colorado bioethicist. "The fundamental issues around NRP still remain unresolved."
Lynch, however, argues the new guidelines will protect donors and that NRP is ethical.

"This is an important first step to make sure NRP care is available but that the safety of the family's loved one is always at the forefront," Lynch says. "This is life-saving care that will extend the supply and improve the quality of organs that patients can get in transplant. And if it is done properly, it is safe."

nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/politics/congr.headline: As Congress Plans Investigations, White House Prepares Ferocious Response
nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/politics/congr.author: Luke Broadwater, Zolan Kanno-Youngs, Devlin Barrett

paragraphs.text: In his first term, President Trump approached congressional investigations with a strategy of resisting and stonewalling, hoping to stall the inquiries until Democrats ran out of time.

But in anticipation of Democrats’ return to control of Congress in his second term, Mr. Trump has embarked on an even more aggressive maneuver: threatening to treat some legislative oversight as a potential crime.
That tactic is expected to be part of an all-out effort by the White House to block Democratic congressional oversight over the next two years.

The pushback will be led in part by Mr. Trump’s new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, a political brawler with extensive experience on Capitol Hill. It will be bolstered by a Justice Department and a White House Counsel’s Office that have been quietly laying the groundwork for the fight.

At stake: whether the Trump administration can prevent Democrats from getting access to its decision-making and scrutinizing the actions of top officials and powerful people, in and out of government. Mr. Trump has also become increasingly concerned that some of his biggest supporters who give money toward his prized construction projects will be targeted, according to aides and his public statements.
The White House is bracing for a spate of investigations, and officials say they are ready to punch back.

“If you’re not ready for these fights, you’re going to be in a whole lot of trouble legally and politically,” said Hogan Gidley, a White House deputy press secretary in the first Trump administration. “They have a really good plan and have a good leader at the top in Stephen Miller. He is primed and ready for this fight, like no one else would be.”

While clashes between lawmakers and the White House over congressional investigations are not unusual, the escalating threats could result in a remarkable battle that reshapes the balance of power between the two branches of government. Legal experts have said the White House’s contention that congressional investigations “may cross the line into blatant criminality” pushes the bounds of the law, but much remains unclear about how the courts might handle the coming fights.

“As the president has said, he’s willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hard-working Americans,” said Lauren Bis, a White House spokeswoman. “If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people.”

Top Democrats have shown no indications they are intimidated or plan to slow down. They have already sent letters to scores of potential targets of investigations, on everything from cuts to scientific research to donors for Mr. Trump’s White House ballroom.

On Thursday, Senator Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts, Representative Robert Garcia of California and Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut announced an investigation into a top Trump fund-raiser, Meredith O’Rourke, after reports indicated that she coordinated more than $800 million in contributions to the president’s favorite construction projects.

“The fund-raising operation that President Trump reportedly directs with your assistance reeks of potential corruption and the potential for quid pro quo politics,” the lawmakers wrote to Ms. O’Rourke.
A spokesman for Ms. O’Rourke said that Mr. Trump could not be bought, and that Democrats’ accusations were baseless.
The White House plan to shield Mr. Trump’s donors and threaten Democrats has been taking shape for months in response to what they believe will be an unrelenting pace of oversight.

The Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel over the summer quietly published an opinion asserting that even communications by those outside government could be covered by executive privilege if they concerned Mr. Trump and his top aides.

Rachel Jag, a former staff member to Representative Jim Jordan of Ohio, the newly elected Republican leader in the House, will coordinate the department’s response to Democratic subpoenas, records requests and accusations. She is overseeing a large staff, but the department is seeking experienced lawyers to fill out what are expected to be high-workload jobs.

The department has been hit by a wave of departures, and Ms. Jag took over the role on an interim basis after Patrick Davis, who served as the department’s head of legislative affairs, quit just before the midterm elections for reasons that remain unclear.
At the White House, Mr. Trump appointed Mr. Miller chief of staff after Democrats swept to victory last week.
“Stephen Miller is President Trump’s wartime general,” said Mike Davis, a former chief counsel for nominations on the Senate Judiciary Committee. “He’s very experienced, including on the Hill.”
And the White House Counsel’s Office began beefing up its staff, hiring two lawyers to deal with oversight.

On Saturday, the president posted on social media: “Threatening letters have been sent to many people, all innocent, from Democrat Political Leaders. By copy of this statement, I am ordering the Department of Justice to look into this criminal act, immediately!”
Top lawyers across the federal government snapped into action.

Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, sent a letter to Mr. Blumenthal on Wednesday, warning of “significant legal consequences” should he continue to pursue an investigation into the ballroom donors.
Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Thursday that top leaders at the Justice Department had been working with Mr. Reitz.

At a news conference, Mr. Blanche said there were “no ongoing criminal investigations” into statements made by incoming members of Congress. Nevertheless, he said, Justice Department officials were concerned about some of the statements made after the election.
“There can come a point when a criticism becomes a threat,” Mr. Blanche said, adding, “There are threats, which can be allowed as well, but at some point it does become a crime.”
Then, Will Scharf, the White House counsel, put Mr. Garcia, the incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee, on notice that he could be committing criminal acts by pursuing investigations.
Asked about his letter to Mr. Garcia and whether it meant the White House was prepared to prosecute lawmakers, Mr. Scharf said that “the letter stands for itself.”

“I meant everything I said,” Mr. Scharf added in an interview on Thursday. He declined to address how the administration’s efforts squared with the “speech or debate” clause of the Constitution, which shields lawmakers from being subpoenaed or prosecuted by the executive branch over their legislative work.
Congress, at its core, is a legislative body, not a prosecutorial one. To the extent Congress has investigative powers, they are to obtain information to help in the act of legislating.
If administration officials fight congressional subpoenas, federal courts would have to referee — litigation that could take months or years to resolve.
Mr. Scharf and others are collecting examples of lawmakers who they say are making clear their investigations have no legislative purpose.
Donald F. McGahn II, the White House counsel for part of Mr. Trump’s first term, said the White House had long prepared for the oversight.
“They’ve talked to a lot of people who’ve done it before,” he said.

Of Mr. Scharf’s letter, Mr. McGahn said, “It’s smart to chronicle in writing all of the things that the various Democratic congressmen will say about oversight that shows that they’re not doing it for a legislative purpose.”

Stanley M. Brand, the top lawyer in the House under Speaker Thomas P. (Tip) O’Neill Jr., said the White House threats against lawmakers carried little legal power. But he said Congress would have difficulty enforcing any subpoena should the administration refuse to comply, because any criminal referral would go to the Justice Department. And the attorney general reports to Mr. Trump.

“Although the Democrats control the Congress, the administration still controls the Department of Justice, and so to the extent that people get referred for contempt under the criminal statute, I don’t expect that to go anywhere,” he said.

Either chamber of Congress could also consider trying to use its long-dormant “inherent contempt” powers. Such a move would direct the sergeant-at-arms to arrest an official who refused to comply with the directives of Congress.
It would be another escalation in a fight that has been full of them even before it has begun.

nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/elections/alas.headline: ‘Democrat’ in Alaska’s House Race Is Doing Time in a New York Prison
nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/elections/alas.author: Anna Griffin

paragraphs.text: In the midterm election’s closing days, the phones of left-leaning Alaskans pinged with texts urging them to back Eric Hafner, the lone Democrat on the four-person ballot for a U.S. House seat.

But Democratic Party leaders in Alaska and Washington were actually backing an independent on the ballot, Bill Hill, and for good reason: Mr. Hafner is a felon serving a 20-year sentence in a federal prison in Otisville, N.Y., about 4,351 miles from Anchorage.

Who paid for those text messages is of particular interest in Alaska, where purportedly dirty tricks by Democratic operatives put an alternative Dan Sullivan on the Senate ballot against the incumbent Republican, Senator Dan Sullivan.

Mr. Hafner’s unknown benefactor was likely hoping to confuse voters and aid the Republican incumbent, Representative Nick Begich. Democrats point to the texts as proof that nobody’s hands are clean in Alaska.
Mr. Hafner and his chief supporter — his mother — say the motive doesn’t matter, even as the mysterious outside help has elevated his jailhouse bid into a potential spoiler.
“Why should we care where they came from?” Ms. Hafner asked.

Official results may not come for days in the races for Alaska’s Senate seat and its lone House seat. The winners will likely be determined after officials tabulate second- and third-place choices on the state’s ranked-choice ballots.

In the House contest, Mr. Begich, the scion of an Alaska political dynasty, holds 48.5 percent of counted votes, and Mr. Hill, 41.2 percent. Mr. Hafner, who has never visited Alaska, has nearly 8 percent.
“This guy may actually matter,” Eric Croft, the state Democratic Party chairman, said.

If enough supporters of Mr. Hafner and the fourth candidate, the Libertarian Jim McDermott, ranked Mr. Hill ahead of Mr. Begich, the independent could still win. But preliminary ballot data suggest that Mr. Hill faces an uphill battle. Only about 45 percent of Mr. Hafner’s votes would ultimately transfer to Mr. Hill, while nearly half would be exhausted because voters did not rank either of the two leading candidates.

Carol Gray, a University of Alaska Fairbanks political scientist, said most of Mr. Hafner’s votes — “maybe all of them” — came from Alaskans angry at Republicans and backing any Democrat on the ballot. Mr. Hill’s decision not to run as a Democrat — no decision at all for the lifelong independent, according to his team — may prove to be his campaign’s undoing.
Mr. Croft was not so sure. Eight percent for someone like Mr. Hafner? “That just feels too hard to believe,” he said. “That becomes a dirty trick that worked.”
Mr. Begich has denied any involvement by his campaign to boost Mr. Hafner. The only clear Republican fingerprints on the caper are actually on the similar electoral efforts of Mr. Hafner’s mother.
“We’re a politically engaged family,” she said.

She ran as a Democrat in Alaska’s nonpartisan U.S. Senate primary, backed by $346,000 in ads from Fair Deal Alaska, a super PAC funded almost entirely by committees tied to Senate Republicans and the incumbent, Dan S. Sullivan. Ms. Hafner won less than 1 percent of the primary vote and failed to advance.
She finished third in Alaska’s Democratic House primary in 2018 and second in Wyoming’s Democratic primary two years later.

Ms. Hafner and her son both use a South Dakota mail-forwarding service as their campaign addresses. She said Republicans did not recruit either of them, denied any connection to the Republican-bought ads and described both her and her son’s politics as “progressive through and through.”

Still, Mr. Hafner’s handwritten filing for a Florida U.S. House special election last year listed ancillary committees including “MAGA Republicans Victory Fund,” “Secure the Border Florida” and “America First Florida Always.” His entry in Alaska’s official voter guide this year called on voters to unite against short-term greed.
Ballot stacking — essentially, recruiting candidates to siphon votes and split the opposition — is a time-honored tradition in Alaska and other states with low hurdles to run for office.

In Mr. Hafner’s case, Mr. Begich’s allies appear to have capitalized on a history of quixotic campaigns dating back to 2016, when “the Rev. Dr. Eric Hafner” finished second in the Republican primary for Hawaii’s 2nd Congressional District.

Two years later, Mr. Hafner ran as a Democrat for a U.S. House seat in Oregon, another place he had never lived, telling a reporter that Portland’s live-and-let-live vibe — especially on marijuana — matched his own.
Mr. Hafner, who his mother says “runs to win,” has plenty of time for politics.

Between 2016 and 2018, according to court records, Mr. Hafner threatened to kill lawyers, police officers and judges in Monmouth County, N.J., tied to his past juvenile and family court cases. He pleaded guilty in 2022 to two counts of making interstate threats and one count of making false bomb threats and received a 20-year prison sentence.

In 2024, Mr. Hafner paid the $100 fee to run for Alaska’s U.S. House seat from prison. He won fewer than 500 primary votes, but reached the general election after several Republicans ahead of him dropped out to aid Mr. Begich.

Alaska Democrats, worried about confusing voters and hurting the Democratic incumbent, Mary Peltola, sued to block his candidacy. Republicans fought to keep him on the ballot and won. But Mr. Hafner’s 3,417 votes — one percent of the total — were not decisive in Ms. Peltola’s loss.

This year, Democrats lacked a big-name contender for the House seat after an Anchorage pastor, Matt Schultz, dropped out. So they backed Mr. Hill, a commercial fisherman and former teacher and school administrator.

Mr. Hafner filed on May 10 via another handwritten form mailed from his cell. This time, fearing voter confusion, independent groups spent nearly $500,000 urging people not to rank him. Online and radio spots said the “D” next to Mr. Hafner’s name stood for “doing time.”

At the same time, thousands of Alaskans received text messages supporting Mr. Hafner. The messages accused Mr. Hill of being a closet conservative and noting that Mr. Hafner supported “Medicare for All, the Green New Deal, and will fight back against Trump and his enablers.”

The texts did not include any detail about who sent them, which may violate federal election law, depending on how many went out and how they were sent. So far, no outside group has reported spending money supporting Mr. Hafner.
Ms. Hafner doesn’t care who paid for the messages. She’s just grateful.
“If something lands in your lap, you’re not going to say ‘no thanks,’” she said.
Mr. Hafner is already barred from serving, because the Constitution requires U.S. House members to live in the state they represent when elected.
His mother sees a path around that: “Somebody needs to tell President Trump that Eric has earned a pardon,” she said.

nytimes.com/2026/11/14/technology/jensen.headline: The Jensen Huang Scandal Has Shocked Even Scandal-Prone Silicon Valley
nytimes.com/2026/11/14/technology/jensen.author: David Streitfeld

paragraphs.text: Artificial intelligence promises transcendence. We will ditch our tired and inefficient bodies, say farewell to tedious work and trips to the grocery store. The computer will tend to all human needs and solve all human problems.

Well, that was the idea. A.I. was supposed to achieve a new level of reality this month with the public sale of shares of Anthropic, one of the two start-ups that have created and defined this young industry. A trillion-dollar company will be born, yielding billionaires galore.

A.I. is the biggest Silicon Valley story ever. But last Sunday it was suddenly pushed aside when the chief executive of the company whose chips are literally powering this intelligence revolution confessed to cheating on his wife with a woman, Alice Huang, who U.S. officials believe was spying for China. By Thursday morning he had resigned, something few thought possible just days earlier.

The scandal that took down Nvidia chief Jensen Huang is full of implications for national security and the global A.I. boom. Mr. Huang ranked among Mark Zuckerberg, Steve Jobs, Elon Musk and Bill Gates as tech leaders who were considered by the world to be inseparable from the companies they built.

In Silicon Valley, people were mostly just stunned by the news. Those who have been around for a long time, and seen the stretch of territory south of San Francisco evolve from hardware manufacturing to software development to the dot-com frenzy and now the A.I. boom, said they had never seen anything like it.

Tech veterans have witnessed amazing ascensions and equally abrupt falls. They have seen abundant arrogance. Fortunes made and fortunes lost in an instant. But there’s something that stands out this time: Transcendence was never supposed to be tawdry.

“We’re told A.I. will change all of our lives in ways we can’t even understand and then suddenly here we are: the oldest story in the world,” said John Gage, a longtime Sun Microsystems executive who, like many in the valley, has been following new developments avidly. “And it’s not hard to understand at all.”
What is harder for tech people to understand is why it happened. How could someone supposedly so smart, and entrusted with so much of humankind’s future, be so casually stupid?

After all, intrigue in Silicon Valley is ubiquitous — everyone is looking for the secret sauce to help their start-up, or their country, get ahead. As a result, secrecy is an obsession. Silicon Valley did not invent the concept of nondisclosure agreements but has used them zealously. Everything and everyone is guarded.
Mr. Gage recalled working with a tech executive making his first trip to Korea decades ago.

“At two in the morning some woman sent by some technology rival taps on his hotel door,” Mr. Gage said. “That sort of thing was routine. When you’re attempting to persuade someone to buy something or sell something, you use every possible tool.”

If scheming and spying are almost inevitable in tech circles, for a long time women were not. Every woman in tech above a certain age has memories of being the only female in the room. Silicon Valley was as much a boys’ club as Wall Street or the military.

It was an engineering culture and the men who flourished had a particular aptitude. “It’s like the engineering half of their brain had taken over,” said Lynnea Johnson, who began working at Apple in the early 1980s. “The other half, the part with emotional clarity and judgment, was kind of immature.”

What struck Ms. Johnson as puzzling in Mr. Huang’s case was that he seemed not know or care that Ms. Huang was possibly in the employ of the Chinese government. He was reckless, which wasn’t his reputation.

These are dizzying days in Silicon Valley, which needs to present A.I. as unavoidable but beneficial and the executives as in control but nonthreatening. Mr. Huang was the prototype of the new transcendent man.

He did a terrific job of branding himself. He talked about his devotion to his wife Lori, who handled all the routine aspects of their lives since they met at Oregon State University. He didn’t know his address or phone number. The machines did, and that was good enough for him. Material things seemed of little interest beyond his ubiquitous leather jackets. When California debated a wealth tax, he didn’t whine it was unfair like some of his fellow billionaires. “I don’t mind paying taxes,” he proclaimed. Nvidia was his only passion. “If I’m not working, I’m thinking about working,” he said.
But it looks like he was thinking about something else, too. On Wednesday, The New York Times reported that Mr. Huang was having an affair with a second woman, who worked at Nvidia.

Powerful men are often drawn to risk. And their power seems to increase their sense of impunity. It’s a plotline as old as King David and Bathsheba, the wife of one of David’s top soldiers. (For those who have forgotten their Bible studies: God was really irked). A woman who has worked closely with the tech elite thinks that they are obsessed with two things they can’t control: how long they get to live on this earth, and certain primal urges.

“There’s no feeling in the world like the thrill of a new romance,” the woman said. “You can’t buy it or compel it. It’s perhaps the only emotion wealthy and powerful men can’t create at will, so naturally for them it’s irresistible. And that’s why it overrides the better judgment of the most intelligent and disciplined men on the planet.”

The woman asked to remain anonymous because she thought even talking about sex in Silicon Valley would somehow taint her. It underscores the unease that still endures between men and women in the tech world in 2026.

Others in Silicon Valley were reticent to talk, at least early in the week, because they thought Mr. Huang was likely to hang on and they feared his power. A publicist explained that her clients were not available to comment because selling their start-ups to Nvidia was their exit strategy.

Mr. Huang also had his defenders, at least until the second affair surfaced. “Just because it’s salacious does not mean it is treasonous,” said Joanna Hoffman, an early Apple executive. “It was bad judgment, but it’s as old as the human race.”
If Mr. Huang’s problems were only sex, he might still have a job. But there is also the spying angle, which China denies.
“I know of no precedent here,” said Margaret O’Mara, a Silicon Valley historian. “Corporate espionage, yes; real espionage involving anyone notable, no. Wild times.”

Espionage cases in the tech world that are discovered and prosecuted usually involve low-level employees. Their actions often play out like farces, as if it never occurred to them they could be caught.

A new employee of OpenAI, Abdulrahman Alfozan, was arrested last month and charged with wiretapping after he was allegedly discovered putting a recording device wrapped in toilet paper in a conference room. Mr. Alfozan, a Saudi national, has pleaded not guilty.

OpenAI found the device during a routine sweep. Google was not as lucky with its own employee. Linwei Ding, who started working for the company as a software engineer in 2019, uploaded confidential information about A.I. technology to his personal Google Cloud account using Apple Notes, according to court papers.

Mr. Ding simultaneously started spending a lot of time in China raising money for an A.I. start-up. To evade detection while he was 6,000 miles away from his California office, he had a colleague swipe his access badge, a process known as “ghost-badging.”

A few days before planning to flee the U.S. for good, Mr. Ding was arrested. After an 11-day trial in January, a federal jury convicted the 38-year-old engineer on seven counts of economic espionage and seven counts of theft. He was sentenced to nearly a year in prison.

Mr. Huang seemed to have had a similar carefree attitude toward his relationship with Ms. Huang, as if he wouldn’t be caught, and if he were, it wouldn’t matter. With his power and wealth and importance, that was probably true — until it wasn’t.

Regis McKenna is the grand old man of Silicon Valley, who came here in the early 1960s when it was still apricot orchards. The tech industry then was an arm of the defense industry, and pioneers like Gordon Moore and Robert Noyce had a Midwestern, almost military rectitude. Mr. McKenna, a marketer who worked for America Online, Apple, Genentech, Lotus, Microsoft and other companies, had dinner plans when I called. He only had time for one question.
Does too much money —
“Yes, yes,” he interrupted. “Does it turn their heads, does it turn their morals? Yes. Money changes people, and it started changing Silicon Valley a long time ago.”

In just a few days, if all goes as planned, will finally come the Anthropic public offering. How big a deal is it? In 1999 and 2000, the peak years of the dot-com boom, 800 companies went public. Their combined value on their first day of trading will likely be less than Anthropic, according to calculations by the finance expert Jay Ritter.

Never have so few made so much so fast. The world will be in awe. Look for some of these technologists to believe their press coverage, shrug off any natural caution and, in the great tradition of Silicon Valley, do something transcendently stupid.

washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/13/h.headline: Hidden homeownership costs can catch first-time buyers off guard
washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/13/h.author: Natasha Etzel

paragraphs.text: For hopeful first-time buyers who have only ever rented, it can be easy to misjudge what they can realistically afford as they start looking at home listings. To avoid starting your first few months of homeownership in financial stress, it’s important to understand the true cost of homeownership and set a realistic budget before you begin touring homes or making offers.

Beyond the mortgage itself, there are other expenses that add to the cost of owning a home. Property taxes, homeowners insurance, private mortgage insurance (PMI) and maintenance and repair costs can add hundreds, or even thousands, of dollars to your monthly housing expenses.

First-time buyers who don’t account for these costs risk stretching their budget by overbuying from the start. Here’s what to know about the hidden costs of homeownership and why financial experts say you should never buy at the top of your budget.
These homeownership costs can change

With a fixed-rate mortgage, your interest rate is locked in, and your principal and interest costs won’t change. But that doesn’t mean your monthly mortgage payment will stay the same. Other costs tied to homeownership can change over time.

Your property tax bill could increase if your home is reassessed or if local property tax rates rise. Homeowners insurance premiums can increase at renewal, and rate hikes are unfortunately becoming the norm. A LendingTree study found that between 2020 and 2025, homeowners insurance rates rose nearly 47 percent nationally.

It’s good practice to assume that your property taxes and insurance premiums will go up, because they usually do, said Stephanie Bucko, a CPA and chief investment officer and co-founder at Mana Financial Life Design.

Many lenders collect a portion of your annual property tax bill and homeowners insurance premium with each monthly mortgage payment and place those funds in an escrow account. But these amounts aren’t fixed.

“Your lender reviews your escrow account each year and can raise your monthly payment if taxes or premiums increase, so leave some room in your budget beyond what your first statement shows,” said Bucko.

To better budget for future property tax increases, Bucko suggests first-time buyers learn more about how property taxes and reassessments are handled locally. “It’s also worth learning how your area handles property taxes, since some states cap how much they can rise each year and others reassess closer to market value,” she said.
The costs many first-time home buyers forget about

When you make a down payment of less than 20 percent, your lender will typically require you to buy private mortgage insurance, or PMI. This insurance protects the lender if you default on the loan. The monthly premium is added to your mortgage payment, increasing your total monthly housing cost.

PMI costs vary depending on your loan amount and down payment, but according to Freddie Mac, you can expect to pay $30 to $70 per month for every $100,000 borrowed. On a $300,000 home loan, that’s about $90 to $210 per month. You can request cancellation once your home equity reaches 20 percent. It terminates automatically once you reach 22 percent.

Home maintenance is another expense many first-time buyers aren’t used to thinking about. Unlike renting, there’s no landlord to call when something breaks. You want to make sure you can afford general upkeep and any necessary repairs.

Regularly setting aside money is a good way to prepare for ongoing maintenance. “Plan on 1% to 2% of the home’s price each year, and lean toward the higher end if the home is older or has things like a pool or a big yard,” said Bucko.
On a $350,000 home, that’s $3,500 to $7,000 a year, or about $290 to $580 a month.

Bucko gave two suggestions to help buyers better understand what maintenance and repair costs to expect. “Before you buy, hire a great inspector and talk with the previous owner about what they’ve historically spent on maintenance,” she said.
Here’s how to set a realistic homebuying budget
If you have a mortgage preapproval letter in hand with a maximum loan amount listed, you may be tempted to use that number as your budget as you begin touring properties. But that’s risky.

“Your maximum approval is the lender’s limit, not your budget,” said Martin Mulyadi, PhD, an accounting professor at Shenandoah University. “I’d suggest building the budget from your own monthly numbers, with every ownership cost included and savings still intact, and then seeing what price that supports,” he said.
Here’s an example: If your take-home pay is $6,700 a month, your bills and debt payments total $2,700, and you set aside $1,000 for savings and investments, that would leave $3,000 for housing costs.

For a home priced around $350,000, your budget would need to cover more than just principal and interest. It should also include property taxes, homeowners insurance, PMI (if applicable), and $290 to $580 a month for maintenance based on the 1% to 2% rule mentioned earlier. If the total comes in under $3,000, the home may fit your budget. But if it’s higher, you may need to look at properties in a lower price range.

Bucko said she often sees clients looking at homes that are on the edge of their budget. With prices climbing and rates much higher than they were a few years ago, the approval number can feel like permission to stretch. “At the end of the day, remember, the lender makes money on a bigger loan. It’s not necessarily what you can comfortably afford,” said Bucko.
She recommends keeping essential expenses, including housing costs, to about 60 percent of your take-home pay. “That leaves room to keep saving, handle surprises and still enjoy your life,” she said.

To make sure your budget works before you commit, Bucko recommends a practice run: start saving the difference between your current rent and your estimated housing costs each month. “It shows you pretty quickly whether the number works for your life,” she said. “And if it does, you’ve also built up extra savings for the down payment or the first big repair.”

Buying a home is one of the biggest financial decisions most people will make. Understanding the full cost of homeownership before you buy your first home can help you avoid financial stress down the road.

nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/politics/house.headline: Top Democrat Eyes Filibuster-Proof Budget Bill to Unlock Affordability Agenda
nytimes.com/2026/11/14/us/politics/house.author: Catie Edmondson

paragraphs.text: A top House Democrat mapping out how to leverage his party’s vast majorities in Congress next year to push through a sweeping economic agenda is considering using a filibuster-proof bill to muscle it through both chambers and to President Trump’s desk.

The approach, outlined by Representative Brendan Boyle, the Pennsylvania Democrat in line to be chairman of the House Budget Committee in January, would be one way of forcing Mr. Trump to either embrace or veto broadly popular measures to lower living costs.

Triumphant after electoral victories delivered them more than 255 seats in the House and at least 55 seats in the Senate, Democrats are weighing the best strategy for quickly delivering the affordability agenda they promised voters, including tackling the soaring costs of health care, child care and housing.

Mr. Boyle, the 49-year-old son of a janitor for Pennsylvania’s transportation authority and a school crossing guard, is now positioned to lead the way from his perch at the helm of the House panel that handles budget matters and sets spending priorities.

In an interview, Mr. Boyle said it was “worth exploring” using budget reconciliation — a tool that allows the party in power to bypass opposition from the minority and push through fiscal legislation on majority votes — to unlock the affordability agenda Democrats ran on, including reversing Medicaid cuts Republicans enacted unilaterally in 2025.
“I think any time we can pass good, popular, meaningful legislation, that only strengthens our hand in any ultimate negotiation with the White House,” Mr. Boyle said.

He also said he would like Democrats to forge a deal with Mr. Trump on the statutory limit on the national debt, ending what has become a perennial cycle of high-stakes fiscal clashes between the president and Congress that have repeatedly brought the country dangerously close to a federal default. Mr. Boyle has long pushed for legislation that would allow the Treasury Department to suspend the debt limit, subject to congressional override, rather than requiring an affirmative vote by Congress to increase it.

“He wants it raised,” he said of Mr. Trump. “We never again want to see a Democratic president have to have this held like a gun against their head, the same way it happened to Joe Biden and to Barack Obama.”

A sharp but sociable communicator, Mr. Boyle is part of a younger vanguard of House Democrats rising to the top echelons of the party. He said that no final decisions had been made, but outlined a scenario in which Democrats early next year would first try to pass their economic agenda with some Republican backing, which they would need to steer around a filibuster in the Senate. He suggested Democrats could then move to a partisan reconciliation package if they failed to win over G.O.P. supporters.

“It’s worth exploring reconciliation now that we have both the House and the Senate; however, I think it’s also worth exploring the fact that we’re 56,” Mr. Boyle said, referring to the number of Senate seats Democrats would control if they won a seat in Alaska, where their candidate was leading. “Are there four Senate Republicans who we could work with on issue X, on issue Y, to get things passed in a more expeditious manner?”

That strategy would be in step with what Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, has privately outlined to his caucus. He has said he is prepared to move to a filibuster-proof effort if Republicans will not back Democratic legislation meant to address cost-of-living issues.

Mr. Boyle said he would defer to Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the Democratic leader who is expected to become speaker, on whether the costs of an economic package would need to be offset by new taxes.
Democrats could try to pay for the cost of such a plan by rolling back tax cuts for the “megawealthy” that Republicans enacted during the first and second Trump administrations, he said.

Or they could not pay for them at all. Mr. Boyle said Democrats could argue: “Look, those folks passed a massive, $5 trillion bill and only paid for a fraction of it; we certainly shouldn’t be held to a different standard.”

In 2021, when Democrats used their governing trifecta in Congress under President Joseph R. Biden Jr. to advance a legislative package through reconciliation, feuding broke out between the moderate and progressive flanks of the party over the scope and cost of the bill.

The House eventually passed a $2.2 trillion measure known as “Build Back Better.” But in the months of debate, centrists in the Senate pushed to narrow the measure substantially, outraging progressives, who then threatened to withhold their support for a separate $1 trillion bipartisan infrastructure bill.
Not yet at the helm of the budget panel, Mr. Boyle still vividly remembers the internal party churn that threatened to tank both bills and the multiday slogs he endured to pass them out of committee.

“When it got to the Senate, because of the math of 50-50, where every Senate Democrat could be king or queen, the bill got slimmed down considerably, about half of the size,” he said. “The name changed, and a lot of the things that I felt the best about in that bill were stripped out.”
“The biggest difference now,” Mr. Boyle said, “is 56 is a lot easier than 50.”

washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/14/w.headline: Why homeowners who go electric have a secret advantage
washingtonpost.com/business/2026/11/14/w.author: John Csiszar

paragraphs.text: Owning a home has long been one of the most effective ways to build long-term wealth. And now homeowners have a new financial advantage that has nothing to do with equity or rising property values: electrification.

Homeowners who take advantage of green energy to power their homes and cars can potentially save money on electricity bills and transportation costs. But for renters, this benefit might be out of reach.

Data recently released by the Census Bureau show that 6.4 percent of homeowner households have an electric or plug-in hybrid vehicle, compared with only 3.6 percent of renter households. Another Census finding shows that 7 percent of owner-occupied homes have solar panels, compared with 2.8 percent of renter-occupied homes.
While using solar panels or an EV can help, the real financial advantage comes from using them together.
Getting more out of the same investment
Say a homeowner installs solar panels to cut their electric bill. During the day, those panels might generate more electricity than the home needs, with the rest going back to the utility company.
The catch is that the utility might pay considerably less for that electricity than it charges customers to buy it back.
In California, for example, state regulators say compensation for excess solar electricity under the state’s newer billing system is generally lower than retail electricity rates.
That’s where owning an EV can pay off.
“The less your utility pays you for exported solar, the more it’s worth to keep that energy and put it in your car,” said Alexis Abramson, dean of Columbia University’s Climate School.

If you’re paying 20 cents per kilowatt hour to use electricity, for example, but the utility buys your excess solar-generated power for only 5 cents, you’re on the losing end of that trade. By using that electricity to charge up your EV, you could get an additional 15 cents of value per kilowatt hour.

Jesslyn Pei, a former infrastructure investment and asset management professional, estimated that a $24,000 solar installation could pay for itself in about 10 years if the homeowner uses the solar-generated electricity to charge an electric vehicle at home, assuming favorable conditions. Solar alone, she said, might take 13 to 14 years.

But if homeowners use the electricity they generate instead of selling it to the grid at a low rate, they can recoup the high upfront cost of a solar installation much more rapidly. “The more use cases for utilization, the shorter the payback period,” Pei said.
Making the numbers work
Of course, homeowners don’t necessarily have to make two expensive purchases at once to start saving money.

The Department of Energy says some EVs can add two to five miles of driving range per hour using an ordinary household outlet. For drivers with shorter commutes, that might eliminate the need for a more expensive charging installation.
Other opportunities include charging during cheaper overnight hours, checking utility discounts for EV owners and comparing the value of using solar electricity against selling it back to the grid.

But going electric isn’t automatically a good financial decision. Abramson cautioned that a shaded roof, an aging roof that may soon need replacing or particularly low electricity prices in a community can make solar a poor investment. Financing costs can also eat into any savings.
She recommended running the numbers with a local installer, including the cost of financing and any available state or local incentives, before committing to a system.
What about renters?

As renters by definition don’t own their properties, they’re usually limited in how they can modify them. For example, renters generally can’t install rooftop solar panels or home chargers without their landlord’s cooperation.
Other options might be available, however.

Abramson says community solar subscriptions can reduce electricity bills by 5 percent to 15 percent, with potentially greater savings for qualifying low-income households. Renters with an EV can benefit from workplace chargers, potentially cheaper overnight charging rates and buying an affordable used EV to lower the upfront cost.

More innovative solutions might be coming. Abramson pointed to plug-in balcony solar systems, which are gaining attention as a lower-cost alternative to traditional rooftop installations. They can be used with regular wall plugs and are portable. While not eliminating the benefit gap with homeowners, these types of options provide renters with choices.

Before spending thousands of dollars, homeowners should compare the total upfront costs against their expected annual savings, including financing expenses and any available incentives. They should also consider how long they plan to stay in the home. The longer you plan on staying put, the bigger the potential savings.

nytimes.com/2026/11/14/business/zhang-li.headline: He Was China’s Man in Panama. Then He Became a Wanted Man.
nytimes.com/2026/11/14/business/zhang-li.author: Alexandra Stevenson, Murphy Zhao, David C. Adams, Daniel Berehulak

paragraphs.text: For years, Zhang Liang warned that powerful people in his former homeland, China, would try to drag him back. Then one Saturday morning in July, it happened.

In Panama City, two police officers on motorbikes pulled alongside his black Mercedes-Benz and motioned him to stop. A check of his identification turned up an Interpol red notice from the Chinese authorities, who wanted him extradited on charges of embezzling around $300 million.

Mr. Zhang, a 44-year-old dealmaker, barely had time to remove his gray suit jacket and wrap it around his head before officers handcuffed him and paraded him before cameras at Interpol’s National Central Bureau in Panama.
He has been behind bars ever since.

It was a remarkable fall for Mr. Zhang, one that traces the arc of China’s dealings with the West. He went to Panama ready to make deals and help China extend its influence. He oversaw a port project that promised to turn a former U.S. military base near the Panama Canal’s Atlantic entrance into Latin America’s largest container terminal, establishing a base for Chinese interests near one of the world’s busiest trade routes.

Today, China’s ruling Communist Party holds much tighter reins on entrepreneurs like Mr. Zhang. At the same time, Panama has been caught in a showdown between the United States and China: President Trump claims that China exercises too much control over the Panama Canal.
Mr. Zhang believes he is a pawn in a larger political game — a way for Beijing to regain direct control over key infrastructure he helped build in Panama.

“China is seeing its influence in the Panama Canal slipping away and is now putting pressure on Panama,” Mr. Zhang said from prison in a letter responding to written questions from The New York Times.

To his aggrieved former business partners, though, Mr. Zhang is a corporate fugitive who used offshore jurisdictions and other people’s money to enrich himself. He wooed Panama’s elite with promises of deals and funding that never materialized. He continued to earn a salary of $6,300 a month, his lawyers said at a bail hearing, a substantial sum in Panama.

His tailored suits, A. Lange & Söhne wristwatch and black Mercedes all pointed to a lavish lifestyle. Mr. Zhang has faced lawsuits, criminal complaints and judicial proceedings in multiple jurisdictions. He is also pursuing an international arbitration claim against Panama.

The competing accounts of victim and culprit are difficult to reconcile. The ownership of the port is disputed, and the financial dealings behind it are opaque. After reviewing the case, Panama’s Foreign Affairs Ministry agreed last month to proceed with Mr. Zhang’s extradition to China, according to a document seen by The Times.
The Foreign Affairs Ministries of China and Panama did not respond to emailed questions.

For a decade, Mr. Zhang had used China’s growing interest in Panama to expand his influence. Now, as Beijing and Washington battle over the canal, his business empire has unraveled, and the political connections that once helped him prosper offer little protection.

This account, with previously unreported details, is based on official documents, legal filings and interviews with lawyers and associates, including a former colleague who has accused local authorities in China of harassment, coercion and the falsifying of records in Mr. Zhang’s case.
China Moves In
Mr. Zhang arrived in Panama in 2016 to oversee investments for a wealthy Chinese financier. A lawyer licensed in New York and China, he had been named a “leading talent” by China’s Justice Ministry.
From an 18th-floor office overlooking Panama Bay, Mr. Zhang secured Panama’s approval to build, own and operate a major container terminal in a free-trade zone on Margarita Island.

Chinese state-controlled media celebrated the deal as a diplomatic coup, advancing investment interests in Panama. Mr. Zhang also secured a deal to build a gas-fired power plant. He promised officials that the project would create 1,000 jobs and lower energy costs.
As deals were made, Mr. Zhang became a go-between for officials in Beijing and Panama City.

His success coincided with Beijing’s courtship of Juan Carlos Varela, who was Panama’s president. In 2017, Panama severed diplomatic ties with Taiwan and aligned with China. It also became the first Latin American country to join the Belt and Road Initiative, China’s signature global infrastructure program.
Washington watched the growing relationship with alarm. Mr. Zhang’s proposed terminal would sit beside the Panama Canal, a strategic artery for the United States.

“Margarita Island gave them a lot of access and intelligence value,” said Isaac B. Kardon, an adjunct professor at the Johns Hopkins School of Advanced International Studies who specializes in Chinese maritime strategy.
But the political opening started to close.
Mr. Varela left office in 2019, and his successor was far less receptive to Chinese investment. The Panamanian government began moving against the Margarita Island project.

Mr. Zhang sought Beijing’s help. Tingyun Han, his former assistant and translator, said she had gone to the Chinese Embassy in Panama City, hoping officials could persuade the Panamanian government to reconsider. The plea went nowhere.
The new Panamanian government “no longer wanted any Asian faces or Chinese enterprises involved,” Ms. Han told The Times from China.

Mr. Zhang’s problems deepened when his backer, a wealthy property financier named Gao Tianguo, lost his fortune. Mr. Gao’s lending businesses in China collapsed under billions of dollars of debt. He was arrested in 2020 and died two years later.

In 2022, Mr. Zhang agreed to transfer the port assets to Notarc Management Group, a Bahamas and Florida-based private equity firm. Within months, the deal incited an ownership dispute. Ye Cheng, a politically connected Chinese businessman who claimed a controlling stake in the project, accused Mr. Zhang of illegally seizing the company.

But Panamanian authorities declined to bring charges, concluding that Mr. Ye’s allegations amounted to a commercial dispute. Mr. Ye’s company, the Landbridge Group, did not reply to requests for comment.
China took a different view.

In 2023, police officers pulled Ms. Han, Mr. Zhang’s former assistant, off a plane in her home city of Xian and drove her 12 hours to Rizhao, where Mr. Ye’s company has its headquarters, she said. Officers interrogated her so intensely about Mr. Zhang and the port deal, she said, that she vomited and was taken to a hospital. She later accused the local police of torture.

Mr. Zhang became convinced that his adversaries in China were coming after him. In court filings in 2024, he described being followed to work by a white Nissan and chased through Panama City. He requested and received police protection.
Panama in the Middle
By the time the police stopped Mr. Zhang’s Mercedes in July, Panama had become the focus of tensions between Washington and Beijing.

Shortly after starting his second term, President Trump demanded that Panama loosen China’s grip on the Panama Canal. He accused a Hong Kong conglomerate that operated two major ports at the canal, one at either end, of being controlled by Beijing. In January, Panama’s Supreme Court declared the company’s port contract unconstitutional.
China vowed to “take all necessary measures” to defend its interests in Panama. Chinese authorities started detaining hundreds of Panamanian-flagged vessels in China for inspection, disrupting trade.
Mr. Zhang was arrested the same week that China’s new ambassador arrived in Panama — and just five days before Panamanian officials were due in Beijing for talks to defuse the diplomatic standoff.
Panama’s foreign minister later said China had renewed a key maritime agreement that grants Panamanian-flagged ships preferential access to its ports.
“From the moment they arrested him — and that is no coincidence — the disputes between China and Panama disappeared,” said Guillermo Cochez, a Panamanian diplomat and one of Mr. Zhang’s lawyers.

No evidence links his arrest to the diplomatic negotiations. But relations between China and Panama improved afterward. Extradition documents revealed that Beijing wanted control of Mr. Zhang’s assets in Panama without explicitly asking for the port project.

On Aug. 21, a Panamanian court denied Mr. Zhang bail and ruled that the seriousness of the charges outweighed his claims of personal roots in Panama. In September, Panama’s Foreign Ministry said China’s extradition request was “appropriate.”
Mr. Zhang was moved from La Gran Joya, a high-security prison outside Panama City, to another detention center nearby, while his lawyers pursue a final appeal.

China has said Mr. Zhang is a Chinese national, although he said he had renounced his Chinese citizenship and obtained citizenship from Saint Lucia in 2020. The Times reviewed copies of his permanent residency card, his Saint Lucia passport and his Chinese passport.

Chinese authorities said Mr. Zhang’s transfer of the port terminal to Notarc had constituted embezzlement. He dismissed the allegations as a “sham.” (Notarc also sued him, seeking compensation for losses it says it incurred in the dispute.) Notarc did not respond to requests for comment.
Mr. Zhang said the criminal case was a pretext for Beijing to seize the Margarita Island project and “get back into the canal.”
But, he warned, “what Panama doesn’t realize is the pressure won’t stop with extraditing me.”

cbsnews.com/news/trump-putin-xi-jinping-.headline: Trump, Putin and Xi Jinping expected to meet in first-ever trilateral of its kind, officials say

paragraphs.text: November 14, 2026 / 5:59 AM EST / CBS/AFP

President Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and China's President Xi Jinping will hold the first three-way meeting among the three leaders at a summit in China next week, the White House said Friday.
The three leaders will meet on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese city, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.

Mr. Trump wants to talk about reducing nuclear arsenals at the trilateral talks on Thursday and is also set to bring up his war in Iran — but he is not expected to discuss Russia's war in Ukraine, officials said.
"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world. This proliferation, President Trump believes, is very dangerous," Wales said.
One of the major conflicts dominating Mr. Trump's second term as president will feature, but the other will not, the U.S. officials said.

"I think the president does intend to talk about Iran in the trilateral meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin," a senior U.S. official, speaking on condition of anonymity, told reporters on a call.

Washington has a "whole other track" of negotiations with Kyiv and Moscow aimed at ending the war in Ukraine, the official added, referring to talks that U.S. envoys have had in recent days with Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky.
"China is not really a part of that track, so it doesn't seem appropriate to have the Ukraine discussion there," the official added.
Mr. Trump will also hold a bilateral working lunch and meeting with the Chinese president on Thursday — their fourth meeting since the president's return to power last year.
The United States also did not plan to discuss export controls on sensitive chip technology, which were at the heart of the Nvidia scandal.

"We do not negotiate American export controls. These are national security matters that we develop in the administration... and we don't expect it to figure at all in any of our conversations with the Chinese while we're there," the second official said.
Tesla and SpaceX boss Elon Musk will accompany Trump on his trip to China but will not be involved in the meeting with Xi and Putin, the officials said.
Trump will leave Washington on Monday and arrive in the Philippines on Tuesday for a summit of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) before heading to Shenzhen.
2 top Trump advisers are in Russia for talks with Putin

bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckjwj03w4w0qo.headline: Hungarian authorities uncover $20m during probe of Orbán-era minister
bbc.co.uk/news/articles/ckjwj03w4w0qo.author: Alicia Curry

paragraphs.text: Nearly $20m (£14.8m) in cash has been found hidden in farm buildings and buried in forests as part of an investigation into a former minister of Viktor Orbán, authorities have said.

Miklós Seszták, who served as minister of national development for four of the ex-prime minister's 16-year rule, is accused of accepting bribes as part of a scheme involving the state transport company. He has denied any wrongdoing.
Hungary's new Prime Minister Péter Magyar unseated Orbán in a landslide election in April on the promise of launching a sweeping anti-corruption drive.
On Friday, following the two-day search for the cash - found in secluded locations across the country - Magyar described it as the end of the "mafia".

Investigators found wads of banknotes in safes, buried in woodlands and hidden in agricultural and residential buildings and warehouses, as part of the probe into Seszták, the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) said in a statement.
The cash amounted to "5,071,632,000 forints, €2,658,350 and $1,257,100", it added, bringing the combined value to $19.5m. It has been deposited into the Hungarian State Treasury, the body said.
The NVVH was established to investigate allegations of corruption during the Orbán rule, which Magyar has dubbed "Operation Purgatory".
Magyar promised Hungarians "regime change" during the election earlier this year and has set about undoing many Orbán-era policies since entering office.
Allegations of corruption and cronyism have long dogged Orbán, who during the course of his tenure turned Hungary into what the EU characterised as an "electoral autocracy".
His government faced accusations of offering lucrative government projects to allies. Orbán has strongly denied the claims.

Two of his former ministers, including Seszták, and the former central bank chief Gyorgy Matolcsy have been under arrest since September over accusations of graft in separate investigations. They all deny wrongdoing.
On Monday, Hungarian authorities also detained Orbán's brother and three others as part of a people-smuggling case.
The former prime minister dismissed it as political revenge, saying: "In this dirty game, the aim is the elimination of the political opponent and the establishment of a one-party system.
"I am the target, my younger brother is just a tool."

nytimes.com/live/2026/11/14/us/faa-natio.headline: Disruptions Persist as Air Travel Recovers from Nationwide Ground Stop: Live Updates

paragraphs.text: Latest
Karoun DemirjianNiraj Chokshi and Hari Raj
Here’s the latest.

Travelers across the United States and beyond were still facing delays and uncertainty on Saturday as airlines and airports sought to recover from the ground stop the day before that brought air travel to a halt for hours.

Thousands of passengers were stranded on Friday after the Federal Aviation Administration ordered the ground stop. More than 8,200 flights — or over 31 percent of those scheduled for Friday — were canceled nationwide, according to Cirium, an aviation data firm, though some international flights received permission to take off.

Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, said at a news conference on Friday night that the authorities had decided to issue the ground stop after aging air traffic communications equipment became overloaded and began to falter on Friday afternoon.
He said that it would take “some time” for airlines to recover, predicting that flight schedules would return to normal in time for the busy Thanksgiving travel season.

Many who waited at airports until late Friday night had to scramble to find accommodation after their flights were canceled. Some carriers, including United Airlines and American Airlines, began to restore flights after flight traffic was restored on Friday night. Aviation experts have said it could take days to fully restore flight schedules after a halt of this scale.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who appeared alongside Mr. Duffy at the news conference on Friday, said there was no indication that the communications failures had been caused by a cyberattack, though he said that an investigation was underway and that he could not rule out such an attack. He stressed that lives were never in danger.

Mr. Duffy blamed lawmakers for not fully funding upgrades that he said were needed to prevent similar failures. To upgrade aging air traffic facilities and technology, he said, he wanted another $50 billion from the Republican-controlled Congress, which last year approved $12.5 billion for the project.
He said the new amount should be delivered in emergency funding by the end of the year, before control of Congress — and the budget — switches to Democrats.
Here’s what else to know:

• If your flight is canceled: You are entitled to a refund if your flight is canceled in the United States, regardless of the reason, or if a flight is significantly delayed or changed and you decide not to take it. Here are other travel tips that might be helpful. Read more ›
• Handling the chaos: Radio transmissions between air traffic controllers and pilots at major airports offered a peek at how they navigated the ground stop. Read more ›

• Rare halt: Friday’s nationwide ground stop was only the third that the F.A.A. has issued this century. It ranks as the second-longest, after the stop issued in the wake of the terrorist attacks on Sept. 11, 2001. There was a shorter one on Jan. 11, 2023, because of an outage in the F.A.A.’s safety-alert system. Read more ›

• Democrats’ response: Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the House’s top-ranking Democrat, said the stop was “the latest in a series of unacceptable air travel incidents” under the Trump administration. He added that Americans deserved timely answers about how and why it happened.

At Los Angeles International Airport, a number of travelers who had been hoping to get a late flight out have now been notified that their flights have been canceled. Many travelers here are scrambling to find new flights for Saturday as well as accommodation for the night.

Their flight to Jacksonville cancelled, longtime friends Ann Bruns, 79, and Janice Simpson, 78, opted to hire a driver to shuttle them six hours from Atlanta to Florida, where they hope to catch a cruise ship departing on Sunday.
“We’re about to go on a cruise ship with no clothes,” Simpson explained, because their luggage had already been loaded onto a plane bound for Jacksonville.

Bruns described a day punctuated by confusion, saying when the duo arrived in Atlanta from Kansas City, “We saw pilots just standing there, and we knew something was up.” They still feel like they have almost no idea what went wrong to send air travel into turmoil.

Nationwide, more than 8,200 flights — or over 31 percent of those scheduled in the United States for Friday — were canceled, according to Cirium, an aviation data firm. And the disruption was already spilling over into Saturday, usually a slower day for travel, with more than 5 percent of flights canceled before the day had even begun.
Reid J. Epstein and Lisa Lerer
Reporting from Denver, where they are stranded along with much of the Democratic Party.
The ground stop stranded some Democratic leaders in Denver.

Pete Buttigieg could not believe what he had just watched. The former transportation secretary stood at the corner of the hotel bar in Denver, where CNN had just finished broadcasting the Trump administration’s news conference about the ground stop that stopped flights nationwide on Friday.

Mr. Buttigieg was among the thousands of Democrats who had gathered in Denver this week for a conference designed to chart the party’s future and celebrate their midterm wins. The ground stop stranded some of the party’s top rising stars and their staffs.
People accustomed to having inside information suddenly had very little.

At a table to Mr. Buttigieg’s left sat Gov. Abigail Spanberger of Virginia, Gov. Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey and Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan. They munched on Parmesan fries and checked their phones as they waited for news of their flights.
To his right, Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia scanned his Senate group chats to check for updates from secure channels and Senator Mark Warner of Virginia.
But Mr. Buttigieg, glancing up at the television, struggled to comprehend the performance of his successor, Secretary Sean Duffy.
“You can just write down the comic book asterisk swearing characters,” Mr. Buttigieg said when a New York Times reporter asked for his impressions of the news conference. “I have questions.”
The downtown hotel bar resembled the famous bar scene in “Star Wars.” The stranded politicians bemoaned the lack of information from the federal government and their inability to get home.

One New England-based operative booked a rental car and planned to drive back to Boston. Others looked up how many hours it would take to get to the East Coast on Amtrak. (The answer: more than 40.) Aides to one prominent Democratic governor, who had flown to Denver on a private jet, fielded questions from others in the bar about whether they could hitch a ride home.

A few people working for Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois — who did not come to Denver — commandeered a long table where Anne Caprara, his chief of staff, worked two phones as she juggled rumors, emergencies back home and calls from the boss. She said Mr. Pritzker was furious about the lack of information coming from the Trump administration.
“Welcome to Denver’s hottest bar, the Mos Eisley Cantina of politics,” Ms. Caprara said, referring to the “Star Wars” bar. “With ‘Veep’ characters and a ‘Terminator 2’ vibe.”

Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the leader of the House Democrats, shifted the blame for Friday’s ground stop back to the Trump administration. In a statement, he called the stop “the latest in a series of unacceptable air travel incidents under the Trump Administration’s failed leadership.”
Earlier Friday night, Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, had blamed Congress for not adequately funding his department’s plans to upgrade the nation’s air traffic infrastructure.
“American travelers deserve timely answers from the Trump Administration about how and why this happened,” Jeffries added.
Pilots and air traffic controllers kept communicating during the outage.
A communications outage on Friday led the Federal Aviation Administration to pause departing flights nationwide, but pilots were not entirely cut off from federal air traffic controllers.
In a Friday night news conference, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said the outage was intermittent, so federal controllers were still able to reach pilots.
“It wasn’t a complete blackout in communication or radar,” he said. “So we were able to keep some of those communications going.”
But even in a complete outage, aviation authorities have multiple backups to maintain contact with pilots.
Pilots and air traffic controllers primarily communicate by voice radio, using primary, backup and emergency frequencies.

Controllers and airline dispatchers can also send text-based messages to pilots. And many commercial planes are equipped with satellite communications, which are especially useful for reaching people on the ground when the planes are flying in remote airspace like over the ocean.

If a control tower loses radio capabilities, it can also communicate with pilots with high-intensity colored lights, which pilots can acknowledge by rocking their wings or flashing lights in response.
The ground stop has scrambled travel plans for sports teams across the country.

Some professional and college sports teams were stuck on runways, or opting to pile into buses, ahead of games this weekend that are now uncertain due to the nationwide ground stop that was lifted Friday night.

Markwayne Mullin, the secretary of homeland security, said at a news conference on Friday that the ground stop was caused by technology upgrades “overwhelming” the flight communication system. Thousands of flights have been canceled, but no high-profile games have been affected so far, ahead of what is set to be a busy weekend in sports.
Dozens of teams had made it out of airports just ahead of the stop. But the N.B.A.’s Brooklyn Nets were not so lucky.
The Athletic reported that the Nets were stuck on a team plane on Friday. They have a game Saturday night against the Memphis Grizzles.

Also stuck at an airport was the University of Texas Longhorns football team, slated to play Louisiana State University in Baton Rouge, La., on Saturday night. Minutes before the stoppage, the Longhorns posted a video of players boarding a plane with the caption “Bayou bound.”
Both teams are in the Southeastern Conference, which said in a statement that it would work “to determine whether any adjustments to scheduled competitions become necessary.”

On Friday night, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told reporters that he encouraged college football teams to coordinate their flights with the Federal Aviation Administration “to make sure we have games going off tomorrow.”
While some teams, including the Longhorns, headed home from the airport to wait out the delay, a handful of others opted to travel the old-fashioned way: By bus.
The Athletic reported that among the longest drives was a 330-mile ride for the Purdue University Boilermakers, who are playing the University of Iowa Hawkeyes on Saturday night.

The University of Southern California women’s basketball team said they were grounded in Los Angeles ahead of a marquee game Sunday against the University of South Carolina Gamecocks, but were preparing to travel on Saturday.
In men’s college basketball, a Saturday game between University of North Carolina Greensboro and Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., was postponed because of the ground stop.
N.F.L. teams typically travel on Saturday for Sunday games. Five teams told The Athletic that their travel plans were not affected.

According to The Athletic, the stakes of the ground stop may be most significant for the National Women’s Soccer League, which is scheduled to hold its semifinals this weekend. The stop affected the Kansas City Current’s flight to New York City ahead of its game against Gotham FC on Sunday. The Utah Royals, playing the Washington Spirit on Saturday, traveled before the stoppage.

The N.B.A.’s Cleveland Cavaliers had planned to catch a flight home after their Friday night game in Miami. Kenny Atkinson, the Cavaliers head coach, told reporters before the game that he didn’t know if the team would make their flight.
“I think we’re scrambling to find hotel rooms in case,” Mr. Atkinson said, adding: “If not, we’ll sleep on the bus.”
Alexander CardiaNeil Bedi and Robin Stein
Hear how air traffic controllers grappled with the ground stoppage chaos.
Radio transmissions between active pilots and air traffic controllers at major airports offer a peek at how they navigated the Federal Aviation Administration’s nationwide ground stoppage on Friday.
An air traffic controller at Newark Liberty International Airport can be heard sharing the news with pilots.
Minutes later, at airports in Atlanta and Chicago, controllers said they had limited information.
