The dramatic, high-stakes account of Artemis II, the first human journey into deep space in fifty years, told from the perspective of astronaut Jeremy Hansen ... A riveting and intimate account of the iconic achievement of Artemis II, Earthrise—written by author John Larsen and based on extensive interviews he conducted with Hansen—is a testament to what can be achieved with unity, teamwork, and a bold belief in humanity’s ability to reach for the stars.

washingtonpost.com/transportation/2026/1.headline: Travel chaos, flight cancellations continue following nationwide ground stop
washingtonpost.com/transportation/2026/1.author: Victoria Craw

paragraphs.text: Travel chaos continued into the weekend following Friday’s rare nationwide ground stop, with thousands of fresh flight cancellations Saturday and international authorities warning flights to and from the United States could be disrupted.
More than 3,200 flights within, into or out of the U.S. were canceled on Saturday alone, FlightAware, which monitors flight disruptions, said.

Delta Air Lines and American Airlines have both canceled more than 2,200 flights through Saturday, flight-tracking site Flight Radar reported late Friday. United Airlines has canceled 1,800 while Southwest had canceled nearly 1,400, it said.

Trump administration officials blamed Friday’s ground stop on an aging air control system that is patched together and in need of modernization. It ended about 8:15 p.m. Eastern time Friday after more than four hours, but is expected to lead to airport chaos throughout the weekend.
By Friday night, more than 15,000 flights across the U.S. had been disrupted, AirNav Radar said, with airports in Chicago, Atlanta, Dallas Fort Worth, New York, Denver and Los Angeles worst affected.
The Federal Aviation Administration said late Friday some departures had resumed, but passengers should contact their airlines for updates.
“Before clearing flights to resume, we thoroughly tested our systems to confirm they were stable and that operations remain reliable,” it said.

Airlines warned customers they needed time to reorganize following the ground stop. Delta Air Lines said Friday while some flights have resumed, “it will take time to reset our operation, including the positioning of aircraft and crews.”

American Airlines said it would prioritize certain flights to non-hub cities and international routes “to position aircraft and crew where they are needed to help restore our operation,” adding that it expected delays and cancellations into Saturday.
United Airlines said it had resumed operations but expected “residual impact” from Friday’s order, while Southwest said customers may experience delays as they work to recover.
The U.K. Civil Aviation Authority also warned of international disruption early Saturday as airlines work to rebook affected passengers.

Customers are entitled to a refund of the ticket price in the event an airline cancels a flight and the traveler chooses not to accept travel, vouchers or other forms of compensation, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation. Passengers are also entitled to refunds if they are subject to a significant delay or changes.
The exact issue that caused the ground stop remains unclear and Friday’s order caused confusion at airports and in the air.

Transportation Secretary Sean P. Duffy said at a news conference Friday that the aging system “went down everywhere,” and that the problem had been sparked in the process of upgrading the system that caused it to overload.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday at a news conference the outage did not appear related to a cyberattack. “It appears that this was mechanically driven. However, we’re still looking, so we’re not going to rule that out,” he said.

aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11/14/usman-nu.headline: Eight sentenced to jail over Nurmagomedov-Dvalishvili Abu Dhabi hotel brawl
aljazeera.com/sports/2026/11/14/usman-nu.author: Manasi Pathak

paragraphs.text: A brawl broke out between the two MMA fighters and their team members inside a hotel before a wrestling event.
The Abu Dhabi Criminal Court has convicted 10 people over a mass brawl ⁠involving mixed ⁠martial artists Usman Nurmagomedov, Merab Dvalishvili and their teammates at a hotel.

The brawl broke out ahead of a wrestling event organised ⁠by Real American Freestyle (RAF), where Usman Nurmagomedov’s brother Umar and Dvalishvili were scheduled for matches against different opponents.
Recommended Stories

“An Abu Dhabi court has convicted 10 defendants in connection with a brawl inside a hotel and has sentenced them to six months’ imprisonment … along with deportation from the country,” read the announcement from the Abu Dhabi Judicial Department on Friday.
ESPN reported that six members of Team Nurmagomedov were sentenced to six months in prison, fined 300,000 dirhams (approximately $81,600) and ordered to be deported after serving their sentences.

According to Abu Dhabi-based The National newspaper, former UFC bantamweight ⁠champion Dvalishvili and a friend were fined 50,000 dirhams ($13,600) for “disturbing public security and assaulting others”.

Two additional people were handed six-month prison sentences for privacy violations after they filmed the ⁠brawl and published the footage online, the reports added. The court also ordered the confiscation of their phones and deletion of the footage.
The brawl broke out on Wednesday when Georgian Dvalishvili, who was scheduled to appear at RAF Abu Dhabi on Saturday, was being interviewed in the lobby of the Yas Hilton.

PFL lightweight champion Usman – the cousin of retired MMA legend Khabib Nurmagomedov – and his associates approached Dvalishvili. Videos shared online showed Usman coming in from behind and slapping Dvalishvili, which started the melee.
Usman was not scheduled to feature at the RAF Abu Dhabi card but travelled to the UAE capital to accompany his older brother, Umar, who was scheduled to face Urijah Faber.
Later on Friday, the event organisers removed Umar from the card, replacing him with Saba Lazishvili, Dvalishvili’s friend who was also involved in the brawl.
RAF cofounder Chad Bronstein said Dvalishvili has been released from custody. He remains available for his scheduled match with Marlon Moraes.

“I’m pleased to share that Merab Dvalishvili is back with us in Abu Dhabi,” Bronstein said in a statement. “We would like to express our sincere appreciation to the relevant authorities in Abu Dhabi for their professionalism and support.”

Dvalishvili posted several videos on social media after the incident and released his personal statement on X, saying: “Just want to let everyone know I have been released, and I am good, healthy and ready to go.
“I want to thank everyone in Abu Dhabi for your help in resolving this matter … I do hope that they release everyone; I would not press charges. I want peace and the best for all,” he added.

Wednesday’s incident wasn’t the first time Dvalishvili and Team Nurmagomedov clashed. Tensions also escalated in January last year after Dvalishvili defeated Usman’s older brother Umar in a UFC bantamweight title fight. They also had a smaller altercation at an RAF event in Georgia in July.

washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/14/she.headline: She was 14 and addicted to Instagram. Could she handle a month without it?
washingtonpost.com/nation/2026/11/14/she.author: Casey Parks

paragraphs.text: PARKER, Colo. — The night before Addisyn Mace started the detox, she tucked herself into a bedroom nook and allowed herself one last binge. She was 14, a month into her freshman year of high school, the kind of kid who went to church every Sunday and never failed a test, but she wasn’t thinking about God or school as she unlocked her phone.
She opened Instagram. Online, a woman curled her hair. Boys yelled. Boys played basketball. A dachshund ate a cucumber. A man in a car ate takeout. A woman in a car shared her opinions.

Addisyn lingered on each video for three seconds or less. She thumbed past a makeup tutorial and a trailer for the movie version of her favorite book. She ignored the sweet calico begging at her feet as she zipped by one cat video then another. In the kitchen, her great-grandmother was baking cinnamon rolls, and, online, Addisyn watched a stranger create the same treat.

She had begged for the right to watch these clips. She had asked when she was 12, then again for her 13th birthday, to download Instagram so she could see what other girls saw as they stared at their phones during hangouts. Addisyn’s mother, Shera, had used social media for nearly two decades, but she’d grown increasingly skeptical of the apps’ influence. She made Addisyn wait until she turned 14 to join.

Addisyn knew why her mother thought social media was bad for her. Every school lecture on bullying warned kids to stay off Snapchat. And just a few weeks earlier, Addisyn had read that Meta agreed to pay Colorado and other states and territories $18 billion after a coalition of attorneys general sued the social networking company for damage they said Instagram and Facebook have done to young people.

Addisyn had been on for just five months, but already she could feel that Instagram had reshaped her days and, most likely, her brain. She used to come home from school and read or practice guitar. Now, she watched other people strum online. She scrolled past her favorite country singer, Morgan Wallen, as he sang the opening lines of “I Got Better,” then she DM’d her mother a cartoon cat meme.

Shera was 15 feet away, curled up with her own phone in the living room, half-watching a Broncos game, half-staring at the inspirational stories that made up her Instagram feed. She had tried to limit how much time her children spent on the internet, but she was an exhausted single mother who worked full-time. Most evenings, she felt like Instagram was all she had.
“Mom,” Addisyn called from her nook. “You didn’t respond to that meme I sent you.”

Shera wandered back to her daughter’s bedroom and found her sitting in a fuzzy pink chair in a room lit only by a makeup vanity. Addisyn had decorated the room with analog entertainment. She had a shelf full of young adult novels and a crate stuffed with records she played on a turntable, but she didn’t engage with them as often as she had before.
“I saw it,” Shera said.
“But you didn’t respond,” Addisyn said. “How do I know you saw it if you don’t respond?”

They had only an hour or two left before they gave up the devices that both entranced and isolated them. A nonprofit had challenged students at Addisyn’s school to quit social media for a month, and Addisyn had agreed — partly because she wanted to be a good student, partly because she knew that she was already addicted to the tiny videos she barely watched and couldn’t remember.
Shera had decided she’d do the detox, too, but as the start of it drew near, they both felt more than a little worried.
“It’s literally how I relax,” Shera said as she looked back at her phone.
“I know,” Addisyn said. “It’s kind of all I want to do.”

THE NEXT MORNING, the assistant principal at Venture Academy of Leadership and Entrepreneurship (VALE) called Addisyn and the other freshmen to a special lecture. It was 8 a.m., early enough that more than half wandered in looking like they’d rather be in bed. Several wore blankets around their shoulders. Without a word, they deposited their phones into pouches on a wall.

Like many schools across the United States, VALE had tried to find ways to break its students’ attachment to their phones. More than half of U.S. states now ban phones “bell-to-bell,” while Colorado and others allow districts to create their own rules.

Last year, VALE partnered with the nonprofit NoSo Connection Collective to lead its entire student body through a month-long detox from social media. The nonprofit was created by a Colorado teenager in the years after she lost 10 classmates to suicide. Maddie Freeman couldn’t say that social media was the only reason her peers had struggled, but she knew her own mental health had tanked soon after she turned 12 and downloaded Snapchat. Within a few months, she was competing in online “thigh gap” weight loss challenges, and she was sneaking out of class to message Justin Bieber. By the time she reached high school, she was spending every waking hour on the platforms.

The average teen spends at least four hours a day on social media sites, and nearly half of U.S. teens say they are on “almost constantly.” That level of participation can have devastating effects on young people’s mental health and attention span, public health experts say. Multiple studies have found that heavy users are twice as likely to be depressed as nonusers. Other researchers have found that social media can be particularly harmful to girls’ self-esteem and self-image.

And so VALE had brought Freeman’s nonprofit back to try to reach Addisyn and her classmates before their burgeoning interest in social media turned dire. To do that, it had to persuade the kids to do exactly what social media was telling them not to: quit. That impossible sales pitch fell to a bouncy University of Colorado at Boulder student named Ben Forman. He’d had the apps since he was 11, he told the group, and he once thought he had “the world in my hands.”
“It was the most powerful 4-by-6 screen I could have ever imagined,” he said. “And I fell in love.”

Forman showed a few silly TikTok videos he had made when he was young, then he got down to business. He asked Addisyn and her classmates how Instagram earned $84 billion in revenue but gave away its service. The class said “ads” in unison. Right, Forman said. Companies pay to place the ads.
“Then what is Instagram selling? What is the product?” he asked.
The teenagers shifted uncomfortably on their stools. No one posited a guess.
“We’re the product,” Forman said. “We are what is being sold.”

A few students pulled their blankets tighter around their shoulders, and Forman explained that to earn money, Instagram had to keep people like them online for as long as possible. The company had found lots of new ways to do that since it launched in 2010, Forman said. It had added stories and push notifications and something called “infinite scroll.”

If Addisyn had logged on a decade earlier, she might have had a more limited relationship with Instagram. She follows just 35 people. In the days before infinite scroll, she would have seen the posts those 35 people made, and then she would have reached the end of her feed. Most likely, she would have logged off after a few minutes. But friends are no longer the point, Forman explained. Today, teenagers spend more time watching content produced by strangers on a stream that never ends.

Meta executives have described these new features as “useful,” but Forman told the class that court documents revealed something more sinister at work. As young people abandoned Facebook, the company’s top leaders began talking about what they described as the “teen problem” that had lost them roughly $12 billion. In a 2018 internal email, company leaders assigned a dollar amount to Addisyn and her classmates:
“The lifetime value of a 13 y/o teen is roughly $270.”

Meta figured it would lose more than a billion dollars a year by 2030 if it didn’t keep teenagers online. Court documents show that Meta employees knew years ago that teenagers struggled to sign off the apps. In 2020, one senior researcher called the app “a drug” that dulls people’s ability to feel rewards. That same year, a marketing employee for the company told a co-worker that teens “feel addicted to IG.” “Like addicts,” she wrote, “they feel that they are unable to stop themselves from being on IG.”

Addisyn knew what they meant. Sometimes, in the middle of reading a book she loved, she’d reach for her phone even if she didn’t really want to scroll. It felt compulsive, beyond a 14-year-old’s power to control.
Forman talked for a while about algorithms and the ways the companies track even the actions users don’t make. Then he invited the students to give up social media for a month.

Most seemed loath to do it. A few agreed to cut down the number of hours they spent on YouTube, but only two said they would do the full detox: Addisyn and a Snapchat-obsessee named Scarlett Sable. Scarlett figured she spent close to four hours every school day messaging friends and posting TikTok dance videos. On the weekends, she almost never logged off.

When Forman finished, the students collected their phones. Some sneaked glances at their notifications. Others opened the apps they had just learned might harm them. Addisyn stepped outside and deleted Instagram without word or fanfare. Scarlett hesitated, then told the assistant principal she needed someone to hold her hand. She squealed as her thumb hovered over the yellow Snapchat icon.
“I did the hardest one first, you guys,” Scarlett said. “I’m shaking!”
The class cheered as she deleted TikTok. A bell rang, then both girls stared in disbelief at their suddenly boring phones.

ADDISYN FELT CONFLICTED the rest of the day. She couldn’t believe someone had designed a product to lure teens into addiction. And yet she couldn’t stop thinking about all the things she’d miss without Instagram. The homecoming dance was coming up. How would she see all the photos girls posted? How would she let them know she thought they looked great?
A few hours into the detox, she checked her phone. Scarlett had texted.
“Girl, I’m dying. I hate this. I just want Snap back like literally so bad,” she wrote.
“That’s how I feel about Insta,” Addisyn wrote back. “What am I going to do?”

That night, as Shera made hamburgers on a George Foreman grill, she and Addisyn talked about how their first few hours had gone. Addisyn’s younger brother, Bentley, had decided to give up Roblox and YouTube for the month, but he had barely noticed their absence that day. The only family member who didn’t want to detox was Addisyn’s 91-year-old great-grandmother, Laverne Bila.
“I’m not giving up YouTube,” Laverne said. “Nooo. That’s my entertainment at night. They have some cute Western stories. And there’s a Canadian fellow I like who makes wreaths.”
The hamburgers sizzled, and Addisyn leaned against the counter.
“I just can’t stop thinking about the fact that I just don’t have it anymore,” she told her mother.
“My lunch break was the worst,” Shera said.
Shera works at a preschool, and, usually, she scrolled while the children napped. That day, she had reached for her phone over and over again and finally decided she could at least browse Amazon.
“I literally was shopping, so it’s going to cost me money,” she said. Once the hamburgers were ready, they sat at the dinner table and talked about Dolly Parton, which led them to Miley Cyrus.
“Her father was quite an entertainer at one time,” Laverne said.
“She just dropped his last name,” Shera said. “I’m not going to know any of this anymore. The only things I know are from Instagram.”
After dinner, they decamped to the living room and set up a bedazzle kit Shera had been meaning to finish for two years. They used pens to apply tiny gems to a picture of a snowman. Addisyn sighed.
“I would rather be on Instagram right now,” she said.
“I would rather be on Instagram right now,” Shera said.

They seemed relieved when it grew too late to work on the snowman. Still, Shera tried to stay positive. They had nothing to show for the hours they spent on Instagram. The bedazzling project was tangible, something they could hold onto.
“One day, we’ll finish,” Shera said, “and I’ll frame this.”
ON DAY THREE OF THE FAST, Scarlett texted Addisyn: “Bro, I gave up.”

Most of Scarlett’s friends from middle school attended a different high school, and the only way they kept up with each other was through Snapchat. She felt lonely and disconnected, she told Addisyn, and she couldn’t imagine spending an entire month that way.

Addisyn wasn’t lonely, exactly, but her thumb did keep reaching for the spot on her phone where Instagram used to be. She watched a lot of TV the first weekend. But soon, she felt her creative juice return. She wrote three songs and learned how to cook crepes. She read whole book chapters without looking at her phone. Her average daily screen time plummeted by hours, and by the end of the second week, she felt lighter than she had in months.

No one touched the bedazzle project again, but they found other things they liked doing together. They tried out pickleball and dusted off the board games they had let sit in the closet. They played mini games of baseball as Bentley worked on his pitching.

Still, Addisyn missed Instagram and counted down the days she had left. Taylor Swift released a new song, and Addisyn missed the initial release because the singer put it on Instagram. She made it through homecoming without giving up, but she felt left out as other girls recorded videos as they got ready at Addisyn’s house. The next morning, all she wanted to do was share the photos her mom had taken under a gazebo in the park.
Still, she didn’t cave. In fact, as the month wound down, she applied to be an ambassador for NoSo, the nonprofit that suggested the detox.

The night before Addisyn’s last day without social media, NoSo hosted a Zoom meeting for its young participants, and she learned that if she was going to serve as an ambassador, she needed to participate in the nonprofit’s marquee event — “No Social Media November.”

She knew she could go a month without Instagram, so she agreed, but the night before the detox ended, she realized she had a new dilemma. November was still two weeks away. She could use Instagram during that break, or she could just push through and do an extra-long detox.

That night, the family sat down to a dinner of white chicken chili, and Shera told her kids she was done with social media. She had more energy in the evenings, and she’d even replaced her nap time scrolling with schoolwork. She was halfway through earning her bachelor’s degree, but most of her classes were self-paced, and she’d often chosen to scroll instead of study. In just three weeks, though, she had made real progress on her marketing and conflict resolution classes.
Addisyn looked down at her food.

“I can’t decide what I want to do,” she said. “I feel like I’m going to miss out on something. I do feel better without social media, like I felt more productive, but also it never crossed my mind to stop having it.”
“I don’t think you should go back on tomorrow,” Shera said.
“I don’t know,” Addisyn said. “We’ll see. I want it back so badly.”
“What is it that you miss?” Shera asked.
“I don’t actually even know,” Addisyn said. “I just want it back.”
THE NEXT MORNING, Addisyn climbed out of her lofted bed and padded into the kitchen. She picked up her phone and considered her options: Instagram or no Instagram?
She put her phone down. First, she’d make muffins, then she’d decide.
By the time she pulled the muffins out of the oven, everyone else was awake. Her mom suggested they window shop along Main Street, so Addisyn put off her decision again.

Downtown, each family member picked out a treat. They found a picnic table in a park, then Addisyn pulled out her phone. She opened the app store, searched for Instagram, and her thumb hovered over the install button.

“I could download it right now and I could see everything that I missed,” she said. “I start thinking of all the notifications I’m going to have, and it’s like, ‘Oh, I could be in total bliss right now.’”
Shera put down her ice cream.

“Tell me one way getting back on social media will enrich your life,” she said. “Did you know Steve Jobs wouldn’t let his kids have an iPad? And Zuckerberg doesn’t let his kids have any social media. They see the fault in it, but they want you to do it.”
“You’re acting like I’m going to rob a bank or something,” Addisyn said.
A whole minute went by. Addisyn’s thumb trembled over the “install” button, then she sighed.
“Let’s go shop,” she said.
They walked down the street and stepped inside local spots hawking candles and handmade ghost art for Halloween. They tried to visit a studio that hosts open mic nights, but it was closed.

They drove to a park with a baseball field, and Bentley and Shera headed to the diamond. Addisyn wheeled her grandma to a spot in the dugout where she could watch, then she sat on a bench and pulled out her phone. Her fingers moved quickly over the screen. Shera asked Addisyn what she was doing.
“I’m looking up open mic nights,” she said.

Going off social media didn’t mean Addisyn or her mother had given up screens. Shera had worked her way up to level 737 on the cellphone game Jewels Legend. Addisyn still Googled things she wondered about. But she wasn’t scrolling. She was looking for opportunities to play music, so Shera left her to it.
After half an hour of searching, Addisyn put down her phone and picked up a bat. She didn’t consider herself athletic, but the more she swung, the more fun she had.

That evening, she made up her mind. She wouldn’t go back on Instagram — at least until the end of November. She stashed her phone in her back pocket and asked her mom and brother if they wanted to try a board game.

phys.org/news/2026-11-spacex-starship-ea.headline: SpaceX's Starship set for return to Earth after booster catch aborted
phys.org/news/2026-11-spacex-starship-ea.author: Anita Chang Beattie with Charlotte Causit

paragraphs.text: edited by Andrew Zinin

SpaceX's Starship spacecraft was "healthy" as it orbited the Earth and on track to return Saturday to its Texas launch site, where Elon Musk's company was planning to "catch" the vehicle for the first time.
It was the 15th test flight of the world's biggest and most powerful rocket system, originally meant to feature a groundbreaking twin capture of both the Super Heavy booster and the Starship.

Successful recoveries of both stages would have marked a milestone in the space industry's decades-long pursuit of fully reusable rocket systems that can drastically reduce mission costs and make frequent launches possible.
But that achievement slipped out of reach minutes after the 124-meter (407-foot) rocket blasted off Friday afternoon from its launch pad at Starbase.
After the midair separation of the two stages, the Super Heavy booster was initially set for capture at Launch Pad 2, SpaceX spokesman Dan Huot said.
But near the end of its descent, "the booster aborted itself for a GNC (guidance, navigation and control) issue that it detected," he said.
It diverted instead to the Gulf of Mexico just off the launch site, where it automatically self-destructed before hitting the water.
Meanwhile, the Starship spacecraft that gives the rocket system its name was orbiting the Earth, which it was expected to do 14 times before returning Saturday.
"Starship and its heat shield are healthy," SpaceX said around seven hours after the mission started.
"We're not tracking any issues right now with the vehicle or with the range for our return, so everything continuing to look good," Huot said.
Starship on Friday launched 26 satellites to join others in Musk's Starlink satellite internet constellation.
Complex catch

Clayton Swope, an aerospace expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, called the mission a "mixed bag so far" after the failure to catch the Super Heavy, something SpaceX has done three times previously.
"At least the Starship made it to orbit, like on the last test flight," he said.
Some versions of the Starship spacecraft are designed to launch internet satellites and data centers into orbit, while other iterations will be made to ferry people to the moon and Mars.

U.S. space agency NASA is counting on Starship to serve as a lunar lander on its Artemis mission, and administrator Jared Isaacman congratulated SpaceX on Friday for "another spectacular launch"—without mentioning the booster disappointment.
SpaceX plans to return Starship to Earth after more than 22 hours of flight and recover it at around 3:20 p.m. (2120 GMT) on Saturday.
The "catch" is extraordinarily complex because the spaceship will be falling much faster and from a much higher altitude than the booster.
Like the three previous Super Heavy recoveries, Starship is meant to carry out a controlled descent and nestle between two mechanical "chopstick arms" at the launch site.
"We'll only go for it if the ship passes all of these system checks and decision gates along the way, and there are lots of them," SpaceX commentator Kate Tice said.
Due to the risks of losing control of Starship, SpaceX has planned for various scenarios where it will shorten the test flight and plunge the spaceship into the Pacific Ocean if necessary.
Refueling challenge

Musk, the world's richest person, has already revolutionized the space sector with the partially reusable Falcon rockets, which regularly launch satellites and carry astronauts to the International Space Station.

But the Starship project has been plagued by years-long delays as SpaceX grapples with novel engineering challenges, including the unsolved problem of transferring fuel to the spaceship while in orbit—a requirement for any journey to the moon or Mars.
Following SpaceX's high-profile stock market debut in June that raised about $85.7 billion, the company is investing heavily in production and launch capabilities.

During a tour of its million-square-foot (93,000-square-meter) factory at Starbase on Friday, SpaceX officials told journalists that it now has the capability to produce a spaceship every two weeks and a booster every four weeks.

aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/14/ukraine-ru.headline: Ukraine, Russia race to build military satellite networks as war rages on
aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/14/ukraine-ru.author: Mansur Mirovalev

paragraphs.text: Kyiv, Ukraine – Looking like a tiny desktop tower with wing-like solar panels, the Obria Nano satellite is a small step that could herald a giant leap for Ukraine’s military.

Launched by Himera, a Ukrainian company known for ergonomic military radios, and GomSpace, a Danish small-satellite manufacturer, the first Obria Nano could eventually grow into Kyiv’s own constellation of military satellites, its creators hope.
Recommended Stories

The nanosatellite marks Ukraine’s “first historical step toward establishing resilient and sovereign satellite communications capabilities,” the company said on October 27, almost four weeks after the Obria Nano had reached orbit.

In mid-October, Kyiv also signed up two Finnish companies, the Nokia telecoms giant and the ICEYE space startup that owns a “self-illuminating” radar technology for obtaining high-resolution satellite imagery in any weather, to look into developing a network of military satellites.

Kyiv’s efforts are rooted in one concern – the nearly total dependence of Ukraine’s military communications on SpaceX, Elon Musk’s satellite communications giant that operates Starlink, a constellation of more than 10,000 low-orbit satellites.

On Thursday, the speeds of Starlink and Starshield, its military component operated by the Pentagon, were limited for Ukraine, leading to “significant disruptions” of their operation along the front line, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Before this, Starlink was also disrupted last month.

Kyiv realises that “it’s possible to create an absolutely new system, but it will take several years,” Anatoly Zak, a US-based space expert, told Al Jazeera. “In the nearest year or two, Starlink and [its military-grade component] Starshield are absolutely necessary.”
Since 2022, Ukraine developed a love-and-hate relationship with Musk, his volatility, shifting loyalties and political demands.

“Musk’s mood swings play a significant role,” Volodymyr Fesenko, head of the Kyiv-based Penta think tank, told Al Jazeera. “There were times when Musk helped Ukraine, and times of very negative reactions.”

Ukrainians hailed Musk’s decision to provide Starlink services and modems to Ukraine free of charge. The military, hospitals and government agencies operating critical infrastructure quickly made a backbone of their communications.
But in late 2022, Musk refused to activate Starlink coverage in Russia-occupied areas, slowing down or stopping Ukraine’s successful counteroffensive.

The world’s wealthiest man also said that Kyiv should remain “politically neutral” in the future, officially cede Crimea to Moscow and conduct United Nations-supervised referendums on Russia-occupied territories.

“If you want to understand what Russia has done here, come to Ukraine and you will see it all for yourself,” Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in response. “And then you will tell me how to end this war, who started it and when it can be ended.”

Meanwhile, Russia has reportedly smuggled thousands of Starlink terminals and used them for comms and drone attacks. This February, Musk put an end to the practice by allowing only certified modems to operate in Ukraine.
Kyiv’s attempts to find an alternative to Starlink followed the October 14-24 speed limits for Ukrainian drones imposed without prior warning by Starlink and Starshield.
Drones and drone interceptors moving faster than 60km/h (37mph) lost signal and could no longer reach their targets.
Musk accused the Pentagon of limiting the speed and admitted that the decision was his only after The Wall Street Journal reported that Musk had personally authorised the slowdown.
Both Musk and Kyiv realise that Starlink and Starshield are the Ukrainian military’s survival tool.

When it comes to his highly publicised position towards Ukraine, Musk has to balance his own emotional outbursts and the interests of SpaceX, the crown jewel of his business empire that comprises two-fifths of his net worth, analyst Fesenko said.
“If he tries to throw Ukraine under the bus, it may work as very negative advertising for his business, including the Starlink system,” Fesenko said.
Russia’s bid to create military satellites
Another factor is Russian President Vladimir Putin’s calculated flattery towards Musk – on October 28, he called him a “real genius”.
“Putin apparently wants to use the methods he’s used towards [US President Donald] Trump – flattery, unlimited flattery,” Fesenko said.
Putin mentioned Musk while talking about Russia’s attempts to create its own version of Starlink.

“We are in close contact with our American partners – including Mr Musk – because it’s very important, in orbit, not to get in each other’s way and to maintain a certain level of discipline and order,” Putin said.
The attempts have not been very successful so far.
The military satellites for the upcoming Rassvet (Dawn) constellation turned out to be Qianfan satellites, which are similar to first-generation Starlink satellites and manufactured in China.
Bureau 1440, a Kremlin-controlled space company that runs the Rassvet system, plans to have 900 satellites in orbit by 2035.
In August, the Institute for the Study of War, an international military think tank, claimed that more than a third of Rassvet satellites failed to reach “sustainable operational altitudes”.
By early November, Moscow lost two of the 32 Rassvet 3 satellites launched in the past seven months.
The second satellite that burned in the Earth’s atmosphere on November 1, failed to launch its propulsion to correct its position, according to The Defence Express, a Ukrainian military publication.
Ukraine can also try negotiating a switch to Starlink’s rivals, but they are smaller and less effective.
The US-based Iridium has 66 satellites flying at about 800km (497 miles) above Earth.
OneWeb, operated by the French Eutelsat company, has up to 650 satellites that orbit the Earth at 1,200 kilometres (746 miles). But it is not authorised to be used for military drone strikes.

An average terminal in Ukraine sees five dozen Starlink satellites simultaneously – and only 11 OneWeb satellites. A light, compact Starlink terminal costs up to $500; a much heavier and bulkier OneWeb one costs $9,000.
According to Pavel Luzin, a space and military analyst with the Jamestown Foundation, a think tank in Washington, DC, Kyiv has two options to get its own satellites.
It could work towards heavy and pricey satellites in geosynchronous orbit – or Earth-centred – that could serve for up to 20 years and cover all of Ukraine’s military needs.

Or option two is a focus on launching a system of hundreds of cheaper low-orbit satellites that will need propulsion engines to maintain position, but they will eventually fall down because of contact with the upper atmosphere, and will constantly need to be replaced, he said.
Kyiv can also use much cheaper alternatives such as stratostats or stratospheric drones that serve as “quasi-satellites,” he told Al Jazeera.

A satellite fleet necessary to provide coordinates to long-range drones makes each drone strike pricier, and AI-driven drones that can be “taught” to recognise their targets could bring the price down – and make the satellites unnecessary.

The development of ballistic missiles is another alternative, because they do not need satellite connection but can cause damage equal to the boom from several drones that have gotten through Russia’s air defence system, he said.
“Such decisions are made with all calculations considered, not because Starlink – that depends on current political trends in Washington – needs to be replaced with an alternative,” Luzin said.

“I don’t rule out that Ukraine won’t have to create any alternatives, because SpaceX is definitely interested – even if someone in the company doesn’t realise that – in Ukraine using it further,” he said.

washingtonpost.com/obituaries/2026/11/14.headline: Juan Atkins pioneered techno music as a teen in his bedroom outside Detroit
washingtonpost.com/obituaries/2026/11/14.author: Amanda Covarrubias

paragraphs.text: Before the huge international electronic music festivals filled with lasers and thumping drum beats, there was techno — gestated in bedrooms around Detroit by young Black artists experimenting with machines and ideas that looked to the future.
Juan Atkins was one of them, improvising as a teenager on a synthesizer that his grandmother bought him.
Starting in the 1970s, he would go on to build a legacy in electronic dance music that added another storied chapter to the rich musical history of his hometown, Detroit.

Mr. Atkins, a DJ, record producer and musical godfather to techno, died Oct. 31 in Mexico City, where he had been scheduled to perform. He was 64. His management agency, Greensmith Artists, did not provide a cause of death.

Influenced by George Clinton’s Parliament-Funkadelic, Prince and Chicago house music, Mr. Atkins began creating danceable electronic music with friends in high school, went on to record his own demo tapes and formed the groundbreaking duo Cybotron, the name a fusing of the words cyborg and cyclotron.

Although many people think of electronic music as originating in Europe, Mr. Atkins is credited with pioneering the sound that would become known as Detroit techno, music created by DJs with synthesizers, electronic instruments and digital workstations.

“Nobody knew that this was some Black kids from Detroit making this record, man,” he said in a 2011 interview with NPR, referring to Cybotron’s “Alleys of Your Mind,” released in 1981. “They thought it was, like, from Europe.”
He even gave this new style of music a name.

“When people asked him what he’d call this type of music, he said, ‘Techno. Short for technology music,’” his daughter, Milan Ariel Atkins, wrote in a remembrance to her father. “... Anyone listening to it just couldn’t help but dance. Those frequencies resonated deeply with a mass of people who needed that outlet, but didn’t know how or where to get it.”
Mr. Atkins was born in Detroit on Sept. 12, 1962. His father was a concert promoter who was incarcerated for much of his son’s life, Mr. Atkins said in interviews.
He told the music newsletter Tone Glow that his mother was young when he was born, and his grandmother did most of the child-rearing.
His father bought him his first electric guitar for his 10th birthday, and his grandmother had an old organ in their house in Belleville, Michigan, outside Detroit.
“I came home from school one day and I saw her playing the boogie-woogie and I was like, ‘Dang, Grandma, I didn’t know you had it like that,’” Mr. Atkins told Tone Glow.

He said he had always listened to music and played bass and lead guitar in funk bands in Detroit when he was 12 or 13. He also experimented with sounds on the organ and would accompany his grandmother to the music store, where he would go into the back room and play the early-generation synthesizers.
“Eventually, I was able to talk her into buying me one,” he told Red Bull Music Academy. “And the rest was kinda history.”
In high school, he began collaborating with two classmates, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson. They would play their music at parties in the Detroit area.

“Juan was the originator of Techno, a true visionary who opened the door for so many of us, myself included,” Saunderson wrote on social media after Mr. Atkins’s death. “I’ll never forget how he showed me how to finish my first record, Triangle of Love. That meant a lot to me then, and it still does today.”

Mr. Atkins began making demo tapes and connected with community college classmate and Vietnam War veteran Richard Davis to record as Cybotron in 1981. They released “Alleys of Your Mind,” a seminal work in electronica that year, when Mr. Atkins was 19. “Cosmic Cars” came two years later.
After the duo went their separate ways, Mr. Atkins deejayed at parties and started his label, Metroplex Records, in 1985, producing and recording under the name Model 500.

“This was especially innovative at a time when most musicians were seeking major record deals,” his daughter wrote. “Instead, he decided to do this himself, so that he had creative control and could deliver techno directly to those who resonated with it.
She declined an interview request through her father’s management company. No information on other survivors was immediately available.

In the 2017 documentary “Never Stop: A Music That Resists,” Mr. Atkins said it was only natural that the distinctive sounds of techno-funk would come from Detroit, home of Motown and the once-glorious auto industry.

“The height of the Industrial Revolution and the height of Industrial Age, I mean, Detroit was a big place, man, because the car industry was booming, and jobs and unions and auto unions and things formed,” he said.

“And then when the industry came to a close, of course, the city kind of went down. And I think a lot of good music and a lot of great art and creativity comes from depressed and stressful situations.”
Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield issued a statement after Mr. Atkins’s death that described him as part of the city’s history.
“Alongside his friends Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson, Juan took a sound born in Detroit basements and bedrooms and carried it to clubs and festivals on every continent,” the statement said.
“Today, millions of people dance to music that traces back to him and to our city. That is a Detroit story: genius, grit, and invention, from neighborhoods the world too often overlooked.”

washingtonpost.com/style/2026/11/14/step.headline: Stephen Miller’s suits make the radical look reassuringly routine
washingtonpost.com/style/2026/11/14/step.author: Robin Givhan

paragraphs.text: Like so many of the men and women who populate President Donald Trump’s political ecosystem, Stephen Miller, the new White House chief of staff, has crafted an image that is both gentleman policy wonk and urgent Cassandra, warning of barbarians at the borders. He trades in stereotypes and clichés, looking backward in order to define himself in the present day.

Miller is now the most powerful aide to the world’s most powerful man. He portrays himself as a combatant in a business suit, a clear-eyed patriot in a nation overrun by cowardly globalists. Miller has embraced fashion as an expression of order, power and importance. He dresses like the so-called Establishment, situating himself and his point of view in the mainstream. He makes use of fashion’s cultural clout, of its shorthand form of communication. He uses it to proclaim himself reasonable. Even as his words make both his loyalties and his disposition clear.

“If it wasn’t for President Trump, the United States of America would not exist right now. This man saved America,” Miller said to a glowing commander in chief and an appreciative audience at Mar-a-Lago the day he was promoted last week, seemingly ignoring the avalanche of voters who had rebuked this administration. “I swear to you and I pledge to you, Mr. President, my absolute loyalty, my unwavering commitment and my total devotion to your success, and the success of this country.”

The two men stood side by side in front of a giant swan fountain that looked like it was striving unsuccessfully to be Botticelli-esque. The president wore one of his voluminous suits and below-the-belt red ties. Miller was in a trim gray suit — and he was smiling. He had come for his victory lap, and he was quite put together: tailored, pressed, modern enough in fit without flash, and just shy of upstaging his principal.

Miller is not usually caught on camera looking pleased about anything — except, perhaps, when he is in the company of his wife, Katie. Before Miller stepped into his new role Monday morning, he was best known to casual Washington observers as the president’s lead anti-immigration champion, whose state of outrage often approaches hissing. The policy known as the “Muslim ban” in Trump’s first term and the expansive deportation quotas in his second are examples of Miller’s handiwork.

In conversations it doesn’t seem to matter whether Miller is discussing immigration policy with someone sympathetic to his worldview or appalled by it. He is reliably animated, adamant and argumentative as he insists that certain immigrants — namely brown-skinned, non-English-speaking — do not belong in this country because all they’re going to do is make it as awful as the terrible places from which they’ve fled.

“If Somalians cannot make Somalia successful, why would we think that the track record would be any different in the United States? Go third-world country by third-world country,” he insisted during a Fox News interview last year. “If these societies all over the world continue to fail, you have to ask yourself: If you bring those societies into our country and then give them unlimited, free welfare, what do we think is going to happen? You’re going to replicate the conditions that they left.”

Miller, at 41, has managed to foment a great deal of anger and cruelty. On the surface, he is an inexplicable candidate for such dirty work. He grew up in the progressive city of Santa Monica, California. He hails from a Jewish family of immigrants who generations ago benefitted from chain migration. Professionally, his trajectory has seemed to be nothing but upward. Personally, he and his wife have four sweet-faced children. But Miller seems to have thrown off any expectations of reciprocal tolerance.

“The refugee program is not intended as a solution for global poverty. And historically it’s been used that way,” Miller told a group of reporters outside the White House. “The U.S. refugee program in America has been a catastrophic failure.” Except, it seems to Miller, when those refugees are White and of mostly European extraction. He said all this calmly, with a slight smile, dressed in the soothing manner of a statesman: a dove-gray suit, pristine white shirt, a burgundy-dotted tie and matching pocket square.

In words, deeds and style gestures, Miller is a man of contradictions. He can sound like a 1950s Archie Bunker dressed up in modernity. A firebrand wrapped in worsted wool. His clothes are not provocative, nor are they distracting — in ways that are good or bad. They are a costume of concealment.

Miller is not some stodgy guy in a bow tie, nor is he a disheveled attention hound. His ties are narrow. He likes a pocket square, and he often can’t resist one that matches his tie. Men’s tailoring is in the details, and Miller is attuned to the little things. His suits are two-button — a style more flexible and breezier than a three-button configuration. He doesn’t lean toward the high armholes and pronounced structure of Savile Row and the conservative formality of British tailoring. Nor are his suits fitted to the can-you-even-breathe millimeter in the manner of those fashionable Tom Ford tuxedos worn by Hollywood’s leading men on the red carpet. He favors a notch lapel over peak. And while Miller avoids a break in his trousers, they are not hemmed to Thom Browne’s ankle-bearing proportions.

Miller has chosen a standard configuration that by default makes his style contemporary. It offers a soothing, thoughtful counterpoint to the jarring public mien, enraged words and fabrications of the man who wears them.

Trump “saved our military from collapse. He saved our economy from destruction. He saved our border from annihilation. And he saved our country from threats at home and abroad which would have been the end of the American Dream forever,” Miller said during his remarks at Mar-a-Lago. “He saved the Republican Party from the ash heap of history and has made it stronger, more popular and more resilient than ever before.” Miller said all of this in the aftermath of the midterm elections, in which Republicans lost their majority in both the House and the Senate, and more than a few states made history by electing Democrats to offices they’d been shut out of for generations. He looked like an unassuming insurance salesman while doing so.

Miller may not have respect for the creators of fashion or those who inspire it with their do-it-yourself imaginative spirit — many of whom are immigrants or Black or Brown strivers. But he understands that the right cut of a jacket and length in a pair of trousers can give the impression that a person is relevant rather than old-fashioned. Astute style choices can cloak an outlier in relatability and commonality. We have been conditioned to believe that unemotional men wear suits. Dressed in a suit, even the most horrifying ghouls manage to slide into polite society — at least for a while. In the 21st century, dangerous men do not come wearing white hoods, saggy jeans or balaclavas. They arrive in khakis and polo shirts, overpriced cashmere hoodies and business suits.

“America’s doors are closed, fully, to asylum seekers. We’ve set up agreements where if you want asylum, then we will find a country elsewhere in the world to take you,” Miller said this summer. “It’s a very simple, a very elegant, very complete solution.”

When the public-facing Miller is not chopping the air with his fingers and ratcheting up the volume on his messages about immigrants and American might and force, when he stands silent, he has a habit of folding his arms tightly across his chest and tilting his head downward. In this stance, one in which he is so often photographed, we see a face drained of affect. His eyes go flat. His mouth tightens into a narrow slash. Perhaps this is a defensive mask, or one of exhaustion. Perhaps he is thinking sad thoughts that he would prefer to keep private. A series of protest posters plastered around the nation’s capital accuses him of having a resting fascist face. “Fascism ain’t pretty,” reads the script underneath a close-up of an impenetrable Miller.

Fashion is Miller’s camouflage. It’s a distraction. It’s his social grace note. The viciousness his many critics declaim is couched within the familiar. It’s just business — nothing personal, nothing to see here. Just another menacing plan, laid out by a policy wonk in a nothing-special suit.

theatlantic.com/newsletters/2026/11/jens.headline: 10 Questions to Determine Whether Your Partner Is a Spy

paragraphs.text: Since Jensen Huang stepped down as the CEO of Nvidia amid revelations of his affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset, the whole internet has been consumed with terror. If this can happen to Jensen Huang, the seemingly happily married, leather-jacket-clad leader of the Most Valuable Chip Company in the World, it can happen to anyone! Can’t it?
Fortunately, I have devised a quiz. Ask your partner some simple questions and gauge their responses to determine whether or not you are being honeypotted.
(1) What should we do tonight?
a. What if I told you some fun facts about an interest we do not share and then we went to bed early?
b. Whatever you want to do, babe!
c. How about we [unprintable] on a pile of your favorite chips and then we send them all over the globe, randomly? Definitely to China, though.
d. Let’s go down to the waterfront and eat some bread!
(2) Would you still love me if I were a worm?
a. Probably not. But as a worm, you would lack the higher brain functions to find this fact disappointing, and we would part ways amicably.
b. You bet, babe!
c. If as a worm you still had access to proprietary information about CPUs.
d. I WOULD LOVE YOU MORE THAN ANYTHING! I WOULD DEVOUR YOU.
(3) Are there any secrets you haven’t told me?
a. Probably?
b. Babe, I tell you everything!
c. No! But I like the idea of sharing secrets! Do you have any secrets you want to tell me?
d. I have a cloaca.
(4) How did we meet?
a. Why are you asking me this? You were there. I have to get up in the morning.
b. Love at first sight, babe!
c. The classic way. You were signing a woman’s chest. I was there for normal business reasons.
d. At the park, by the waterfront. You had bread.
(5) Do you want to come with me on my official trip to China with President Trump?
a. No.
b. Only if you want me there, babe!
c. (Sexily) Yes
d. Ordinarily I would love to, but I have to sit on these eggs.
(6) What do you love most about me?
a. Why are you asking me all of these questions? Is this one of those memes about being a spy?
b. Everything about you!
c. How good you look in your leather jacket!
d. When you have bread in your pocket.
(7) If I weren’t the billionaire CEO of a wildly successful company that makes a restricted chip, would you still love me?
a. Well, you aren’t, and I do!
c. Obviously, but I do think it’s really, really cool that you are! But obviously I would. Although we probably wouldn’t have met if you weren’t! But obviously I would.
d. Yes, if you still had access to bread.
(8) Talk dirty to me.
a. I took the trash out already so we can go to bed early.
b. (Growls.)
c. Baby, this bra must be a restriction on the export of sensitive high-tech goods, and you must be the Commerce Department, because I want you to Take! It! Off!
d. (Quacks.)
(9) What frightens you?
a. Losing the people I love; having a bug fly into my mouth.
b. Spending even a second without you, babe!
c. The Commerce Department’s export-control list.
d. LOUD NOISE! DON’T KNOW WHAT IT WAS! SOUNDED LIKE A PREDATOR.
(10) What’s something you wish I would do for you?
a. Watch even a single Hallmark movie voluntarily.
b. Just be yourself, babe!
c. Complete this multifactor authentication.
d. Help me get my long, beautiful neck out of this bag of chips.
Answer Key:
Mostly A’s: Your partner is likely not a spy.
Mostly B’s: Your partner could be a spy; more info needed.
Mostly C’s: Your partner is almost certainly a spy.
Mostly D’s: Your partner is a duck.

cnbc.com/2026/11/14/foundation-payroll-c.headline: Eric Trump-backed robot soldier startup can't pay staff after founder borrowed $4.6 million from company to buy home
cnbc.com/2026/11/14/foundation-payroll-c.author: Hugh Son

paragraphs.text: Foundation Future Industries, a maker of military humanoid robots advised and backed by Eric Trump, failed to pay employees last month as its cash reserves dwindled, according to people with direct knowledge of the matter.
Workers have yet to receive paychecks after San Francisco-based Foundation missed payroll on Oct. 30, said the people, who asked for anonymity to speak candidly about a private company.

The situation has particularly angered some inside the startup because its CEO and co-founder, Sankaet Pathak, borrowed $4.6 million from the company last year to buy a luxury home, money that could have been used to pay workers, the people said.
Public records show that an LLC that names Pathak as sole principal purchased a $4.6 million Sausalito, California, property with "sweeping, cinematic views" of the San Francisco Bay in October 2025.

A spokesman for Pathak acknowledged receiving a detailed list of the major points from this story on Thursday, but didn't respond to requests for comment. Pathak's previous startup, a fintech firm named Synapse, collapsed in 2024, leaving thousands of Americans locked out of their savings accounts.

Foundation's cash crunch comes at a precarious moment for the company, which Pathak has said is close to unveiling a next-generation, weapons-ready robot that will help the U.S. compete against Chinese rivals. At the same time, Pathak is seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars in funding at a $3 billion valuation.

The company has garnered headlines this year for Pathak's claims that his robots could soon take on battlefield tasks in Ukraine or patrol the U.S. border with Mexico. Broadcast interviews and articles about Foundation also include claims that the company has won $24 million in Pentagon contracts.

"What we're about to unveil in the next couple of months [is] going to be the strongest humanoid robot that exists anywhere in the world, including China," Pathak said in an April television interview.
'Plain sight'
That April interview introduced Eric Trump, the son of the U.S. president, as a Foundation investor and chief strategy advisor. It is unclear how large his stake is.

Eric Trump and his brother Donald Trump Jr. have invested in an array of defense firms, including makers of military drones and autonomous weapons. A July Washington Post investigation found that startups backed by investment vehicles linked to the brothers had secured at least $3.2 billion in government business.

"We have to win robotics in the United States of America," Eric Trump said in April. "When you go up and interact with these robots ... they fist bump you, they high five you, they follow your commands."
Eric Trump's involvement in Foundation drew the swift ire of Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., who asked whether Foundation won U.S. defense contracts because of nepotism.

"Eric Trump went on FOX to brag about winning ANOTHER multimillion-dollar contract from the Trump administration," Warren said in an April 23 social media post. "This looks like corruption in plain sight."

Eric Trump didn't respond to requests for comment. His spokesperson recently told the Financial Times that Eric Trump had "no involvement in Foundation's management, operations, strategic decisions or commercial activities, including the solicitation, negotiation, procurement or execution of any government contracts."

While the Eric Trump announcement created speculation within Foundation that a Democratic-led Congress may look to investigate the company, Foundation itself didn't actually win the $24 million in contracts, despite that assertion being widely reported across news outlets.

Instead, it acquired Florida-based Boardwalk Robotics in late 2024, and government research contracts won by that firm account for the claim, said a person with knowledge of the matter. Foundation used Boardwalk's robot Alex as the basis for its first robot, the Phantom MK-1, this person said.
Foundation's deal for Boardwalk included performance milestones for the robot that haven't been reached, said a separate person with direct knowledge of the deal.
In 2024, CNBC reported that letters Pathak sent to prospective investors cited an imminent investment and $300 million purchase order from General Motors, claims the automaker rejected.
Foundation co-founder Mike LeBlanc said at the time he was "embarrassed" about the marketing materials.
Rescue loan?

Insiders fret that Foundation could soon fold if Pathak doesn't secure fresh funding. Pathak has been seeking to raise hundreds of millions of dollars at a $3 billion valuation since at least January.

Pathak is Foundation's sole board member, a structure that has raised concerns among prospective investors about corporate governance, said the people familiar with the matter. He also owns most of the firm's shares.

That setup allowed Pathak to borrow $4.6 million last year, which he called a short-term loan at the time, the people said. Existing investors are aware of the loan through the company's financial disclosures, the people said.
"This is what happens in a company with no governance," said one of the people. "Are you just going to let it ride into the ground, and you ride off into the sunset?"
Foundation also ran out of cash for payroll in August, though employees only had to wait about two days to get paid after the company secured a bridge loan from an existing investor, the people said.
Pathak told employees this week in a memo that he was working on sourcing money to pay back wages.

The company was founded in April 2024 by Pathak, Tribe Capital CEO Arjun Sethi and LeBlanc, co-founder of Cobalt Robotics, a maker of autonomous security guards, according to a fundraising pitch at the time.
Foundation went on to hire dozens of robotics engineers and artificial intelligence experts, managing to lure some from Tesla and Amazon-owned autonomous vehicle company Zoox.
Missing money

Before Foundation, Pathak was known as the founder of Synapse, a kind of middleman that enabled fintech firms like Mercury, Dave and YieldStreet to offer savings accounts and credit cards with the help of small community banks.
Synapse was a behind-the-scenes player until its collapse left more than 100,000 Americans with a combined $265 million in deposits locked out of their FDIC-backed accounts.

While some customers received partial payments during Synapse's bankruptcy proceedings, thousands remain without access to their money after more than two years. A bankruptcy trustee, the former FDIC chair Jelena McWilliams, said as much as $96 million in customer funds went missing.

The bankruptcy proceedings concluded last year without uncovering where the funds went; Pathak blamed a banking partner named Evolve, and Evolve blamed Synapse for the mess. U.S. regulators didn't intervene until the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau sued Synapse last year, opening up a $55 million fund for customer relief.
Pathak withdrew $320,000 in loans from Synapse as it spiraled toward bankruptcy in 2024 amid disputes over unmatched ledgers, according to the consultant and independent journalist Jason Mikula.
Federal prosecutors convened a grand jury to investigate possible criminal misconduct at Synapse, the Wall Street Journal reported last year. The WSJ report didn't mention Pathak specifically.
The controversy didn't dissuade Eric Trump from investing in Foundation and Pathak, who he called a friend in the April broadcast interview.
"I walked into his factory, and I couldn't believe what I saw," Eric Trump said. "I'm telling you, he's doing a phenomenal job."

fortune.com/2026/11/14/new-congress-affo.headline: A warning for the new Congress: Don’t stop at ‘affordability’
fortune.com/2026/11/14/new-congress-affo.author: Samantha Tweedy

paragraphs.text: It was a night of historic wins for the candidates who understood that “affordability” was at the heart of this election. But the lesson of this election is bigger than the price of eggs and gas, and every candidate – Democrat and Republican – who won should be careful not to miss the point of what voters really want.

As Black business leaders who are experts in navigating and building economic opportunity when the system doesn’t deliver, we had a hunch “affordability” wasn’t telling the whole story. So we spent months before Election Day asking voters and confirmed we were right.

Through internal polling conducted by Workbench Strategies during July 2026 of 1,400 voters, including an oversample of 400 Black voters, and our two-way texting conversations with voters, we found that they gravitated toward a combination of solutions that provide immediate relief from rising costs and build pathways to help them get ahead. For example, nearly half of all voters chose both caps on medical and prescription costs (45 percent) and increasing wages to keep up with the cost of living (43 percent) as a top-three priority. Black voters were even more focused on higher wages, with 56 percent choosing it as a top-three priority.
And over and over again, voters in focus groups conducted by HIT Strategies said that they wanted to take control of their own economic futures and for leaders to remove barriers to opportunity.

It was easy to see leading up to the election that candidates who recognized these concerns and built agendas around addressing both affordability and economic opportunity would be rewarded at the ballot box. Now that we can sit with the results of the election, it’s clear that what voters were calling an affordability crisis is also an economic mobility crisis. And now, the newly elected Congress has only 18 months to demonstrate it understands the difference and begin to deliver on both.
Yes, lowering prices matters – but that only helps Americans get to the end of the month.

Helping Americans really get ahead will take solutions that make it possible to own a home, finance a business, compete for a contract, and turn a lifetime of work into lasting financial security for their children and grandchildren – in other words, it will take building pathways to work, wages, and wealth.
This conversation matters for more than economic reasons: our democracy is still on the line.

A growing body of research finds links between economic inequality, institutional distrust, and democratic backsliding. If elected officials fail to create meaningful pathways for far more Americans to get ahead – making sure work pays, wages rise, and wealth can be built – they should not be surprised when voters look elsewhere for answers in 2028 and beyond. Nor should they expect trust in our economy, our institutions, or our democracy to rebound on its own.

Fixing this requires a bold, affirmative economic plan – and for our leaders to realize they’re on the clock with voters to deliver. The good news is that there are solutions that address both sides of the challenge: actions that can help families manage rising costs today while expanding the pathways that help people get ahead over the long term.

Lawmakers should lower costs where families feel the greatest pressure. That means promoting competition in prescription drugs, lowering grocery costs, and expanding proven tax credits that help working families keep more of what they earn.
But lowering costs alone is not enough.

Leaders must also expand pathways to work, wages, and wealth by increasing access to homeownership, supporting entrepreneurship and small business growth, expanding opportunities for workers to own a piece of corporate profits, raising wages, and ensuring that economic growth reaches communities too often left behind.

Finally, leaders must restore trust that the economic rules are fair. That means increasing transparency in concentrated markets, enforcing fair competition, and ensuring tax regulations do not disproportionately reward those who accumulate wealth.

If leaders do not take immediate steps to address rising costs and make the country’s founding promise of opportunity a reality for more Black Americans, and consequently all Americans, we’ll continue in a downward spiral: lack of faith in economic opportunity causes lack of faith in democracy, which harms the whole economy.
Every leader who won in 2026 should take this warning seriously and signal to voters that they understand the mandate underpinning those wins. The clock starts now.
The opinions expressed in Fortune.com commentary pieces are solely the views of their authors and do not necessarily reflect the opinions and beliefs of Fortune.

phys.org/news/2026-11-alaska-laments-dec.headline: Alaska laments decline of its prized salmon populations
phys.org/news/2026-11-alaska-laments-dec.author: Romain Fonsegrives

paragraphs.text: edited by Andrew Zinin
In his Alaskan community, fisherman Bob Candopoulos has long welcomed tourists to his business that's showcased by a sign featuring a king salmon.
But this local fish emblematic of the region is growing increasingly rare.

"Ten years ago, we could go out every single day" and hit catch limits, the sports fisherman and charter boat operator told AFP. "Now sometimes we're lucky if we even find any salmon when we're out there fishing."
"It's terrible," Candopoulos said with a sigh, standing on the docks of the small port of Seward, a municipality surrounded by snow-capped mountains along the shores of the North Pacific.
Like many residents of this vast, frigid state, the 64-year-old blames massive trawlers that scour the Gulf of Alaska and the Bering Sea for impacting the king salmon runs.
Industrial vessels target pollock, which is used in products like breaded fish sticks and imitation crab products worldwide.
Their nets are as wide as four commercial airliners and routinely scoop up thousands of tons of fish other than pollock each year.
This bycatch includes salmon, which then die in the ocean instead of returning to spawn in their native rivers.

The waste is particularly difficult to bear because salmon fishing has been severely restricted—and even outright banned—for years among the Indigenous communities along the Yukon and Kuskokwim rivers.
"Our rivers are running dry of fish, but the trawl industry isn't regulated to stop killing them," says Candopoulos.
'Preyed on by a billion-dollar industry'
Most of the trawlers are based in Seattle, Washington state—and roughly two-thirds of the economic output generated by the pollock fishing industry ends up outside Alaska.
"Alaska is definitely being preyed on by a billion-dollar industry," fumes Candopoulos.
This inequity fuels distrust in a region that's long witnessed the arrival of opportunists eager to exploit its rich resources, including beaver pelts, gold and oil.
Polling has indicated the majority of Alaskans are angry enough they'd like to see trawling banned.
In Seward, fishermen are not necessarily calling for that extreme.
"I'm not necessarily on the 'kill all trawlers' wagon," Chance Miller, 42, told AFP.
The sports fisherman noted that Alaska has a significant fleet of local trawlers, some of which operate on behalf of coastal Indigenous communities.
He also voiced concern over the economic implications.
"Towns are built around processors," Miller said. "If those guys weren't bringing fish in, those processors might not be able to afford to stay open."
Climate change impacts
The thorny issue even found its way into Alaska's recent Senate election.
But science points to another culprit: climate change.

Research from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) shows the decline in Chinook (king) salmon primarily stems from marine heat waves in the Bering Sea, which render the waters uninhabitable for the fish's prey.
Brett Watson, a natural resource economist at the University of Alaska Anchorage, said a trawling ban would have "unclear" impacts on salmon runs.
"Climate change has been identified as probably a larger contributor to the declines of salmon runs on the Yukon and Kuskokwim rivers," he told AFP. "That's a much more difficult issue to deal with."

In a state where residents receive an annual dividend from oil production, commercial fisherman Ian Raab laments that politicians squabble over trawlers while failing to mention the impacts of climate change.
"One would think Americans would talk more about it," he said. "I would love if we did, if we were more concerned about it."
Raab pivoted from salmon years ago, and instead prioritizes catching halibut and sablefish.
At 58, he is concerned about the Trump administration's dramatic budget cuts to NOAA.
He said the agency's marine weather forecasts have grown less reliable, and he fears reduced research will undermine policies for managing fish stocks.
"We should let them do their job," Raab said, "so I can do mine."
