aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/14/three-kill.headline: Three killed in Russia as Ukraine claims US floated NATO membership option
aljazeera.com/news/2026/11/14/three-kill.author: Al Jazeera Staff

paragraphs.text: Zelenskyy says the US asked for the first time whether Kyiv would cede land to Moscow in exchange for Ukraine’s NATO bid.
A Ukrainian drone attack has killed a mother, father and their 24-month-old daughter at their home in Belgorod, a Russian region bordering Ukraine, according to Russian authorities.

The deadly attack came on Saturday in Proletarsky, about 20km (12 miles) from Ukraine’s border as Russia’s Ministry of Defence claimed the army intercepted 29 Ukrainian drones overnight, including several over the Moscow region.

In turn, Ukraine’s air force said Russia launched 96 drones from Friday evening, of which 81 were shot down or electronically suppressed as of early Saturday. It reported hits at eight locations and falling debris at two others, while a local power supplier reported outages in parts of northeastern Sumy.

Meanwhile, in Friday’s comments to reporters that were under embargo until Saturday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said United States negotiators had asked during this week’s Abu Dhabi talks whether Ukraine would withdraw its troops from its eastern region of Donbas in exchange for joining NATO, the transatlantic military alliance.

Zelenskyy said the question had been raised for the first time but that no concrete offer existed. Zelenskyy maintained that Ukraine would not withdraw its troops but could put the issue to a referendum if Kyiv received firm security guarantees, funding for its armed forces and money for reconstruction.
“NATO is back on the agenda,” he said.
Donbas comprises Donetsk and Luhansk, two eastern Ukrainian regions partly occupied by Russia.
Moscow demands a Ukrainian withdrawal from areas Kyiv still controls, while also opposing Ukraine joining NATO, whose members pledge to defend one another.
Zelenskyy said on Friday that he would not amend Ukraine’s constitution to make it neutral, arguing the move would not guarantee lasting security.
Ukraine has been defending itself, with Western assistance, against a full-scale Russian invasion since February 2022.
This past week brought a resumption of US-mediated direct talks between the Russians and Ukrainians, which raised hopes of an early end to the war.
However, apart from renewed prisoner exchanges, there appears to have been little progress. European representatives are set to take part in the next round of talks.

Zelenskyy said the European Union and NATO are Europe’s “only real security” and that Moscow’s bid to review the continent’s security was “dangerous because … it is precisely things like this that lead to wars or escalations”.

theatlantic.com/politics/2026/11/tomb-un.headline: What the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier Means to Its Guards

paragraphs.text: In the autumn of 1921, the U.S. Army faced a difficult choice. Among four identical, flag-draped caskets—each containing the unidentified remains of an American soldier killed in World War I—only one would be laid to rest at the new Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at Arlington National Cemetery.

It seemed only appropriate that an experienced commissioned officer ought to make the selection. All four men had died in the war and been buried at American cemeteries in France. But when word came that the French military had asked an enlisted man to pick France’s Unknown Soldier, the Americans quickly determined that they would not be one-upped by French egalitarianism on that day. That is how the selection came to be made by Edward Younger, a 23-year-old sergeant and one of the pallbearers who had carried the four caskets under consideration. Younger had survived being knocked unconscious by a shell and later being shot through the left thigh during vicious fighting in World War I. But he later wrote that being told to make this choice, standing alone with the four coffins, left him overwhelmed and numb.

“Maybe these buddies had once been my pals,” Younger wrote in This Week, a syndicated magazine supplement, 15 years later. “Perhaps one of them had fought with me, had befriended me, had possibly shielded me from a bullet that might have put me in his place. Who would even know?”

Younger left roses on the second casket to his right and reported that his duty was complete. The Unknown Soldier traveled that night by train to Paris and westward the following day to Le Havre, where his casket was carried aboard the USS Olympia en route for Arlington. The Unknown Soldier was buried under a marble slab atop a hill overlooking the nation’s capital from across the Potomac River. Among thousands of those who died in the Civil War, the Spanish-American War, World War I, and other conflicts, Younger’s choice offered a place to mourn for every parent whose child never returned home from battle.

The tomb soon became a destination for tens of thousands of visitors to pay their respects to America’s war dead. In 1926, military guards were posted to discourage visitors from climbing or stepping on it. The large marble monument familiar to anyone on today’s tours was completed in 1932, and the watch became a 24-hour duty in 1937. Like Younger, the guards today belong to an infantry unit.

Also like Younger, Thomas Iglesias, a specialist, was almost certainly not expecting to become famous just by showing up for work. On Wednesday, Veterans Day, senior officials gathered for the annual observance. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, his wife, and three of his top advisers posed for photographs near the tomb. But, as they departed, the group began talking and someone laughed. Iglesias paused, then did his job. “All visitors will maintain an atmosphere of silence and respect at all times!” Iglesias shouted. A CNN camera captured the moment.

Warnings aren’t unusual at the tomb. A 2022 Army article quotes a tomb guard saying that sentinels issue two or three of them a day, usually to oblivious tourists. It’s another thing entirely to admonish Hegseth and his entourage.

Hegseth’s detractors quickly scolded him for the group’s misbehavior or lauded the young specialist for correcting the behavior of a man who has regularly disparaged members of his department for lack of decorum, be they “fat” generals or bearded soldiers. Others, on Hegseth’s side, chided the soldier for failing to show proper respect to his boss.
Hegseth, at least in this moment, chose not to pick a fight. His press office affirmed the warning as appropriate, and Hegseth awarded Iglesias the Joint Service Commendation Medal.
I didn’t read any grand motive into Iglesias’s assertive correction of Pentagon leadership, because I’ve witnessed the devotion of the tomb guards many times.

In October 2021, I traveled to the town where Younger had made his choice 100 years before, since renamed Châlons-en-Champagne. Active-duty tomb guards, all part of the 3rd Infantry Regiment “Old Guard,” were there with former soldiers who belonged to the Society of the Honor Guard, Tomb of the Unknown Soldier. They had joined a 10-day pilgrimage across France.

They gathered in a broad town square, where French and American flags adorned the way to the neoclassical city hall, completed, as it happens, in 1776. Gavin McIlvenna, the society’s president at the time, spoke with me just outside, while visitors filed in to pay their respects in the room where Younger once stood.
“I don’t know how many times I can say this is overwhelming. But it is,” McIlvenna said.
I appreciated his passion for the moment. I also didn’t totally get it at the time.

I initially saw their jobs as honorable but tedious. Walk 21 steps, turn and face the tomb for 21 seconds more. Turn again, shift the rifle to the outside shoulder, count another 21 seconds and walk. During visiting hours, repeat for 30 minutes in the warmer months and an hour in the colder months. After the cemetery closes, each watch lasts two hours. During a 24-hour shift, guards alternate time on the plaza with rest and preparation for their next watch. If the weather is miserable, that’s part of the mission.
[From the November 2023 issue: The patriot]
If any of the tomb guards in France that week ever saw their duty as I once did, they never let on. The Old Guard soldiers spend an average of 18 months at the tomb.

Standing watch on a busy day means inspecting your surroundings, keeping your rifle at the correct angle, and maintaining a steady walk. There is no casual conversation, so guards communicate through scrapes and clicks of the steel plates attached to their shoes. A sentinel scrapes a heel to acknowledge veterans and distinguished guests or strikes the plates together on the inside of his heels to signal to another guard.

The same standards of behavior apply once visitors leave the cemetery for the night, though the solitude provides plenty of time for the soldiers’ introspection. Several sentinels told me that, during the watch, they think about the tomb and all those it honors. An Unknown Soldier has no backstory to limit what others see in him. On those walks in the darkness, he can embody the courage and selflessness of combat or a remembrance of loved ones the guards have lost in their own lives. Many tomb guards have deployed to Iraq or Afghanistan, while others served as far back as the Vietnam War. Some are never far from friends buried in other sections of the cemetery.

In France, shared devotion brought together guards whose service spanned generations. From Châlons-en-Champagne, they traveled to Paris with other military organizations for a ceremony under the Arc de Triomphe, followed by dinner at the École Militaire.

At dinner, they lived it up and mostly kept the conversation light, while accommodating my interest in their jobs. I remember the look in the eyes of one former tomb guard when he talked about his service. I began to understand that every moment on that walk, and every little detail performed with precision, was an expression of gratitude for a debt that will never be fully repaid. And so it continues, uninterrupted.
[Read: The inside story of what happened at Stars and Stripes]

The World War I Unknown Soldier would later be joined by unidentified service members from World War II and the Korean War, buried in separate crypts beside his tomb. But scientific advances have made future unknown burials very unlikely in the U.S. armed forces. In 1998, the Vietnam Unknown was identified as First Lieutenant Michael J. Blassie, an Air Force pilot shot down in 1972. The Vietnam Unknown’s crypt has been kept empty since Blassie’s remains were exhumed.

DNA-based evidence can restore a fallen soldier’s identity. But people still have to choose to remember them. Edward Younger never forgot the Unknown Soldier he picked. He traveled to Arlington in 1930, telling The Washington Post that it was “real nice to get a chance to visit him again.” Twelve years later, Younger himself was laid to rest at the national cemetery.

Younger described himself and his comrades as just “good, average soldiers.” He always imagined the man in the tomb to be a lot like him. That’s why the unidentified man in that tomb is paradoxically so easy to identify with. Few of us will be remembered by name for long. But what good, average people accomplish can outlast the memory of any one of them.

phys.org/news/2026-11-california-steels-.headline: California steels for storms that could trigger massive waves, flooding
phys.org/news/2026-11-california-steels-.author: Science X

paragraphs.text: edited by Andrew Zinin
California was bracing Friday for a storm series packing heavy rain and surf that could once again flood coastal communities and potentially send monster waves pounding shores.

Off the coast of San Francisco, southern Monterey Bay and the Big Sur coast, forecasters warned that up to 30-foot (9-meter) breaking waves could arrive Friday evening, with occasional monstrous sets of 40 to 50 feet (12 to 15 meters) possible.

Such violent waves in the Pacific are a trademark of the El Niño weather pattern, which this year has driven disruptions around the globe as it turbocharges the impacts of human-caused climate change.
"Large breaking waves will run up beaches and crash over seawalls, inundating adjacent, low-lying infrastructure," read the latest National Weather Service advisory.
The U.S. weather agency urged against entering the water and said to stay off waterside infrastructure including jetties, piers and rocks.
"NEVER turn your back on the ocean," NWS meteorologists wrote.
Farther south, near Los Angeles, forecasters said widespread rainfall would begin Friday and continue into Saturday, and elevated surf could fuel dangerous rip currents and breaking waves.
The surf's impact was expected to peak on Saturday and potentially again Monday, the NWS said.
"There is potential for moderate coastal flooding impacts at times, especially Saturday," read the latest advisory from the weather agency.
"Some of these impacts may be moderate to significant beach erosion and shallow flooding of normally dry beaches and walkways."

Storm systems as well as high tides have triggered flooding in recent months in California, causing dramatic property destruction and leaving communities along the coasts feeling particularly vulnerable.
Forecasters anticipate giant storms off the coast will continue to whip up large waves as the El Niño phenomenon is expected to strengthen into the winter.
El Niño raises surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean and causes global changes in winds and rainfall, and this year's edition has proven particularly extreme.
Human-caused climate change can worsen El Niño's impacts. A warmer atmosphere holds more moisture, making rains more intense.
Sea levels off California will likely soon bump even higher due to especially high tides known as king tides, which generally occur in the late fall and winter months.

In the spring of 1943, Walter C. Langer, a psychoanalyst at Harvard, received a query from William J. Donovan, the head of the U.S. government’s Office of Strategic Services, the covert-operations predecessor to the CIA. Donovan was interested in commissioning Langer to prepare a psychological profile of Adolf Hitler.

“What we need is a realistic appraisal of the German situation,” Donovan told Langer. “If Hitler is running the show, what kind of a person is he? What are his ambitions? How does he appear to the German people? What is he like with his associates?” The OSS chief wanted to understand Hitler’s “psychological make-up—the things that make him tick.” Donovan was especially keen to know how Hitler might respond to increasing adversity.

Hitler was used to winning. From 1933 to 1943, the Nazi leader had marched from one stunning political and military triumph to the next, securing the chancellorship, crushing the German constitutional order, annexing Austria, dismembering Czechoslovakia, and then invading Poland, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Denmark, countries across North Africa, and Russia. Until 1943, Hitler had seemed to be an inexorable political and military force, smashing constitutional guardrails, shredding international treaties, breaking trade alliances, upending the international order, and ultimately plunging the entire world into war.

But then came military reversals that stopped Hitler in his tracks: El Alamein, in November 1942, then Stalingrad, in January 1943. Donovan wanted to know how Hitler would react—militarily, politically, personally—if the tides of war began to change. “Do you suppose you could come up with something along these lines?” Donovan asked Langer.

This was the first time the U.S. government would commission a psychological profile of a foreign leader to determine his possible future courses of action. Donovan was not interested in an academic study. Rather, he wanted a “realistic appraisal” that might provide actionable intelligence about what the führer might do next.
[Read: Hitler could have been stopped]

Langer engaged three fellow psychoanalysts—one from Harvard, one from the New School for Social Research, and one of the New York Psychoanalytic Institute—and set to work. He immersed himself in Hitler’s speeches and writings. He read both volumes of Mein Kampf front to back. He collected newspaper clippings and magazine articles. He interviewed former Hitler associates who had broken with the Nazi leader and were now living in exile.

“The world has come to know Adolph Hitler for his insatiable greed for power, his ruthlessness, cruelty and utter lack of feeling, his contempt for established institutions and his lack of moral restraints,” Langer wrote in framing the scope of his work. “In the course of relatively few years he has contrived to usurp such tremendous power that a few veiled threats, accusations or insinuations were enough to make the world tremble.” It was only when the world wearied of Hitler’s threats and bluster, “and concluded that it was all a bluff,” Langer wrote, that the Nazi leader had “initiated the most brutal and devastating war in history.”

Hitler was a man, Langer was told repeatedly, with an insatiable ego who needed to be the center of attention, always, everywhere. Hitler saw himself as the ultimate authority in all matters regardless of their import or insignificance. “It makes little difference whether the field be economics, education, foreign affairs, propaganda, movies, music or women’s dress,” Langer reported. “In each and every field he believes himself to be an unquestioned authority.”

One former Hitler associate described to Langer what had happened when he tried to correct the Nazi leader about something. “I cannot be mistaken,” Hitler said. “What I do and say is historical.” Langer attributed this “infantile thinking” to an arrested emotional development that also resulted in frequent tantrums, both in private and public.

Langer heard repeated stories about Hitler’s unbridled rages against his staff. Otto Strasser, an early Nazi Party member who had broken with Hitler over economic policy, told Langer that Hitler regularly browbeat members of his inner circle. “Rage and abuse became the favorite weapons in his armory,” Langer wrote, along with public degradation, humiliation, and, occasionally, murder. Strasser’s brother Gregor Strasser, another Nazi Party member who had also broken with Hitler over policy matters, was killed on the Night of the Long Knives.

“Some of his closest associates have felt that he induces these rages consciously to frighten those around him,” Langer wrote. Hermann Rauschning, another early Nazi Party official, told Langer that some of Hitler’s “well-timed fits of rage” were intended to throw his entourage into confusion and submission.

Langer reported that Hitler used a social gathering attended by his propaganda minister, Joseph Goebbels, and his Luftwaffe chief, Hermann Göring, to disparage both with juvenile humor. “You all know what a volt is and an ampere, don’t you?” Hitler said to the assembled crowd. “But do you know what a goebbels, a goering are? A goebbels is the amount of nonsense a man speaks in an hour and a goering is the amount of metal that can be pinned on a man’s breast.”

Langer observed that Hitler used radio and rallies to spew lies and hatred, in order to manipulate public opinion. “Hitler’s speaking has been aptly described as a ‘verbal diarrhea,’” Langer wrote, and he reported that Rauschning had compared a Hitler speech to “an oral enema.”

Langer also heard much about Hitler’s obsession with women. “Hitler likes to be surrounded with pretty women and usually requests the moving picture companies to send over a number of actresses whenever there is a party in the Chancellory,” Langer wrote, supporting this with an Associated Press photograph of Hitler surrounded by young film stars.

Langer also cited unverified accounts of Hitler’s sexual proclivities and capacities, ranging from impotence to homosexuality to myriad perversions. Hitler, Langer wrote, “derives sexual gratification from the act of having a woman urinate or defecate on him.”

Although this was likely not the kind of “actionable intelligence” that the OSS chief had been seeking, Langer, schooled in Freudian psychology, devoted much of his report to psychoanalysis of the Nazi leader. “Hitler’s outstanding defense mechanism is one commonly called projection,” Langer wrote. “It is a technique by which the ego of an individual defends itself against unpleasant impulses, tendencies or characteristics by denying their existence in himself while he attributes them to others.”

As evidence, Langer noted that Hitler accused his political opponents of the “bombardment of lies” that Hitler himself assailed them with. Hitler’s hatred of the Jews, Langer theorized, emanated from hatred of himself: Hitler’s “own personal problems and conflicts were transferred from within himself to the external world where they assumed the proportions of racial and national conflicts.”

Langer attributed Hitler’s rages, hatreds, obsessions, and delusions to an unhappy childhood with a brutish father and an emotionally battered but loving mother. Langer also spent considerable time analyzing Hitler’s preoccupation with architectural projects—in particular, the Eagle’s Nest, outside Berchtesgaden, Germany.

“First there is a long hard road, then a heavily guarded entrance, a trip through a long tunnel to an extremely inaccessible place. There one can be alone, safe and undisturbed, and revel in the joys that Mother Nature bestows,” Langer wrote. “From a symbolic point of view one can easily imagine that this is a materialization of a child’s conception of the return to the womb.”

By October 1943, when Langer’s report was rushed to completion at Donovan’s insistence, Hitler was on his back heel but hardly finished. London was being pummelled. Rumors of a Wunderwaffe, a “miracle weapon,” that could change the course of the war proliferated. German physicists, led by Werner Heisenberg, were at work on an atomic bomb.

Göring had already developed a prototype for a delivery mechanism—the Messerschmitt Me 264, dubbed the “Amerika Bomber”—and Manhattan was its first target. Hitler “described the skyscrapers being turned into gigantic burning torches, collapsing upon one another, the glow of the exploding city illuminating the dark sky,” Hitler’s armament minister, Albert Speer, recalled. “With such range we could repay America a thousandfold for the destruction of our cities.”

Not until the final three pages of his long report did Langer provide the “realistic appraisal” of Hitler’s potential courses of action that Donovan had been seeking. Based on his interviews and his review of 11,000 pages of source materials, Langer discerned scenarios for Hitler’s possible reactions were he to face ultimate defeat. Langer thought it unlikely that Hitler would try to escape to another country, as dictators were known to do—because “nothing would break the myth” of Hitler as a great leader more assuredly than running away.
[Read: Trump: ‘I need the kind of generals that Hitler had’]

Although Langer doubted that Hitler would allow himself to fall into the hands of the Allies, he did not rule out the possibility that the führer’s warped personality could welcome such an outcome, citing the case of a 16th-century religious fanatic who, when his theocratic cult was disbanded, asked to be paraded around in a cage. “In Hitler’s case such an outcome seems remote,” Langer wrote, “but it is difficult to estimate the extent to which an extreme masochist will go in order to gratify these tendencies.”

Langer did think it possible that Hitler would sacrifice himself in combat. “When he is convinced that he cannot win, he may lead his troops into battle and expose himself as the fearless and fanatical leader,” Langer wrote. But it was equally likely, Langer concluded, that Hitler would suffer a complete nervous breakdown. “Hitler has many characteristics which border on the schizophrenic,” Langer continued. “This would not be an undesirable eventuality from our point of view since it would do much to undermine the Hitler legend.”

Langer presciently posited suicide as the most likely scenario. He knew that Hitler had always been a man whose “infantile thinking” drove him to extremes and blinded him to compromise. Hitler sacrificed an entire army at Stalingrad, and his entire Afrika Korps in Tunisia. Langer cited Hitler’s fatalistic fanaticism verbatim: “We shall not capitulate … no, never. We may be destroyed, but if we are, we shall drag a world with us … a world in flames.”

If anything, Langer suggested, the worse things got for Hitler, the more intransigent he would become. “He will fight as long as he can with any weapon or technique that can be conjured up to meet the emergency,” Langer concluded. “The course he will follow will almost certainly be the one that seems to him to be the surest road to immortality and that at the same time wreaks the greatest vengeance on a world he despises.” It is fortunate that Hitler never had access to a nuclear button.
My home is full of honey pots.

In the front hall hangs a vintage poster from World War II, a sultry blonde at a cocktail party with three British officers leaning over her and the warning: “Keep mum, she’s not so dumb! Careless talk costs lives.”

I also have a Cold War honey trap: a photograph of the bewitching Tatiana Romanova, wearing nothing but a black velvet choker and black stockings, looking up saucily at James Bond after sneaking into his bed in “From Russia With Love.”

On my TV at night is the new season of “Black Doves,” the Netflix thriller in which the comely Keira Knightley is spying on her husband, the British prime minister, and working for a spidery organization that sells state secrets to the highest bidder.

And on my coffee table is a DVD of the 1946 Hitchcock spy noir, “Notorious,” in which Ingrid Bergman honeytraps a Nazi played by Claude Rains. When the Rains character is forced to confess to his Nazi mother that he married an American spy, the mother sneers at him: “We are protected by the enormity of your stupidity.”
Suffice it to say, Jensen Huang was not protected by the enormity of his stupidity.

Sexpionage in Silicon Valley looks too easy. It barely requires any real tradecraft. All it takes is a smile from the sort of femme fatale these nerdy brainiacs couldn’t get when they were young — before the billions, the makeovers, the personal trainers, the yachts and Huang’s ubiquitous Tom Ford black leather jacket.
Some Silicon Valley executives have warned their scientists and engineers to beware if they find themselves dating women who are “out of their league,” as one tech leader put it to me.

For a 2023 New Yorker profile, Huang told Stephen Witt that he was anything but a player, noting: “I did not have a girlfriend” in high school. His future wife, Lori, was his college lab partner in an introductory electrical engineering class.

Our future is being molded by a sketchy pantheon of stunted tech bros. Many of these boys with toys are immature, awkward and hubristic, high on their own supply, believing themselves to be the gods of a new religion, the creators of a new species.

And Trumpworld is not reining them in — just the reverse. In return for lavish flattery and donations to President Trump’s inaugural fun and pet projects, they’re getting all kinds of leeway, creating threats to national security and a glide path for artificial intelligence to conquer us.

As Julian Gewirtz wrote in The Atlantic, “American strategy has come to depend, to an extraordinary degree, on powerful private-sector actors whose incentives the government cannot simply assume will align with the national interest.”

Though Huang once said at a summit at Stanford that “greatness comes from character,” the lords of the cloud often seem clueless about character, motivations and, indeed, human beings. That’s how Elon Musk threw away close to half a billion dollars on the midterms.

Huang, who went from video games to crackerjack chips that fueled the A.I. boom, dismissed the risks of A.I. and lobbied Trump to lift export restrictions on selling advanced chips to China. Asked if it mattered whether China or the U.S. won the A.I. contest, he said, “I don’t think it does.”

In April, at a $1 million-a-head Mar-a-Lago dinner, Huang made his case to Trump to allow Nvidia to do business with China as the administration weighed an export ban on its chips. The administration shut down sales days after, only for Trump to reverse course a few months later and allow the company to sell certain chips to our chief adversary, provided the government got 15 percent of the revenue.
Trump brays that America can’t slow the pace of A.I. because we have to stay ahead of China. But then he makes perverse moves that will help China catch up to — and maybe overtake — us.

It’s hard to believe Huang wasn’t suspicious of the woman he was involved with, Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence identified as a Chinese spy. After all, over a year ago, The Times reported on their cozy friendship, noting that Alice Huang’s firm, Megaspeed, was getting its mitts on billions worth of Nvidia’s most advanced products and distributing them to data centers in Malaysia and Indonesia, and perhaps passing them on to China.

This is a dangerous loophole that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has apparently done nothing to rectify. On Nov. 5, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent confronted Lutnick, hotly asking why the administration had not already banned chip sales to Megaspeed. Bessent told CNBC on Friday that the Treasury Department had been pushing for it for months. The president, according to The Times, was more sympathetic to Lutnick’s position.

Marco Rubio, a China hawk, began warning top Trump officials this spring about the dangerous liaison of the two Huangs. But Trump, no stranger to risky encounters, brushed it off. He likes rich, powerful, dominating men. And he surely liked hearing Jensen’s happy talk on A.I. because, as everything else around him faltered, the beleaguered president needed the rising stock market, disproportionately buoyed by Nvidia, more than ever.
Trump is a peerless con man, but he’s also an easy mark. He is so eager to have good relationships with Vladimir Putin and China’s President Xi Jinping that he sometimes seems like a patsy.

When A.I. models began blackmailing programmers, giving creepy advice to teens and hacking into other systems, many top tech executives and over 1,000 employees at A.I. companies signed a letter urging that we slow our roll and figure out some guardrails.
Seems like a no-brainer. But Huang wasn’t onboard.

As Witt wrote in The Times, the fallen Nvidia chief liked to present a facade of a humble family man. But in truth, Witt said, Huang was an arrogant narcissist with a penchant for dressing down members of his staff and was reportedly willing to have a widely known affair with a subordinate even though both of his children held senior roles at the company.

The chip king named his company after the Latin word for envy, invidia. But Huang is not someone to be envied; he is someone to hold in contempt. At a perilous moment, when we need to get control over A.I. before it gets control over us, Huang, Lutnick and Trump aren’t looking out for us.
Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies ever, has lost over a trillion in market cap since the spy story broke, causing some headline writers to call this the most expensive peccadillo in history.
Never mind artificial intelligence. What about a little intelligence?

nytimes.com/2026/11/14/opinion/midterm-e.headline: Opinion | ‘There’s No Juice Left to Squeeze From MAGA’
nytimes.com/2026/11/14/opinion/midterm-e.author: Robert Siegel, E.J. Dionne Jr., Timothy P. Carney, Vishakha Darbha

paragraphs.text: The midterms last week upended assumptions about where — and how — both political parties can win. So what comes next? The Opinion contributor Robert Siegel joins the contributing writer E.J. Dionne Jr. and the senior political columnist for The Washington Examiner, Tim Carney, to debate whether MAGA can outlast Donald Trump and what Democrats can do with their new power.

Below is a transcript of an episode of “The Opinions.” We recommend listening to it in its original form for the full effect. You can do so using the player above or on the NYTimes app, Apple, Spotify, Amazon Music, YouTube, iHeartRadio or wherever you get your podcasts.
The transcript has been lightly edited for length and clarity.

Robert Siegel: Since the three of us last talked, the political map of America has been redrawn. Assumptions about which party can win which state have been thrown out, and past speculation about the future has been replaced with fresh speculation about the future. And before we dig into some of the big questions that arose from the 2026 elections, I’d like to hear, briefly, from each of us about what impression of the election sticks in the mind?
What sums up what’s happened most vividly for you? Tim?

Tim Carney: For me, it’s proof that the Donald Trump realignment that we first started to see in 2016 was not really a partisan realignment, but an emergence of what I call “the Trumpy vote.” If you look at the counties in Ohio, for instance, that swung most from Mitt Romney to Trump — the places where they’re not necessarily conservative Republicans, but they were Trump voters — those Trumpy counties, those were the counties that had the biggest blue wave. Same thing happened — I looked precinct by precinct level — in Lower Bucks County, the blue collar part right outside of Philadelphia.
Siegel: In Pennsylvania.

Carney: In Pennsylvania, right outside of Philadelphia. Trump came in and won these, what Sean Trende used to call, “the missing white voter.” Those guys, sons of former factory workers, those are the precincts that swung back to give Democrats a House seat, the State Senate, that sort of thing. So I don’t know whether it’s a matter of Trump voters staying home, or what seems more likely from the numbers so far, that the Trump voter was never a conservative, never a Republican, and now he just voted Democrat.
Siegel: E.J.?

E.J. Dionne Jr.: I got two numbers and two little postcards from my experience of the campaign. Two numbers: Democrats got 56 percent of the popular House vote on the basis of the count right now. That is exceptional. We’ve never seen a blowout like that in decades. The Gingrich “revolution” was with 51 and a half percent of the vote.
Siegel: In ’94.

Dionne: In ’94. Apparently, Republicans haven’t hit 56 percent since 1928. Four and a half million fewer Republicans at the latest count; 15 million more Democratic votes. So this was both a dispirited Democratic base and mobilization. Two postcards: Covering Adam Hamilton — Rev. Senator-elect Adam Hamilton. It’s the only campaign I ever covered, where part of my work was going to a wedding that he performed as a minister, and a baptism — and I think that tells us something about him and the nature of this campaign.

And lastly, I went down to Mississippi, because I’d heard some really good things about the kind of candidate Scott Colom was. I walked into a place called Johnny T.’s Bistro and Blues in Jackson, and I sat down with Scott Colom. He laid out exactly how he could win that race. And it was an extraordinary understanding of that race. And I’ve got to say, he made me a believer — that this really could happen. And he proved, as he said in his speech, that it wasn’t just about faith, it was also about work, because he wouldn’t leave Johnny T.’s before he had shaken every hand in the house. He really worked that race.

Siegel: To which I would add, from myself, the political power exercised by Southern Black voters, even after, and in large part in reaction to, the gutting of the Voting Rights Act. It was so great in Georgia, in Mississippi, in North Carolina — you can say Texas is part of the South. It was pretty strong in Louisiana. And it left me wondering if the Voting Rights Act, a great landmark piece of legislation of the 1960s, really had, as many conservatives argue, outlived its necessity. E.J., feel free to scold me for that heretical statement.

Dionne: How’d you know I disagree with you, Robert? When you look at Colom’s victory, what did it take? You still had very quite racialized voting in Mississippi. It just happened that Colom was skillful at bringing over enough white voters and a massive turnout of Black voters. Why? Because they fundamentally disagree, obviously, with what you just said. They believe — and I think they’re right — that knocking down the Voting Rights Act enables the kind of gerrymandering that you saw in Tennessee that also happened. In Tennessee, the Republicans split up Memphis, which is about 60, 65 percent Black, not into two pieces, but into three pieces, just to make sure that that vote couldn’t affect the results.

Justin Pearson, a brave state legislator who’s Black, ran in one of those districts. He ran a great race. The national wave was with him, and he still could only get to within one point. So I think what we really need is a new Voting Rights Act, but we also should have national outlawing of gerrymandering. Because I think that when you think about environmental laws, we have them so that somebody doesn’t try to cut their price by polluting a river. We say to employers, people, manufacturers: “Sell a better product, but don’t pollute the river.” And I think we’re polluting the river of American politics with competitive gerrymandering, which is going to keep going until we outlaw it.

Carney: I agree that partisan gerrymandering — it’s a scourge on democracy. I also agree that part of what the Voting Rights Act was being used to do was to mandate racial gerrymandering. This is part of the case in Louisiana. If you remember those horrible districts in North Carolina a couple decades ago, that were drawn with these little threads along a highway — that was racial gerrymandering to make sure that there are enough majority-minority districts.

So I absolutely agree that we need to get rid of the gerrymandering, the partisan stuff. We also need to get rid of racial gerrymandering. And Democrats would not be happy with that, because in some states they depend on tying together two different minority precincts.
Siegel: Let’s talk about the two big parties right now. The devastating defeat the Republicans suffered this year raises the question: Is MAGA dead? Who wants to start on this one?

Carney: I mean, the political analysis that I was mentioning earlier, the Trump vote, the working-class white vote that Trump brought into the party, never became reliably conservative and Republican. These people weren’t made into Paul Ryan acolytes who love the idea of reforming Social Security. And frankly, they’re not the Ted Cruz vote from 2016. Remember, you could chart by county. The places where people were more likely to go to church every week in the 2016 primaries, they were voting for Ted Cruz.

The places where you had the white evangelicals who don’t attend church, they were more likely to be the Trump voter. So the less religiously observant, the less fiscally conservative — that was the Trump vote. And the Republicans cannot rely on them now that Trump is leaving the stage. And then, you combine with that the fact that the party started selecting for loyalty to Trump, rather than either conservatism or quality of candidate — and that also hurt the party. So going forward, the Republicans, there’s no juice left to squeeze from MAGA. And if anybody tries to be a mini MAGA — if JD Vance says, “I’m going to be the next Donald Trump” — you can’t be the next Donald Trump.

I mean, we’re New Yorkers. We remember this guy. He is sui generis, thanks be to God, and there isn’t another one of him. I basically think Trump blew up what existed before the consensus — the Reagan consensus that lasted for a while — but nothing has filled that space.

Siegel: I just want to underscore what you said about candidates. I was thinking, boy, a lot of Senate Democrats who won Senate elections were lucky to have a terrible opponent. And then it occurred to me it’s not luck that you get Herschel Walker running for the Senate, only because loyalty and fame have been elevated to values that dwarf every other talent that a candidate might have.

Dionne: Look, I think that MAGA is dead as such, because it was always rooted in a contradiction. The great economics writer for the Financial Times, Martin Wolf, once described it as “pluto-populism,” which was plutocratic populism.

And I think, in this version of Trump, he gave voters the pluto without the populism. And that his ties to very, very wealthy people were just so obvious to so many of these voters, and the obsessions with things like the ballroom and the like, that they just walked away. Now, does it mean that a strongly conservative wing of the Republican Party is gone? No. There’s always been that. The Tea Party, in many ways, gave birth to the MAGA movement. So there will be a right wing of the Republican Party, but MAGA specifically defined by Donald Trump — and this odd contradiction of policies that often help the wealthiest people, but rhetoric that was directed to working people, usually using tariffs as his way in — I think that just will not work anymore.
Siegel: Tim, how would you see a Republican Party minus MAGA? Is it back to the Ted Cruz appeal?

Carney: I mean, when I talk to conservative Republican circles, they want to, I say, get the band back together. And they think that the way things were and that when they lost in 2012, you know, Romney should have won that — that is a perfidious pipe dream for conservatives. Part of the problem was that they were ignoring the big difference and why some populism was needed between the elites of both parties and the public of both parties.

I said this last time I was on the show. Both parties’ elites have long been internationalists on war, trade and immigration, while the public was not. So a more nationalist party — and I know that nationalism sounds like a bad word to a lot of people — but you can have nationalism without it requiring what Trump did. Say, in Minnesota, siccing cops on protesters; immigration enforcement that’s basically “bust the heads and haul off anybody.”
Dionne: And kills people.

Carney: Yeah. So there is a nationalism that says our immigration policy should be crafted for the people who are here, and our foreign policy should not be listening to what NATO and the E.U. say, but looking after American interests.

I mean, in my view, the trade policy that serves us best is basically free trade. But all of those things — be more guided towards nationalism, but in a smart way, not driven by a Trump who says: I love tariffs, they’re my favorite word. So a saner, calmer, but more nationalist-focused conservatism could be one of the paths forward for a post-MAGA conservatism.

Dionne: “Perfidious pipe dream.” I’ll have to credit you when I use that. I think that Tim is right about something important, which is that the Trump victory did show that for many years now, the Republican Party has relied a great deal on white working-class voters. And Ross Douthat and Reihan Salam wrote a book years ago, about the Republicans not doing anything for that white working class.

The problem is, they still haven’t done very much about the white working class, and what you saw in this election was something like a more authentic populism, I would argue, coming from the Democratic side, which said, “Look, it’s not populist to cut people’s health care off by cutting Obamacare subsidies. It’s not populist to kowtow to big tech companies. It’s not populist to let data centers run rampant without any local control.” And so, I think what you’ve got is a bunch of loose voters again, who are open to persuasion. But if the Republicans go back to a kind of pure Reaganite or Paul Ryanite politics, I don’t think there’s a majority there for them.

Carney: But I think a conservative populism can be a real thing. For instance, again, immigration. Is the immigration policy directed at driving down low-skilled wages? Which a lot of our immigration policy has been. Let’s bring in guest workers. Maybe we need them for seasonal work, but do we need them in the factories? Maybe that would be better going to the people who are here, natives, or current immigrants who don’t have a college degree or a college education. Similarly, big government, as we saw with Trump’s tariffs — that often serves the guy with the best lobbyists, which is not going to be mom and pop. So I do think a more conservative populism is possible. Obviously, a very different one than Trump’s. And I think you’re right that the Democrats seized the populism mantle this year, but I don’t think that that’s inevitable going forward.
Dionne: You know, under Trump, real wages are down. Manufacturing jobs are not up. And so — if I may channel the late Walter Mondale — where’s the beef?

Siegel: Let’s move on to the Democrats, who won nearly everything that could be won. They have big majorities, but not a veto-proof Senate majority. And some of the people who might have crossed the aisle to vote with them in recent years — Susan Collins of Maine, Thom Tillis of North Carolina — are no longer there. There are Democrats holding those seats. So what can the Democrats actually do with all these seats in Congress?

Carney: They can investigate Donald Trump. And I’m going to say, not that the average Democrat will listen to my advice, but there are places where there is clear evidence of corruption in the Trump administration, which is self-enrichment. Whether it’s selling crypto — worthless crypto tokens that then the top buyers get — a dinner with Trump; whether it’s his son’s business in the United Arab Emirates or Qatar. We could keep going on with a lot of these. The revolving-door lobbyists, the firms that are close to them, what special deals did they get? In short, were there quid pro quos? Did Donald Trump, or anybody in this administration, give any political favors to people who were personally enriching his family or enriching the people close to him?

I bet the answer is yes, and that’s where I’m hoping the Democrats look. I’m afraid they’re going to get distracted by Jeffrey Epstein noise, or by Russia again, or something like that. They need to focus on what really corrodes policymaking in this country, and what Trump was pretty guilty of, it seems to me, which is selling policy for personal favors to the president and the people close to him.

Dionne: So I’m going to do something dangerous. I’m going to say that the Democrats actually will be more disciplined than Tim suspects. And if you listen to one of the leading people who’s going to be looking into all this, Jamie Raskin, he is speaking in a very disciplined way, because he knows what the Democrats are up against here.
Siegel: We should say he’s poised to be the next chair of the Judiciary [Committee].

Dionne: Thank you. And so, I think they do know that a mishmash of too many hearings doesn’t penetrate anything. But they’re also not going to make the mistake of all investigations, no legislation. And I think they already have a plan to pass some very simple, broadly popular things in the party as early as they can, particularly reversing these health care cuts, trying to hem Trump in on the tariffs, particularly with Canada, which are very unpopular in the country. And also, take steps to end the war in Iran. And I think the problem Democrats have is that they don’t know which Trump they’re going to be dealing with. I was so struck that on the same day ——
Siegel: When he said he would work with the Democrats?

Dionne: Trump gave our former colleague, Ross Douthat, an interview in which he said that the immigration policy was too tough, and he’d like to negotiate a deal with the Democrats. Later that day, he named Stephen Miller, the architect of that policy that was too tough, as his chief of staff. They’re now threatening criminal action, if the Democrats exercise their constitutional right to oversight. So they don’t know what they’re going to be dealing with. The rubber will really hit the road on the budget, because the one thing they have to agree on, at some point, is a budget. The budget can pass on reconciliation, the rules that allow a party to pass stuff in the Senate without 60 votes.
Siegel: Without a filibuster.

Dionne: Without a filibuster. And then you’re going to have a negotiation, and I think Democrats will put some of the stuff they want that is very popular — like restoring health care money — in that bill, and we’re going to see what Trump really wants to do.

Carney: Also, we’re going to see if Democrats believe in taxes anymore. It used to be that Democrats would say: “We’re going to tax people.” Now the Democrats are piling on finding new people to not tax. Four hundred thousand — is that now the limit? If you make less than $400,000, so many Democrats say, “We’re not going to hike your taxes.” So, that’s one point of pressure on them: Are they willing to say, to balance the budget, to reduce the deficit, etc., “we need to increase taxes”?

Democrats of old loved increasing taxes on anybody who was above the middle class, or even in the middle class; and now it seems that they’re allergic to it, in part because that upper middle-class electorate has moved so far to the Dems.

Dionne: Two things: One, there is so much money given away to the super rich in the tax code, since 2000 — the two Bush tax cuts and the two Trump tax cuts. I think there is a lot of money to be raised just there, to fund what the Democrats think they might be able to do in this period. But I think the honest, most likely thing is neither party is going to deal with tax increases until after the 2028 election, because I think Trump would veto that anyway. And we’re going to have the big argument about budgets and the future of Social Security after 2028.
Siegel: Who are some stars of the Democratic landslide and how might they figure in the coming presidential election?

Carney: I think Jon Ossoff is the one that won all the buzz coming out. Georgia was a state that 20 years ago the Republicans took over, and now it’s got — statewide — Democratic elected officials. And Ossoff seemed like he was at the cutting edge of that.

On the other side, though, I would say I think Josh Shapiro, the governor of Pennsylvania, is the one who comes out of this the biggest loser, in part because now he has a trifecta. He was pretty good working across parties, and Dems would say: Hey, he gets stuff done. Remember, he fixed I-95 in a week or something.

But now he’s going to have the pressure from the liberals who are now controlling the state legislature to pass stuff that Tim Walz was handicapped by — the governor of Minnesota who was Kamala Harris’s running mate. He was handicapped because he got pushed to pass all sorts of things, either the special interest asks from the teachers’ unions or massively high minimum wage or other things that could really hobble the economy.
So I think of Ossoff as a winner and Shapiro as a loser.

Dionne: Tim thinks everything progressives want to do is unpopular. Strengthening health care is popular, child care is popular, building more housing is popular, raising the minimum wage is popular. I think that’s actually good for Shapiro because he needs to move to the left a little bit to have a chance to win the nomination.
But you can go down the list. James Talarico is a star. Roy Cooper is an unheralded star. I think Roy ——
Siegel: Governor of North Carolina.

Dionne: Yes, of North Carolina. I think Roy has not gotten enough kudos because he put the race away so early that it really didn’t get a lot of attention. I don’t think he’s a presidential candidate, but I think his achievement is really going to be studied.

And I think that Abdul El-Sayed is going to be one of the most interesting people in the Congress. I think you’re going to see El-Sayed try to develop into more of a national candidate. For example, he started out being Medicare for all, and then he amended a little bit to Medicare for all who want it, which is really the public option, which is the compromise position Democrats can agree on. So I think he’s going to be a fascinating person to watch.

Siegel: According to Gallup, close to half of Americans identify as independents, even if they lean one way or the other, they go out of their way not to identify as Democrats or Republicans, perhaps just to avoid fund-raising phone calls. I don’t know why they do it.
Dionne: I get emails from President Trump trying to raise money.
Siegel: Does the shrinkage of party identity, party affiliation in the country, mean that there is this vast pool of people who are up for grabs in every election?

Carney: Up for grabs, yes. But one of the dreams that people get is, oh, well, if half of the country — and that’s bigger, that’s a plurality if it’s 49 percent — we can form a third party that can win. That 49 percent doesn’t agree on very much, so this includes, again, your working-class white guy, who wants more spending on Social Security, but also tariffs. And it includes your moderate country-club voter who wants lower taxes, medium regulation. It includes every sort of thing. So a key thing to remember is that 49 percent might agree that both parties stink, but the next item on the agenda, you’re going to have a lot of disagreement.

Dionne: Tim has found something we emphatically agree on. But what I want to say is, somebody years ago wrote a book called “The Myth of the Independent Voter,” and a lot of independents aren’t really independents. The pollsters now ask, do you lean ——
Carney: Who did you vote for last time? Who did you vote for?

Dionne: But I do think there’s something that friends of a party system — and I think you can’t have a democracy without parties — have to acknowledge that the rising desire to identify as independent is, in some ways, a sign of alienation from the system.
Carney: Yeah.
Dionne: A sense that the system isn’t delivering. We are not happy with these politicians. I think there is something real there that both parties have to grapple with.

Siegel: One interesting feature of this year’s Democratic candidates was the relative comfort that several showed with the language of religion, in describing themselves and their ideas about governing. Senator-elect Hamilton of Kansas is a pastor. James Talarico of Texas is a seminarian. Scott Colom in Mississippi began his victory speech with a long riff on prayer and faith. Just a coincidence or is there something big at work here?

Carney: This was the silver lining of the election for me, that these were Democrats who were very comfortable in talking about faith and not just as a personal thing. If I can quote from some E.J. Dionne columns here — Adam Hamilton said: “The gospel isn’t just about a personal faith. It’s about the call to be in the world.” Scott Colom: “When we talk about policy issues we need to talk about it through a faith and values lens.” This is a very important thing that, I think, we struggle with as a country because we rightly see that religion shouldn’t be legislated.

We shouldn’t mandate that people go to church. We shouldn’t impose, through legislation, some specific religion. We can’t establish a religion. But there’s this myth that we should just take our religion out of our brain when we’re talking about politics, or ask our elected officials to do that, too. And the fact is that, if you’re passing a policy — if you’re going to go ahead and say, actually, no, we’re going to expand Medicaid. Why are they doing that? Again, Scott Colom says, well, it’s a biblical duty to serve the poor, not just that it would be good to keep people from starving.

As a Christian, you have to believe that you have to feed the hungry. You have to clothe the naked, house the homeless. This is actually a duty. They think you can do it through the government, and the point is that they are informed by their religion in their policymaking. I think that this needs to be more broadly accepted. And as we become more pluralist, as we get Muslims in the United States Senate, maybe it’ll be easier for us to say, “OK, yes, individual lawmakers and voters are going to be informed by their religion, nobody’s going to impose their own.” But the idea that religion has no place in the public square, that’s a really destructive idea.

Dionne: That was a warmly, “love thy neighbor” thing to do, to quote my column. So thank you for that. And maybe this whole thing is affecting, coming into this room. Two things: I broadly agree with that. A lot of Democrats were religious before and didn’t talk about it. John Kerry is a good example, where he spent a year, after 2004, talking to a lot of theologians; basically asking, “Why was I tongue-tied on this? How could I talk about it?” So it is a myth that Democrats were all godless all those years. That just wasn’t true.

On the other hand, it is very clear that Democrats did find a way, partly because of the nature of the candidates themselves, to talk more about this. And by the way, just if I can put a parenthetical in here, Black politicians have always been very good at talking about faith. And what you saw with Scott Colom was deep in his own tradition. But yes, I think what you’ve got is Democrats being much braver about saying, “We want to have an argument about faith. We want to talk about what faith really demands of us.” And I think they are trying to replace the culture wars with a much broader moral argument. I’ve been writing about this, this year. And the biggest compliment to Democrats is that they talk so much about faith that when the Republicans couldn’t attack them as being anti-religion, they attack them as heretics. And as I tell some Democratic friends, that’s a big improvement for Democrats.

Robert Siegel: But are northern liberal Democrats — who might attend a house of worship for weddings and funerals and little else — ready for a Jimmy Carter-like invocation of faith in political discourse?

Dionne: I think these candidates have found ways of making very clear that they know they live in a pluralist democracy with a First Amendment. Adam Hamilton has been very clear on that. The Republicans actually attacked Adam Hamilton for saying that non-Christians could go to heaven. And Ted Cruz did that. And I actually wrote, what will Senator Cruz tell his Muslim constituents down in Texas about their eternal life? So I think all these candidates signal that they’re pluralists at heart, but they’re believing pluralists.

Carney: And again, an important thing is that religion does belong in the public square and in the public discussion, not as one religion imposing on the other. But Nancy Pelosi once said, when she was being asked about how the Democrats could support the case against the Little Sisters of the Poor, and said: Well, you’re a Catholic. Why are you going to force these nuns to provide contraception? And she said: “I do my religion on Sundays.” A poor slip of words, but you can’t just do your religion on Sundays. To be a Christian, a Jew, a Muslim, etc., it has to be part of your life. And so, that religion belongs in the public square is something I’m really hoping that a Hamilton and a Colom can advance.
Dionne: If you look at the record, Pelosi actually has talked a lot about the public implications of religion, but ——
Carney: And she goes to Mass too, not just on Sundays. So yes.

Siegel: OK, one last question. What did you guys make of the vote to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, and the Democrats who were stuck in traffic and deprived that motion of a possible majority?

Dionne: You know, Italians have this wonderful word that translates as “behindology,” and you never take anything at its surface. And I would love to know why those 11 were not there. I agree that Beltway traffic can be awful, but that was rather astonishing. And is there some move to postpone this to their time in office? Because I think that should have gone through. We should have a debate, in the Senate, where there are a lot of Republican critics. So I still am not satisfied with the explanations we’ve heard.

Carney: And yeah, a dog caught the ambulance that it was chasing, and it didn’t know what to do with it. That’s the interpretation that this wasn’t just an accident. If it was an accident, it doesn’t speak to Democrats being good at governing. But some of those charges, why they would be brought against Hegseth as opposed to the president — going to war without congressional authorization, too. Is Congress really who handed this ball over, who were derelict on their duty to declare war? Are they now going to try to impeach the defense secretary for doing it?

Dionne: This is one of the most destructive defense secretaries in history. I think it’s a good idea, and you would be the first to say endless impeachments of Trump didn’t work out so well. Really zeroing in on abuses here, I think, is a good idea — and we should do it.

Siegel: OK. Well, listen, it’s been great hearing you guys on politics. It’s time now for us to wrap up, as we do in every one of these conversations, with something, some source of joy in your life over the past week or more, that you would share with us. Who wants to start?
Dionne: Go ahead. You start it.

Carney: So Twitter was actually good for a day. And that was Veterans Day. First, my brother went ahead and posted that our dad, John Carney, was a captain in the U.S. Army, but both of my grandparents were in the military. I had a great-grandfather who was a brigadier general in the Marine Corps. You can go back to the Irish Legion, in the Civil War, to find my ancestors. And then to watch other people proudly post their husband or their wife as a veteran, and posting pictures of their dads.

And something about the Vietnam generation, they just looked a little cooler in uniform than anybody else. And so, to watch the celebration of veterans in people’s families and communities, I thought, “Wow, I’m going onto Twitter and coming away feeling better.” That’s a rarity. So that brought me joy.

Dionne: I appreciate that. You know, my dad and sister, and a lot of my students at Georgetown, actually were, or are, in the military, and thank you for that. I’ve got to say my joy is political this week, and it’s particular. One is we had a free and fair election. A lot of us were worried about whether we would. A lot of us worried about where the administration would intervene. Now, I think the lack of intervention was in part because a lot of people, including a lot of lawyers, organized and stopped certain things in their tracks. But maybe somebody inside the administration said, “No, there’s a limit to how far we can go here.” We still have to always be alert, but that was a great thing.

My other joy was just to be part of history and go down to Mississippi, and watch Scott Colom do what he did there, and be a figure who, at the same time, recognized the sacrifice of earlier generations of civil rights heroes and martyrs — and he talked about them — and also spoke resolutely about building a multiracial coalition: Now your kids are going to be as important to me as my kids.

He really did an extraordinary historic thing. And I don’t care what your politics are, to have Mississippi elect the first Black senator since Reconstruction is a big deal for the country, and it was really cool to be able, in a small way, to be a witness to that.

Siegel: You bet. And for my part, I would say that my wife and I gave in, to the urgings of a daughter and various friends who told us all to go see, “You Can See Everything,” a three-hour-long documentary. But to call it a documentary doesn’t do justice to the improvised form of this movie. It’s fascinating, and it’s all about how to determine what is true, what is sincere, what’s fraudulent, what’s phony. And I found it just one of the most thought-provoking things I’ve seen in a movie theater in quite a while. I recommend it to you all.
Guys, thank you for that. Tim, E.J. — wonderful seeing you again.
Carney: My pleasure.
Dionne: And may all elections be as fun to discuss.
Thoughts? Email us at theopinions@nytimes.com.

Sometime in my mid-20s, I stopped wearing jeans.

I’d spent my youth romping around in baggy hand-me-down Gap jeans, their knees stained with grass. As a mopey teenager, maturing under the twin moons of skateboarding and hard-core punk, I favored dark skinny jeans that hugged my calves. Emerging from college, I saved up for a plywood-stiff pair of raw denim from the French label A.P.C. I wore those slim-straight jeans into oblivion, until holes sprouted at the pockets and they grew feline-like whiskers at the knees.

And then one day, I just quit them. As I slid into the work force, I became preoccupied with being taken seriously. I had a beard but looked younger than my 22 years, my face still bearing the aftershocks of acne. Jeans, to me, underscored that.
I migrated instead to dress trousers, cotton in summer, wool in winter. They were wider than the J.Crew norm, but I had only black and navy. The whole idea was for no one to notice them.
I vacillated between crewneck and V-neck sweaters, and cycled between striped shirts and solid ones. But for years, those pants were a constant.
A few years ago though, I tired of them. It was as if I had eaten the same coconut-flavored yogurt for breakfast for a decade until one day, even the thought of it made me retch.
I decided my wool pants were a stylistic void, a dark wormhole where something more varied, or just something worth even a split-second of closer inspection, could’ve gone instead.

This is what can happen to all of us with clothes. Our eyes wander, taking in new influences. You see someone in a chartreuse sweater and suddenly your gray knits feel creaky. A friend arrives to dinner in a tweed coat that you can’t stop looking at, and with that, your peacoat is cooked. It’s good to be open to change.

I was open enough on a reporting trip in Paris — cry for me! — three years ago that when a pair of beautifully battered bluejeans beckoned to me from across a vintage store, I bought them. They were by Yohji Yamamoto, fleecy from decades of wear, and priced at $175. When I became a dad a yearish later, I put on those jeans day after sleep-deprived day of my paternity leave. They became my literal Dad Jeans.

Despite their princely sounding provenance, the Yamamotos are essentially recreation straight-legged Levis, only a bit crisper in shape. Their indigo hue gives way to white from wear; their knees are frosted with cloudlike wisps. They’re like something James Dean would have worn in “Giant.”
I wear them at least three times a week now.

I’ve learned that my fears about appearing unserious were unfounded. Glance around on your commute and you’ll realize it’s nearly impossible now to discern someone’s job based on how they dress. Jeans are really a norm in most offices.

And now I can’t seem to stop buying them. I’m up to seven pairs in a range of washes and fits, in a foolhardy pursuit of perfection. In the wearing, deficiencies come into focus: One pair is too short, another too wide, a third too … blue? I’m currently hunting the utopian pair of dusty, straight-legged black jeans. A pair of Levi’s from eBay is en route to me as I write this. I’m sure when they arrive, I’ll love them. Well, that is, until I get sick of them.
