It's China's duty-free retail mecca and a tropical oasis, to boot. For Beijing that's no longer enough.

fortune.com/2026/11/14/ai-corruption-nvi.headline: The case of Nvidia and the growing risk of AI and corruption
fortune.com/2026/11/14/ai-corruption-nvi.author: Susan Ariel Aaronson

paragraphs.text: In 2025, the UN Office of Drugs and Crime and the Organization of American States co-convened a panel (slideshow & video) which examined whether AI is the biggest corruption risk in history. In November 2026, the panelists’ deepest fears about the AI-corruption relationship came true, but not in the way they expected.

The panelists feared that AI would enable corruption by making it easier to launder money, give bribes, or produce disinformation. Instead, they learned that the corruption of AI did not start inside the technology itself but with its leaders, heads of state, government officials, and tech CEOs, steering the direction of AI governance. As we see today, America’s approach to AI governance, using export controls to regulate the supply of AI and its components, is fueling corruption. We utilize Transparency International’s definition herein– the abuse of entrusted authority for private gain.

I believe that one company, Nvidia, has become the poster child for corruption in the U.S. Last year, the Trump Administration restricted sales of chips to China under U.S. law out of fears that would provide the Chinese military with an advantage or could undermine U.S. leadership in AI. The now former CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, used flattery and donations to influence the Trump Administration’s AI export policies. And in December, Mr. Trump gave Nvidia permission to sell the H200, an older but still powerful A.I. chip, to China, as long as the U.S. government was given a cut of the sales. (Another company AMD also received an exemption). In so doing, the U.S. gained a financial incentive for loosening controls of AI infrastructure to China However, the Congressional Research Service reported that .”Article I, Section 9, Clause 5 of the U.S. Constitution,prohibits the federal imposition of export taxes and duties (not user fees), and 50 U.S.C. §4815(c), which prohibits BIS from collecting fees for considering or issuing export licenses.”

Additionally, last year, Nvidia’s General Counsel, Tim Teter, seemed to interfere in an investigation of Nvidia’s sales to Chinese and Malaysian entities. And now we’ve learned that although senior administration officials such as Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick were warned about the dangers surrounding Nvidia and its now former CEO, they took no action. This corruption and inaction puts U.S. national security and the American people at risk.

While export controls may be useful and necessary, they are particularly vulnerable to corruption because they sit at the intersection of high-value restricted goods, bureaucratic gatekeeping, in customs, business, and trade policymaking agencies, and complex cross-border supply chains. When governments restrict access to lucrative technologies, including dual use items such as chips or AI, they can create massive financial incentives for bad actors to bribe officials or exploit regulatory blind spots to bypass the rules. Export control systems rely on government officials to issue licenses, classify goods, and clear shipments through customs. This concentration of discretionary power allows corrupt officials to solicit bribes in exchange for faster approvals or looking the other way. At the same time, U.S. agencies struggle to coordinate trade, customs, and anti-corruption efforts, which are controlled by different agencies.

Export controls also create situations of artificial scarcity and high profits, particularly for dual use items such as AI systems. Some buyers may be willing to pay extremely high prices to receive a limited supply of AI services. Not surprisingly, both competitors of Nvidia that produce high speed chips such as Google, and, as well as Open AI, Amazon, Anthropic, and Microsoft—three of Nvidia’s biggest clients—support legislation that would further limit Nvidia’s ability to export chips to China.

Finally, export controls often involve opaque national security exemptions. Because export decisions often involve classified intelligence or sensitive defense deals, licensing and procurement processes frequently lack transparency and accountability. Such situations make it difficult for independent watchdogs to spot irregularities However, the Trump Administration fired many inspector generals in 2025, including at the Department of Commerce, along with antiorruption prosecutors. .

Given these problems, export controls are not the best tool to prevent our adversaries from acquiring advanced AI systems or chips because they present many opportunities for corruption. Yet Politico has reported that it is almost impossible for members of Congress to support loosening export controls. Studies have shown such controls are rarely effective. Hence, Congress should weigh a different approach Morreover, current export control implementation can harm U.S. economic and technological competitiveness. . While there are no easy answers, , the U.S. should work with its Western allies to to manage technology transfers that might threaten our shared security interests

nytimes.com/2026/11/14/world/europe/ukra.headline: Ukraine’s Starshield Access Is Being Restricted Again, Zelensky Says
nytimes.com/2026/11/14/world/europe/ukra.author: Kim Barker

paragraphs.text: Ukrainian military operations were disrupted again this week along the front lines because of restrictions on Starshield, the satellite internet system developed by Elon Musk’s SpaceX and controlled by the U.S. government, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Friday.

Mr. Zelensky told reporters that speed limits of about 100 miles per hour were being enforced for Ukrainian devices connected to the system. It would be the second time in recent weeks that Ukraine’s Starshield connectivity had been throttled. The previous restrictions caused Ukrainian drones to lose their connection to the system if they flew above certain speeds.

Mr. Zelensky said that the latest speed limits took effect on Monday and were being enforced over Russian-occupied territories, not over all of Ukraine. That hurts Ukraine’s ability to strike Russian troops with drones in those territories.

Imposing restrictions on occupied territories is “very dangerous, because it already has political implications,” Mr. Zelensky said. “If you impose restrictions there, you are already partially recognizing the temporarily occupied territories as not ours,” he added.

Mr. Zelensky said separately in his nightly speech that the Starshield limits hurt Ukraine’s ability to use newly developed interceptors to protect its cities from Russia’s jet-powered drones. It is likely, however, that those limits would not affect interceptors in Kyiv, the capital, which is being battered by jet-powered drones but is far from the front lines.
Mr. Musk and SpaceX did not respond to requests for comment on Friday evening. SpaceX had earlier told Axios that the Ukrainian claim about throttled connectivity was false.

Limits on Starshield were first imposed in all of Ukraine for about 10 days in October as President Trump and his administration were pressuring its leaders to stop attacking Russian oil refineries, hoping to lower diesel prices before the U.S. midterm elections.

At the time, Ukrainian officials expressed fears that the limits were meant to force Kyiv to capitulate to Moscow. The changes, which caused drones to fall from the skies on the front line, still have not been fully explained.

Starshield is the military version of SpaceX’s Starlink, which is also used by the Ukrainian military. Ukraine uses Starlink for communication, while it uses Starshield for certain kinds of air defense and to guide drones in Russian-occupied territory.

Last month, SpaceX said in a letter to Congress about the previous disruptions that no changes had been made to Starshield because it was under the control of the U.S. government. But changes were made to Starlink, the company said, because Ukraine had violated the system’s terms of service by using it for “offensive military aviation missions.”
On Friday, Mr. Zelensky did not mention any renewed limits on Starlink, and Ukrainian officials this week only referred to restrictions on Starshield.

Serhiy Beskrestnov, a Ukrainian military expert who advises Mr. Zelensky on weapons technologies, wrote on social media on Thursday that “the operating speed of Starshield while in motion has been restricted again.”
“Our relief didn’t last long,” he added.

Mr. Beskrestnov said the Ukrainian military was once again having communication problems with its helicopters that pursue drones targeting cities, and with the jet-powered interceptors used to shoot down Russia’s jet-powered drones.

The Ukrainian claims of another Starshield slowdown came shortly after the latest round of trilateral peace talks between officials from the United States, Russia and Ukraine in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates. It was the first time since February that Russian and Ukrainian representatives had met in person.
Mr. Zelensky also told reporters on Friday that Ukraine planned to ask Congress for more U.S. weapons and for additional sanctions against Russia.

He said that “if Ukraine can move in this direction, and the U.S. Congress can consider supporting such an idea, then by the end of the year the parties really have an opportunity to try to reach an agreement on at least some de-escalation.”

Such a package would likely have to wait until the newly elected Congress, which will be fully controlled by Democrats, takes office in January. Republicans in Congress have largely bowed to Mr. Trump’s desire to lower military support for Ukraine.
Andrew E. Kramer, Oleksandra Mykolyshyn, Dzvinka Pinchuk and Ryan Mac contributed reporting.

sports.yahoo.com/articles/key-matchups-p.headline: Key matchups for Panthers vs. Saints in Week 10

paragraphs.text: Who wants to win the NFC South?

Sometimes, it seems like the answer to that question is "nobody" based on how this season has played out. In any case, first place in the division will be on the line Sunday when the Carolina Panthers visit the New Orleans Saints at Caesars Superdome.
If the Panthers are going to hang onto their division lead, they'll need to win some crucial one-on-one matchups. Here are four to keep a close eye on . . .
Panthers WR Jalen Coker vs. Saints CB Jonas Sanker
The Panthers need their slumping wide receiver corps to step up in this one—especially Coker, who has only totaled 84 receiving yards over the team's three-game losing streak.

Well, the good news is that Coker should have an advantage in the slot over Sanker, who he has two inches and a few pounds on. This year, Sanker has allowed a 65.9-percent completion rate and a 92.5 passer rating in coverage.
Panthers RB Chuba Hubbard vs. Saints LB Pete Werner
Aside from one bad game against Tampa Bay, nobody has been more consistent for the Panthers offense this season than Hubbard.

Through eight games, he's totaled 619 rushing yards, which puts him on pace for a new career high. Hubbard also has a 53-percent success rate going and is averaging 77.4 yards per game on the ground, just a couple shy of his career-best 79.7 set in 2024.
The guy he'll have to get past is Werner, who leads the Saints with 65 combined tackles.
Panthers CBs vs. Saints WR Chris Olave
Whether or not the doubtful Mike Jackson is a go, Carolina's corners will have their hands full with Olave. He leads the Saints with 734 receiving yards, and no other player has more than 365.
If the Panthers' depleted cornerback room can contain Olave, it will leave their offense practically without any true weapons at the skill positions.
Panthers OLB Princely Umanmielen vs. Saints QB Tyler Shough

The Saints also don't have any run game to speak of, with Shough leading them at just 162 rushing yards on the year. That means if the Panthers can get pressure on Shough in the pocket, their offense may effectively be toast.

Carolina has to get more out of Umanmielen—who posted 3.0 sacks in the team's first four games, but has gone quiet since. Although the defense is likely to get fellow pass rusher Jaelan Phillips back in the fold, they might need Umanmielen to step back up.
A sack or two on Shough may be all it takes to secure a much-needed win.

sports.yahoo.com/articles/wales-v-zealan.headline: Is Wales v New Zealand on TV? Channel, kick-off time and how to watch All Blacks clash

paragraphs.text: After edging past Japan in their November opener, Wales face a significantly stiffer test as New Zealand come to Cardiff in the Nations Championship.
Steve Tandy’s side could not quite find top gear in a seven-point win in their first outing of the autumn, and know they will have to improve considerably against the All Blacks.
The tourists were victors at Murrayfield last Saturday as they saw off Scotland with a second-half surge, and Dave Rennie takes the opportunity to freshen up his side.
New Zealand are assured of a top-two finish in their pool as the inaugural finals weekend nears at Twickenham.
Here’s everything you need to know.
When is Wales vs New Zealand?
Wales vs New Zealand is due to kick off at 2.10pm GMT on Saturday 14 November at the Principality Stadium in Cardiff.
How can I watch it?
Viewers in the United Kingdom can watch the match live on ITV1, with coverage from 1.40pm GMT. A live stream will be available via ITVX.
Team news

Wales are without No 8 Aaron Wainwright, which leads to a bit of a back row reshuffle from Steve Tandy. Taine Basham makes his first Wales appearance in nearly three years at the base of the scrum with James Botham brought in on the flank, while Adam Beard’s experience and lineout nous are favoured in the second row.
Josh Adams is rested, which allows Tandy to reward Gabriel Hamer-Webb for a good start to the season at Leicester.

Wales XV: 1 Nicky Smith, 2 Dewi Lake (capt.), 3 Archie Griffin; 4 Dafydd Jenkins, 5 Adam Beard; 6 James Botham, 7 Jac Morgan, 8 Taine Basham; 9 Tomos Williams, 10 Sam Costelow; 11 Gabriel Hamer-Webb, 12 Max Llewellyn, 13 Eddie James, 14 Louis Rees-Zammit; 15 Blair Murray.
Replacements: 16 Ryan Elias, 17 Gareth Thomas, 18 Dillon Lewis, 19 Ben Carter, 20 Taine Plumtree; 21 Reuben Morgan-Williams, 22 Dan Edwards, 23 Louie Hennessey.

New Zealand ring the changes from the win over Scotland as Beauden Barrett captains the All Blacks for the first time on the occasion of his 149th cap. Richie Mo’unga comes in as his playmaking partner at fly half, while Fehi Fineanganofo and Anton Segner start for the first time at flanker and on the wing respectively.
There are six forwards on the bench, in a sense: Leicester Fainga’anuku has featured regularly in the back row for the Crusaders this year having forged his reputation as a hard-running outside back.

New Zealand XV: 1 George Bower, 2 Asafo Aumua, 3 Fletcher Newell; 4 Scott Barrett, 5 Josh Lord; 6 Anton Segner, 7 Peter Lakai, 8 Wallace Sititi; 9 Cortez Ratima, 10 Richie Mo’unga; 11 Josh Moorby, 12 Anton Lienert-Brown, 13 Quinn Tupaea, 14 Fehi Fineanganofo; 15 Beauden Barrett (capt.).
Replacements: 16 George Bell, 17 Xavier Numia, 18 Pasilio Tosi, 19 Jamie Hannah, 20 Ethan Blackadder, 21 Leicester Fainga’anuku; 22 Kyle Preston, 23 Rieko Ioane.

nytimes.com/2026/11/13/us/politics/trump.headline: Trump to Meet With Putin and Xi in China, With Nuclear Proliferation on the Agenda
nytimes.com/2026/11/13/us/politics/trump.author: Katie Rogers

paragraphs.text: President Trump will have a joint meeting with Xi Jinping, China’s leader, and President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia during a summit in China next week, a White House spokeswoman said on Friday.

It will be the first trilateral meeting the three leaders have held together, and the third meeting Mr. Trump has had with Mr. Xi in person this year. At the meeting with Mr. Putin and Mr. Xi, Mr. Trump plans to discuss the war against Iran, but is not expected to bring up Russia’s war with Ukraine.

Olivia Wales, the White House spokeswoman, said that Mr. Trump would also address the threat of nuclear proliferation. U.S. officials have expressed concerns about a steady buildup of China’s arsenal in recent years, and a U.S. nuclear arms control treaty with Russia expired in February.

“The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” Ms. Wales said in a telephone briefing with reporters.

Two senior administration officials, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe the president’s travel plans, said that Mr. Trump would travel to the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in Manila early next week. The officials said he would then travel to Shenzhen for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, where he will meet with Mr. Xi and then both Mr. Xi and Mr. Putin.
The officials said that Mr. Trump would be joined by the billionaire Elon Musk in Shenzhen, but added that Mr. Musk would not be part of the trilateral meeting.
Mr. Trump is prepared to discuss the “difficult” topic of Beijing’s nuclear arsenal with Mr. Xi, one of the officials said.

China maintains secretive nuclear facilities and is on track to have 1,000 nuclear warheads by 2030, producing the weapons at a pace that has worried U.S. officials and analysts. On the call, the administration officials said that they did not expect any agreements on nuclear proliferation, and characterized the talks as a starting point.

Mr. Trump said this week that he had no plans to discuss with Mr. Xi the scandal that had engulfed Jensen Huang, who until this week was the chief executive of Nvidia, one of the largest companies in the world. Mr. Huang stepped down from his role in the wake of revelations that he had engaged in extramarital affairs, including one with Alice Huang, a woman whom U.S. intelligence officials believe is an asset of Beijing.
The officials said that the matter involving Ms. Huang was a national security issue, and did not expect Mr. Trump to discuss it with Mr. Xi during a diplomatic meeting.
